Speaking as a newcomer to the series, I can say that Saints Row IV is the most unexpectedly awesome experience I've played in a long time. Since I'd heard through word-of-mouth that the series has traditionally followed in the shadow of Grand Theft Auto, I expected this to be a pale imitation, but I was wrong. This enormously fresh and novel game, with its insane superpowers and sharp, witty banter between our lovably sociopathic protagonist and his or her homies was an absolute joy to play through.
The story is very cliched, but it's clearly not meant to be taken seriously. The narrative is stuffed to bursting points with references (which range from friendly homages to biting satire) to the likes of Mass Effect, Metal Gear Solid, and... Jane Austen?? Saints Row IV is a smarter game than it lets on, and it's very subtle about it.
I've heard from those in the know that the open world of Saints Row IV is copy-pasted straight from Saints Row the Third, which may irritate folks who've played The Third. In that way, it may be more fun and fresh for newcomers to the series. On the other hand, investment in the previous games is definitely necessary to properly enjoy the storyline and the concluding arcs of all the characters, so in that way, the game rewards returning fans. It's an unavoidable tradeoff.
At times SRIV runs the risk of becoming unfocused and sloppy, as new gameplay mechanics are constantly being thrown at you to be used a few times, then never picked up again. The highly extensive and customizable vehicles, which are promptly replaced by the super sprint ability, is the biggest example of this. However, the jumbled mess of the gameplay lends to the crazy, schizophrenic atmosphere they seemed to be going for with this game, and it all somehow melds together into a great big ball of violent, vulgar, childish fun.
It's a game carrying around a ton of tiny flaws, but it's just so much fun that I can easily overlook them. It's a rip-snortin' good time, and I'd recommend it to anyone who doesn't mind the crude and violent content.

This is one of those choose your own adventure type games. You read text, you make choices, those choices affect your stats. The art reminds me of Gustave Dore's art for Paradise Lost (which is actually kind of fitting given the subject matter) and is mostly black and white with a bit of brown thrown in. You can choose one of three characters. Your choice doesn't really impact the game that much, although they appear to get different events. There's some great writing and atmosphere in this game, from cannibal priests to ritual murders to attending swanky parties at the Sultan's Palace, you'll find all that here and more.
The game reminds me very much of the Yawhg (also a text-based horror game( but unlike the Yawgh, it seems to lack any random elements. Events seem to play out the same way for each character regardless of stats, your stats only really seem to have an effect during the final battle and that.....is very disappointing..... it's also really short, my first playthrough maybe took me twenty minutes because I was carefully reading everything, subsequent playthroughs took about five minutes.
Despite being disappointing in a number of ways, I'm giving it a tentative recommendation because I love text-based games like this one, and if you liked The Yawhg you should definitely check this one out. If the game were a bit more random I'd certainly recommend it, but as it is now, I like it, I think it definitely has potential, but the execution is....not as great as I'd hoped. I would definitely recommend waiting for a sale at this time.

How would you describe this game? The best way I can think of to classify is as an illustrated choose your adventure novel with RPG elements. It's a has very dark, ominous, macabre atmosphere. Each part is backed by hand drawn greyscale scenes illustrating events which are described in text. You have the city screen where you choose where to go and investigate next. You are only able to visit 1 to 2 place each turn. You are not able to keep tabs on the entire city everyday because there will be anywhere from 5 or more locations to choose from. Within each scene you will be presented with two choices and have to make on of them. For example whether or not to carry a weak woman off a boat, I chose to help. But it turned out that she was a vampire and the reason she needed assitance was because she was unable to cross moving water. You actions have consequences. Usually choices result in the increase or decrease of your stats such as strength and magic or a change in your reputation. So, yeah basically the game boils down to choosing which places to visit each day and which choices to make in each place. That's how you interact with the story.
There is basically no animation and virtually no colour in this game. But I really liked the literally very black artwork. I liked the omninous, atmospheric music. I really liked the written narrative and the setting. For example it was cool to be able descend into catacombs and be confronted by some pretty ghoulish characters. Some of scenes are pretty gruesome, terribly mutilated bodies strewn around the city's streets and some brutally violent events. For example my poor guide through the catacombs basically had a chunk of her skull ripped out by the jaws of a ghoul. Even I gasped a little when I came to some parts. The game has a very strong horror theme!
So, so far I'm really impressed by this game (doesn't that make me sound horrible straight the previous paragraph lol). Okay so I haven't put replayability or variety of twists and turns of the story or it's outcomes to the test yet. But I sort of got the feeling that with only being able to choose 1 to 2 out of 5 or so locations per turn and different choices made at each place that the game has potential for different experiences for each player and playthrough. In addition there are two other character classes you can choose from that I haven't looked at yet which should affect things further. Also I got up turn 10 of 15 turns in only around 30 minutes. So if the ends at turn 15 then it's a pretty short game. But to be honest as long as I enjoy the rest of the game I would consider it is short and sweet and that would enough to satisfy me.
As much as I loved this I have to admit for such a short game it may be a bit expensive for those who wish to get the most gaming time for their hard earned cash. Also I have to let you guys that the game seemed to bug out slightly at the end for me, in place of like the last paragraph of the story there was a wierd message with underscores through it. Also I've looked at one of the other reviews here and apparently at end of the some of the images didn't render properly and they could only see a big blue mass or something. But hopefully more people don't have these problems.

There is a specific reason why I write this review so sure of my opinion after only 2 hours of play. That reason, my cyber friends, is that I love you. And XCOM is on sale. And you should GET IT, like, RIGHT ABOUT THE ♥♥♥♥ NOW.
When it first went on sale, it was way too pricey for me. When the price went down, I had other games to play. This summer sale, I didn't plan to get it, but when I saw it's on sale, alongside the The Bureau sequel (get both for 7 € or equivalent in dollars in the next 18 hours or choose XCOM: Enemy Unknown alonside DLC Enemy Within and DLC's for 9 € or equivalent in dollars), I said to myself - it's now or never, man. Now or never. And am I so glad it's now.
XCOM slams you in the middle of galactical war - it's humanity VS traditional depiction of aliens - it makes you wanna watch "Mars Attacks" and "X-Files" marathon. Now, the game is pretty simple to get a hold on, yet impressive and pretty hard to be perfect at. The core of the game is tactical combat in the vein of turn-based strategies. You move your squad, turn after turn and you shoot if you have any action points left. You need to deal with objectives which are mainly - survive and kill the aliens, but also extractions, bomb defusals, tecnology capturing etc. Beside 70+ missions that you get in original game, you also gave a great deal of work to do in your base: you need to build and upgrade your facilities - your engineers stand to produce deadly weaponry for you, your scientific labs are exploring alien technology and making it useful for humans, you're hiring new soldiers, you're constructing new base options. You also need to get your soldiers in shape. Some of them panic. Some of them get wounded. You need to treat 'em right. Imagine your base building as something you've already seen in CIV games, in a way - your collagues are something like your advisors and your work with them is something like building and technology tree unlocking in Civilization games. No wonder, it's Firaxis game.
You upgrade, you build, you train your squad, you make rookies learn to kill and you weep in pain and despair when your soldiers get killed because in this game, the war and death are eternal, and only thing you have is a memorial wall to remember the fallen.
XCOM oozes in traditional SF atmosphere; it's an turn based strategy game of epic proportions and generic, although great story that will keep you hooked for many hours (I can already feel habit building up inside of me).
And it has a multiplayer I haven't even tried yet.
So, what to pick? I've picked XCOM + The Bureau. You may want to pick XCOM Complete with DLC's, but I couldn't resist The Bureau's setting.
The bottom line is this: it's not only a great strategy game, it's A FANTASTIC GAME, whether you like strategies or not.
GET IT. You'll thank me later.

ENGLISH :
It's a strict transposition of Steve Jackson's 1984 gamebook published by Puffin.
A great classic but extremely tough : you will wander during many tries in in the Manor's corridors, always encountering a tragic end before finding the one true path to victory.
Production value is decent but nothing stellar thought.
FRANCAIS :
Ce jeu est une strict adaptation du Défi Fantastique 'Le Manoir de l'Enfer' de Steve Jackson, publié pour la première fois en 1984. Un grand classique du genre !
C'est également un des défis fantastiques parmi les plus difficiles de la série : il n'existe qu'un seul chemin qui vous permettra de sortir vainqueur du Manoir. Vous allez errer pendant des heures dans les sombres corridors et y rencontrer un destin funeste de bien nombreuses fois.
On peut déplorer une fidélité extrême à l'oeuvre de base (le texte est le même à la virgule près) et le fait que le support informatique n'apporte rien de particulier à l'oeuvre originelle. C'est correct, sans plus. A signaler une musique assez irritante à la longue. Quelques bugs essentiellement cosmétiques sont également à déplorer.
Dans l'ensemble, un peu cher et le soft n'a pas grand intérêt si vous possédez déjà le livre.

By far the best sandbox game I ever played.  The camera angle takes a bit of getting used to but it's all fun after that.
I likethe progression of levels.  Every piece of equipment, clothing, food recipes, weapons, buildings etc. get better as you level but you must supply the resources.  You need to save everything, yes, even the poisonous mushrooms.  If you can’t build storage containers (barrels and chests) fast enough to accommodate your resources, you can pile them in neat stacks anywhere on the ground and no one will disturb them. The scenery is fantastic, the terrain is great.  Here are some highlights:
1.) All animals are wild, you catch them with net traps, tame them and tell them to follow you.  Make sure you have fenced in areas to lead and keep the animals securely inside.  Cows will give milk, chickens, eggs, etc. etc. But you need to feed them.
2.) You need to gather plants, seeds and fruit but after that you can grow most of them in planting beds at home.
3.) Mining for ore, building a smelter and an anvil is all part of the game.
3.) Hunting for meat, pelts and other animal resources is fun as well.
4.) You can make your own trails through the thick brush by cutting trees and bushes and saving the logs and sticks.
5.) You can build Portals to teleport from one place to another anywhere on the map and it is huge.
I could go on and on.  Just watch out for the goblins, they will attack anything but they do drop gold coins, the only resource you have for making gold ingots, which you will need later in the game.  These ugly little creatures are everywhere and they are a pain, until you reach the level where you can actually trap one and he becomes your sidekick.  He will be the funniest thing in the game as you both go on adventures. Only thing is that he dies if he’s killed, unlike you, who resurrects at home, minus some inventory items, sometimes,  valuable stuff.  So, you make more chain traps and catch another one!!!!
My hats off to the developers, now for the extension package and multiplayer ability.

I probably should stop buying these darned gamebooks, lest I should render my transformation into a broken record complete.  Tin Man Games really have done a fantastic job of recapturing my childhood with both their literal Fighting Fantasy adaptations, as well as their self-penned "Gamebook Adventures" titles:  Even back then I really did want to utterly ADORE these attempts to create a single-player "roleplay"-style adventure, and even back then I somehow never quite felt that these gamebooks played fair.  This particular one gains a point over the others for so specifically catering to my horror-loving needs, then promptly loses that point again for handing out so many "Fear Points" left, right, and centre that merely choosing to OPEN A DOOR in this game is a perilous enough proposition.

Now, this digital version is fortunately generous in handing out regular "bookmarks" (read: save points) which ensure that you can essentially cheat and skip over any rooms which prove to be a source of naught but a one-way ticket to the funny farm, but even my shameless exploitation of such mechanics has led me to a point where I need to have fluked the attainment of a particular item or it's GAME OVER anyway.  For better or for worse, that's just how these books always worked...so unless you're someone who firmly believes it's somehow for the "better", you'll probably just get the ♥♥♥♥♥ and put the game aside until the NEXT time you feel like facing the utter humiliation of a defeat which you haven't quite rightly earned.

If, after reading the above, you STILL can't help but cave in to your masochistic impulses, at least wait for a sale.  Whatever worth these gamebooks still hold in the modern marketplace, it certainly doesn't resemble ten U.S. dollars (unless you're a really, really slow reader, and/or a voracious "achievement hunter", in which case the price may be slightly more justified).

XCOM: Enemy Unknown, and the expansion, Enemy Within, provide a solid experience for strategy game fans. A turn-based game, its steady pace of new resources, abilities and enemies delivers a rewarding experience.
As the commander of the newly initiated XCOM project, you must lead your Soldiers (in squads of 4-6 in each mission) against an emergent alien threat.  Soldiers are fairly unique (certain options can widen the gap between Soldier base stats); each is made up of a mix of RP stats (gender, race and a voice type for personality) and battle stats (Health, Aim, willpower). While unit health and Aim are determined only by class and rank, will power can vary wildly between 2 Soldiers, based on that Soldiers service.  In addition to stats, classes determine weapon loadouts, skill trees and movement ranges.  Variations in the class (2 choices of skills at 2 separate ranks) can turn two SOldiers of the same class into completely different specialists.
As the Commander, you are also responsible for maintaining order planet-wide via manegement of "panic levels" for each of your member countries; let panic rise too high and you loose support, loose too much support and your project may be disbanded.  Panic levels can be lowered or maintained via performance on missions and selection of missions in a member-states territory or missions provided by your ominous counsel of ominousness.
R&D, base staffing, construction and funding is also your responsability.  While staffing occurs naturaly over time, you will sometimes need to choose between extra funds or R&D personel.  R&D itself is a standard fair, set your labrats on a task and they'll knock it out in time; which projects are available depends on prior research and your dedication to capturing/killing the aliens. Construction of your base is slightlly randomized (several "tiles" have special facilities that can be made only there), and grants bonuses for construction similar facilities on like "tiles"
The challenge of the game is completely customizable, though I would recomend default settings for first time players. Despite the main story remaining the same, adjustments in difficulty (something as small as selecting a different starting country) can give an entirely different experience.
The expansion content enhances the main story line, making it unnecessary* to play the base game, even for first time players.  In fact, I would recomend against playing without the expansion if possible, as the added maps help keep the experience fresh. However, the base game still delivers on a fantastic experience.
*As of this writting, there is 1 achievement that cannot be acquired through playing the expansion content

Before I start, I'll just say now that I'm going to be looking at this game from an objective standpoint and not comparing it to Anniversary Collection. While it would be easy to say that Anniversary Collection is the better purchase because it has more games, gives you more options like fast weapon switch, and all that good stuff, it is also a game that’s not on Steam, Xbox One, PlayStation 4, nor the Nintendo 3DS. The game also has its own fair share of problems, such as the god-awful sound quality for example, so it’s not like either game is free of problems and why I’ll only exclusively look at Legacy Collection by itself.
Mega Man Legacy Collection is a game that’s torn me both ways on really liking certain things about it and hating others, as well as unfortunately being indifferent to most of it. The goal of Legacy Collection is to try and be as accurate to the original NES titles as possible, so it does not make the games lagless nor does it fix any graphical issues or glitches found in the original games like zipping. The game also includes extra content such as a museum of high resolution official and concept art for all six games and a challenge mode with leaderboards. The challenge mode consists of timed objectives to do that range from defeating Yellow Devil in Mega Man 1 to completing an assortment of sections from stages from each game in the Megamix challenges. The game doesn’t do much else aside from these kinds of extras and then just the games themselves, so let’s look at the good and bad things about Legacy Collection.
THE GOOD:
+Colors are bright and vibrant
+Sound is really good, very crisp and clear (I swear there’s some instrumentation I hadn’t had heard before in some tracks)
+Some of the Megamix challenges are actually pretty fun
+Most of the border art looks fine
+Concept art in museum is incredibly detailed and is interesting to look through
+Database provides descriptions and weaknesses for enemies and bosses for all six games
THE BAD:
-Only has native controller support for Xbox 360 pads (you would need to use something like JoyToKey if you want to use an NES controller through an adapter like I do)
-No scans of each game’s manual in the museum
-Noticeable input delay if you’ve played these games before (I’d guess around 1 to 3 frames)
-Certain rooms are reused A LOT in challenge mode (Guts Man room 1 and Quick Man beam section is ridiculously overused in the MM1 and MM2 challenges) and some that are used don’t have anything going on besides just walking forward or climbing a ladder (one room used is near the end of Bomb Man’s level that only involves walking forward under two Flying Shell’s and then climbing a ladder)
-Autofire is not authentic to the original games and makes challenges like Yellow Devil MK-II and Mecha Dragon way too easy
-Main menu is very bugged and can improperly display everything to be white squares or can just randomly crash on startup if options were changed (this can be fixed by deleteing Options.sav under \AppData\Roaming\MegaMan\011000010009159F\)
-Severe lack of basic options (only controller mapping for keyboard, no sound options or anything)
As a whole I can only give this game a recommendation if you’re someone who hasn’t played Mega Man and wants to do so on an officially released title. The input lag likely won’t be noticeable enough for it to ruin the experience and the games themselves are preserved well enough that you’d get an experience close to the original NES. For someone who has played these games countless times and wants something more, I can’t really recommend buying this game. Obviously the six games aren’t what you’d be looking for if you’ve played them again and with the added input delay you’re not going to get much out of playing them again on this. The challenge mode does provide some fun stuff to play through, but with the amount of them that are either boring or flat out not fun to play through I can only really recommend this game on a sale. The best implemented features in this game are the museum and the soundtracks for each game, but even at that $14.99 is too steep of a price to pay for this rahter lacking title. Hopefully with the release and sales of this game, Capcom can develop an original Mega Man title, but at this point I’m not really expecting anything. So as far as new Mega Man content goes, the challenge mode in this is likely as close as we’ll get for a while.

I grew up playing Mega Man on the NES and I resisted purchasing this for about 3 days. I want to show support and interest for the series, though, and enough reviews convinced me to buy it. I'm glad I did.
So, technical stuff:
As others have noted, these games are recreated identically to their NES origins, warts and all. Honestly, Mega Man 1 is fun until Wily's castle, after which the amount of slowdown plagueing boss fights makes the save states almost a necessity. The same is true for MM2 in one fight, and the early games suffer from poor game design (weapon energy doesn't recharge between Wily stages, for example). Save states make up for this, but players who are unaware of these odd problems in the first two games may find them especially frustrating. I'm wondering if people have mistaken the slowdown for poor performance or software bugs. Given how rough it is in MM1, it's a questionable decision not to fix some of it.
That said - I experience no performance issues on my fairly low-end machine, and zero input lag. These games look and feel exactly as they did when I was 8 years old, which is great for me but may frustrate new players.
The monitor filter is great. Initially I didn't care for it, but once I got used to it, it looks exactly like my old tube TV did on NES games. I've hated these filters on emulators before but this one feels perfect.
Given there are a multitude of ways to purchase and play these games legitimately, this is certainly the best way to do so. At $5 a game on Virtual Console services, getting this package for essentially $2.50 per game on top of all the challenges is a great deal. Truly wish they included MM9-10 though, since they were done just like NES games.

There isn't much can be said about the game's visuals asides from that they're high quality. There isn't much can be said about the game's audio asides from that they're top-notch and it kind of reminds me of the audio from Mario games. The visual and audio can be adjusted in the game's option menu.
There are four different themes, the first theme is automatically unlock, but the other three themes are locked; they all required certain amount of flowers in order to unlock them.
There are roughly hundred unique puzzles to solve. They're divided into ten clusters with ten different unique puzzles to solve. Each of the clusters are locked with a requirement. The requirement is the number of flowers that's needed to unlock them. The first cluster is automatically unlock.
The developer of this game has given an option to replay any or all of the puzzles for a better score.
This is a fair warning, there's no reset button in this game, the puzzle will reset itself if an error has been made by the individual. Solving these kinds of puzzles is all about trials and errors. If it doesn't workout then keep trying until it does.
Collecting the sunflowers is the main objective. The amount flowers varies from puzzles to puzzles. The scoring multiplier is connected to how fast the puzzle is completed. The scoring multiplier increases as the game progresses on.
It's recommended to play through the tutorial to understand how variety of puzzles functions before actually playing them.
There are twenty-five different achievements to be earned while playing the game. Each of these achievements has certain requirements before they can be unlocked.
Final thoughts, I definitely enjoying playing this game all the way through to the end. The replay value for this game I would say moderately high. I would recommend this game but not at the full price.

A nice little addition to any Megaman fan's library.  I'll get the one nitpick out of the way first:  There seems to be a very bad crashing problem when viewing the Leaderboards after accessing them straight away from completing a challenge.  Encountered a crashing problem while starting up the game, but was remedied by restarting Steam.
Onto the actual gameplay:  As far as I can tell, the controls are the exact same and behave the same as the cartridges I have sitting here right next to me.  Most of the input lag that people are experiencing may be first-timers or people who have seemed to forget that there are little silly control mechanics embedded in these games.  Like in Megaman 4, while in water you cannot jump out of a slide.  In Megaman 6, you cannot jump out of a slide at all.  Megaman 3 has awful lag issues, but it's always had that,  It can also eat you jump/megabuster if you press the button slightly before picking up a weapon energy or life capsule.   Say in Shadowman's stage, when you have to cross the ravine with the parachute bots coming from above, if you jump at the same time you kill them (say with Magnet Missle) and they drop a weapon energy that you then run into, it will eat your jump input and you will fall into the death pit.
It's just small things that some of us tend to forget after 20+ years of not playing these games.
I have played around with challenge modes for a few hours, and they're an enjoyable little addition.  Great to hone in on your platforming skills.  I have also completed all 6 games start to finish and I cannot distinguish any greatly disparaging differences from the original titles.  They play 99% the same.
I do not think the $15 price point is steep at all, considering the original games can cost you anywhere from the $15 itself, to upwards of $60 depending on where you look.

A short little Weird West shooting gallery game.  Highly thematic, retro pixel graphics and matching audio.  VERY short (~10 minutes) but also very enjoyable for the duration.  Ending theme music is pretty good too.

Nothing, really.  With a game this small, there's really not a lot to critique.  You either like it or you don't, and I liked it.
Some people have been putting up "it's too short" as a negative, but I'm not so sure about that one, myself.  The game is great just the way it is, but I suspect it would get boring
if it were significantly longer (and had nothing else different.)  In other words, a longer game would also require more depth, both of story and of game mechanics, to keep things interesting.  This one hit the sweet spot just the way it is.
Hard to say, but it won't take long to find out for yourself.  Plus, it's free!
It's quick and stylish.  There are certainly worse ways to kill 10 minutes.

What is RISK OF RAIN?
Risk of Rain is a unique game that emphasizes combat on platform-style levels to collect loot that will make your character stronger (and more survive-able) overtime. This is no RPG--your character's health will go up as you gain levels, but the true key to beating each level lies in how many items you can stack into your arsenal before you unlock the boss and exit the stage. All of this needs to be done promptly, because every second you spend walking around and killing enemies adds to the ever-increasing timer that ramps up the difficulty roughly every five minutes. This goes from Easy to levels such as Insane, I SEE YOU, and HAHAHAHA. Each difficulty spike adds a greater spawn rate for enemies and spawns colorful variations of enemies with more health and increased damage. The last few ranks of difficulty start to spawn boss monsters instead of regular ones and the timer keeps going until you beat the game--so move quickly!
Each level has a set number of chests and shrines in it, and to unlock them all you will need MONEY. Cold hard cash. How do you get money? Why, you kill monsters, of course! Unlocking a chest will get you a random item of loot (with more items becoming available the more collectables you get and the more challenges you complete, adding to replayability). Shrines, which cost either money or a percentage of health, only have a chance to give an item--you could find yourself spending all your hard earned gold on a big pile of nothing or be pleasantly surprised with a great item! It's all about how lucky you are.
The items you get vary and there are quite a few different ones, adding variety to your strategy as you see what playstyle works best with the new enhancements these items bring. Most of them have effects that are passive, such as giving your attacks an electric shock that hits multiple enemies, adding a health regen, or increasing the amount of money that drops from creatures, but you can hold one useable item that will give you a special ability on a cooldown timer.
Multiplayer is an option, and very fun, but at the time of this review it requires port-forwarding from a host. The result is hours of challenging fun with friends. :)
CONCLUSION:
Risk of Rain is the kind of game that challenges you to get better and better each time you play. It has enough playable characters and unlockables to keep you entertained for hours, and replayability that is remarkably high for the type of game that it is. You will quickly learn which items you prefer, and which ones you think are just bad luck to get--and there is no limit. The items stack with one another, so it's possible to get a x2 run speed....4 different times. My maximum items so far in one playthrough was around 74, but that could be way higher, and it was not uncommon when playing with my friends for one of us to get three double jump items that made us insanely mobile. I highly recommend this game to anyone looking for a good, fun challenge.

You've probably heard Half-Life 2 is THE GREATEST GAME OF ALL TIME or something. From every ♥♥♥♥ing person on Earth. Well, here's a diferent opinion!
Half-Life 2 is a hugely disappointing waste of goddamn potential. There are many times throughout where I just sad to myself: "What could have been done!" It's decent, but it could have been so much more...
You start in a train to an Eastern European town 20 years after HL1. None of the characters seem to have aged 20 years (assuming that the characters shown are the dozens of same-looking scientists and security guards, but now they're one person? Ok). Apart from that slight plot-hole, the world after the invasion of alien life is interesting; It's turned into an Orwellian dystopia. You go around, run from the Combine (the police force tasked with repressing the populace) and then you run into Alyx Vance. Here, the game starts to give hints on how it's going to treat you. I mean, Gordon, the player character. Throughout the game, everyone keeps raving about how amazing you are through the cutscenes that aren't cutscenes because you can move around waiting for everyone to shut the bloody hell up so they can open the door and you can progress throghout the game. It comes to a point where everyone calls you the One Free Man and appoints you as leader because, well... It's you! The One Free Man! In 20 years, no one in the resistance force against the invaders has bothered to appoint a leader. 'k... I guess.
The other bad thing about this game, as I said previously, is that it could have been so much more. There are gameplay elements (Gravity Gun, antlions) that are used on 1 level primarily, and then barely have a use anymore. This game could have been a Deus Ex-like where all of these weapons and items can be used for you to get to your objective, but... I guess that would have meant the game had to have a non-linear level design, which it doesn't have. It's strictly linear.
Gunplay is very interesting, since Valve decided that the best weapons (more specifically, the alien/sci-fi weapons and the revolver) are barely used because you rarely find ammor for them. Instead, you get a crappy Glock pistol, a peashooter SMG and a... decent shotgun. Movement is good when you're sprinting (which is pretty much sliding around at a fast speed) but unfortunately you can't spint all the time.
HL2 gets more interesting to the end, it feels more sci-fi on its final levels, but it's too little, too late.
So, why the hell is it so praised? Because, when it came out, it was pretty revolutionary. The graphics looked really good (and still do, thanks to the graphic enhancements that Valve did.) The lead artist is the same as Dishonored (Viktor Antonov) and both games look fantastic and have a great art direction. It still has better facial animations (both HL2 and Vampire Bloodlines, released in the same day with the same engine) than a lot of games today! And it had a physics engine, which is again squandered for awful teeter-totter physics puzzles instead of any meaningful gameplay.
I'm probab ly being too harsh, giving it a negative review, but yeah, whatever.

I recommend XCOM:EW only to someone who has play Enemy Unknown through once and has gotten used to what objects provide what cover, as it can be difficult to tell sometimes without the visual cue. There has been very little support for the game's bugs, but I found the game to be worth it regardless.

The original Master of Orion truly puts you in the position of galactic dictator; there is no red tape for you to cut through. When you decide on a whim over a two 'turn' span to allocate a planet's resources from being the primary Shipbuilder world in your empire to a population breeding ground: your nameless subordinates get to figure out how to meet your absurd milestones, and you get to enjoy the end result of all of their struggles... from building your 32,000 pelican miracle fleet to crapping/(cloning?) out +18M pop/turn.
Rather than you, the EMPEROR, deciding whether one of your colonies should build a children's hospital or a factory on a given square, and which square of land gets to house the missile base or hydroponic's lab: you adjust your desired metrics using 6 simple sliders, and let your theoretical archetects and imaginary planetary governors work out the specifics for you.
Which means that you get to focus on the really interesting facets of a 4X game: the security and expansion of your borders, observation and predation of your neighbors, and praying to your ancestors that Plantary Shield V is in your force field tree.
I'm very happy that this game has come to steam... I've now owned it in at least 3 different versions (GOG had a similar deal with MoO + MoO2)(am not sure if the game was released to both Mac and DOS, but I have a memory of it, might have been the sequel on the big green/silverwhite old iMac though). Techland have done this magical thing that alot of other developers should definately take a note of. They made a game that actually works.
Technically I've had no problems, it's ran persistantly sweet as a nut for me and not crashed once. The game mechanics themselves also work. They've synthesised several types of game into one and actually pulled it all off remarkably well. You've got Parkour (I'd say offering a better experiance than Mirrors Edge), survival, scavenging, action, and at night a quite creepy stealth game. Other games have tried to mix and match genres (I'm thinking of things like Rage here), but often fail to make everything gel. Dying light does succeed and makes all it's constituent parts seem credible. Of course you want to use Parkour to avoid the ground it's covered in Zombies, of course you want to be quiet and move slow at night the Night Stalkers will rip you a new one. Oh and you can boot Zombies off buildings!
Minuses? A few minor quibbles, sound doesn't seem as well implemented as it could have been. It's not bad, but there were no noises that were really memorably nasty like the screamers in Dead Island. Also their Zombies are all lifted from other games. You've got Tanks and Spiter like things from L4D, Screamers and the big bruiser types from Dead Island and a smattering of Stalker. They had a good game here, but could have come up with at least a few of their own ideas.
Overall highly recommended 4.5 our of 5 I'd say.

Ok, gang, everyone that loved Dead Island, will love this. It's mucvh better implimented, graphics, and improved menus (and yea, TL did away with the 'auto equip of DI)
The parkour part takes a bit of getting used to, but once you got it, it's great and I'm not one for this style of play. Being able to jump and climb give you so much more than DI ever did.
Sadly TL kept the less than stellar 'check point saving system', but did improve it slightly by adding the ability to save should you have to leave the game suddenly by:
1) Whatever mission you're on have it highlighted and you die, you'll lost points, but respawn at the nearest safe house. (so make sure you clear all safe houses and make them secure...it'll pay off later)
2) Go to a safe house, use the bed and sleep, and then quit. You should respawn at that location as long as you had that mission highlighted.
I played through the game in about 45-50 hours and didn't do a lot of the side missions. After completeing the game you'll have the chance to go back and do the side missions, so don't worry if you miss a lot of them.
You'll also get a warning before you go into the final mission to bow out and do side quests...Just be aforewarned that once starting the final mission (quite long compared to the other missions) you CANNOT STOP and go back. So go on finish the final battle and return to have more fun...or start a completely new game.
From the boards TL seems to still have some problems with AMD systems (hopefully fixed soon) My intel system ran the game good. (I built my rig last spring, so it's not the latest)
If not fo rthe saving system, I'd give it 5 stars...so Dying Light only gets 4.

The puzzles are all very innovative and every new one makes you think a little. One of my favorite parts were the signs, they were very poignant. I'll recommend this game to anyone that likes playing a puzzle game with patience, learning how the world works and thinking of new ways of solving problems. It may be taxing on the mind and tiresome if played for too long, but if you play with peace of mind, this game is very enjoyable. Don't let the world get you frustrated and enjoy this unforgiving world. Antichamber is a maze and a puzzle at the same time.

One of the most enjoyable platformers I have played, Risk of Rain is a procedurally generated platformer with rougelike elements (according to the store page). After landing on a hostile alien planet, your charachter is assaulted by legions of enemies as you complete each stage. Completing stages quickly is essential to not dying, as the difficulty increases the longer you are in the game. HOWEVER, spending more time on a stage allows you to collect more powerups. Well, where to start on probably the best game in the industry?
Story:
Brilliant, Marc Laidlaw and the Valve team write great immersive stories that really make you feel a part of the universe. Half-Life has a great way of making the filler moments, when you don't have any weapons or you're not blowing things away, feel almost as fun as the action. Although I do not like the convenient G-Man sequences, and how HL2 started in comparison to how HL1 ended, I think the overall mood is definitely defined.
Gameplay:
Pretty standard FPS, but feels so liquid and smooth on the Source engine. Can be fast-paced and millitant as well as slow-paced and camperish. It feels good, but what I did dislike is Valve showing off their physics capabilities. I do appreciate that it's pretty good, but it's not perfect enough yet for usage (too often did I get snagged by a unhinged door on the floor, or a piece of crate), but there were some fun physics puzzles.
Graphics:
Considering the game is 11yrs old, it has aged beatifully. Runs way above 30 FPS on any of today's standard gaming rigs. Only once did I look at something and think: "That looks like crap". Environment, to lighting to particle effects are all really nice to look at, and I suspect it will still look beautiful in another 10yrs.
Music/Sound:
Sound effects are great and nostalgic (loading up HUV's armour from wall-mounts). The music is a weird nerd-electro mix, but fits weirdly well in what I imagine Gordon Freeman's persona to be.

This is the best way to play the best Dead Rising game in the series.
Dead Rising 1 is a game crafted by a passionate team for those looking for a completely unique zombie survival experience. Please play this game, and try to keep an open mind with regard to the way the game is structured. Understand that accomplishing everything on your first playthrough is nearly impossible for someone new to this game. You're meant to struggle against time, and when you fail you're encouraged to tackle the mall again when both you (the player) and Frank have more experience.
But you're also free to ignore the main plot of the game, and let the trail go cold while you goof around and gain XP and knowledge of the mall. You're free to ignore every survivor and let them all die, or even kill them yourself. Hell, you're free to stand on the helipad for three in-game days and be rescued without having accomplished anything.
Try using everything you can pick up as a weapon. See what works well and what doesn't. Memorize the locations of the most effective items, weapons, and food. Figure out how to most effectively navigate the mall and it's underground maintenance tunnels. Then realize why you should be cautious about walking through the park at night...
If any of this sounds interesting to you, I implore you to give Dead Rising a shot. Please don't let Dead Rising 3 or Dead Rising 4 be your first or only Dead Rising experience. They're not faithful at all to the original teams ambition.

1 – GENERAL
Killing Floor 2 it's a co-op, survival, multiplayer FPS. We join in teams and we have to kill hordes of zombies (or monsters if you prefer), listening to a relaxing rock/metal soundtrack.
So great. Nothing more to say, the game is good. End.
But I can add some stuff to the pack. The graphics are a bit exaggerated, but that suits the game very well.
To be honest I do not know if there's some story into the game, but who cares?

2 – GAMEPLAY
The game mechanics are very simple. Kill zeds, earn money, upgrade your weapons, kill more zeds. And that's it. Is this enough to make a good game? Yes, if at the same time the gameplay is incredible, we are playing with other people, and at the end we can leave the game with a huge smile in our face.
There're different classes to choose from, but at the beginning they feel very similar between them, and you will just notice major differences when you start to level up and unlocking some of the perks each one has.
Most of the zeds are only hard when in massive numbers, but there are some of them very hard to kill, and the final bosses, despite being only 2, are always hard to kill. So if a team is not very well built, or doesn't play as a team, everyone will have a hard time in staying alive.
I've tried the versus survivor also, where we can be the human, or the zed, any of the games have passed the first or second rounds, so I can't talk much about this, just to say that it isn't very fun to play as a low tear zed. Insta kill.

3 – CONCLUSION
I've spent some hours into this game in the free weekend on steam, and I really enjoyed it. Sure it can be a bit repetitive on paper, but I guess you will only feel that after you spent an absurd amount of hours playing it. You can say the price is high, but if in a sale this game is a great purchase.

-Pros-
+ Good graphics
+ Good optimization thanks to unreal engine
+ Great game mechanics
+ Good amount of weapon choices and perks for different classes
+ Unique classes with their own personality and voice lines (+1 for accents)
+ 1-6 players with appropriate scaling to the difficulty with more or less players (this is applied at the start of the wave)
+ The maps are great and the design is spot on (there are custom ones available as well if you get bored of the stock ones)
+ The background music is great (you can turn on the vocals for them as well if you'd like)
+ Solid menu and in-game UI design
+ Weekly challenges that as the name suggest are actually challenging and keep you busy (after completion you get a reward item but it is not marketable or tradeable, still it is a nice addition I think altough everyone uses those items after getting it which is annoying sometimes)
+ Great community
+ Collectibles (small items) are hidden on stock maps for a bit more fun if you have time between waves going looking for them (achievements can be earned per map after collecting 10 of them)
-Neutral-
~ Micro transactions and cosmetics: In some games it is a crate or a case, here it is a usb that can be opened. However what is different and better is that instead of being useless you can recycle the usbs into tokens which I liked cause after collecting 10 of the same type you can craft either a weapon skin or a cosmetic depending on the type you have.
-Cons-
- Long game launch time (~3-4 mins that can be reduced by installing on an SSD instead)
- Matchmaker sometimes can put you on servers with 200-300ms ping (unplayable) -> use the server browser instead
- Rarely but it can happen that items such as your weapon or dosh (money) bugs out or gets out of the reachable area so it becomes unreachable for the players
- Only 2 bosses available at the end of the match
- I kinda wish there was an option to upgrade your weapons, for example buy better bullets for more damage or something because in the end-game you can get a lot of cash saved up (unless you are playing with suicidal or hell on earth difficulty)
- For some, the French trader robot lady can get annoying with her constant tips on what to do
- I wish there was a story mode or some text about how the zeds were created and get to know the background story better

Let me start my review with the negatives:
1. THE FREE DEMO YOU CAN DOWNLOAD GIVES ABSOLUTELY NO INDICATION OF SOME OF THE GAME'S FEATURES. For instance, I was pleasantly surprised to find that 16:9 resolutions are actually available in the full version, including 1080p and anti-aliasing. The demo only had some really silly resolutions, meaning it was still playable, but didn't fit my screen. The full version also has its own achievement system and themes (visual styles), which are unlocked after you've collected enough flowers for each one.
2. The controls are keyboard only, which gives  great control of the ball, but takes some getting used to!
Now the positives:
1. There's no time limit, which means you can take your time figuring out the solution for each puzzle.
2. The "playing field" is made up of blocks, which all have different properties. The cracked block, for instance, disappears after one use, while the ice block makes the ball roll forward (and potentially roll off, unless it encounters another block!). There are about 10 different types of blocks in total, so collecting the flowers needed to complete each level can sometimes be a real challenge!
3. The game can be started from any level you've previously unlocked, and once you've figured out the solution, each level takes about one and a half minutes. This makes for a perfect casual title.
4. The game is an absolute joy to play if you like pretty graphics and imaginative puzzles!
Score: 12 out of 10

I like the game very much, but before you play it, please realize some brutal facts:
1) Prologue AND Epilogue is single-player only. This means that before the epilogue kicks in, you'll be greeted with a message saying that from now you'll be playing single player only. So, if you wanted to play co-op in Dying Light, you can, but the ending part of the game will be single-player only. Epilogue is not only cinematic, there are zombies to be fought, volatiles to run form, etc. I was very irritated by this.
2) Ranged weapons are broken. In the first hours of the game you can buy i.e. a shotgun with over 2400 damage. If you can, buy it, because it will be the best shotgun you'll encounter whole game. Same thing with a rifle with over 200dmg -- you won't find better one in the whole game. I bought two weapons in first hours of playing and they stayed with me the whole campaign, because every weapon in a drop was worse. Also, there are maybe 3 types of pistols (including 1 unique type that can't be bought), 2 types of rifles, and probably 1 type of shotgun.
3) Two-handed weapons are broken. They are stronger, but with smaller weapons you hit 3-4x faster and 5x longer. So, if you have a two-handed weapon with 1000dmg, and one-handed with 500dmg, you probably should realize that DPS of one-handed one is bigger. I haven't noticed any advantages of two-handed over one-handed weapons.
4) You can't choose female character. You're playing Kyle Crane and that's it. Even in coop - you're both playing the same person.
That said, the game was very fun and the co-op was better than expected. "Parkour" aspect was very nice, I will miss it in every zombie game from now on, same thing with day-night cycle, very nice idea and realization.

This collection is a pretty extensive love letter to the NES days of old. While it may not contain 7, 8, Soccer, or Power Battles, it does include the whole NES sextilogy along with comprehensive challenge modes, leaderboards, music player, a ton of concept art, your choice of filter (raw pixels, scanlines (monitor), and CRT fuzz), and nice 16:9 backdrops all rolled up in a tidy package.
By default, the games run in fullscreen windowed mode at "original" resolution (integer scaling in emulator terms, meaning some horizontal borders depending on your display resolution), with black vertical borders and no screen filter. Since the games are run emulated, sprite flicker and slowdown are present, although this was also true of the original NES games (not "bad emulation"). Fans of accurate emulation should find it leaving a pleasant taste in their mouths, though it would have been nice to have the option as in many emulators to remove the sprite limit.
Understand, however, that because this collection is emulated, removing the slowdown would have thrown off the game's timing, and would have required significant edits to the original code. The only way to do that is to "overclock" the emulated NES. Most games of this era react poorly to this, because the common method to get accurate timing was to use the CPU or PPU clock; This is why PAL territory ports of the day ran slower - The CPU and PPU were clocked differently (1.79MHz/5.37MHz vs 1.66MHz/5.32MHz) - not simply because of their 50Hz TV's. Editing the original code to allow for that could alter the intended timing across the board, so this is probably why it wasn't done.
Would an updated release of Anniversary Collection, which actually ported the titles to its release platforms, have been better? Maybe. But it's not likely that the source code for it still exists; The developer, Atomic Planet Entertainment, folded in 2009. Besides that, the Anniversary Collection had its share of bugs and changes from the original titles as well.
Given the low price point, I think this package is more than worth it for purists and nostalgia-seekers, along with those looking to give themselves some new challenges. If you're looking for a remaster of the original titles or a re-release of Anniversary Collection, this isn't it.

Mirror's Edge got some pretty mixed reviews when it came out. Some people liked it, some didn't. The most common complaint I hear from people is that they think the controls suck and it's an example of why platforming shouldn't be done in first-person. I disagree. I played through this game several times, and I earned almost all of the speed-run achievements on 360. Even completely out of practice I can beat this game in about two hours. I love the controls, and I think it's a perfect example of how to do first-person platforming right. It's just one of those games where the controls either click for someone or they don't.
As far as the rest of the package goes, I admit that it leaves something to be desired. The story isn't great, and while it is definitely possible to avoid shooting anyone in this game, there are a couple parts where shooting makes it SO much easier. It shouldn't be that way. It should ALWAYS be easier to avoid conflict. That being said, the other main complaint I hear is that the combat sucks and you can't avoid it. This is also a bit of a misconception if you ask me. Besides those couple parts I mentioned, it is actually easier to learn how to avoid the fight most of the time, but, well, it controls like a first-person shooter and killing folks is how people are used to progressing in a game like this. If you're fighting dudes, you're probably doing it wrong.
Besides that though, it is a fantastic game. I love the look of it, and the abstract-art-esque DLC is absolutely gorgeous.

The release of Mega Man Legacy Collection has been rather controversial with fans. Here are a few facts everyone should know:
-The NES cartridges have suffered remarkably from inflation, and aren't equipped with frustration pain killers (quick save features). Buy them if you want them. The controller is certainly more suitable.
-The slowdown and flicker plagued our beloved Mega Man NES cartridges, too.
-You have the choice to emulate. Use it if you choose it.
-The Mega Man Anniversary Collection on GCN included Mega Man 7&8 and some sweet little JP only fighting games, but it also reversed the shoot and jump buttons for a crippling button layout. Regardless, it was a great collection and you can buy it.
-Mega Man Legacy Collection doesn't include 9&10. It would have been better if it did, just like if it had also included 7,8, Mega Man & Bass, and the entire X and Zero collections.
-Fifteen dollars is really not a lot of money, ya know? I've spent more for broken Early Access games. These are six of our favorite games of all time, with trophies, art, music, and challenges.
-You may think Capcom sucks because of their recent business methods, or for their treatment of the Mega Man producer and product in the past. That doesn't mean this package sucks.

Where to start.... This game has great potential, I will say that.
But it's crippled by several KEY factors.
1. Camera, Movement, Inventory/Menus - They are not intuitive. There's nothing wrong with using a control scheme that everyone is familiar with guys...
2. The game in it's ENTIRETY is very restrictive. You MUST unlock things by leveling up, and completing quests. I know if I was personally stranded on an island, I wouldnt waste my time doing most of that nonsense, besides building a shelter, and making sure I had a fresh water supply. - Suggestion - Remove leveling, unlock all stuff from the beginning. That simple.
3. Creative Mode... I dont even know where to start with this. First of all, you can't call it creative mode, if the player doesnt have unlimited supplies. Creative mode refers to a game mode, in which the player has the power to inspect every part about the game. Creative mode should have its own separate menu. To give players access to a creative mode without any of this, you have effectively fixed #2, BUT YOU STILL MAKE US LEVEL UP, AND COLLECT ALL RESOURCES. - Suggestion - Change the name of this mode to normal mode, and change normal games to be hard mode. Add unlimited resources, and separate creative menus.
4. Movement - Movement is overly complicated to begin with, coupled with your run speed being just barely faster than your walk speed, makes it abhorrent. Stamina recharges too slow, and the character should move faster overall.
5. Shards - These are relatively easy to get, however, it takes FOREVER to get to a place where you are ready to go after these. Not to mention, they spawn SO FAR APART, that by the time you reach your 3rd one, you're ready to quit the game.
6. Chests - They dont hold enough. Nuff said. - Suggestion - Just double it. Then it would be perfect.
7. Replayability - Once you have played for a couple days, everything gets ridiculously repetitive. As a progressive gaming generation, there should be new content every few weeks, to let your players know, you are listening, and actually adding things to the game. Even if it's just a single item every week or so.
8. Bugs - I dont have the time in the day to list the bugs that I have encountered thus far. There are some horrible crashes the player can encounter. They always seem to happen when you havent saved the game after a large accomplishment, thus severely diminishing the replay value...
9. Enemies - Enemies arent spawned properly. I started a brand new game to test. The minute you leave your starting area, there is a chance to encounter level 20+ enemies. This is a death sentence, even to an somewhat experienced player.
10. Heat/Cold - They drain your stamina WAY TOO FAST.
There are a lot more that I could list, but I don't have all day.
If you are interested in this type of game, you are better off spending your money on something else. I got this game on a sale, when it was much cheaper, so it's not a TOTAL loss. It only started being a loss after the initial excitement wore off, and I started encountering features (not even bugs) that are game ruining.
Features: 6/10

Story: 3/10
Options: 5/10
Overall Score: 4.5/10

Man, this game is a mixed bag.  Do I think it's worth the $8 price tag?  Absolutely.  Do I think it stacks up to other similar-ish titles like Starbound or Subnautica?  No.
Here's the best way of describing it: do you want a crafting game that's a bit on the "rails"?  Because this game is definitely on "rails" - you've got an extremely linear progression of what you have to do, with little room for variation.  In Minecraft survival, for instance, you can within the first 2 minutes be doing any number of completely different things: sailing on an ocean, beginning a farm, mining deep under the soil, starting a ranch, etc.  This game basically requires you do all aspects before you can proceed onward.  Want to build an epic farm?  Too bad - you can't have any more seedbeds until you level up, and that level-up requires you to defeat enough monsters to get 30 gold coins and to build a cooking table.
If you're up for a crafting game that's less open-ended?  You'll probably like this, especially for an extremely reasonable price tag ($8 is an awesome price for the game, which easily makes up for its gameplay irks.)
If what you love in crafting games is absolute freedom?  Then this might not be what you're looking for (still, for a price tag of only $8, it might still be worth a try.)

Important stuff first, rambling and shambling to follow......
The game is basically....
= Ho hum, classic shambling zombies that will swarm you in packs. Interesting enough to keep you engaged
= Brilliant! A shopping mall and a very nice shopping mall to boot. The open world isn't as huge as most open world games but heck, this is a perfectly sized shopping mall for this game.

A suplex? A hammer throw? Wall jump kick? I pretty much got eaten alive by the time I could pull these moves off. This is not Batman, there is no freeflow combat....that's exactly what this game needed to make the hand to hand combat perfect.....zombies dont think too quickly though.
The guns are a little better ( headshots work well ), if somewhat limited.
Don't get me started on the survivor/escorts AI.....There are ample comments about how much more stupid the "living" are than the zombies.
Taking photo's is an afterthought eventually....
Some very entertaining moments!
So, you really need to put in a little work and try to understand HOW this game works before you get some enjoyment out of it.
Now my 10 cents....
Because of the stupid amount of games I have on steam, I've started to get through them all with a specific system.
Firstly, decide on a game to play (a no brainer), then dedicate a good 2-3 hours to it. Secondly, if I'm not having fun (because games are supposed to be fun), quit it, delete, leave a negative review but with constructive criticism and put the game in my hidden list. Thirdly, if it's a game I'm enjoying, play it through and repeat the steps.
Funny thing about this game, I got to step 2, hated the game then thought " I'm missing something here...there has to be more of a point to this...". I went into Dead rising without knowing too much about it, expecting something like State of decay or Dead island with a combat system that made you feel badass. I didn't get what I was expecting....
You have to dig a bit deeper to enjoy this game, it's not a jump in and bash the crap out of everything game, though you can do that eventually, you don't do it from the get go. There are things you have to understand before you can get to the point of feeling like a badass....
For starters, you have to understand this game is based on a "triage" system when it comes to completing a "scoop" or "case file". You are timed in missions but not so much that you're overwhelmed and frustrated.
Secondly, you have to understand the save system. You can save the game in certain areas only and to a number of different slots. However, anytime you die and save to start again, you have all of your stats and character progress intact! This opens up a hell of a lot of possibilities. The level cap (of 50 I think), can easily be reached in one playthrough.

This game is a classic. Released back in 2006 as what felt like a third party launch title for the Xbox 360, Dead Rising has had a great transition over to Steam in August of 2016 as a part of its 10th Anniversary. It feels great to play on either a Controller or a Mouse and Keyboard, and while it has some dated aspects such as aiming a gun with the left stick when you aim or the stiff mouth movements in cutscenes, it doesnt hurt the experience much at all. The game, while fun, has some pretty big balancing issues, primarily the Small Chainsaw (which Capcom should never nerf). If you gather 2 books from the Bookstore underneath Columbian Roastmasters in Paradise Plaza (The Engineering and the Entertainment books) and then went over to Sir Book-a-lot in Wonderland Plaza and grabbed the Criminal Biography book, it lasts for about 27,000 swings, which is about the entire game. Also, some of the achievements are very annoying to get, mostly the 5 and 7 Day Survivor, Saint, and Transmissionary achievements. They are brutal and require you to know EXACTLY what you're doing.
Other than that, the story is servicable and some people call the best in the series, though I prefer Dead Rising 2's story. The combat is one of the more fun things in this game like performing the special moves which are unlockable by, wait for it --- leveling up. Doing stuff like rescuing survivors (which have the worst AI known to man and made me want to claw my eyes out), completing scoops, case files and defeating Psychopaths gives you experience, where you can max out your level to level 50. Beware though, driving in this game is AWFUL and if you can avoid it, please do so. Frank is a good character, and to me hes just plain awesome. Another unique aspect is that you can also get rewarded for mixing food in blenders, like if you put a Coffee Creamer along with another food, lets say Orange Juice, you will get Quickstep, which makes you run like Sonic in the middle of a bathroom emergency for a short period of time. This game is incredibly hard to 100% though, so beware of that. To sum up what I said, while it doesnt have co-op or a true sandbox mode, if you can forgive that --- its the definition of old but gold.

Deathsmiles is a bullet-hell shoot-'em-up game from masters of the genre - CAVE. You take the role of one of five Angels to defend the magical land of Gilverado from an invasion by Hell itself!
This one is your typical CAVE high quality shoot'em up. This Steam version has actually several versions of the game, the arcade one, the home console one, the 1.1 version with slightly changed enemies, and respective Mega Black Label (MBL) versions, with one added character, new difficulty level and some further modified enemies. The game itself is pretty short and can be finished in 30(ish) minutes, but that's per mode and per character, so the replayability is normal for these kind of shooter games.
Mechanically it's a horizontal shooter, you can shoot left and right or bomb everything on the screen, after picking up enough enemy skulls pressing both shoot buttons together starts semi-invincibility mode where bullets still hurt you, but you can fly through enemies. There are three levels of difficulty, with the fourth one added in MBL version of the game. The first one is kinda normal shooter, the third one is kinda normal bullet-hell, the middle one is somewhat in-between. Shocker, I know. And the hardest lvl from MBL is just crazy. One thing I didn't like is that there are no weapon modifiers, so you have the same weapon start to finish. Each character has a different weapon at least, so it's not all that bad. The game is fun, as all CAVE shooters and if you like shooters you should give it a go.
I liked:
* another colorful CAVE shooter!
* only shooter I know that has cow as a boss
* also tyrannosatan, TYRANNOSATAN
* several difficulty levels catering to different skill levels
I disliked:
* no weapon upgrades throughout the game
Get this if:
* you like horizontal shooters
* you like anything by CAVE
* you'd like an easy introduction to bullet hell games (lvl 1 is more of a standard shooter than bullet hell)
Don't get this if:
* you enjoy shooters for their story
* you'd like cutting edge graphics
* screen full of bullets seem scary to you

You'll also want these DosBox commands:
Alt-Enter (full-screen/windowed toggle)
Alt-F12 (increase cycles; not sure if this is critical but it was running slow on my tablet when I didn't have this and ran without lag on my desktop cranked up to 18000 cycles).
The game doesn't actually rely on cycles for timing so you can crank it up with no issues, but 3000 may give you lag.
The game has a very small view window (old resolutions are crap) but otherwise I think the graphics generally hold up; you can tell what's happening and it still looks good.

This game took me back to the days I used to play in the arcades and waste all my money there attempting to get just a slightly better score than the one I already had. This game delivered the bullet hell and I am a gothic lover and just the entire game has a gothic feel to it that is unique to bullet hells. This game rewarded me for buying it on sale for 8$ but I would pay the full price knowing how good it is now. It's become an instant favorite for me. You will die ALOT lol.
The game mechanics are really unique, I play Mega Black Label mode the most as I find it the most fun, But the game has many unique game modes that don't "Seem" too different at a glance but you will find they are different enough to change the entire way you have to handle enemies. Positioning is much more important than in other bullet hells since certain modes make enemies explode into bullut hell bombs on top of enemies coming from both sides of the screen at the same time..and sometimes even from below or above.
The bosses were quite difficult, I don't know about anyone else here but I absolutely hate it when a game is so difficult to get to the end boss and then you get to the end boss and you slaughter it and you're left feeling like it was pretty anti climactic. I didn't get that feeling at all from this game..It was a rough ride after the 1st few stages and one I thoroughly enjoyed. I plan to go back at some point and play it in 2 player local co-op again, I'll likely come back here and say more good things after that :3

After my 2 Player Co-Op of this game my view on it has not changed. This is probably one of, if not my absolute favorite bullet hell game.

Dead Horizon has the interesting style for point and click and storytelling but it is weakened by the exteremely short duration of the game.
Story: Dead Hoizion tells the story of a women who during the game gains a deadly repuation for her duels and how and who many she killed. What i liked from this is that it doesn't show the glory of winning in duels and being a feared shooter. As an example, in the story, the main charcter would tell about the townfolk heard of her would either want to buy drinks for her and tell story of her battles but also different folks would fear her becuase of her high skills in duels. Surpirisingly, the story is quite set grounded in the way of the real wild west even though it is inspired heavily of Spaghetti westerns as the character first duel with a man is becuase of something trvial such as gambling cards which happens quite a lot to the real historical west.The game also delves into topics of death, life and the interesting meaning from all of this. But sadly there are problems in the story, which firstly is the problem of the main charcter herself. Before i say this, i know the devs are intenional for not giving much focus on the person rather her expolits in duels and it affect her life. But the problem is that the story is told so brief with so little detail that it is hard to fully understand the emtional turmoil of the character and the player doesn't know much about her to begin with to the point that i forgot something basic as her name becuase the dialogue only say it only twice or three times in the entire game. While it is well written, the pacing of it is all over the place and feel incomplete rather than simple short and sweet.
Gameplay: The gamplay is a first person point and click in the most basic of terms. The game is broken up to stationy section where there only one control which is the mouse and the player can click to interact with the enviroment to only read information from this. But there is another mechanic that is all focused on is the shooting. The closest i can compare is arcade shooters such as Time Crisis and House of the Dead but you can only shoot once to kill the opponent. This can be used by simply moving the mouse down the screen to equip it. It simple, but effective and easy to understand for all people which is fine for me. For 4 of the 5 sections of the game is focued on the duels and the enamies throughout will test your refelxes similar to duels in Red Dead Redemption but without the dead eye. Sadly there are no ways to change the outcome of the duels as no matter where you shot on the enemy, he will die in on hit beside missing and dying. It's a shame as it could be cool to shoot the arm of a person to drop their weapon or talk them out of it.
Presentation: The Game presentaion is set in pixel art and sound effects and music are in chip-tune clearly to be a throw-back to 16bit genertaion of the Super Nintendo and Sega Mega Drive/ Genesis. While i am assured some people would eb groaning at this becuase of the large amoult of saturation of this on steam for years. But i don't mind at this usually, as this actually in my opinion works well esspecially the well done music that add a tense but gritty atmosphere.
Conculsion: Dead Horizon has it's faults that in any other narative-focused game would be lethal but for this game, it doesn't dectract the experience too much as the main core theme are still able to be expressed and the simplisitic gameplay isn't bogged down on unnessary mechinics and design like other games. Being the game is free and can be beaten in a few minutes, i suggest you should at least try.

Dead Horizon is like a short, sweet ride through a western film as you play as the infamous gunslinger, Bonnie Starr. While there is some gameplay here with you having to shoot multiple people in a quickdraw with your mouse and while that aspect of the gameplay is fun and done well, the writing is what makes Dead Horizon great. While Bonnie herself has no shown dialogue, the narration of her life helps to develop her and really draws you into the world of Dead Horizon and helps you sympathize her place in the world.
While the gameplay is incredibly simple, gunning down anyone dumb enough to cross your way is really saitsfying as the shooting is accompanied by a great sound design and detailed animations of your opponents going down. You can even inspect various parts of each screen too if you want to see more of the excellent writing that the game offers. However, there's not much variety in the gameplay as all you do is just shoot people but that's not much of a fault at all considering how short the game is (like less than an hour).
Overall, Dead Horizon is a really, really good short game and you really have no excuse not to play it since its free and all. Hope you enjoyed my 300 word essay on this excellent game

Well, where to start on probably the best game in the industry?
Story:
Brilliant, Marc Laidlaw and the Valve team write great immersive stories that really make you feel a part of the universe. Half-Life has a great way of making the filler moments, when you don't have any weapons or you're not blowing things away, feel almost as fun as the action. Although I do not like the convenient G-Man sequences, and how HL2 started in comparison to how HL1 ended, I think the overall mood is definitely defined.
Gameplay:
Pretty standard FPS, but feels so liquid and smooth on the Source engine. Can be fast-paced and millitant as well as slow-paced and camperish. It feels good, but what I did dislike is Valve showing off their physics capabilities. I do appreciate that it's pretty good, but it's not perfect enough yet for usage (too often did I get snagged by a unhinged door on the floor, or a piece of crate), but there were some fun physics puzzles.
Graphics:
Considering the game is 11yrs old, it has aged beatifully. Runs way above 30 FPS on any of today's standard gaming rigs. Only once did I look at something and think: "That looks like crap". Environment, to lighting to particle effects are all really nice to look at, and I suspect it will still look beautiful in another 10yrs.
Music/Sound:
Sound effects are great and nostalgic (loading up HUV's armour from wall-mounts). The music is a weird nerd-electro mix, but fits weirdly well in what I imagine Gordon Freeman's persona to be.

Deadrising was originally released on the xbox360 and at the time proved that vast zombie hordes were capable of being rendered with good graphics. This PC variant doesn't state that it is a remastering of the original even though it is and improves upon many aspects of the original game. The AI has also improved(more so for the zombies than the humans) the psychos react more appropriately to combat and the humans follow commands better. It also seems as though all dlc is included and controller support is fully functional. The story for this thing is not entirely required to complete the game but I highly recommend playing through the story as it can be pretty interesting compared to most zombie games. The story pushes you to do things quickly so pathway flow from survivor to survivor to psycho to safe house can and is very important(be sure to plan ahead and map your route). The variety of weapons, toys, abilities, and costumes is almost unrivaled only to its sequels(some special costumes grant powerful abilities or weapons as well). There is also drivable vehicles though very few. In conclusion I highly recommend this game and I thoroughly enjoyed playing through it again.

Techland have done this magical thing that alot of other developers should definately take a note of. They made a game that actually works.
Technically I've had no problems, it's ran persistantly sweet as a nut for me and not crashed once. The game mechanics themselves also work. They've synthesised several types of game into one and actually pulled it all off remarkably well. You've got Parkour (I'd say offering a better experiance than Mirrors Edge), survival, scavenging, action, and at night a quite creepy stealth game. Other games have tried to mix and match genres (I'm thinking of things like Rage here), but often fail to make everything gel. Dying light does succeed and makes all it's constituent parts seem credible. Of course you want to use Parkour to avoid the ground it's covered in Zombies, of course you want to be quiet and move slow at night the Night Stalkers will rip you a new one. Oh and you can boot Zombies off buildings!
Minuses? A few minor quibbles, sound doesn't seem as well implemented as it could have been. It's not bad, but there were no noises that were really memorably nasty like the screamers in Dead Island. Also their Zombies are all lifted from other games. You've got Tanks and Spiter like things from L4D, Screamers and the big bruiser types from Dead Island and a smattering of Stalker. They had a good game here, but could have come up with at least a few of their own ideas.
Overall highly recommended 4.5 our of 5 I'd say.
