I'm surprised by how little I like this game, actually. I quite liked SR3, since it was ♥♥♥♥ing bonkers, but this just feels... too bonkers.
Well for one, all the destruction you're doing is inside a simulation. It just doesn't feel right knowing that you have all these balls-to-the-walls powers and the ability to do so much damage when ultimately none of it really matters. The game is also permanently fixed with this ugly-looking dark♥♥♥♥♥filter all the time, which is just really depressing to look at.
In addition, there's no option for massive stand-offs with the authorities with your new powers either! Sure, you can wreck♥♥♥♥♥♥for a good few minutes and cause large amounts of damage, but what happens after all this? A monster which you have to fight comes out (one which is excruciatingly annoying to fight, I might add.) and after beating it, what happens?
YOUR WANTED LEVEL JUST VANISHES.
Yeah, because lord knows freezing and subsequntly shattering an entire wave of authorities would be MUCH less fun than that.
On the topic of the powers themselves, I feel like they actually detract from the game. Sure, there is some challenge to be found when you first start out, but as soon as you upgrade them even slightly, the game becomes a ♥♥♥♥ing breeze. Nothing is a challenge beyond the missions which take your powers away. You can essentially freeze-blast whoever you're fighting, blow them up/shatter them with a few shots from whatever weapon you have and that's it.
The powers are indeed rather varied, but most of them I never found myself using. There's one for a stomp move which I never used, one which gives you some aura♥♥♥♥♥powers which once again never got used, and Telekinesis which was never used beyond challenges. Everything feels just so easy with the upgraded powers you have at the start.
Also, they might as well have removed cars from this game entirely, because there's VEEEERY little reason to use them. You can dash much faster than any car, knock things out of the way, be ready to attack as soon as you stop... unless you're using a jet with rockets/lasers whatever attached, you'll never have a reason to drive anywhere once your dash is upgraded.
And of course it suffers from what Saints Row 3 suffered from, the mundanity. While everyone spouts off about how crazy and off-the-wall insane the game is, that's also one of it's biggest downfalls. If you see and experience all this crazy stuff, it eventually just becomes normal. You don't think, "Wow, that was really over the top and cool!" because EVERYTHING is over the top, to the point where it's just annoyingt to deal with.
Now despite how much I've♥♥♥♥♥♥on this game there ARE some parts that I liked. Weapon customisation is better, since you can choose from a range of models and skins which look quite nice. I had a blunderbuss, old-timey pistols and a Tommy gun for instance, which was really cool. The pratfalls mingames are also much more fun since you can jump super high, meaning you fly for miles and then smack off some poor bugger's car and fly even further. The ice ability also has the fun side effect of making any cars that are moving slide along out of control, which is always fun to abuse.
In spite of all this however, I regret buying this for the full price, it just doesn't feel worth it on top of all the ♥♥♥♥ing DLC being brought out. Unless you can get this for REALLY cheap, I'd give it a miss.

You're a little bitty hexagon flying either clockwise or counterclockwise around a pulsating hexagon* (*can change into other regular polygons). This hexagon pulses along with the beat of the FANTASTIC sound track that is playing as you try to find the few lanes with no deadly walls coming in to squish you. It's quick, it's fun, and when you die(It is WHEN, not IF), the next game is only one spacebar press away from starting. If you're too hesitant you'll die, if you're too confident you'll die, if you pause for just a moment too long before trying to escape the next set of barriers... well, you get the idea. I can't stress enough the ease of travelling in between the menues and the actual game. There are NO loading times! This is a very fun game that can be played casually, but you'll find yourself trying very very hard to not die.

I really wanted to love this collection.
I've been a Megaman fan from a very, very young age. I own a variety of MM games, from NES carts, to the X games, to the Legends series, to some of the digital editions, etcetc.
If you're looking for a direct port of the NES versions, you're in luck. The problem however is that this game markets itself as a 'faithful reproduction' with 'HD flair'. As far as I played, neither of these key elements are actually there.
The game suffers from really strange input lag. It's hard to describe but everything feels really off and unresponsive. In a game where quick reflexes can be the different between life and death via pitfall, this is already a pretty major error.
As mentioned earlier though ontop of that, they are literally direct NES ports (as far as I could tell, anyway). This means every game in the collection (including the new challenge mode) suffers from buggy audio, flickering sprites, and EXTREMELY frequent framerate drops, to name a few.
Back on the NES this would be forgiven because of hardware limitations. But in what should be an HD reproduction in 2015, this is an absolute deal-breaker. Emulators that you can download for free literally do the job so much better, meaning you can save your £11.99 for something else.
I've already received my refund from Steam. If these errors are fixed later and the price drops by half, then all is well. But now though, just emulate.

Deathsmiles gets a 3.5/5
-Graphics: Decent until you increase the size of that small screen, obviously the quality drops a little.
-Sound: The sound effects and music really suit the situations nicely.
-Story: Not much of a story until you reach the end. After defeating the final boss you will get glimpses of the characters backstory.
-Multiplayer: No online Multiplayer. Only Single Player or Local Co-op.
-Controls: Very nice when using a controller and you have the ability to customize your settings in the options.
-Setting: The levels are all very nice and unique. A couple of the levels are perfect settings for fighting the forces of hell.
-Characters: Pleasant variety between the characters, their attacks, and their familiars. You will also be treated with some snippets of background information on each individual if you defeat the final boss.
-Gameplay: Overall smooth and enjoyable with the variety of enemies and bosses. You are also able to choose which stage to go to next instead of a completely linear progression.
-Customization: No customization of characters, which isn't necessarily a bad thing since players compete for high-score. Plenty of settings to configure like the amount of damage you recieve when running into an enemy or damage you recieve from enemy attacks.
-Dialogue/Well Written: Not a lot of cut scenes or dialogue. Most appear at the end.
-Tutorial: There's a training option that will allow you to play individual stages to practice on.
-Worth the price tag: For bullet-hell enthusiasts I would say yes. For anyone who is not sure if they'll enjoy a bullet-hell game I would say wait for a sale or find a free to play one to try out first.

The atmosphere which the player interacts with, while not at it's full potential, couples with the game pretty well. There aren't any small, worthless things to inspect. In fact, all you do inspect ends up being relevant to advance the game at some point or are just empty boxes. Angels of Death isn't very long, either. The game only lasts about 5-6 hours.
Overall, the greatest, and some may say, only, selling point of this game is the strange but unique storyline. However, it is still a game worth playing simply to enjoy a new story.
Oh, not to mention, I absolutely love the character designs.

FTL is a roguelike space simulation strategy game where you are the captain who runs the ship.
Your objective is to move from galaxy to galaxy, keeping ahead of the rebel fleet that's pursuing you. Sounds simple? Nope. Definitely not. In your travels you will encounter many events, all randomly generated each playthough, where you have to make the decisions on what to do. These events can range from battles to distress signals.
You will have to manage your resources and crew, building and powering up your ship, fighting battles, and dealing with a myriad of situations that will put your decision-making skills to the test. If you run into an enemy spaceship, will you fight or run? Are you going to fire at your enemy's weapons systems or try to disable their engine? How will you respond if the enemy has set your medic bay on fire? Will you send a boarding party to the enemy ship? How will you deal if you've been boarded? You see a ship that badly needs fuel. Will you give them some of yours and hopefully get something good out of it? These are just some of the scenarios that you may encounter.
Once you're defeated, there is no continue button and you will have to restart. But each playthough is always different, and with all the new ships to unlock, new areas to discover, achievements to be earned, there is plenty of replay value.
In terms of graphics, this is a pixel game. And a well-executed on at that. And in terms of the audio... The soundtrack is just plain amazing. I have never gotten tired of the music here.
Overall this is a must have if this is the type of game you are looking for. Awesome story and music. Challenging gameplay, and a lot of replay value. A great deal for the price.
Btw it's been years since I bought this game and I'm still playing it every now and then.

If you are looking for a top-notch puzzle game that cleverly uses three-dimensional space, Puzzle Dimension is definately the game for you. The puzzles are mindboggling and each one is both clever and unique. You're goal is simple: traverse the puzzle to collect all the sunflowers and get to the goal without falling infinitely, being spiked, roasted alive, or otherwise incapacitated.
The game creatively adds new mechanics as the levels get more and more difficult, and each add a whole new level (or should I say, a new set of levels, for each mechanic has its own group of levels focused on intorducing and using it) to the already deep puzzler that it is. The levels complement the mechanics well, and they are all challenging and fun to solve. I've finished about two thirds, and it never stops dropping new ideas and challenges on you.
The graphics are simple, and they do the job well. There are four options to choose from (all showcased in the trailer), so you can change how the game looks to your liking. In each texture, you can still easily tell the difference between the different types of tiles, even if it does take a little getting used to if you just switched. Music is also quite catchy with a nice retro-ish style to it.
The biggest issue with this game is the controls. This is a console port, and boy do you know it after a minute of rolling the ball around. Arrow keys for movement, okay. WASD for six-directional camera, I'll live. The jumping however, is very clunky. Once you hit space to jump, you cannot change the direction you are going. This means you have to time your jumps between the time you press an arrow key to the time you roll off the edge of the block. This certainly isn't a dealbreaker, and I stand by my reccomendation wholeheartedly, but this is easily my biggest gripe with the game. That and invisible platforms.
All in all, Puzzle Dimension is certainly worth the low price of admission, and if you can get it at one of the many times it is on sale, it's a steal. It is easily one of the best puzzle games I have played and one that uses 3-D space in ways most puzzle games don't bother to explore. At the very least try the demo. It will show you if you can stand the controls and how much this game has to offer.

I will start out by saying Deathsmiles is my favourite Bullet Hell shooter of all time and to finally see the game released on PC is a big deal. I originally bought Deathsmiles along with a Japanese Xbox 360 back in 2010. Along with Mushihimesama, Deathsmiles is part of bullet hell shooter Cave’s new decision to bring its catalogue to PC and I really hope this is the first… well the second of many.
Deathsmiles first appeared in arcades back in 2007 and unusually for Cave is a horizontal bullet hell shooter featuring a very strong lolita gothic visual style. While the game has not aged amazingly in the visual stakes its theme and gameplay remain as fresh today as they did back then.
One of the main reasons I always liked Deathsmiles is due to the multi-directional gameplay that sees you travel and fire in both directions as you move through the game on rails. As you progress through the game you can choose the order in which you play the various stages along with the individual difficulty which mixes up things in terms of gameplay and style.
Mechanically Deathsmiles isn’t the most complicated of shmups with you controlling a familiar which orbits your main Lolita and allows multi-directional shooting. Once 1000 skulls are collected, a special state mode can be activated to boost your damage & score. Waiting for the correct time to activate this is key to achieving high scores.
There are a number of different version in the game such as the original arcade version, normal mode which is graphically improved and Mega Black Label version which adds and extra stage, and extra character and is probably the best version to play for people looking for the most complete version.
Sadly I had hoped for a shiny new PC version but this is essentially a port of the game I bought on my Japanese 360 back in 2010 (I always found it odd that the 360, a system that was essentially DOA in Japan was the only place to play Cave shooters). I would 100% recommend playing the game with a 360 pad or a stick as playing with the keyboard just doesn't offer the needed level of accuracy.
If you are a Cave fan this is a must buy, if you are a shooter fan then this is well worth a stab and to be honest this is one of the more accessible bullet hell shooters out there so for anyone remotely interested in a very Japanese genre lets go and dodge some bullets.

It's easy to forget just how good 8-bit Mega Man is if you dont play for awhile. It's been along time since I had the drive to play through these classic games and oh man does this collection make me never want to stop. As far as recreations of these games go, this is the most faithful reproduction of the original game experience I have seen. The slowdown is there, every little flickering sprite glitch is remade in crisp 8-bit. If you dont like the crispness they have a couple filters to simulate the blur of a CRT which gave me some instant feelings of nostalgia. Outside of the games there is a good amount of production and concept art to look through for each game, there is a music player where you can listen to every song in the game, and then there is a challenge mode. The challenge mode reminds me a bit of NES Remix in that it mixes and reorganizes the games in different, more bite size ways to play. There are around 50 challenges I belive. Every challenge keeps track of your time and there are online leaderboards where you can see how you line up against other mega man players. If you just want to practice and get good at mega man as a genre, this is a cool way to learn and push yourself. I would say, I reccomend the PC version over the console versions, purley because of the display lag inherint in most modern TV's. I have also been playing on my PS4 and it is absurd how much better the games feel when I play them on the PC. The tightness of the controls really starts to shine, something I havnt felt since I played these games all thoose years ago. Overall it is well worth the 15$ to play through these games again and bring foward this formative time in video game design to a modern audience.

Suicide bullets are a bigger feature in the 1.1 strain. Everyone you shoot has them, but the game makes them easier to manage. In all strains, suicide bullets are annulled by your satellite helper - in Deathsmile’s case, an adorable mascot familiar. Outside of 1.1, you control them in a similar fashion to BioHazard Battle, wherein they rotate round you in the opposite direction in which you move. So, for them to cycle through to your left, for example, you would have to move to the right. You could use them to eat up the extra bullets with some pre-planning, but the greater numbers 1.1 offers make it a bit of an ask. As such, the familiar becomes directly controllable and can be easily nudged into the path of bullets, which it gobbles up and turns into points. To make it all a little bit easier, prompt for any of the MLB versions and you’ll find previous enemy, Sakara the Swamp Witch, playable.
Which is handy, because she has two familiars. That makes it easier to plough through the swarms of bullets you produce when you turn uncountable enemies into corpses. Deathsmiles is too stylish to lean on overused fighter crafts to slip through the constant bullet walls, so instead has you wage war with a handful of loligoth girls who each possess unique quirks. The youngest of the bunch, Casper, has a bloodthirsty bat familiar who can spit out arcing balls of rolling plasma. Shy, bespectacled Collete’s dragon chum offers powerful but short-ranged tongues of flame. I’ve talked a lot about the mechanics of this game -- and I’m not done doing so just yet -- but the gothic fantasy world is stunningly realised here, and absolutely obsessed with trying to kill you. Graveyards spawn plasma-spitting crows from shadowy tombstones, while bipedal ram-headed monstrosities mingle with mammoth ogres, all firing skywards from opposite sides of the screen. Other stages fling out serpentine plants that belch tadpole-shaped lasers that lazily wriggle around the screen, along with cycloptic swarming bats pinging bullets at you from their singular eyeballs. Slice your way through them - Cave kindly supply a very well-defined hit box to help you wiggle through all the bullets - and maybe you’ll see a few of the bosses.
Which gives me a chance to talk about Mary. She’s a giant cow. She wants to kill you.

The selling point of 'Mirror's Edge' is the gameplay -- that is the parkour-inspired platforming in the first-person perspective. There was nothing like it at the time of the game's release, and there is nothing like it now at the time of this review. There is a story in 'Mirror's Edge', but it is not that interesting and is merely there to move the action along. As a fan of good stories in video games, I can overlook that because the first-person platforming is fun, albeit much, much trial and error is needed to complete a level most of the time.
The game's clean, bright visuals are refreshing given the predominantly dark, brownish, shadowy looks of contemporary first-person shooters. The look of the game makes the gaming experience uplifting, which is much needed when you get frustrated from falling to your death many times in the game. There is an in-game system called "Runner Vision" that highlights environmental elements that are useful in solving the platforming puzzles, but those elements can still be hard to see as you may be in fast motion at the time. In later parts of the game, objects are highlighted less and less.
The game is plagued with strange technical flaws that are hard to overlook though. First, if the PhysX option is turned on, it will cause debilitating drops in framerates if you are not using an nVidia GPU. (It should have been disabled automatically.) Second, you can't change a game's video settings mid-game and you will need to quit your current game to do so. Lastly, the checkpoints where you resume your game can vary, seemingly based on whether you are in the same game session (e.g. after an in-game death) or you are continuing a previously saved game (e.g. you start the game and click "Continue Game"). That means you may find yourself playing a level all over again just because you decided to quit the game mid-level. More frequent checkpoint saves would have been nice.
At the time of this review, I have not played the game for over three months. I have uninstalled it even though I have not finished it because there is just not enough good points to lure me back for more. (Ironically in short, I have lost my momentum with the game.) Despite its flaws, I am still recommending 'Mirror's Edge', but not as enthusiastically as I had for games like 'Dishonored' and the 'Tomb Raider' reboot. There is much to improve on to make 'Mirror's Edge' an even better game, but what we have here is good enough to experience at a discount price.

Mirror’s Edge is a first-person action-adventure platformer which focuses on free running and parkour in a very unique concept even to this day. You take the role of Faith who is part of a Runner gang acting as couriers to transmit messages while evading government surveillance. The gameplay essentially allows you to run, climb and slide over many obstacles around town, from rooftops to ventilation shafts.
Graphically, it is artistically breathtaking and well optimised even for old computers. Its choice of colour pallet is great; the intense red and very vibrant whiteness of the city are very compelling in particular. Looking around town is amazing and sometimes you just wish you stop for a while to admire the landscape. The soundtrack is also pretty solid too.
While the concept is unique with its breathtaking skyscrapers and that vertigo sensation, Mirror’s Edge has several major design flaws which can cause major irritations. Firstly, the combat was not well planned out and is rather clunky throughout most of the game. Getting shot unfairly by helicopters can be frustrating at times and seeing security guards being so deadly can be underwhelming. These would not have been a problem if the combat system was not poorly designed, because in a way it is understandable why you would die so fast in close combat with no weapon (unless snatched from a guard) or bulletproof vest to protect you. But more frustrating is the fact that some sections of the game have you running around at least five or so guards in front of you in somewhat claustrophobic corridors, attempting to take them down. The most efficient way is by beating up one guy and using his weapon to clear the area, this way you will not be pestered again. On the other hand, with time and practice, you can get used to the combat and eventually master it, but in the end it is still a lacklustre experience. It makes sense why the game advices the player to stay out of combat as much as possible (for the reasons mentioned previously), but it would have been nice to see a good balance between solid free running and a functional combat system because as much as I personally prefer to take the combat totally out of the equation, what is left? A bland gameplay which gets repetitive quickly after a while.
And this leads to the second problem. Playing about an hour is all you need to see and expect from the gameplay. While the game is relatively still classified as short in length, it simply lacks variety which makes it bland. There are some very small and easy puzzles to solve from time to time, but they all boil down to finding a way to travel from A to B. Sincerely, the game hardly has any concrete puzzles. For an educational comparison, despite disliking analysing a different game in a review not meant for it in the first place, I will take the first Portal as an example in terms of variety in gameplay since many people do draw comparisons between them. It can be argued that while Portal was considered one of the most unique and unexpected games in years at the time, much like Mirror’s Edge alluded, playing the first few test chambers would be enough to see its entire gameplay. So why criticise Mirror’s Edge for this lack of variety when Portal gets a free pass? Principally, Portal got away with this by its even shorter length (3 hours) which managed to stick to the point. For what it had to offer, it had the perfect time. If Portal were to be longer in length, despite its very clever mechanics and actual puzzles, it would have been turning into something noticeably repetitive and tedious. With Mirror’s Edge, the lack of variety gets very noticeable after merely an hour in, with still a few hours left to play. And yes, tedious is a good word to describe Mirror’s Edge especially from midpoint onwards. To clarify, “by variety” I am clearly talking about approaching things in new interesting ways aside from simply jumping around walls and obstacles, which is what you only do almost all the time. For example, it would have been nice to be able to take different paths leading to the same point instead of its one-way obviously linear path. Linearity in itself is not a problem, but here the core of the gameplay is just running, so it would have been nice to see a bit more than being oblivious about variety.
So okey, it is all about free running. What more can you want and expect (erm, maybe some actual clever puzzles)? Perhaps its receptiveness could have been forgiven if the story was at least memorable (fastfoward a few years to Spec Ops: The Line), but instead it is generic from start to finish. You live in a utopian city where everything seems perfect and crime is almost non-existed, but behind curtains the system and government are in fact corrupted. That is as deep as the story gets, so it is obvious what the player’s role in this story is. Take the system down, restore order and freedom. Oh, and rescuing your sister. Furthermore, the support characters (not even many though) are also uninteresting and there is not a single one to get attached to; Faith is most likely the only interesting character who is the protagonist. The story does not feel like it is building up to anything grandiose nor takes you by surprise with any huge twists because the only twist in the story is predictable quite early in the game. The narration has some passing issues as well. There are occasions where more time could have been allocated to some character development instead of quickly introducing characters straight into your face for the sake of having something to advance the plot. In summary, it works like this: "I am this person doing this thing. We actually know each other, but no time for any backstories. Just follow what I tell you. Trust me". There is a backstory regarding Faith's past though, but that it is all. Ultimately, the story is average, easily forgettable and definitely one of Mirror’s Edge’s weak assets. The ending is nothing spectacular either, however the song “Still Alive” (Portal? Again?) sets the final mood nicely. Then again, its selling point is not the story but its parkour gameplay.
Lastly, possibly the most annoying design flaw is Mirror’s Edge’s poor auto-save system. Considering you will never get the first moves correctly in the first place, dying is frequent in this game; whether falling off a building by a misstep or getting shot by the security. With no manual saves such as quick-saves, the game usually sets you back quite far from where you died which makes it painfully unforgiving at times. There are sections where you just wish to get them over with and move on because, as mentioned previously, the gameplay gets bland from a point and you do not want to go through the same section again to see failing it again due to poor saving system.
Conclusively, Mirror’s Edge is a game with a very unique concept, beautiful visuals and an interesting albeit repetitive running mechanic, but as a gaming experience it has design flaws which detriment it from what could have been the next Portal. And sadly, it is not a game where you invest time in the story either. It is only there to fill the space, otherwise this might as well could have been called Parkour Simulator 2009. In summary, it is a nice looking game about running over obstacles around town and that it is the best it can offer; nothing too ambitious and rather bland at best. Also, its age is not important here. If it were designed flawlessly all around from the start, it would've still been enjoyable a decade later. Defending its flaws for its age is invalid. If all you care about is parkouring around, then Mirror’s Edge delivers it with flying colours. The mechanic is functional. If you are expecting something a bit more elaborate with variety and maybe some actual clever puzzles in its 6-hour campaign, it is only something you should play it once just for the aesthetic experience.

Great platform shooter that grows on you. The premise is pretty simple with the controls consisting in left/right/jump and 4 skills that don't look terribly different one from the other. Find the exit gate, activate it, survive the enemy waves and warp to the next level. But the execution is brilliant. The scale for a start, with tiny characters facing wave on wave of critters and giant boss creatures. Then the escalation: the difficulty increases over time, and tons of powerups massively increase your firepower and mobility as you go along. When on a good run, it becomes exhilarating.
Be aware that the first few runs will be disastrous. Many powerups are locked behind relatively basic achievements that naturally happen as you keep playing, making your future runs easier. A number of artifacts can also be found in the levels at fixed locations, and one collected, these can be activated for any new game to add a twist to the game mechanics. The Command artifact for example allows you to choose your powerups from chests, making it a very different game. Then there are a fair few characters that get unlocked as you play, each with a distinct set of 4 basic moves which will dictate your engagement technique. For what it's worth, I find the starting Commando class to be the best, so don't despair if you struggle a bit to unlock the others.
And finally, there's the music. This game's soundtrack is incredible. You can listen to it here:
I didn't expect much while picking this game as part of a Humble Bundle, but I fell in love and keep coming back to it every now and then for a run.

Never thought I would be able to play this. I had seen some videos about it when it was an xbox exclusive, but I never had an xbox 360.
There was a Wii spinoff, which I did not try because back then I was not interested in the series. Just like with other game misunderstandings of how the game was or how it played.
Years later, I had read and heard good stuff on a remixed version of the sequel, Dead Rising 2 Off The Record. I rented the PS3 version and...
Honestly? I loved it.
The humor,  the design philosophy that was similar to Breath of Fire V, where you are not lost if you lose, but you get to try again, the limits it had.
And the sandbox mode it added. That was important.
Off The Record was my first experience with Dead Rising. And it was enough to make me a fan of the series. OR  at least a fan of that particular entry.
Afterwards I ctually LOOKED at how this played, I saw videos, I saw a good LP of it
. I started to understand what was done for OTR and why.
And then I started getting the entire series on Steam. Or at least I did this year.
Dead Rising 2 OTR is  CONSIDERABLY more accessible. The first Dead Rising is VERY strict about what it does and what it wants. The timing to rescue the survivors in the first game is much  more strict than it is in the sequels, but that is how it goes.
The first game is  very strict.  Dead Rising 2 eased up the  requirements, even though it  added  a bit more complication with the zombrex, but it was looser, as well as adding new things, like combination  weapons.
Off The Record did it again there, and even more, added a mode where the  time limit is REMOVED. The Sandbox mode.
Dead Rising 3 removed the photography, which is an element I GREATLY enjoyed in OTR and in this one, but made it more accessible, as well as making the weapon combination more important and flexible, but the focus on having to save survivors and managing a strict time table was made completely optional. It is still a very fun game but  what made the first game so special was diluted by then.
On the other hand, that does not make me like it any less. Since I started with one that was  MUCH more  flexible.
Dead Rising 4 seems to have removed all of that. Seems like its design is a much expanded  Sandbox mode from OTR.
I will be getting that when it gets on Steam.

Dead Rising, originally an Xbox 360 release title (well, around that time at least) was a zombie game before the zombie craze went off the rails. Nowadays we have co-op campaigns like Left 4 Dead to apocalpyse survival games like H1Z1. But Dead Rising (along with Resident Evil to an extent, where the focus was less on zombies and more on horror) is where it all started and it's influence is absolutely felt in every zombie game today regardless of whether or not you played it. It's intelligent game design and time based gameplay make for an extremely challenging and fun experience where gameplay decisions and skill come hand in hand.
You play Frank West, a photojournalist trying to uncover a strange ongoing mystery happening at a mall in a place called Williamette, a town somewhere in Colorado. He's covered wars you know, so he organizes a helicopter pickup 3 days after he is dropped off in which he'll enravel the mystery that is going on and learn the dark secret of what is causing the zombie outbreak and make his escape.
As far as stories go, it's as Japanese as you would expect. The lipsync quite frankly is terrible, and you can tell English was a second thought and no effort was made to try and fix this. It's definitely immersion breaking at times but the voice acting here is surprisingly pretty good. The actual mystery itself is pretty compelling and has, while not subtle at all, a pretty disturbingly true message about first world countries and human consumption. The psychopaths that you meet along the way (boss fights) are again, surprisingly intriguing. They all have a specific way of fighting meaning you have to adjust your playstyle slightly in order to combat them which can be quite tricky if you aren't prepared. What's most surprising is the in which these psychopaths are humanized, making you feel sorry for killing them. Cliff especially has a pretty sad story along with one or two others. Of course, there are genuine crazy people who do crazy things because they're crazy but I personally feel that there should have been more emotionally moving psychopaths as opposed to insane people who act in anger for no reason.
As for gameplay, like I mentioned in the beginning of the interview, time is everything. You really need to manage your time effectively if you want to be able to save all the survivors and unravel the mystery of the outbreak which for most people causes the most frustration. Personally, I think these people are misunderstanding why that is such a good mechanic, it forces you to learn the paths of the mall, where the food is, where the best weapons are, what's the best way to approach a case and so on. Dead Rising is a game MEANT to be played more than once. You will succeed, then fail, but you  will always learn from your mistakes. I think the complaints are from people who just need to, quite honestly, git gud. That being said, the things this game does wrong are quite bad.
The worst, without a doubt for me, is the AI. The AI half the time get caught on stupid pieces of terrain or stop moving after defending themselves from a zombie attack. Infact, the AI is SO BAD that it's actually easier to carry the injured survivors through a horde of zombies than an able bodied one wielded with a gun because they will not be able to run past all the zombies and rush to the saferoom without getting attacked or failing to defend themselves. This is where the game shows it's age, as well as in the shooting controls. The shooting controls are simiarly like Resident Evil 4, except funnily enough, less clunky as you can move a full 360 degrees which you can't do reliably in Resi 4 without turning your character the whole way.
That said, even with the frustrating AI, the game is still a lot of fun. The amount of weapons in the game is insane for a game made in 2006. It has more weapons than Left 4 Dead 2 for christ sake, although not all of those weapons are neccesarily 'good', but they are actual weapons that can be used.  There's just something hilariously unique about shoving a horse head mask on a zombie then using a bowling ball to 'strike' them down. All the survivors have different personalities and while they can be annoying to escort at times, it's really satisfying getting a group of survivors to the safehouse and be rewarded for it. What's great is that you can get through the game just fine ignoring them at all but the game makes you feel guilty with it's bright red 'JASON SMITH HAS DIED' in big bold red writing as well as their screams for help that you can't help but feel you have to. The game rewards you with PP (haha pp...ugh) which is basically XP that let's Frank level up and improves how fast he walks, how much damage he does and how many items he can carry.
One of the most unique things to the character of Frank West is that he's a photojournalist, which means you'll be taking pictures of the events that happen. Certain specific moments like two family members reuniting can give you a ton of PP if you manage to snap a moment of it at the right moment as well as more perverted photos like taking a picture of a zombie womans cleavage (god damn it Japan). These don't feel gimickly at all and it flows really nicely. I found myself taking pictures of things that wouldn't neccesarily give me a lot of PP but I would take them anyway because I thought the image was just super cool.
With that all being said, Dead Rising is a fun game that sometimes requires you to wrestle with the mechanics a little but is absolutely worth it's price in challenge, story and exploration. It's a game made 10 years ago that is still miles ahead of games being released today, as pathetic as that is. If you're looking for a game that challenges your timing and skill or if you're just looking to see how zombie games got started, this is definitely a game you want to pick up.

Puzzle Dimension has got to me one of my top favorite puzzle games. It has a simple objective in gathering all of the sun flowers; however, the trick is getting to each and everyone of them and then getting to the exit portal (granted that you took the correct route in getting to that point).
Different set-ups, tiles with different properties, map rotating (both movement and vision), and falling off edges to get to other places on the map makes many of these levels difficult and tricky to solve. I have thoroughly enjoyed it to this point and will continue to complete each level, as there are quite a few...

This is a 'fun' straight-forward 'casual' wave based survival 'twin-stick' shooter.
As the name would suggest I assume there are 99 waves, so far I have made it to wave 52.
Some noticeable features;
1) You don't have to kill all enemies, only the required number for that wave.
2) Enemies start to shoot at you wave 22 (not wave 50 like another reviewer stated)
3) Enemy types behave differently; EG: some will move in a pattern and some will home in on you.
4) Enemy worm holes can kind of spawn randomly and ships can appear from them to either side so sometimes if you are not observant enough they spawn right beside you and ships right on top of you.
5) If one ship or projectile hits you then you die, there is no health or shield as far as I know.
There are random powerup upgrades and bomb drops you can pickup, you also get downgraded a little each time you die. This can have a snowball effect in that against the advanced enemies it is harder to survive with weakened weapons. A number of times I was able to claw my way back but past level 50 it can have a 'doomed spiral' effect.
I recommend this game for someone wanting a casual shoot-em-up to pass the time as there is no story mode, etc.
Four things I would like to see added; a pause button, a save/load feature, steam achievements, friend leaderboard.

I bought 'Antichamber' out of sheer curiosity. I was entertained by the variety and uniqueness of puzzles that are not found in many AAA games that I play, the general creativity of the game, the minimalistic art design, and the paltry directions or clues for most puzzles. However, 'Antichamber' felt like a barrage of puzzles, with barely any moment for players to soak in the moments -- similar to trying to get out an escape room before the timer runs out.
While I do recommend 'Antichamber', I cannot say I am highly entertained by it. If you enjoy solving puzzles for the sake of solving puzzles, I think this game is for you. I personally prefer games that give me a purpose to solve the puzzles and a clear end goal; 'Antichamber', in this regard, felt like an escape room game in which you have no idea why you want to escape and what you're escaping from.

And - as always - I've catalogued my playtime of this game:

PROS
While this is a first-person puzzler, it's not like ones you've played. The puzzles are very cleverly designed, and once you get over the initial disorientation, you'll love the originality. Unfortunately, I cannot describe any of the puzzles without giving them away, but they give you that feeling of "coolness" you got the very first time you solved a challenging puzzle in
. You will see things that you did not expect.
NEUTRAL
The game is awfully short, but it's also inexpensive and very rewarding for the time spent.
CONS
The game can be just baffling for a while at the start. I understand that they wanted this neat little Skinner box experience where you figure out the game's goals as you go, but a LITTLE more help understanding what the game actually
would have been appreciated. If you get frustrated early, just cheat (watch a video on YouTube). You will see how the first puzzle or two works, and you'll understand the game's themes.
The game has no plot, characters, or world. It's literally just puzzles within puzzles. But so are chess and sudoku, so maybe that's not a bad thing for some of us. I would have preferred a bit of plot, but no plot is actually better than a BAD plot.

Avalon Lords is a game very much like the Total War series but without a campaign mode. It's fun, it's intuitive, it's buggy. The bugs aren't game breaking. They're, from my experience, just graphical errors, performance errors and generally the smaller things. The AI is just flat out dumb. They send out their troops one by one when they're ready. They do not do any type of formation. This causes very long battles since only the side with more units will win... Right? Well, to a point, yes. You just need to have some more ranged units such as artillery and archers. They do massive amounts of damage to the opposition. You can finish a battle with less than five groups of T2 infantry and around 5 groups of archers, the rest can be artillery. It's highly unbalanced, artillery wipe out any enemy before they even come close to the artillery. I get that they are end-game units, but the only way for me to lose my artillery is for the opposition to have even more of them than I do. The units are slow. Very slow. It takes anywhere between five to ten minutes to travel to help out your neighbouring factions which are quite close together. Even the cavarly feels slow. Now, onto the good. Large battles are fun. You can zoom in very far to see the mass destruction you have caused. There's many upgrades, something I love in any game. Progression is highly demanding but highly rewarding. Currently, there's tons of buildings to build and then upgrade. The units are many in number and all have a different usage. Graphically, the game is not impressive even for a 2012 game. Optimization isn't really great at all. The AI needs to be improved. The game is too easy even in 3V3 all Hard/Nightmare bots (then again, I've recently played some older commander-strategy games so it might just be experience), I'd like to see some more difficulties. Mass upgrading takes a long while, maybe add a button to select multiple building units and upgrade them all at once? Maybe even automatically when resources are plentiful. Also, there's one one map at this time.
Buggy but fun. That's the simplest description I could write about this game. It's the good ol' Total War battles. Command your people into battle and watch your enemies either burn or your units be ultimately defeated. The battles are on a large scale during end-game. Watch units pass right through your walls as if they never existed and kill your swordsmen. As buggy is it fun, though. It's difficult to explain. Only people who have played Total War games will understand. When you lose a group of units, the frustration is real. If you triumph over the dead bodies of your enemies, it's a true reward. The largest downside is only how slow the units are, not the bugs.

Dead Rising, originally an Xbox 360 release title (well, around that time at least) was a zombie game before the zombie craze went off the rails. Nowadays we have co-op campaigns like Left 4 Dead to apocalpyse survival games like H1Z1. But Dead Rising (along with Resident Evil to an extent, where the focus was less on zombies and more on horror) is where it all started and it's influence is absolutely felt in every zombie game today regardless of whether or not you played it. It's intelligent game design and time based gameplay make for an extremely challenging and fun experience where gameplay decisions and skill come hand in hand.
You play Frank West, a photojournalist trying to uncover a strange ongoing mystery happening at a mall in a place called Williamette, a town somewhere in Colorado. He's covered wars you know, so he organizes a helicopter pickup 3 days after he is dropped off in which he'll enravel the mystery that is going on and learn the dark secret of what is causing the zombie outbreak and make his escape.
As far as stories go, it's as Japanese as you would expect. The lipsync quite frankly is terrible, and you can tell English was a second thought and no effort was made to try and fix this. It's definitely immersion breaking at times but the voice acting here is surprisingly pretty good. The actual mystery itself is pretty compelling and has, while not subtle at all, a pretty disturbingly true message about first world countries and human consumption. The psychopaths that you meet along the way (boss fights) are again, surprisingly intriguing. They all have a specific way of fighting meaning you have to adjust your playstyle slightly in order to combat them which can be quite tricky if you aren't prepared. What's most surprising is the in which these psychopaths are humanized, making you feel sorry for killing them. Cliff especially has a pretty sad story along with one or two others. Of course, there are genuine crazy people who do crazy things because they're crazy but I personally feel that there should have been more emotionally moving psychopaths as opposed to insane people who act in anger for no reason.
As for gameplay, like I mentioned in the beginning of the interview, time is everything. You really need to manage your time effectively if you want to be able to save all the survivors and unravel the mystery of the outbreak which for most people causes the most frustration. Personally, I think these people are misunderstanding why that is such a good mechanic, it forces you to learn the paths of the mall, where the food is, where the best weapons are, what's the best way to approach a case and so on. Dead Rising is a game MEANT to be played more than once. You will succeed, then fail, but you  will always learn from your mistakes. I think the complaints are from people who just need to, quite honestly, git gud. That being said, the things this game does wrong are quite bad.
The worst, without a doubt for me, is the AI. The AI half the time get caught on stupid pieces of terrain or stop moving after defending themselves from a zombie attack. Infact, the AI is SO BAD that it's actually easier to carry the injured survivors through a horde of zombies than an able bodied one wielded with a gun because they will not be able to run past all the zombies and rush to the saferoom without getting attacked or failing to defend themselves. This is where the game shows it's age, as well as in the shooting controls. The shooting controls are simiarly like Resident Evil 4, except funnily enough, less clunky as you can move a full 360 degrees which you can't do reliably in Resi 4 without turning your character the whole way.
That said, even with the frustrating AI, the game is still a lot of fun. The amount of weapons in the game is insane for a game made in 2006. It has more weapons than Left 4 Dead 2 for christ sake, although not all of those weapons are neccesarily 'good', but they are actual weapons that can be used.  There's just something hilariously unique about shoving a horse head mask on a zombie then using a bowling ball to 'strike' them down. All the survivors have different personalities and while they can be annoying to escort at times, it's really satisfying getting a group of survivors to the safehouse and be rewarded for it. What's great is that you can get through the game just fine ignoring them at all but the game makes you feel guilty with it's bright red 'JASON SMITH HAS DIED' in big bold red writing as well as their screams for help that you can't help but feel you have to. The game rewards you with PP (haha pp...ugh) which is basically XP that let's Frank level up and improves how fast he walks, how much damage he does and how many items he can carry.
One of the most unique things to the character of Frank West is that he's a photojournalist, which means you'll be taking pictures of the events that happen. Certain specific moments like two family members reuniting can give you a ton of PP if you manage to snap a moment of it at the right moment as well as more perverted photos like taking a picture of a zombie womans cleavage (god damn it Japan). These don't feel gimickly at all and it flows really nicely. I found myself taking pictures of things that wouldn't neccesarily give me a lot of PP but I would take them anyway because I thought the image was just super cool.
With that all being said, Dead Rising is a fun game that sometimes requires you to wrestle with the mechanics a little but is absolutely worth it's price in challenge, story and exploration. It's a game made 10 years ago that is still miles ahead of games being released today, as pathetic as that is. If you're looking for a game that challenges your timing and skill or if you're just looking to see how zombie games got started, this is definitely a game you want to pick up.

Surprisingly innovative for a game from 2006, Dead Rising® is basically ''Time® Management®: The® Game®''. Or more adequately, ''Escort® Missions®: The® Game®''
An entire game consisting of escort missions rightfully gained the ire of some people that gave this a shot back in '06. The escortee's sometimes have their pathing screwed up and get stuck behind a wall; they can't navigate the hordes as easily aas you can, which means as little as 10 zombies can stop their movement; some move somewhat slow -- there's nothing more obnoxious than seeing them 6 miles away from you as you turn around to check up on them.
It doesn't help that the VERY FIRST escort mission in the game is QUITE POSSIBLY the hardest one, which means a lot of people probably rage quit this game back in the day. Add to that the fact that you have a set amount of time to get these survivors and escort them, as well as doing main storyline missions and some people probably grew exhasperated at such constraints.
But that's a misunderstanding of how the game was designed.
For one thing: the game is constantly on a timer that constantly ticks down, even during boss fights. How much real world time does the game have?
6 hours.
This is a 6 hour long game. And all of your upgrades from one playthrough carry over to the next. Upgrades like improved walkspeed (CRUCIAL) to attack strength and life-meter. Additionally, upon death you can save and restart the game, or reload.
In other words, the game is made in such a way so as to allow you to get right back to where you previously where. It's meant to be replayed, wherein the game becomes much easier due to upgrades. granted, you CAN save all people in a single playthrough and the only difficult escort mission is the first one, so replays aren't necessary. But missing something  and restarting isn't as obnoxious as you might think since you can get right back to where you where in less than 3 hours.
Tell anyone this game is 6 hours long and they'll probably scoff, because it feels much longer and bigger than that. Every mission, including escort missions, are on a timer. You typically get a slew of them with each ''chapter'', and some come in the middle of said chapters. They're all neatly lined up on your screen with their timers displayed; it's all a matter of rushing to save people and bringing them back to the safe room whilst having time to also continue the main storyline.
With so much running about the game feels much longer than it actually is. The sense of accomplishment in seeing the survivors pile up in the safe rooms is immense. You can completely ignore survivors if you want, but there's really nothing more to the game other than rescuing survivors and doing the story mode. It's all the more exciting if you're juggling time, otherwise the story itself is really easy and you'll never miss any mission.
At it's core Dead Rising is a game meant to be replayed. If you don't want to replay the game for whatever reason: you can play for an hour or so and purposefully let the zombies kill you, then commence once more with knowledge of the malls layout and your experience poitns carrying over. The main goal isn't necessarily completing the story, as that isn't hard. It's getting all the survivors along with the previous goal-Dead Rising is a completionists game. It's short enough to make replays not feel like a chore to get back to where you were, but has a lot going on so as to surprise you when you realize you reached where you previously were in under 6 hours.
A first playthrough will probably take over 8 or so hours, and thats because of reloads to better manage time. But subsequent playthroughs will most likely take under 6 hours.
Overall A++. There are some flaws in how the ai for the escorts is programmed, but otherwise it's not a big deal and overall highly enjoyable.

This game was fun! It took me about 11 hours total to beat, but I was distracted through bits of it. Here's some points.
- I generally like RPGmaker games, such as Ib, OFF, and Yume Nikki, etc. I had fun playing this game, although the 'gameplay' of it felt more like a visual novel than an actual game. There are some chase sequences, and some puzzles, but it's rarely more intense than that. I would probably have felt alright paying $10 to play OFF or Ib. I don't really feel like the amount of content in this game matches up to a $10 price tag. Maybe if it's on sale for less than 5, give it a shot!
- A big draw to this game is the characters and dialogue. I don't think the story was groundbreaking, but I found myself liking the main character quite a bit.
- The sound effects, and the translation, were a bit, uh.. immersion-breaking, I guess? Distracting. For example, there's a character who every time she appears she has a high-pitched laugh track play-- and it gets overused very quickly. Another character says the word 'peepers' nearly every sentence he speaks, and it can make scenes he appears in lose whatever 'serious' tone they had.
I don't want to be that guy who says "Maybe you should just watch an LP", because I did like this game, but if you're interested in getting it, I would suggest waiting until it goes on sale rather than pay the full $9.99. There's not much reason to replay it and it plays like a lot of other RPGmaker games out there, which is more of a story being told through a game engine than a gameplay-focused game itself.

This is an enhanced port of the 2007 arcade shooter from Cave, which was also ported to Xbox 360 (and later to mobile platforms). It feels and plays like a very high quality old school arcade game.
The chosen theme here is nothing new for Japanese shoot'em'ups - witches and castles entourage, bizarre enemies and story which doesn't take itself seriously (well, if you choose Rosa, that is), and it reminds me of games like Parodius and Cho Aniki. You will fight bosses like giant cow and giant man head, it's that kind of game.
...is fantastic. Gorgeous art, highly detailed everything. Non-stop action, bright colors, little touches here and there. It features both pixel art and pre-rendered sprites (some of the enemies and bosses like Mary).
The controls are simple, yet not really common - you have one button to shoot right and another one to shoot left. You also have a bomb / spell which kills everything on the screen and “Targeting Magic”, which is an alternate attack which features lock-on mechanics.
Bullet hell shooters are known for being very unforgiving. But Deathsmiles has...how would you say...democracy? All stages except the last one (and the bonus one) have Rank system (difficulty level). You choose 1, you get a walk in the park, you choose 3, you get the true bullet hell.
So both groups of players would be happy – the ones who play shoot'em'ups for entertainment and the ones who play it hardcore, for scores and ranks.
Every stage is different and the game introduces new enemies with each one. I never felt like something was recycled.
Its length is exactly would you expect from an arcade game – 30-40 minutes and it's GREAT. The replayability is there – choose different characters (all have different attacks), choose different ranks, choose a different mode, heck, choose a different ending (quite literally, you just choose the ending you want in the end of the game, A or B).
There are many options to customize your experience. Make it 4:3 or 16:9, choose background image, zoom the screen how you want, etc.
The game has framerate slowdowns. They're not common, and they usually occur when there are hundreds objects on screen at the same time. In such games it's something that people see as both good and bad, so it's up to you to judge is it a problem or not.
A quality port and great game, a must have for shoot'em'up fans.
Fantastic replay value, simple and effective UI, lots to unlock for future playthroughs, and always a challenge. This game really makes you think on your feet and try to plan ahead.

This game is just what it describes itself as - a two-sticks arcade shooter where you have limited lives and try to get as far as you can.
I was recently thinking about such simple "pick up and just be playing" games again, so this hits the spot. It's fun, and while it starts easy enough to warm you up (or to be OK to pick up for a young kid who's early to games) it gets more and more swarmy with each wave. I like that it's challenging enough for me to enjoy but that little family members who can't do major games can play something out of this too.
Note that I had the benefit of playing it with a gamepad where I used both sticks - I haven't looked at what the mouse/keyboard controls are, but with a two-sticks gamepad you move with the left stick and fire with the right stick. Like if you push the right stick to the left you're firing to the left, even if you're moving up and down. For those who haven't played two-sticks shooters, be aware that if you're moving down to get away from an enemy (for example) you'll want to adjust the direction you're pressing on your right stick as you go since the enemy is not on your left now but above you. (I realize this is a given to anyone who has played this kind of game before, but this is for those who haven't.)
I like this game. For the price, it's great. It also reminds me of when in the 90s you could find fun little gems in PC game software that weren't overly-done-up but that you kept going back to when you were at that certain aunt's house looking for something to do.

On the human side, it failed. Free to Play seemed to be grabbing at any heart-tug it can find. There's a guy who plays Dota (and Dota2) so much that he gets kicked out of his parents house. There's a guy who lost his girlfriend. (spoilers - he gets her back) There's another kid who wants to go to the contest but will miss all of his college finals. But these 'journeys' that the story sets up doesn't build up beyond the initial start. Then it comes to a conclusion.
It's as if the film makers started filming without a real story to tell. Then halfway through, finally found an idea - only to have it slip away and now stuck piecing it all together.

Game looks nice with that survival "arc" and immersive feel, but it is barely fun; the game is ultimately time consuming and boring. Force of Nature has in its core a badly implemented leveling/building system. You need to find resources very hard to obtain in order to level up. In order to unlock critical items you need, you are forced to do tedious quests in order to gain the next level. But... it only gets worse. The game is very strict. There is hardly any freedom in this game even though it claims to be an open world... game mechanics such as your stamina is horribly awful (for example if you are out of stamina, you cannot defend yourself or mine for resources + you can't run), obstacles (SOOOO MANY, like trees or even bushes) get in your way that you want to go hence you are forced to spend a really long time grinding your way through them (only to completely destroy your stamina), enemies run away from you all the time and it is extremely difficult to kill them or even catch up to them (so expect various enemies to take away your health then run away all the time if hurt), AND FINALLY the worst part of this game, progression!!
The progression in this game is terrible. Let me point out it has taken me 16 hours just to get to LEVEL SEVEN (7)! You need to get to level 2 just to get an axe to chop down trees, yeah it's that bad. The time and effort needed to be put in this game in order to do anything is worse than even space engineers, and that game's survival mechanics sucks too. But anyway, if you are tired of the items you got and you wanna get even better stuff, prepare to grind another 10 hours out of your life.
Limits placed on what you can build is another BIG issue. First off, why can't I put chests on grass or nature ground? Outside of the little cramed area that is so called a house? The chests also don't contain a lot of space to store items. That is pretty disgusting in itself as I am forced to litter my own yard with useless items you can't even get arrid of. Inventory space is a problem, interior spacing is bad, and by the time you are at level 7, you can only build 2 houses and 2 other that costs a heck ton of resources. You can only build one of this building and one of that building, why not unlimited and freely expand my territory?
- Camera angle unadjustable, I hate the top down view.
- Limitations placed on all of what you can build.
- Wonky GUI, not fluid. You have to spend time dragging items from your inventory to a chest for example (no control or shift click).
- Enemies run away from you all the time and are hard to kill at that point. No rewards for loss of health and stamina.
- In hot weather and out of food to eat to cure stamina? RIP
- Lack of hotkeys.
- GUI wonky implementation (hard to explain, just copy Minecraft/factorio mechanics and scrap this GUI).
- Forced obstacle removal to get to where you need to go.
- Forced direction, hardly any freedom.
- Incredibly bad leveling system (why can't you just kill things for XP?)
- Incredibly tedious resource gathering.
- Incredibly bad stamina implementation.
- Agonizing progression system.
- 8 hotbars instead of 10 for your quickslots (WHY ONLY 8??)
- Bad controls.
- Some rigid sound affects are present, specifically the goblins.
- Lack of paliside Gates.
- Iron axe/pickaxe at level 8? Progression gap.
- Spelling errors.
- Half naked until 10+ hours of gameplay.
- Feels unfinished.
BUT...
- Very nice immersive playstyle.
- Has lots of potential.
- I like the portals idea.
- I like the click and hold mechanic where you can gather like 100 wheat in 2 seconds. Not even minecraft has that.
- 5 feathers given from a rooster? SWEET!
- Tame an ally to fight with you? Nice.
- I like the beginning choices of your cudgel, stone cudgel or fang cudgel. Why can't you add more weapon variants?
- Art style is almost flawless.
- AI is very good (EXCEPT WHEN THEY RUN AWAY!)
- I like the compass mechanic.
Overall, this review seems harsh, but not bad. It can compete as it has that spark of potential and I WANT to like the game. So if the game improves and these major errors are fixed, then I'll gladly change my review and play it again. But for now? $7 ... I guess it is almost worth it if you removed at least the creatures running away ALL THE TIME, obstacles in your path, the stamina mechanic improvements, and finally rehauled the leveling system or give the game more freedom.

Puzzle Dimension was a game I got on a whim because it was on sale for 79 cents. I figure that there really wasn’t much to lose for a puzzle game like this, and much like my other purchases I get for a really low price, I loved it. It’s a really fun puzzle solving game that really twists the way you think about a puzzle. Like 3D chess, Puzzle Dimension requires you to look at all the right angles before pushing forward.
That’s what I like about puzzle dimension so much, it made me think of other ways to approach a problem. Much of the game relies on camera tricks and thinking in more than one dimension. While the objective is simple, collect all the flowers and leave through the portal, getting there usually isn’t. And while most of the game certainly isn’t as challenging as say Toki Tori, Puzzle Dimension focuses on a different mindset to solve a puzzle. It’s not trying to outwit you, more so it’s making you think differently about solving a problem. While some puzzles in Puzzle Dimension do require a certain order to solve it, if you know how to do all the right tricks and what to leave in and out in order to get to where you want to go, you can solve it however you see fit. As long as you get that marble to the end, it doesn’t matter how many trips you took to get there.
I really don’t have so much complaining, but more of a warning that some puzzles are simply harder than others. While I did the majority of these puzzles without any help, a few select number of them I needed to look up. The game simply didn’t set up a well enough overview for me to see where I was going, and having only a few chances before I messed up again meant I wasn’t always so daring. Such a case could be solved with a rewind button or something like it, but the puzzles were never too trying for that to be a complaint.
Aesthetically the game looks beautiful and the music has a nice chip-tune beat too it. The standard settings of the game don’t really ruin the puzzle solving and provide for a better standing of what you are doing. Although a lot of the newer tiles you unlock throughout the game do provide to be far too distracting compared to the first one.
Final Thoughts:
Puzzle Dimension is a different kind of puzzle game; it’s not really one to challenge your mind as it is to challenge your view on how to solve problems. Aesthetically the game looks great, but when using the non-default skins the game can be a bit more distracting. The game can also be a bit of a trial and error run, but it never gets too mind numbing to turn the game off. Overall Puzzle Dimension was an enjoyable puzzle experience that any fan of the genre should play.

It's definitely worth getting for the price of £1.99, especially if you enjoyed Kula World.

Half-Life 2 (stylized as HλLF-LIFE2) is a first-person shooter video game and the sequel to Half-Life. Developed by Valve Corporation, it was released on November 16, 2004, following a protracted five-year $40 million development, during which a substantial part of the project was leaked and distributed on the Internet.
The game follows some years after the events of Half-Life, where the protagonist, Gordon Freeman, is woken by the enigmatic G-Man to find the world has been taken over by the alien Combine due to events that occurred at the Black Mesa Research Facility, the setting of the first game. Gordon encounters human resistance forces that aid him, including former associates from Black Mesa, among them Dr. Eli Vance and his daughter Alyx. Alyx joins Gordon as they search for a way to eliminate the Combine from Earth and free humanity. The game is a first-person shooter played from Gordon's perspective, with the player using a variety of weapons including the gravity gun to eliminate hostile forces and solve physics-based puzzles to progress forward in the game.
The game won 39 "Game of the Year" awards and the title of "Game Of The Decade" at the 2012 Spike Video Game Awards.
Over 6.5 million copies of Half-Life 2 were sold at retail by December 3, 2008
As of February 9, 2011, Half-Life 2 had sold over 12 million copies.
Half-Life 2 is often considered to be one of the greatest video games of all time.

I've always been a fan of the Horror RPG Adventure genre, so once I've started playing Angels of Death, it just clicked in naturally for me (I should also note that; I've NEVER completely finished a true Horror RPG Adventure title before, so it was the first time for me with Angels of Death!) However it is not a perfect nor a complete game, it certainly has some downfalls, with Gameplay Aspects, Dialogue Pacing, a few Textbox Errors (which was a huge pain) and the unfortunate Translation mishap.


What makes Angels of Death stick out the most from the genre was; their Characters, Worldbuilding, Theme & Storytelling! I’d find myself feeling invested in the story, wanting to learn more about the characters and backstory (which is currently possible, though the lack of any English Official Translation of the Angels of Death Manga series)

The worldbuilding may seem lacking, but would come through very subtly and unappreciated! (something that I admire a lot!) And as for the character development… it just leaves me very speechless; I could only assume it would be a, “You either Love them or Hate them” scenario, but in MOST cases it would be the former.

What I do praise the game the MOST was for the Character Designs! They are all equally memorable for the low numbers of casts (in their respected themes) making them very unique and complementary to each other!

The Soundtrack however was not very well balanced throughout the entire game; so it was rare for me to find a track I REALLY enjoyed, or find it to be awfully unfitting (for the appropriate theme or timing)

As I mentioned before, the Dialogue Pacing in the game wasn’t Angels of Death strong suit; but I would give credit for the game’s attempt of changing the gameplay pacing and theme in each Episode! For me, I very much appreciate the game for keeping me on my toes, during each Credits sequence!!


MY FINAL OVERVIEW IS; I would ‘Love’ to replay Angels of Death in due time, once it receives an Improved and Finalised Update on the Translations, that would do justice on Angels of Death!
Till then, I still find myself feeling very disappointed on the misuse of rephrasing, it’s a shame that 星屑KRNKRN’s games (especially a PAID game) would have to receive this kind of treatment on their work.

But for anyone looking to try out the game, I encourage you to give Angels of Deaths a shot! It’s definitely a game you shouldn’t miss, especially from the Horror RPG Adventure Library.
I guarantee that you would find ‘some kind of “weird” enjoyment’ from the game, for its unique charms!

I want to start this review off by saying I am not bored by RPG Maker style games that focus on story with minimal gameplay and I adore story rich games in general. However my entire experience with Angels of Death felt half-baked in that every gameplay element it tries to pull off feels unfinished and not well thought out.
The "puzzles" are flawed in that I never once had to stop and think about what I was doing. The answers were either incredibly obvious or it was a matter of "use everything in my inventory on this one thing," which would take about 15 seconds and then the puzzle would practically solve itself, lacking the "AHA!" moment which makes puzzles fun in the first place.
The other piece of gameplay is very occasionally evading killers, which actually sounds like a fun concept until you realise that this just means running along a path and hoping you don't take a wrong turn. Don't worry if you do though, you just have to wait a few seconds to load and then try again with absolutely no consequence for your failure because the game autosaves right before any part where you could potentially get a game over. This completely kills any tension that could have been established with these scenes.
The last thing that could be considered gameplay is walking around the world exploring and interacting with things, and they somehow ♥♥♥♥ed this up the most. A game is meant to make you feel that you as a player occupy a space in a virtual world which functions even when you're not playing it. However this game feels manufactured in a cookie-cutter way in that everything you have the option to interact with is only there to advance the story. There are no interesting little things you can find hidden away that offer world building or more information about the characters. It lacks the hand-crafted charm that is often the reason I play small indie titles like this one.
The main problem with Angels of Death is that it has no reason to be a video game. Completely failing in all it's gameplay elements, all that's left to this title is a dialouge only story that most people have much lower standards of writing for because it's "just a video game."
TLDR: Angels of Death attempts to tell a story which can be told much better and more completely using any other medium of storytelling. It's almost as if the developers wanted to make a visual novel, but couldn't afford artists so instead they downloaded rpg maker.

It has the three essential games (1,2,3) and a couple of filler games. Presentation is fantastic, with a lovely aspect-corrected nearest neighbour mode; an even lovelier TV mode with a light dot crawl effect, scanlines, and a bit of motion blur; and just a regular scanline mode that basically looks like an RGB-modded NES running through an XRGB.
From everything I read, it sounds like they put a lot of effort into getting it to be as accurate to the games running on an original NES as possible. To that effect, there's no emulator weirdness, you get all the flicker and slowdown you'd expect, the palette is completely accurate, and it sounds fantastic.
Not much to say about the games themselves, because they're classics of the medium and among the best games ever made - at least the first three - and everyone who likes action games should play them. The latter three are technical showpieces that demonstrate the NES running at its absolute maximum capacity, but feel like they're starting to run out of steam.
The fact that this collection is only these games is fine, because these games ARE Megaman. The awkward late SNES/PSX years weren't kind on the little blue boy, so we're best left forgetting them. The only game I really wish was there was the triumphant return of classic Megaman, Megaman 9, but that does kind of exceed the scope of this collection. Wish there was a way to play Megaman 9 on the PC that doesn't involve ugly emulation through a Wii emulator, though...
Support classic rereleases that actually put effort into the presentation and accuracy of the games - buy this.

I'm really torn... I love Mega Man.  It's my favorite series of all time!  I've played through the NES versions, the Genesis version, emulators on Windows, Android, PSP, and Dreamcast, the PlayStation Store releases of the Japanese PlayStation versions, the 3DS Virtual Console, the Wii Virtual Console, the Wii U Virtual Console, and the PS2 Anniversary Collection.  All told, I've probably played any given game in this collection hundreds of times.  But...
Pros:
-Mega Man 1-6, legitimately on PC.
-Recreates the slowdown and glitching of the NES, including stuff like rapid-pausing trick in MM1.
-Lots of cool artwork.
-Uses a save state (as any MM fan will tell you, passwords sucked because they didn't save E-Tanks)
Cons:
-Feels off.  It's hard to explain why/how, but I'm finding myself making a lot of mistakes and moving with less precision than I normally do.
-Kind of glitchy in ways I don't recall from the NES days.  For example, I beat Guts Man but got hit with the last block he threw still hit me.  Normally no big deal, but this time it somehow knocked me back outside the boss room with no music.  I go back in, and Guts Man reappears with full health.  WTF?
-Straight ports, with none of the cool extras or remixed music from the Anniversary Collection.
-Where's MM7-10?
-Only one save state slot per game, and it saves your options every time you save or load a state.
I'm not exactly sorry I bought it... I do want to support Mega Man and show Capcom that the franchise deserves better.  But for serious play I'll probably go back to emulators.

Cons:

death)
