My first two entries into the Dead Rising series were Dead Rising 2 and Dead Rising 2: Off the Record, though I've never actually finished any of them. I've never played the original Dead Rising on the Xbox 360 so this Dead Rising remaster on the PC will be my first time playing it.
:
👍
:
Think Saints Row, both game series are silly in their own ways. With Dead Rising, you have the main character, Frank West who's just a normal person trying to report an apocalypse, you have a number of fun weapons and clothes to try out, you have the camera system which helps you in levelling up slightly. Of course, like Saints Row, the game can be serious at times.
👍
:
With the levelling system present, the game allows you to start a new game using your progress from your previous save, making the game much easier for you, especially to complete the side-missions and defeat psychopaths you didn't manage to do in your first playthrough. You can play "freeroam" to level up Frank and start a new game with that progress when you feel ready to do the missions. You can also unlock the sandbox mode '∞ Mode'.
👍
:
The day/night cycle makes the world feel real rather than constantly having the game at night just because it's a zombie game. It also gives challenge to the player, to either stay inside the shelter and wait out night time or to risk going out at night having to deal with stronger zombies but with a potentially more rewarding experience.
👍
:
There is a wide variety of weapons to choose from in the game. I lost count after picking up twenty-five different ones. My favourite weapons would probably be the Sickle and Excavator, no regrets going into that hardware store out of curiosity.
👍
:
The game allows you to change Frank's clothing, though in order to do so you'd need to explore the mall and try out the outfits that are available to be worn, in some of the stores.
:
👎
:
It's not terrible, just that I felt it wasn't very smooth and fluid. Trying to aim with a weapon can be difficult especially since you're not able to move when you're aiming the gun or to throw a weapon. Fighting against psychopaths, especially when you're still starting the game can be very frustrating. Maybe it's not the bad combat, maybe I'm just bad at the game, who knows.
👎
:
Terrible, you encounter survivors who say they want to live but as you try to escort them and look back, they're often standing still or running slowly as if they want to be eaten alive. You can give them a weapon for their self-defense but it's not like they'll be able to use it effectively. It's infuriating but pretty satisfying when you're actually able to escort at least two or more at once to the shelter though. Kindell was the best survivor I've encountered in the game though.
👎
:
Imagine a triangle, you're at point A, you want to reach to point C without looking at the map so you trust the waypoint system to lead you there, so you keep following the waypoint until you realise it made you take a detour through point B even though the risk of going straight to point C or taking the detour is more or less the same, just that you wasted an amount of time because of the waypoint system. Seriously, you're better off navigating on your own using the map. It's as if it was designed to waste the player's time as much as possible. Once you've played enough of the game you'll probably remember all the locations of the mall anyway.
👎
:
There were numerous times when a survivor would be crying right in front of me and I'd only hear them from the right side of my headphones as if they were to the right of my character. I don't know if it's just me or it really is the game.
:
👌
:
Dead Rising has a time limit system for the missions, in which you only have a limited amount of time to complete missions. You're able to ignore the missions but with consequences, you might lose survivors when skipping side missions and you won't be able to continue playing the main mission if you skip them. However, you're still able to continue on playing freeroam after skipping and failing the main mission. Initially, I wasn't the biggest fan of this when I first tried out the Dead Rising series but then as I played more, my opinion changed in favour of it, especially since it's one of the features that makes Dead Rising unique compared to other open-world sandbox zombie games.
👌
:
The game can be quite challenging, especially with the lack of difficulty choices, save locations and the stupid survivor AI.
👌 The chances of having a perfect playthrough, with all side-missions completed, psychopaths killed and survivors saved, on the first try is very slim. The game was designed with replayability in mind, with each playthrough you do, everything becomes easier because of the progress system works. With this in mind, I would not recommend this game for those who are looking to have a perfect playthrough on their first try, you will fail and you will be retrying numerous times.
👌
:
1. The convicts on the humvee in Leisure Park can be annoying especially after you've already beaten them the first time. (The music too.)
2. You can sometimes get stuck in the 'jumping animation' when you try to jump on some cramped locations.
3. Otis' messages being unskippable without losing side-missions is very annoying.
It's a shame Dead Rising 4 will not feature most, if not all of the things I liked about Dead Rising.

It's a shame that Steam does not allow me to differentiate any more finely than recommending a game or not. This binary is useless without a target, whereas at least a scale can have some usefullness in the generic sense; it at least tells you how the game lines up with MY taste, if not how it lines up with YOURS.
My agnst over this comes about becasue Half Life 2 has a lot of interesting elements, but it ultimately a bit boring. It hasn't aged well, but this is true for many 3D action games. This is not news. What has aged the worst, I think, isn't the stingy level design or the mid-level loading or the  shooting gallery mechanics or the stiff feeling of everything. What has aged the worst is the crowning sense of ambition that gave the game so much praise when it first arrived.
So often Half Life 2 is said to be a game that belongs in a particular place in time, a time when it was oh so ambitious and new. It doesn't have to be this way. Every game is a product of it's time, but that gives us no obligation to preserve a game's cannonical criticism across the decades. If steam were asking me if I thought Half-Life was an interesting piece of design and of gaming history I'd happily explain why I think it is both of those things! But Steam wants me to recommend it or not.
To that end, I cannot recommend Half Life 2. The silence of the protagonist, perfectly acceptable to me in many games, feels downright unearthly in this game where everyone you meet interacts so personally and humanely towards you. This isn't a big silent lump in a cartoonish and empty world. This is a big silent lump in a world of color and love and humanity struggling against anihiliation. The spaces, so nicely designed for the theater of Half Life 2, are rather poorly designed for it's action something exacerbated by the awkward physics of the oft-touted Gravity Gun. It was delightful in Multiplayer Death Match, but in single player it is awkward alternating between uninterestingly powerful and frustratingly imprecise--something turned up to 11 at the very end of the game in what is, again, a half-decent piece of theater and a half-terrible piece of play.
Half Life 2 is scattershot, bouncing from mechanical idea to mechanical idea, but it is oddly that scattershot sensability that makes it feel coherent as an experience. Gordon Freeman bounces from place to place. Running, hiding, fighting, leading, following. Freeman's peculiar oddyssey works for me, as does the strange, clinical color pallatte. Despite chasing photo-realism in many ways--something that usually ages horrendously--looking back at it Half Life 2 managed to visually age about as well as possible, as well as some much more stylized and unique art styles. I'm sure tweaking of the Source engine and revisiting of the game post-launch have aided this feeling in places, but mostly I get the distinct impression that this game was built with a lot of care.
If only that care had been applied to what I actually do as a player, who Freeman actually is to these people. Imagine, for a moment, a Half Life 2 that visits the same places, carries the same pace ... but occurs in vingettes. You see Kliener and Alex and the major characters repeatedly, of course, perhaps even Gordon Freeman for that matter but maybe he's best left talked about in hushed tones by your fellows and exuberant ones by the main cast. Either way, you play as other figures, with other objectives that take you through the world. Sometimes toting guns, sometimes tools. Sometimes making deliveries, others escapes. Sometimes surivving, sometimes dying, always cutting away to see some other part of the struggle for humanity against the Combine.
But that wouldn't be an ambitiously medicore first person shooter. That would be taking Half Life 2's strengths--well cast and directed characters, impeccable attention to background detail, a consistent sense of atmosphere, a road-trip narrative sensability, etc--to their natural conclusion. What we have feels a bit more awkward with lots of mechanical dead ends that quite possibly excited their designers as little as they now excite me given how the episodes tried to break out of those spaces while still struggling to stay close enough to the mechanics to work both in-engine and in-fandom.
It is a strange road trip. The timbre and atmosphere of each new environment is effective at first, but Freeman inevitably wobbles silently through the same dead performances we had once come to expect as the only option from first person games, sucking the novelty of gravity guns, cars, turrets and ant-lions out of the proceedings as he continues to get his gun off much the same way against much the same soulless, unchallenging canon fodder.
Half Life 2 isn't without fun and isn't without quality. But if Steam isn't intersted in letting me communicate that in a more robust shorthand, I'll have to go with an even greater oversimplificaiton: I can't *recommend* it. But I am fond of it.

Wow!  Really, really fun game.  This is a fantastic FPS.  I'm sorry I missed it when it first came out.  Way better than the first Half-Life game.   This time they got almost everything right.
Pros:
- Controls are very responsive in this game, unlike the original HL, which makes this a blast to play.
- Story is simple but compels you to play to try and find out WTFudge is going on.
- HL had tedious puzzle-lite sections where you had to push crates around to progress to the next part of the game.  I found these boring and annoying.  HL2  also has these simple puzzle aspects, but for some reason they got it right this time.  Hard to explain, but this time around I did not find it tedious or boring.
-Fun variety of weapons which you do switch around for various reasons.  Not just a 1 gun run.
-The vehicles were a nice change of pace.
- The AI on the Combine soldiers is pretty good but not perfect.  Once in a while they would do something stupid, but for the most part they would offer a good fight.  And they are annoyingly good at aiming thier gernades.  8 out of 10 on the Combine AI.
Cons:
- The WTFudge aspect of the story does not go away.  But that may be a Pro because you want more.
- The AI on the rebels who insist on trying to help you is BAD.  No wonder the aliens are in control!  These humans are so stupid, they deserve to be oppressed.  They were often in the way and got me killed several times because it was difficult to move around them in tight quarters.  And they constantly apologized for being in my way which made them more annoying.  And they had no tactics and no idea of duck and cover.  They are cannon fodder and they play the part well because of the stupid AI.  I will admit, I was amused several times just watching them get creamed.  The annoying thing was, more kept popping up to take the place of the ones that kept getting killed.  3 out 0f 10 on stupid rebel AI.
-Bugs and Glitches.  Yep, the game has some, at least for me,  None make me want to stop playing, but they can be annoying.
---At one point within 48 hours of play time, screen crashed to a black screen, had to reboot PC.  So far this only happened once.
---Game crashed on 2 other occasions, just had to restart the game.
---Several times audio has glitched.  The game will freeze for about half a second, then when it starts again, the audio is messed up.  Either there is no audio or now you only get one sound effect, like machinery droning and no other sounds.  This has happened a few times.
---And the most annoying glitch, getting stuck in the terrain or stuck to moveable objects.  This happened often enough to really annoy me. The worst of this was in a fight with a gunship.  You have to use wrecked cars as cover so you hide behind them.  The gunship shoots at you, hitting the wrecked car, causing it to move slightly.  And because it moved while you were next to it, you are now perma-stuck to it like glue!  frozen in one spot, unable to move.  The gunship swings around to the other side and tears you a new one.  And even if you do not die, you can never unstick your self.  You have to reload the last saved game.  This kept happening over and over for this particular fight so I finally just abandoned that fight and moved on.
Bottom Line:  9 out of 10  (no glitches and better rebel AI would have been a perfect 10)

They changed way too much from the Xbox 360 version. I'm going to list the pros and cons of the PC version to help clarify to those that just keep disliking this review. This is not a hate review this is a review of what I have physically seen playing this game. These issues should have never made its way to the remastered version.
Pros
------
(+) Better textures and visuals (Increased draw distance)
(+) 60 FPS (Stable)
(+) 4K support (Xbox 360 maxed at 1080i)
(+) Best Dead Rising game in the series
(+) Fun gameplay with great cut scenes
Cons
-------
(-) The prisoners in Leisure Park keep respawing even after you kill all three. This goes on numerous times and makes it nearly impossible to escourt surviors to the security room. I know this was in the Xbox 360 version I just thought it was important to add. This issue should have been fixed but apparently it wasn't since it's in the PC version.
(-) Terrible survivor ai plagues this game like the Xbox 360 version but worse. The survivors never seem to follow you even when calling them. They always seem to walk right into a horde of zombies and die within a few seconds. Try giving them a weapon? Your results will be even worse because now they'll just target any zombie whether close or far and waste more precious time.
(-) Zombie capacity increase. This was something I noticed right away. It appears the amount of zombies have been doubled or even tripled in certain areas making escourting survivors even more challenging. Stocking up on quickstep barely helps avoiding confrontations because it doesn't last long enough. I understand this is a zombie game and all but this was not how the Xbox 360 version was. The Xbox 360 version couldn't possibly have these amount of zombies due to hardware limitations but on PC the amounts are just ridiculous. Even veteran players like myself struggle to complete missions with enough time. It's only logical that if the amount of zombies were increased so should the intelligence of the survivors.
(-) No indicator to determine the quality of your weapons. This was never in the Xbox 360 version but thought it should have been included in the remastered version. When you attack zombies your weapons gradually begin to get weaker eventually breaking. There should have been a percentage bar under each weapon showing how much is left. This would enable the player to have more strategy in fights.
(-) Long dialogue with survivors. In order to have survivors team up you must first interact with them. The amount of dialogue there is before the survivor joins is way too long. There should have been an ability to speed past the dialogue to avoid sneaky zombies from attacking you from behind or even the survivor.
Conclusion
----------------
I personally love Dead Rising. I still believe this game is and will always be the best but this applies to the Xbox 360 version not PC. The gradual changes that have been applied have modified this game making it something different then what it once was. If you truly want the best experience play the Xbox 360 version.

In 2006, Dead Rising was a technical achievement and the sole reason I bought an Xbox 360. It felt like something familiar, but still like something I hadn't played yet. This game has a silly tone to start, but quickly shifts into horror as soon as the malls automated power is cut after close. The atmosphere alone is one to be experienced first hand. By yesteryear's standard, the graphics were goofy, sure, but some of the best I had seen a video game offer on a console. Couldn't read the text too well, but ooh what's that sound? It sounds so good! Hearing glass shattering, the difference in running machines, each slice, dice and every single drop of blood hitting the floor, I can honestly say that this is easily one of the best sounding video games I've ever played. I'm still basking in the aural pool of it's warm waves.
But of course the most significant feature was rendering six hundred plus characters on screen at one time without massive dips in frame rate or performance. It was amazing! With Dead Rising, Capcom created a survival horror comedy beat-em up that had introduced RPG elements, photography, time, inventory, resource and human management. It's like, ♥♥♥♥, I can do whatever I want and there's so much to do! Sure, the sequels have opened up the playground, added more in-depth combat systems and packed it all to the brim with more zombies, but the original did it best. It's the simplicity of the gameplay and a variety of activities that helps Dead Rising age so finely, like a nice pack of smokes.
Now, old fans and new comers can enjoy this game without having to get an Xbox 360, A decision I was facing a few months before I discovered it's release on Steam. And it runs like my frozen dinner into the toilet. Smooth. Now, if only we can get Saints Row, Conker Live and Reloaded with Halo 2, I might just make myself some bathtub Gamer Fuel. Code Red y'all! Red allert! You gotta pick this up if you're on the fence. It's well worth the twenty bucks. It'll make you laugh, then♥♥♥♥♥♥you off, but don't take it too seriously. This game sure as ♥♥♥♥ doesn't. If you're interested in trying Mega Man out, this is the place to start as it includes the first six entries. (Keep in mind, Mega Man 1 is less polished than the rest of the series, try starting out with MM2)

Tried it on the free weekend.  It's pretty fun at first, but it gets boring fast.
It's wave fighting with "large zeds" being hard-hitting bullet sponges, with that only increasing the harder the difficulty.  And harder difficulty = playing with the worse weapons while enemies hit harder as you try to save up enough to buy a decent weapon.
There are a lot of weapons, granted.  The gun variety is cool at first, but you quickly realize it's not worth it to use the mid-tier upgrades; you're better off slogging through the first few waves with trash gear while saving up for the top-tier weapons.  The unique weapons tend not to be even worth it.  The crossbow is laughable and the railgun doesn't hold enough ammo to be worth it.  Those last two are part of the Sharpshooter class ("perk"), and I think it's telling that no one ever chooses the Sharpshooter class on Hard.
I don't like that there are only 2 bosses.  Some people make it a point to say that each time you fight them, they have different traits (hitting harder, chasing down runners, "arrogance"), but these traits are few in number and negligible in practice.  I've not noticed any of the traits affecting how the boss behaves.
And speaking of varying playstyles, I didn't notice any.  You can weld doors shut to block off hordes, but I didn't see a single person bother.  You're constantly moving around the map, so welding doors just becomes a hindrance as it limits your mobility.  Maybe on Nightmare and Hell modes it matters, but on Normal and Hard, it's a pointless novelty to boost your Support experience.
One last thing: The servers are in need of repair.  Even on the official Tripwire servers, I was disconnected constantly or experienced mid-game lag spikes, going from <50ms up to >200ms, which affected the entire server.  For a first person shooter, let alone a wave-based FPS, that's just not fun.  I only have so many grenades in my grenade launcher and if a zed rubberbands into my line of sight, the round gets wasted as it sits undetonated in its skull, instead of 10m downrange where it should have exploded.
Bottom line:  It's fun, but repetitive.  There are a lot of guns, but they're pretty interchangeable and boring.  The maps are cool but you can't interact much with them at all (there aren't even exploding barrels).  Healing is a nightmare, unless you like playing as Ana from Overwatch with even less healing capabilities.  You move slowly, even while running, even with a light build.
I did play for six hours, and after my last round I just asked myself, "Why bother playing another?"

What's more all the things I loved from the original were still there such as the infamous zed time to reward gory kills with yet more gory fun, and significantly better hit regristration and gore effects.
Several updates later, and several more classes maxed out and new maps released, I'm happy to say that the game is better than the original, even if there had been a few hiccups along the way.
Though one thing I am a little dissappointed about is the susposed loss of the original 10th class nick named "The Dragon" due to one of the pins out of a set sold during early access depicting an eastern style dragon. Not saying I dislike the Survivalist class, in fact I love it since it's the most flexible of all classes, even if some of it's traits are kinda meh, but despite the the potential loss of "The Dragon", lookin at you TripWire, with all the awesome ideas you've guys have had so far I'm sure you can think of something for "The Dragon", I am happy to recommend it to anyone looking for a horde survival game with roots in a HL2 mod.

An interesting conclusion to the Arkham series. It's been an amazing ride indeed...
OK let's get the elephant out of the room, the game's optimization has never been fixed. After 2 years of it's release the game still crashes and the fps drops from time to time, but in my case it wasn't unbearable except when i started the game (in which the game crashed almost always when i tried to open it) and i've managed to get fixed 60 fps majority of the game.
So, Arkham Knight is way bigger than City and the Atmosphere is more neon-ish rather than City's almost Claustrophobic and Dark tone. The map is as dense as ever with numeroes secrets, riddles and easter eggs. Stuff you'd expect from an Arkham game. (Thugs are still interesting and funny to listen to as well)
The combat is faster, more varied and feels as satisfying as ever with some new types of enemies put in. The addition of buddy fights (?) add a nice touch to the combat.
Now, since we got those out of the way my main gripe with the game is side quests. There are some, now cliched, tower liberation missions, beat a bunch of militia missions and bomb defusing missions. These missions feel extremely repetetive and you do each one more than 10 times. They could be more varied with different twists to each one to break it's repetetive nature but i think Rocksteady has been lazy with them. There are also a couple side quests with EXTREMELY underused villians (Such as
).
Most people say that the batmobile is overused and while i kind of agree with that statement (especially with tank parts) i think there is enough variation to keep it from becoming stale, and the Batmobile controls well enough.
Lastly, i think the main story was great (Even though the identity of the Arkham Knight is predictable). Better than the first two games. MAJOR SPOILERS
All and all even though it has it's shortcomings this is a great game and a pretty good ending to one of my most beloved gaming Franchises.

Just finished the game. If you like lots of crafting, some fighting, loads of base building and farming then you may enjoy this game. That being said, it is very very very grindy- building and crafting takes a variety of materials which you'll spend most of the game collecting. In-game content could use a bit of tweaking (ie wells refilling to a more reasonable amount- I think I spent around a third of the game getting water for crops, cooking, livestock. Very slow and somewhat frustrating as the well only refills to 4 units and even with 6 wells at the end I was still short on water) Oddly there's also no way at present to destroy items so after a while you end up with a pile of old gear, assorted junk and a ton of wheat seeds strewn all over the place.
If you're keen on combat then you may not like this. Your character is very squishy and the wilderness is populated by plenty of monsters who hit a lot harder than you do. Very basic click to whack something with a sword and see if you or it dies first. No skills, nothing fancy, stuff your face with food to recover health and stamina. Combat may be a bit difficult for first time players. Armour doesn't provide much in the way of protection and even wearing the endgame gear I had to duck behind trees and bushes in order to survive pulling more than one mob at a time. Your weapons, while they don't have durability or need repairing, don't do much damage so expect to spent a lot of time poking bears with swords and getting mauled. Part of the game involves killing large numbers of enemies guarding quest-related rocks (which you mine for Force of Nature shards needed to craft said FoN) and you'll spend a lot of time cutting and chopping narrow paths through flora and fauna to survive any kind of combat- most mobs can't slip through small spaces so despite aggro they're unable to reach you. This sounds a bit odd but if you play the game for a bit you'll understand.
Most of your time though will be spent building up your base so you can craft better gear, farm more ingredients and cook a mountain of food that you'll end up going through each time you venture out into the forest. No rushing headlong into battle, you'll need to plan ahead and prepare before getting into a fight. I think I ended up eating around 500 apple pies towards the end.
Hoping that there will be more content updates in the future but for $9 it offers a fair amount of gameplay and so long as you're ok with grinding a whole bunch I'd say it's worth getting.

Gameplay
Simple yet complex, The Stick of Truth has an intricate system of battle stances, status effects and turn based mechanics. It is essential to have a frim understanding of these factors, as one mistake way cost you dearly. Every class has something unique to add to the table, with fighters breaking through any deffences with ease and soking up damage, the mage controlling the flow of the battlefeild with magic, the theif piling on status effects or the jew, whose complex, risky playstyle I haven't had the confidence to try yet.
Sound
The music is realitivly passable in the open world; however it gets considerably better in boss battles, to the point that it almost sounds too badarse to be in a South Park game. The original voice actors all make an appearance and makes it feel like you're really a part of the world despite your muteness. The battle noises themselves are meaty and appropriatley brutal for what is essentialy a game about leaving a string of battered, vomiting, bleeding children in your wake.
Humor
Thankfully, the humor never wanes from this experience as I feared it would, nor becomes overfrequent and purile. This is largely thanks to the original creators of South Park overseeing the development of the game. As a result, the humor is far more present than most boring, grey, triple A games that have been appearing these days. Almost every joke made me chuckle at least a little, especially those that comment on the nature of children playing made up games together.
Is it Fun?
Yes. The combat system alone is enough to tell me that this isn't a genric game with the South Park brand clumsily slapped on as an afterthought. Real love and pride for the series went into this and it shows. Seeing the game now makes me wish a could have seen more of the series than I was allowed to by my parents, although I can see why they'd be squirmish about it. All in all, its a solid, interesting RPG that I still have yet to tire of.
This is the most unadulterated fun I've had in a game for I don't know how many years. Screw your escapism, screw your story and improvment of games as a literary medium. This game is pure game

Shortly put, the Jump button in this game is adhorrently unresponsive, which alone says it all. Jumping is as important in Mega Man as stealth in Metal Gear or flying in Flight Simulator. And if such core mechanics won't work, you just can't shrug that off. It fundamentally breaks the game. Just imagine if you suddenly were unable to pick up blocks in Minecraft (in survival or creative mode, that is).
Far too often, jumping doesn't even register. And the times it does, there's commonly a delay from when you press the button till you actually jump. These things make pixel-perfect edge jumping and similar almost impossible, and there's a plethora of situations in this game where jumping multiple times in a row and timing it correctly is key. And you can forget about speed running these games, as it stands now.
I've played these games on both the NES and through emulators, so this isn't about the games being too hard for me. Mega Man 2 is my most played-through game of all time - easily 200+ playthroughs, culminating in a 27-minute speed run. For the Mega Man Legacy Collection, I also happened to have a new keyboard (that works perfectly with every other game I have, old as well as new ones).
In MMLC's defense, I have NOT tested the game on a controller.
If Capcom fixes the shoddy controls and makes the games feel properly responsive, you are in for an amazing game experience. The Mega Man series has some of the best NES games ever, and Mega Man 2 is, imo, the greatest NES game ever designed (from a level design perspective).
The fact that 7, 8 and 9 aren't included in this collection, is incidental IMO. Those games are barely worth playing - it's always been Mega Man 1 thru 5 that have been acclaimed as pinnacle titles, and I guess Mega Man 6 too. I can understand how the bigger fans would like 7, 8, 9 though - it makes the collection feel incomplete.
In either case, for my own sake, I just have to go with what I'm experiencing right now. And right now, I have very little good to say about the experience.
Booh, CAPCOM. Please fix this!

If you don't mind, I'll copy/paste parts of my review for the first episode, because some remarks for it is valid for Patriot Frames
The core mechanics is a point-and-click. But I wish that the inventory/utility belt was easier to use. I mean, why should I open the inventory for combining items and use the utility belt to... use them in the scene? Being original is good. But being practical is also a good option. I was really confused at that. I would have prefer the combine option in the utility belt. Why? Because I can easily the utility belt by placing my cursor at the bottom of the screen instead of opening the top of my screen and make a click on the box to open the inventory.
Another gameplay problem is that you can easily obtain items... but can't use them before speaking to a character. I don't have an exact example in the head - though I know that for episode 3, I had to ask help to Melvin (as he's also the one giving hints) and it was the only way to go forward.
The dialogues are still in the comedy mood: with the Purple Patriot being "mean" (Kyle is a sweet guy, when he's Kyle and you'll see it only once in episode 2). Besides, while I had a little hard time sometimes to solve the puzzles, I must say that I warmed up to the game.
Yet, achievements unlocking every five minutes is really boring after a while. And some are missable, as they're kinda all "hidden".
Anyway, the graphics or the soundtrack are still the same: in a comedy mood, cartoonish and with new locations.
Buy it when it's discounted or in a bundle but I suggest you strongly to play the first episode if you want to follow the story and understand all the references.

Supreme League of Patriots is a point and click game wiwth a dash of humor and comedy. The game let's you take the role of both Kyle and Mel as they venture through the world of superheroes and supervillains. The story is a bit slow on the build up but the actual plot is very unique and original. Each issue comprises about 3-4 hours of gameplay depending on how you solve the puzzles in the game. The puzzles are easy and you won't get off track much since Melvin is there to guide you when you don't know/forgot what you should be doing. The dialgoues and voices are great especially Melvin's british accent.
Pros:
+ A great funny story plot
+ Great voice acting
+ Great Music (especially each character's BGM)
+ Good Graphics
+ Narrative guide (Mel gives you a hint when you get lost)
Cons:
+ There's a bit of bugs whenever you make Kyle go to an obtacle-full area
+ There are times that the voices become out of sync with the balloons/text that appear
If you're looking for a point and click adventure game full of humor, comedy, patriotism, superheroes and supervillains, then Supreme League of Patriots is a must try for you.

Bread-and-Butter Turn Based Tactical Skirmish Game. Has all the basic elements you expect from this kind of games: ranged vs. melee, tactical positioning, support, flanking, cover in buildings, terrain, etc. etc. Uses slightly more units than other games in this genre. However - the unit capabilities seem rather limited, there is limited rock-paper-scissors type strength/weakness matching. A hex-layout would have been more suitable than square-based, and pacing seems pretty slow.
Thus it feels like a tablet/mobile port, or some basic tabletop skirmish game ported to PC. Pre-battle setup customisation is very limited and unit experience does not carry over between matches. Also, crashed on me about 100 Minutes into the game. Personally, I think there are better games of similar type around (but also much worse). I will refund this as it is to generic for my taste, without really unique points that would set it apart.
I would rate it 6 out of 10. It's by no means a bad game, and if there were a "meh" rating I'd use that.
However, if you like those type of games it may still be OK for you.

Story is cliche, and text certainly has its share of spelling errors, but it seemed simple to play and a fun way to pass time. Art is decent (kind of like Warcraft, cartoonish), and relatively easy to figure out. A manual would have been nice, but most nowadays don't provide more than the basics anyway, certainly little in the way of tactics or strategy. Didn't find a manual for this game, but didn't find one, just tutorials.  A couple other points: Your units gain experience and level up...but that doesn't seem to carry over from one battle to another (you have to start from scratch each battle). Also, in the later battles you're able to choose some of the units you can bring in with you, but your choice is quite limited. For example, in some battles you get longbowmen, but others only crossbowmen. Or if you get longbowmen, you can only take two perhaps. I'm guessing this is the way the game designers ensure the game stayed balanced.
Anyway, spent a fair amount of time this weekend playing the game, but am now going to uninstall: the game has crashed three times in the past few hours, not only freezing up the game itself but forcing me to log out in order to be able to do anything in windows. This is ridiculous: It's one thing to have bugs that cause your software to freeze or crash, but another thing entirely to force me to log out of windows to fix. Those kind of errors belong in the '90s, not now. I was finally able to shut down the game using task manager and the keyboard, mouse was not functional until I shut it down.
So, if you don't have any problems running the game, great. Still nothing that really stands out. With bugs it just makes it another piece of shelfware.

On the surface, Hell is a casual, light hearted cartoonish affair. It doesn't take itself seriously at all, and instead plays off the fantasy cliches for comedic effect. The maps and models are simple and beautiful, making the overall aesthetic colorful and easy on the eyes. Some tactical turn based fans might be turned off by the cartoon comedy feel of this game, but it works as intended.
Beneath the surface is a surprising amount of tactical depth. You get a good mix of units. Melee, short and long ranged missile, cavalry, scouts, magic; everything you'd expect from the genre. Units level up through combat experience, and have unique abilities that can turn the tide when used correctly. Units gain support bonuses from adjacent allies, and flanking bonuses for attacking the enemy from the rear. You get terrain bonuses and penalties, and the maps lend them well to strategic gameplay.
I'm running the game on a crappy laptop with no crashes or technical issues. The price point is prohibitive, but on sale I recommend it highly.

This is the pinnacle of story-telling that can be found in RPGMaker games. It managed to keep me enthralled in it the whole time I was playing it, making my eyes very pleased with the splendid art design and entertained me with its witty and charming dialogue and well-designed, interesting characters that can rival games like Alicemare and LiEat, (Both very good games, I suggest them if you like Angels of Death) and threw me for an emotional rollercoaster that had me smiling and laughing at Zack's expression, to sobbing and crying because of the story's compelling events. The writing and the visuals accented each other very well.
However, it is a very niche game that only certain people will enjoy. The gameplay is comprised of puzzles that go from simple to average, and text boxes that can sometimes feel like they go on for half an hour. (Which they sometimes do, but I'm not at all complaining; I loved every second of it) Overall, if you like Psychological Horror and Story-Based games with some Strategy involved, this game will please you.
The game does have flaws that are common in Japanese games translated into English, including grammatical and spelling mistakes, and some text boxes having words that go beyond the box and are unreadable, (I counted five, and all of them only cut off the last word of the sentence, making it not that much of a problem) and is almost exclusive to Zack. However, these are few and far-between and are hardly noticeable unless you are actively looking for them. The translators and programmers did very well.
In case you want a brief verison: Amazing story and characters, with charming and witty dialogue that has very little grammatical and spelling mistakes, but is very niche and will appeal only to certain people.

Lots of people harbor disdain for RPGMaker titles, and for good reason. With the exception of a few gems like
, most of them aren't worth playing, with stock sprites, unoriginal story, poor world design, uninspired combat...
Thankfully,
has none of these. It's well-made enough to have garnered a sizable following among Japanese doujin game fans. At heart, it is a mystery story with similar "horror" vibes to
. That is to say, it is more of a atmospheric/psychological horror game, without any real jumpscares or gore. Which is great, because I'm a queasy guy :<
(In case you're unaware,
is a fantastic, cheap non-RPGMaker title on Steam. Also from the makers of
).
Right at the start, you are introduced to Zack and Ray. They are lost in a mysterious facility filled with other psychopathic axe murderers. Zack happens to be one of them as well, underneath his edgelord bandaged exterior. Ray is a mysterious young girl who begs Zack to murder her. Zack promises to do so...only on the condition that she helps him escape. The game is split into 4 episodes, much like
. Be sure to play them in order!
The real meat of the game, and its most enjoyable aspect, lies in unravelling the mysteries behind the characters, with a strange and unlikely rapport building up between these two oddballs as the narrative progresses.
Both
and
excel in this regard of storytelling - all the characters are genuinely likable and relatable in their dialogue and interactions. If you enjoyed one of them, I'm certain you'll enjoy the other as well.
In the end though, you still can't escape from the limitations of the RPGMaker engine. The game is locked at a miniscule resolution, with gritty pixel graphics. The puzzles that you have to solve are limited to the 2D physics engines of RPGMaker. Not that they aren't challenging or fun, but they aren't anything too novel.
The art isn't anything to write home about as well either. I'd label it as serviceable, for lack of a better word. Better than most RPGMaker titles out there, but
has it cleanly beat on this level.
Overall, if you're after a quick dose of episodic psycho-horror + mystery story,
is a decent choice.
I still feel the price is a little high though - I could get both
and
for $10. Considering that this game was released as freeware in Japan, you're essentially paying for 4 hours worth of in-game translation. Wait for a 50% sale?

Nice and very challenging strategy game with good graphics. Play on the lowest difficulty unless you're a true wargame grognard!
Pros:
- Deep gameplay: Zones of Control, flanking and mutual unit support; special abilities for all units; terrain elevation and cover matters; morale system. This is not your average Advance Wars clone, it's closer to a real wargame.
- Easy to play despite the deep rules (but reading the manual helps to understand all the details)
- Nice graphics, adequate art style
- Mission and campaign editor, interestingly while units don't carry over from scenario to scenario in the current campaigns you can enable that feature in the editor. So you could make the current campaign a lot easier, or create a new balanced campaign around that feature.
- Full campaign for both sides of the conflict.
- You can save your game at any time and play any campaign scenario whenever you want.
Cons:
- Atrocious learning curve, the first campaign scenario is very difficult and does not ease you into playing. (DEVS: Wanna fix this easily? Extend the tutorial campaign to be more like the one in Panzer Corps, actual scenarios where you have to take decisions but where the odds are initially heavily stacked in your favor and get harder as you progress.)
- Scenarios like to spawn enemy reinforcements right on top of you, and they can move on the same turn they appear. That sucks, so be wary of map edges.
- Interface is functional but slightly clumsy, and it should have included some information that is only found in the manual. It lacks keyboard shortcuts for some things such as closing dialogs, and betrays its iPad cross-platformness (yup I did just invent that word) by inefficient use of space and by looking stretched (or just badly skinned?) in widescreen.
- Generic universe and story that does the job but isn't captivating.
Overall despite the flaws there's a lot of fun to be had if you go in expecting a good challenge, not a walk in the park. Units don't carry over with their XP from scenario to scenario (contrary to, say, Battle for Wesnoth), so unlike other games where losing one or two major units means reload, here you can definitely win despite some heavy losses. Some players are complaining about this lack of campaign continuity, but I find it different and refreshing. Fight to the death instead of XP farming! Another misguided player complaint is the turn limit in every scenario: every serious wargame has it (notably the amazing Panzer Corps), a time constraint is part of the challenge and gives a realistic element to any battle. In war you're always under pressure from something, be it dwindling supplies, attrition, the coming of winter or incoming enemy reinforcements. And war, war never changes.

Published by Slitherine, its no surprise that Hell is a highly addictive turn-based strategy game that offers challenging gameplay for even the most battle-tested tacticians among us. Still, the game manages to offer an inviting platform for beginners, complete with a helpful tutorial and an in-depth game manual. Moreover, it is a "skirmish" style of strategic warfare, meaning that the game skips the often tedious and mind-boggling affairs  found in grand strategy games and thrusts players right into the action. By doing so, the game is easier for newcomers to the genre to catch on and since combat is the central focal point, more effort and development has been put into the tactical aspect of it and the results are impressive.
So what exactly can players expect? For starters, the maps are much smaller, which keeps the speed and intensity of each battle moving at a fast, steady pace. While the maps (and the graphics in general) are amazingly rich and lustrious for this type of game, they are so much more. Players must utilize the various terrains and vantage points craftily in order to gain the upper hand on the battlefield. The use of higher ground, hidden units in a treeline, obstructed fields of vision, slower paths of travel, and choke points are some of the things to be considered with each turn. Additionally, combat tactics include using unit support, flanking, and other maneuvers as well. These things must all be considered both offensively and defensively in order to be successful.
There are a variety of units in the game with their own abilities, strengths and weaknesses to be considered. Units gain experience on the battlefield which increase their strength as they level up. This is all done automatically, much like everything else non-combat related in order to keep the micromanagement aspects out of the game.
The game offers a solid storyline that plays out over two full-length campaigns, one having players defend the mystical realm using the armies of "The Order of Radiance" and the other commanding hordes of the "Demons of Hell" to prevent being vanquished from the lands. These campaigns are broken down into individual missions, or skirmishes, and offer individual battle achievements for each map to further challenge players. Unfortunately, these are not in the form of Steam Achievements and as far as I can tell, attaining these offer no additional benefits other than personal glory.
Some of the other nice features about this game include good background music and sound effects, attractive graphics including battle animations (for this type of game), a cross-platform multiplayer feature, a skirmish mode, a rotating camera with smooth controls to enable better views of the battlefield, and an editting tool to create custom maps and campaigns.
Honestly, there isn't much to not like about this game. The one thing I personally would like to see added to this game is a way to reverse, or undo, a unit's movement before performing an action in combat. Several times I accidentally clicked a spot on the map not realizing I had the wrong unit highlighted or without knowing support units would not be able to reach the location in time. The results are perilous and for a game that has done so well in removing the micromanagement aspects of strategy in order to keep from distracting players from the battle, I found it a bit disappointing that managing my mouse is a determining factor in overall success. Another area that could use some work is the AI. Its not bad and it does offer a good challenge to players, but since this is a skirmish game whose focus is on the combat, the AI should be superb. It feels a bit random at times and often unpredictable for no apparent reason. Enemy units sometimes back off when they clearly have the upper hand or fail to capitalize on a player's mistake. The lack of intuitive thinking is more obvious at some times and less at others, but it is clearly visible for true veterans of the genre. Overall, its still not bad and can be challenging on higher difficulty settings.

Overall, Hell is a solid turn-based tactical game that offers plenty of challenge for beginners and veterans alike. Being a skirmish strategy game makes it a great alternative to fire up when you don't have time to fully engage in a grand strategy since you can jump straight into the action. For all strategy fans and for players looking for a new type of challenge I encourage you to pick up a copy of Hell. Its devilishly fun.

Preliminary review after only 1.8 hours [I will update as I play more].
It is a story driven game at the strategic level, you fight one tactical scenario/battle after another, each increasing in difficulty and number of enemies.
If you like turn based tacticaly battles, this looks like a lot of fun.
PROS:
- good graphics
- easy UI
- no bugs
- good AI (I am playing on easiest level and it took me until the last turn to win the first scenario)
- turned based strategy (gotta love it)
- a little like Fantasy General of old (but not quite there, see RPG issues below).
- I am a supporter of Slitherine, the Lords, Matrix Games, and other small, independent, turn-based, war game makers, and this game is so close to having great potential just from the little I have seen. Once it is balanced, I think it will be great.  Keep up the good works guys!
CONS:
- No Undo button. It is such a pain to fight a battle for an hour and then due to a misclick get screwed because you can't undo an errant click that had no affect on anything.  I hope they add an UNDO button.
- Lacking true RPG from what I can tell so far.  Units within a scenario gain experience and can increase in rank, but apparently that unit doesn't carry over to the next scenario/battle, so what is the point?
- There is NO fun RPG things to find on the map, no magic weapons, etc., to outfit your troops.
- If they add the two features listed above, this game could rival Fantasy General and become a classic hit.  If you are unfamiliar with Fantasy General (old DOS game) you can play it for free here:
-Also the game is quite difficult, even on easy setting.  The game needs balancing for recreational gamers who want to enjoy the game but not spend endless hours repeating battles that are too difficult.
- I am having a hard time getting past the first battle without losing troops.  I am not sure if you need to not lose troops as I don't know if they and their experience carry over.  WHen I start the second battle I have different troops, but I don't know if my earlier troops come back later. If not, then this game has little RPG factor.
- Some of the enemy units (HELL HOUNDS) seem over powered for first scenario.  Game needs balancing.

~I would like to see the farming plot numbers pushed upwards per level, as farming can be a bit tedious. Maybe an option to exchange the small plots up to the bigger plot sizes?

~More uses of gems, such as embrodered into armors and engraved into weapons? (Tailor Bench and Anvil?)
~Maybe I haven't played far enough into the game yet but I'd love to see a few more different types of monsters. Maybe in an expansion?

`First review of the game. Who knows, it may change.  This is a set scenario tactical turn based war game.  If you found it, you likely know that or play strategy games already.  There is a base "story" that the scenario goes thru.  The rule set is very good.  The "zones of control" that limit movement around enemy lines really change tactics up.  I am only on the beginning few scenarios of the "good" side, but so far,the unit choices are normal.  People complain that they arent varied enough, but most other games don't have many more options, unless they are reskins of similar units.  Far ranged longbowmen, mid range crossbowmen, knights, calvalry, grunts (men at arms), heavy infantry (spearmen) and more.
The only thing I can't praise is the feeling of rails.  Being a limited turn scenario, it really forces your hand into one or two main strategies, especially if you want the bonus objectives.  I assume this is to keep the difficulty up.  This is, and may be, easily fixed with patches, dlc, or user generated content (dev kit included as usual these days).  Some wargamers like the feeling of being pressed for time by the turn limits, however, I feel as if it makes the scenarios into puzzles, that barring horrible luck on many dicerolls, make it so once solved there is little reason to replay.  Once you've been thru the scenario and know about the behavior of the AI, you know how to approach the level.  It's also likely that I dislike turn limits because I have always been a "sniper" tactician and really like to set up before I attack.  In Hell, I can't waste turns being timid.  I'm sure more campaigns will be made available at some point.
This game uses the Battle Academy engine.  I am not an old school slitherine fanboy, I just found out about them.  I got this game for $20, and that price is great for what we get.  At $30, it is still a good game.  If the developers support it with small content changes for free, it would definitely be worth it.  There is already a patch coming, and eventually a skirmish mode, as mentioned on the forum by the developers. If they release full campaigns as dlc for $5 or less, then that would be ok as well.  All in all, there are many games that I paid much more for that are not as good.  The tactics are solid, the unit variety is there, and although it is presented in a "Blizzardesque" cartoony way, the subject of saving the world from hell, or bringing hell upon the world, is  different than some made up warring factions.  The demons aren't scary, or funny.  More board game styled (obviously..slitherine makers digital boardgames)  I highly reccomend if you like tactical wargames, and aren't married to AAA graphics.  These games are all in the system, not the graphics.  Hunted Cow seems to have taken the BA engine and gave it a different kind of feel, which I like.

This game is more of a time and resource management game than a sandbox rpg. There is no survival elements at all other than staying alive if you want. Dying doesn't have any real consequence other than loosing a few inventory items and at times letting yourself die is advantagious.  This game is a time sink and one of the grindiest games out there but that is not saying it is bad. Contrary, it is a very addictive game the grind is done well but could use a few minor balancing tweaks.   If you are looking for a crafting/building/survival game this is not it. Even though it has those elements they are extremely limited and are only there to get you to the next level.  The developers are not active in the Steam forums and that leaves a lot of guessing on where/when/what is planned for this game. As far as I know the game is out of Early Access and no major changes are expected.  Hope this review helps a you make an informed decision on the purchase.  I have over 100 hours in the game and really enjoy it for what it is.﻿

First let me say that performance-wise I had no problems, looks like they fixed all the issues the game had at launch.
This is a direct sequel to Arkham city, so if you liked that game you're sure to like this!
I got the premium edition that has all the skins and DLC stuff and what not. There's a lot of content here, first there's the main story, then there are side quests, then there are DLC side-quests, then the Riddler challenges (if you're into those, I am), then the challenge maps (racing, fighting, etc), and thennn expansion missions where you play as Batgirl or Harley and other characters. Villains from previous games' side missions make a comeback too so everything ties together nicely.
Some of the content is repetitive and some of the boss battles will disappoint, but there's also lots of neat puzzles (environmental and otherwise), a few truly teriffic moments, and then there's the Batmobile which is just a blast to drive once you get the hang of it. And without spoiling anything a character pops up often that is a constant joy to see. They nailed the look of Gotham too - it's a glorious mess of art deco, Gothic architecture, art nuveau, industrial pipes and bricks, and neon. I'm reminded of Joel Schumacher's vision of Gotham... but in a good way, if you can believe that.
Parts of the city feel like there's nothing to do but enjoy the art design, that's just an inevitable fact of making such a huge environment. But bless Rocksteady they really tried to populate the city with challenges. If you want to fight, or chase cars, or do predator missions, there's plenty of those just lying around!
Is this the best Arkham game? I still think Arkham City is mroe satisfying, but it's certainly a good game with lots to do, tons of gadgets to do it with, a veteran voice actor from this series gives perhaps his best performance yet, and if nothing else gliding between the buildings in the pouring rain looks and feels absolutely amazing!
PS
Off topic, but the Bale Batsuit skin is phenomenal, they nailed every detail of it and it looks really amazing, the way it looks in the environment and how it catches the light is perfect. Driving around in the tumbler batmobile is a dream come true!
Also, the Adam West suit is a console exclusive, but here is a mod that integrates it into the PC version, easy to install, works just like the console one.
In a way I find this game incredibly relaxing. Takes my mind of everything around me letting me fully focus on this one task.  Also has an incredible sound track.

Dying Light is one of the best games I've played and by far the best game within the last year. This isn't just "another zombie game", this is a very unique game in itself and definitely THE best zombie game. The parkour/running mechanics are fast and fluid and the combat is fun and can get intense. The crafting system is fun and there are plenty of varieties to to choose from.
The game puts you on edge when it starts nearing dusk, and when the sun goes down is when the game gets really scary and ups the ante. At night time, this game is one of the only games where I genuienly am scared and full of anxiety.
As for performance...the game can be demanding the higher the graphical settings are, and favors Nvidia GPU's and features Nvidia's Gameworks technologies such as DoF, HBAO+, etc... The game is actually optimized pretty well and the graphics and environment are beautiful indeed. The game runs silky smooth for me at 2560x1440, all settings maxed with vsync enabled and doesn't drop below 60 fps.
Do yourself a favor and pick up this game and be ready to have a blast. I highly recommend this game
*My setup: i7 3770k @ 4.2 Ghz, 16 GB 1866, 2x EVGA 780 ti SC SLI, SSD*

I love the game and whole-heartedly recommend it. But for my review, it's going to be frank and include the gritty parts which annoyed me and may contain progression spoilers. You can read the positives elsewhere.
Early on in the game, everything you do has an impact to your survival, such as, scavenging for materials, lockpicking chests for weapons, cash and vendor items, however, like Dead Island, later on there is no point in doing so.
My reasons for saying this is because I am on the second map, at about 80% complete and have amassed 200+ of every crafting material, I have $500,000 and nothing to spend it on, all weapons looted after vendors start selling orange items are worthless, and when you reach maximum survivor rank, airdrops aren't worth your time either. I achieved all this by approximately 65% completion.
Mods and materials are so abundant, that there's no real survival element to the game. The only part which can be considered so, is the weapon durability and permanent loss when it finally breaks. However, a fully upgraded orange weapon (3 King mods) will last you so long, that you will only need to find/buy a new one every 30% of the story. That, and with the perk that gives the possibility of a free repair (it's given me 4 free repairs on my current weapon, with 3 repairs remaining), I haven't had to replace the weapon since the previous map. But that could be attributed to picking my fights, rather than mindlessly slaughtering zombies.
Vendors also have this annoying trait of advertising weapons for higher survivor ranks, which you cannot purchase until you reach that level, and then rejigging their inventory when you level up. Then advertising even higher level weapons, thus rendering having them in their shop inventory 'effing pointless. "Look at this lovely orange katana. Want it?... Tough.". Also regarding weapon purchases, the docket system they employed as part of pre-purchase, is a complete waste of time. From survivor rank 1 to 25, not one of my 16 dockets gave me a weapon that wasn't instantly vendored, because it was less than total trash.
Most of the blueprints in the game are useless. I have around 20 of them, but have only used 3 types. "Puke 'N Nuke", "Toxic Reaper" and "Bolter Poison". Puke 'N Nuke is terrible, as more often than not, it makes the zombies explode, attracting volatiles, which you then have fight off, which makes them explode, attracting more... rinse and repeat. I use bladed weapons, so I hack the zombies heads off in one click, rendering the weapon's elemental effect pointless. They only come in handy for the larger zombies (late game Goons and Demolishers... which I kill in 2 power strikes anyway). Any of the fire or toxic effects will more than likely hurt you as much as it does the zombies, so you're best going for something that adds bleeding, because at least you won't die along with them. I hated this self damage mechanic in Dead Island and I hate it now.
And I don't know about anyone else, but I'm sick of exploding zombies. How does a poppable, fleshy, bloody mess, even hurt a person, let alone kill them in one?. I'd much rather have the explosive effect disorient me, or blind me because I'm covered in gore.
Other than all of the outlined grievances (of which there are more, but my hands hurt from typing) Dying Light is a satisfying zombie Hack 'N Slash, with replayability, especially if you play in coop mode after the single player experience.

Dying Light sets itself as what could have made Dead Island more fun and less hated, developed by Techland, as in the same people that made Dead Island and Dead Island: Riptide, you can already imagine the simillar gameplay and the frequent feeling where you're really just playing an improved version of Dead Island.
Story has you playing as Kyle Crane, a GRE operative who's mission is to find some file or whatever that is being kept by an infamous and cruel psycopath named Rais. In the quarantined city of Haran, which obviously enough is set in some fictional area in the Middle East, a zombie virus is spreading and you need to find the file for whatever unknown reason only to realise that all of this is some big conspiracy to weaponize the virus (Original..?)
Like Dead Island, combat is advanced on a very severe level and the weapon customization is back, altogh not as great as it was in Dead Island. However the game includes First Person parkour around the city of Haran and I must say, I found it rather fun once I got the hang it of it. Way better than Mirror's Edge parkouring in my opinion anyway.
Gunplay, of course like in Dead Island also exists in this game, both of which only give the idea of how gunplay is a real asset only when encountering bossess or human enemies. Crafting also makes a return but it can be done just about anywhere unlike Dead Island.
So far no cars added in yet, but they are told to make an appearance in a later update, tho the parkouring of course is an amazing form of transportation so I bearly even mind that.
Enemy types come in very severe veriety.
You got the typical zombie, you know the ones...The infected rusher AKA beserker zombies, The spitters, the giants with concrete hammers, gasmask wearing zombies which are just so joyful to blow up their back gas tank when you get the chance, and of course the charging tankers and more...
The amazing feature about Dying Light is how it sets itself apart from your typical Zombie Survival action game by also having horror elements at the night sections. This is due to the zombies being twice as powerful while also adding almost unkillable zombie types that you WILL run away from if you know what's good for you, thankfully the night sections aren't always forced upon you since they are skippable, or if you're feeling like the daredevil you are you can always play in the night instead...
The missions are just what you'd expect them to be sadly...Fetch quests...Guh, can't have too many of those huh?
Co Op in Dying Light is amazingly fun and is a very good time for you and your friends so I definently think you should play this with a partner.
I managed to run Dying Light on high settings without all of the required specs, and that alone shows that the port is good.
With all that said, I'd give Dying Light a 9/10. Possibly THE best if  not one of the best zombie games I've ever played. And it sets itself apart from your typical L4D or Dead Rising game, it's good, and you should get it if you can buy it.

This game is a good example of why graphics don't make a game good. This game is from a different time, where games weren't really games. There were software limitations at the time. However! Despite it's simplistic look, it is actually a good game. The story is imersive as it describes a geneticly created being and his life cycle. Think of it like the Talos Principle of it's time.
Pros:
-Good story
-Can run on any computer (No points for guessing why)
-The OG Talos Principle
-Immersive
-Fun
Cons: (For any underdeveloped brains wondering... I will be excluding graphics and sound from the cons list as it's like making fun of a kid in a wheelchair).
-Too short :(
-If you close the game... THE WHOLE GAME RESTARTS >:( (To be fair it is like an hour long game).
-No tutorial. Litterally thrown in the deep end.
Overall 8/10 - Would recommend to anyone looking for a short, immersive, singleplayer game from 1984

Hey, I haven't posted a review in awhile (or ever for that matter), so I thought I'd share my experiences with this game because of how much I loved it  (and because I have nothing better way to spend my time on a saturday night). So, I guess I'll start out with the bads and then finish strong with the selling points of the game. One of the "meh" parts of the game is the soundtrack... It doesn't make me feel certain emotions when they're played as well as I'd like, and everything just sounds the same throughout the game, but not really... I'm not sure if that makes sense but whatever. Other minor flaws include annoying sfx that play too often, and the occasional typo in the dialogue. With the bad out of the way, lets talk about the stuff that makes this game SUPER FANTASTICLY AWESOMELY EPIC!!! I LOVE the characters, from their artwork to their dialogue, they all manage to keep me engaged till the very end. The story itself is pretty good too. The plot twist had me so off guard, and the ending is a real tear jerker! The game comes with a few minigames and some (simple) escape puzzles to keep the game feeling fresh until the very end. I don't know how to end one of these reviews so I'll just give a summary of a sort: It's not the perfect game ever, but the characters and story made up for what the game lacks. I highly reccomend this to anyone that is eager to play a new game, with a fantastic story and characters!

This is a difficult review to do as it is hard to think of Deus Ex Machina in gaming terms, moving a cursor around a screen to either avoid or hit things might make you think, “well it's rubbish” and taking it these terms it would be considered rubbish. However, instead I'd rather think of it as a piece of art and what does art do?
Well, art tries to make us think, tries to convey a message to the person observing it. Deus Ex Machina does this through either simple 8bit graphics of the very first iteration or with an enhanced Retina version. In both cases the graphics serve their purpose, which is to give you something to look at, a context if you will and setting the stage for what it has to say. Which brings us then to how Deus Ex Machina does this. It comes from it's soundtrack. The songs reinforce the message the graphics try to depict. It melds sound and form to tell you a story. A story about life, in which (as it is with us all) always has the same end. The “score” you get in it is less important than understanding what it has to say.
So what is it all about? It's about the “game” then of life itself. ;)
And that is all I wrote.....

Before I say anything else, let me start off with a few words: this game is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing.
Now that that's out of the way, let me give you the nitty-gritty.
So, the premise of this game is that a girl wants to be killed and a serial-killer promises to do that after they make it out of this facility.
Now, at first, you might be wondering, "How good of a game could this possibly be with a premise like that?"
My answer to you, would be, "Trust me, it gets good."
At the outset (meaning most of the first episode), it may not seem as great as I make it out to be, but that's because it's not supposed to be like that so early. The main thing that makes this game great is a little thing called character-development. There is so much of it in this game, it's insane. You'd never think an emotionless 13 year old girl and a ruthless murderer would be such great and likeable characters, much less be a good team.
Honestly, the gameplay is secondary to the story besides maybe a few parts, so if you're thinking of playing it for gameplay, you might be disappointed. The story, however, is masterfully written and played out. The script is always entertaining, always brimming with character (though there are a lot of elipses, I must say). Even the non-main characters are interesting, and I say non-main characters because saying they're entirely supporting would be an insult. Every character plays a part in the story in a way. It's set up so that you'll understand some things better towards the end than when you first encounter them.
Oh, and the music is creepy, epic, emotional, or wacky whenever it needs to be, perfectly matching the situation. The art is also very original, not "original" as in disgusting to look at either, I mean original as in very well designed. It's not like there are too many hidden details within the character art, it's just really nice to look at.
This has become one of my favorite stories afrer playing through such a great game, the ending is perfectly suited to the story, that's all I'll say about it.
All in all, this is a great game. I'd even say it was 10/10. I'd definitely recommend if you have $10 to spend and want a masterpiece of a story.

It should go without saying that Mega Man is one of those games that defined the action platformer genre back in the late 80's and early 90's. Though it doesn't seem like I've put many hours into this game here, trust me when I say that I've played and finished every game included in this set (1-6), 7, 9 and 10 (I never got the chance to play 8 unfortunately), and that these games are worth the current price of 15€.
There are extras included in this set, such as art, music and gameplay challenges. And while it does seem all well and good, it does feel like it was rushed a bit. The art isn't really categorized by any other way except which game it belongs to, a lot of the challenges are just small parts of the games put into a section that you have to clear, little things like these. They don't really take away from the experience, but they sort of make it seem like everything was rushed.
There are also some decisions made that I don't really agree with, such as autofire and having the ability to save your game at any point in the game and then being able to load it up pretty much any time you want. First of all, autofire is for wimps! Am I right? ... No? ... Ok, sorry. Second, I'm not entirely comfortable with being able to save and load at will, because you can just come up to a hard part, save, die and then load your game again like nothing happened. It sort of negates the reason why the Mega Man games had lives to begin with. Maybe if you used the saving system after every boss instead of the password system from 2-6, I'd be happy with it. But overall, I can't say that they're bad things to have. If anything, it will probably make more people enjoy the Mega Man series. Besides, they're entirely optional. If you want to play the games without saving or using autofire, you can choose to do so by not even acknowledging that they exist.
In conclusion, it's classic Mega Man with a built in autofire and the option to save and load your game at will, along with gameplay challenges, soundtrack and art. What's not to love?

3) No Resolution Option: Playing in Fullscreen or Full-Window just locks the game to your monitor's resolution, Windowed Mode does allow you to drag the window to resize it, but it would be nice to have an actual resoultion option (would make recording video at the right resolution much easier)

Emotional nostalgia aside, Mega Man is a great series but is this collection worth the price of admission? Short answer,  no.
I live in Canada, and the dollar is♥♥♥♥♥♥right now so this cost me 20 bucks... pretty ridiculous in all honesty considering I've had these games downloaded for almost 20 years now in ROM form and have beaten them multiple times. I've purchased these games multiple times over in digital and hard copy formats over the years and there's really nothing different about this version of the game.
It's essentially an emulator (built from the ground up, so you know that holds some kind of merit /sarcasm) with a fancy front end menu on it. For those who are unfamiliar with "front ends" they were basically just add-ons to emulators that made them look fancy and bogged down your system more than playing the actual game did. For example: Callus, the Capcom arcade emulator had a front end on it that would display the cabinet art instead of just boring old text when you wanted to choose a game to play... that's essentially what this collection is... An emulator with a nice front end on it... nothing more.
The achievements are insanely lacking, 1 achievement per game (beat the game) doesn't matter how you do it, whether you cheat and use save states, do a buster only run, a no death or damage run... whatever, just deliever the final blow to Wily in each game and achievement unlocked... so that's 6 games, with 1 achievement each... what a disappointment. No creativity went in to the making of this collection, and this is cold hard proof.
However there's 24 achievements so where does that leave us with the other 18? Well... the newly tacked on remix / challenge mode. In this mode you run through random areas of each game spliced together or do full boss runs. This means, every single boss from every single game, back to back... like... why? This isn't even fun, or creative it's just boring and dumb... how many times is someone going to play this mode before losing their mind due to frustration?
I'm severely disappointed, it had so much potential and it fell flat, not really sure what the developers were thinking but they don't know these games well enough to put in real achievements based on each game... like how about, not using the #2 Jet Item in Heat Mans stage? Like ever.... meaning you have to do that ridiculously long disappearing block section legit... wow, look at that, 1 solid, fun achievement for MM2.
Even if they only did 4 achievements per game, I would of been satisfied. How about beat MM2 on Difficult mode? Or Beat Wily in MM3 without using the Search Snake? There's a fun one that might actually enlighten some people that there's two ways of beating Gamma in MM3... again, just not very well thought out.
Also MM1 is incredibly dated, it's such a basturd of a game I had no choice but to use save states and pause tricks to complete it... It's just such a lame MM game, obviously the prototype for a truely balanced game like MM2 and onwards.
The controls in the first MM game are also incredibly unresponsive, it doesn't actually start to really shine until MM3 when your gamepad feels like it actually works. Even though they built this engine from the ground up, it fixed nothing... the games are basically just emulated.
It's just unfortunate more MM games weren't added like MM7 and 8.... the biggest gripe I have about this collection is that it starts and ends with the two worst Mega Man games in the entire franchise... MM1 and MM6... so that's kind of a downer. I started playing MM1 and felt, my God this series has come such a long way since this garbage, I almost couldn't bare beating it, but I pushed through....
Knowing that I have to trudge through the boring and lame MM6 for my final game just annoys the hell out of me, the music sucks, the game is boring and obnoxious because the level design is♥♥♥♥♥♥ iI's basically just running through straight hallways until you fight a boss... there's literally nothing fun about MM6 at all... not even the music is good, none of it, it's horrible in comparison to MM1 - MM5.
Either way, this collection starts out tough and ends on a bitter note but all the stuff in between is amazing, so it's kind of like an oreo cookie or something with a sugary filling inside... or you could look at it like two book ends... book ends are just book ends but the literature inbetween them, oh baby.
So in other words, you're paying for MM2, 3, 4 and 5.... and getting forced to play MM1 and MM6... We know no body likes those games... and those that do are in the minority and their opinions don't matter.
I would of rather this collection ended it on MM7 or MM8 in all honesty, the tacked on challenge mode isn't going to do much for me but I'll definitely give it a whirl just to get my crappy medal achievements the dev's are forcing upon me.
All in all, I'd wait for a 50% off sale, it's not worth the cost if you already have these games downloaded.
P.S. The save state system is such trash, emulators actually do it better. You only get 1 slot per game and it takes forever to save your postion, you should of just been able to hotkey save and load buttons to the controller (like the LT and RT - which by the way can't be mapped at all - LOL) I swear these programmers are just chimps looking to get paid.
