Critics of this game list 'problems' like "the world is too big", "there are so many fights" and "cool things happen repeatedly". I shall now refute these complaints, as I believe them to be inaccurate:
First off, as cool as it would be to have every single encounter, event, puzzle and challenge be unique, programmers only have so much time and energy to code things, and re-using little or no code would mean a shorter game with less content. Doesn't mean nothing unique should ever happen, just that it is difficult and impractical to do all the time.
As for 'too many fights' and 'punch through 3-15 gangs of goons' and so forth... should Arkham Knight have been studded with burger-flipping cookery sections, trivia questionnaires, and perhaps an ultra-realistically unmanageable flight simulator? He's Batman! Punching goons is his bread and butter. If you don't want to punch goons, by all means avoid the Arkham series...
Thirdly, the world felt just about the right size to me. A matter of taste, certainly, but there seems to be a good balance here between wanting the world to be big and wanting it to be full of interesting architecture and other features. Sure, it got a little annoying to spend multiple play sessions solely poking around looking for the remaining Riddler trophies, destructibles and such, but the game world looks nice enough that I actually felt like doing it anyway; the rain on Batman's cape glistens nicely, the lighting and buildings are varied, there are a lot of things to do, with varying degrees of challenge... I find it just a bit ungrateful for players to be complaining about a world this well-crafted. Sure, it
have been done even better, just as Da Vinci could have painted the Mona Lisa even better, or the statue of liberty could have been sculpted even better. How about we take a step back, take a breath, actually look at the thing we were about to criticize and chin-strokingly realize that, oh, hey, it's more than good enough when you think about it.
All that said, I do have some personal issues with the game...
One, the controls are still a bit dodgy. For instance, using the new Fear Multi-Takedown ability is... well, largely a matter of "get to vantage point, wait for group of enemies to cluster together, pray to the powers that be that the ability will actually register it can be used and pop up a pretty little button prompt so you can actually activate it before the baddies spot you and shoot you full of holes". In the prized FreeFlow melee combat, there is a disturbing tendency for the inexact targeting (i.e. 'turn camera toward target enemy, press key/click mouse button for the attack you want to use) to select the worst possible target. Example: three enemies approach from the same direction. One has a shield, the other two do not. You turn in that direction and toss a quickfire Batarang at them. It hits the guy with the shield, ending your combo and leaving you vulnerable and annoyed at having lost your momentum when you were clearly pointing more toward the guys with no shields. Another example: You activate a special combo move to disable one enemy. You are pointing directly toward one with a shield, who would be very handy to get out of the way so you can keep hitting less awkward-to-eliminate opponents. Instead, Batman grabs a guy off camera to his right and disables him instead, because he was a few inches closer or something. The shield guy moves up close and bangs you with his shield, ending your combo and ruining your chances of racking up a decent score/experience gain.
Two, it is not the 'final game of the trilogy'. It is the last game in a quadrilogy, unpopular as that word seems to be... Arkham Origins was a prequel, yes, but it also contributed a large number of gameplay elements which make a comeback in Arkham Knight -for instance, Shock Gloves allowing you to attack otherwise invulnerable enemies temporarily in Origins, weapon steal serving the same purpose in Knight. Placing Origins somehow outside of the 'main' series is nonsense, possible hurt feelings about some other developer being called in notwithstanding.
Three, the DLC is fairly underwhelming. The pricier pieces do offer a few hours of fun, but it is worth knowing that the entire set of "Story Packs" can be played through in a single long-ish session. It's not a bad experience, but short. Worse yet, the skin packs and batmobile variants feel very token; the alternative batmobiles, notably, cannot transform... and thus are only really usable in AR racing challenges, as opposed to the batmobile combat sections that feature prominently throughout the main storyline. Granted, resources were probably limited, and a transforming batmobile is probably a great deal more work to create, but again: worth knowing about before making a purchase.
Four, the female characters take a very definite back seat, which is puzzling considering how extensively they've been implemented; Catwoman has more or less the same rich set of moves and takedowns she had in City, and is joined for those who shelled out for a couple of the DLCs by Batgirl and everyone's favorite giggling loony gal, Harley Quinn. Catwoman gets a few brief play sessions in the main story, while the other two get a half hour or so each in their story packs, apart from also being playable in most of the combat and predator AR challenges -basically recreations of various story encounters, some more modified than others, and the occasional new scenario, generally set in recycled main story or story pack DLC locations. It would have been nice to see them each get a bit more screen time, is what I'm getting at... and of course, none of them have half the gadgets Batman does. Well, maybe Batgirl, but only by the grace of copy-pasting Batman's utility belt onto her... and that's still just half.
Five, the AR challenges... As mentioned above, these are one of the few opportunities to play as the female characters (as well as fellas of the supporting/DLC cast), so it would have been nice to see some of the mood-setting features like villain commentary implemented a little more enthusiastically. As it is, it tends to just be the Arkham Knight -if anyone- ranting, minus the most obvious "kill the Batman!" lines... which ends up being rather awkward. I seem to recall Riddler dynamically commenting on the progress of the eternal minions vs. protagonist struggle in Arkham City's counterpart choose-your-hero predator challenges, which worked a lot better. Not to mention those cool special challenges where Joker or Penguin would send lots of goons at you in a big endless arena fight, and then offer commentary as you fought. Considering some of the AR challenges literally appear to be rehashes of those from previous games, I would have liked to see the awesome ones again... no such luck, sadly.
Six, the whole 'investigate the crime scene, reconstruct the events' schtick was done very, very well in Arkham Origins. Here, it's reverted to the same "scan a thing, scan a thing, done" stuff you got in Arkham City.
All in all, I found this to be a prominently enjoyable experience. A bit workmanlike in places, perhaps, but that expression still carries connotations of competence that I think are appropriate. Is it the best in the series? Could be. Is it the worst? ...I'm not sure there needs to be a worst. In fact, does there need to be a best? It's a Batman: Arkham Something-Or-Other game. If that sounds good to you, play it. If you're sick of the series, don't.
...You'd be missing out on a pretty flippin' awesome Batmobile, though. And that's coming from someone who doesn't even like driving games. Oh, and if you still want to glide too (and you should), there are
upgrades to the grapple-booster. Yeah, as a series-ender and general fun-filled thrill ride, I'd say it more than passes muster.

Okay.  This is the sort of game that Valve REALLY needs to have a better rating system for.  Officially I’d give it a neutral or slightly below neutral. Four out of ten so to speak.  But the question is "Do you recommend this game."  The answer is no.  If I had paid full price ($30 at the time) I would have been furious.  Definitely would have been a return.  I paid $3 on a Steam Sale and am satisfied enough to say $3 worked for me.
Truth be told there is a lot of decent stuff in here.  The art work is very good even if the animation is... well the animation is somewhere in between Visual Novel and Harmony Gold if you understand the reference.  Actually, most of the bits in between dungeon crawling (and some during D.C.ing) are very much visual novel style.  The afore mentioned Dungeon Crawling is average.  Similar to the Atelier series.  Combats are good.  Turn based with free movement.  (No grids or anything.)  The leveling system is... I'm on the fence about is.  There seems to be a lot to it but there’s also not a lot of control over it.  Purely leveling gives you stat bonuses that you have no say in.  There is a secondary XP system to raise weapon stats.  You can change out fairies and EQ but there’s mostly stat upgrades in them as far as I have seen.  So that bit COULD be better but could also be way worse.
Buuut then you have to deal with the story and the characters.  Thus far I have seen three main characters that do most of the talking and a half dozen cameos that had not a lot to say.  The acting is... frankly I can't tell if these are amazing actors/actresses doing a stellar job trying to save unsalvageable lines or mediocre actors doing their best with... unsalvageable lines.  So far as the main three characters I have thus far seen...  Frankly, I have never in my life seen a story in any medium go to such great lengths to make me hate every protagonist.    I was truly disappointed to find the lava in the second dungeon was just the edge of the map and not something I could jump into to shut them up.  I THINK this is intended to be comedy.  But it fails on every level.  Then it invents and constructs new levels to fail on.  Then I think they may hire some contractors...
I am, in fact, quitting playing fairly early in the game because I simply cannot face another cut scene.  I think there is a good game in here somewhere.  If only we could change the past and drop every bit of dialog and plot and completely redo the story line.  Okay the actual story isn't that horrific.  It's pretty standard JRPG stuff.  Light and dark deities sealed off after an ancient battle before the dawn of time.  Blah blah.  But, it is conveyed by three people I have no interest in spending any time with… Okay, I have an active desire to avoid them… So the story sort of falls flat.
Short version, if you can put up with the never-ending tirade of motivation to hate the characters and thus the story and, by extension, the world they live in, then the game is not so bad.  My recommendation:  Do not pay full price.
And, to the Devs:  I know you guys worked really hard on this.  Believe it or not you CAN tell.  But somewhere along the line…  *sigh* The review has to reflect the final and whole product.  Better luck next time.  8)

I love their Neptunia series so had high hopes that another turn based RPG from the creators of that would hit similar highs, yet the end product is just boring.
On the plus side the humour found in that other series is present and accounted for. No fourth wall demolishing here but the characters inject plenty of in-universe humour into the story and it was pretty cool to learn more about people. Some scenes and ideas can drag on a bit though, like Fang's abrasiveness to most people he meets.
Unfortunately, the combat that makes up the majority of the experience is just dull. Characters have special attacks, but using them takes away SP you need to either use items or leave the dungeon to restore, which resulted in me saving them for the bosses or healing. Especially due to the amount of enemies you can run across in any given stage. This left just normal attacks, but these are very limited as well. Neptunia's combo system for normal attacks was a lot of fun with the choice available from the start. Here you get one attack per turn until you pump earned WP into adding additional slots. Even when you do have more attacks the tactics come down to figuring out which damage type the enemy is weak to and then using nothing but that on them. No switching between different types during the battle or readjusting combos between fights. There also seems to be an unnecessary split between physical and magic special moves, but since each character is generally more proficient with one over the other it can lead to some moves just never seeing use outside of maybe curiosity.
Then there is the grind. You start off with very little as the game uses two experience systems. The first is the standard XP that grants boosts to stats on level up. The other is WP, which is a resource you can spend to unlock various things of characters. Stuff such as aforementioned attack slots, new specials or boosting stats further. The ability to choose is nice but so much WP is needed to give characters the same amount of options those in other RPGs would have at the same point without a WP system that it can drag earning enough to unlock sufficient options. The big selling point of the game - fairy partners you can assign to characters - ended up being little more than the equivalent of accessories that gain experience from battles too. Not exactly the clever twist on RPG mechanics I was hoping for and just adds another grind to the game.
It's kinda a shame, because when I got to the bosses and felt free to actually go all out with specials and items (especially once I'd used WP to unlock a variety of options) there was an element of fun. They had significant special moves and multiple health bars in most cases so indulging in those hard hitting moves or making use of buff techniques made me feel more involved that mindlessly hitting the normal attack command. I just don't feel like the payoff of those boss battles is worth the grind though all the common monsters on the way.
At this point I feel like I've been pushing on just because it's an IF/CH RPG and not getting anything back out of it.

Xcom: Enemy Unknown
Pros: Turn based strategy, base building, Difficult
Cons: Unforgiving.
Who do they call when the world gets invaded and the military has been swept aside. That right they call you commander!  You are the leader of an elite military unit whose job is to take the fight back to the aliens and protect earth population. You are earths first and last line of defence, if you fail the world will fall to this alien threat.
Great replay value: By for one of the most fun aspects of Xcom is its replay value. Once you beat the game for the first time you unlock more options to change how the game will play out, from randomizing traits of your recruits, to how much money each country will give you or if you find yourself good at xcom then you can turn on iron mode. You get one save so clear your weekend!
Unforgiving: Xcom is by far the most unforgiving game i have ever played. If you make a mistake mid mission you can watch your troopers pay the ultimate price. This is especially sad when its one of your highest ranked soldiers is killed in the field and you have to level up a noobie and pray he lives long enough to become useful. The harsh truth of this game is if you fail to spot something or leave your troopers unsupported they will die, it will hurt and cost you a lot of time and energy training replacements.
Winning: Over all the ability to win the game isn't hard, each mission will set you with challenges and you will have the time when you are grateful that you are able to evac the last few soldiers.
.
Maps/ Gameplay: Make no mistake, this is a turn based strategic thinking game that challenges commanders to think about the small picture, where and how to position troops to give them the best shot and most cover but also keep in mind the goal is to save the earth from invasion. You will have to make sacrifices and decide how to deal with problems and certain situations that arise.
Price: Xcom Enemy Unknown can be yours for only $30, however if you wait for the summer steam sale that is coming im sure it will be significantly cheaper and is a must have for any tactical thinker that has dreams of defeating an alien apocalypse!

You know the top-down, pseudo-strategic gameplay of a lot of free-to-play titles offer these days?  Heroes of Shadow Guard minimizes that to a first-person, claustrophobic dungeon crawler, where the longer you take to navigate literal labyrinths means more encounters to drain your health, mana, and items.
I originally thought to write this off, but came back to it on a whim and now realize how complex this game really is.  I didn’t appreciate it until I invested the time and head knowledge to really understand the gameplay.
Yes, it’s a mobile port.  Who cares?!  It’s very deep for a mobile game and not at all as simple as it looks.  You can play it very simply: apply XP potions, auto-equip better gear, instantly complete unlocked quests, let the computer run your battles for you.  Most daily bonuses take a few minutes of your day and provide many bonuses and rewards.  You can slowly rise your party to sufficient power to a point you just auto-resolve every encounter with ease.
Or, you can go hardcore, nitpicking which Gems to apply 4% bonuses to, max out specific skills, mix and match Pets between party members, swap out Heroes to evenly distribute XP earned.  You can fight tooth and nail wading through enemy players’ mazes, scraping by to maximize rank points.
Completing a labyrinth is often no easy task.  It requires lots of concentration to minimize steps (thus minimizing number of encounters).  I frequently find myself frantically rushing the final chest, one-shotting the boss with a javelin, and completing the maze.  Staying and grinding is a huge risk to your success.
I feel like a lot of balancing is warranted, but it doesn’t bother me a lot.  Just because you have access to the strongest items doesn’t make them viable for low-level players: they’ll drain your Gold sooner or later.  The $3, 100 premium currency daily for a month is a steal, and I’m not complaining; it’s another great reason to log in and check dailies.  The shield (preventing other players from raiding you) is reset every day and after every time you’re raided; probably also needs balance, but I’m still not complaining.
Heroes of Shadow Guard strikes a special mix of casualness and involvement.  The amount of time you spend grinding and customizing labyrinths is a lot longer than you’d think.  The amount of time you spend just checkin’ in for daily rewards is appropriately short.  There’s a world of complexity waiting for proper capitalization.  Ignore the plain visuals: this game has a lot to offer for the low price of “free.”

As I played Pokémon Alpha Sapphire and Omega Ruby, my memories of certain trainers’ one-liners and their Pokémon teams came rushing back from my time with the original Pokémon Sapphire and Ruby in 2002. Experiencing this classic role-playing game again in beautified 3D was truly a nostalgic trip, from the cute friendship-themed plot to the touching end-credits sequence. However, as a remake, it does represent a big missed opportunity to fix several significant balance issues and mechanical problems — the difficulty I had going back after playing the much more modern Pokémon X shows how far Pokémon games have come in 12 years.
For the uninitiated, Ruby and Sapphire were the third installments in the Pokémon RPG series and the best-selling Game Boy Advance games of all time. They follow the tried-and-true Pokémon model of journeying to catch new monsters, challenging eight boss-like Gyms, and eventually fighting the Elite Four trainers and the Champion. Like most other Pokémon games they also put you at odds with a villainous team of Pokémon trainers, in this instance Team Magma for Ruby and Team Aqua for Sapphire, who want to use legendary Pokémon to forever change the region of Hoenn, where the games are set.
Now they’re the first of the earlier games to receive the 3D treatment. Generation III was a big change from the first two for many reasons, most notably the introduction of Abilities (attributes that add advantages to battle, among other things), Natures (which affect how stats develop) and double battles (using two Pokémon at once was unheard of back in the day). Different areas had their own weather patterns, and the region contained varied topography, from a desert to a volcano to sandy beaches.
In 2002 I reveled in the newness and feel of having an untouched world to explore, and that sense of wonder carries over in Omega and Alpha. The scenery is rich, the adorable characters are even more adorable (especially little Wally!), and there’s more to many of the cities than there was before. I walked into Mauville City for the first time while playing Alpha and didn’t even recognize it. In the original games it was comparatively small and boasted only the bike shop and the Game Corner, but now it’s like a smaller Lumiose City from X and Y: full of little shops and tons of NPCs to chat with. I actually got lost in Mauville City more than once, and had a lot of fun rediscovering something I thought I knew well.



















Alpha and Omega also bear some resemblance to X and Y in that certain app-like features — Pokémon Amie, Super Training, the Player Search System — have all been integrated as part of the PokéNav Plus. The interface is overcrowded as a result and really cumbersome, but the online apps are welcome additions (especially Wonder Trade) It’s the new Pokémon search app, the DexNav, that is perhaps the most interesting addition for Poképhiles. Every so often, a wild Pokémon will peek its ears or tail out of the tall grass (or sand or water), and DexNav will alert you to things like the Pokémon’s level, ability, and even rare moves it might have. I found two Poochyena this way: a female with Ice Fang and a male with Poison Fang, two “egg moves” that you can usually only get by carefully breeding. Easy-access breeding material! The app has the potential to help EV trainers as well, since you can see what Pokémon you’ll face before you battle it, and in that regard it provides another alternative to Super Training aside from traditional, less-accessible methods.
There’s also an updated Berry map, first introduced in Gen IV, which is a serious help to anyone who needs Berries for competitive battle... or even Pokéblocks! Remember Pokéblocks? They help your Pokémon up their beauty or cuteness or what have you for Contests, which are of course a part of Alpha and Omega. These Pokémon talent shows have a Japanese pop-idol feel this time, which makes it all seem more modern and updated. Playing as the female trainer, I was literally and figuratively taken under the wing of number-one Contest star Lisia and her Altaria, Ali. Lisia is absolutely adorable, but the best part of Contests for me is undoubtedly the Cosplay Pikachu you receive after winning your first one. Change Pikachu’s outfit according to the five Contest attributes and Pikachu gets a different move! I might just be a super nerd, but it’s the best thing since Surfing Pikachu.
Really, all the tweaks of original Hoenn features are improvements. Unfortunately, there are still a few big flaws that weren’t addressed, and they’re even more noticeable in light of more recent Pokémon RPGs. My least favorite part of every Pokémon game is the unnecessary inclusion of too many hidden moves, commonly referred to as HMs (Hidden Machines), which you must teach to your Pokémon in order to progress through the region and aren’t so easily unlearned. Anything more than Surf and Fly is too much, as far as I’m concerned, and Hoenn is one of the worst HM offenders. Alpha and Omega dropped Flash for a total of seven HMs this time around — and in the late-game you can summon Latias or Latios to fly you places, which means you won’t need a Pokémon in your team with Fly — but compared to X and Y’s five HMs, it’s obvious why the decision was made to pare them back in subsequent games.
Secret Power factors into this too. It isn’t an HM, but it is another move that interacts with the overworld and is necessary for building Super Secret Bases. Maybe I’m just stingy with what moves I teach my Pokémon, but I wish I didn’t need a move at all to check out potential bases during my travels. That aside, having a home base I could decorate in 3D was a lot of fun, and sharing via StreetPass or setting it up for other players to fight through as a mini-Gym are both neat touches.
It’s not a new complaint, but Hoenn is still imbalanced type-wise, heavily favoring water. It’s especially noticeable in Alpha Sapphire, in which Team Aqua (the villains of the piece) use a lot of water types. It feels like there are water Pokémon in nearly every battle, and I have an overleveled Pikachu to show for it. You also have to navigate many bodies of water, since much of the late-game involves the HMs Surf and Dive to get from place to place. Diving was really neat back in 2002 when it was new, but I found it incredibly tedious in Alpha and Omega — an obvious example of how superfluous some HMs are.
The water itself is absolutely gorgeous with the new graphics and details, though. One of my favorite parts of the entire adventure was splashing through puddles that reflected the starry skies at night, and even diving was made better by seeing a school of Luvdisc swimming by. Building my Super Secret Base on the rainy Route 119 had an extra-comfy, drinking-tea-on-a-rainy-day feel. Everything in Hoenn, water or not, is either delightfully cute or strikingly beautiful, and I enjoyed seeing the entire region anew — despite the tediousness associated with navigating all that pretty water.
The Verdict
As a 3D remake, Pokémon Alpha Sapphire and Omega Ruby do a fantastic job of reintroducing Hoenn. Little details, like characters turning their heads to look as you pass or flocks of Wingulls flying overhead, make the region really come to life, and small updates and tweaks help make the journey smoother. Out of the Park Baseball 18 is just as complex and in-depth as it's predecessor, maybe even moreso. Jumping in as a relative newbie to baseball, but relatively well-versed in sports management games (Football Manager, Eastside Hockey Manager etc), I found OOTP tough early on. There's very little hand-holding, but both the developers and fans have put out a plethora of great tutorial-type videos, explaining what is going on and how to make sense of it. Once it clicks, OOTP 18 is as extremely addictive as 17. (I should probably point out that most of my hours are offline.)
The breadth of gameplay options - slowly working through seasons as a manager, or burning through one in roughly an hour wheeling and dealing your way to a World Series as a GM - is complemented by the scale of clubs to manage and leagues to work in: fictional, present day and past. As a Football Manager player, the latter of these interested me especially. Being able to do-over certain seasons with past players can be great fun. Similarly, the game is extremely freeing: if you want to simply build a team of All-Stars and see how they fare, you can prise players away from teams through options like Commissioner mode. If you want a stiff challenge where you can't 'cheat' the AI in trading, there's the new Challenge Mode. However you want to play, OOTP tries to cover it, and the attention to detail is absolutely staggering.
Though not as flashy as big-budget sims like FM, Out of the Park's 3D visuals and FaceGen is nice enough. 18 is perhaps not worth it if you are an owner of 17, or not into baseball: unlike other sports sims I've played with only a passing interest in the sport and enjoyed, OOTP needs a level of interest in baseball to really be fun. Otherwise, OOTP is the most complete, detailied and freeing sports sim I have ever played.

Stilton, Pear and Walnut bread
(Makes one small loaf)
Ingredients:
500g Strong White Bread Flour
10g Salt
7g satchet instant yeast
20g Unsalted Butter, diced and softened
320ml water
200g Stilton Cheese
100g Walnut Peices
1 pear, peeled, cored and diced
1. Tip the flour into a large bowl. Add the salt to one side, yeast into the other. Add the butter and 3/4ths of the water, then turn the mixture with the fingers of one hand. Add the remaining water a little at a time, continuing to mix untill all the flour is taken in and the dough is soft and sticky; you may not need all the water.
2. Coat the work surface with a little oil to prevent the dough sticking. Turn out the dough and knead for at least 5 mins, until smooth and no longer sticky. Lightly oil a bowl, return the dough to it, and cover with cling film. Put in fride for an hour, so it has doubled in size.
3. Line a baking tray with grease-proof paper. Scrape the dough out of the bowl and fold it inwards again and again until all the air is knocked out and it is smooth. Add the stilton, walnut and pear peices to the dough and work them in well.
4. Shape the dough into a rectangle 30 cm long, roll it up into a sausage, then flatten it out again and roll it up a bit tighter this time. Tuck the edges under and neaten the loaf by rolling the edges to taper them slightly. Put the dogh on the baking tray with greaseproof paperwith the join underneath. Place the tray in a plastic bag and leave to prove for about 40 mins, until the loaf has doubled in size. Heat the oven too 200C, or Gas 6.
5. Just before baking, gently rub flour over the loaf, then make deep diagonal cuts alo9ng the top, first in one direction, then the other, to make a criss-cross pattern. Bake for about 30 mins, until well-risen and golden brown. Cool on a wire rack.

One of the rare treats I ran across in a Humble Bundle.  I bought the bundle for other games and did't play this until a while after.  If I'd known how fun the game is, I'd have bought it at full price long ago.
At the core, it's like Devil May Cry or Bayonetta in 2D, but with a large emphasis on knocking enemies into each other.  As you learn the game and upgrade your skills you start to build crazier combos, which I think gets really fun (I'm up to about 550 hits in a combo).  If you like action/combo oriented games, this is a great game.  I've heard the game be compared to Smash Brothers.  In my opinion, it is not anything like it (and I have competed in and won large tournaments in Melee and Brawl).  It is single player and much more combo-based.  On Smash, when was the last time you got a combo greater than 20 on someone that knew how to play the game?
All of the levels are arena based.  Some may not like this, but I thought it was perect for the game because it keeps the action fast-paced, which is what the game is all about.
A major point of criticism for the game might be it's length.  It only takes 1 - 2 hours to beat the game.  That being said, there is a new game plus mode along with several difficulty settings.  Personally, I beat the game and turned right around and played it most of the way through again in the same sitting (I've now beaten it three times).  Beyond the story mode, there is another mode which runs much longer.  It is a survival mode of sorts that challenges you to go through 99 phases with only occasional saving, which can be a greater challenge than the main story.
Overall, the controls are perfect, the action is intense, the replay value is incredible.  The story and characters are lame, but there is little emphasis on this, so it didn't bother me much.  I thought the music was pretty forgettable.
I know this is not the kind of game everyone will enjoy, but for me as a serious action/brawler game fan, it has landed a place in my "Greats" category.  I will definitely be returning to this game many times over the years.

East Tower Takashi is much better than Akio, and i enjoyed it way more. It felt more natural and balanced drama-humour better than Akio, and i grew to love Takashi as a character. But still, the first two, they're only the beginning.
I fell in love with East Tower during Kuon's story. In my opinion, it's much better written than the first two, and balances out everything surprisingly well, even though plot gets more complicated than in previous games. It completely sucked me in and made me enjoy every second i spent playing.
And then, finally, Kurenai. Now that one is good. I shouldn't be surprised, since there are signs like, you know, order of routes or increasing price, and yet. I still can't believe how Kurenai managed to meet all my expectations and then exceed them.
Kurenai tells you everything you wanted to know and more. It uncovers the whole story, and doesn't leave anybody out. The amount of choices combinations is just stunning, and it took me about half of my play time to hunt everything down. Which is both a good and bad thing (i can now recite some choices order from memory after clicking them repeatedly a couple of times), depending if you like that kind of thing or not. The whole story is actually really interesting and even though some things are predictable i still found myself thinking "but... maybe it's actually not true?". East Tower manages to make you wonder and teases you all the time. I, for one, couldn't resists and beat both Kuon and Kurenai in one sitting.
The best thing in all of the routes is heroine. She isn't your typical shoujo/otoge heroine, oh no, she is a character in her own right and it's impossible to overlook her. I think i loved her the most in Kuon's route - her comments and thoughts were just so relatable! She's absolutely irreplacable and that is a thing many games with female protagonists fail to deliver well.
The other characters are just as good. I guess with Akio and Takashi you just don't spend as much time as you do with Kuon or Kurenai, so naturally they don't feel as developed and complex, but they have their good moments. Kuon is really interesting, and i personally like that sort of character with that sort of plot (avoiding spoilers is so hard!). Same goes for Kurenai, who managed to capture my heart almost instantly. Even the side characters are great and i liked them all.
I know some people make fun of/dislike East Tower's graphics, but i genuinely like them. Although sometimes they look weird/anatomy is wrong, i absolutely love colouring, textures, and how diverse positions/expressions are. I think only in Akio i was frowning at art, but East Tower captures you with its plot and completely overshadows its graphics. It should also be noted that there's a lot of cgs, the winner being Kurenai (117 cgs, although a lot of them are different versions depicting one scene; still, that's impressive!).
The music is also really good, some of the tracks are still stuck in my mind. Music also completes the picture; when i turned it off for a while i felt like something was lacking and playing was less enjoyable.
All the voice actors are good, and i'm so glad we can enjoy japanese voice acting in these games! It feels so right.
So, to sum up my review: East Tower series is really good. I enjoyed every second while playing it and felt it was so worth my money. I recommend it to anyone, whether they like visual novels or not, because East Tower is a good, solid story, that definitely deserves more praise.

Sakuya is a woman wishing to be a man since an incident in her childhood. She makes everything in her power to look like one. Her cousin Daiki works for Dreamworld and needs her help to try a new virtual attraction called West Tower, reserved for women. However, Sakuya managed to convince him to let her try the East Tower, reserved for men. She ends with four other testers, trapped in the virtual world, though she's happy to see that she's a man in it...
This is the same beginning in each Each Tower game. Once in the virtual world, Sakuya will team up with one of the guys. In the first of the series, she's Akio's partner, whose virtual form is a child. East Tower is an attraction that will confront everyone to their own insecurities and fears.
I will go straight the point: this is a visual novel, where you have choices to make. Each stage must be cleared to advance in the story, you don't have any skills or relationships to improve/destroy. However, choices are mattering: you can get a bad ending immediately where you have to begin the stage again (not the entire story), a best friend ending (by scoring A on each stage) and a romance ending (by clearing each stage with a S). If you follow the romance route, you'll end up with an extra chapter. However, some stages don't have a A rank, only a S one - in that case, for the best friend route, it's considered as if it was a A.
Choices are generally made during the challenges proposed for the team. It's much rare to see them outside of them, before or after them. True, without skills or anything to worry, the game is easier than any other visuel novel I've already played (apart Shan Gui, which is more an interactive book), even the first Heileen was more complex and even Blue Rose was more complicated. I don't mind at all this lack of difficulty.
I find very interesting the fact that the guy will be your best friend at the end, as the bad ending isn't a "you're alone", "you're killed", etc.. However, should you choose to pursue him, it means that your character is also evolving and accepting herself more.
Let's speak about Akio. He seems very calm, cold and trusting no one than himself. However, thanks to Sakuya, Akio will reveal the reason of this attitude and will also evolve and be more friendly. It's a very interesting evolution. I really liked being in a team with him. I'm now with Takashi and while it's also interesting, I still prefer Akio, maybe because his voice was soothing.
Indeed, the visual novel has voice acting... in Japanese. I don't understand a thing but as the subtitles are in French (else, they're in English), I could follow the story. The only character not voiced is you. However, I find it really good. It's always fun to hear something in a foreign language, it's reminding me some good memories with some anime.
As for the style, it's really in a manga style, reminding me of The Rose of Versailles or anything directed to girls - because it's clearly stated in the official website that it's a visual novel for them (but everyone is welcome to play it). I loved it, even if Akio seemed a little weird. I also loved the HUD, kinda hi-tech and with a good shade of green.
The music is very good too, very adapted to each scene. I really liked it.
East Tower: Akio is a little good moment I've spent. without having to think too much. It's not the best visual novel out there, I admit that, however, it's still worthy of a purchase.

Its about time a game like Fairy Bloom Freesia has come across my way. Featuring a endearing loli-esque protagonist to dive into the conglomeration of Beat 'em up games available on Steam, you can only infer by the gallery and thumbnail that you are in for a treat. Should the average player overlook a handful of flaws that were evident already by its kawaii demeanor, Freesia will be one to dazzle.
Did the kawaii tag applied to this game grab your attention? Well, that's because this game exudes moe profusely. Character models, particularly Freesia and Plum-chan, are given a very cute essence to them, which will automatically secure a good 60% percent of the weeaboo consumer-base for this game,
. Hell, I'd be damned if I didn't give heed to the fact that even the ♥♥♥♥ing golems have a anomalous charm to them, they're just so small and squishy and- getting ahead of myself here. The playing stages are given a seasonal makeover occasionally as the game progresses, keeping the eyes fed when it starts to get boring. In contrast, the enemies never recieve that same variation other than a color palette swap to accomodate to the background in question. Besides that, the game offers something different than the norm we regularly see here on Steam, so the aesthetic direction is something that is has going for it.
With remote intuition from playing fighters of any kind, you can anticipate a sub-par or at least mediocre story. This is where Fairy Bloom Freesia will most likely meet those expectations. The narrative provided here spans across 25 days as you assume control of Freesia, a fairy-figured dollface as you defend Lita Forest and your Master, the omnipotent Jomon Tree from golems (I think that's what they are) and humans who come to the forest under the pretext of taking away the gem encompassing the life of Jomon with orders of fueling an ultimate weapon...or something of the sort. The story here is presented to the player in a style equivilant to that of a visual novel, which may either lead some astray or captivate fans of the genre, which even then will most likely lead to the former. This is due to the fact that the way visual novels play out have the propensity of stressing the specific quriks of characters that make them different from others, and in this case they just so happen to be vapid and once again uninspired. Going under the preconcieved notion that you have not been living under a rock, chances are you have seen the personalities showcased here before. The zealous protag, the pervert, the calm and composed colleague, the eerie weapon of destruction, etc.. You've been there. But nothing will bewilder players more than that ending, which by the way, leaves a ponderous amount of unanswered questions and opportunites that will never come to fruition unless a sequel is in the works, which I doubt there is one if sufficient research was done. I wasn't expecting much from the Story Mode but it for some reason left quite a bit to be desired.
A rather dense and humdrum story, yes, but that doesn't nullify it's ability to entertain the player, as the gameplay is rich with fun. One can argue that Fairy Bloom Freesia is essentially a button masher, which the game is to some degree, but the game also allows for more intricate styles of play. Learning how to manuever properly is going to be players' utmost priority, as later on in the game it becomes impossible to not die instantly without the right "stepping". With continuous play of the game, Freesia will transform to a one-loli arsenal as you will unlock an impressive variety of stat boosts and special moves for players to sort as they see fit. Some special attacks are harder to use than others, but the time frame between combo hits is broad, and enemies can collide with eachother, so this grants you the power to land sublime combos nonetheless. It is this metamorphosis of Freesia and the 300+ number displayed on the combo counter that will drive players to stetch through any ordeals they might endure as the game is played. Overall, the game is simple to pick up once you get a knack for the fundamentals, which might bring about a discernable blemish in the game. The game is♥♥♥♥♥♥easy for it's majority. The average beat 'em up player can feasibly pass Story Mode on Normal in about 2 hours max, and again on Difficult in another 2 since you are provided the ease of preserving your upgrades when you start another new game. Only when you reach Day 70 on Guardian Mode (Which is in essence a Horde/Wave defense mode) or attempt to conquer the story on Cruel will you truly begin to pull your hairs and bargain with the devil. Shynie in general is also another nightmare of boss, the difficulty spike induced by her is unparalleled. Despite the lack of replayability, Fairy Bloom Freesia succeeded to build a solid brawler experience from the foundation up.
FYI: If you can, it would behoove you to play this game with some sort of gamepad (X360, DS3, a ♥♥♥♥ing Nyko for all I care) because the keyboard contols are a tad-bit awkward. It's also adds convienience, no matter what the glut of PC elitists insist.
To reiterate from the intro paragraph, if you are so good as to pardon the shortcomings that mostly stem from the story itself, be ready to have a great amount of fun. Its $8 dollars and well worth that price tag. Combos and lolis. Like come on. I'm getting tired of typing here. I'd recommend it for sure.

Xcom: Enemy Unknown
Pros: Turn based strategy, base building, Difficult
Cons: Unforgiving.
Who do they call when the world gets invaded and the military has been swept aside. That right they call you commander!  You are the leader of an elite military unit whose job is to take the fight back to the aliens and protect earth population. You are earths first and last line of defence, if you fail the world will fall to this alien threat.
Great replay value: By for one of the most fun aspects of Xcom is its replay value. Once you beat the game for the first time you unlock more options to change how the game will play out, from randomizing traits of your recruits, to how much money each country will give you or if you find yourself good at xcom then you can turn on iron mode. You get one save so clear your weekend!
Unforgiving: Xcom is by far the most unforgiving game i have ever played. If you make a mistake mid mission you can watch your troopers pay the ultimate price. This is especially sad when its one of your highest ranked soldiers is killed in the field and you have to level up a noobie and pray he lives long enough to become useful. The harsh truth of this game is if you fail to spot something or leave your troopers unsupported they will die, it will hurt and cost you a lot of time and energy training replacements.
Winning: Over all the ability to win the game isn't hard, each mission will set you with challenges and you will have the time when you are grateful that you are able to evac the last few soldiers.
.
Maps/ Gameplay: Make no mistake, this is a turn based strategic thinking game that challenges commanders to think about the small picture, where and how to position troops to give them the best shot and most cover but also keep in mind the goal is to save the earth from invasion. You will have to make sacrifices and decide how to deal with problems and certain situations that arise.
Price: Xcom Enemy Unknown can be yours for only $30, however if you wait for the summer steam sale that is coming im sure it will be significantly cheaper and is a must have for any tactical thinker that has dreams of defeating an alien apocalypse!

This game is beautiful.  It has a dramatic soundtrack and solid voice acting.  The base design and combat mechanics are wonderful ... with a few soul-crushing game-killing flaws.
tl;dr, I'm glad this game was gifted to me.  I can't force myself to finish it or buy the expansions.
--The two action points are a grand improvement over the original x-com ... but restricting their use in any way was a mistake.  What if I want to fire first and then move or reload?
--The AI mobs should NOT get a free movement the moment you spot them.
--Why the hell can't I build more than one actual base and/or develop enough teams to respond to more than one terror attack at a time?  You're pitting me against arbitrary mechanics, not my ability to fight aliens.
--All equipment held by an alien explodes if the wielder of that equipment dies ... are you kidding?  You know, you could've just adjusted the economy to account for me picking apart all the stuff the AI's drop and it wouldn't have felt like you were intentionally screwing me here.
-- Why can't I specify what class of trooper I'd like to recruit?  The class system is cool, but it's crippling to have to fight a few battles with a guy only to find out he randomly rolled a class I do not need at the moment and be forced to give him the boot.

How does one begin to make sense of Saints Row IV?  Take a regular sandbox game and add a barrel of ridiculous.  Then add a bucket of laughs and a bottle of♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes.  Within the first half-hour, you get superpowers.  And not ones that you use for a mission and are never used again, either.  Jump halfway up a skyscraper, run the rest of the way up, jump off the top and fly your way across the whole city?  Why bother with traffic?  The side missions, mostly minigames of one sort or another, never feel forced or laborious, nor do they feel like the developers were looking for a way to pad out the game.  A decent plot, delivered with tongue firmly in cheek, which reminds you that games are supposed to be fun, and revels in the stupid kind of fun that just lets you sit back, crack open your beverage of choice, and puts a smile on your face.
So, how does one begin to make sense of Saints Row IV? Maybe it's easier not to.
Don't let the long list of DLC give you pause--it's mostly cosmetic and you won't miss much.  Pick up the Season Pass for the story DLC (one already out, one coming soon) and a new weapon.  Other recommended DLC: GATV Pack (it's got a gun that shoots combat knives, a heavy machine gun, and some costumes) and the Commander-In-Chief pack (Screaming Eagle jet, Uncle Sam costume, and 'Merica weapon--rockets, fireworks, machine gun all in one handy gadget).
Verdict:  A great time and worth every penny, even at its regular price.

The design of this game is laughably bad. The "spotted enemies get a free turn so often they can just move to flank/surround your squad and murder them freely in their turn" rule is enough for it to be shown in a circus to be poked with sticks and laughed at. The classic difficulty is not classic at all, it's just a losing game against rng roulette where aliens get instakill crits from maximum distance while your guize have 40% hit while standing two meters away, because "hardocre yo!".
Due to the above the game can randomly just lose itself for you. Example: one of these mind-numbingly boring VIP search and rescue council missions. I spot the VIP. I have to approach him for him to notice me. I cannot approach him without triggering two thin men spawns (that get a free turn). After I approach him, I cannot move him to a place where he won't be hit with a poisoning attack. After he gets poisoned, he panics. After he panics, he gets one-shot by one of the thin men that literally fall from the sky behind my line in automatic overwatch. Mission failed. 8/10, would rage again.
The tactical battle mechanics have literally nothing to do with classic UFO games bar the "secret organization fights aliens in turns" premise. Even the most basic stuff like being able to shoot whenever and at whatever you want is not there. Instead, the game carbon copies the core mechanics (one move-one attack instead of ap, no free movement, 4 slot "inventory", attacking through skills with "action camera" animations and so on) from the so-called tactical jrpgs. Which is not surprising, considering this is a console game after all.
The strategic layer is more akin to EU, but of course horribly castrated with things like one base, one skyranger, one (scripted) alien base etc., because that's apparently what 20 years of advancements in gaming brings us.

A really atmospheric first-person puzzle game that is well worth the price of admission when on sale.  Antichamber has a minimalist art style and a soundscape of extremely bizarre yet soothing noises and sounds that play while you solve puzzles that involve good amounts of logic as well as occasionally forcing you to think way outside the box.
Though, it's hard to recommend Antichamber on the merits of its puzzles. Most of the puzzles will have you playing around until you finally have that "Aha!" moment, and in that sense it is really quite rewarding. However, there's nothing too difficult even when finding the secret rooms though more than anything it's the experience of Antichamber that makes it worth playing. The rules of physics and reality are thrown out the window as you walk around this strange place reading signs and wondering what the hell is going on or how it's possible that reality seems to warp around you the second you look away.
Give Antichamber a shot if it sells for $5 or less. I can't recommend it at anything above that, but it's an experience well worth the price of admission otherwise!

Out of the Park Baseball 18 is just as complex and in-depth as it's predecessor, maybe even moreso. Jumping in as a relative newbie to baseball, but relatively well-versed in sports management games (Football Manager, Eastside Hockey Manager etc), I found OOTP tough early on. There's very little hand-holding, but both the developers and fans have put out a plethora of great tutorial-type videos, explaining what is going on and how to make sense of it. Once it clicks, OOTP 18 is as extremely addictive as 17. (I should probably point out that most of my hours are offline.)
The breadth of gameplay options - slowly working through seasons as a manager, or burning through one in roughly an hour wheeling and dealing your way to a World Series as a GM - is complemented by the scale of clubs to manage and leagues to work in: fictional, present day and past. As a Football Manager player, the latter of these interested me especially. Being able to do-over certain seasons with past players can be great fun. Similarly, the game is extremely freeing: if you want to simply build a team of All-Stars and see how they fare, you can prise players away from teams through options like Commissioner mode. If you want a stiff challenge where you can't 'cheat' the AI in trading, there's the new Challenge Mode. However you want to play, OOTP tries to cover it, and the attention to detail is absolutely staggering.
Though not as flashy as big-budget sims like FM, Out of the Park's 3D visuals and FaceGen is nice enough. 18 is perhaps not worth it if you are an owner of 17, or not into baseball: unlike other sports sims I've played with only a passing interest in the sport and enjoyed, OOTP needs a level of interest in baseball to really be fun. Otherwise, OOTP is the most complete, detailied and freeing sports sim I have ever played.

I have mixed feeling about this game. On the one hand, I appreciate original concept, on the other there are some issues with it. So basically our female protagonist is taking part in some sort of virtual reality contest. There's an important gender-bender element - she wakes up in a male's body. This is something she clearly wants, not only inside this game, but in general. At the same time she's still interested in other males... But for same reason she's creeped out by the two males dating...? I didn't really understand that part and the logic behind it. Also, although she clearly want to be a man, whenever she find herself interested in her teammate, she's transforming back to girl....? It's another weird thing, because even though this game don't get too much into serious issues, there are few moments that seems to show and critique how judgefull people can be. While in the same time, I feel like the message is: "Well, she may acted like she want to be man herself, but nope, she just need this right man to change her mind". I like the whole explanation that this is: "about person, not about their gender", but still, the "I wanted to be a man, because everyone says girls are weak, but now I just want you" it's just... Meh. It's not something important in terms of gameplay, it's just something that bugged me within the plot and I couldn't get past it.
As for general things:
Pros:
+ writing is pretty good. Nothing spectacular, but there are funny and cute moments.
+ interesting concept
+ interesting protagonist (especially if we compare her to regular female protagonists in VNs)...
Cons:
- ... but as the game progress and I've learn her motives, she seemed more childish than strong
- short, even as for part of a series
- romance is so... out of nowhere, really. The "seduction" scene felt very awkward and rushed
If the other parts are about the same length and quality, I can't imagine it being worth almost 30 euros.
But as for game that I've got as a part of a bundle, it was still rather enjoyable experience, despite all the flaws. Try it if you like visual novels.

The East Tower series is a set of otome visual novels that are different than your standard Japanese otome game. If this review peaks your interest, I would recommend buying the whole bundle as it is cheaper than buying each one individually. And the 4 games together give about 15+ hours of game play.
I was surprised at how much I ended up liking game. I think a lot of that has to do as a Otome game addict I was getting a little burnt out on the mobile games. (When I say burnt out, I think I have played the main story line of more than 80 characters on mobile otome games.) East Tower Akio is the first installment the series. The order which the game is recommended is Akio, Takashi, Kuon then Kurenai. I would recommend this game even to just VN fans (not necessarily otome fans) because it explores interesting themes and has a great overarching plot.
The story is what got me hooked on this game, I love a different story than your more standard otome game that ET has. The Akio story line is just the very start of the whole ET series and made me interested in buying the whole ET series. It is the first building block to the whole ET series. I especially like how this game explores gender related sexuality in a very interesting way. Gender fluidity is something much different to be explored in a VN/Otome game, especially for a Japanese market. Sakuya (the MC, name changeable) bends the standard female protagonist role, rebelling against the female stereotype, actually starts the virtual game as a male character.  I think that Akio maybe my favorite character out of all the boys.
The voice acting is very nice for an indie game. I liked some of the unique voices in the game (Daiki specifically). I wouldn't say that there is any blaring miscasts in the voice acting. Of course this being an indie game, there aren't the big shot seiyuus (voice actors) to really make the voice acting really shine.
I was not big on the art style that ET has, but I grew attached to the characters anyway, which is a good sign as the likeability of the character is not just based on the art. I would say the thing that bothers me the most is the roundness of the faces, especially the young versions of the characters. I think of all the VN/Otome games ET has to take the cake on roundness of faces. There are more CGs than I was expecting for an indie game. The backgrounds in ET are interesting, I really like how the game world is portrayed. I would really say that the only (slight) drawback to this game is the art style, but it is still nice in its own way.

How does one begin to make sense of Saints Row IV?  Take a regular sandbox game and add a barrel of ridiculous.  Then add a bucket of laughs and a bottle of♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes.  Within the first half-hour, you get superpowers.  And not ones that you use for a mission and are never used again, either.  Jump halfway up a skyscraper, run the rest of the way up, jump off the top and fly your way across the whole city?  Why bother with traffic?  The side missions, mostly minigames of one sort or another, never feel forced or laborious, nor do they feel like the developers were looking for a way to pad out the game.  A decent plot, delivered with tongue firmly in cheek, which reminds you that games are supposed to be fun, and revels in the stupid kind of fun that just lets you sit back, crack open your beverage of choice, and puts a smile on your face.
So, how does one begin to make sense of Saints Row IV? Maybe it's easier not to.
Don't let the long list of DLC give you pause--it's mostly cosmetic and you won't miss much.  Pick up the Season Pass for the story DLC (one already out, one coming soon) and a new weapon.  Other recommended DLC: GATV Pack (it's got a gun that shoots combat knives, a heavy machine gun, and some costumes) and the Commander-In-Chief pack (Screaming Eagle jet, Uncle Sam costume, and 'Merica weapon--rockets, fireworks, machine gun all in one handy gadget).
Verdict:  A great time and worth every penny, even at its regular price.

The design of this game is laughably bad. The "spotted enemies get a free turn so often they can just move to flank/surround your squad and murder them freely in their turn" rule is enough for it to be shown in a circus to be poked with sticks and laughed at. The classic difficulty is not classic at all, it's just a losing game against rng roulette where aliens get instakill crits from maximum distance while your guize have 40% hit while standing two meters away, because "hardocre yo!".
Due to the above the game can randomly just lose itself for you. Example: one of these mind-numbingly boring VIP search and rescue council missions. I spot the VIP. I have to approach him for him to notice me. I cannot approach him without triggering two thin men spawns (that get a free turn). After I approach him, I cannot move him to a place where he won't be hit with a poisoning attack. After he gets poisoned, he panics. After he panics, he gets one-shot by one of the thin men that literally fall from the sky behind my line in automatic overwatch. Mission failed. 8/10, would rage again.
The tactical battle mechanics have literally nothing to do with classic UFO games bar the "secret organization fights aliens in turns" premise. Even the most basic stuff like being able to shoot whenever and at whatever you want is not there. Instead, the game carbon copies the core mechanics (one move-one attack instead of ap, no free movement, 4 slot "inventory", attacking through skills with "action camera" animations and so on) from the so-called tactical jrpgs. I love the Saints Row series, I've been a fan since the early ones where it was just a step off of a Grand Theft Auto rip-off then blossomed into more of a parody.  As it grew, it got more ridiculous.  This latest one is, far and away, the most over the top and insane of the entire series.  The game is amazing to play coop, but even single player it is a blast.
A wide number of collectibles to run around gathering, a ton of side missions, a great main story, Keith David voicing the VP is also a win.    There is a sore spot for fans of Saints Row 2 as they, once again, fail to get Eliza Dushku back to voice Shaundi.  But you take what you can get.  The new voice actress is still great, just not what older fans got used to as Shaundi.   She did great in three, as well.
You get super powers, you'll do insane games like Genki Bowl telekinesis challenges and super power fights, you'll fight aliens and try to save your friends in a story that rips off the Matrix more than a little bit and parodies a number of popular shows and movies.
I love the series, I'm bias.  But I'd highly recommend it.

Coming back to this game was the best 25$ I've ever spent. Even after 7 years, the nostalgia held up better than I expected while I was reminded of what the Dead Rising series used to be. The zombies, though far sparser than in the sequels, present a much more dangerous and present threat within the environment than they did in DR2 and especially DR3. The pshycopaths are more unique than I ever cared to remember back then, and they kept every single tiny element from the original game(excluding the save slot, Hurrah!), which i find both infuriating and but even more absolutely love("Don't cut me off like that! It's rude!"). This game is for lack of a better description a perfect port, forgiving the frame drops from when you gib multiple zombies with weapons like the sledgehammer. I would highly suggest this to both returning players as well as anyone looking for a solid game with replay value and a linear story that you can just flip the bird and ignore for some good ole slaughter and rescueing to get that level up. It's the best in the entire series in my personal opinion(and im sure many others), and provides a guaranteed 7-8 hours of awesome story, zombie slaughter and if you wanna try and rescue everyone, it can also be one hell of a challenge(Courtesy of the perfectly ported atrocious AI). Buy it and love it.
One other thing of note for fans, the remastered graphics were fantastically done. Not in the sense that the textures were out of this world(they look damn good though), but because for a seasoned fan like me used to more graphically intense games these days, the textures and fps made it feel like the game hadn't aged a day, hell it looked clearly better even. And really, that's all I could really ask for. Well done, Capcom!

A really atmospheric first-person puzzle game that is well worth the price of admission when on sale.  Antichamber has a minimalist art style and a soundscape of extremely bizarre yet soothing noises and sounds that play while you solve puzzles that involve good amounts of logic as well as occasionally forcing you to think way outside the box.
Though, it's hard to recommend Antichamber on the merits of its puzzles. Most of the puzzles will have you playing around until you finally have that "Aha!" moment, and in that sense it is really quite rewarding. However, there's nothing too difficult even when finding the secret rooms though more than anything it's the experience of Antichamber that makes it worth playing. The rules of physics and reality are thrown out the window as you walk around this strange place reading signs and wondering what the hell is going on or how it's possible that reality seems to warp around you the second you look away.
Give Antichamber a shot if it sells for $5 or less. I can't recommend it at anything above that, but it's an experience well worth the price of admission otherwise!

East Tower - Akio redefines visual novels by removing branching storylines and replacing them with a linear story. For example, in a typical level, the first choice you make will decide whether to progress to the next choice or whether you'll have to start the stage again. Get all the romantic scenes and you'll get the big romantic ending at the end of the game.

A short average Visual Novel with an entertaining storyline, the first part of the East Tower series delivers an hour of acceptable immersion as we are introduced to the struggling female protagonist entering a virtual dream world attraction with a group of men, one of which serves as the romance interest for this particular game, competing their way through stages contributing to increasingly contrived feelings and advancing the deeper plot.
The game itself is divided into seven stages of the meta-level game, each of which must be passed during a complete playthrough. Being a practically linear VN, the story only branches extremely lightly with bad choices leading to restarts of each stage, while good choices lead to either S- or A-rank passes, depending on the quality of the choice. These are the only decisions the player makes throughout the game.
Apart from the very superficial first impressions of the characters, the VN does accomplish to use the stage design to gradually form a bond between the protagonists, slowly revealing their pasts and secrets and bringing them closer. With that said, the entire romance part is still dangerously cliché. Thanks to the unusual setting, the overall combination, while definitely not groundbreaking, does manage to deliver some fresh air to the genre, but not in the sense that it would lure in many people that are not positive towards VNs in the first place.
The ending is simplisticly conclusive but does provide a cliffhanger for the next episodes in the series.
As many recent VNs suffer from, both characters and backgrounds are crudely rendered and severely lack dimension. Faces are portrayed awkwardly and it subtracts from the realism in an otherwise fine story. The amount of backgrounds and character expressions is extremely limited and some are repeatedly used in less appropriate settings. This is an example of many recent VN publishers that have started to favour quantity over quality, and is overall reducing the average of the genre.
The main protagonist is supposedly the player's avatar, despite a lot of events in the game seemingly not designed for that. Because of this, her speech is not voiced, while all the male characters' are. I find this to be a very poor choice from the developers as not only could this be interpreted in the wrong way, but it simply destroys the atmosphere when one character is mute while others talk (GTA V anyone?) It makes the game feel incomplete.
The cutscenes are also the trademark of low-budget VNs, a mixture of theme music with clippings from the game's character portraits and with random quotes from the game passing by the screen (as seen in the Steam trailer). In my opinion, if you cannot make a proper intro, you'd be better off not passing off that kind of work as one and just skip it entirely.
On a positive note, the various mood music throughout the game does manage to hit its cues and set the atmosphere as it should.
All achievements in the game are very easy to obtain by the length of two playthroughs, picking S-rank and A-rank choices, respectively (saving at a branching point to obtain the carrot ending). By completing S-ranks you unlock each stage's epilogue which eventually unlocks all the CGs. There is a great 100% in the Community Guides section.
East Tower - Akio manages to deliver a decent, refreshing story covered in the average artwork of mediocricy that is dominating certain mainstream VNs today. It is quite short, and prospective buyers should most likely obtain this in a bundle key or similar for it to be worth it. However, if your mind is tuned for a little trip down VN lane with a drop of feels, then I do believe you can get a good experience out of it.

Fairy Bloom Freesia is a 2d anime beat-em-up style combat game where you
play as Fresia, a fairy of the forest that protects it from invaders.  The game
finds a happy medium between combat and story, and I never felt that the story
took over the game.

The game offers a surprising amount of personalization and customization
of play style, and the interface is sleek and well designed.  The combat has a
simplistic beauty to it with a fast paced style, a multitude of enemies, and
challenging bosses.  The high paced tempo combined with the fancy fighting
combos allows you to feel satisfied  as you battle.  They did a good job of putting
just enough variation in the environment to give a sense of progression, despite
this being a 2d game.
My time in this game was enjoyable;  the controls are a little annoying
at first to adapt to, and the leveling up system makes me feel as if my character
was progressing.  The graphics were simple, but it handles and plays well, and
I never felt that it was wasting my time.  If you like this style of game, it is
an easy recommend.

The story of East Tower: Akio shocked me a bit at first. It is about a girl that likes to dress like a man and act like a man. She is given the opportunity to test a new virtual reality game, in which everything she imagines comes true. And, as anticipated, she chooses to have a male appearance in this game. Because of some hacker, she becomes trapped in this virtual world with other 4 people and she teams up with another boy to find the escape. This is an Otome, so I think we can all imagine where this is going...
I didn't know at first how to feel about this opposite gender orientation but I decided to continue playing and what seemed in the beginning to be a game about transsexuals turned to be Sakuya's story of discovering herself and accepting her gender through love. And this is the only reason for which I decided to give this game an upvote (because I enjoyed the idea of “Love conquers/changes everything”), despite the fact that I didn't like quite a few aspects.
First of all, her love interest is a bit controversial too, he often makes you wonder if he is bisexual or not, since he is attracted to Sakuya despite her male appearance in the game -- all of this culminating in
.
Secondly, the dialogues are a bit childish and nonsensical at times, and there's a whole chapter before the end that did not make any sense at all to me. I tried to find a deeper meaning to it, but I failed miserably.
Thirdly, it is a visual novel so we expect to have only a few backgrounds, but I didn't expect them to be THAT few. Even more so, most of them have a lot of repeating elements.
As gameplay, you are supposed to get through 7 stages of the virtual game. Each of them has a set of 2-3 choices. There are usually two right combinations, one that counts towards the romance ending and the other one that counts for the normal ending. All others result in an immediate ending and you are required to play through the stage again, starting from the beginning. The normal ending seems quite dull and emotionless, while the romance path unlocks an extra steamy scene. The effects of the choices you make while playing aren’t always easily foreseeable according to the ending you are going for, so you have to play through pretty much all of them to see their results.
Akio is the first episode of the 4 which the series consists of; considering how short this visual novel is (a bit over 1h for unlocking both endings and achievements), I think its price (4,99€) is a bit too high for the quality that the game offers.  And considering that you might want to try the other 3 episodes, the price of the full series becomes excruciatingly high.

Killing Floor 2 is the follow up to one of the best Co-op experiences I have ever had. Killing Floor sucked out well over at least 4000 hours of my life since I started playing the original game back when it was just a free mod for Unreal Tournament in 2005. On the first day of playing the somewhat lackluster mod, I knew that this game had the potential for being something truly great. I followed its development over several years up until its Tripwire retail release in 2009. Even after launch the new devs kept adding new content which kept me playing for years to come. I can remember after playing for quite some time (1000+ hours retail), I started hearing rumours of Killing Floor 2's potential existence. At first I was dismayed and saw this only as a bad thing however a part of me was truly interested in its potential.
When the early access version of Killing Floor 2 released on steam I had mixed feelings regarding the title. I praised the fantastic gore system and weaponry however the game still needed major balancing and bug fixing. Time passed and improvements and fixing came through. As the game is now it is definitely one of the finest co-op shooters out there. Wider array of classes over the original, Fun to use weaponry and the gore, Oh man the gore.
To most people games like Killing Floor 2 may seem mundane and repetitive but lets face facts. I am a man with simple tastes. I love my games to be as Brutal/Gory as possible. And Killing Floor 2 delivers that by the bucket load. If you want a game that allows you to massacre zombie like foes with over the top weaponry along with your friends, You have come to the right place...
Final score: 90/100

To me Arkham Knight will always be my personal favourite SP game ever made, their attention to detail, comic references and appeal to traditions have always made me love Rocksteady and the effort they put into their games.
Arkham knight clearly represents Rocksteady's attempt in stepping into the next generation platform, utilizing Nvidia's physX engine, 4K ready support and of course gamepad support from cross platforms. To simplify the review nicely, I have made a list of pro's and cons:
Pro's:
• Awesome Story; the presence of many DC comic characters such as clayface and Hush just make the gameplay so much more enjoyable. Comic readers don't feel as if they are being outshined by movie watchers and the referneces send shivers down the spine (espicially when discovering the Arkham Knight's identity).
• Graphics; They are unique and amazing.
• Showcase; amazing <3 - my favourite part of the game, being any batman from all of his different universes along with many of his batmobiles to go with it.
• The Joker's Absensce; I love the joker and arkham's joker with Matt Hamill (from the DC:AU) is incredible to this day but rocksteady did so well to not over use him.
• Combat; still the simple but brilliant arkham combat with a few more gadgets and moves to make it newer.
Con's:
• Optimization; you guessed it and here it is. I love AK but the optimization is horrific. The system requirements do not match the true specs needed and even with my current rig I still fail to keep a solid 60 frames. The RAM requirement is at least 12GB if you don't want the stutters and even with a juicy rig, as soon as you get in the arkham mobile, good bye frames.
• Map; sure it's gotham but its so compressed and just doesn't feel as expected from a company who smashed their previous games. If the city showed as close attention to detail as the story did then it would be insane.
• Finally, the DLC's. Okay, I love them sure - the stories were all references to the original standalone comics such as the killing joke, but the pricing for indeviduals stories that last about 40 mins tops is a joke. With that too, the batmobiles purchased cannot be used during hte campaign or game plus rendering them pointless and a waste of money.
I do reccomend this game, I've had my fun and still do to the time of this review. Do not let other people fool you into staying away from it - however look into benchmarks with a similar set up to yours as it will be your only regret.
