I can only review this from the standpoint of what it advertises itself to be, and that is as a Japanese visual romance novel especially designed for female interests.
Before I begin with my normal rant I must confess to you that this is my first ever Japanese visual romance novel and hopefully it will also be my last Japanese visual romance novel.
I'm so much in shock after playing this I really don't know where to begin.
Let's start with the artistic style or the lack there of. From the very first chapter nearly right up to the last chapter you will be staring for 1.5 hrs at basically the same stenciled forefront, with the same animated background running on a loop, over and over again. It NEVER changes. Things that should look 3D, look fake even on a 2D scale. The only thing that changes is the characters which fade in and out as you click your way through a hodge podge thrown together romance story.
Now don't get me wrong this is not my first visual novel, i've played through a few and they were all pretty good and entertaining and many cool pictures or backgrounds, but such is not the case here. Though the story mentions things like dream chambers, rooms of treasure, hideous monsters, none of them will look good. In fact even the game 'Biglands a game made by kids' has better and  more interesting art work and that's really saying something.
Now lets look at the story. A girl who wants to be a man is paired together with a man who wants to be a woman in a new attraction at an amusement theme world where participants enter dream chambers and have to go through a series of 7 tests and save the princess in the end. Once inside they find out that there is a hacker controlling the game from within preventing them all to leave. They also realize that this dream chamber serves to make all their darkest desires come true. Hence before you know it, hotel rooms with King Sized beds are popping up everywhere.
The romance side of this story is as cute as a seagull dry reaching a half eaten sardine and the morals that you will learn from this story were no doubt drafted up by a blonde sniffing painted dry salts. The only thing this game has taught me is that it is apparently wrong to prefer meat over curry rice. It is also wrong to aim a rocket launcher at a puppy that snarls at you and more ultimately it is unforgivable to hold a carrot with two hands or kiss someone who looks exactly like you, just to see what happens. This game has made me so sexually confused that I was praying that the amusement park would forget to pay their electricity bill and be turned off, so I could watch everyone suffocate to death in their dream capsules. Alas that did not happen in the LOVE ENDING!!!???
The biggest thing that really gets my frilly knickers knotted up is the price and the sly advertising behind it all. They recommend that you play all characters of the game in a particular order to get the full sense of the story. They recommend Akio - Takashi - Kuon - Kurenshai. What they don't tell you is that only one of them is playable with the price here which is $5.00. There is no way on this planet that this novel is worth $5.00. Plus the further you go the more it costs. Each one progressively gets more expensive and the whole collection will eventually cost you $30.00. I can only gauge the worthiness of that price from what's available in the first episode. To play through the story it will take you 1.5 hrs - 3hrs if you want all achievements. Also the last episode has a R rating in comparison to the PG  rating which is in this first episode.
Instead of buying this I would recommend buying for $5.00 a bag of carrots and hold them in your hands and then go and eat some beef knowing your being really, really naughty...

Hands down one of the GREATEST Zombie Survival games ever made. Period.
Myself like many others got this game back when it was released on the Xbox 360 in 2006. I was TEN years old at the time and I remember the day I got it being amazed at how no other game was like this. Keep in mind there was no zombie games like Left 4 Dead (2007) or Killing Floor (2009) around at the time or any of these other Zombie Games that could potentially compete with it, they all came out afterwards. You ever had that conversation late at night with a friend where it's along the lines of "I wish there was a zombie game where you could run around and survive in an open world and get clothes and guns and do whatever you want"? That was what I was like during the time and then I found this masterpiece. What's funny is that when I first got this game, I never finished it. I always hid in the saferoom or on the rooftop and waited for the helicopter. Browsing on the early days of youtube, early in the morning, watching youtubers play the game. A year later after building up the courage to play it my Xbox broke down, I never got it repaired and that was the last time I played Dead Rising 1. I switched back over to PC Gaming and years on I would search for a Emulator of a sort so I could play it on my PC, never found one. ;(
Then on September 13th 2016, as I was browsing the Store Page I saw this masterpiece featured. Such a good feeling.
Anyway, story time out of the way. I'll list the pro's and cons below!
- Great Story
- Great Characters
- Lots of Replayability, so many different endings, one that leads to further progession of the game ;)
- Manages to capture that comedic effect at certain times which is a great touch to a Zombie game.
- Interesting Psychopaths, all of them are different and require different strategies to beat.
- Best map out of the franchise, I do wish it was a bit bigger but still it is great.
- Interesting Protagonist
- Great Port, surprising since many Developers can't do that right. Feels very smooth and crisp.
- Infinity Mode.
- Wide range of weaponry and clothing.
- Interesting and fun missions.
- Terrible AI, nothing more frustrating than escorting 4+ survivors back to the saferoom only to have them run into walls, bump into each other, stop, fall behind and die.
- Game mechanics are quite clunky at times.
- Rare occasions of crashing (Has happened to me twice, hopefully will be fixed soon)
- No CO-OP, I wish for the 10 Year Anniversary they added it. I mean they have CO-OP for DR2/DR3.
- Hit Detection on Zombies can be annoying at times.
- Otis calling you every single time you're in the middle of doing something important, he doesn't stop calling until you answer either and if you hang up, he'll call back. This disables jump, attack and makes it hard to defend yourself
I rate this game a 9/10, It is truly a masterpiece and EVERY gamer should at least play this. Don't worry about playing the sequels, they are good but will never touch the original. BUY IT.

So, spoiler alert, this review will be positive regarding the game. Dead Rising is one of my favorite zombie games of all time and with the remaster it finally deserves, I was genuinely excited to dive back into this game, so while I may sound like I'm reviewing this game from the perspective of someone who's a die-hard fan of the game, please understand that while I think the game is fantastic, I still know the game is not without its flaws, so without further ado, lets get started.
It's been approximately 10 years since the original Dead Rising debuted on Xbox 360 and it still reigns supreme as one of my favorite, if not favorite, zombie game of all time, despite it's problems with various aspects of the game itself regarding AI and time management. However, despite its flaws, I still consider Dead Rising to be my favorite zombie game of all time, so just a heads up in case you haven't figured it out yet, this will be a positive review on the game, so yeah.
So what is Dead Rising?
Dead Rising, as I have said already, is a zombie "sandbox" game released as a console exclusive for the Xbox 360 in 2006 and became one of the first games that really tested the power of the console itself with the amount of zombies the game could render on screen. As freelance photojournalist Frank West, you are tipped off about a potential story taking place in the small town of Willamette, Colorado and find yourself in a fight for survival and a fight to uncover the truth behind the events taking place. With 72 hours to uncover the story and an endless amount of zombies around you, you have to use your wits and your resourcefulness in order to survive.
Story:
While the story of Dead Rising is nothing really special or memorable, the game's story does take itself semi-seriously even though it's a zombie game. With a story that is interesting and clear, although the theme's and messages of the story are pretty much black and white, it's still a good and followable story.
Gameplay:
Dead Rising's gameplay is broken up into 3 aspects: Zombies, survivors, and camera work. Being a zombie game, you of course need to have a means of defending yourself, and as advertised immensly in the game's marketing, anything and everything is a weapon. Set in an open shopping mall, you have access to a variety of weapons ranging from the standards such as guns, knifes, and home hardware, to the more oddball such as teddy bears, boomerangs, and gems. In addition to the insane amount of weapons, you also have access to a variety of books scattered around the mall that can increase the efficiency of certain items. Suffice it to say, there's a lot of weapons in the game, but what if you get bored just killing zombies? Well that leads us into the second aspect of the game: Survivors. While wandering through the mall, you will occasionally recieve calls from the safe room regarding the spotting of survivors located in the mall and if you have the time, you can choose to try and save them, and while I want to talk abou the AI of the game, I'M NOT TALKING ABOUT THAT YET, as I will discuss that aspect later. Regardless, the survivors mostly vary in personality, ranging from the physically and emotionally traumatized to the strong and resilient, giving the game a more challenging and realistic approach to them. The last aspect, the camera, is the most underlooked aspect of the game. Being a photojournalist, you can use your camera as a means of capturing the events taking place right before you, and doing so can also give you immense experience for leveling up Frank, but sadly the camera is more than less just an added feature to the game that doesn't really enhance or lessen the experience of the game.
Atmosphere:
If I can appreciate anything in a game is how well it establishes tone and atmosphere, and boy does Dead Rising set a unique setting for itself. Taking place in the Willamette Shopping Mall, the interior design's of each area in the mall all give off an eerie and hopeless feeling that perfectly matches with the feeling of dread and mystery that is present with the story. Areas populated with the sounds of the dead and the cheerful and informative mall PA system to accompany the sounds of said dead all add immensly to the game.
Difficulty/Bugs:
Although I don't find the game to be particularly difficult, going into this game for the first time, you are going to be frustrated. Starting the game you are basically powerless; you have no good attributes, you're slow, don't have much inventory space, low on life, essentially you're nothing. However, what point is there to a game that gives you no challenge? Now depending how you play the game it can either be somewhat challenging or a nightmare. Playing the game vanilla, the game is somewhat challenging as there is little to no stress pressed upon you, but playing the game with the intention of saving survivors, you're going to find yourself immensly frustrated, which leads us to the bugs portion of this review. Now as I have said already, most of the difficulty in Dead Rising comes from the bugs and design decisions in the game. With♥♥♥♥♥♥poor survivor AI and a somewhat poorly constructed time system, it's easy to find the game to be overly challenging, but with a little bit of dedication and experience, it can be a rewarding experience. Overall, the game is challenging but not to a point where you can't find enjoyment in the game.
Changes:
Being a remaster, the burning question about what the remaster has done to improve the original comes to mind, and in all honesty the remaster is an excellent improvement on the original game, with the game now rendering at 1080p quality at 60fps, with the original on Xbox 360 rendering at 720p at 30fps. In addition to the improvement in quality, the game also introduces multiple save slots, which if you have played the original, you'll be thankful for. Other than that, the original game still remains intact, and that's the point of remastering a game: to improve the quality of the original.
Overall:
Dead Rising still reigns supreme as my favorite zombie game of all time. Dark, addictive, challenging, replayable, and fun, Dead Rising is a must own for the zombie gamer at heart. The story is a perfect blend of cheese and dread, something that most zombie games don't do nowadays sadly, and the gameplay is challenging and variable. However, the bugs present in the game are very noticeable and can take away and somewhat ruin your experience with the game.
Overall, 8/10

This game is what got me interested in roguelikes.
Every game is a new experience thanks to randomized maps, events, items, and enemies.
Combat is the heart of FTL, and there are a few strategies you might employ. Whether you choose to just focus on destroying enemy ships, or killing their crew to salvage the ships, you have options. There are bombs and missiles which ignore shields, EMP weapons that disable shields, energy weapons effective against both the shields and the hull... You can teleport boarders onto the enemy ship, create hull breaches to suffocate them, set their ship on fire...
Oh, and of course, you have to worry about all the same stuff happening to you! Luckily, you can press the space bar to pause the game at any time and issue orders, making all this chaos manageable!
A crazy game where a little luck is always required, but experience and skill are much more important.

Like a good book, this title deserves to be in everyone's library.

Let me tell you what's wrong with this game.
Think of adventure and RPG games, you are given choices and you have to make decisions. It's rewarding when you see the outcome of your own decision, even it is a scripted scene rather than physics-sandbox games like Kerbal Space Program. At the end, you get the illusion of controlling your own adventure and that's satisfying enough to have fun.
This game, being a visual novel, is already in "lazy programmer's game" category. No physics. No real time mechanics. Just displays images and text, yeah? The only thing it has to do right, is to give you the illusion of you controlling the adventure.
It fails miserably. For example, you are given two choices, and the choices seem to depend on your own personal thoughts (like "which meal you want to eat", meaning there's no clue which one is correct choice) and one of those choices always leads to "GAME OVER / BAD ENDING". And worst of all, it makes you play the stupid level all over from the start.
It's so annoying I didn't even want to proceed into further levels after getting a few BAD ENDING screens. The only thing that has been good for me is the foil trading card... so.
Nothing to do here.

This game is fantastic for learning and playing baseball on a managerial level. Personally I have a league for places in Maryland. When the first Killing Floor was released, it was a fantastic survival FPS, one of the best ones at the time, with great visuals, gunplay, progression system, music. A wide variety of maps, weapons and enemies! Now get ready for all of that again, but with huge improvements. It's the same gameplay, but is much more fluid.  The same familiar aesthetics, but visually enchanted. More of the same guns, with better recoil.
For games like this it's hard to find many negative things to discuss. This is a very calculate and linear shooter. You're faced with hordes of monsters and you have to stay alive until the final boss, which Killing Floor 2 now has two. The Patriarch is back, bigger and unglier than ever, along side Dr. Hans Volter who is just as menacing with his exo-suit that can shield him. We might see a third one in the future. So, if you are not familiar with KF, yes, it does get repetitive since there are only three mods in the game so far. Lots of gunning and killing and it would be difficult to say it's not fun as hell. I would say it's one of the greatest stress relieving games you could play. If you have good taste in shooters then I'm pretty sure you will love this.
There are 10 perks to choose from. Each with 10 sets of skills that you can customize. Depending on how you want to help your team, whether you want to the healer, the one with the explosives, the gunslinger, or maybe you prefer full melee. You can do it! But whatever you choose make sure you plan to level up that perk since you will be grinding with it for the next 10+ hours or so.
It's so satisfying to team up with other players and try not to be wiped out by the upcoming zeds and it can get really intense on the harder difficulties, which you should always aim for in order to get the full experience of facing wave after wave as you can slay every single mutant coming your way and building up that experience. The amazing soundtrack only helps to solidify just how badass it feels to unleash havoc on your enemies.
Killing Floor 2 is a damn good game and you should own it if you are a fan of horde survival!

There is something quite quaint about this game. I have sunk a little over 80 hours in this little gem over three years?  Something like that doesnt seem like a lot when look at some of the other users here with 100+. But bear with me. This game has really been the only game I can play the crap outa and still keep on coming back. I start games maybe finish one or two of them and then never come back. This one without friends is fun with friends is even more fun! And as of a patch a few months ago YOU DON'T NEED HAMACHI/VLAN THINGS ANYMORE!!!!!!!!!!!!!! That was my biggest issue with it (but even then opening a quick port was faster than those silly things). Enough flarin up this post. What makes this game great? Great enough to stand the "Test of time"? Well as stated up top by the nifty video and images of the game. It's a rogue like. Oh now hear me out yes Rogue likes are the new mandatory tag. But this one takes the cake in a odd direction? It has the familiar semi changing enviroments, many enemies on screen drops are random (until things are changed with secret additives!) But it adds characters in a pre set manner. As in your first character is a Commando who has four abilities this four abilities only he has and will only have them. You learn to master this character in order to progress through the tough but relativly short game. Other characters are unlocked by playing through multiple times finding secrets and completeting certain tasks. The game has some very fun items some a little weird and somewhat obscure with their funcions but they are found often enough that with a little bit of trial you start to get your groove down. The art OH MAN this team one man/woman army at Hopo games has made some wonderful art for this game (and their other Deadbolt). There is enough detail in these odd interesting creatures to bring them out from the mostly dark and purple layerd levels (fun dangling arms of the Engineer are my favorite). I get the feeling I am rambling here and have honestly lost my train of thought. But all in all this game is great, lots of fun. Recent additions to the game made multiplayer almost seemless( tend to see my friends teleport around the map or kill things while hanging from chains) and super easy to set up. The combat is fast and fun.

"Can't Drive This" is a party-game to give you and your friends a lot of reasons to yell at each other and a reason for that making-it-all-up-again-cold-beverage afterwards.
The objective is simple: One builds a neat driving track, while the other has to drive it (yes, WHILE it is being built) and the driver must (in all Speed-ish style) not drop below a certain speed.
But that'd be way too simple, there is un-simplifying obstacles like windmills you can crash into, trapdoors you can fall down in, pinball bumpers that almost literally bump'n'kick you out of the screen, and many, many more the driver will hate the builder for placing right in front of them.
So, yeah, lots of chaos, lots of fun, lots of yelling :-D
Quick rundown of the most important features:
- LOCAL PLAY! While you CAN play online, this features local play, both players on one computer, a.k.a. "Couch CoOp"
- Multiple gamemodes (as of writing this some are still in development)
- Multiple vehicles to chosse from (that also differ in driving behaviour!)
- Customizable track visuals
....and more being constantly added (the game is in Early Access and being updated often at the time of this review).
So, if you need another hit for your next party, try this :-)

An import game with a basic but nice anime coat of paint with a story to pull it along, but it only can pull so much.  The game is as thin as they come with some very bland and ultimately cheap as sin game play where it's one against an ever growing/spawning army of golems and other creatures in an arena that changes graphics but never changes in quality, a floor, a few platforms, and nothing more.  You can add some moves and spells, but ultimately the game is not fun, and more of a mix of being boring and infuriating with the hits you end up unavoidably taking in this fairly small closed area which in particular is magnified in boss fights where they can easy break defense and use a few support creatures in the area to make the fights unpalatable and infuriating when they're not just boring on some of the others.

The worst part of this game is that a lot of the times when you die, it's not clear why. Was it because I just wasn't fast enough to get past the enemies shooting at me? Or did I jump too soon to clear the gap? (this will happen all to often due to the first person perspective; you simply can't judge where you are properly) Or was I just going in the wrong direction, which the game punishes, not by telling you to turn around, but by killing you. Which make you wonder whether it *is* the wrong direction, or that you just weren't good enough.
The levels seem large and expansive, but are actually incredibly restrictive as there is only one correct route to take. The game tries to highlight this correct route by highlighting things in red, but if you need to press a button it's very easy to overlook, and often the place you're supposed to jump to isn't highlighted, leaving you roaming about the area looking for where you need to be, which breaks the games flow.
If you do find yourself in a section where you know what you're doing and where to go it's a great experience, but such are the flaws I can't recommend it. Play Assassins Creed if you want a fun parkour experience

In most games, if it's difficult to get someplace, it means you're not supposed to go there. The opposite is true in Mirror's edge. You have to jump over rooftops, scale fences, slide down cables, crawl through ventilation shafts etc. You'll run into an occasional fight with the police, but your superior speed and dexterity will usually help you leave unscathed. This means that you can usually outrun them, or knock out and disarm one of them and use the gun against the rest.
The gameplay itself is very casual. You only need a few buttons to do all your actions. The game autosaves often and at the right places. Obstacles that you have to overcome are often highlighted. You can always ask for a hint as to what direction to go next. Health works like in Call of Duty - if you're hurt, just wait a while and it gets better. You cannot get stuck - if you get somewhere, you're always able to either continue from that point or return back.
However, being casual does not mean that this game cannot be stressful sometimes. Often the police are chasing you, so you have to run constantly and make your decisions quickly.
Note that on some graphic cards (e.g. mine), the game's PhysX engine (that is turned on by default) makes the game stutter horribly whenever a glass pane shatters. This is quite a problem if you're being shot at in an office area. However, all that you need to do in this case is to turn PhysX off. Apart from this one bug, the game is well polished and it's very pleasant to play.

This is a fast-paced fighter with an attractive art style and a neat little upgrade system.  As a bonus, there's a small but quite servicable story that keeps you moving through the game.  You can expect your first run-through of the game to take about 90 minutes and to be moderately challenging. After completion, you will unlock harder difficulties and additional modes, which adds playtime.
I sure am a sucker for cute heroines, which was why I was originally drawn to the game.  Your adorable fairy will fight off waves of enemies that drop on screen.  You've got a repitoire of regular attacks to use, and specials that can be obtained and re-mapped in between levels.  Every so often, there's a boss level, or there will be a level that requires you to protect one or more portals that heal you if you're near them, but if destroyed, it's game over.
In terms of fighting, Freesia behaves for the most part exactly as you would want her to.  Attacks are quick and responsive, specials work as advertised, and you feel like you pack a punch, because the right combos will send enemies flying, but if you try to button-mash, you'll be quickly punished.  Special mention goes to the block button, which works perfectly - it's not laggy or glitchy or broken, and actually blocks attacks, unlike similar functions in other games.  My only complaint is with Freesia's horizontal movement speed in both air and on land - it's slightly too slow and results in missed combo oppertunities, difficult jumps in one or two later levels, and difficulty approaching some enemies (some of whom have huge attack ranges).  All in all, though, the combat flows very nicely.
This one's a positive addition to any library - it's solid, enjoyable, cute, and, while ultimately forgettable, will keep you company for a few fun-filled hours.

This game is a wee gem in my opinion.
The game is basically: you choose your surviver from a mysterious spaceship crash where each surviver has it's own skillset. On the planet you figure that as time goes on, your enemies become stronger but so can you. Killing monsters nets xp and gold and that gold you can use to open chests or buy support drones. Clearing an area isn't necessary (but recommended) and the goal is to find the teleporter in each area, proceed to the final area and defeat that which caused the crash of your damn cargo-spaceship (and then fly out into space with whatever is left again).
You can have shorter sessions (especially the first time you play you'll likely die in the first area..) but my personal sessions have lasted longer than a couple of hours (not normal by the way, but playing around with artifacts is just that fun hehe. There is something quite quaint about this game. I have sunk a little over 80 hours in this little gem over three years?  Something like that doesnt seem like a lot when look at some of the other users here with 100+. But bear with me. This game has really been the only game I can play the crap outa and still keep on coming back. I start games maybe finish one or two of them and then never come back. This one without friends is fun with friends is even more fun! And as of a patch a few months ago YOU DON'T NEED HAMACHI/VLAN THINGS ANYMORE!!!!!!!!!!!!!! That was my biggest issue with it (but even then opening a quick port was faster than those silly things). Enough flarin up this post. What makes this game great? Great enough to stand the "Test of time"? Well as stated up top by the nifty video and images of the game. It's a rogue like. Oh now hear me out yes Rogue likes are the new mandatory tag. But this one takes the cake in a odd direction? It has the familiar semi changing enviroments, many enemies on screen drops are random (until things are changed with secret additives!) But it adds characters in a pre set manner. As in your first character is a Commando who has four abilities this four abilities only he has and will only have them. You learn to master this character in order to progress through the tough but relativly short game. Other characters are unlocked by playing through multiple times finding secrets and completeting certain tasks. The game has some very fun items some a little weird and somewhat obscure with their funcions but they are found often enough that with a little bit of trial you start to get your groove down. The art OH MAN this team one man/woman army at Hopo games has made some wonderful art for this game (and their other Deadbolt). There is enough detail in these odd interesting creatures to bring them out from the mostly dark and purple layerd levels (fun dangling arms of the Engineer are my favorite). I get the feeling I am rambling here and have honestly lost my train of thought. But all in all this game is great, lots of fun. Recent additions to the game made multiplayer almost seemless( tend to see my friends teleport around the map or kill things while hanging from chains) and super easy to set up. The combat is fast and fun.

...
I quess I could grumble a bit about the turn-based combat system, it feels a bit too standard, run-of-the-mill, copy-paste..
Several battles became too easy after I found the most optimal way around them, I believe (if my tally is to be believed) that I died the total of 4-times. During the total of.... 15-hours of gameplay that it took me to finish the game, I feel that's a rather positive ratio.
Whilst on the subject of combat, I'm not that impressed by the small amount of input lag I got when using a 360-pad. I've heard that it might have something to do with the game being locked at 30fps, it's a bit annoying when a perfectly timed block decides that it happened a split second too late and this happened way too many times to count.
The Audio-Visual style follows that of the TV-series, characters bob around imitating walking, the original cast does what it does best, everything looks like paper cut-outs.. The works.
The game has a lot of in-jokes and references to the TV-series and those who haven't seen much of the series might feel a bit left-out, but luckily being a keen fan of the series is not reguired.
There are collectables, yay... (HURRRGGGGGHHHH)
There are items to use, the same way as they do in other RPG's..
...
SIGH
...
Do you know how hard it is to find something to grumble about this game?...
You know what? I'l just give up now.. I'm going to Skeeters.

Dead Rising is one of my top 3 favorite games of all time.
It is absolutely a classic, and has aged rather well.
The game's 10 years old, so I can't really say much about it that hasn't been said. I'm still gonna gush over this game though.
For starters- The game is built on MT Framework. It's the same engine behind most of Capcom's games from the gen, and it means this port is beautiful. No discernable problems at all.
Wilamette Mall is cozy. You can decide to just roam around and explore, and while the game penalizes your story progression for it, you can just ignore the scoops. There's alot of nooks and crannies to explore, and while the mall stores themselves are somewhat sparse with what you can actually use, there's still alot of novelty weapons and items.
The story hits that perfect spot between B movie cheese and a legitimately interesting storyline with memorable characters. This entire game is a commentary on consumerism, much like the Romero movie it pretty heavily "borrows" from. There's depth in the characters, surprisingly.
OST is cozy. Mall Music 3 is still amazing.
The difficulty in this game is all over the place, which can be good and bad. You will almost immediately be smacked in the face with a limited save system and a punishing difficulty spike the second your first nighttime switch happens. The missions are all doable though, and you can actually save nearly every survivor in the game in one playthrough (though this is almost impossible without NG+). DR is not really a game you can just jump into and breeze through. The rough survivor AI and some of the ridiclous Psychopath fights are enough to cause rage quits. There is a reason people remember the "WEEELLLLLLLLLLL" meme.
tl;dr - DR is a fantastic game. It has a ridiculous amount of content, high replay value and an atmosphere that you can't really find anywhere else. If you haven't played the original 360 version, pick up this game and enjoy all the magic that MT Framework offers.

UPDATE 2016: My first review was done shortly after the game was released. Now that all of the dust has settled and the game has had numerous updates and DLCs and a GOTY style package with everything, I'd say it is absolutely worth the current retail price of $19.99 USD. I still think there were some valid points in my original review, so I'm going to leave it below. However, I've changed my recommendation from a No to a Yes.
BELOW IS MY ORIGINAL REVIEW:
Is this a fun game? Yes. Is this a game that is worth paying retail for? No. This game was originally supposed to be just an expansion DLC for Saint's Row: The Third. Then someone said, "With all the work we are putting in, we should charge three times as much." And Saint's Row IV was born. Don't get me wrong....the game is quite enjoyable and has a fair amount of content to keep you busy for a while. But it is very clear this game was not meant to be a stand-alone product, and that shows in the details (polish, bugs, etc). Then we get to the DLC....the real issue here. This company has a history of nickel & diming their customers to death with tons of small DLC packs. Pay 3 dollars for new outfits. Pay 2 dollars for a new skin for your guns. Pay 7 bucks for a new set of generic missions that are no different than the already-included missions. Or my personal favorite...pay 10 bucks for a "Season Pass" that, in any other game, would entitle you to ALL the DLC that will be released for the game. Except in this game, it doesn't do that. The name is completely misleading, and entitles you to 2 of the larger DLC packs, one of which has yet to be released. You STILL get nickel & dimed for everything else. Sure, you'll discover this if you read the fine print. But it's this spirit of "Let's milk our customers" that really leaves a bad taste in your mouth when playing games by this company. It isn't anything new, but keep in mind that they are leaving elements of this game out with the intention of getting MORE money from you at a later date. I, for one, will not be purchasing games from this company again. Consumers don't need to encourage this type of parasitic behavior.

Not really the best position on the jRPG market.
First of all, the storyline / characters are TERRIBLE. The main character has absolutely no depth whatsoever, he's a totally cliche "let's save everyone / reluctant hero" type of guy without any backstory and real motivations (half of the game is about the main character wanting to get good food to eat - seriously?). Out of the main cast, probably only Tiara has some real backstory going for her and even that isn't too well fleshed out.
Second of all, all the story is presented in a Visual Novel, "talking heads" style. There are no cutscenes, even ones rendered with the in-game engine, so basically every scene, even the most dramatic / important ones, are just talking heads.
Third of all, the combat is simply repetitive and boring. The locations are totally empty, there's nothing in them besides monsters and the occasional treasure. No story, no setting nothing. Plus, they all look and feel more or less the same. The ratio of fun fights to dreary fights is strongly in favor of the second - especially since there are not that many  monster types and the later variants do not really add a new mechanic - just more firepower.
The leveling system, based on a typical double resource XP (autolevel) / WP (invest in skills) is somewhat fun, but the fact that you need to grind the boring and repetitive fights to get any real number of WP makes it a chore.
Overall, I've had much more fun with the Legends' series, with the Tales' series, hell, even with The Last Remnant and Final Fantasy XIII. If you want quality jRPG entertainment, I'd suggest you start with those.

Refreshing and accessible, FTL provides an addictive and fun, albeit difficult, gaming experience.  What's FTL, exactly, you may ask?  It's basically a rogue-like style game set on a spaceship escaping from an encroaching and relentlessly advancing Rebel fleet.  As you parse your way across each sector of space, you'll have various missions and events to tackle, each of which offers potential rewards as well as pitfalls.  Managing your limited crew, equipment and resources (in the form of scrap materials, weapons, and other goodies) is at the heart of the gameplay and you'll never quite feel like you have enough time to do everything successfully or to upgrade your ship fully.  Adding a bit of frustration to the process is an overly difficult learning curve (at least in Normal mode - there is no Hard mode) but with some careful observation and trial and error, players can gradually learn how to best proceed.  I'd rate this at a 7.5 out of 10 with extra props for the creativity and addictiveness but some negative vibes due to the initial difficulty level.

This is an excellent game, but it's not exactly for everyone if you get my drift.  Though it plays a lot like a First Person Shooter, the object isn't to race through it as quickly as possible and shoot everything in sight; rather, it's appeal lies in the opportunity to explore the world in which you find yourself.  I used to enjoy playing games like Quake, not to blow up monsters, but to try and find all of the secrets and bonuses - this game appeals in the same way.
Another thing to note is that, even though the game is advertised as "breaking all the rules" as far as gameplay expectations are concerned, the key to solving the game's puzzles is to work out that there actually ARE rules (while the map is definitely non-linear, you can still fidn your way around if you remember how places are connected - and certain symbolic features of the game all work the same way).
In short, while Antichamber isn't *truly* a rule-breaker, it *is* a game changer, and a welcome breath of fresh air.  I'd love to see a sequel - if that's possible.

I bought this game not knowing what to expect.  I am a baseball fan, which is obvious, but I've always liked baseball games that were more interactive, e.g., MLB 17 The Show, etc.  If that's solely the kind of baseball game you want, don't buy this game; if you like a regular baseball game and also like the behind the scenes nuances of baseball, like putting a team together, managing free agents, running a draft, and analyzing WAR and BABIP figures, then you should strongly consider buying this game.  The interface does take some time to adapt to, but once you do, you'll already be hooked on the game.  The game presents multiple challenges to overcome, on either the manager or general manager track, and there is nothing quite like putting a team together in the winter and watching it evolve over the season.  You have to manage injuries, slow starts, rising minor league stars, and aging veterans; you have to keep your attendance figures up and your fans happs as you spar with miserly owners, micromanaging GMs, and the public at large.  You do all of these during the course of the full season, and you watch with agony as you go through each game, getting closer and closer to September and (hopefully) October.  While the game's large database does often take too long to load, it remains the sole criticism I have for the game overall.  In short, this is a game that's designed for a particular type of baseball video game fan, but has enough of everything for the average baseball fan.

You know a game's gonna be hard when you're having a helluva time just making it through the Tutorial. Fortunately, Draw Slasher is one game whose novel mechanics you gradually get the hang of, and for a short while thereafter you might even fool yourself into believing you're pretty good at it. Don't get too cocky, though. Get your guard down for more than a second, and this game knows how to hand your♥♥♥♥♥♥back to you, in several more pieces than it started.
Even the so-called "Easy" mode will give you a run for your money, especially if your hand-eye coordination and reflexes are as dodgy as those of the person writing these words. But rest assured: persistence can pay off, and it's in the personal rewards department (y'know, pride an' all that stuff) that Draw Slasher truly pays off. Almost every new enemy requires its own strategies to take 'em down, e.g. attack 'em only from behind, look for the chink in their armour, etc. Learning each of these strategies, then becoming increasingly competent at executing them, is enough to convince even the crappiest of gamers that they can make it one checkpoint further (and maybe, just maybe, get past that pesky boss once and for all).
I've alluded to the mechanics, but have yet to describe them. One of the great "gimmicks" of Draw Slasher is the fact that it began life as a mobile game, and while it shows, it still translates surprisingly well to PC. All of your ninja's nifty moves are executed by moving the mouse whilst holding down the left button, "drawing" the path from where your warrior begins his run-up to where he ends his mighty slashing blow against the foe (which can zig-zag through an enemy and thereby 'cause them multiple blows with a single strike, earning combo bonuses and so forth).
It's both simpler than it sounds, and much, much harder to MASTER than it sounds. Like all clever mobile games, though - Plants vs. Zombies being another excellent example - its success ultimately lies in that very paradox of deceptive simplicity versus actual difficulty.
Oh, and you do get to use the right mouse button occasionally too, but only to summon up special enemy-obliterating "ki" powers, which you earn by killing bucket-loads of baddies. So yes, it's a fairly traditional "arcade" game in many ways, with enough of a twist to make it something fairly fresh and modern in its own right (with all due credit to the influence of Fruit Ninja, which the game itself cheekily acknowledges in one sequence).
Aesthetically, the game is simply gorgeous. Beautiful animations, evocative music, quality sound effects, charmingly quirky voice acting and dialogue - "Stink like dead baboon in here!" - and the kind of chintzy gore which only a haemophiliac couldn't love. And who on Buddha's good earth doesn't like slaughtering hordes of evil Pirate Monkey Zombies? 'Nuff said.
Okay, so it's a tad repetitive. Like many a side-scrolling arcade game before it, new enemies are only unveiled sporadically, though the thoroughly unique bosses are frequent enough to keep even the nimblest of ninjas on their toes.
Not that the bosses themselves don't get "old" quickly when you have to fight them over and over and over again - I'm looking at you, Mr Cannonballs - but at least the game allows you to go back to the beginning of levels while still retaining all the experience you've accrued. So even if that early-ish boss is proving too much for your meagre skillz, you can at least re-confront him with more health and/or stamina than you had the last time (after you grind all the way back to him, of course)!
One major downfall of the game is the fact that the difficulty curve of the levels isn't quite incremental. The fourth boss, for example, is basically an EASIER variation on the second: one throws cannonballs which you have to dodge in real time, while the other merely plants stationary bombs for you to jump over. Quite why anyone would find the latter more challenging than the first, I have no idea. I think I beat bomb-boy on about the second try, while Mr Cannonballs killed me at least twenty times or more.
And no, it wasn't just that I was better at the game by that point, nor that I had higher health and stamina through the leveling-up process. It's simply the fact that I could take my sweet time leaping over the bombs, as opposed to panicking when two or three cannonballs were thrown at me in quick succession. So the level design does, unfortunately, leave a little to be desired.
Draw Slasher is not a long game, but it's also not one I'd recommend to anyone looking for a "casual" or "easy" gaming experience. Sure, it's not Super Meat Boy...but nor is it, well, Fruit Ninja. It's pretty hard, even on Easy level, and has the kind of mechanics which will require patience from the average PC gamer. As much as I enjoyed it, I can't help but feel that it's probably a game better suited to mobile touch-screen technology, as a mouse isn't the most intuitive way to quickly draw a line from one side of the screen to another.
Beyond this, however, it would appear to be a quality port, and there's no denying the game its more-than-fair share of charm. It also has a lot of additional Challenge and Arcade modes to give it some longevity, though how much replayability the Story mode itself has is really up to the tolerance of the individual. Don't come expecting an awful amount of bang for your buck, and you may well be pleasantly surprised.
Verdict: 8/10.

This is a pretty neat, quite unique game based around freerunning. The controls are simple: space to jump/climb/vault, shift to crouch/roll/slide. Levels tend to follow a set recipe; first, you have a fairly casual run where the path is generally straightforward. Then you have a more intense run while being shot at (seriously, these segments are really intense!), interspersed with more puzzling indoor areas where the skill lies in deciphering the route. If you ever get lost, you can press Left-Alt and the game will point you in the right direction, but this is not always helpful as it doesn't show you HOW to get there. It can be frustrating at times when it's not clear where you're supposed to go, or when you have to climb the same drainpipe over and over again because you keep dying, but on the whole the game is fun. It does get quite repetitive, but the combat spices things up a little, allowing you to perform flying kicks and cool slow-motion attacks that disarm opponents. The story isn't hugely gripping and is hard to follow at times, and the music isn't outstanding, but it fits the game well, as do the graphics, which are fairly simple so as not to detract from the gameplay.

While I recommend this game, if it had been more expensive I would have decided not to recommend it because it is pretty flawed. I had fun playing it, because the gameplay itself was quite entertaining but you are mostly fighting the same 4 kinds of monster and the ones that appear the most are the small ones and the tall ones. The flying ones an the big golems appear in some levels, but the big golems don't appear as much. This lack of variety can make the game quite repetitive but once you get the hang of the game, the levels go by pretty quickly.
The boss fights are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t hard. In the second boss fight I did, I may have simply not performed well because I wasn't entirely used to the combat system. The problem is, the human or fairy opponents can still attack you while being attacked while every other enemy and Freesia, can not attack whilst being hit. This puts you at a clear disadvantage because while you are trying to hit the opponent, and often succeeding, they will suddenly kick your♥♥♥♥♥
Fighting the first female boss who shoots projectiles took me a long time to beat since she can just spam projectiles at you the whole time and it gets pretty unfair. Again, she can also still throw projectiles and hit you while being hit herself. There is also a large gap in the difficulty between the regular enemies, and the boss fights as the regular enemies are extremely easy while the boss fights are extremely hard.
On the plus side, the character models for the humans and fairies are quite good and some of the backgrounds are really nice. The arenas seem to get bigger progressively with more platforms to jump on which can help strategically as well.
One thing I didn't like about this game, was the artwork for the sort of Visual Novel style bits (where they tell the story). The artwork looks like the kinds of stuff I drew as a 16 year old and not something I would expect to see in a game of this quality. I think to be honest, the game would have been better without the visual novel sections entirely because the story is not very entertaining and the sprites look pretty bad. Freesia's sprite looks good when compared with the others but could still use improvement.
6/10 - It was satisfying to finish, but overall it isn't one of the best games. When you consider the price though, it is definitely well worth it.

TLDR: The pinnacle of Batman's crusade against crime.

Arkham Knight is a masterpiece in its size, gameplay, and graphics. Even after years past launch, it looks stunning. The cape dynamics while gliding with rain sliding off the cowl particualrily get me everytime. The combat and exploration is improved from previous titles, and I somehow feel even better as the Caped Crusader. It is amazing how the devs have upgraded the controls. I will admit, in some places the writing lies on the weaker side, and the plot can be predictable, but this is often times overshadowed by the numerous easter eggs, cool finds, and villains littered throughout the game.
The game is already 1/3 of its price for a AAA masterpiece, and with sales it is even below the $10 mark. Do yourself a favor and pick up a copy of this game if you're a Batman fan, love fighting games, love graphics, enjoy a nuanced plot, or just want to beat up on some street thugs.

tl;dr It's a neptunia game reskined with stereotypical light novel story. I'm going to spoil it so  people don't bother playing it.
This game has an interesting turn based battle system that lets you customize your combo attacks. It tries to be fresh with the seal unlocking side plot. Other than that, the attractive and colorful character design are the selling point for this game.
Now that we are done with the half decent elements about this game, everything will go downhill. The most glaring aspect that you will notice at the first dungeon is that the control, CG models, map, and battle system are all ripped from Neptunia games.  You can say that it is natural because both games have the same developer, but I would argue that it reflects the effort that are put into this game.
The story is not amazing, it is rather generic and overdone. A boy adventuring with a fairy, and later friends, to save the world. An overdone plot can be done well and subverted but this game done none of them. Now, I am going to move to the characters because, no matter how generic the story is, the characters are the downfall of this game.
The main character is the typical teenage wish fulfillment light novel protagonist. He is lazy and doesn’t want to do anything, but at the same time he is talented and dependable. A bit perverted; therefore hated by girls, but at the same time romantic enough to make them interested in him. So yes, he is everything that the story demands him to be, not relatable and realistic at all. The other cast are as tropey as the main characters, ranging from tsundere girl, chunni girl, genki boy, fan service girl, butler guy, to some random mascot character; because every games need a mascot character. Most of them are just appearing to join the party and throw random jokes mid game. Most of them can be omitted with the only consequence that the game will be boring because there will only be the  main guy, fairy, and tsundere girl.
The plot actually tried to be subversive by introducing time travel; however, none of this opportunity to redo the plot was dedicated for exploring the characters. It is just giving a second chance to the main character to do better, while also making the gameplay longer. Now imagine all the problems that I mentioned warped up perfectly with a Japanese dub that is recorded with a quite low quality mic (yes, the English dub is actually better sounding), I hope you can relate to my claim about how there is not much effort put in this game.
I will not suggest people to buy this game, especially if you are a jaded RPG player.

I didn't really like this game a lot.
It had the good premises of a (maybe too) simple-drawn turn-based JRPG, and it has a lot of customization capacities (at a first glance, but in the end you'll stick to the same 2-3 attack patterns..), but it adds really nothing to a market that already in the '90s was at its finest.
Since Fairy Fencer F it's a new game (2013, PC version 2015) we could expect much many things. The graphics are colorful and light-hearted, but too simple and not in that retro-way à-la Ys that we all love, grown up with games such as Final Fantasy IV, Chrono Trigger, Ys, and the later sagas like Golden Sun.
It's like an in-between an old graphic and a new 3D one, and it fails in both.
The gameplay is way too easy, even if it is highly customizable. Maybe it's -too- customizable, like in upgrading everything.. you end up grinding and using the same things over and over.
Uematsu is not here, and even if everyone praises the voice acting and so on, the soundtrack is really adoidable.. like one of those games during which you prefer to put on some EDM on your old computer.
So, a combination of poor graphics, overgrinding in recycled dungeons and a general lack of depth and length hasn't made me a fan of this series, although I'll give a try to the other Neptunia games for PC.
Overall, easy and repetitive. I'm gonna borrow some lines from an Italian review I read some months ago: "each of the dungeons, no more than ten, is made up by a single corridor in which you can collect one or two items and fight the same enemies; going through these areas is so exceedingly boring that the gameplay becomes pathetic".

The Definition of Antichamber is “Brainteaser”. Antichamber is an indie puzzle game developed by Alexander Bruce
, Antichamber was released 2013 and is an excellent puzzle game that you should get right now.
To my understanding there really isn't a “story”, not in the literal sense. You start the game working your way through puzzle after puzzle trying to get to the exit. There is a strong sense of progression and rewards for completing various puzzles, so in a way that's the story driving you... completing the puzzles and getting to the end.
The controls are very straightforward, and the game explains how to play as you play... Unless you miss one of the hints like I did once I got the yellow gun. I had to wander around the game for hours before returning to the original place I picked up the gun and noticed the tutorial tip.
As you progress through the game you obtain a gun, then upgrade that gun to get a different unique ability that will help you solve new puzzles and sometimes make the old puzzles easier. Just like any good puzzle game, each puzzle is tougher then the last, and often times dynamically different.
This is probably one of the hardest puzzle games I've ever played, Antichamber forces you to think about puzzle games in a whole different way
, and after you've gotten used to thinking a certain way for one puzzle the next requires you to think of a solution a different way.
There were a number of times playing Antichamber I thought “Yeah! I broke that puzzle with my creative solution” only to find out that the game actually
me to figure that solution out the way I did. Expect twisted solutions, creative planning, strategic thinking, and down right mind screwing.
At the time that I'm writing this review, there aren't any achievements
but they could easily be added later with a patch. The game already has many goals and hidden pathways that you can find. Including added difficulty if you're trying to beat the game in a short time.
Antichamber is priced at $19.99, as most people who have consistently read my reviews knows, I like to spend an hour playing a game for every dollar.
So far I've spent 6.3 hours in the game, but it has a high replay value because puzzle games are always easy to come back to play, even after beating them.
All in all, this game is definitely worth it to me, because I've enjoyed the challenges and the puzzles I've figured out on my own.

Antichamber feels like what I imagine Portal would have been if M.C. Escher designed it. The similarities to Portal are obvious: Antichamber is a first-person puzzle-platform game in which a key tool to solving the levels is a kind of gun for manipulating the world. But those similarities are big structural elements, as far as the actual experience of gameplay and the nature of the puzzles Antichamber is unique, and well worth attention in its own right.
Antichamber is very abstract; it essentially omits characters and plot altogether. As a player, you are not even told who you are. Instead, you simply find yourself in a world of stark geometric forms from which you are seeking an escape. The system of interconnected rooms and corridors you find yourself in is essentially one big level, without any marked division into stages. But as you discover solution to various puzzles, and gain new tools, more and more areas will become accessible to you. To help with disorientation you may return at any time to a kind of antechamber which provides a map of your progress and also doubles as the game’s only menu.
All this sounds rather stark, but the real delight of antechamber is its hard-edged surreality. This is where Escher comes into it. Instead of trying, like most 3D games, to give you the impression that you are in a real, physical space, Antichamber revels in the fact that you aren’t. Instead you are in a world where the geometrically impossible is actual: staircases deposit your back where you started, hallways connect to different places depending on how you use them, doors change where they open to when you turn your back. Relatedly, the game eschews realistic-looking textures for vivid monochrome, including a lot of white.
The puzzles also defy expectations. If you’ve played a lot of puzzle games you’ll notice this right away. Unlike many games which tell you what sort of solution you’re looking for and give you a series of puzzles on a common theme, Antichamber leaves you to figure it out for yourself—to wander around and play with the world until you have insight. Some puzzles are of a type players of puzzle platformers will more or less recognize, but others require an entirely different approach, more like lateral thinking. This makes each breakthrough feel like a flash of brilliance. Enigmatic little clues are found on the walls at intervals, some to help you have the needed insight, others just to provide general good advice.
All this to say, Antichamber is a great game for the puzzle aficionado, provided she is somewhat patient. Solving this game was really engaging and satisfying. Even after accomplishing your main objective various rooms will, likely, still have something hidden in them. But, also, Antichamber gives you the fun of simply exploring. The place you find yourself is not conventionally beautiful, but it is fascinating, and much has been included simply to fascinate. Among other things, there are several hidden rooms in antechamber which preserve artifacts from its development, and others where it seems the level designers are simply showing off what they can do with the faux physics of their world. Antichamber provides you with a digital artifact worth simply looking at.
There are a few downsides to this. That you are not restricted to working on a single, clearly delineated problem is both a blessing and a curse. Being dropped into this labyrinth without much direction, unsure where to even start looking for solutions, can seem daunting. There were points in my first play through where I had to just put the game down to come back to later, and others where I spent a lot of time on challenges that turned out not to really advance me (for instance because I’d been trying to access a point which was meant to be easily reachable much later in the game). Also, this would be a poor choice for somebody not already familiar with this sort of videogame. This is a puzzle game for gamers.
But, overall, I’d rate this as one of the very best puzzle platformers I’ve played, in a category with things like Braid and Portal. It is well worth a look.

OOTP Baseball 18 - A Game With Promise
First off I would like to commend Out Of The Park Developments on a great and addicting game, there are not many MLB Liscensed titles out there and the few that do exist today are either exclusive or don't live up to expectations, in my personal opinion.
The Bad:
There really isn't anything hugely bad about this game for me to critique, the game has it's obvious faults but those faults were not advertised in order to make a profit, the game is what it claims to be.
The Good:
Historical Simulation at it's finest, This game lets you go all the way back to the late 19th century and take over your favorite MLB Teams to rewrite history or to create your own teams and leagues.
Franchise Mode is honestly the best thing here, my personal favorite thing to do is create my towns team as a professional independent and create a dynasty, which is much more challenging than I make it out to be.
Game Balance is pretty good, nothing is too hard or too easy, the game has a ton of things to micromanage, however you can always diliberate that to your AI Manager to help you out. I reccomend taking the game slowly at first by using an MLB team to learn the basic principles of how the game works.
The Potential:
Currently this game has 3D stadiums for all the current MLB franchises, and the modding community here has some they have created too. The Dynamic Crowd is a great idea and I feel like if the developers took a little more time with the next game we could potentially move away from the low poly crowd and pawn characters in the actual games. The models and animations don't even need to be that good, I just think that if they existed the game would be that much better.
Final Score:
85/100

Killing Floor 2. Not much to be said about this game although that is not to say it is bad, in fact it is quite the contrary.
A sequal to the first game titled, as you'd expect, Killing Floor, KF2 remains the same concept but with a bunch of extra stuff. Killing Floor 2 is a wave survival game which pits you (solo or with friends) against waves of escaped specimens from a ♥♥♥♥ed up cloning experiment. Refered to simply as "Zeds" your objective is to survive the waves by killing all Zeds. After finishing a wave you will be given a brief moment of respite where you can visit the trading pod to buy new weapons, get some armor and ammo. After surviving all the waves you will face one of two bosses and after killing them you will win the match. Simple concept, surprisingly fun.
The game features 10 perks (classes) with each one being suited to different weapons and they can be leveled up through a simple "as you play and kill♥♥♥♥♥♥with your class' weapons you earn XP" system. The game features an alright amount of weapons although that could be expanded on and there are also a good variety of Zeds to keep you on your toes.
Overall I find this game to be worth grabbing due to it being a good game that you can boot up if you find yourself with nothing to do as the games don't take too long. Plus the game features utterly ♥♥♥♥ing stupid amounts of violence which is what all games should have.

Saints Row IV is, in many ways, Saints Row III with the volume turned up to 11.  The game is faster, the powerups are more powerful, and the silly is ridiculous.  While the humor in SR3 tickeled the 12-year-old part of my brain, there are many truly funny parts in the sequel.
On the downside, much of the environment is just a slight modification of the map from SR3.  On the upside, most of the development effort seems to have gone into creating an interesting, entertaining story with many memorable moments.  A multitude of small touches on top of fairly well-written dialogue shows the team was really invested in making a great product rather than just cranking out a sequel.
Outside of the story,  SR4 is not significantly different from SR3 which is either a good thing or a bad thing depending on how much you enjoyed SR3.
The biggest difference in gameplay comes from the new abilities your character has.  This gives combat a new dimension but in many cases you'll likely just pick your favorite power and use it over and over again.  The downside to the new abilities is that they make cars, planes, and helicopters a pretty uncompelling choice for travel or combat.  On the other hand, the ADD part of your brain will appreciate being able to move quickly from mission to mission rather than playing the "carjack then squeeze between traffic" minigame so prevalant in sandbox games.  However, the Saints Row series has combat that seems geared toward the intoxicated gamer, so dwelling on the particulars seems like missing the point.
While SR4 is definitely a "console port," there are some nice graphic options which help ease the sting of some pretty basic character models and astoundingly low-resolution textures.  Another nod to the PC gaming crowd is flawless and instant transition from from gamepad to keyboard + mouse.  I personally experienced a sound bug that never got patched and the game crashed a few times, but austosave combined with the ability to save at almost any point kept this from spoiling my fun.
While the game is open-ended, the quests drive the action and the action moves quickly.  The game is full of fun and ridiculous things to do, but the well-paced storyline will lead you through thirty or forty hours of gameplay before you even pause to wonder how many brain cells have died as a result of playing this very stupid and entertaining game.

This is the game that would be called a masterpiece, and a prime example used to demonstrate that video games can truly be viewed as art if not for some of its technicalities. The scenery and atmosphere is astonishing, and roaming this world feels like a genuine adventure in physical endurance. Despite some of the flaws noted above, it's a great game even as is, but close to what with more creativity and thought could have been the game of the decade.

There is no escaping the fact that SR 4 is in fact Saints Row the Third with a new paint job, but it just so happens to be one hell of a paint job.  At least 75% of SR 4 comes directly from SRTT, however that little extra bit changes everything, and presents a new and unique experiance.  Though the franchise began as a GTA clone, it has developed into an all out freak show and bares little to no resemblence to it's roots.  From the first moments of gameplay SR 4 takes every chance to push the limit of crazy as hell, and sometimes leaps over it.  Actually it's quite simple to explain what makes SR 4 unique.  You play as the United States of America, who gains super powers, and fights aliens in a simulated world.  It's as simple as that.
Graphically, SR 4 comes off as crisp and animated.  Controls are exact and intuitive, and the gameplay is fluid and nonstop.  However, not everything is sunny and bright.  SR4 wreaks of the fact that it was more of a product of economics then proper game developement.  Much like Saints Row the Third, you find yourself 100%ing the game far sooner then you'd like, with literally nothing to do, other then running around fighting the same enemies over and over.  With games like GTA which easily can keep you busy for 100 hours while constantly finding new things to do, SR 4 is wrapped up pretty solid in around 40 hours, and even some of that is just screwing around.  The lack of mission replay, or activity high scores compound the problem.  Not to say that just being a jackass in SR 4 isn't fun, it's just that even that leads to it's own problem. Finally after years and years of waiting we're able to relive the original zombie slashing mayhem fest on the best platform known to man. For those of you who have played the subsequent Dead Rising games but never played this game I have a word of warning: it has aged some and if you've never played this one before you might not like it based on that alone.
But, on to the good stuff. This is a rather loyal port with few issues so far. The main one was the save data corruption that's already being patched (and I was able to get around by launching steam as an admin). Weapons will be where you remembered and encounters will happen where you know they would. This does also mean that there are some negatives. Once you get that certain weapon that respawns you're pretty much set for the game (you know which one) with most bosses falling to it in a matter of a few hits. You're still planted firmly in place whenever you aim a weapon and the defualt aiming is with the stick you'd use to move (if you use a controller). This can be changed in the controls menu but it's not an obvious option.
Compared to the second game in the series I have to say that this one was definitely harder when I came back to it. The hordes were denser and the survivors like to get stuck on a few zombies only to promptly be swarmed by dozens more. Unfortunately, the only way to get them out is to slice at all the zombies around them and hit them in the process. During the final few side missions for rescuing the survivors this became especially apparent and rather tiresome.
Despite all this, I still found myself enjoying the game and wanting to play it. Running around with a chainsaw is still fun and using the silly weapons here and there is good for a chuckle. The psychopaths are still memorable and a very nice change of pace. The story is still there (though only picks up in the latter half) and now you have five (5!) save slots so you don' get ♥♥♥♥ed hours in by a deadline.
TLDR: If you played this game when it came out and enjoyed it then you'll enjoy it now. If you've never played it before but liked the second then you'll probably like this one, just keep in mind that this game is ten years old and it shows in certain mechanics. However, if you can get past that then it's still a fun game.

Okay, so I gave the remake a good, honest try that extended past the hour of bull hooey on Danny's computer....
I won't bother going over an exhaustive list of the differences between the two games because honestly, the remake is different enough to warrant being its own game *inspired* by the original. The premise is the same, the missions are nice, but I don't think that it's either fair (or possible) for the remake to 'stand up' against the original-- simply put, I don't think that a younger audience would be able to deal with the old interface, graphics, and flat-out-butt-kickin'-nonsense that was XCOM: UFO Defense.
A couple of key notes here:
1) The class base system is nice but almost completely random. You'll find yourself particularly attracted to some, not liking others, and winding up with a mixed bag of both. The game does absolutely nothing to help here, making you purchase rookies like they're going out of style to find the right grab bag of combinations that you want. A mixed squad of the base classes *can* be nice, but only if you play a certain way.
2) This is no longer the nuanced 'laser or plasma' debate: flat out, plasma wins because laser needs to be reloaded. Don't ask, don't tell-- the younger generation is going to miss out on all of that. Maybe even for the best.
3) The tutorial will run you on rails so hard you'll check for scorch marks in your crotch. You have been warned.
4) Stats? What stats? The class base system overrides stats so completely you'll never notice them, randomized or no.
5) The game is trying to tell a story, a sequential story which can be exploited. Unless you're playing the tutorial, in which case, enjoy hell.
6) The game has limited the strategic elements of the game and has narrowed it down to a tactical level. Nice, if you like that kind of game. Far less grand strategy (if you could even say that of the original) because all of your things are in a single base with a well-thought out, fairly streamlined interface.
7) For those of you who want to complain about ammo management: they did it, it's done, it's not bad. You have to reload WAY more often than in the original but it adds a tactical dimension not otherwise noticed (except for those who played small-squad games).
8) For those who want to complain about reaction skill removal: overwatch is a great mechanic and actually makes sense to those who couldn't/didn't/wouldn't do the math from the original. Dumbed-down isn't always stupid, it's functional.
9) For those who want to complain about the interceptions: no person in their right mind played a game that deliberately required them to send up multiple Interceptors who didn't lose before the first year. Yeah, it's not as hardcore as the original, see 8.
10) For those who want to complain about the inability to purchase certain items, *cough*personnel*cough*, etc etc: it makes the plot decisions more interesting.
All in all Firaxis has done a great job re-envisioning XCom. It's fun, it's fast, and it's not even close. 8/10

Well, we can get to that in a minute, but don't you want to ask me some more specific questions first?
Well, the title lies. It's not Antichamber. It's (lots of)Antichamber(s). Lots and lots of antichambers.
It's a game set in a highly linear, and highly surreal maze. In order to proceed through the area, you must solve physical puzzles. Sometimes based on resource management, sometimes based on clue decifering, and sometimes just based on trial and error, the puzzes often prove to be challenging. Ususally when I finish playing Antichamber my brain is sore.
The best word to describe it is unique.
There are plenty of other first person physical puzzle games, such as Portal or the Talos Principle, but this one stands as a completely different game.
The world is very surreal. There are parts where you fall through the floor when you look down. Where a room changes depending on where you're looking from. Where a hallway changes if you walk backwards rather than forwards.
And I love the unpredictability of it. There's no experience like it.
Sure.
To match the surreality of the environment, the graphics are simple, yet abstract. They fall into the same category as the gameplay: unique.
Colors are bold, and the visual contrast between different materials in the game make it easier for one to distinguish key items that are vital in the solving of puzzIes.
They're also high resolution. *oooooooo, high resolutionnnn*
I think you're asking about replay value. If so, I wouldn't say it has a lot of it.
Granted, though, Antichamber is a puzzle game, and as the puzzles can only be solved in one way, there really isn't any point of returning to replay the game. Unless you just freaking love it.
However, it must be remembered that few puzzle games do have very much replay value, due to their linearity.

I've been playing KF2 since early days when game didn't have many weapons, classes and official maps.
Initially the devs were slow but now that this game has been fully released it's very close to perfect! Also, they promised that alpha release buyers will get all the future DLCs for free. So far so good :D
Pros -
1. There are 10 classes to choose from with every class having different skill set.
2. A good community base. You can easily get many servers to play with low pings. However, servers with custom maps are relatively low. Also, some of the custom maps are epic.
3. Hell on Earth mode can be quite challenging even for maxed out players; which is great!
4. A lot of weapons are now available and they have also introduced cross-perk weapons,
5. Versus game mode has been improved but it is still challenging. Low level players will struggle in playing versus as survivors.
6. No overpowered class. Initially, berserker, medic and some perks which increased headshot damage continously were overpowered but now they have been nerfed, which is good. Berserker was very resilient ( and still is, to some extent ) and medic could restore whole armor of players with continous darts ( I've done this! ). However, all of this is now a thing of past.
7. Friendly community people who will help you in-game ( at least in SEA servers ).
8. You will learn/discover new tactics to beat different zeds everytime to play. In crowded servers however, you won't get many opportunities as it is just shoot shoot shoot!
Cons -
1. Some small bugs like display of a random person killing a player who had left the game. It doesn't affect the gameplay though.
2. Some of the in-game objects are not 'climbable'. Like some cars, fences and other things. I got killed many times initially when zeds were chasing me and I couldn't jump on objects. It's like a trump wall surrounding things, but invisible. A more free and easy movement across map would be really helpful.
3. It is very rare but sometimes fleshpounds won't appear till wave 10(on Suicidal/HoE) even though they should appear in the waves before as well. It's only scrakes and scrakes then. This has happened only twice in over 100 gameplays.
The bugs associated are very minute now and I think most of them will be removed as the post development team maintains the game. Overall, a fun and enjoyable game. Highly recommended! ;)

I thought I'd check this game out, assuming it would be a cheap Battlefield spin-off. That's exactly what this game is. It's based mostly on Russian equipment (only 2 Russian helicopters, 2 Russian tanks, and a Russian jeep are usable vehicles), but uses both NATO and Warsaw Pact gear and weapons. Consumables include airstrikes, artillery strikes, usable miniguns, parachutes, medic kits- all of which cost in-game money, but this money is earned, not purchased (which I think is a plus). The graphics are mediocre early 2000's quality, but hey, the game is free, are you really expecting amazing graphics? It has a few glitches, especially when using their vehicles, but they're mostly comical glitches and the game developers have a glitch reporting tool at the start menu; they clearly want to take a proactive stance on any errors. At first I found this game a little boring, but once you learn the complex controls (which can be eased by carrying less consumables) it's actually a very fun game, and the controls really aren't that hard to learn if you just go through the keyboard and see what happens when you press different keys. I really like their first to third person feature: you can toggle between first and third person both in and out of vehicles, making this both a first and third person shooter.
In conclusion, I would recommend this if you aren't picky about graphics, don't mind a few glitches on vehicle maps, and want a fun game that you really can play for free.
