Antichamber is a unique experience that challenges (and sometimes outright defies) conventional gaming logic. The majority of the game is set in a sprawling labyrinth of corridors, which usually don't quite follow the rules of 3-dimensional space. There were segments where I felt I was experiencing the fourth dimension, which was exhilarating and confusing in its own strange way.
Early on, the game establishes its own fairly unique logic; that, combined with its unusual spatial properties, tells you that the game is not quite as mundane as first appearances might indicate. However, once you get used to Antichamber's special brand of reality, many of the puzzles are relatively straightforward (although you will still have to make a few unexpected solutions as you progress).
The minimalist aesthetics make for stark visuals: Most of the game consists of blank monochromatic corridors, contrasted by occasional explosions of extremely saturated colors. There were even a few instances where I had to briefly shield my eyes from the sudden change of scenery. Overall, Antichamber has a minimalistic striking beauty about it, and the bright colors will be a welcome sight after you've been looking at white walls for a while.
DESIGN/TECHNICAL ISSUES
It has some bugs and instability. The game is mostly solid, but you will almost inevitably encounter a few problems as you progress through the game. Fortunately, none of them are permanently game-breaking, and everything goes back to how they should be when the game is restarted.
Crashing the game becomes fairly easy as your abilities progress later in the game; you can even cause a crash just by trying to solve various puzzles.
In addition to instability, several puzzles can be permanently broken until you restart the game. These are probably the most infuriating bugs you can encounter, because it may not be immediately obvious that the game is broken; due to the game's inherently "illogical" puzzles, one might think a particular broken puzzle just requires a different solution to the obvious one. You can waste hours trying to solve it, only to slowly realize that it is, in fact, unsolvable.
Fortunately, all broken puzzle woes are alleviated by a simple game restart, since the game world resets after every exit. It's mildly annoying, but it's better than having a permanently broken game save.
While there is a fast-travel system in place, you'll be spending a lot of time running through corridors to get from point A to point B. This can quickly get boring, since most of the game consists of featureless white surfaces.
You cannot crouch. Well, you can technically make yourself "crouch", but it involves placing cubes in your head until you get squashed into the floor. It is by no means an intuitive method, and it can get downright annoying if it doesn't work as intended (since it's basically a collision exploit, it's not exactly reliable). You might encounter multiple occasions throughout the game where crouching would be useful and perfectly reasonable, but there is no intuitive way to do so.
There is no control rebinding menu. You have to dig into the game's configuration files to change the controls. Doing so is not particularly difficult, but it's not intuitive, and can waste far more time than decent in-game control rebinding.
CONCLUSION
Despite its flaws, Antichamber is a refreshing, mildly psychological puzzle game that manages to not feel pretentious. I recommend it to anyone who likes puzzles, or simply wants a change of pace from most other games.

The Gate is the perfect combination of Card Game and RPG with Fast Forward and Auto-play mechanics.
In The Gate you create a combat deck of 4 cards; each having any of the 4 elements in the game; Earth > Liquid > Fire > Wind which beats earth. The cards are divided into 4 rarities and each can be leveled up to a max Level of 25. Each card can have up to 6 unique skills with only 3 that can be equipped at a time, becoming unlocked as you level them up.
The cards are treated as actual monsters, creatures or disciples as they are called in this game and have Stats like an RPG, Health, Attack/DPS, Defense etc. They can be evolved by combining them with other copies of themselves to become much more powerful.
The game has a huge variety of missions, ranging from regular Boss battles, Raids, PvP arena and battles where you acquire Equipment you can equip to your Disciples to make them stronger. Events are held every week with unique and rare rewards and you get login rewards for consecutive daily visits and remaining online longer.
Sadly; the game has one big downside and that is HOPE.
Hope is what you use to play Missions. Every mission requires a certain amount of Hope to begin; and without Hope you cannot play any missions. You replenish 1 Hope every 5 minutes whether you are online or not, and every 12 hours you get rewarded an additional 40 on top of your base cap.
Sadly again however, the higher level missions require 10 Hope on average to begin; so you end up running out of Hope after a few missions.
Your Hope replenishes to the base max if you Level Up your player level, but this doesn't always happen.
I'd recommend giving the game a try and seeing if it is something you want to invest your time in. I was able to get a good 10 hours out of it before I started running into "NOT ENOUGH HOPE PROBLEMS" because of the cost of higher level missions. This problem becomes worse because of the fact Hope is consumed even if you fail the mission; which will happen at higher level missions.
Hopefully the devs do something about the lack of Hope issue.

This is one of those games that (assuming you like this kind of stuff) you start to enjoy more and more the longer you play. At the start, you've only got one pretty generic character and a handful of items that will randomly spawn for you when you open treasure chests. As you play the game and unlock more achievements, however, you open up a cast of characters that include the bow and arrow-wielding Huntress, the punch-happy robot called "HAN-D", and more. Playing on different types of characters also allows you to unlock more items by completing character-specific achievements. Along with all this, there's a few different artifacts that radically change gameplay rules that can be found on various levels. (For those of you that hate the random items factor, one of these lets you pick which items you're given from chests!)
Each item and monster in this game also has a sort of lore page that you can acquire either from picking up the item for the first time or killing enough monsters to drop a monster log. None of these are particularly long, but some are pretty funny and they're a nice little detail to add to the game. The music is also very well done and the composer responds pretty frequently to comments on his youtube page.
One thing to note is that the levels aren't randomly generated. Each tier of levels picks a level from a specific area, meaning at some point you'll see all the levels the game has to offer. This doesn't bother me, but it might be a deal breaker for some people. Along with that, if you extend your runs through the game past a certain point, you'll have so many weapons firing off particles that the game can slow down and possibly crash on you. If you only do a run or two through the levels before challenging the final boss though, you should be fine.
Anyways, I think this is a great game that I play whenever I need something quick and enjoyable.

What an absolutely brilliant game from start to finish. I have just finished it and I'm honestly stunned at just how good it was, I was expecting it to be good but not this good. Fairy Bloom Freesia is the successor to the original doujin game, Fairy Bloom.
In this Beat 'Em Up game, you take on the role of a young fairy named Freesia, fairy guardian of Lita Forest. You fight monsters by mixing together various attacks and special attacks. There's many possible methods of beating the heads of your opponents ranging from a simple beatdown to throwing them into the ground or you can even play an impromptu game of pinball... using your enemies as the ball.
While the game has a short story, you should be looking at this game for the gameplay.
It's fun.
It's an Action RPG Beat 'Em Up style game where you can learn new skills to demolish hordes of little (and quite a few not-so-little) clay golems with. The game is challenging, but it never gets to the point where you want to rip out your hair in frustration. Experimenting with new combos is a big part of the charm in the game and whether you're playing to get the best combos and do the best you can or simply playing as a passtime, this game will be worth a look.
As a small game, it's quite short in terms of story. But it makes up for that with "Guardian Mode", which is effectively a glorified survival mode. Unlike the story, however, Guardian Mode will test your abilities and will push your skills in this game to the limit as it is quite punishing.
All in all, the game definitely deserves a mention and for a $7.99 price tag is a great way to kill time.

After all said and done, this game is still a pretty good game which is why I gave it a 8/10.

Now for the autistic part: the breakdown of this PC port.
This port has numerous incompatibility issues. Putting anecdotal evidence aside, the discussion forum is literally flooded with topics asking for technical assistance or to complain about the issues on their end. Every other topic is a complaint about a common techincal issue because some people are too dumb to read the stickies. And the tech-support thread that does exist got flooded within the first day.
At first, I thought the game had incompatibilities with the 2014 C++ Redistributable, but I checked the files and saw it utilized the 2012 Redistributable. So that was obviously not the problem. The issue was the driver. If you're on a legacy Nvidja card, be prepared to di
ck around with drivers that are compatible with the game and - at the same time - won't make your card poop out early. For the record, any video card older than the GTX 1000 series is considered "legacy" by the Nbidia - The Way You're Meant To Be Played. So what's the deal? Why do we need to adopt new drivers that could potentially gimp performance in other games but Dead But Not Phallic Rising? Could a Capcom rep care to explain?
The game runs on the MT Framework engine, the most scalable and efficient engine created in the last generation. It could be herald as Capcom's Barry-magnum opus. It was capable of squeezing Marvel 3 down to the Vita, and it was responsible for making DMC4 and Lost Planet 1 the best PC ports Capcom had ever produced. It pretty much made all of Capcom's games run smooth like butter on the PC, barring Tameem may Cry which used a build of the UE3 that was capable of rendering different hues of grey (DM me for the color values if you're interested). So why is it that Dead Rising 1 doesn't run the same as DMC4 and LP1, ports that came out in 2008? I looked at the menu in the graphical buffet, and I was poorly disappointed in the servings. You get the standard, no, barebone, settings for a PC game. The textures cannot be scaled at all; you have to deal with 2006-tier textures that reek of a 3megapixel camera importing its dump to Photoshop or Green Is My Pepper 1.2. At the very least, we can turn motion blur on and off, but I would keep it on since the animations look tramautizing with the blur off. Compare and contrast DR1's graphical settings to the DMC4's graphcial settings. DMC4's original PC port had several different options and went up to extremes with anti-aliasing. If you downloaded the update that supported DX10, you were playing on what was considered next-gen, ala 2010.
The game also has terrible aiming acceleration. It's just really bad, especially when you jerk your mouse around at the highest dpi settings. You could potentially break the game by bending the mesh; its values might have been null.
In addition to that, the game has a lot of mission bugs. Very first side-mission with Kent, I snapped a 4000pp photo of him and the dude wouldn't shut up. Obviously the if statements were coded to be introspective, instead of just werks. What disappointed me was the fact that Capcom half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥this PC port. They had a good track record of producing amazing PC ports since the beginning of last gen; the failures of the original PC ports of RE4 and DMC3 motivated them to git gud. They squandered our good will, and sold it to GoodWill for tax breaks.
Don't listen to that elitest homo known as Totalbizkit, who would say all Japanese games have bad PC ports. That dumb rand doesn't even realize that a majority Japanese games at the arcade run on PC's, and that a lot of developers have to use Winblows PC's for toolkits. In particular, the Sega Lindbergh uses Montavista, an enterprise distro that you have to pay for - similar to Red Hat, but not a Fedora. Biscuit brags about being PCMR, but in reality he's a tech-illit, so he's uses Ubuntu; in that case, he can apt-get f
ucked. Either that, or we can wait for London's new mayor to establish a caliphat so Sharia patrols can throw Totalbiscuit off a roof for being a bundle of twigs.
As of now, I give this port of Dead Rising a 3.2/10 because it still has a lot of problems that need to be fixed in a patch. Honestly, I'm fond of this game. I come from RTSes such as SC2 and WC3, and I've played demos of Civilization games. I was never really fond of turn by turn games because they enabled almost to much vision of the enemy movements and thus it was very predictable. Additionally, you could legitimately see turns ahead in those games due to the simplicity of combat and enemy AI.
I'm proud to say XCOM: Enemy Unknown is entirely different than that. While it is turn based combat, having two "Actions" per turn is something you don't see in many turn-by-turn games, and with that different classes for your units with different actions they can do, and the permanence when a soldier dies all add up to a very strategically intense game.
Some of the naysayers complain the game is to easy. I'm willing to bet those naysayers haven't yet tried the game on Hardcore on maximum difficulty with "Second Wave" options on. If they did, they would likely rescind their earlier statements and cringe as the enemies beat them every time. Every. Single. Time.
Truly, this game is quite fun and worth the money!

Been playing for a couple of days, and while it's not the best game there is, it's definitely not the worst either. I haven't spent any money on it, so I can only talk on the free part of the game.
It's easy to play in the beginning, and then gets pretty hard. So, easy to learn, hard to master, and all that. Probably gets hard, because I didn't spend money, but oh well.
If you're a bit of a pack rat like me, the limited inventory will most likely annoy you, but seeing as I'm also a tad OCD, then it becomes less annoying as you spend the weaker cards to level up your main hand.
I do fairly well in both PvE and PvP - again, without spending money - so the people talking about pay to win are most likely just annoyed it's an option to spend money. By the time I get through my stamina (hope pool), I'm pretty much done with the game for the day, anyways. The hope pool does increase (albeit slowly) with levels, so it's not a fixed amount.
The battles are a bit tedious, I have to admit, usually because I choose the easy way and let my troops do their own thing. There is, however, ample opportunity for micro management, and you can choose precisely when to use which skill, and where to position your troops.
As for gold (premium currency) it's not limited to those who pay. You get a bit of gold every day, just for playing an hour. And with all the stuff there is to do - PvE, PvP, upgrading cards and weapons, training skills, and enhancing and evolving and well... yeah... - an hour is quickly spent. Probably too much to do, I guess :P
But generally, as a free game, it's recommended. As a paid game, I don't know.

Developed by Just1337 Studio and published by KupiKey, Neon Space is tagged as being a casual game but as late levels have proved to me, it can be quite hard as well. Make sure you might not confuse this title with Neon Space ULTRA, which is a another genre and with different devs & publishers.

Neon Space establishes some fairly straightforward objectives. You must travel across the levels with your glowing orb and avoid certain puzzles, namely the stationary red lines. The moving lines are bit more tricky and with some form of teleportation, the first few levels were a breeze compared to the later ones. With 50 of them in total, you can’t even say the game is short and as expected, we have an in-game scoring system as well as Steam Achievements.

The graphic style is minimalist and with neon (the title MIGHT have hinted at that, right?) overtones. It found it quite easy on the eyes and enjoyed its different stylistic approach to recently released arcade titles. More color diversity would have been welcomed but even as it stands now, the game looks and feels different enough from similar titles, to warrant a purchase.

The sounds had a limited diversity to them but at least they can be skipped or muted for something better you might want to listen to instead. Considering its asking price, it would be unfair of me to flag this as a con, though.

+ Steam Trading Cards & Achievements
+ Decently priced

- Difficulty spikes on late levels

As simple as it may look, Neon Space proved an entertaining experience and a good break from heavly detailed titles. It contains both the aforementioned Achivements and Tranding Cards, to add even more value than it provides already. It is true what they say sometimes. Less is more.

Super Hexagon is best described as a rhythm/music game, in which you the hexagon must be facing away from the walls as they close in on you, all to a very pumped up soundtrack. The arrow keys are all the keys you need as you jam away to an increasingly difficult game.
The difficulty of the game scales as the time goes by, the walls coming closer increasingly faster. Significant changes can be seen every ten seconds (there is an in-game timer).
The game is very simple, but requires a lot of practice and finger finesse in order to achieve longer times. Think the Super Gravitron from VVVVVV, another game by this developer.
Overall, this game is a 7/10. Fun to play for awhile, but it can get repetitve over time and the difficulty can be seen as too much for new players.

I got this for $3 when it was on sale. It's a really simple game but it's pretty fun. You play as a guardian fairy that protects a magical forest or some such, and a human city nearby ends up looking for a stone that is giving some tree that you talk to life. You fight their golems they send it which pretty much look like muk from pokemon at first. Said fairy is (Stronger than 300 spartans) according to some game dialog. And she does, in fact,♥♥♥♥♥♥face. I think it's part of the games charm having a main character that looks like a small girl but then giving her special attacks that send people flying across the maps and blasting into one another. If it's on sale when you're considering it I'd say it's worth the money.
Pros:
Good combat with the ability to choose the 4 special abilities you want to use.
A cartoony (anime like) art style
Cute character, fairy looks like a young girl and for some reason seems to use a green onion as a weapon.
Japanese voices (honestly no need for ♥♥♥♥♥♥ dubs given how little is voiced)
Throwing enemies into each other is a blast, trying to do some crazy combos is fun as well.
Cons:
At least as far as I've gotten the enemies don't have very detailed models, aside from bosses.
The story isn't terrible but it's not going to keep you on the edge of your seat.
Levels where you have to protect a vortex can be pretty tedious, if your attack send an enemy flying and it hits the vortex it'll damage it, and given that the enemies cluster around the vortex to attack it that happens quite often. You lose if every vortex is destroyed.
The game has controller support, which is good to have the option, but I don't think it's really an option to NOT use a controller. Given the combat style I think keyboard controls would be really difficult and awkward to play with. I don't know for a fact though as I simply used a controller.

If you love fighting games, play this beat'em up. You might play as a cutesy fairy girl, but you absolutely decimate hordes of invading monsters and warriors with beat'em up combos and mechanics reminiscent of Street Fighter, Marvel, and Devil May Cry. Basic strings of impressive strikes, launchers, area effect sweeps, and more along with a huge library of new basic attacks and special moves (which use a regenerating mana bar) for you to unlock using experience you gain beating the ever loving snot out of your foes.
While enemy and level variety leave something to be desire (it's the sludge monster again but NOW ITS GREEN!), you're constantly unlocking new moves and passives for you to experiment new combos with, letting you explore new strings such as primarily grounded ones, ones that knock away and have projectiles, extended aerial combos, and more. The sky's the limit with Freesia's fighting style and the waves and waves of endless enemies is your canvas.

Alright... where do I even start with this one... Oh, right, the completely insane difficulty! If you want to get anywhere in this game, you need every single ounce of gaming prowess you have in your body, your friends' bodies and your whole family. And that's just for the easiest difficulty "Hexagon". Your reactions have to be perfect, but if you watch for your reactions to be fast enough, you're unable to see what's coming. So it's like "Pick your poison"...
This game has some redeeming factors though. First, the gameplay is "easy" to learn, as it only requires three buttons. Left to move left, right to move right. What's the third button? Enter to reset after you die again and again and again (insert endless loop of me saying "and again")...
Secondly, the music, oh damn, the music. Superb fast-paced techno/electronic with lots of bass and synth put to use. I would praise it even more... if it didn't distract so much from the barriers you're running into while being into the music.
Third and last, the visuals. They are simplistic and flashy, perfectly complementing the techno beat, making this game super-addicting just to see the flashy graphics and hear the soundtrack.
- - - - - - - - - -
Final conclusion:
Difficulty: 9001/10
Presentation: 7/10
Addictive: Definitely, you will play for hours straight (if you can keep yourself from ragequitting)
- - - - - - - - - -
So, considering all that was said, this game is very addictive and fun, despite the difficulty. If you're into techno, flashy visuals and extreme masochism, this game is for you.

The music is fantastic and really sets the mood. First thing I did before playing the game was listen through the whole menu track. Also, the menu is really pretty and the graphics will scale to your resolution which keeps things running fantastically well -- I cleared this game on a
laptop and apart from a slow down here and there it ran really, really smoothly!
The difficulty curve goes from naught-to-ninety and then some, but levels out a bit when you learn what you're doing. The story is short, feelng more like a single chapter in length, but it's nice that it's there.
The combat is a bit on the hard side until you get to grips with defending and dodging, and even when you do get into the flow you still end up taking damage in seemingly unavoidable ways. The battles are tough for this reason, but after a while you realise that avoiding damage is sort of the name of the game and it becomes all the more fun – I wouldn't call it bullet-hell exactly
but the game can definitely throw a lot at you. Choosing which skills to use to take down a particular foe gives the game a genuine strategic side, and it's here that you'll find most of Fairy Bloom Freesia's depth. The difficulty can drive a player to rage-quit, but victory is always a different skill choice or better approach away.
At less than a tenner it's well worth it, but I stress that this game isn't for beginners! If you enjoy fighting games and games where you can restart with the same high-leveled character at a greater difficulty
, then I'd say this one is for you. If you only ever play through something once, then get it on special offer and you'll still have your money's worth.
I just really hope Edelweiss takes the core concepts of this game and expand on it, as the potential is huge.

Every single decision you make, whether be a draft pick, a trade, or a substitution in the game, has an impact on your franchise. It doesn't feel like anything is scripted and it truly is a game of skill.
Some people like to simulate through seasons fast and bring a team from the ashes and turn it into a dynasty of superstars, others like to control your team every single game of the season, monitoring every single decision. If you're a new baseball fan or a baseball fan that has never played a baseball sim before, I would highly recommend this game. It's challenging, exciting and flexible all at once.

Mirror's Edge is one of my all-time favorite games. It's one that I just keep coming back to, even after having completed it many times.
The soundtrack, expertly crafted by Solar Fields, is a standout. The art direction is one of the most interesting and unusual I've seen, seamlessly combining sterile utopian architecture with bold, modern color. The gameplay is mostly very fresh and enjoyable, but not entirely without problems.
A common criticism is the combat system, which is somewhat poorly designed. This was never an issue for me, since I realize that the protagonist, Faith, is trained as a runner, not a fighter. Running should be, and almost always is, the best way out of sticky situations. The levels are also sometimes said to be too linear, but there are actually lots of alternative paths to find, if the player is willing to think outside the box.
The campaign is short (about 8 hours) - a decent speedrunner can complete it in less than an hour. The story is also a bit sparse; but the dialogue, for the most part, is well written and voiced.
Although it has its faults, Mirror's Edge stands out as one of the most unique, exhilarating, and visually striking games of its generation. I highly recommend it.

A solid port that features everything from the original Xbox360 version but with the option to run at a higher resolution and framerate. The only performance problem I've run into is that a few weapons (like the sledgehammer) cause massive stuttering when you kill zombies. This appears to be a problem with the remaster itself and not the PC version as this issue exists on the XboxOne/PS4 version as well.
As for the game itself, it's brutally difficult with some poorly done AI and outdated controls/graphics. The map design is great with some interesting locations and lots of secrets to explore. The story is a typical Dead Rising story with terrible voice acting, stupid plotline, and terrible boss fights.
So why bother with this game? Well, it's the original open world zombie game that started it all. It's a lot of fun to explore the mall and kill zombies, but just know now that it's a stupid, silly game that should never be taken seriously. The missions are poorly done and are often frustrating to complete so only the most dedicated players will even get to the end of the main questline.
Overall, the $20 asking price is not high and the game is definitely worth it for that price. Though the micro-stutter issue needs to be fixed immedietly. If it's not, then you're better off waiting for a sale.

It's baffling that it's really been ten whole years since the definitive zombie game was released for the Xbox 360 in all of its clunky, infuriating glory- I was in high school. Now it's a decade later, i've graduated college with a full time job- plus hundreds of zombie games- and three (soon to be four) sequels later its still the best in the series and possibly the best zombie game i've played yet.
Getting into the port itself, it runs like a dream. The kb+m controls are practically seamless, but you can change the settings if you need to if the bindings don't suit your motor skills. It looks better than ever, adds multiple save slots to make you want to tear your hair out just a little bit less when you die trying to get a survivor to walk through an automatic door for the nth time that day, and even more impressively, the soundtrack remains the same! That means being able to relive the stomach-churning apocalyptic trumpets once again as they begin the minute your feet touch the grass of the courtyard in all their glory.
Some people have reported having saving issues, troubles with directx, and audio problems. I have personally not had a problem with any of those, but my sympathies go out to those who do and I hope there's a fix released for it soon. So... the port isn't perfect. But it's pretty damn good. In retrospect, it could have turned out much worse.
The bottom line is, if you feel as if zombie games have oversaturated the market and become passe, do yourself a favor and return to one of the classics. It's frusturating, it's hard, and it's got a timer, but it'll be the best time killing the undead you've had in ten bloody years.

Another day another RPG that is made by the same developers who did the hyperdimension series. I will be reviewing the game on a pro/ con style and end with my final conclusion.
Pro:
Great story. The story is full of laughter and moments that are sad or shocking. Those last two are very notable since the game is a cutesy RPG so dealing with the concept of death of a beloved character is very sudden. It really helps attach the player with the characters and plot.
The characters are all likeable. The main party members are very memerable with their crazy dialog and unique personality. Each character is special and tied with the story, they all play a pivital role to and their personalities remain constant to a degree.
Music is phenonenal. Each track is very nice especially the sad tune since that really tied with the overall mood at times but there are other songs that i enjoyed which begs the question....why is there not a sound track that can be purchased on steam.
The level design is for the most part varied. Some levels are pretty much palet swaps. The rest of the levels are unqiue since they have a gemic such as a windy level or lava, or forest. The one set back is how the second half of the game uses the stages already visited to because of time travel which feels lazy but it is whatever.
con:
The grind is real for those who want those achievements like getting 100million gold.
Unlocking secret characters like lola has to be done every playthrough even if on a previous playthrough you have gained all the furies.
Conclusion:
The game is great. Great characters and story that make the game very lively. The rpg elements work well since every level up makes you feel much more stronger. It is debatable on whether it is better than the hyperdimension seres but it was a blast to see how things worked out. I reccomend the game to any rpg gamer.

Honestly, I'm fond of this game. I come from RTSes such as SC2 and WC3, and I've played demos of Civilization games. I was never really fond of turn by turn games because they enabled almost to much vision of the enemy movements and thus it was very predictable. Additionally, you could legitimately see turns ahead in those games due to the simplicity of combat and enemy AI.
I'm proud to say XCOM: Enemy Unknown is entirely different than that. While it is turn based combat, having two "Actions" per turn is something you don't see in many turn-by-turn games, and with that different classes for your units with different actions they can do, and the permanence when a soldier dies all add up to a very strategically intense game.
Some of the naysayers complain the game is to easy. I'm willing to bet those naysayers haven't yet tried the game on Hardcore on maximum difficulty with "Second Wave" options on. If they did, they would likely rescind their earlier statements and cringe as the enemies beat them every time. Every. Single. Time.
Truly, this game is quite fun and worth the money!

This game isn't bad, but I don't think it's anything exceptional. If you've played QUBE or Talos Principle, you should know what to expect here. The game has its couple of unique mechanics, and you'll use those to walk around and solve puzzles.
The start of the game is very well done. It's confusing in a good way, and the novelty of the spatial tricks is fresh.
Unfortunately as you proceed the puzzles start to become surprisingly mundane block placement puzzles. The strange world physics and the block placement almost never mix, which leads to an odd situation where you're walking through a bizarre world to solve completely ordinary puzzles. What makes these frustrating is that the controls feel sloppy -- it's difficult to position blocks in 3D space since you have no control over depth of your cursor.There are also a good amount of jumping block puzzles which are tedious at best.

Dying Light is Dead Island re-animated... er... zombified? Worst parts of DI have been rotten out, so you now have actually playable game.
Gameplay is heavily parkour-styled, so your character, Kyle Crane, will climb and jump around the city of Harran in search of cure research for the zombie virus.
Harran is made up from two large areas Slums and Old Town, which are enough distinct to spark your EXPLORE!-fire again when you change the map. The game world is quite amazing and graphics developers have been doing marvelous job to add lots of details all around. Exploring the world will give you XP, but when you hit the level cap the rewards from exploring won't account much unless you play for Steam achievements. On the other hand, as there aren't any practical reason to explore more, two large map areas will suffice.
Movement is fluid and usually you get intended action (grab a ledge, jump off from the wall) so you actually feel like you're doing parkour moves. If surface looks like it could be grapped or climbed, that's usually the case. Movement skill level also adds to the feeling that Kyle Crane physically learns more as he goes on. Having seen some games which kind of sucked (Mirror World *cough* *cough*) and some games where all surfaces are fair game (Ninja Gaiden), doing parkour in DL is simply fun. Of course some movement restrictions are in place as game world is finite, there are surfaces you can't grab and gameplay area is confined by magical invisible walls. Later on you get grappling hook, while it speeds up gameplay considerably, you lose most of the illusion of being parkour runner.
Combat system is fairly simple. Neverthless it's entertaining enough for few hours just to bash, slash, maul and maim zombies with whatever weapon you get on your hands. Zombies react to physics, so they can tackled, toppled over fences or forced to climb on high places to even reach you (and then they get kick in the face). You're able to target generic body area so usually button mashing is a great combat tactic. There is unfortunate auto-targetting when doing some combat moves but I guess it's price to pay for playing console game.
Story is kind of mixed bag, as side quests have more story than the main quest. Most of NPCs have at least somewhat interesting dialogue and voice acting & animations are ok, some overacting, but also some really excellent performances. Most of the default story line aspects living in the city full of undead are handled in way or another through side quests or collectibles. Unfortunately main quest includes some really dumb forced story events, bad boss seems to have constant grip from Crane's balls whatever Kyle tries to do. Kyle Crane voice acting shows him as quite strong-willed character, he's not on par with JC Denton but delivers his punch lines with real punch well enough (except every time when Kyle meets evil boss he puts whimp clothes on so he can receive good spanking). I have kind of insight after my playthrough that Techland can't make a game without horrible main story twists. Dead Island was such a dog puke, DL is bit better though as side quests will give some credibility for the story writer.
Of course the zombie game aren't zombie game at all if there aren't any gibs! In DL zombie gibs are also finite, for example you can't cut only fingers off, then palm off, wrist off and so on, you only chop off whole hand from elbow. Gore effects are fairly well done and stay within reasonable limits so you can enjoy the effects and do not get WTFs every time. Gore with taste, I say! Also splatter effects on walls seems to correspond with weapon you're using.
User Interface is designed for consoles, game has "hold this key and move mouse"-style weapon/item menu. This might work if you have gamepad or such, but I played this with keyboard and mouse. You can rebind the keys, but you need to limit yourself to only some items or juggle through awkward inventory if you want to use more items (especially elixirs). Also keybinding on Linux version is horrible and mouse recognizes only 3 buttons.
Also final battle with the boss is just one facepalm moment you can't forget. So, you're ready with best weapons with best upgrades, holding boss' own gun to give it back one bullet at time and lots of invulnerability elixirs to gulp. You climb on the final ledge ready to pump this guy full of lead and then chop him to tiny grilled evil zombi-snack bits with your Fiery Sword of Death. Well, that's how it should go? Instead you're treated with Quick-Time Event (QTE) where one-handed man beats your zombi-killing hero to ground only using one hand and whole battle...  no, not battle... watching interactive movie... consist of pressing seven buttons in certain order. WTF? In fact, here's pro-tip for you: in this game you can discard your weapons before playing any main quests against boss as you can't never use them.
Conclusion: despite some shortcomings this is quite fun game. Main story sucks but as one NPC said to Crane, blockbuster movies are all about happy endings and badly told stories. Here's story for 70€ (incl. Season Pass). As long you remember to turn your brain off for the main story quest, you should have fun.
On the bright side, gameplay is fun and entertaining for one playthrough. Multiplayer might add some more hours, but I'll suggest you first try the game on single player or with newbie friends as best parts of the game experience is at the beginning of the game. I would say with more experienced story designer,
and adapting interface more for keyboard/mouse this could have been excellent gem.

Fairy Bloom Freesia is a game well loved for it's combat mechanics, but other elements also makes me want to recommend this game so much.
I'll start with the combat. It's pretty difficult for me to explain, but it has the gameplay of Action RPG games like Tales of, but much more simplified, which isn't necessarely a bad thing. The only disadvantage to this gameplay is that there are only a few enemies throughout the game which just come back with different color schemes.
You fight as an anime fairy forest girl who is protecting said forest from bad things. There is no exploration though, as you just fight enemy waves with bosses after a select amount. Don't worry though, after every wave you go back to the intermission, where you can equip and upgrade skills, and save so you can take a break from the game. A shout out to Edelweiss for making some really good and interesting boss battles, with the exception of the first boss.
The graphics and music are really appealing, but that might be different according to your taste. Another thing I like is personal, but a big reason why I love this game. It comes in the form of references, though some are incorrect. For example, the main girl is not a reference, but looks and acts like one of my favorite Anime characters ever called Last Order. And lets not forget the achievement which is a direct reference to Madoka Magica, one of my favorite Animes of all time.
This game also has a great replay value. After you have completed the main story, several different modes unlock, with much more challenges than you have faced before in this game.
I might be a little biased when it comes to this game because it had several things that I look forward to in a game. But these are somewhat personal preferences, so I'd advise you to check out the demo first. And if you enjoyed the demo, then you will for sure enjoy the game.

Look, this isn't difficult, by which I mean the decision.  The game on the other hand is extremely difficult, and potentially super frustrating.  It's easiest difficulty setting, perhaps mockingly, is Hard.  Every level is some N-th degree incrementally more difficult, with your choices ranging from "Hard" to "Hardestest".  That second 'est' was not a typo.  It's not complicated, you just rotate a small triangle around a hexagon and try to make sure the front tip of the triangle doesn't touch anything oncoming, or you lose.  Your goal is not so much to win, but to survive, and trust when I say the game is going to make you struggle for it, SUFFER for just a couple more seconds, before taking it all away.  And you know that it's your fault.
The decision is much easier.  You should get this game.  It has a pricetag that might convince you that the product is being digitally stolen when it hits your cart, but then you remember the internet somehow considers under $5 some form of "murder" if it isn't also "free".
In all seriousness though, the game is magnificent.  Delightfully simple, excellently designed, and practically the perfect time sink if the only window you have is "a couple minutes long".  Play it for a minute.  Play it for an hour.  You probably won't play it for multiple hours in a row, it's not quite deep enough for that, but you'll have SO MUCH FUN(?).
You know what it does well?  Most things.  Great music, great visual design, excellent idea executed perfectly, and probably one of the most non-commital easiest to replay games I have ever seen.  And it's so challenging, but you will definitely feel yourself adjusting, as if your skill level is somehow escaping your grasp.  It does some things not so well also.  There's not much to the game; the simplicity is also a drawback since there isn't a whole lot to do outside of, well, THE ENTIRE GAME, which isn't much sadly.  And for the not so dexterous gamer, I'm sorry to say this game will not cater to you.  Either you catch up or get left behind.  Luckily, I do feel like most people will be able to follow the game at its lowest difficulty and not feel like they are missing out on the experience.
It's so easy to recommend this game.  It's like giving someone a sour jawbreaker and telling them it only gets more sour the further you go, and finding out that most people get "enough" just from the outer layer.  And honestly, the outer layer of this bs is enough for most people.

Mirror's Edge is one of my all-time favorite games. It's one that I just keep coming back to, even after having completed it many times.
The soundtrack, expertly crafted by Solar Fields, is a standout. The art direction is one of the most interesting and unusual I've seen, seamlessly combining sterile utopian architecture with bold, modern color. The gameplay is mostly very fresh and enjoyable, but not entirely without problems.
A common criticism is the combat system, which is somewhat poorly designed. This was never an issue for me, since I realize that the protagonist, Faith, is trained as a runner, not a fighter. Running should be, and almost always is, the best way out of sticky situations. The levels are also sometimes said to be too linear, but there are actually lots of alternative paths to find, if the player is willing to think outside the box.
The campaign is short (about 8 hours) - a decent speedrunner can complete it in less than an hour. The story is also a bit sparse; but the dialogue, for the most part, is well written and voiced.
Although it has its faults, Mirror's Edge stands out as one of the most unique, exhilarating, and visually striking games of its generation. I highly recommend it.

Going into this experience, I expected something great. After playing for some time, I expected something admirable. After finishing it, I thought, “That was it?”
I’m not sure what others see in Mirror’s Edge, but the overall experience left me unsatisfied with all but the fact that I didn’t have to frustratedly search for the next path to continue the level. The visuals of the city and even of the characters were beautiful, and for more than an hour that qualified as a reason to play the game for me. However, after those assets wore off, the rest of the game failed to impress.
The gameplay, while an innovative and powerful idea, was crippled by the unnecessary difficulty of performing the simplest parkour moves (frequently resulting in a thousand restarts). This was only made worse by the clumsy combat system; in order to take down an enemy, the player needs to either punch them a certain number of times, counter them, or shoot them. You don’t start with a gun, so shooting them is out, and if you have more than one or two enemies around, then punching them becomes near impossible. This would all be fine if the countering mechanic didn’t require what seemed to be lucky timing. Ergo, numerous more restarts due to combat deaths.
The sound design was mediocre, and the level design was interesting at first but became monotonous quickly. The between-level cutscenes were 2D animations that didn’t fit with the game’s visual themes and were noticeably lower quality than the rest of the game—obviously a cut expense for production. These made me less interested in what was already a decent-at-best storyline, which is hard to follow and uninteresting. It drew no emotional response from me and could have been completely removed from the game without changing the value of the game.

Have you played Dead Rising 2 and 3 but not 1 yet? Haven't played any of them? Do yourself a damn favor and get this game. This port of the original from 2006 runs perfectly, and it is a blast to run around in the confines of Willamette Mall once again. Although its more serious in tone than 2&3, I feel that Dead Rising is the best one and always will be because of that serious tone. As you play through the game you need (well not really but you should) to rescue any survivors that you see and are told about, while completing the main quest line, taking some pictures and dealing with psychopaths. The game truly makes you feel on edge in certain moments, like you're racing against the time that has been given to you in order to complete all the tasks that you have been put up to. And just when you think you've caught up, the clunky AI will have the 6 survivors you're transporting back to the safe house sprint endlessley into a potted plant as they get horded by zombies and scream your name for help. And then some of them die and all is lost because you really wanted to save all of them. And now your last save was an hour ago, and in Dead Rising you can only save in the bathrooms (or security room), and there's rarely auto saves (unless it's for a main quest). Frustrating, but it's part of what gives Dead Rising its charm. Having to not only deal with zombies, psychopaths, survivors and the main storyline but also the games little nuances is enough to make anyone drop the game and say "This sucks!" But for me it makes me appreciate it that much more, because it's just another challenge that you have to adapt to and tackle. So if you get this game, don't give up easily, or early. Keep on trying to play and beat the game. And have some perseverance through the beginning, because the more you play it gets easier and more fun :)

Neon Space is a small $1 arcade puzzle/timing game. Your goal, in the world of this little and simple yet fun and highly addictive classic, is to navigate your spaceship through and around numerous still and moving obstacles, in an attempt to advance through and end up completing the game.
The game’s mechanics are a prime example of “easy to learn but hard to master,” where you change the direction of your little round character by using the left and right arrows, then moving forward and backward using the up and down arrows (it also supports gamepads.) It sounds simple, and it is, but under pressure it is incredibly easy to press the arrows a little bit longer than you should, causing you to undoubtedly fail as the red lines collide with you.
It is a game of timing - patience as much as swift reflexes. You can wait for the perfect moment, but wait half a second too long and you can say goodbye to your little spaceship. It can also be very frustrating when you’ve tried and failed a level ten times, but stick at it and you will be greatly rewarded with the feeling of accomplishment once you succeed.
Talking about timing, there is a timer on the screen, constantly reminding you of just how bad at the game you are, but also a reminder that you can beat that time displayed. A few more tries and you can get to 20 seconds instead of 25, then a few more and you can beat that score too!
You play in front of a few beautiful space-based backgrounds and through the neon curves and lines (that explains why it is called “Neon Space,”) which combine and make a great, somewhat retro-futuristic feel. Music is one of the most important things in Neon Space, being as it is an arcade game and can’t really be atmospheric, so you play alongside some sweet techno tracks (is it techno? I don’t know, the music of this generation is so confusing, I just try to sound cool.)
Conclusively, I believe you should spend $1, something you would usually find lying on your bench or under your sofa, on this great little arcade game.

This game isn't bad, but I don't think it's anything exceptional. If you've played QUBE or Talos Principle, you should know what to expect here. The game has its couple of unique mechanics, and you'll use those to walk around and solve puzzles.
The start of the game is very well done. It's confusing in a good way, and the novelty of the spatial tricks is fresh.
Unfortunately as you proceed the puzzles start to become surprisingly mundane block placement puzzles. The strange world physics and the block placement almost never mix, which leads to an odd situation where you're walking through a bizarre world to solve completely ordinary puzzles. What makes these frustrating is that the controls feel sloppy -- it's difficult to position blocks in 3D space since you have no control over depth of your cursor.There are also a good amount of jumping block puzzles which are tedious at best.
I got this game since the reviews were making it out to be something really extraordinary and groundbreaking. The game is neat, but it isn't much you haven't seen before and I don't think it's worth a $20 price tag.
As a side note, this game gives me terrible motion sickness. I usually don't get it in games, but if you're prone to it this game will probably make you feel very ill.

The idea of Neon Space is pretty simple. Your goal is to guide your orb (which is your spaceship) to certain points on each level avoiding the various objects and things you’ll encounter which will result in your untimely death. Though the base gameplay sounds easy, it gets pretty challenging as the levels progress and when you find yourself dying you’re hit with a severe case of the ‘just-one-more-try’ bug. You have two abilities at your disposal, ‘blink’ and ‘slow’ and these will be all you have to help you through the levels besides your amazing sense of timing (sadly this is not provided with the game). Blink allows you to dash forward which comes in handy for dodging lasers or as a speed boost if you’re impatient like me. ‘Slow’ will allow you to slow all enemies for a few seconds giving you that edge on those levels that are a little too hard. Some levels will be as easy as travelling to one checkpoint but others will have you weaving around the levels, unlocking new routes and hitting multiple checkpoints.
The enemies you encounter (red lasers) follow specific route usually so timing is the main challenge to the game. If you have no timing, then I suggest you avoid this like the plague.
The game takes around an hour to complete so it's rather short but at a dollar the content more than matches the price. (my gametime is incorrect due to card dropping)
The soundtrack of the game is one of my favorite things about Neon Space. Every track seems to fit perfectly with the game and i’ve loved every single one on the soundtrack. You can switch between tracks as you’re playing with just one button so you can choose what you want to listen to without having to navigate to the menu. I was really disappointed I couldn’t buy the soundtrack on Steam and there are no links to download it even which I would love if the devs would change.
The graphics are another great feature, everything is clean and bright and the really nice background space images that change with each level are very atmospheric.
--- Easy to grasp gameplay.
--- Surprisingly large amount of content for $1 (50ish levels).
--- Highly addictive.
--- Simple yet stunning graphics.
--- Balanced levels, never too challenging but not too easy either.
--- Really amazing soundtrack.
--- No option to rebind keys.
--- Short soundtrack for 50 levels.
--- Controller causes the main menu and pause menu to not function correctly.
--- Cannot see the medal you earn after each level.
For $1 you can’t go wrong with Neon Space. The gameplay is fantastically addictive, there are plenty of levels to keep you busy and the soundtrack is well worth the money alone in my opinion. Anyone who likes simple puzzle games with straightforward mechanics won’t be disappointed with this one.

I gave this game a No, but it's a soft one.
I got this game as part of a bundle and thought "what the hell, I'll try it."
I expected it to be a sort of sidescrolling action platformer. It isn't.
Fairy Bloom Freesia is essentially one of the Multi-Man Melee challenges from Super Smash Bros.
If you don't know what I'm talking about, you're set down in a 2D arena and besieged by a bunch of enemies until you've defeated them all.
So far I've seen two different arenas and neither has been different enough to matter in terms of gameplay. After each level (they're more like rounds) you're given the option to spend points you've earned on upgrading your abilities and aquiring moves. All this is fine. It isn't great, some isn't even good, but it's baseline decent.
What's really terrible about this game are the endless text-based story segments you have to click through to get to the next piece of gameplay. These might be alright if the story made any sense or was interesting at all.
If you're 12 and really into anime of all kinds, you might enjoy the story. That's not a value judgement, that's the demographic I think this game is aimed at, and I think it's probably alright if you're in that demographic. As a 26 year old dude, the story does nothing for me, and frankly it's a bit weird playing as what appears to be a 10 year old fairy girl.
If you're looking at this game and thinking maybe the gameplay will make up for everything else, I have to tell you that it doesn't. That doesn't mean this is a terrible game. You'll probably get some enjoyment out of punching weird plant things for a few rounds, but really I wouldn't buy this unless you meet any two of the following criteria:
A) Know it's arena-based
B) Saw the characters and thought "Hey that looks like my kind of thing"
C) Can get it for $2 or under.

Look, this isn't difficult, by which I mean the decision.  The game on the other hand is extremely difficult, and potentially super frustrating.  It's easiest difficulty setting, perhaps mockingly, is Hard.  Every level is some N-th degree incrementally more difficult, with your choices ranging from "Hard" to "Hardestest".  That second 'est' was not a typo.  It's not complicated, you just rotate a small triangle around a hexagon and try to make sure the front tip of the triangle doesn't touch anything oncoming, or you lose.  Your goal is not so much to win, but to survive, and trust when I say the game is going to make you struggle for it, SUFFER for just a couple more seconds, before taking it all away.  And you know that it's your fault.
The decision is much easier.  You should get this game.  It has a pricetag that might convince you that the product is being digitally stolen when it hits your cart, but then you remember the internet somehow considers under $5 some form of "murder" if it isn't also "free".
In all seriousness though, the game is magnificent.  Delightfully simple, excellently designed, and practically the perfect time sink if the only window you have is "a couple minutes long".  Play it for a minute.  Play it for an hour.  You probably won't play it for multiple hours in a row, it's not quite deep enough for that, but you'll have SO MUCH FUN(?).
You know what it does well?  Most things.  Great music, great visual design, excellent idea executed perfectly, and probably one of the most non-commital easiest to replay games I have ever seen.  And it's so challenging, but you will definitely feel yourself adjusting, as if your skill level is somehow escaping your grasp.  It does some things not so well also.  There's not much to the game; the simplicity is also a drawback since there isn't a whole lot to do outside of, well, THE ENTIRE GAME, which isn't much sadly.  And for the not so dexterous gamer, I'm sorry to say this game will not cater to you.  Either you catch up or get left behind.  Luckily, I do feel like most people will be able to follow the game at its lowest difficulty and not feel like they are missing out on the experience.
It's so easy to recommend this game.  It's like giving someone a sour jawbreaker and telling them it only gets more sour the further you go, and finding out that most people get "enough" just from the outer layer.  And honestly, the outer layer of this bs is enough for most people.

An excellent game! The main thing I loved about it is that it has heart. The characters are so interesting and make you feel engrossed in their stories and problems. They make you feel as you are a real part of their world, and a part that matters. There are many funny and frustrating moments, and by frustrating I mean in a good way because it makes you feel something, makes you care. The story is solid and keeps you going right until the end with some great cliffhangers.
The gameplay... ahhh, what a delight! The parkour style hopping across the rooftops and the melee combat from first perspective are done so well that you almost feel like you are really physically jumping from one rooftop to the next and barely managing to grab a ledge and avoid a very damaging fall. Also, swinging the katana and literally splitting people and zombies in half, never felt so natural. I wish Bethesda would learn from this for their next Elder Scrolls game.
It took me around 32 hours to finish the game, and I didn't finish all of the side quests, most of which are interesting. I definitely recommend it to anyone who likes an engrossing game with excellent gameplay and a story that keeps you going and care what happens.

Arkham Knight is a great game.
Arkham games have a distinct feel to them. This is true not only as a franchise, but as every individual entry as well. Every game has similar core features, yet feels very distinct to the next one. Arkham Asylum is one of my all time favourite games for a lot of reasons. It captured the essence of being powerful ye powerless all the time. It made us feel trapped, something that was essential to the gaming experience. City amped up the feeling, bringing in a more open world, and giving us another look at the Caped Crusaders life. Origins featured an interesting premise, which always managed to keep feeling fresh, but the gameplay began to feel aged. Knight came at a new Video Game Generation, and it shows. It looks beautiful. Always.
Arkham games have always had beautiful scenery brought to life straight from the comics. The characters look alive, the villains always menacing, and batman, at the centre of it, calm and confident.
This one in particular features amazing performances by the now-staple Kevin Conroy, and Mark Hamill as the Batman and Joker. John Nable as the Scarecrow stands out as well.
Gameplay is a lot similar yet different from the past games. The older mechanics are present, mixed with newer elements. The Batmobile felt new and different, and is pure fun to ride.
The story feels slow to start, but picks up during the second and third act, Paul Dini's absence shows during various aspects. But overall, feels complete and provides a good conclusion to the tale of the Dark Knight.
Technical aspects are amazing as well, which is something I feared playing on a computer. But on my present rig, it felt right in place.
Overall 9/10.
Definite buy.

tl;dr: Absolutely stunning and vibrant visuals, a masterfully performed soundtrack, unique, heart-pumping gameplay that tests your spatial awareness skills and encourages you to run the levels as smoothly as possible, and a lifelike world. It is a bit short however (my playthrough took 4 hours). All in all, Mirror's Edge is most definitely worth your money. Buy it now.
Mirror's Edge, developed by DICE (makers of the Battlefield series), released in 2008, is a first person running game. You play as Faith Connors, a Runner in a futuristic unnamed city in which the government monitors all forms of communication. Runners were established to send messages without the government knowing about it. The plot revolves around Faith's sister being framed for a murder she didn't commit, and Faith unraveling the web of truth, forgive my simplistic metaphor. There are 9 chapters in the game, each one separated by an animated cutscene.
Mirror's Edge, however, is not praised for it's intricate story. The component that shines is the unique gameplay. Despite being developed by the makers of the Battlefield series, combat is far from the focus of this game. The main objective is to traverse from point A to point B via rooftops, air vents, hallways, whatever stands in Faith's way. All of this is done on foot. Occasionally, the police force (referred to as "Blues" by the characters) show up to try and kill Faith. The Blues are dangerous, and should not be confronted head-on. The main strategy of survival is avoiding enemies and escaping them. Faith is not a fighter, she's a runner. Her only weapons are the environment around her and her limbs.
A neat mechanic that greatly enhances the experience of Mirror's Edge is "Runner Vision". What this does is highlight possible pathways through the level, making it easy for the player to focus on the immersive world and parkour experience. Certain objects such as ramps, ziplines, and doors are highlighted to guide the player along. If the player is stuck and does not know where to go, pressing a key (or B on an Xbox 360 controller) will snap the camera to the direction of the objective.
While Mirror's Edge is a fantastic experience, it is lacking in the length department. I completed the main story in under 5 hours, and that was with countless deaths and moments of "What the hell am I supposed to do here?". The game makes up for it by including a separate "speed run" mode for each level, and additional time trials.
Overall, Mirror's Edge is a fulfilling and satisfying experience that delivers on all levels. The visuals are vibrant and memorable, the soundtrack adds the perfect amounts of ambience and tension, the plot is interesting enough, and the gameplay keeps you coming back for more. I highly recommend playing this at least once in your gaming career.

Dead Rising is a classic game for the Xbox 360, and this port keeps all gameplay mechanics intact although the KB+M control scheme is less clunky than using a controller. I highly recommend the game, but for a more in-depth review I would recommend looking on Google or YouTube. However, keep in mind that these reviews are for a 2006 game and may not mention some inconveniences such as Otis constantly calling you or the survivor AI being poor. I should note that this is a port and not a remaster like some people are saying, but it still looks beautiful for what it is.
About technical notes about this version of the game:
Pros:
*True unlocked framerate (no FPS cap at 120 like DR3)
*21:9 native resolution support.
*Great performance, solid 144hz@1440p w/ 8xMSAA with an i5 2500K CPU, nVidia GTX 1070 FTW GPU - should run on about any computer out there, certainly much better than the DR2/DR3 ports.
*Remappable controller and KB+M controls.
*Texture filtering and MSAA options.
Cons:
*MAJOR: It appears that some boss attacks do more damage at framerates above 60, such as some of Adam's and Cliff's attacks, even to the point where they can oneshot Frank.
*Game requires admin permissions to save properly, although some users are reporting that this game doesn't save even with permissions.
*Controller controls are clunky (like the original) and unfortunately remapping can't do much to help this.
*Mouse aim is floaty, the player model will change orientation with the mouse but the camera and reticle take time to catch up, there seems to be heavy camera smoothing.
*Some of the item/weapon icons in the HUD have bad aliasing on them, and the some HUD textures are slightly blurry.
Would recommend at the price of $19.99 or less.

A few years ago, a friend let me borrow Batman: Arkham City for the PS3. I really enjoyed it, so I bought it along with the other games in the series (Arkham Asylum and Arkham Origins). Although there were moments of frustration, I enjoyed them all. That’s why I was looking forward to Arkham Knight. It was one of the few reasons I had for getting a PS4, but it came out on Steam and I picked it up on sale.
These games are essentially “open world.” That world has grown since the first game came out. The typical usual characters are in them, perhaps with some surprises. There is a lot to do, like collecting Riddler trophies. Each installment in the series seems to have improved upon the original by expanding the world, giving you more to do, or just more story. The game play doesn’t really change too much or too drastically, but it does evolve. Some battles can be tough and it can take some practice to land some perfect combos. The death penalty isn’t really harsh, you basically just get to try again. Arkham Knight automatically saves your game and often you won’t be too far from where you died.
I seem to recall the release of Arkham Knight on Steam and that it got bad reviews or many people were having problems with it. It’s clear to me that those issues have either been resolved, or non-existent in my case. This game looks great and performed quite near perfectly on my PC. It’s definitely a game that makes me happy with my PC. I love games that make it shine.
I think this is something I would recommend to fans of Batman. I think this game series is great and I believe it’s also quite popular. Since you get to drive the Bat-mobile around Gotham in Arkham Knight, I’ve often felt like I was playing GTAV again.
I also like the voice acting in these games. Most notably, Mark Hamill is the voice of Joker.

The team who did the Dragon's Dogma PC port once again did a great job of bringing this 10 year old game to PC.  The game allows you to switch between KBM and controller schemes on the fly, and controls are completely rebindable.  Good selection of graphic options, including borderless windowed and choosing between 30, 60 or unlimited framerate.  Entire time I've been playing I have experienced no crashing or game stopping bugs, except for the infamously idiotic survivor AI, which isn't a result of a bad port but more a lack of polish on the original thing.
As for the game, the first Dead Rising I played was 2, and I must say the lack of the more gimmicky features of the later games makes DR1 refreshing to play.  The later changes to include more and more powerful weapons comes at the price of making the zombies feel less threatening; one combo weapon in DR3 makes entire zombie hordes a complete joke, letting you simply mash X in large groups and get immense amounts of PP.  Combine that with being able to create said weapon at any point, so long as you have the parts (which get brain dead easy later), and the game loses an incredible amount of tension, making the game a lot more boring as a result.  It's almost a reverse effect: the crazier the weapons and attacks get, the less interesting the game becomes.  In Dead Rising 1 this isn't the case; zombies are a bigger threat due to not having overpowered weapons readily available, and the zombies themselves being more aggressive and not so easy to shove aside, espeically in large groups.  The zombies being an actual threat make the game a hell of a lot more interesting to play.  This is looking waaay far into the future, but if a Dead Rising 5 happens, I only hope the zany combo weapons get toned down so it feels there's at least some resistance to moving around.
Like I said earlier, the first Dead Rising I played was 2, because I had never owned a 360.  This port is my first time ever playing this game, and if this port had never happened, I might've never played this game.  Same goes with Dragon's Dogma (although it was on PS3, I'll take 60 fps any day).  I'm very thankful for Capcom putting money into gambling a rerelease of a 10 year old game, and I hope they decide to make more smart moves in the future, either with great port jobs or WHERE THE HELL IS DEEP DOWN CAPCOM

i played this game on Kongregate a while ago. i got up to a fairly middle-range strength without paying anything, so to those who cry about it being p2w... it's more like "pay to be top of leaderboards". in that respect, it's kinda similar to web-based MMOs like wartune.
however, this is SpicyHorse, so it's not a china-based milk-players-dry MMO sweat shop (they do hire some china-based artists, but that's it). First off, it's a straight mobile port so expect all (or most of) the problems that typically come with mobile games. Heavy monetization, stamina systems, grinding, limited inventory space (with the option to expand it for money), and timers. Timers to get assistance from friends, 5 hour cooldown, but you can spend 50 gold coins (the premium currency) to lift that cooldown. It is definitely not the most egregious of its kind, but I still don't think it's worth the time for a variety of reasons either.
=====
It doesn't feel like they even tried to make a proper PC port of the game. Options are almost nonexistent, no volume sliders, just toggles for sound effects and music. No resolution or resizing the window if you want to play windowed.
Description of the game is pretty laughable, they couldn't even bother trying to convince people to download it and it still ended up kind of misleading ("3D + RTS + CCG + 666 = The Gate" apparently that's the best they could do to convince you). It's not an rts, or an action rpg or anything event remotely resembling any of those things. It's 90% ccg with microtransactions (a lot of them).
The battles you see in the trailer, that's the entire level. One screen. Monsters typically spawn off screen and come towards you, you have a party of 4 so there aren't much tactics involved with the battles. Just keep healers and mages safe. Team composition can maybe count for strategy but the demons you get is RNG since you gotta buy card packs. Most battles (at least starting out) are incredibly easy to the point where you can alt tab out to do something else while the game plays itself. I did this and got through the first 2 areas without even upgrading any cards. Decided to upgrade after that because I ran out of inventory space. You also have an auto battle system where they use skills on their own too. Up until the second continent I didn't have to do anything but upgrade a little bit. Once I got there and died I upgraded a bit again and was fine for a few missions until I started dying again. At that point there wasn't a whole lot more I could do with the resources I had (playing for free) to progress. This is with user interaction and trying to position my team properly, keep the squishy ones away from enemies and focus on the tougher monsters. So by the second continent (which will take you maybe an hour at most to get to) you'll probably begin the massive upgrading/evolving grind you find in a lot of mobile ccgs.
There is the tedious and annoying stamina system that comes with most mobile games. Run out of stamina and you're going to have to spend real money to refill it (or wait), etc... It's about 1 dollar for two energy refills (50 max stamina). Starter dungeons use 5 stamina per run. There is a "VIP" system where the more money you spend the more benefits you get in-game. I absolutely hate this as its blatant p2w and I feel it's exploitative. It's 1 dollar for 100 "gold coins," the premium currency. It costs 2 dollars for one premium summon (guaranteed to be at least a rare), 50 cents for a equipment summon, 2 dollars for summoning "exp" cards used for leveling up your cards. The exp are what you might be spending most of your money on since upgrading your cards takes FOREVER.
UI wasn't optimized for PC either. Using the skills for example. You have to click the orbs at the top. Even larger orbs pop up on the entire screen after that and then have to click again to use em. We don't need 4 orbs taking up the entire screen because we're using a mouse. We have the ability to be precise and can accurately click on the normal sized ones in the UI. Obviously this just feels lazy to me and some of you might think I'm nit picking. Maybe I am, if it doesn't bother you then just ignore that. No way to cancel targetable spells as far as I could find either. Right clicking or pressing escape didn't work. A lot of functions you'd expect from a PC game don't exist. You have to click and drag to move up and down through your list of cards, or drag left and right to move through horizontal lists. Not the worst thing in the world but again just a sign of laziness in my opinion.
The only pros this has vs the mobile version is that you can control your team much easier since a mouse is more precise and quicker than your finger. And if you're someone who wants to spend money on the game it's a bit cheaper to do so on the PC.
The game hands out various gifts on a fairly regular basis, including stamina. This is pretty common in mobile games though so it's expected as far as I'm concerned. Right from the start it gives you some decent cards.
I will also mention that after a certain point the game spiked in difficulty pretty hard, I assume that's the point they want you to start spending money to get better demons for your party.
If you don't mind mobile games, go 'head and try it, but for everyone else who might be expecting a legit game with some depth, this is definitely not for you. Personally, I can't recommend it. It's a straight mobile game on PC. If I wanted that I could get an android emulator or bluestacks. That just doesn't work for me, there needs to be more to the game if you're going to put it on PC.
