-GAMEPLAY-
> Overall gameplay is close to the Hyperdimension Neptunia specifically Re;birth 1.
> Recommended to be played using a controller.
> Fairy Fencer F is a turn based role playing game.
> Features up to 3 active members in the party.
> Switching of members is allowed during a member's turn.
> "Weapon Boost" system allows players to make adjustments to a character's stats using "Weapon Points(WP)" which can be earned through battles.
> Support characters known as "Fairies" are collectible throughout the game. This support characters can be equipped to your party members and can give them passive skills and stat boosts according to the "Fairy" you equipped to them. Of course, 1 "Fairy" per party member only. They vary from Rank C being the lowest and Rank S being the highest and they can level up to level 10. The number of passive skills they provide and the boosts they give to stats increases as they level up.
> The conditions in the dungeons in Fairy Fencer F can be adjusted using your "Fairies". The system is called "World Shaping" But first, your "Fairies" must first go through the "Godly Revival". A little bit of storytelling. In the lore of Fairy Fencer F, there was once two deities that have fought each other for a long. The Vile God and the Goddess. The two sealed each other using multiple "Furies", which are magical swords that contain "Fairies" and gives the user immense power, and they both are now in a state of a deep slumber. When you enter "Godly Revival", you will see the statues of the two along with the "Furies" stabbed through them. "Godly Revival" allows you to remove this "Furies" from either of them using the "Fairies" you possess. Each "Fury" stabbed in the deities have their own passive skills and conditions for "World Shaping". The "Furies" stabbed through the deities have their own ranks and in order to remove them, you have to use a "Fairy" of the same rank as the "Fury" you wish to remove.
> In order to change the conditions of a dungeon, you have to stab the "Fury" that went through "Godly Revival" near the dungeon whose condition you want to change. No "Fury" must be near another. The area of effect of the "Fury" increases as they level up. The higher the level your "Furies" have, the better.
> Each party member has their own unique skill called "Special Command". This "Special Commands" does not require SP(or mana in Layman's Terms) in order to use. Some provides additional damage at the cost of using SP per attack you execute. Some allows to take down any foe, except bosses, in one hit.
> Each party member has combos which are set of attacks you can execute in your turn if you used the "Attack" command. This are customizable. The number of attacks in a combo are upgradeable up to 3 through "Weapon Boost".
> Each type of monster in Fairy Fencer F has their own weakness in weapons and luckily, the weapons of your party members can transform to different weapon types according to the attack they do in the combo. When a monster is hit with a weapon that is its weakness, there is a chance that an "Avalanche Attack" may occur. "Avalanche Attack" allows the player to execute the combos of the other active members to one enemy using only the turn of the active member that attacked the monster that triggered the "Avalanche Attack".
> Dungeon crawling is the main play of the game. You get to walk through different dungeons in the map of Fairy Fencer F. Some maps are are simply re-color or re-organized versions of the other maps in the game. Dungeons in the aren't that long so it really wouldn't consume much time for you to walk through them not unless you are grinding or hunting or item collecting.
> Quests are offered in the game. This won't affect the story whether you do them or not. It's a different story if you want to get the achievements. The Quests are offered in "Guillermo's Pub" and this quests have their own ranks from Rank E to Rank S. You start with Quest Rank E and after clearing a few quests of that rank, a promotion quest appears and if you do that, your Quest Rank steps up.
> "Synthesis" is also a system present in Fairy Fencer F that allows the player to craft items and equipments using items that are required. The "Picture Gallery", which presents the artworks, CGs and backgrounds of the game you have previously seen, and "Sound Gallery", which presents the BGMs that you have heard in-game previously, are unlockable through "Synthesis".
> A location called "Shukesoo's Tower" is present in the map of Fairy Fencer F. It is a collection of floors that features their own set of monsters to battle and their own rewards to give. It has 40 floors in the main section and 40 floors in the DLC section. The DLC section features super high leveled monsters which are a challenge to those who are grindy enough to face them. The height of "Shukesoo's Tower" depends on how many "Furies", which is also the same as "Fairies", are stabbed on the map. The more "Furies" stabbed on the map, the more floors will be available in "Shukesoo's Tower".
> The storytelling is done through using visual novel presentation. It also, although rarely, features an in-game animated cutscenes.
> New Game+ carries over all your stats although you have to recollect all your members again and you have to remove the "Furies" again in the "Godly Revival".
> The game has 3 endings. Each of them are relatively easy to get.
-STORY-
> Once upon a time, a hungry young man named Fang is loitering around a city to find some food. In his search, he discovered a sword that is stabbed on the ground that was said to grant any wish although many have tried to pull it but no one was successful. Out of desperation, he pulled the sword and effortlessly, he removed it from the ground. A Fairy living in the sword named Eryn appeared before him and told Fang that he is now a Fencer for he was able to remove the Fury from the ground and it was now his task to recover the 100 Furies scattered throughout the world. Fang refused and decided to leave Eryn alone. One day, Fang was caught for stealing food and was thrown to jail. After 3 days, Eryn rescued Fang and went out the prison until the guards found him. Eryn powered the Fury and Fang fought the guards and defeated them easily. After the fight, Fang still declines the role as a Fencer until Eryn declares she has no recollection of her memories. Only the task of collecting the Furies to revive the Goddess and her name was all she can remember. Forced by conscience, despite declaring he has none, Fang decided to help Eryn get her memories back as repaying for her rescue. Now, they set on a journey to reclaim the Furies and revive the Goddess and bring peace to the entire world. Of course, they will face hordes of monsters, encounter villains who wish to revive the Vile God, handle a masochistic rich girl, fight an edgy edgelord, resist a hottie fairyologist, fight hunger, hate on a damn pretty boy, contemplate on what the heck is one of their party member for the rest of the game, look for ways for money to get those info of Furies from that cute kid who is obssessed with money, spend hours of level grinding, search google for walkthroughs and guides, do multiple playthroughs, skip everything in New Game+, do everything all over again. BUT! Those things will not stop our heroes from collecting the Furies. Join the Fang Gang in their quest for the Goddess! Stay tuned in FAIRY FENCER F!
-GRAPHICS + PERFORMANCE-
> Graphics are pretty basic. They may not be the most beautiful there is but they fit quite nice in the game.
> The game itself has low requirements in order to be played HOWEVER knowing Idea Factory+Compile Heart, optimization is not good. Fairy Fencer F places the workload on the processor.
-CONCLUSION-
> I am near the character limit of this review.
> Recommend the game? Yes

The biggest difference [from other sandbox games] is that SR IV has a ton of mini games embedded into it.  Many parts of the game are specific instances or action sequences.  There are a lot of games "types" included in the total package.
This mix of mini games and open world exploration does hurt in some ways.  Its makes the game feel disjointed at times and occasionally it feels like the open world really doesn't matter except to just blow stuff up.  Its mostly a sandbox games, mixed with a shooter, mixed with some mindless action and awesome explosions.  Is it better than GTA5?  Depends on what you are looking for.
Overall I give it a solid B and recommend it to anyone who likes GTA clones and action shooters,

After playing through this game, aswell as the 2 other episodes, it's no wonder people are begging Valve to make a 3rd installment. The game as a whole is absolutely amazing. It has a great story, tricky puzzle elements, great action, and fun gameplay elements. Almost all of this game's main characters are likeable, you genuinely care about all of them; Alyx, Eli, Barney, Kleiner, even Father Grigori whom you only see for one chapter! The game's various gameplay mechanics are stunning, (especially if you consider it was made in 2004) segments such as controlling an antlion army in Nova Prospekt or driving through the canals on the airboat armed with a hunter chopper gun are awesome to play through and the music really assists with this. The game isn't exactly easy though, it will occasionally get difficult to keep things interesting and it doesn't always lay out the path or the way to open the path to progress right in front of you, it can either be right infront of your face or hidden somewhere nearby, it challenges you to think, similar to Portal. There is much more to this game but some of which you should find out on your own. I know I may seem like some super-fan of Valve gushing and over exaggerating it's awesomeness like I see good 'ol GabeN as God, but no I just really like the game, Valve is popular for a reason and it's not that people are suckers, they just make really good games. Which is why people are either violently upset or insanely desperate towards Valve to make a 3rd game(for any of their games mind you). Also the ending of Half Life2 ep2 is also a big reason people want a Half Life 3, (trust me you want to save that one for last so you may understand). I highly reccommend playing this game and the other episodes, specifically in order, you will not be disappointed.

I would have hoped for this puzzle game to be a bit more... puzzly. Most puzzle games that I enjoy require some kind of insight to proceed, or at least, are designed such that strategic thinking is superior to trial and error. You apply logic, derive a pattern and act on it.
This game on the other hand does not reward thinking much. The best strategy seems to be: Find pieces that fit the border (usually this will yield a unique partial solution) and go from there (usually there is a unique way to do so). This took me through the hundred levels in roughly six hours with little cause to reconsider my strategy. It's not super boring (you can listen to music or podcasts in the background) but does not provide an interesting challenge either.
I would have hoped for more clever puzzles. There are topological and graph theoretic insights that levels could be built upon, such as:
• Any cut through the level crosses an even number of lines (of each colour).
• The curvature of each loop must sum up to a multiple of 360°.
• If there are crossings between red and blue lines, then this number of crossings must be even.
• The number of times line segments connect to the left end of a hexagon equals the number of times that a connects to the right (for each colour. the same for the other two directions).
I think it would have been possible to build new mechanics and levels around those mechanics that encourage and reward thinking about these things. Sadly, the existing levels are designed such that considerations of this kind are either useless or more tedious than just applying trial and error.
There are puzzle games out there that convey interesting logical insights and reward the application of them, making the player feel smart when solving a challenge. This is not one of these games.

I tried this game so far only for 4 hours, passed the tutorial and started expanding my village and in nearby territories and from my first impression I would recommend this game.
As the description goes it's an action game with a big component of strategy and character building.
Therefore it's a mixture of different genres, but does it excel in all those? No, absolutely not. Does it mix them nicely? I believe so, so let’s analyze the different components of this game:
You have a group of heroes, in time you expand your roster and you have always to choose between 3 of them for each mission. Every other hero’s level you can choose between two different skills per hero, forcing you to try to specialize your heroes so they complement each other. In theory a good idea, but then each hero has also an element associated to them in a sort of paper-rock-scissors with 5 elements that makes some heroes especially vulnerable in certain levels (for example a nature hero would be weaker in a level with many metal enemies). Some may argue this is part of the strategy. Would you have only one support guy risking to not use him/her in certain battles and have an unbalanced party without weaknesses or bring him along and acknowledge he/she could be your weak spot? Others may argue that this approach seems “forcing” some tactical aspect in a combat that is not otherwise rich of many options.
The combat is real-time with pause and the ability to input a sequence of commands. For the most part this works, but certain abilities require to write trajectories and by the time the character is in position the enemies moved and the character will faithfully execute your commands even if the enemies are not there anymore, therefore forcing to pause the game before that action is executed and change trajectory before the ability is used and becomes unavailable for X seconds.  So far the fights have been challenging but not difficult, I’m at the first fights and can’t afford to kill everything that moves having to choose where to put my efforts or risk to obtain a too expensive victory (or worse). During combat is also possible to use potions and objects that work mostly as missile devices doing certain damage depending on the type (remember the 5 elements circle?).
The last component is the character building that is intertwined with the village building. Each turn you obtain a certain amount of resources depending on the buildings built in your village or in the map and the territories conquered. One of these resources is “Renown” that allows you to unlock either new buildings or new plans for new armor, new devices, new potions, etc. When you spend enough renown you unlock new areas of the village and every few milestones you unlock a new level for all your characters. The good aspect is that all your heroes level up at the same time. In theory they could level up also if you don’t do anything for few turns (but your enemies can attack you or keep expanding in the map). The other side of the coin is that there’s not much interest in levelling up the heroes as you can only choose one skill out of two and after actions that do not strictly depend on how good you performed in a battle (getting most territories with renown will allow you to advance faster, but then you’ll not have enough coins or other resources to buy better equipment, so really, your choice).
All in all I recommend this game, a fresh approach on the genre with few things not seen at the same time on titles on this type (but not necessarily new). I didn’t try the demo as I trust BlueByte since the time of The Settlers, but I expect it to give a rough idea of how the game is and if you would like it. I was interested after playing for 2 hours, tutorial included (I believe Steam policy is less than 2 hours? That and the demo should give you a good idea). The humorous dialogues (definitely not a game that pretends to be serious) add a nice touch to the game and the graphics are really pleasant reminding me Settlers 7.

If you're a longtime player of OOTP then you know what you're getting in a sense. A slick user interface, a speedy simulation engine and a bizarre array of poorly rationalized decisions that every game comes with. I think the problem with OOTP is every year is more sheen over substance. Back when the game was a plucky indie without the MLB license, this made sense. But now that the game has "mainstream" interest, there's just no reason that the dev team can't prioritize some of the nagging issues that have persisted for decades.
Online leagues still suffer through a poorly compiled HTML setup that takes too long to generate, financials could be way better and many people (incuding me) have spent countless hours providing tools, mockups and ways to make them better and they're generally ignored.
To be fair, I don't care about 3D and rarely play games out, preferring to use the game as a simulation first and foremost.
That said, none of that will matter to the majority of baseball fans who come from other games like tabletop and older sims and for you, this is the game you'll have wished existed when you were younger and had tons of time to play it. There's just SO much you can do with the game, even with its warts, that I can't not recommend it if you're a fan of baseball, have interest in baseball or simply like sports and/or simulations and want a powerful game engine that works really well for you.
If you have OOTP17, it's absolutely not worth the upgrade at full price. If you have an older version, then you'll get the full benefit of the upgrade because essentially that's what it is -- an upgrade.

XCOM Enemy Unknown is a modern version of the 1994 version of the XCOM game. If you're not familiar with it you manage a covert organization that's charged with protecting Earth from an alien invasion.
As the organization's leader you must manage your resources, keep the countries that supply funds happy, improve your base, decide what to research, and decide who to send on missions. The missions to fight alien incursions use a turn based combat system. Strategy on the battle field is more important than speed.
There is no strong cental character and story thread as in Halo or Mass Effect. Your play determines what happens and any of your team can be killed. You can, and probably will, enjoy playing through several times. You want to see the sights on the road not taken.
This game, and the "Enemy Within" variant are very true to the original game. I thought they captured the spirit of the original games but made them much more enjoyable to play.

I would love to say this game is good, I really would love to.
It has a very stable engine, the mechanics/controls are well done and implemented and the combat system feels fluid and you can nicely rack up combos...
...As the game throws (spams) a total of 4 differently-colored enemy types at you.
If it's any issue I have with the game and which in overall removes most of the pleasure I would have with the game is something you do 95% of the time (the other 5% being fighting bosses; I will get to that in awhile); and that is killing monsters.
There are a total of 4 monsters in the game (small ones, medium ones, huge annoying ones and flying ones... such variety) which may vary in future levels through color which will make them more powerful. Letting aside that the developers clearly have a goo fetish, the selection is extremely weak and everything results to the same strategies. Always. No exceptions. When they are grouped regardless of the kind of enemy it's actually pretty fun to simply slam them into each other racking up combos and all, but if you are to put them aside and consider, it's very weak on the main aspect. Then there are the general backgrounds and scenarios which also lack in variety, having to go through 5 waves (there are a total of 30 waves; 5 of which are bosses) on the same level.
Then there are the bossess which do kind of recover, the bosses have clear variety, their difficulty always bases on your skill to block and how to manage things and generally fun. Except the first one, which is a enormous version of the "huge slime", which is annoying enough already; so I am not really happy with the first boss. But bosses after that felt really vivid and were fun to fight. However it's what I would expect from a fighting game on a daily bases; so I am afraid that does not save the rating.
Visually the game is a individual JRPG so I am not expecting next gen graphics. If I am going to go with the artstyle I could say it's cute enough and everything fits well together.
Regarding the characters (even though there is barely any interaction), I think too much lolicon is going on regarding Listine. I don't /particularly/ mind it but it's completely out of hand and makes you go like "...what". Outside of that the game also offers a tiny story which comes up with a twist. I will keep this spolier-free but I will still say that the ending is very dissapointing and not expanded upon at all.
Overally this is a good game with potential. If it had a bigger enemy and map variation, maybe more useful skills (I found many of the skills you unlock later pretty pointless, but they may just not fit to my playlist) and perhaps a rehash of the storyline and this could be a pretty good release. The game is extremely stable otherwise and enjoyable.

If you're a longtime player of OOTP then you know what you're getting in a sense. A slick user interface, a speedy simulation engine and a bizarre array of poorly rationalized decisions that every game comes with. I think the problem with OOTP is every year is more sheen over substance. Back when the game was a plucky indie without the MLB license, this made sense. But now that the game has "mainstream" interest, there's just no reason that the dev team can't prioritize some of the nagging issues that have persisted for decades.
Online leagues still suffer through a poorly compiled HTML setup that takes too long to generate, financials could be way better and many people (incuding me) have spent countless hours providing tools, mockups and ways to make them better and they're generally ignored.
To be fair, I don't care about 3D and rarely play games out, preferring to use the game as a simulation first and foremost.
That said, none of that will matter to the majority of baseball fans who come from other games like tabletop and older sims and for you, this is the game you'll have wished existed when you were younger and had tons of time to play it. There's just SO much you can do with the game, even with its warts, that I can't not recommend it if you're a fan of baseball, have interest in baseball or simply like sports and/or simulations and want a powerful game engine that works really well for you.
If you have OOTP17, it's absolutely not worth the upgrade at full price. If you have an older version, then you'll get the full benefit of the upgrade because essentially that's what it is -- an upgrade.

OOTP18 is the latest version of a great baseball simulator.  I noticed two significant changes from OOTP16 (last version that I owned).  First, the 3D view of the game.  Pervious versions that I played was basically text-only with minimal graphical reflections of the action.  This addition is a very nice touch and aligns with the play-by-play text that is presented.  Since I tend to play all the games (not sim), I have enjoyed this feature much  more than I would have thought.  Another little nuance that I thought was great is after a completed game, there is a nice recap of the game along with player "quotes" and a probability of winning line as the game progressed.  The other significant change that I found is the new "challenge mode."  Although this does not fundamentally change the game, you can now compare your results to the other OOTP18 players out there.  Challenge mode restricts a couple things in the game (e.g. player editor, long-term simulation), but does enable your score to be recorded against other players.  These two changes were worth getting OOTP18.
For those that are unfamiliar with the series, OOTP18 is a baseball game for all of the armchair GMs and Managers that are out there.  This is the third iteration that I have played (OOTP16 and OOTP10) and the game continues to evolve very well.  As with the pervious couple of versions, OOTP has the MLB and Player's Association license.  As a sports fan, you always wonder about how you would remake your favorite team into a dynasty and now is your chance.  You start with the ability to manage a MLB team today or any year from 1871.  You may also choose one of several International Leagues that are available.  From day one, you can delegate authority to the AI or control everything.  From the GM perspective, this includes player and staff contracts, free agent signings, major/minor league roster moves, drafts, trades, and organizational budget allocations.  From the manager perspective, you set your pitching rotations and lineups.  At that point, you can dive into playing each baseball game or sim through the days.  All the statistics from MLB history is available and its fun starting from scratch in 1871 to learn about the early pioneers in baseball.  The other great thing about the OOTP series is the ability to create your own fictional leagues, uniforms, and designs with the large user-mod community.
The bottom line is that this game is a must have for people who love baseball.

Greetings Everyone!  First of all I want to say I enjoyed this game and just recently finished the game on Normal Difficulty.  Overall it is an enjoyable game that has some minor flaws and infrequent crashes.  The game is comprised of three major genres:  City Building, Fiction and Tactical RPG.
Fiction:  Largely forgettable, it tries to be funny and in some parts it is but largely it is eye rolling and simplistic fiction.  I almost feel this was intention as a pun towards other RPGs but we aren’t getting the classic satire you’d get from some other games attempting the same.  To be honest, I’d rather have seen a story that was less satire if nothing else to hope for a better overall narrative.
City Building:  This was a fun addition that I wish more RPGs would emulate.  Though lacking the depth of actual city building games it creates a good break in between the action.
Tactical RPG:  This is the main focus of the game, the reason you are probably considering buying this.  Let me start by saying overall this is a solid addition to the library of Tactical RPGs, though nowhere near as good as games like Aarklash.  The real-time pause / play mechanic was done solidly if a bit more shallow compared to some of the other ones out there.  My biggest complaint is that the pause play mechanics were not needed on normal.  Now, I know one might argue that the game was played on normal but the entire mechanic is based around the pause play and lining up skill shots.  I would have liked more customization and a deeper equipment line but the fact that the game even includes crafting is a great benefit to other games.

Plenty of descriptions already on here, so I'll say what I like and don't like about the game.
Ups: There's a decent amount of Strategy in the different ways you can build your town, how you conquer territories, your research path and what abilities you give your heroes. That should make for some replayability. The missions are interesting tactically because you have to choose 3 heroes from 5, decide how to approach the map and what/when hero abilities and consumables get used. I like the ability to pause and plan, like XCom and similar games, although the ability to chain commands isn't as useful as it might seem at first sight (e.g. if using an area attack and your opponents move you will need to interrupt the chain). I'm glad it's not a micro transactions game. The game runs very smoothly for me on Ultra settings and I don't have all the latest kit (GT970 card, but older motherboard/CPU).
Downs: No MP of any description limits the long term replayability. The graphics are a bit too cartoony for my taste (a bit twee - I prefer a look more like AoW or HOMM). Gameplay wise: the caravan missions are too linear (some units only spawn when the caravan passes so you can't do advance cleaning, or try to come at them from a different direction) and the NPC units you sometimes get run around like mad things attracting mobs (hopefully this will get fixed).
So so:  The funny narrator is OK, but isn't that funny IMO; but then I'm quite demanding on humour.

This is quite likely the best manager sim I have ever played. It is very deep, with a lot of different statistics and tables that allow you to see every little detail of every player and every team, psychological model with distinct personalities that can have very different impact on your chemistry, yet very adjustable, and you can delegate simply everything to the AI which is more than capable. But what really sets this game apart from virtually every other one is ability to play every single team from 1870s, with real players, real stats, and real rules. There is a huge difference between a team from the 19th century, the deadball era, and today. Each period has its own rules, and each will play very differently.
To sum up - this game should be the example for Sports Interactive. Make your Football Manager like this, and I might even consider buying it again.
1. The deep system of statistics and personalities that make every player unique.
2. Team chemistry which makes your players interact and work together, with results based on their personality. Some people are nice and make it fun, some will disrupt your team, and a few ones are great leaders who can make a huge difference. Choose wisely.
3. Customizability - you can customize everything in this game - easily create your own leagues, stadiums, players, personnel, rules, and edit whole countries, without the need to buy in-game editor or some other *** as in Football Manager. Commissioner mode gives you a lot of power, and you are really in charge. Want to create your own award? Done. Add your player to the Basseball Hall of Fame. Done. Create a third Major League? No problem.
4. Really good AI that is quite capable and fallible like a human.
5. Game seems very realistic. Outcomes of games are believable and baseball is as unpredictable as in real life.
6. Your club's owner has his own personality, goals, and a different vision. Act accordingly or else... you're fired.
7. There are literally thousands of clubs to choose from, including many historical ones. You can play Major League team or a minor one - your call.
8. The game is very stable, but also offers you a backup feature, so you won't lose your precious database after several decades of playing.
9. It's baseball so you will literally play almost every day which means even more fun in one season than in soccer.
10. Other modes are also fun - you can for example play as New York Yankees from the times of Lou Gehring and Joe DiMaggio against 2017 Boston Red Sox or 1960 Milwaukee Braves. You can even play with real players from any period playing together. Lou Gehrig, Ty Cobb, Mike Piazza and Sandy Koufax in one team? No problem.
11. Face-gen system is amazing and customizable. You can for example choose how many percent of your players will have beards and then how popular each of the beard styles will be, with dozens of them. You can even make them black-white or sepia to be compatible with your era. It's probably the best system in any manager game.
12. Developers are real baseball afficionados and made everything work wonderfully great - if you will it, it is no dream.
13. Despite hundreds of teams the game runs pretty fast for me.
1. There are still some minor bugs, especially with minor leagues in the 1920s, but those are beint patched quite efficiently and developer support is good.
2. Game could definitely use some built-in real pictures and 3D models of stadiums (at least major ones) - bur then again, you can find them on the internet and on Steam Workshop.

As an avid movie buff and a Dota2 player, I was really looking forward to seeing this, but the end product just doesn't cut it.
*** WARNING: SOME SPOILERS BELOW ***
While they touch upon the fact that the DOTA pro scene has exploded from beer money to tournaments such as The International, they don't do a very good job of covering DOTA2 or eSports in general. It's mostly just a human interest fluff piece for Fear, Dendi, and hyhy.
I realize this movie has been years in the making, but to leave out poignant details such as the recent changes to grant "athlete visas" for eSports, the magnitude of eSports in Korea (only covered for maybe 1 min), the lengths to which gamers go to find better competition (i.e. Moving to other countries to live in a team house, etc), or even TI3 selling out Benaroya Hall in Seattle.
A typical mistake made by sub-par documentaries is telling you that someone is skilled or talented instead of showing/convincing you of that fact. Showing a picture of Dendi or Fear sitting in a booth in front of a computer just doesn't cut it. Other than the brief talk about EHome's 2010 run of dominance, there were very few points of comparison that could be shown. I'm sure if you looked at the stats you could find SOMETHING that demonstrated why these players are the best of the best. Doesn't even have to be real. Make something up! Somewhere buried in the mountains of data for WL records, % first blood, Avg GPM, K+A/D ratios, etc. there has to be something that tells us that these guys are head and shoulders above others. Even something like versatility could be demonstrated by # of heroes used in tournament play. Give us a frame of reference for someone that doesn't already know Dota and exactly who they are.
Compare "Free to Play" with any of the following documentaries and you'll see exactly what I mean: "Senna", "More than a Game", "The Fab Five", "Hoop Dreams", "King of Kong", or any of the 1hr episodes of  "A Football Life". In all of those cases, you see the human side as well as the skill side.
The only thing this movie does pretty well is show you the human side of EG.Fear and Na'Vi.Dendi. I personally didn't find hyhy's story to be particularly compelling, but maybe that's just me. In both cases we see little snippets of the sacrifices they've made and adversity they've encountered. In particular, everything about Dendi makes for a heartwarming story, but that alone doesn't make this a good documentary. Most of the movie is a fairly typical treatise of kids who game. The parents don't relate and/or protest because they think they spend too much time in front of a computer. They use gaming as a temporary escape from reality or a coping mechanism. They work pretty hard at their craft. None of those facts alone are news or noteworthy. SHOW us why Dendi is dominant or explain it to us other than just saying he's creative and skilled.
For reference, I was able to convince a friend and my girlfriend (neither of whom know anything about DOTA) to watch coverage of The International 3 and they actually enjoyed it. The end product with Kaci Aitchison and the casters was actually entertaining enough for them to watch. This doc? Not so much.
P.S. while the animated 3D effects were mildly interesting, they mostly just confused matters. My guess is that someone decided to weave them into the film because it looked cool. It mostly just made the action more confusing.

Shadowverse is a collectible card game similar to Hearthstone. Infact, the two are so similar, that I'm not going to just review Shadowverse here, I'm going to make this a direct comparison of the two games: I feel like this approach would be somewhat more helpful, since many people coming here are probably at least somewhat familiar with Hearthstone.
Before I start, however, I'd like to point out that I'm not deeply invested in neither Shadowverse nor Hearthstone yet. I spent just several months with Hearthstone, and just a few hours with Shadowverse, so I can't speak of things like balance with any level of authority just yet. I will, however, note down my observations in this regard anyway, simply based on how the games "feel" so far.
A simple fact: Hearthstone runs horribly. There's an entirely unnecessary 30FPS cap, the game will hang for several moments before a match begins for no reason whatsoever, and will often lag without any discernible cause. Shadowverse isn't having any of that: the game runs at a solid 60FPS, and there isn't any lag whatsoever. Cygames did take care to put in a few settings for those with poor hardware, too: you can disable various animations and such to make the game run better should you encounter any performance issues after all. In other words, Shadowverse wins in this regard, hands down. It might not seem too important, but the better performance makes the game a lot more enjoyable in the long run.
I've touched upon this above, but Hearthstone has very few options of any sort. Some aspects of the Hearthstone UI are simply clunky. To name a major example, if you buy a bunch of packs in Hearthstone, you have to open them one by one and flip every single card over. It gets tiring. Shadowverse still lets you do that, if you enjoy the "unboxing" process... but it also lets you just see what cards you got from all the packs in one list. Hearthstone's card tooltips are also worse compared to those of Shadowverse. Cygames chose to put the so-called "card text" in a separate box, rather than on the actual card image itself. It may sound weird if you're used to Blizzard's design, but this actually has a bit of an advantage: it allows the card text to be more descriptive, and therefore reduces the need for mysterious keywords denoting complex mechanics. Speaking of keywords (Shadowverse still has those, but only for very common traits), Cygames seems to have a better naming sense for various effects. You have "Ward" instead of "Taunt", which just makes more sense, for example. Shadowverse also includes a built-in replay system, that lets you review past games, which I sincerely appreciate.
Now we're getting to the actual "game" part of the game. The game modes in Shadowverse and Hearthstone are similar, but not the same, so I feel the need to point out the differences. First off, a major one: there is no equivalent to the Tavern Brawl. The obvious ranked/unranked/friendly duels are all there, of course, no worries in that regard. Arena is vastly different: you don't pick cards one-by-one, but rather, you pick between pairs of cards. You get 5 attempts in arena, no matter whether those attempts are wins or losses: wins improve your reward, but you can't straight up "lose" an arena run in Shadowverse. Additionally, you
, which is awesome and I have no idea why on Earth Blizz doesn't implement something like this in Hearthstone. There's even a funny variation which lets you build the deck for your opponent rather than for yourself.
Then there's the singleplayer. Holy cow, the singleplayer. Cygames went all out on that aspect of the game, it is
. There's an entire story mode, with visual novel style cutscenes, voice acting and all that, with AI that gets progressively harder and teaches you to play on a level far beyond what a simple tutorial would provide. I have to commend this.
All in all, Shadowverse offers more variety with its game modes than Hearthstone does. I still wish there was some kind of weekly challenge thing, however.
This is a highly subjective topic, of course, so I won't be saying which of the two is "better", I'll simply describe the differences. The art style in Shadowverse is very Japanese and "anime-like". The music is more upbeat compared to that of Hearthstone: whereas Blizzard is going for a calm and relaxed atmosphere, Cygames tries to make you feel like there's an actual fight to the death going on in their game. Unlike Hearthstone, the majority of the default heroes are female.
The gameplay is similar to Hearthstone. The mana system is identical, the concept of different classes having access to different cards is the same. However, Shadowverse features just three types of cards: Followers (equivalent to Hearthstone minions), Spells, and Amulets, which are persistent, hard-to-destroy modifiers that grant various bonuses to their creator. You'll notice the lack of hero powers and weapons in that list, and, indeed, they don't exist in Shadowverse. However, Shadowverse features an interesting, and very different, gameplay mechanic known as "evolutions". They unlock on the fifth turn of any match, and they allow you to effectively replace any of the followers currently in-play with better versions of them. You only get to do this a few times per game. Evolution grants your followers the ability to immediately attack on the same turn they are played, so you have to keep that in mind and decide between getting an extra hit in a turn early with a weak follower, or giving a good follower a buff later on. I have noticed that there don't seem to be any cards (at least, from my experience as of now) that are insanely random. Some cards do have random effects, but they are all more along the lines of "Deal 1 damage to a random enemy follower", as opposed to insane things like Yogg-Saron that Blizz comes up with. Classes have unique characteristics, too, but I can't cover all of them here, it's best to see it for yourself. The game also feels a lot more fast-paced, with matches ending fairly quickly.
Here, I mean to compare how easy it is for a new player to get started with either game. Hearthstone is a slug in this regard: it locks a new player out of all but one class, and forces them to grind to unlock basic cards. In other words, you're probably going to spend several hours in Hearthstone before you actually start being able to play the game. Shadowverse does no such thing: a brief tutorial and off you go, with the singleplayer story sitting there, offering its help for you to learn the details of how to fight with each class. The game also feels a lot more generous, it just showers you with card packs. In other words, Shadowverse
, since it does a phenomenal job of teaching you how to play.
Finally, a few words on how the games are distributed. Both Hearthstone and Shadowverse are available for all the same platforms: Windows, OS X, Android and iOS. In other words, if you could play Hearthstone, you can most definitely play this game. However, Cygames did what NORMAL PEOPLE do and put their game on Steam. Blizz has their dumb launcher. Shadowverse also doesn't have the region/server issues that have plagued Hearthstone for the longest time: it doesn't matter if a person you want to play with lives on the other end of the world, you won't have to create an entirely new account and start your whole card collection over just because they're on a different server than you are.
To me, Shadowverse was more enjoyable than Hearthstone. I like the art, the music, the gameplay a lot better. It's just more fun. But this is just an opinion of mine: try the game for yourself and see if I'm right or not.

Fairy Fencer F is the typical Idea Factory/Compile Heart JRPG. If you've played any of the main series of Hyperdimension Neptunia games, then you know what this is. I'll give it a recommended rating, but it's a very close call. If you enjoyed the Hyperdimension Neptunia series, then you'll probably like this. If you disliked the Hyperdimension Neptunia series, then this game probably isn't for you, but may be worth it depending on why you disliked Hyperdimension Neptunia. If you never played the other series, then it's really up to you whether or not you want to take a risk on a comedy JRPG with a plot written by a pubescent middle schooler.
Pros:
-Most of the characters don't look like middle school girls, so people won't judge you as much.
-The scenery style and color looks slightly less like cotton candy vomit than in Hyperdimension Neptunia.
-Animations and models look good.
-Voice acting isn't awful.
-Can be run on lower-end machines if you edit the files to remove shadows, or sometimes with no editing at all.
-Additional playthroughs are much quicker, and you can skip cutscenes, so you don't have to dread New Game+.
-All endings can be obtained on one playthrough if you save at the right time.
-Great soundtrack.
Cons:
-It's Hyperdimension Neptunia in traditional JRPG clothing. You know it, I know it, IF knows it, and the people judging your taste in games know it.
-Grinding is necessary to unlock certain characters on the first playthrough.
-Some of the plot and much of the dialog is cringey, but you should expect that at this point.
-Combat is very easy, even on the first playthrough. Even more so if you grinded to unlock certain characters. This follows an apparent trend with JRPGs becoming increasingly easy these days.
-Characters are largely one-dimensional, and all plot-twists are revealed within the first half of the game.
-Battles against bosses and villains is the typical "boss in battle is a giant monster but is human in the field". Many of them are recolors, or appear as regular monsters with a recolor later in the game.
If Steam used a numerical scale, I'd give Fairy Fencer F a 6.5/10. It's not a very long JRPG, and it's certainly far from being the most entertaining or well-written, but it isn't awful and that's saying something in a market that is flooded by cringe-inducing games and television series that operate on the assumption that if it's anime, somebody will buy it.

Antichamber is a very special game. It requiers you to think outside the boundaries of game design, logic, and everything you ever known. This is really amazing, but some people might not exactly like this sort of aproach.
First of all, presentation. The graphics are nice. It is an indie game, so don't expect anything incredible, but they work, and make you feel like in a testing chamber, similiar to Portal. The music is quiet and atmospheric, which is really nice, since it doesn't break you concentration.
The gameplay. It is really hard to talk about the gameplay, since every puzzle is mindblowing, and I don't want to spoil anything. You really have to think what to do, do it backwards or even leave and start again elsewhere. This can be a problem, if you played games for your entire life, like me, because of the backtracking. If there is a sign that says go forward, and you return to it 10 minutes later, you may think that you just went back and have to find another way, but you have to remember this game is playing with you. You may also get lost, and that can be fatal in some occasions.
The challenge, along with the puzzles, comes with the time limit. Anyone played the original Prince of Persia? You had one hour to finish the game, otherwise game over. This game is the same. You have 1 hour and 30 minutes, otherwise you start again. The second time you figured out some puzzles, so you can go through the game faster, but it can be tedious for some people to replay the game multiple times in one sitting.
TL;DR - If you are up for the challenge, go ahead. This game creates some very interesting elements and makes you think every second of your playthrough. It is difficult, but it is so refreshing and creative, that this is a must for any puzzle game fan.

A very aesthetically pleasing arena brawler that offers average speed combat with responsive controls that can compare to AAA fighting games.  With its anime theme and its wide array of skills, spells, and buffs, players will suddenly find themselves completing their first play through only to jump back in to unlock what they couldn't do during the first run.  The skills reward the player with blur effects, screen shaking, bright lights, and loud percussive explosions and generally feel really good as they're slicing through their targets.  With an EXP per kill system that is used to unlock spells, players are tasked with chaining the most absurd amount of combos in an attempt to hit the mother load that never ceases to entertain.  The story is very light, however, and can be finished in an hour or two.  There are also very few enemies and gameplay may get stale after noticing that monsters in the final levels are the same as the roster from the first.  Overall, I recommend this game to any anime enthusiast and brawler battler.

Who wouldn't know Half-Life 2? At least here on Steam, Valve's online distribution platform? The game that brought fame and the main reason for people actually installing Steam (at first at least)?
No introductions are necessary, Half-Life 2 is the perfect first-person shooter that introduced a revolutionary engine, that still looks very good even by today's standards (just take a look at the water or the shiny tip of the crowbar) with excellent physics (introduced in Jurassic Park Tresspasser) and had memorable action scenes (not really something first-person shooters were known for at that time, except the original Unreal, Deus-Ex and maybe Far Cry).
And of course who wouldn't remember the fast paced chase sequence with the airboat trying to the shake off the helicopter behind us? Or the first time we grabbed the gravity gun either in it's "normal" or overcharged state? The spooky zombie infested old town section? The prison assault commandeering the giant insects, the antlions?
Valve successfully managed to create from Half-Life's silent protagonist a (still silent) superhero for Half-Life 2, who can turn the tide and fight off the puppets of an unknown invading alien species: Gordon Freeman. The secret is that it's completely from his (or rather your) perspective with no interruption of cutscenes and no third-person camera view. Also after loading screens there are no breaks between the sections so you really get the illusion of having travelled a long way.
What I loved the most is the atmosphere and the semi-post-apocalyptic urban setting. The ravaged blocks of flats or the ruined houses along the (still) beautiful coastline and the police state controlled society reminiscent of Orwell's 1984, are the greatest strength of the game in my opinion. It's really immersive.
Half-Life 2 has its flaws however. We get no explanation whatsoever regarding most things (why is the mysterious man with the suitcase called G man and who is he anyway - a constant riddle left over from the original Half-Life) leaving us only guessing and the further episodes (which are also very good) can't really shed more light on the plot, leading us to believe that the creators didn't really focus on the storyline and were thinking 'aah, we're going to figure out something later on'. Too bad, because with a decent story Half-Life 2 could have been the GAME.
Still it is one of the best games in gaming history and everyone who has a registered steam account should give it a try. It is a very memorable experience (along with its sequels, Episode 1 & 2) and maybe Valve should make its playthrough obligatory for new users in their subscriber agreement (for free of course :))
PROS
+ amazing graphics, water effects, even on weaker systems
+ excellent engine with great physics
+ good sound effects and voice acting
+ high-speed chase sequences
+ beautiful, diverse scenery and great overall atmosphere
CONS
- story is functional
- due to scripting some enemies are impossible to kill early on
RATING
9/10

8/10: Mirror's Edge is a very cool game. I thought I'd better try it out since Mirror's Edge 2 will be coming out, and I'm sure glad I did. Mirror's Edge offers a really unique and entertaining form of gameplay with its free-running mechanics and a beautiful world with vibrant colors to enjoy them in. The story isn't amazing, but it works well with the gameplay. The gunplay/combat is pretty poor (though you can pull off a pretty sweet dropkick), and I wish you had the option of simply avoiding fighting altogether, so you could focus on the aspect of the game that really shines: its core mechanics. Running, jumping, and navigating the city feels extremely satisfying, and the game presents you with many exciting environments to test your parkour skills. The chase scenes in particular can be quite exhilarating. There are some moments of frustration and minor annoying details, but overall the free-running system is done very well. There is also definitely some good replay value as there are time trials, and the main story could easily be enjoyed for multiple playthroughs. I will definitely be looking forward to the sequel.

It has an Overwhelmingly Positive review for a reason.
If you just need to take a moment to relax, because you had an annoying time in Overwatch or CSGO and your teammates were legitimately bad and really, really tilted you, so you want to let all that anger out on some ugly♥♥♥♥♥zeds in a very satisfying yet also challenging game, then this is for you.
You team up with people that if you are good enough, you can carry, Pathfinder - a youtuber, has soloed Hell on Earth (The highest difficulty.) with a level 0 class with an emulated full party (6 people.) what does this mean?
It means if you are good enough at kiting, understanding which weapon to use, when, and aiming, then you can carry an entire team by yourself, but it also means, you are going to have an insanely tough time doing it.
You need to memorize each attack pattern on each Zed, each Zeds weakness, each weapons strength, every weapon has its use in some way, and every role can turn the tide.
This also means, though its going to be insanely hard (Though pathfinder makes it look easy, its not.) to carry a full party of really bad players, its also very easy to find that "just right" difficulty just for you for how you feel. You can make it either too easy if you want to sit back and relax or really challenging if you want to keep your A game up but got sick of other PVP games and just need something to wind down to.
Each game is a mastery of a set of patterns, each pattern needs a reaction to said pattern, this game offers just that in a PVE style setup for even the most hardcore gamers and helps you improve as a player without the neccessity of others, but they can still be there if you want to chat others up.
TLDR: The game is good, its for everyone, buy it. You WILL get at least 60 hours of pure enjoyment out of this game and thats already 50 cents an hour you are paying to have a good time. I already got 200 hours of pure enjoyment and STILL COUNTING. I literally just paid 0.6 cents an hour so far for pure entertainment.

Every morning I walk to work and consider what food I should buy on the way. Maybe i'll go into the supermarket and buy a Melon Medley for £1.40, or a Pork Pie for a £1. Maybe i'll go into the little shop at the top of the hill and purchase a bacon and cheese turnover for £1.20 they are pretty damn good. Or if I am feeling really hungry i'll swing by the burger van and buy a slab of greasy beef in a bun with cheese and spend at least £3. All of these options are pretty decent and will saite my hunger for at least a short while. But once they are gone, they are exactly that... gone.
For less than the price of a cheap breakfast you could be in black smokey bullet hell (or heaven depending on your preference). This game doesn't bog you down with story, cutscenes or long loading sequences. You jump in, you get swarmed, you shoot back, pretty simple! The art style reminds me of the real world sections of the Matrix,
the gameplay also evokes the Nebuchadnezzar being attacked by robot squid things, and the soundtrack is a pumping rock jam that goes perfectly with you shooting everything to oblivion.
There isn't much more to say about this game really, it's fun and can be played in short bursts. It scratches that bullet hell twin stick shooter itch, and it's cheaper than breakfast, even really awful breakfast.

Don't let my hours on record fool you as I've spent more time on the mobile version.
This is a Hearthstone clone that pretty much surpasses Hearthstone in most aspects provided you don't mind the anime asthetic. It has something for everyone. There's a fair payment model which allows those who pay money to advance faster while also giving you plenty of ways to earn card packs for free without it feeling like a complete grind. There are some interesting mechanics that can really add to the experience like evolving monsters which boosts their stats and sometimes activates secondary effects. In my experience, there is much better game balancing than most of the competing online CCGs, Hearthstone included. The game also has a single player story mode where you play through the perspective of different characters whilst simultaenously allowing you to earn more cards to use in the multiplayer modes. It won't win any awards for the writing but it does keep you engaged and is suprisingly deep for what was originally a free to play mobile game. ¨
Bottom line, if you're looking for a deep CCG or just a fun way to kill time, you have nothing to lose by checking this game out.

The game wasn't bad, but I give it a cautious recommendation.  If you're looking for smooth difficulty in a JRPG, look elsewhere.  More on that later.
I found the story to be decent, got a few laughs from it and generally enjoyed myself while playing.  Combat is simple, if not a bit easy; you set up combos for your basic attacks(shortly after you start you unlock the ability to exploit weaknesses), use skills/magic, and use a mechanic called Fairize which gives you a boost to your stats, starts a side song, and unlocks a high damage but risky ultimate move.  The cast is not too uncommon for a JRPG, especially if you're familiar with Idea Factory's other games, and whether this is a good or bad thing is up to you.  Art style is not bad, it is the same style that IF uses for their other games(along with how overworld exploration is handled) and mixes JRPG elements with a bit of a VN style for talking.
I give this game a cautious recommendation for a reason though.  While I find it rather solid, there's things that bother me a lot.  The first, and most blatant thing, is how the difficulty is.  Overall I didn't find my journey to be too difficult, and this is including picking up what side Furies(equivalent to a sidequest) I could.  The game is MOSTLY easy, save for several sticking points at seemingly random intervals where the fights are more difficult than anything else in the area(or next area), and that's not even counting area bosses.  Second, a certain major plot point makes it feel like you're playing the same exact stuff again without a change.  Third(this one is more a personal gripe), it felt like the game didn't know where it wanted to go to end until sudden railroad, not as much a buildup other than certain macguffins.  Last, I felt that characters didn't develop as much as I think they should have.
As I've thought more and reflected, I'm going to stick to my guns and give the cautious recommendation.  Will I play it again?  Maybe if I feel like going back to it later, but the postgame stuff doesn't interest me too much.

The original Swarmriders was an absolute blast. High octane action gunning down a swarm while riding in a super fast motorcycle (and also the start point of the titular Blade Saint). But this version improves on the original immensely. As well as the core gameplay of gunning down the huge swarm, there's also the introduction of the Manastrike and the Melter/Shield powerups from the later UBERMOSH games.
The music is just as intense as the action and it really gets the heart racing.
If I did have any complaints then it would be that there is some occasional slowdown when there's a lot going on at once but that doesn't detract from the fun at all.
All in all, very fun and highly recommended. (Though if you're not sure, try the original Swarmriders first. It's free to play.)

TL;DR -> Even if I recommend you play this game, be aware that it's NOT for everyone. This is a jrpg (and a fairly easy one I'd say) with a visual novel-like narration and very interesting characters, lots of grinding and several "meh" plot twists, so if any of this bothers you, you're probably not gonna enjoy it. Otherwise, go for it.
There's plenty of things to dislike in FFF: Running into dungeons for hours because Fire Stones aren't spawning. Those stupid plot twists where almighty gods and creatures are inside people and objects. The fact that the boss hit you for 50 damage and the cutscene's like "AW, MAN, HE'S SOOO STRONG, WE NEED TO RUN AWAY". And about this point, the game's too easy. Enemies do very little damage, and if they do, you've plenty of healing magic to deal with them. Also, Fang is in the game. And even if with time he gest a little better, your first impression of him is that he's a patented ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Not a good quality for your supposed protagonist, isn't it?
But what FFF does good, it does VERY GOOD.
The music is FANTASTIC.
The fact that everytime you break a seal of the Goddess she loses a shard that covers her, and reveals her voluptuous body, keeps you motivated.
The characters are wonderful, and probably the best aspect of the game. Everyone of them has a fairy companion, so you basically interact with a "couple" instead of a single character. These couples are funny and have very well defined personalities: there's the noble-like girl with her pokemon, the lazy girl with a big bald man that scolds her, a dumb and lovely fellow with her fairymom, and, well, a green cat with a blue afro and a sword through his skull, and his sexy male butler. I couldn't make this up even if I wanted.
The point is, it's a funny bunch. It's lively, it's noisy, and it feels like a real adventuring party where everyone is given a bit of spotlight.
Also Harley is the best thing in the game and so is the fanservice regarding all of the female characters.
The combat is also good. You've got this weird combo system instead of a single attack, you can chain combos between allies and air juggle enemies with the right setup. It's not really intuitive, but as soon as you get it, you're gonna go full Soul Calibur on those bizarre monsters.
You can transform, or Fairize if you'd like, and use super-final abilities. Both of those things feel AWESOME every time you watch them, it really spices up your regular jrpg turn-based combat. So even if you're levelling up or grinding WPs, you're not gonna get bored. Well not immediately at least.
WPs are basically experience points to upgrade your characters. It's fun to have it, but you're soon gonna find yourself in the mental state that "you're gonna unlock everything", so it's not like you can "build" characters. Keep that in mind.

This game (and likewise its standalone expansion) is simply stellar. A masterpiece of game design and thoroughly enjoyable and engrossing. Not normally a fan of turn based games, Enemy Unknown/Within is challenging, often brutally so, rewarding and varied.
The game has two main components: a base management side which involves researching new tech, building new facilities, manufacturing weapons/armours and managing "Panic" levels across the world. Picking missions (and their associated rewards) is just as important as actually completing the mission. The other side is the tactical missions during which the player commands a squad of XCOM soldiers on various alien related missions. Soldiers belong to one of four base classes and gain new skills as they level up through experience, making them more powerful, giving more tactical options and so on.
I've played and replayed this multiple times, lost often but despite how difficult it can sometimes be it's so much fun I go back for more. This game cannot be recommended highly enough, a genuine must-buy.

Antichamber is a very special game. It requiers you to think outside the boundaries of game design, logic, and everything you ever known. This is really amazing, but some people might not exactly like this sort of aproach.
First of all, presentation. The graphics are nice. It is an indie game, so don't expect anything incredible, but they work, and make you feel like in a testing chamber, similiar to Portal. The music is quiet and atmospheric, which is really nice, since it doesn't break you concentration.
The gameplay. It is really hard to talk about the gameplay, since every puzzle is mindblowing, and I don't want to spoil anything. You really have to think what to do, do it backwards or even leave and start again elsewhere. This can be a problem, if you played games for your entire life, like me, because of the backtracking. If there is a sign that says go forward, and you return to it 10 minutes later, you may think that you just went back and have to find another way, but you have to remember this game is playing with you. You may also get lost, and that can be fatal in some occasions.
The challenge, along with the puzzles, comes with the time limit. Anyone played the original Prince of Persia? You had one hour to finish the game, otherwise game over. This game is the same. You have 1 hour and 30 minutes, otherwise you start again. The second time you figured out some puzzles, so you can go through the game faster, but it can be tedious for some people to replay the game multiple times in one sitting.
TL;DR - If you are up for the challenge, go ahead. This game creates some very interesting elements and makes you think every second of your playthrough. It is difficult, but it is so refreshing and creative, that this is a must for any puzzle game fan.

Great game. Bought it 4 weeks ago and already played it for 70 hours, of which half singleplayer and half multiplayer.
The economic system is deep, but very easy to get started with. Every resource plays a distinct role and can help (or ruin) you just as much as the others, and each resource can boost the other resources in its own way. Even happiness is a resource that can destroy your civ if you don't have enough of it, and it still all just makes sense.
Talking about military, you won't be managing thousands of units, but just a few. Even though you can see 10 men standing on one tile, the game treats them as one. I'm surprised how simple things are kept in this game, though there's a lot more to discover while playing.
I got it with all DLC during a sale for €10, but if you're used to paying a lot for games, it's worth the full price too. Do NOT buy it without the DLC, the 33% extra for the complete pack is worth it.

At first I thought it was just about dodging walls and awesome music.
Now I realise it's much more than that.
The triangle which you play as wanders aimlessly on a hexagonal plane dodging trapezoids that fall towards it. It realizes it has no friends and only obstacles, and yet even still it tries its best to dodge as many as it can. Try as it might, it will not succeed the first time. It makes you wonder what motive it has to make it through even a minute of this madness. The answer is simple:
It is a thunderous feeling of courage in its heart. It will not give up on its quest to impress even though no one is there to watch. It will prove it is the mightiest of all triangles to ever exist.
Yes, this game is a dangerous and epic quest with a lot of story behind it that just makes you want to shout,
"YOU GOTTA BE KIDDING ME! I DIED AGAIN?"
10/10 best trapezoid dodging simulator I've ever played.

Disregard my hours, I play(ed) this game a lot offline, as well as some on my xbox version of the game.
It's okay. It isn't great, but it is fun in some spots. It has an odd patchwork way of doing things that leave the game feeling like the developers only really worked on the combat and kind of just threw the rest together in a month or so.
The story is terrible and paper-thin, and it isn't the focus of the game. It's just your basic "Oh my god, Aliens! Save us Men-In Black/CIA/X-Com!" And at the very end there's a minor...plot twist? Can you even call it that? Where the enemy reveals why they're here, but the story is lame and not the focus. This is a shame as the game builds up the mystery fairly well, with your advisors comeing up with ponderings and theories off-handedly and leaving players guessing what the enemy wants, but the payoff is pretty weak.
The tech trees are okay, the machinery and Psi powers (And Meld in EU) are all fun to explore, whereas the armor and other ones are just kind of "Meh". Armor is mostly just health upgrades, with the only choices between protection and extra abilities are at the very end, and guns are mostly just more damage, with no real reason to even buy laser before skipping right to plasma.
Base expansion is kind of weird. It feels like it would be better if you were given more building options, but as is there are only a few worthwhile structures and once you have a few of those, then there's really no need to keep building.
Dancing around foreign parties, trying to balance risk and rewards by helping them is great fun for a while, but later on satilites and airforces minimalize this, leaving you with something that used to be heart-racing and fun being just kind of old and dry.
You are given the chance to upgrade your soldiers however you want, but it's a hit and miss system, as some levels for soldiers you really have to make a difficult choice between one really good ability and others there's one good one and one lame one and even a few where both choices are weak.
Be forwarned, this game will not hold you hand at all, and in your first game you'll likely find yourself saving and reloading your saves a lot, even with max tech. This isn't "acceptable" in the community, but this game forced my hand more than once and forced me to do this.
Now what you'll hear critics say how amazing the combat is and it's damn good, easily the best part of the game. With the exceptions of the scripted ones (more on those later) the missions and their combat are well balanced, knowing just how many enemies to throw at you to make the situation dire without throwing so many that it is just bad and no longer fun. It manages to find the perfect spacing for itself and every skimish, no matter how large or small, is a ton of fun and is more than enough to get myself into the zone of the alien invasion. The game is much easier if you carefully prepare for every mission beforehand, but if you merely are competent in your loadouts, you'll be okay if you play carefully.
Some of the missions, especially the ones in EU, are complete and utter garbage. The Newfoundlands mission in EU where there's literally twenty Chrysallids on screen at once?  A terror mission in Siberia where there are literally five Muton brutes where are all meleeing your squad to death? The final mission where I found myself being outnumbered twenty to one? Garbage. The scripted missions seems to fall to the mindset of "The randomly generated missions are fun and well balanced, mixing good combat with a healthy but not overwhelming amount of enemies. So for our scripted ones, let's forgo that and just throw ALL OF THE ENEMIES!!!!!!!1!!!!! at them. Game ot the year.", which is just frustrating. This is one of the only games where the randomly generated missions are way better than the scripted ones, the scripted ones are the ones that I dislike more as the random gen ones seem to be better balanced.
So, overall, this game is fun, but it is also only Okay. The combat and fighting is a ton of fun, but everything else ranges from decent to wall-punchingly bad. This game had the potential to be one of the masterpieces of the generation, but as is it's patchwork strategy is odd. I recommend it, but be ready to take some punishment and be bored with everything that isn't a mission.

This is a fighting game done right, it blocks when you block and attacks when you attack. There's nearly no delay between you pressing the button and your character doing the action. Even more important, almost nothing can keep you from blocking, even if you just pressed the button to attack. There's a gauge filling up every time you successfully block, when it gets full, your character gets knocked down.
When you fail, it feels as if it was your fault and not the game.
Every fight, you gain points (mana) which you can use to spend on skills, some of them are attacks while others are passives.
Choosing and assigning the right skills for the right buttons is essential and quite satisfying when you get a good setup.
Enemies will spawn while you're fighting and will shoot magic at you, which at a certain point, becomes frustrating as you cannot dodge or block them all. On the other hand, if you had killed them more efficiently, they wouldn't have gathered up and bombarded you that much.
Personally I love this game, everything is simple and efficient. You're playing the game, the game is not playing itself.
By that I mean the difference between a defeat and a victory is a combination of how fast your reflex were, how fast thinking and adaptive you are, which skills you've allocated and how aware you are of the current situation.
You can fail a hard level many times, to end up summoning your 1337 skills and beating the very same level with full health.
That's how much control you have over the game.
Important facts,
The story is short but there's at least two modes (Story and Guardian) and unlockable difficulty levels.
There's only one playable character, which is Freesia.
You cannot play this game without a gamepad or USB controller. (You can use gamepad emulators such as VJoy)
