earned a lot of hate for its launch issues on PC, but the publishers at least did the right thing: offered refunds, pulled the PC version off the market, fixed it, and re-released.  That initial PR debacle did a lot to taint PC gamers' views of the game, though.
Many patches later, the game runs just fine, at least on my rig.  I encountered no issues on my playthrough, though, unlike some hardcore gamers, I don't keep an eagle eye on my framerate -- so long as the action continues to look smooth and clear, I'm content.  So, now that the technical aspects pass muster, how's the actual gameplay?
Epic, yet still slightly disappointing.
Content-wise,
is definitely king of the heap, with an enormous main storyline, even before adding in all the option sidequests and DLC.  Riddler puzzles are everywhere, and all the most infamous of Batman's foes come back for one last hurrah.  Lesser lights of the rogue's gallery, like Calendar Man, receive shout-outs, but no screen time, to keep the already-lengthy story from becoming unmanageably bloated.
For this final outing of Rocksteady's Batman, the big selling point was that you could finally drive the Batmobile.  And a good thing, too.  Before
the Batmobile had made some appearances, but was never under player control, making it the single most iconic Bat-gadget that you never got to use. (The second-most iconic gadget withheld from you is probably the Bat-Shark-Repellent, which would have been handy in
.)  Ending the series without putting you behind the wheel of Batman's legendary ride would have felt incomplete.
The result, however, feels a bit like
. Designing the map around the possibility of driving meant opening up from the impossibly cramped, narrow streets of
and
which could never have supported car chases and vehicular battles.  The resulting Gotham, therefore, feels less like a labyrinthine urban rat-warren of decay and corruption. Highways and boulevards allow Batman to experience, at ground level, a sense of freedom that previous titles made available only if you took to the rooftops.  I'm sure that
's Gotham is a much nicer place to live than any previous
environment, but that makes it a bit less atmospheric than the previous games.
Make no mistake, Gotham is still Gotham, rife with corruption, filth, decay, poverty, crime, injustice, desperation, and appallingly bad urban planning. The underbelly of the city is still openly on display.  The needs of the Batmobile-based gameplay simply required an environment that could no longer be composed of 100% underbelly.
The Batmobile ends up being as much a liability as an asset to the game, though.  While driving the Batmobile is fun, swooping around the city with your grapnel gun and hang-glider cape remains more fun, as well as a more efficient way to get around.  So, once the initial thrill of driving the Batmobile has faded, the game has to keep finding ways to force you back into the car.  Sometimes these are logical and plausible (e.g. transporting a prisoner in the Batmobile while evading pursuers) and sometimes they are blatantly contrived -- the Riddler has constructed a series of underground racetracks at evidently tremendous effort and expense, so he can prove that he is your intellectual superior because... you don't drive fast enough???  Like many of the driving-based elements in
, it doesn't make much sense in any context beyond "We put a lot of work into that car, so you're going to bloody well
it!"
The "scene reconstruction" mechanic that
added to the investigative parts of the game is here again, and works better than last time.  Free Flow combat, too, is better than ever.  Predator segments, conversely, feel largely the same as before, despite the addition of a few new tricks and enemy types. Predator play was the best part of the game ever since
, though, so it's not much of a complaint that Rocksteady couldn't seriously improve on something already great.
Chasing APCs through the streets of Gotham is a new element of play, and rather fun, though I feel that it gets somewhat overused.  Switching the Batmobile into a highly mobile "tank" mode and battling it out with killer drone vehicles also comes in for heavy repetition.
This latter part of the game has come in for a lot of criticism.  Tank battles, many say, even if you find them fun, have no place in Batman's world.  Batman, this reasoning goes, should lurk in the shadows and punch goons in the head.  He should use darkness, fear, deception, gadgetry, and his own physical strength to battle foes, not machine guns and anti-materiel cannons.  I disagree. To me, a Batman who's out in the middle of the street using high-powered weapons to battle scores of robot tanks still feels like Batman... just not business-as-usual Batman.  This is a desperate Batman, a Batman pushed to the wall, a Batman who has pulled out all the stops and called up his entire array of reserve tools and contingency plans.  This is a Batman who might even cross his one uncrossable line.  For a series finale, the sense that the Dark Knight has held nothing back this time around is particularly appropriate.
Greater emphasis on Bat-family characters is extremely fitting here, too.  While in
Batman outright states that he has no objection to dying to protect Gotham, in
he isn't merely accepting his own end -- he's expecting it. Accordingly, this post-Arkham-City Batman is suddenly concerned about issues of legacy: whether his efforts will ultimately have made Gotham a better or worse place, once he's no longer around to solve problems in person; whether he has helped those he took as allies, or harmed them in service of his own crusade; how he can ensure his protection of Gotham extends past his own demise.  There's an undergoing meditation on death running through this game; when the ethos of a hero is "win, or die trying," how can the hero accept the inevitability of death without also accepting defeat?
I view
as second-best of the
games, after
, and that only because of how often Batmobile segments seem to have been forcibly shoehorned in to a plotline that didn't need them.  The DLC, sadly, is another matter altogether, but if considering the base game alone, this series ended on a high note.

Note: I've played this game since 2011, when it was still a browser game called Red Crucible 2 and probably have more like 50 hours of game time.
Essentially, Red Crucible: Firestorm is still a browser game, just Red Crucible 2 with a fancy (and annoyingly convoluted) new UI slapped on. It's just another generic first person shooter with no personality.
"Don't be too hard on it. It's free-to-play!" -a reasonable point.
However, to call this game free-to-play would be a stretch at best.
"Features of the "free-to-play" model:
1. Consumables-LOTS of consumables. They sell experience and damage boosts that last 10 MINUTES. That's right, folks. Just pay about 25 cents worth of premium currency or some in game currency and you can get a little extra experience for a single round. You want to have extra experience for an hour? That will cost you about $1.50. Same thing goes for grenades, airstrikes, and medpacks. You have to buy all of those with currency or premium currency 1 at a time, which may seem cheap, but it adds up.
2. Weapon upgrades. Most FPS games have a variety of different weapons that suit different roles but have tradeoffs i.e. higher damage but higher recoil, higher accuracy but lower rate of fire. Not in Red Crucible: Firestorm.
In Red Crucible Firestorm, you PAY a lot of in game currency or real money to UPGRADE your weapons. That's right: the damage goes up with NO DOWNSIDES. You do unlock new weapons as you level up, BUT they are essentialy carbon copies of each other with higher damage.
3. Armor upgrades-To go along with the weapon upgrades, you can buy and upgrade your armor with a lot of in game currency or real money. This offsets the advantage from upgrading your weapons.
4. Premium weapons. You can buy premium weapons for 300-1000 coins or 30,000-100,000 "honor points," in game currency. This translates to prices of $10-$15 for a single weapon!!! And you can only buy coins in weird increments of 250, 750, 875, etc., forcing you to pay for more than you need. And buying with honor points? Forget it. It would take thousands of hours to get that many honor points from playing the games.
IN CONCLUSION: In addition to tons of crappy consumables, you have to constantly upgrade your weapons and armor as you level up. These armor and weapon upgrades cancel each other out, leaving you with a net gain of 0, but if you don't upgrade or get better ones, you'll get left in the dust. The top tier automatic weapons can one-shot kill you many times over if you don't pay a ton to upgrade your armor. Also premium weapons are really expensive.
Other cons:
1. Graphics-They're what you'd expect from an internet flash game: bad by today's standards, maybe decent back in 2007.
2. User Interface-It's terrible. Tons of nested menus and drop down bars. It's bad.
3. Matchmaking-You often get placed in matches with people many levels above you. This means that they can one shot you with an upgraded version of the same gun you're using. You don't stand a chance.
TL;DR: 3/10 Play it for the laughs. NEVER spend money.

I didn't know where to put this review. I've gone from Pokemon to MTG to Hearthstone to a brief stint in Duelyst to this, and I don't really think it's the strongest out there. Like Hearthstone, it's very snowball-ey. where aggro wins because they dictate trades. In a game like MTG, defenders control much more of the pace, which inherently allows slower decks to operate. The game also has a lot of pretty weird mechanics and busted cards, and while thats nice for a new player to know what the first card the should craft is, it's not really as fun as a diverse game. Similar to Patches in Hearthstone, it sucks the joy out of the game.
However, despite all this, the "gimmick" of evolving guys is well done, and it feels more balanced than, say, the coin. Some mechanics are pretty solid, easy to learn, and reward both slow and fast decks. Ultimately, it's a good experience, but I like MTG and Hearthstone more than I do this game. If you don't have the budget for those games, though, this is a really F2P-friendly game that offers you so much reward if you put in the time, so for those players, this game is great.
Tl;dr - good F2P and a good experience, but I prefer Hearthstone and MTG

I am definitely a fan of this 3D asset creation software.  It is like a more powerful version of Sculptris that can actually handle editing models made elsewhere as well.
This is something (along with a seemingly natural companion of Silo 2) that really helped save my interest in learning to create and work with 3D models.  Many other suites are insanely overwhelming to get started with, such as the admirable but frustrating for many Blender.  Curvy is fast, you can start creating and manipulating shapes immediately without even studying up, even for a total first time user.
As I've progressed, learned about the pipelines and purchased far more expensive programs - I find myself still using Curvy.  It really is great for fast organic shaped model creation.  The ability to sketch a 2D shape and have it pop into 3D is fairly handy.  Surprisingly I also find myself using it as a sculpting tool for models I've created elsewhere as well.  Sure it is not Zbrush or Mudbox or even 3D Coat, but for my purposes as an indie game dev (working within the constraints of multiple platforms) those programs are total overkill anyway.  The power they provide (I do own 3D Coat) requires too much time investment to make it worth it to me and even if utilized, would be fairly wasted somewhere like Unity where a single mesh is limited to 65k polys (unless you are ok with it being chopped into parts like perhaps a static prop).
The one thing I really wish Curvy could do is import and edit 3D models in FBX file format.  This would allow me to work on models that have already been rigged (for this I must use 3D Coat).  However I find Curvy worth using in the early prototype stages of all my models even still.
There are some tricks to learn, such as the fact that importing an OBJ will collapse all of the 'subparts' into a single mesh listed in the scene... however this can be easily 'exploded' into all the parts it was built with in some other program through a menu option.
All in all I think this software would be good for anyone looking to enter the 3D creation world, and probably a very fun quick prototyping tool for anyone that is already familiar with 3D assets.
PS - It seems like all the negative reviews are from people misusing this software - trying to use the sketching like it is CAD or trying to create hardedge extrusion styled models.  As long as you understand what Curvy is and need the functionality, I think you'll be happy.

Let's get the good stuff out of the way first. Great destructible environment, longer story mode, more side quests and tougher riddles.  Good depth in the story (predictable villain reveal but good build-up) plus quality voice acting as usual. Higher number of upgrades and more grappling strength makes it more fun to glide around compared to previous Arkham games. But that's about where it all ends.
Now, having played the first 3 games of the series, I had decent expectations from this game despite this being the only Arkham game to have a number of thumbs down reviews right on the first page of the game's review section. I really wanted to give this game a chance but the clunky controls and horribly mistimed, overcomplicated combat blew it. Aside from repeating what others have said about the quality of the PC port, the gameplay is extremely flawed.
Let's first explore the combat system - it's been absolutely butchered. Why fix something that was never broken in the first place?! I can't time my moves with the same fluidity as Origins let alone City. Then there's the overcomplicated combo takedown prompt which prompts me to perform the worst combo at the worst time on the enemy it will be LEAST effective so I end up punching enemies with shields or electric batons and shooting myself in the foot. Not to mention the badly-timed Batmobile and Oracle takedowns which are THE worst ways to take down any enemy. I lost count of the number of times I wanted to throttle Bats since he kept doing the opposite of what I wanted in pretty much every situation, stealth and combat. Also, for some odd reason Bat's sliding fluency has decreased, proving that once again as a developer you can ruin the most simplest of things if you put enough lack of effort into it.
Speaking of the Batmobile, apart from constantly shoving it down our throats, Rocksteady seemed to think it was a good idea to replace proper boss battles with a World of Tanks emulator, ruining a potentially epic fistfight between Bats and the AK.  Oh and since the Batmobile's handling is SO great, we're given another chance to smash our heads in by having to go through Riddler's mind-numbingly frustrating races. To be fair, it was a good idea but was almost completely ruined by the Shitmobile's 'fabulous' handling.
All in all, the Batmobile's inclusion and campaign length could potentially have made this the best game of the franchise. But what we got was an absolutely horrendous piece of game development and Batmobile-saturation, totally ruining what was once a great franchise.
Do not buy under any circumstances unless you're a die-die-die hard Arkham fan. In terms of ruining franchises this game is right up there with what Ubisoft did with Assassins's Creed 3, Unity and Syndicate. It's games like these that  turn loyal franchise fans into pirates.

FTL is a fantastic roguelike indie title set in space. I highly recommend picking it up (there's a free expansion comming in 2014 too)
The aim of the game is to control a ship and its crew to explore sectors of space and keep one step ahead of the rebels, who will follow you through the stars in hopes of destroying you.
Can you survive to the last sector and destroy the Rebel flagship? -I wouldn't count on it in your first play through!

FTL can be very challenging at times and you'll see your self die a lot(permadeath) before getting to the final stand, but just start a new save, choose your ship, and you have a completely different universe to explore complete with randomly generated events and sectors, keeping the experience fresh each time.
There is also a huge amount of replayability and diversity of tactics in this game. There are huge array of tactics you may employ; from laser beams, ion cannons that disable systems on ships, missiles that penetrate sheilds, teleporting devices to raid enemy ships and many more weapons and systems you can upgrade and buy for your ship. You may also unlock new ships by following certain quests and befriending various races in the game.
FTL also has an active modding community adding even more features to the game. All-in-all this is a fantastic game for £6.99 adding many hours of replayability and fun.

When playing ranked matches as a beginner in Beginner rank, nearly every opponent (like 4/5) played against has a netdeck full of legendary and gold cards. A new player normally would not be able to get these rare, expensive cards, but some players will continually reroll (starting the entire game over) to make use of the starting 10 packs per expansion. Players get to keep trying to get lots of legendary cards. Once they do, they liquefy all those cards besides the ones they need for the netdeck, obtaining vials. These vials are then used to purchase the exact cards from the chosen netdeck. In this way, many new players instantly have competitive decks, but can only use that one deck. All other players who did not do this are then forced to fight against competitive decks in beginner rank, making them lose over and over again.
In summary, beginners either have to get themselves stuck with one deck or use the basic cards and be overwhelmed by netdecks right from the start.

I've bought OOTP almost every year since before OOTP 6 (when it was part of the Sports Interactive stable). I think to make this review different and add something worthwhile I'll compare it very briefly to Football Manager.
Wheras in FM the main gets more complex every year, adding aspects to the role of a manager that no real life manager would ever deal with.
For instance a Premiership manager who deals with what a right back in his under 19 squad does in training on a Wednesday afternoon  - to the point they have had to create a second game (3 really) with "Touch" and "Handheld" being lighter and probably more realistic analogies of what a manager - a single person in the organisation - actually does.
OOTP adds depth but NOT complexity. The game has for many years been split in two Manager and General Manager with the option to do both if you want, but never to confuse the roles in the way FM seems to confuse manager and coach (and trainer and physio and marketing director and media manager and boot boy and....). The amount of micro managing in OOTP is still pretty high, (though this can be varied with game options) but it's also pretty consistent. It's the game engine that adds the depth - not just piling on more responsibilities onto one man in the way FM does.
The problem is the way FM feels when you lose and you HAVEN'T micromanaged down to the Nth degree. Like "I could have dug deeper and done something to prevent that) - and in that way madness lies. I've played a 6 hour session of FM before now and in that time the club played 9 games.  Then you get sick of the time it's taking -  turn on all the auto options, the club loses 4 out of 5 games and you think "I'd better go back to spending almost an hour prep on each game doing stuff that no RL manager would ever even consider doing - just to prevent that happening again". For me that's when FM feels a lot more like a crazy time management job than a game. I tinker with aspects and sit there thinking "Who in the hell does all of this IRL?"
In OOTP I never feel like that. My remit is clear
Importantly
in OOTP your success as a GM or M are based on your performance in that specific role. You can be a great manager getting the best out of a poor club or some poor decisions made by the GM - and vice versa. The game acknowledges your own success in your own specific role without making you think you need to jump a fence and take on extra "plate spinning" responsibilities and do the work other members of your organisation should be doing. FM will be adding "Emmersive boot shining and shirt ironing" responsibilities for premiership managers next - just to add depth to the game... no thanks. That's not what a manager does - that's what a game developer does when he thinks they HAVE TO add more "STUFF" every year
Sorry I think I've made the point :)
Simming?
--------------
Simming - Almost every OOTP player sims by week or month or even by season. Perhaps playing "inning by inning" or" at bat by at bat" just in key games here and there. Baseball is about long lasting trends of players. A rookie might take 2 seasons to develop - and needs playing time at the appropriate level to do so. Your owner might set you a goal to win the division or pennant in 4 years and expect you to do pretty poorly as"rebuild years" are a real thing in Baseball that are accepted by almost everyone - even the fans. It's a very different sort of game though back in 2006 they looked pretty similar
If you love Baseball this is THE management game management version of the game - with  MLB The Show (sadly only on PS4) being the arcade version. If you love text based sims (spreadsheet sims) then this rivals or beats FM but actually plays quite differently
Of course I recommend it. A fantastic game that, if you love text sports sims and/or baseball will swallow hundreds of hours and you'll enjoy almost every second of it.

Been playing this game since '16 came out.  I now no longer play fanatasy sports of any kind.  Honeslty, I'm trying to get me old FB league to move to this.  The game is so deep and there is so much to do.  You can do it all or you can hire people and assign them tasks to take over.  I started with a fictional league based on the teams that existed (but not the players) and league structure from when Ken Griffey Jr. Presents MLB was made for the SNES.  That was the first great baseball game I ever played.  I kept the structure with no wild card, but my league my eventually adopt one.  I wanted the Pirate's GM job at first, being from PGH but it wasn't available.  So I took over the White Sox and held a league inagural draft.  I did pretty well and within 5 seasons I won the Series.  I immediately (and I mean before the parade), jumped ship to Pittsburgh, who coincidentially I had just beaten for the crown.
One of the best parts is that I find myself following both teams,  After the move I wondered if I had sold out the CWS for my one ring before I went to the team I wanted to really make great.  Turns out I didn't even make the playoffs in PGH but the CWS went back-to-back WS champs.  I felt a sense of accomplishment for that though only the shadow of my influence was left there.  Regardless, I was rooting for them.  I also find myself rooting for players, be they guys I took a flyer on or guys I had to let go.  Following careers and debating HOF qualifications in my head for this league has been an absolute blast.
In my opinion, the game is better than just a spreadsheet manager type game.  If you allow yourself to get immersed in the goings on of your league it can be like an encyclopedia of a history of baseball that only exisits as 1s and 0s on your hard drive.
I highly recommend.

This program has a lot of potential, but altogether I can't suggest it. Especially not for the absurd original price of $99.99. I was fortunate to get this program for free from a friend, and I feel bad for him having spent $25 on this, in my opinion this program falls short of even delivering what someone would expect from a $25 pricetag.
Here's what I think is wrong with this program.
1) It's big deal is that it has sculping capabilities. However, there is a free program out there named Sculptris that does this function 100 times better, is easier to learn, works faster, and is overall less of a headache.
2) This program has very basic CAD features (if you could call it that). I tried making some very basic models in this such as an early-era tank, you can't ask for something more blocky or basic than that. With a software of this asking price, you should EXPECT an experienced 3d sculptor to produce a convincing 3d tank in short order... however this program was so backwards that even the CAD in it isn't worth your time.
So who would want this software?
If you're a professional, or trying to produce professional work, I don't advise this software unless you have a lot of time on your hands to get really good with it. The program itself isn't very intuitive compared to other ones I've seen. And for the pricetag, this program seems like a joke when there's so many free programs out there that you can pick up, and out-perform this one. If you really want to get some sculpting software, save yourself a lot of money and just pick up Sculptris. If you want to blend CAD and sculpting, you can import models (in .obj format) into Sculptris and work on them from there.
I can't advise this to hobbyists because as I've said a number of times, there's free softwares out there now for this sort of thing, and honestly this program seems to have a lot less love or thought put into it, making you have to work harder to produce the same thing you could elsewhere... I can't imagine who'd want to spend $100 on software when there's a free alternative that works better.
So my final verdict of who would want this software is merely someone who's okay with spending $100 for an advanced sculpting toy and don't mind taking your time to play around, then this might be a bit of fun. It's true you can produce some great things with this software, but you're going to have to spend a lot of time learning it.

I feel that after spending about 3 - 4 hours with the PC port and many, MANY hours in Dead Rising as a whole, I can safely write a relatively well constructed review.
I imagine most of you out there are reading this because you want to gauge whether or not this is a good port, and I am happy to say that it is a great one.
There aren't an absurd amount of customizable options, however, I feel that there are enough options that allow you to alter the graphical settings as well as the controller/keyboard settings. Plus, changes can be made on the fly and don't require restarts or launchers, which is always nice.
The framerate is uncapped if you so desire and the keyboard controls can be completely rebound, which is excellent.
Even during the most hectic of moments I found that the framerate was very stable, only noticing the occasional minor drop as the screen is completely flooded with zombies.
Loading screens are nice and fast too, barely giving you enough time to register the image on screen before you're instantly loaded back into the next location, which is superb as you will be passing through loading screens quite often throughout the game.
Lastly, the addition of 5 save slots is very welcome as the original only had one, but being able to save onto multiple slots throughout allows for you to split off from the story and try out other possibilites without having to start over, which I adore due to the always ticking clock and time management aspects of the game.
In terms of negatives, I personally don't have any, but I wish to include some anyway just in case they affect you.
- It has been reported that save files have known to become corrupted on a number of different systems, I'm not entirely sure of what causes this, but I hope they fix it soon.
- It has also been reported in other reviews that occasionally the user is greeted with a "Failed to Initialize DirectX" message when trying to launch the game, which affects a number of systems and is fixable, however, this issue really shouldn't be here at all and I hope they get around to fixing that too.
While none of these issues affect me, that doesn't mean that they don't exist and it's possible that they will affect you as a result, so please do a little bit of research prior to purchase so you know what you're getting into. The Steam Refund is there for a reason, after all.
Finally, in terms of Dead Rising itself, I adore it.
It's one of my favourite games of all time from "way back" on the 360 over 10 years ago, and to this day I still feel that it holds up remarkably well despite it's problems, boasting some over-the-top violence while still sporting a well thought out story with lots of neat little ideas to boot.
I have played through this game so many times in the past, and I fully intend to play through it many more now that it has finally come to PC.
I'm giving it a very solid recommendation, for both newcomers to the series and to those that played it when it was first released.

When Killing Floor 2 was still in Early Access I wrote a negative review for it. One of the biggest complaints that I had was underpowered weapons, warping enemies, neglective developer feedback amongst other things, but the microtransaction system took the cake. Killing Floor 2 was still months from being finished, but they already had a working, fully finished microtransaction system cashing  players. Ironically Tripwire advertised their title as being "Early Access Done Right".
I chose to forget the game and let it sink to it's own oblivion, but after it's release Killing Floor 2 has been gathering a steady influx of positive reviews and my curiosity was awekened. Seems like Tripwire began listening to players and tailored the game more to their will. I bought the game, and now after couple of hours I really think that Killing Floor is back. There's no annoying enemy warping, guns feel better, action is better than ever and overall the whole game play tastes sweet as ever. The game has been updated recently with a new map, weapon and a gamemode, and this came in for free. As it should be. Tripwire has earned their respect back.
If you liked Killing Floor, you'll like Killing Floor 2 too. It's similar enough to Killing Floor to make old fans feel like home, but it has enough new stuff to earn it's title as a sequel.

Sick of Heathstone with its ever-increasing barrier of entry and difficulty of keeping up with the meta? Spending hundreds/thousands of dollars on a game, only to be rewarded with higher pack prices, and a forced meta they decide with every expansion? Or maybe you just aren’t a fan of the RNG “clown fiesta” that most matches become. To be fair, I used to love the game. Blizzard took a lot of elements I liked about Magic: The Gathering and did away with some things I disliked, and made a really great game. I’ve played off and on for months at a time since open beta, and have had some of the most fun I’ve had in a game while playing it. With all of the money I’ve invested in it, I’ve been pretty bummed out by recent design decisions along with some of their commercial shifts. So much so that I uninstalled the app from my phone and haven’t logged in on desktop for quite some time.
Enter Shadowverse. Before I offer my opinions on the game, I should also say that I also played a lot of Rage of Bahamut on my phone (the order I was in was ranked #5 in the world competitively). To be quite honest, it wasn’t that great of a game mechanically, but I was hooked – mainly on the social aspect and the artwork. I stopped playing a bit before they shut down their servers in North America, but I was pretty sad to see it go. So along comes this offering from Cygames. I was surprised to see they had repurposed (and preserved) a lot of the art from RoB. As a huge fan of it (I’m still an anime nerd, after all), I was immediately intrigued. I soon discovered the game plays a lot like Hearthstone but also has some really interesting design choices. Things like being able to evolve followers (minions, creatures etc.) at certain points in the match, making them much stronger and in some cases activating certain abilities. It has a lot of mechanics that you’d expect in a game like this (ambush = stealth, storm = charge, fanfare = battlecry, last words = deathrattle and so on). There are class-specific cards that can only be played with that leader (hero, basically) and a pool of neutral cards that can be used in any deck. The cards you get can be liquefied (dusted) for vials that you use to create the cards you want, with the rarity determining their respective worth. The meta on the ladder is pretty healthy at the moment, and there are a myriad of ways to build decks within their respective archetypes. The classes all have distinct mechanics akin to Hero Powers that differentiate them from one another, making their identities really stand out. They also have a pretty engaging solo story mode for each class you can play, allowing you to earn rewards while learning how the play the class. This makes it a unique digital CCG while remaining intuitively familiar.
Where it really shines though is its F2P system. While not as generous as say, Eternal, you are handsomely rewarded for your playtime and efforts. You get a ton of free packs as a new player (10 from each expansion, if I'm not mistaken), and a lot of tickets for packs and gold to buy them with as you play the various solo and multiplayer game modes. I don’t play a lot of Take Two, the Shadowverse equivalent of Hearthstone’s Arena, but its reward system is also nice. You’re provided 4 cards in a 2 pairs at a time, and you a pick a pair of them until the deck is complete. As with Hearthstone, these aren’t yours to keep, however (unlike Eternal’s drafting system). You then play a 5 match game – 5 matches total, win or lose, and are rewarded at the very least a ticket for a free card pack. You can play this mode by entering with tickets or gold you earn throughout the game. If you’re any good at it, it may be more profitable than outright buying packs themselves (I personally don’t play it that much is I have a hard time evaluating the best choices to make.). With all of that said, they are a business after all, and developers need to get paid, so pretty much all of this can be bought with crystals, an in-game currency you can buy with cash. I’ve spent a bit on it, but its reasonably priced, and considering the fun I’ve had and the amount of time I’ve been playing, I figure it’s worth it.
I didn’t touch on the ladder ranking system (it’s pretty grindy, but the rewards are worth it), the rest of the MTX available for purchase, or some of the other features in the game because those are worth checking out on your own. If you’re over Hearthstone – or even if you completely love it (or perhaps you have never played it all, but enjoy CCGs like MTG, Hex, Eternal etc.) this game is definitely one you should consider trying out.

Teleglitch is a top-down roguelike game. Instantly familiar if you've played the multitude of other titles in this hybrid genre such as Binding of Isaac or Enter the Gungeon. For those not in the know the concept is simple. You (typically) have one life and must traverse as much of the procedurally generated hostile environment presented to you as possible, delving deeper into the dungeon, upgrading your character and weapons along the way.

Where Teleglitch diverges significantly, in my opinion, however is the level variety, item management and aforementioned player upgrades. Unlike similar titles there is very little in Teleglitch which is permanent or can be taken for granted. A fairly comprehensive crafting system ups the tension massively, meaning the next crate or enemy could hold those rifle rounds or metal plate you desperately need to restock your guns or create an extra layer of armour or some revolver bullets that you don't even have a gun to fire out of.
In more depth, the levels, while procedurally generated avoid feeling samey. There are certain set pieces that recur but the oppressive tight corridors never really lose their impact, wide open spaces always make your hairs stand up, not sure if you should be expecting a rush of zombies, or...nothing at all. Myriad secret areas carefully hidden in the walls keep things fresh despite multiple playthroughs and the option on where to go next at the end of each stage allow you to tailor your game experience easily, a surprisingly detailed story is also present for you to explore, hidden away in text form on terminals in each level allowing to expand your knowledge of the facility you are trying to escape from.

The weapons are also very much worth writing about. When you first start you are usually provided with a unique weapon or item to aid you on your journey, however your melee attack will become very familiar very quickly as you pick apart the facility looking for any trace of ammunition. Not only can weapons be upgraded, they can also be combined, making for some staggering firepower if you're lucky, but 'use it or lose it' has never been more relevant since a few points of health or armour lost in an encounter can be the difference between success or failure.
In short, if you're tired of other roguelike shooters, try this one. The difficulty can be crushing at first, but each small success is so much more rewarding that simply getting lucky at the end of the stage and rolling that one upgrade that carries you to endgame. A comprehensive in-game encyclopaedia of enemies, items and crafting combos (that decode as you find them) also provides a great incentive to progress, maybe this time you'll kill that Armoured Walker with the Quad-Barrel Nailgun?
Average Game Length? Minutes to an hour or so, depending on skill and a little luck.

A Bit Like? Binding of Isaac, Smash TV, Quake
Is It Fun? Absolutely. Few games nail experience, aesthetic and gameplay quite as hard as Teleglitch. Don't be put off by the graphics.

Everyone will have a different opinion about things - for
, this game is one of my favourites. I have never uninstalled it. We have a special relationship; probably one of those relationships that involves a "safe word."
This game consistently kicks me around, no matter how many times I try playing it. It's like a suspense-heavy Quake, only 2D. This lets it be 'twin-stick.'
I love the lo-fi sci-fi atmosphere, like "Alien."
I love the gritty, visceral gunplay. This shotgun is
a fallback weapon.
I love the UI, after figuring it out... it's elegant. Crafting things really gives an edge, too.
I love doing a whole bunch of things, like selecting a new machine gun, pressing "q" to empty its ammo, then loading all those bullets into the monster drum-fed tommygun I just patched together from scavenged parts. That's a lot of interaction, for a simple-looking 2D shooter.
There are lots of things that crunch, or click, or buzz, or hum, and for an abandoned military facility there's no shortage of character here.
It's like a modern horror film with zombies that sprint, in a retro Ridley Scott future, where Sigourney Weaver decides it's time to play Hotline Miami. I am not kidding you.
I have
gotten far in this game, I've had it for years, and I still indulge myself in it frequently. If you get it on sale or not, throw a couple bucks at this thing. Money comes and goes, right? This has been a lurking presence on my hard-drive that gives me nostalgia, and curiosity, and an endless dark well of dread. This game is my little icky undead cyberzombie sweetheart. A surprisingly good hidden gem, this game's combo and skill system leave a lot of room for depth and mastery, and while the story is a little short, the game sports a "Guardian Mode" that pits you against wave after wave of enemies which beefs up the length of the game quite a bit.
The gameplay itself is like an extremely well fleshed out 2D beat em up, and if you've played games like Devil May Cry 3 and 4, then fimiliar skills like Just Defense and a launcher attack used to juggle enemies in air combos will stick out immediately, though the game's 2D environment adds mechanics like launching enemies into other enemies for crowd control.
A fair warning though, if you do buy this game, buy it for the gameplay only. The story is essentially spelled out in the box blurb it's so simple, and the character art and enemy design is nothing special, even bland at times. Overall though, Fairy Bloom Freesia will more than satisfy 2D action lovers, and is well worth it's low price point.

It has potential. Its also a little odd that people who played it for only a few minutes bash it. Early Access games are always in different stages of completion when released to us and I think a lot of people forget that. rather they think that being a Steam member means that they get exclusive access to a nearly finished game...because they were awesome enough to install Steam. I really enjoy watching Early Access games develop while others seem to become disenchanted with the process. Those folks should just stay away from Early Access. It only aggravates them.
After playing for a little while (and Im not sure why Steam has my time so low) I can tell what they are trying to achieve. It feels like a cross between Battlefield, Insurgency, and older CoD. Since the player has the ability to set various mine types, toss various grenades, AND call in an air strike, it really give each player the ability to change the course of a battle. That is something that is missing in certain games like Insurgency or the other two aforementioned. Since a class system limits your ability to effect change during a battle, you do not always have an opportunity to be a "game-changer". If the devs stick with this, and polish the game to completion, this will become the central feature that will make this game different than others. Just try it out and you'll see what I mean. How many times were you playing BF, CoD, or even Insurgency and you see an opportunity to do something but cant due to class restriction? I know there are many times that I see a tactical strike or manuever that I cant do but someone else can...and they miss that window...and Im screaming at the monitor. In Red Crucible there are less missed opportunities. And that makes the basic structure of the gameplay and character foundation refreshing.
BTW, its free. Just try it out. It downloads in seconds...literally.

This game bounced back pretty well after one of the worst PC launches of all time, but it still has its problems. It wouldn't be judged as harshly as it is if we didn't have the gold standards of Arkham Asylum and City to compare it to, but thankfully those two exist, so the shortcomings of Knight are a lot more visible.
First off though, the game looks absolutely amazing. And they really worked on the optimisation to make it run pretty decently on older systems as well. Music is ok, good but nothing memorable. Voice work is, as expected, stellar from Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamill, but Jonathan Banks (Mike from Breaking Bad) sounds a bit flat as Jim Gordon. The others are fine, though Riddler's voice will start to annoy the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you after a while.
On to gameplay, it's the same tried and tested formula of the Arkham series with some minor improvements, and a major one: the Batmobile. It really does feel like a billion dollar toy to ♥♥♥♥ up the bad guys' day with, but if I have one problem with it, it's that it's way overused. It would've great for just conveyance and the occasional fights, but it's clear that a lot of story and side missions were put in with the express purpose of using it without much thought. Why would the riddler create gigantic, badly booby-trapped race courses in the tunnels under the city? Why would the most skilled mercenary in the DC Universe, who's also a hand-to-hand combat expert, choose to face Batman in a tank battle, when Batman's destroyed hundreds of weaponized drones with the same tank in one night?
Finally coming to the most important part, that is the story, and to me, it's the weakest of the series even counting Arkham Origins. It might be a bit better for those who aren't familiar with one of the most acclaimed Batman stories ever told, but it borrows heavily from that story while making certain changes that I feel were not for the better. They certainly lied when they said the Arkham Knight was a "completely new" character in the lead-up to releasing the game; repackaging something doesn't make it new. Setting aside the Knight, Scarecrow is an OK main antagonist, though he doesn't get too much to do aside from monologue you about fear throughout the game.
Final thoughts: it's a pretty great game gameplay-wise, though it most probably
get repetitive after a certain point. Rocksteady tried to stuff too much into the game instead of the delicate balance between quality and quantity they had achieved in Asylum and City. But I'll still rate it positive because I did have a good time with it, flaws and all.
Final final thought: 243 stupid Riddler trophies for the honor of fighting him in a bad boss battle and an ending cutscene? ♥♥♥♥ing seriously?! I'll just watch that♥♥♥♥♥♥on Youtube, thank you very much.

WARNING: this game will frustrate you to no end.  Even on Easy mode.  Hours and hours of playtime later, I have not managed to beat the Rebel Fleet Leader.  But I was *SO* close...
In FTL, you have to jump across the universe, one sector of space at a time, fighting things that get in your way, in order to find the last remnants of the Federation and confront the massive leader of the Rebel Fleet.  There are a variety of ways to do this and a variety of ships to do it with, but what's important to note is the following:
1. Every choice you make will come out slightly differently in every playthrough of the game.  Effectively, virtual dice rolls are the reason that on your first playthrough the giant spiders killed you, but when you find them again on your third playthrough, you crush them and rescue the space station.
2. Death is permanent.  As soon as you die, that's it.  No save games, no restore points, no extra lives.  Be smart about your hull strength!
3. Every playthrough will be completely different because the universal map is randomized every time.  You could find yourself choosing between Engi and Zoltan worlds at one junction one game (they're both quasi-friendly races), and Rock and Slug worlds at the next (they are *not* quasi-friendly...in fact, more often than not, they're usually just not friendly).  And the different locations in each sector are different every time.  (As in, if you're running out of fuel, you had better hope that this sector contains a store to buy fuel from...)
The game is amazing because of all of this, though.  There are literally hundreds of different strategies to try on each playthrough!  Maybe this time you want to focus on all energy weapons, and you can; next time you could put shields to max instead and rely on drones, or destroy your enemies from the inside by beaming an away team to the opposing ship and killing their captain.  The choices you make are what makes the game fun.  And the infuriating nature of the game is so well directed that it makes you want to take out your frustration on the "New Game" button until you win!
Oh, and it's made by an independent game studio.  Which, in and of itself, is full of win.

Reasons to like Curvy:
1- Can I run it?  Yep... Curvy runs on nearly anything, doesn't even need a separate graphics card.  Desktop, Laptop, Windows Pro Tablet... it doesn't matter (This benefit probably requires the UI to be barebones.)
2- What are licensing restrictions?  None.  Short of trying to sell Curvy's code, UI, or pictures associated with it... the License is quite friendly.  If you can make money commercially with Curvy, then do it.  There's no cap limitations.
3- It has a Wine option for Linux users
4- It has increasing and decreasing geometry tools in fractions.(update: this seems to be percents now)
5- It is the only 3D program that is ready for 3d work in 4 seconds on my laptop
Reasons not to like Curvy:
1- You don't own a tablet
2- You can't draw well enough that other people know what you are drawing
3- You wouldn't watch videos on how to use this software unless it would keep a zombie apocalypse at bay.
4- You don't like drawing living things
5- You are entirely unwilling to learn the 1 to 4 line(s) lathe first, magic glue second, sculpt third workflow and instead figure, I'll just use it like sculptris. (this is called throwing efficiency out of the window... of a 20 story building.)
* a 64 bit version is now included, so the million count issues should be a thing of the past.
Things to Know:
1- Curvy has redraw options.  You know you shouldn't draw with that mouse, but you wish there was some forgiveness?  Well, select your mess of a line and pick the redraw option that you want.  No keyboard shortcuts for this.
2- There's 32 layers available.
3- Scale your geometry down before importing... Curvy likes a certain size range

A long overdue port of one the main games that made me love my Xbox 360 in the early days. The port itself is quite good. Not perfect, but it has been perfectly functional for me.
Graphics options are limited, though you can uncap the framerate and enable/disable vsync. MSAA at varying levels is your only antialiasing option. The textures are noticably aged, but are fine for a game that's a decade old. Hopefully some mods can provide some higher resolution textures.
Sound works fine most of the time, though some audio samples are of varying quality. I think this may have been the original quality though, not an issue with the port.
The game performance is good, with stable framerates when running around grabbing stuff. Hitting a big cluster of zombies with a big object may cause a lag spike, however it is very brief. Loading times are monumentally improved compared to the original.
The game itself is a joy to play. It is simplistic compared to DR2 and beyond, but I prefer this. No running around for money like a neurotic Hebrew; no overpowered combo weapons from "Wrestlemania meets backyard warriors;" just you, a mall and a big bunch of zombies in your way with some believable psychopaths for you to overcome.
The game is more serious compared to the other games, though it can be goofy if you choose to dress up and use silly items. This humour contrasts nicely against the gravity of the situation, which can make it all the funnier. The other games tried to play the humour straight and it was overbearing.

My first impression of Saints Row IV was that the game was simply, more or less a rehash of Saints Row the Third. It's very easy for a new player to the game to get that impression, as SRIV uses many of the same resources as SR3, up to and including the city it takes place in. However, this first impression was quickly broken after I had gotten deeper into the game. Saints Row IV has proven itself to be not simply a good sandbox game in general, but also a viable and legitimate successor to Saints Row 2. SRIV made many improvements where SR3 failed, most notably in the writing department, but also in almost every other aspect where SR3 was lacklustre.
Unlike SR3, SRIV has interesting mechanics, mostly in the form of the super powers granted to the player. Although the game has around the same amount of content as SR3, (which had a notable lack of content for a game its size, especially when compared to its predecessor, SR2) SRIV manages to keep the player interested in the game far better than SR3 did, with both its mechanics and storytelling.
Although the super powers granted to the player are quite numerous and intriguing, they are not without their fair share of problems. Their implementation into this game sometimes feels like an afterthought, as they don't have much synergy with the rest of the gameplay at large. Since the powers were built on top of the game, rather than the game being built around the powers, they were understandably difficult to balance properly. They also do not complement the other gameplay mechanics very well. The best example for this that I can give is how the movement powers (sprinting and jumping) render most types of vehicles obsolete except for vanity reasons. Little thought had been put into how the inclusion of super powers would affect the gameplay otherwise. The biggest problem with the role of the powers within the gameplay is that they simply make the game too easy. SR3 was already far too easy, and all you had there were some guns and military attach choppers. What about when you can jump skyscrapers and turn into a nuke?
From a story perspective, most of SRIV felt like a giant throwback to the Saints Row series. Saints Row IV had a lot of amusing references to both the rest of the Saints Row games and to other media, like The Matrix and Blade Runner. The writing was generally good and the game didn't ride on the back of those references as a placebo for having a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ story, rather using them to improve the narrative as a whole. The whole game paid homage to the earlier games in the series, even to the point where it retconned unfavourable aspects of SR3's story like Johnny Gat's death. SRIV felt like an original product rather than a parody, and the story managed to maintain an engrossing and serious tone a fair portion of the time.
Besides the game being too easy overall, my biggest issue with SRIV is that the game is shoddily optimized. I found it difficult to maintain more than 40 frames per second on high settings, despite not looking very good graphically, and the game often randomly dropped to as low as 20 FPS.
If the ease of play and somewhat low amount of content doesn't bother you, you'll find that Saints Row IV is a much, much better game than Saints Row the Third. I highly suggest playing it if you're looking for a fun, interesting sandbox experience that gives you a large degree of freedom with little in the way of consequences.

Years ago, I read an essay about
that praised it as a "video game" of the purest possible sort: no narrative, no simulation, an experience not expressible in any other medium than the digital arcade. That essay stuck with me, and it comes to mind whenever I play a minimalist arcade game. Super Hexagon falls into that rarefied genre.
is a neuron trainer, an activity of mental self-construction on a basal level. You can't think your way to victory; there's no time for that. Instead you relax, empty your mind, and let your eyes, reflexes, and fingers play and learn. There are no patterns to memorize or level layouts to rehearse; each sub-minute "game" unfurls randomly enough to prevent rote training. There are no powerups to acquire or new abilities to unlock; the only thing leveling up is you, the player. You fail, and fail, and yet your best times slowly creep higher as the substrate of your brain manufactures a
layer. Then perhaps you take a break, and the pulsing soundtrack and whirling geometric shapes linger in your skull, reinforcing your neural net for the next session. It's as much meditative practice as game.
Don't expect to beat this one without many hours of practice on what is, to all accounts, an otherwise useless skill set. But for a few dollars, you can partake of a pastime with no analogue, a memorable artifact with the soul of
,
, and all the other pure video games of our era.

When I saw screenshots, the game did not seem to be of much interest to me, especially because I don't like puzzle games.
I did enjoy Portal though, so I decided to give Antichamber a go. This game has no story, and a very simplistic visuals. Audio does add to the atmosphere though. The game begins with extremely easy tasks, but the difficulty slowly raises the further you go. What surprised me is that this is not a portal clone at all, whatever screenshots suggest, but it's a puzzle game nonetheless, and the chaces are that if you enjoyed Portal, then you will also enjoy Antichamber. To every puzzle you encounter there is a hint provided. Hints are philosophical reflections, which also give solutions to puzzles - but they are not straightforward and require some logical thinking (you may figure out every puzzle the first time without trial & error style of play - which was the case in Portal too many a time - but as the puzzles become more and more complex you will finally encounter ones that are too difficult for that, unless you are smarter than the developer or me at least). Fortunately, the philosophical reflections are not of 2deep4u kind, so you are not constantly molested with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stuff. They are very simple and kind of cute. It's like the guy who made this game wasn't a typical recluse indie developer suffering from affective disorders and egocentrism, but actually a reasonable and smart dude. The gameworld consist of multiple corridors, which branch in many ways and it's the player who chooses which way he prefers to go (or rather - how he solves puzzles, because they often have multiple solutions). At any time you may come back to any previously encountered puzzle and solve it again, perhaps in a different way leading you to another branch of the "chamber".
Overall, I enjoy this game a lot, despite my inner prejudice towards puzzle and adventure games.

Interesting tools are available to customize your character and combos in the engaging, twitch based combat.
However, despite the excellent groundwork, the game falls short in its execution. They should not have neglected level design and monster AI. The regular stages all seem an unending slog of motionless targets on relatively unchanging platform orientations. The only difficulty in these portions of the game seems to be the often obscured spew of projectiles that will unavoidably juggle you to death with no chance of recovery beyond the initial hit. That, and perhaps mindlessly keeping track of your own combo count for no other reason than to have a high combo count.
The game definitely shines in its boss battles, really forcing the player to fight efficiently with an effective character build. Yet even this can be easily cheesed using broken defensive abilities and homing magic, not to mention the boss battles themselves are far and few between. Most disparagingly, the final boss fight ends up being extremely simple and much easier than earlier ones, regardless of unlocked abilities and player skill, as it still holds true in a higher difficulty mode in NG+ which pits you against a hardier variant of each of the bosses to scale with maxed out stats.
It's enough fun for a pick up and play kind of approach, or for anyone who really gets deep into optimal play, but the longevity doesn't extend much further than an achievement farm. I would definetely consider a sequel or extension, but I cannot recommend this game as a complete package.

Mirror's Edge is a first person parkour/platformer and one of the few EA franchises that hasn't been milked to death. The story, a classic Film Noir style story of someone being framed for a murder they did not commit is juxtaposed with a post-cyberpunk dysthopian future that averts most tropes associated with the genre by being incredibly colourful and visually unique.
The city's design is beautiful, filled with stunning vistas and a heavy focus on primary colours, as well as being whiter than a celebrity's teeth. The movement controls are easy to master and with the help of Faith's (the main character) Runner Vision it's easy to see where you're supposed to go without breaking the flow of the game.
Although the game does feature gunplay, it's not really forced on you and the few times you do get your hands on a gun you're more than happy to lose the thing as fast as possible because the gunplay feels tacked on.
Lastly, the music (made by Swedish producer Solar Fields) is absolutely incredible. Beautiful melodies are mixed in with airy and synthetic sounding ambient tracks. The main theme is one of my favourite pieces of music ever and it's sure to stay in your head for years to come.

So, I've been using this software on-and-off again for about two weeks now.  It's a fantastic tool for doing curvy objects -- think humans, vases, crab-alients, tribbles, squirrels, etc.  It is NOT really a tool you would expect to use if you were carving, say, a house or other strict geometric objects because the port to .OBJ leaves you too many extra vertices to clean up.
Of course, if your video game takes place in a Dr. Seuss world, maybe that is the house for you.
When it comes to quick, rounded objects and characters, this software compares favorable to it's competition (in my opinion) as it allows you to easily rock between low and high poly, do intrecate detailing, add textures, add bones, and then port to .OBJ (and only .OBJ I might add).
It serves a singular purpose, so it's not as broad as it's competitors.  But then again, it's not as expensive.  And when it comes to putting out quality meshes, the tools in this program are up to the task.

Mirror's Edge is a beautiful game. It's fast paced and doesn't have to ever slow down if you are a good enough free-runner. But, this game isn't perfect, and as a hug fan of this game I'm going to be completely honest.
The good things about Mirror's Edge:
The Look - The City is amazingly gorgeous and dynamic. Different color schemes for certain buildings really help piece the city together.
The Feel - The controls are decent enough to get you where you need to go without looking like an idiot, but it's the animations and the lightweight feel of Faith that really make you feel like a runner. The way she vaults and slides across the floor look fantastic.
The Soundtrack - One of my favorite videogame OST's, Mirror's Edge has a distinctive feel that's core comes from listening to it's music.
The Bad things about Mirror's Edge:
Wonky parkour controls - At times you'll find that what you want to pull off isn't achievable unless you're a skilled pro at the game. You want to wall run then coil over that fence? Until you're completely familarized with the controls you'll fail 90% of the time.
No Achievements - You wanted to get achievements and cards for your amazing parkouring in this game? You would be better off buying it on console. That's right, Steam doesn't offer any achievements or trading cards for this game. Probably because the game is so old, the port to Steam is missing a lot of things that would make playing Mirror's Edge worth your while.
The combat - Now, this is completely avoidable if you have the skill to evade the police, but the combat isn't all that great. Sure, when you have the chance to pull of wallrun-kicks and leap onto SWAT members it can be enjoyable. But the areas at which you face the police are so open and empty you'll end up walking up to them, waiting for them to hit you with a melee attack, and easily tapping a button and countering them. Then you'll drop their gun, rinse, and repeat this process until all of the police are taken down and you can get on your way.
Short storyline - The story is pretty uninteresting in my opinion. It only picks up at certain parts, and it's easy to tell who the villain is going to be by the final chapters. The game is only 9 missions long, and these missions are usually 10 - 30 minutes long.
In the end, Mirror's Edge is a great game that you will enjoy if you're into parkour and first person combat games. But if you want rewards, achievements, cards, or badges, steer clear of this title. By the end of the game, you'll feel one of two emotions. Satisfied with a great short-but-sweet experience, or you'll be left wanting more out of the game, since you can only now speed-run the same sections of the game or do time trials on certain parts of missions. Also, mentioning the no achievements you'll feel like you just sped-ran the whole game and all of the time trials for nothing, seeing how your scores on the leaderboard are only going to be buried beneath hackers of the game.
6/10 - Good but could be a lot better if Steam supported the features that other titles have on it's store.

When Killing Floor 2 was still in Early Access I wrote a negative review for it. One of the biggest complaints that I had was underpowered weapons, warping enemies, neglective developer feedback amongst other things, but the microtransaction system took the cake. Killing Floor 2 was still months from being finished, but they already had a working, fully finished microtransaction system cashing  players. Ironically Tripwire advertised their title as being "Early Access Done Right".
I chose to forget the game and let it sink to it's own oblivion, but after it's release Killing Floor 2 has been gathering a steady influx of positive reviews and my curiosity was awekened. Seems like Tripwire began listening to players and tailored the game more to their will. I bought the game, and now after couple of hours I really think that Killing Floor is back. There's no annoying enemy warping, guns feel better, action is better than ever and overall the whole game play tastes sweet as ever. The game has been updated recently with a new map, weapon and a gamemode, and this came in for free. As it should be. Tripwire has earned their respect back.
If you liked Killing Floor, you'll like Killing Floor 2 too. It's similar enough to Killing Floor to make old fans feel like home, but it has enough new stuff to earn it's title as a sequel.

WARNING: this game will frustrate you to no end.  Even on Easy mode.  Hours and hours of playtime later, I have not managed to beat the Rebel Fleet Leader.  But I was *SO* close...
In FTL, you have to jump across the universe, one sector of space at a time, fighting things that get in your way, in order to find the last remnants of the Federation and confront the massive leader of the Rebel Fleet.  There are a variety of ways to do this and a variety of ships to do it with, but what's important to note is the following:
1. Every choice you make will come out slightly differently in every playthrough of the game.  Effectively, virtual dice rolls are the reason that on your first playthrough the giant spiders killed you, but when you find them again on your third playthrough, you crush them and rescue the space station.
2. Death is permanent.  As soon as you die, that's it.  No save games, no restore points, no extra lives.  Be smart about your hull strength!
3. Every playthrough will be completely different because the universal map is randomized every time.  You could find yourself choosing between Engi and Zoltan worlds at one junction one game (they're both quasi-friendly races), and Rock and Slug worlds at the next (they are *not* quasi-friendly...in fact, more often than not, they're usually just not friendly).  And the different locations in each sector are different every time.  (As in, if you're running out of fuel, you had better hope that this sector contains a store to buy fuel from...)
The game is amazing because of all of this, though.  There are literally hundreds of different strategies to try on each playthrough!  Maybe this time you want to focus on all energy weapons, and you can; next time you could put shields to max instead and rely on drones, or destroy your enemies from the inside by beaming an away team to the opposing ship and killing their captain.  The choices you make are what makes the game fun.  And the infuriating nature of the game is so well directed that it makes you want to take out your frustration on the "New Game" button until you win!
Oh, and it's made by an independent game studio.  Which, in and of itself, is full of win.

There are so many rouge-like games on Steam that finding a suitable one to play seems like a serious investment of time and money. Rest assured however, if you have purchased TELEGLITCH: Die More Edition because it is FUN and CHALLENGING. Enemies seem to know when you're low on ammo and supplies, and they'll come at you like a raging swarm of bees. You better be good with a mouse or you won't last very long. A nice feature of the game not featured in other rogue-likes is the level saving system. Initially you'll always start at level one however, if you manage to make it to say, level five, the next time you die and load the game again you'll have the option of starting at level one or three.
Aside from mechanics, one thing I really like about this game is the lore. TELEGLITCH could have easily been just another sci-fi flavoured rogue-like, but the world building really sets it apart. Imagine if a defense contractor like Blackwater or Lockheed Martin acquired the technology to reanimate corpses. That's pretty much what Militech, the in-game shady military research firm, is all about. Data logs scattered throughout the levels document the processes of creating, maintaining and interacting with the undead. Most data logs are disturbing. Some are side-splittingly funny. Finding all the data logs and reading through them is just as a potent motivation to get to the next level as the enemies that chase you.
9/10 would highly recommend.

I kept Antichamber on my wishlist for several years before I finally decided to purchase it.  My decision was made based on what little gameplay I'd seen in trailers and my tendency to prefer games that think outside the box.  In that regard, Antichamber did not let me down.
When I went into the game I was fully expecting not only Escher-like rooms, but also Escher-like physics.  The mechanics of the game are often unexpected and unexplained, which I sometimes found annoying, but also easy to rectify.  The draw for me as I got deeper into the game was the overarching philosophy, which I will leave unexplained so as not to spoil the game.
The game is not without its drawbacks, however minor they may be.  There is a significant amount of backtracking, because it is fairly likely you'll need one upgrade or another to discover all the secrets in a particular area, and sometimes in a particular room.  The game compensates by utilizing a very good map system which keeps track not only of which rooms you've completed and which you haven't, but also of which room you were last in before warping back to the main hub, which room you started in the last time you warped out, and what path you took to get there.  The developer was fully aware that the physics in the game allowed for various paths per room, and took the necessary measures to facilitate exploration of each path.
The main issue I took with this game is an unresolvable problem with the game's settings.  There is no way to change settings for FOV and other visual options.  In most games I've played, this is more an annoyance than a serious issue, but in Antichamber, I could not play for extended periods of time without experiencing serious motion sickness.  This was more of an issue in the beginning of the game, as I was getting used to the mechanics and exploring every room to its full extent, rather than focusing on a specific puzzle, but it meant that I could only play the game for periods of 1-2 hours at at time before I had to take a break for the day.
Because of the motion issues, I almost gave up after my first several hours playing the game.  However, I decided to give it another chance because I enjoyed what I had played and wanted to see more.  The hand-drawn graphic style is a nice change of pace from most other first-person puzzle games out there, and the minimalist, ambient soundtrack does a nice job of drawing you in to the otherwise alienating atmosphere.  If you can get past the issues presented by the significantly limited options and settings, do try to beat the game.  The ending sequence and significance presented within are nicely worth the effort.

My first impression of Saints Row IV was that the game was simply, more or less a rehash of Saints Row the Third. It's very easy for a new player to the game to get that impression, as SRIV uses many of the same resources as SR3, up to and including the city it takes place in. However, this first impression was quickly broken after I had gotten deeper into the game. Saints Row IV has proven itself to be not simply a good sandbox game in general, but also a viable and legitimate successor to Saints Row 2. SRIV made many improvements where SR3 failed, most notably in the writing department, but also in almost every other aspect where SR3 was lacklustre.
Unlike SR3, SRIV has interesting mechanics, mostly in the form of the super powers granted to the player. Although the game has around the same amount of content as SR3, (which had a notable lack of content for a game its size, especially when compared to its predecessor, SR2) SRIV manages to keep the player interested in the game far better than SR3 did, with both its mechanics and storytelling.
Although the super powers granted to the player are quite numerous and intriguing, they are not without their fair share of problems. Their implementation into this game sometimes feels like an afterthought, as they don't have much synergy with the rest of the gameplay at large. Since the powers were built on top of the game, rather than the game being built around the powers, they were understandably difficult to balance properly. They also do not complement the other gameplay mechanics very well. The best example for this that I can give is how the movement powers (sprinting and jumping) render most types of vehicles obsolete except for vanity reasons. Little thought had been put into how the inclusion of super powers would affect the gameplay otherwise. The biggest problem with the role of the powers within the gameplay is that they simply make the game too easy. SR3 was already far too easy, and all you had there were some guns and military attach choppers. What about when you can jump skyscrapers and turn into a nuke?
From a story perspective, most of SRIV felt like a giant throwback to the Saints Row series. Saints Row IV had a lot of amusing references to both the rest of the Saints Row games and to other media, like The Matrix and Blade Runner. The writing was generally good and the game didn't ride on the back of those references as a placebo for having a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ story, rather using them to improve the narrative as a whole. The whole game paid homage to the earlier games in the series, even to the point where it retconned unfavourable aspects of SR3's story like Johnny Gat's death. SRIV felt like an original product rather than a parody, and the story managed to maintain an engrossing and serious tone a fair portion of the time.
Besides the game being too easy overall, my biggest issue with SRIV is that the game is shoddily optimized. I found it difficult to maintain more than 40 frames per second on high settings, despite not looking very good graphically, and the game often randomly dropped to as low as 20 FPS.
If the ease of play and somewhat low amount of content doesn't bother you, you'll find that Saints Row IV is a much, much better game than Saints Row the Third. I highly suggest playing it if you're looking for a fun, interesting sandbox experience that gives you a large degree of freedom with little in the way of consequences.

I cannot say enough good things about this game. I got this game for $2.49, which is an absolute steal, even for a sale. I cannot fathom why this game is more popular than it is. So many elements are extremely well crafted, let me list them here.
The first, and my favorite element of this game, is the sound design. As well as the complete lack of an OST. It makes every situation more tense and surreal; whether you're exploring the level and suddenly get ambushed by a group of enemies(which, mind you, can kill you very quickly and easily), or you're fighting a boss and trying to collect yourself under the hail of gunfire and explosions. And that gets me to the second part of the sound design; the crispness of the audio. Gunfire is loud and jarring; explosions even more so. It really helps to reinforce the fact that your weapons are very powerful, but also means the enemies' weapons are as well. Explosions are even better; you're cornered by several enemies with no way to shoot yourself out in time, you pull out a can gun and with a loud "CRACK!", the smoke clears and you have no more enemies. There are so many different scenarios I can list in this game but for the sake of being more concise, I'll move on to the next part.
Visuals. They're very simple, yet have a charm in their vagueness. You can't tell what's under that gargantuan mass of guns and thick armor; all you know is that you have to kill it before it kills you. I also like the distortion effects of bullets and explosions, bullets leave a multi colored trail to show they're ripping through the air, and through you or your enemy. Explosions look like they leave a shockwave that obliterates anything close to it. Now, the adaptive zoom and screen rotation is a neat idea; but for the sake of gameplay it's a bit annoying. With that first bit of negative criticism, let's move onto the gameplay.
Gameplay. Before I say anything else, I'd like to mention that overall, I enjoy the gameplay and can play it over and over. So, let's talk about the rest. In your first couple runs, you'll have no idea what to do except use the controls, which the tutorial teaches you. In fact, without looking at a guide, it'd probably take a long time to get used to the gameplay and tactics. You have to be VERY cautious in this game; this isn't Hotline Miami.  A lot of players probably took a few runs to learn that you should knife all enemies the first couple levels, maybe save for blowing up a very large group or shotgunning a giant zombie on the second level.  Ammo is a precious resource on this game, and automatic weapons are a huge trade off; you're killing a lot of unarmored enemies efficiently, but you're also somewhat inaccurate, and wasting a large amount of ammo if you just go rambo mode. One thing I'd briefly like to touch on are the death messages; they're not ridiculously condescending(like in risk of rain), but can range from flavor messages, to actual gameplay tips. So to add to the ammo point,
"Remember, short, controlled bursts." -one of the death messages
With that out of the way allow me to move onto the final part of this review.
Story. There isn't much to be said here. While it isn't a masterpiece, it's pretty neat and can give you insight on what kind of stuff went down prior to the teleglitch incident, and how the teleglitch incident happened. It also gives some subtle gameplay tips, like saying a certain enemy on that floor is only affected by armor piercing guns or explosions, or how to craft a minigun. So not a huge part of the game, but it's there and it's not bad.
In conclusion, I'd highly recommend this game to anyone who likes brutal, fast paced roguelikes that can change from suspense to terror to brief calm and then back to suspense within just a few seconds. Overall rating: 9.5/10
