Title: XCOM Enemy unknown
Genre: Strategy, Turn based strategy , Aliens.
Developer: Firaxis
Publisher: 2K games
The plot is simple.
Aliens are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and want to invade our planet to experiment on humans, after that take over the planet and terminate all resistance.
You are the commander of a global Elite defenseforce called the XCOM project. Your job as commander is to exterminate all alien threats. Chase them away from the earth. You have some advisors with you. The Chief engineer , the Chief researcher who give you explainations to what is happening and sometimes give commentary and tips. And officer Bradfort. AKA captain obvious.
Find the aliens, cature or kill them, research their bodies, use their own technolagie against them, wipe them out and send them back to where ever they came from. Simple but greatly executed in this game.

This is a turn based strategy game. which means: you take a turn and move your characters, then the enemy does the same. You react to the enemy which keeps it fun and suprising because you dont know where they are based in the beginning. you have to search the area with your soldiers until you run into the aliens. You squad consists of 6 soldiers. (4 at the start of the campaign) and different classes ( Assault, Sniper, Support, Heavy) You can choose who and what you want to take into battle. When you take control of a soldier and move him/her around you have a couple different options. Your soldier can only move a number of tiles every turn. This depends on your soldier's abilities ofcourse. Every class has different abilities and weapons to choose from. Back at base you have a overview of your entire base. Which you can expand underground. you have to be careful with your finances and where you invest them in. You have to research alien technology so you can adapt to the enemy. The mechanics in the game are solid.
Customize your squad their abilities the colors the names  its enough to choose from. Its really enjoyable to name the soldiers after your friends and family. You actually care more about your soldiers that way and you mourn them when they die. If you want more custom option there is a DLC pack for more options.
Its nothing really outstanding but it looks great for a turn based strategy game. Im not a huge graphical fanboy but I do appreciate good graphics which this game delivers. dont get me wrong, its not amazing looking but the graphics do the job for making the world seem believable when you are fighting the aliens on random generated maps. The game has some flaws like the turn not ending, but its nothing game breaking. It just works fine with full 60FPS and no stuttering or anything like that.

Civ is the king of all strategy games. There have been many strategy games since but Civ is the original.  Civ has been and always will be the well from which all others draw their inspiration - to some degree. Civ V specifically is one of the best in the series. It is the modernizing and refining of the Civ concept.  While I have some small misgivings with the way the Brave New World expansion added a needlessly complicated layer of sea trading. there are far more things to be happy about than sour with in this newest edition. The graphics are nicely polished, bugs mostly (if not completely) squashed, mechanics simplified and streamlined without the loss of depth. multiplayer functions well, and lastly the tutorials, learning curve, and difficulty settings have never been more accessible for new players.
If you're new to Civ, feel like trying out a new genre of game or a veteran that for some reason still hasn't picked up this latest edition there's no downside to jumping in. It is a game that easily justifies its price for the amount of content and hours you are likely to spend with it.

If you like Portal you will surely like this game. It's a really great puzzle game with a really deep story and strange event happening (like portal):
Note that's a short but outstanding game.
The gameplay of the game is pretty simple, like every other puzzle game,at the start it's only your movement and body and after a while you have a gun to resolve the problems which can moves and creates cubes to fill or to block lasers. That's the principal idea of the puzzle but what's interesting is that every problems has a lot of solutions and it's up to you to choose the one that you want. Every solutions is personal and this is really new and interesting.Be careful the puzzle can get pretty hard at the end (the last 3 in particular), far harder than Portal.
Also sometimes you will solve a problem and get back at the start of the game: you missed something important and you have to retry this problem(don't worry you can teleport back at this particurarly puzzle and don't redo the entire game).
On the other hand, the game has a really deep reflexion on how we think ,us, humans, and how we can think to solve problems on our own life. What's great is that the game is doing that along with the gameplay and without doing a boring lecture: there's little quotes everywhere after and before each puzzle which tells you and give you hints on how to resolve the puzzle(and don't restart at the start).But those quotes can be applied to everyday life and I find this pretty amazing.The game also gives a summary of these quotes in the menu and after reading them all again, they're all very true(at least that's what i think).
Speaking of the menu, there's no real menu: You start directly in the game and it puts you directly in the spirit of the game: Primary, minimalist but direct with you.
After all, in this game, you don't really know what you are or where you are but maybe that's one of your objectives of the game(you can have the help of a lot of forum for that)? Or maybe you have to find all the quotes ?Or maybe again just reach the credits ?
It's up to you to choose the end that you want and what you want to do with it.
All this game is about CHOICES.

If you're the kind of baseball fan who likes looking at box scores or reading about baseball history, then you'll like OOTP Baseball 18.  IIf you're old enough to have enjoyed stats-oriented baseball boardgames like Strat-O-Matic Baseball, then you owe it to yourself to check out OOTP Baseball 18.  OOTP is the best baseball sim ever made -- full stop.
OOTP puts you in charge of any franchise or league from 1871 to the present.  You can play as GM or Manager or both, or you can play as the Commissioner.   The game allows you to create fictional leagues, to rename your fictional players, to create crazy fictional leagues.  If you want to play out the 2017 season as your favorite team, go for it.  If you want to follow that team into the 2020s and 2030s, no problem.
New features to this year's edition include a better injury system, improved 3D play-by-play graphics (featuring little sprites and baseballs arrayed on a representation of your stadium), and Challenge Mode -- an online leaderboard that tracks your achievements against those of other players using a similar ruleset.
I love this game!  No baseball fan should be without it.

Before I start this quick first impression, I just want to say that just because this game is in early access doesn't mean It should be immune to criticism because:
1. Steam automatically puts a sticker on my review, stating the date and that it was done during early access
2. If a game is bad at the time I'm reviewing it, It will get a bad review. bad game = negative review, good game = positive review. Giving it a positive review because of what it could possibly be is like me saying that In the future, Humans could possibly be able to survive a .50 cal to the face, so right now, I can survive a .50 cal to the face.
3. If you release a product to the public, in the hopes of building some form of a community, you must be willing to accept criticism at any point in development, otherwise as a dev, you can have a feeling of leniency from your consumers and end up not fixing a thing b/c you think everything is fine.
Now, onto the part you REALLY don't care about...
- Economy is awful (Guns and Cosmetics are way too expensive, and paying for maps. This is something that should've been settled on before releasing any form of the game to the public)
- Doesn't feel like It has been being developed for 2 years, as stated in the EA Sticker on the store page.
- P2W; Major Weapon imbalance (Another thing that should've been settled by now)
- Some type of issue where my friend and I joined the same server but couldn't even see each other.
- Unecessarily, locking certain features behind level walls
- Visually unappealing
- Floaty Controls
- Cheezy, bland sound effects
- Paying for certain consumables like grenades and claymores (Which is no better than if you were to force players to pay for ammo, or god forbid, weapon rentals)
- No customizable key bindings

While I'm still waiting for a PC-based baseball game to replace MVP Baseball 2005 (EA Sports), OOTP Baseball has more than satisfied my craving to simulate the dynasty-building experience that I crave in a baseball game. Semi-frequent updates to the game reflect real-world rosters and player abilities, and every facet of the game is very well thought out to simulate real-life results, daring you to make conservative decisions for marginal team improvement, or risky moves which could result in acquiring a superstar or a lemon.
The best part about the game, however, is how totally customizeable it is. Whether you want barely any involvement in managing a team in a single league, or want total control over every single facet of your team's franchise (pitch count for your rookie league starter, or how often your 3rd string right fielder starts against Left Hander's when there's a DH), the game can be absolutely adapted to fit your current appetite.
This is bar none the only baseball game that has satisfied my PC baseball appetite in the last 12 years (and I've been looking pretty hard), and I'm already thinking that OOTP baseball 2019 will be worth my money money as well.

2D arena beat-em-up where you're a cute anime fairy girl who lives in and protects a forest from slimes and flying creature. Story mode consists of the following: four levels (or days) of killing monsters then a boss fight. Rinse and repeat four more times and you complete story mode. You can perform slashes with your dagger and kicks by repeatedly pressing the attack button and juggle enemies into the air. You also have a guard you can perform to block attacks. There's a guard meter that fills as you block more attacks and your guard will break if you block too many hits in a row.
As you kill monsters, you level up and gain Mana (which is the game's currency). Mana is used to purchase three different skills. Mana can be spent after the end of each day in the intermission phase. One category are skills mapped to a button separate from your normal attack button and are special attacks; up to four special attacks can be mapped at once with directional inputs kind of like the Tales of JRPG franchise. The second category is passive skills applied to your attacks for additional properties. The third category is bonuses to your stats ranging from increased HP, increased strength, increasing the amount of hits you can block, increasing physical defense, restoring health from each enemy killed, and so on.
After you complete Story Mode, you unlock new difficulty modes and the ability to carry all of your purchases over. You also unlock Guardian mode, which is a gauntlet of 100 days, only 3 continues, and you get an intermission every two days instead of every day like Story Mode. Once you get the hang of the combat and you're juggling enemies left and right, dashing across the screen, and racking up 100+ hit combos, the game is really fun. It's just that the story can be completed in less than two hours on a first playthrough and the bonus content is more the exact same you just did. The game is really fun and a decent challenge while it lasts. I purchased it for $2 during the Autumn sale and I feel like I definitely got my money's worth out of it. At full price, though, I'd be more hard-pressed to feel like it was worth. This is one of those games that's guaranteed to go on sale. You'd be better off waiting for a sale to get it really cheap and blow through it in no time.

I have been a fan of the Arkham games since back in 2009 when Arkham Asylum came out. The series has delivered to a very high standard (excluding Origins multiplayer) throughout all of its major titles. I can, with confidence say that this is the most ambitious game of the lot.
Asylum introduced us to the franchise, proving it is possible to create fantastic, rich, story driven Superhero games, and we as a gaming community loved it.
City opened our eyes to the potential this platform of game can extend too. An open world filled with all sorts of secrets waiting to be discovered. This is the "Dark Knight" of the franchise, for good reason.
Origins was definately the weakest of the franchise but still, in its essence a solid game. Updated gameplay mechanics and a big graphics upgrade. Sadly they tried to incorporate a multiplayer, let's not talk about that.
Knight at first was a disaster on PC. I'm sure most of you are aware of that, bugs, crashes. You name it, it had it. Thank god rocksteady are a fantastic development team and fixed the problem as soon as possible. If you can look past that, the game is amazing. Yes, some of the Batmobile Missions aren't the best like the tank battles. I definately appreciate the ambition of the developers to add in this whole new mechanic, never tried or tested with the community. As a whole the Batmobile was excellent, it unlocked the full capability of Batman as you race around the large city of Gotham.
Fighting in Knight was the best it has ever been, wicked amounts of variations all polished and smooth, no faults here.
The story was strong, we still have Mark Hamill's Joker with us for the ride so it makes up for the pretty serious side of enemies we have been dealt in this game. I liked the plot, and you feel more like Batman than ever now that you are actually in the heart of Gotham.
Graphically this game is fantastic, if your pc can handle it. On max this game looks incredible with tons of optimization options for you to delve into if you wish.
Overall another fantastic entry/farewell to the series. Sad that it has to end but glad it ended on a good note. Thanks for the ride Rocksteady. Excited for your future products.

(disclaimer: 1140 hours in KF1, finally jumped into KF2 this week)
Absolutely brilliant stuff. Don't hesitate, shooter people.
- AAA quality maps, models, and animations. Some gorgeous levels.
- Really well-optimized engine. Runs locked 60fps ultra on a humble RX 470 rig.
- Fun co-op dynamics. Great overlap of perks.
- Excellent sound design and quality hardcore music.
- Seriously, very good mix of melodic metal and breakbeat tracks.
- Stylish, well-designed UI and menus. Lots of background flourishes, tight, clean HUD.
- Beautiful, persistent gore. All the blood coats the floor and walls, stays there the entire match.
- Outstanding weapons and gunplay backed by top-notch effects. Bullets, fire, explosives, etc. generate huge effects with outstanding enemy reactions, ragdolls, tear-aparts.
- Even when the round is over, you can go poke and chop at the fragments of gore and mangled corpses litering the floor.
- Entertaining character voices and comments. As you're running and gunning away, the characters reference parts of the level, make short comments about the apocalypse, celebrate good kills, say something about an enemy, etc. Non-cheesy, professional voice acting. Short but sweet little bursts of color.
- Plenty of perks and % increases to climb through. Along with ongoing passive gains for every level, each class gets a small selection of assignables every 5 levels.
- A lot of amusing cosmetic items.
- No pressure to buy stuff (no gameplay advantage). You can play and unlock crates anyway, getting crafting materials. The community also sells pre-made stuff (that they've earned and crafted) for under a buck if you don't want to bother.
- Constant stream of free updates, with new maps and modes. Steady as she goes developer interaction with a good tone.
KF2 knows exactly what it wants to be, keeps improving/expanding.
It is, by far, the most technologically impressive co-op horde shooter on the market, has a great vibe, and a very strong community with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s of active servers.

Teleglitch is, dare I say it, perhaps one of the harder roguelikes. A typical run, given that you make it far enough, will yield zombies, mutants, giant armored humanoids of dubious nature, robots, the list goes on, and each and every one of them can kill you in the most colorful fasion that a steampunk shooter on a desolate planet can manage. Teleglitch only has ten levels, which from afar appears to be a cakewalk, if a cakewalk is classified as being assaulted from all sides by gun slinging, flesh rending, laser cutting Lovecraftian horrors then yes, it’s a “cakewalk”. Seriously, despite the fact that these things are only depicted in a topdown pixelart manner, they still succeed in scaring the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me whenever I find one that isn’t just a grunt. For example, around level seven you’ll start to hear a metallic shriek and then a giant be-tentacled robot called a squid will appear, and as if that’s not bad enough, it fires eye lasers that will bore a hole straight through you, it’s not a good time when that happens, and it’s happened to me multiple times.
I think it’s the sound design that helps make the game so frightening at points, and coupled with how difficult it becomes to manage health and ammo? You’ve got yourself a fully fledged top down horror game, which is pretty impressive. You’ll be walking along, minding your business, head through a doorway, which will then shut behind you in a shower of sparks and sharp screeches, and then a motor starts running and two massive zombies in power armor, with Gatling guns by the way, will assault you. High octane points like those contrast so greatly with the nervous jaunt through the destroyed facilities it surprises me that Teleglitch can switch gears so quickly and satisfyingly.
The worst part of the game is definitely the difficulty, I’ve reached level eight at my highest point, at which I was taken down by a menagerie of goons. Which leads to the death screen of the game, which is taken from a random pool of available ones, and recently I just so happened to get the coolest one, which really makes the feeling of dying in game a much more badass and fun moment, which sounds weird but trust me, it’s cool.

Dying Light - I am currently at a 42% game completion within 27 hours of play time. I feel that there is no need to continue beyond this point. Reasons being varied, but mainly concerning with the engagment of the story element.
The story is very cliche and shoehorned in. The AngryJoeShow review details what I've expirenced so far; characters that you will never care for and dialogue that is mere drivel, nor compelling. The antagonist, the villian to our hero, is nothing more than a local mob boss with little to no back story or interesting behavioral characteristics such as in other games like FarCry 3's Voss or FarCry 4's King Min. He's just a bland thug. The dialogue of the main character also is problematic as he seems far too melodramatic during a crisis and sometimes merely annoying in others. The player doesn't really have any envolvment with the fates of other characters they encounter, either to be met with an untimely death in a cutscene or killed off screen.
Besides that, it's just another zombie game from a fragmented team that thought they could bring a more "mature story" from Dead Island. What colminated was an uninteresting set of characters that will soon be forgotten after their fates are met.
Gameplay, however, is satisfying. The athletic movement of the protagonists and plenty of skillset upgrades make for a enternaining romp through a zombie infested foreign city. The por kour system brings speed and a sense of power when in full motion. There are many types of weapons to acquire, either by purchasing them, crafting them, or finding rare ones in hidden areas of the city. They make for the most satisfying gorefest when confronted by the different enemy types.
The night and day cycles within the game give a refreshing expireince and difficulties as zombies and super zombies span the darkness of the night, while the day time is filled with the mundane zombie and many human theives, thus, and henchmen of the alleged villian.
The zombie enemies are varied as you progress in the game or wait until dark for the more powerful and faster super zombies. Though, incountering some of the so called "boss" monsters can be accompanied with familiar troupes that long time gamers are so use to and easily overcome these obstacles. QTE events ruin some very important story line aspects, such as the final battle.
All in all, Dying Light has great game play that is mired by an uninteresting story and cast of characters. I do not currently recommned this games until it falls in price. This would be worthwhile at a cheaper pricepoint, but the unsatisfactory conclusion leaves little room for signle player replayability, where Co-op may give a bit more longevity.

This JRPG is a story about a fight between a Goddess and a Vile God who had different points of view : the Goddess wants to protect the world by bringing peace whereas the Vile God wants to take over the world to make chaos. At the end of the fight, the Goddess and the Vile God were sealed because of the furies which were used during the fight.
A long time later, a young boy Fang who is a normal guy who loves eating. He met Eryn, a fairy who is a part of Fang's sword. Fang became a Fencer and now, he will accomplish his destiny : to collect all the furies in order to ressurect the Goddess who will bring peace to the world. Will he be able to protect the world ? Then, Fang will do a long journey with his friends to grant their common wish.
Positive points :
- An excellent soundtrack
- A simple gameplay which is very effective (similar to Neptunia games)
- The boost points
- 60 FPS
- A great character design
- A game which will take at least 50 hours if you want to earn all the achievements
- The story is original and very interesting
- The characters are endearing
- The backgrounds are beautiful
- The CG gallery is excellent
Negative points :
- The landscapes are repetitive sometimes and the textures can be improved
- The game is a little bit too easy for some gamers maybe
Conclusion : I played this game hundred hours if I add my ps3's stats and I was never bored by it ! I recommend this game to all JRPGs fans without any doubt. By the way, the negative points I mentionned earlier have been improved in the game Fairy Fencer F Advent Dark Force which will be available in 2017 on Steam. Thank you Compile Heart for making great games like Fairy fencer F ! Now I will wait for Fairy Fencer F Advent Dark Force and I already know that this game will be a huge art which will spread you strong feelings.

Before you read this, you need to know one thing. Dying Light doesn't just resemble Dead Island in its setting or style, it repeats entire gameplay features. And they arn't small ones. The focus predominantly is still on melee. The kick is still here. The crafting is identical, in function if not form, allowing you to add elemental damage to your weapons through blueprints and upgrades.
So it won't be much of a shock to you hearing that the Co-OP is the same either, albiet a lot more clumsely implemented, as everyone just plays as a Crane (The protagonist) clone.
These are all solid and reasonable flaws to a game which is neither really original, or unique in many ways. However, when all things are done and dusted; I really dont care, because Dying Light is one of my favourite games of 2015 so far!!
The parkour system is one of my favourite mechanics in a game since the Nemesis system in 'Shadow Of Mordor' and really is one of the best building traversal games ever. Jumping between roof tops and smashing into car roofs. The game in this regard is flaw.
The single player is surprisingly entertaining and lengthy. It's not exactly mass effect, but it serves it's purpose. Side quests are often better than those in the story. Characters arn't always memorable, with more effort given to justify the game world.  Progression comes via a skill tree that unlocks significant character upgrades. You will also learn to craft items like Molotovs and flares to make you more formidable against the various zombie types.
I felt that the game gets a bit too easy once you reach higher ranks however. Weapons (when upgraded to the greatest extent) can kill Volatiles, Goons, and Demolishers in 1 or 2 hits. This effectively destroys the atmosphere and rids Dying Light of one of it's biggest advantages.
My conclusion: Really the biggest issue with Dying Light is a crysis of identity. It's way too similar to Dead Island. It remains a terrific zombie game that really switches up the genre of boring and stale zombie grinder games.
It emphasizes the world and how you move around in it. This isn't just a slap dash map that's been thrown together at the last minute. Everything has it's proper place in responce to the free running elements.  The changes between day and night are refreshing and memorable. There is a healthy amount of content that will provide dozens of hours of entertainment in solo or cooperative play. Entertaining, atmospheric, visceral, and frenzied.

WARNING: this game will frustrate you to no end.  Even on Easy mode.  Hours and hours of playtime later, I have not managed to beat the Rebel Fleet Leader.  But I was *SO* close...
In FTL, you have to jump across the universe, one sector of space at a time, fighting things that get in your way, in order to find the last remnants of the Federation and confront the massive leader of the Rebel Fleet.  There are a variety of ways to do this and a variety of ships to do it with, but what's important to note is the following:
1. Every choice you make will come out slightly differently in every playthrough of the game.  Effectively, virtual dice rolls are the reason that on your first playthrough the giant spiders killed you, but when you find them again on your third playthrough, you crush them and rescue the space station.
2. Death is permanent.  As soon as you die, that's it.  No save games, no restore points, no extra lives.  Be smart about your hull strength!
3. Every playthrough will be completely different because the universal map is randomized every time.  You could find yourself choosing between Engi and Zoltan worlds at one junction one game (they're both quasi-friendly races), and Rock and Slug worlds at the next (they are *not* quasi-friendly...in fact, more often than not, they're usually just not friendly).  And the different locations in each sector are different every time.  (As in, if you're running out of fuel, you had better hope that this sector contains a store to buy fuel from...)
The game is amazing because of all of this, though.  There are literally hundreds of different strategies to try on each playthrough!  Maybe this time you want to focus on all energy weapons, and you can; next time you could put shields to max instead and rely on drones, or destroy your enemies from the inside by beaming an away team to the opposing ship and killing their captain.  The choices you make are what makes the game fun.  And the infuriating nature of the game is so well directed that it makes you want to take out your frustration on the "New Game" button until you win!
Oh, and it's made by an independent game studio.  Which, in and of itself, is full of win.

This game is pretty bad.  I bought it with a coupon, so I'm not terribly bent out of shape, but I still can't give this game much praise.  Ignoring the fact that this game is near unplayable without a controller, the game's set up is terrible.   Basically, you flucuate between two screens.  An 'intermission' screen between each day, where you can spend earned points, and then the combat screen, which is one of several different seasons/mood variations.   This game looks like it was going to be a fairy themed fighting game, but somewhere along the way they dropped the ball on multiplayer and decided to take their fighting arenas and try to inject a story into it at the last second.
Beat'em Ups made in the 90s have more variation to them than this game.
Most of the enemies are literally reskins of the first few enemies you encounter, with some of the advanced enemies being shrunken versions of bosses, so don't expect to fight a huge variety of enemies.  Also, as far as your actual moves go, you do manage to get an impressive selection of special moves, but none of them are anywhere near as powerful as simply knocking one enemy into another repeatedly, like they were gasoline filled balloons holding matches.
Where the game does vary is in its difficulty.  At some point, between Summer and Autumn I think, the game's difficulty spikes.  They remind you that you can 'train' in order to become more powerful in order to complete the day(effectively the levels in the stage), but it amounts to you playing against slightly weaker versions of enemies you've already killed.  Yes, they solve this difficulty spike by letting you grind, giving you very little natural progression.
Ultimately, this game brings together the worst parts of several genres.  The static 'stage' from Arcade styled fighting games(minus the multiplayer), the grinding of legacy RPGs(Without the depth of story).  The only thing that I can say that this game does right is how Freesia herself moves and responds to controller input.  If they took Freesia out of this game, and put her into a game with better level design, better flow, and less grind, it could easily be a great game.  Unfortunately, Freesia is tethered to her tree.

This documentary is meant, and ONLY meant, for Dota 2 (even Dota) lovers, enthusiasts and players (I would actually say all "MOBA" people). So others, in which I particularly include all those who DONT play Dota or even dislike it, please refrain. This isn't simply meant for you guys.
So, here we are. I must say - This is one hell of a documentary! Primarily focused on three professional Dota players, namely hyhy, Fear,and Dendi, it shows their journey, struggles, will to overcome all hurdles on their path, to one of the biggest eSports contest in history, having a booming prize money of a MILLION DOLLARS, The Internationals ! And of course, their attempt to win it.
We get a brief insight into what Dota is. Players struggled to balance their gaming with their education, personal lives etc, while at the same time dealing with parental guilt to a certain extent, and how they struggled to be Professional Dota Player. Or in general, a Professional Gamer. Everything is so subtle, that I bet each one of us can easily relate to. Highly cinematic, where they show you the events of TI, while also taking you inside the lives of the aforementioned players.
A highly inspiring documentary! It's not easy being a gamer. We have multiple obstacles to overcome in that very path; be it financial, social, personal, or even psychological. It's only those who can relate to it, know all the sacrifices one has to do, and the dedication one has to offer.
But at the same time, it does make us realize that to a point, no matter what, we are proud of our gaming ! We see how players falter, how they get back on track, how one BAD move can ruin your entire progress, how patience can get you a well-deserved victory, and how tables can be turned even when your Ancient is at just an inch away from collapsing. It's something we all have come across ! :)
The visuals are interesting, the sequences are highly cinematic, and they make the gameplay seem so dramatic, as if a well-rehearsed play. And as I have said multiple times, we could really connect personally to each of the players. Briefly, if not entirely!
My rating and recommendation ? 10/10 ! Do watch it guys. Definitely, do watch it ! Non-Dota players can watch it as well. But Dota enthusiasts, please do. :)

With so many places I could begin this review, I might as well start with the obvious issues which is the lack content and interesting map design choices. Don't get me wrong, I like chasing shiny things in the street too, but new content updates are few and far between. One map and one or two weapons every few months just feels off especially considering the continuous updates to the "Zedconomy" (Valve tested, Ubisoft approved). Now onto the official area designs. Maps repeat the same formula of small areas with lots of narrow passages that makes me question whether the new engine can actually support large open areas. When compared to the maps from the previous game like farm or wyre it makes it seem like everything is in a clown car. As for things that this game improved upon, the new gore system is something enjoyed by most if not all.  I believe it is time for the list of a bit more subjective things I have with this game.
The first is the idea and creation of the Zedconomy. In the first game if you wanted to put pretty makeup on yourself you could look in the store and see what exactly you are going to get. Instead now you have to gamble with what is essentially keys and crates. It's not like they hold a knife out and demand your wallet because this is all purely optional but the fact that microtransactions exist with rng on a fully priced game makes me uneasy. At least there's more customization to make up for the lack of different characters.
The second is the new artistic design. The theme appears to be big and muscular equals scary and powerful but to me it just comes off as comedically oversized. Think of those before and after ads of people taking experimental performance enhancing drugs. Might as well replace the scrake's chainsaw with a giant cartoon circus mallet and use the old voice to replicate scenes from Tom&Jerry. As much as I disliked how some players would purposely block the door to the trader in the previous installment, the design of the makeshift shops were more pleasing to the eye instead of these pylons with a voice.
The third is with the perks and weapons in general. The saying of too many cooks in the kitchen almost describes the current situation with the creation of the newer perks overlapping the older ones. Berserker's reliance on parrying can become an annoyance when you have to constantly butt heads with the server everytime to see if you either blocked successfully or get reamed without lube. Commando gets to start and end airsoft rifles which are absolutely perfect if your end goal is to imitate a bee and annoy the locals. SWAT tries to copy commando's role with smgs stolen from kf1's medic but falls on its face. Field medic at least no longer has to play matrix dodge simulator so there's a plus. Support players from kf1 who loved the style of weld door from time to time and deal with a single line of enemies are in for a big surprise when muscle pounders come knocking on the door to see if they have heard about lord and savior Kevin Clamely. Sharpshooter gets less weapon variety but still can perform its job. Gunslinger is sharp's younger ADD brother that took half its weapon collection. I guess firebugs are useful as emergency flashlights when they aren't blocking your view with their particle vomit. Demolitionist gets its legs clubbed by the dev's game design with not being able to detonate explosives with other explosives, c4 being remote detonation instead of proximity, and not being able to stack enough explosions to send the boss on an improvised moon voyage. Survivalist was an interesting idea and now that I think about it, I want to know if it live up to its title by being forcefully shoved headfirst into an incinerator. For weapons, I feel as though they aren't as satisfying to fire as the ones from kf1.

A promising title drowned in a grindfest.
Riddled Corpses is a zombie-themed Bullet Hell game, in which persistence is the (only?) key. The game features 6 characters, unlocked via Gold, which you gather in the Arcade and Survival modes. These characters also have levels (max 20) which define the damage they inflict. As far as I am aware, the damage progression is the same for all characters.
The reason to unlock further characters (besides achievements) are their special abilities, respectivelly: items magnet, double gold, extra health, and all of the three. The sixth char is still a mystery to me: she does have items magnet & extra health, but no double gold and... nothing else, apparently.
There is no conceivable way finish the game with a low level character: your damage output will not be able to rid the screen of zombies and you will be overwhelmed. Most players will need, in addition to lvl 20, the MK1000 upgrade which adds to the damage of all characters. It is *very* expensive, though.
And even once you have the
char unlocked and maxed with shiny upgrades, the Arcade mode is short, repetitive and uncreative. I am a bad dexterity player, and I found the game relatively easy too.
However, until you get a lvl20 char (with MK1000 lvl5) you'll be basically farming for Gold - not *really* playing. You'll have to repeat the same stages over and over and over again. It is just a grindfest. More casual players will be wanting to have at least the 4th char (with extra health) to defeat the final stages, and that takes another eternity farming. Sorry, grindfests are always a "no" in my book.
Achievements are natural, but become a burden just as much as the rest of the game due to grind. They would have been fine otherwise. Linux port had problems saving settings; I always had to manually modify some sound options. Otherwise, the port was fine.
Last but not least: there are
beyond the main screen! Shame on you for playing with our hopes!

Riddled Corpses is a very straightforward twin-stick shooter with design and music heavily influenced by the 8 bit / retro / pixelated generation. Although the game can be frustrating, if you are a fan of that era of gaming you will probably enjoy what is on offer here (moreso if you are into Halloween / creature feature creepers as well,) however if you aren't a big fan of that kind of aesthetic you will probably get bored with this game very quickly as its gameplay and presentation are pretty thin.
The game itself is surprisingly grindy, and at first the game was really getting on my nerves with how many bullets the enemies take to eliminate.  Your default guns / weapons are very piddly and weak against the always-encroaching throng of zombies, demon bunnies, and floating skulls, making for an initially-frustrating experience before you use the game's currency to upgrade your weapon. Even after leveling up your gun, however, the effects from the gun don't change all that much and seem to just be a slightly wider or more damaging machine gun.
The gameplay itself consists of little more than what you would find in similar SHMUP games, kiting the enemies around the screen and avoiding their projectile attacks and hitboxes, while using the occassional bomb / screen-clearing pickup or a time freeze which locks enemies in place and allows you to get around them easier. These two items are essential to completing certain sections of the levels as the screen can become VERY crowded with enemies and makes navigating them an exercise in precision and frustration in equal measure. At first I was♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off that the UI would hide where enemies are (before discovering it can be toggled off and on) such as obscuring an enemy sprite spawning behind the icon of how many kills you've done, or behind the icon for the TNT screen-clearing item. This UI / HUD can be toggled off and on by pressing select on the controller, however having to swap between the two to check your life total and/or whether you have any of the special items to use can become annoying when the UI elements could have just been scaled down to avoid this back and forth.
For better or worse you have no option of exploring the levels at all, and instead are shimmied along on-rails style sequences. Occassionally the camera will lock into place and you have to defend an area from a wave of zombies or defeat a boss, but as far as player agency in choosing your own path of which areas to explore there is none, and the levels follow the same linear format each time you play them.
Although I enjoy booting this game up here and there to try my luck at not dying, I would wait until this game is on sale to snag it if you're at all interested, even as a well-done homage to retro titles, its base asking price is a little high for its simplistic gameplay and grindy nature.

Riddled Corpses is a highly imperfect game due to simple problems that could easily be fixed.
While I was looking forward to this game because I like Twin Stick Shooters and the great art style, I came away a bit disappointed as it plays a lot more like a Bullet Hell-lite which I don't care much for, I don't find narrowly dodging nothing but brightly colored objects for hours on end all that fun and to be quite frank I'm pretty bad at them but I'm pretty good at SHMUPS and Twin Stick Shooters.
I'll state the negatives and annoyances first.
It's a grindfest, while I could easily look past this fact because I don't mind grinding, hell, I play quite a few mobile games that are essentially all about grinding, it's kind of fun to an extent, but Riddled Corpses takes it really far. I ended up getting to the boss as level 1 Jon, not an easy feat as I didn't know at the time you could upgrade your character as it's an option on the main menu and not during the player setup or map select menu which threw me off until I backed out to the main menu. It was frustrating and took many tries to get to the boss only to be destroyed pretty easily once the projectile tombs starting spawning in during the fight and my measly little pistol did all of nothing to the two hulks and the little jester dancing around and flinging projectiles like no-one's business.
So, I discovered the upgrades, upgraded to about level 5 with the coins I accumulated. Game was much easier BUT this game also suffers from super wonky hit boxes on certain enemies that hit you from a mile away, some of the ordinary zombies can tap you from a few feet away and take a chunk of your precious health. The UI also completely blocks part of the bottom screen and almost the entire top part of the screen, the overdone, long lasting explosions on the zombies have fooled me so many times into thinking it was clear to proceed past them only to get hit by a zombie that was perfectly concealed by the smoke of the explosion. Happened so many times I decided to just never get near dead enemies. The larger enemies explode all over the screen making it a huge chore to get out of the way without being hit by a lesser enemy.
Enemies also spawn right next to you and probably the most annoying aspect is the fact that a lot of the enemies that will spawn later on fire a projectile when they spawn and only when they spawn, if you're standing anywhere near them when they spawn you WILL probably be hit.
Health is also pretty scarce in this game, most pickups are random though some things can be destroyed in stages and they always hold the same item every time but most levels only hold maybe one or two HP packs, I've gone full levels without an enemy dropping a single pickup or HP pack which makes the game much harder, other times I end up having 5 timers and 6 TNT and full HP plus two HP packs by the end, but that's not usually the case and even then, you'll probably be cheated out of your extra HP anyways. The TIMER pickup is also completely useless, it ONLY pauses enemies movement, not time itself, so projectiles are still moving and enemies are still able to spawn and even fire projectiles as they spawn. So it's essentially useless. It should pause EVERYTHING but the player or make projectiles fall out of the air or slow them down immensely.
In later levels, starting at Level 2 some enemies can fire projectiles every half second or so, the screen quickly becomes filled with these enemies so you'll have projectiles going every which way.
Now back to the grinding. Every character has a max level of 130. The only way to progress is to level up, the only way to get money is to play the game and die countless times to make up that money needed to level up and every level starts out super slow which makes getting money VERY tedious. Survival is the easiest way but again, starts slow but escalates quickly, you're lucky to last a few good minutes at any level under 30 with all the combined annoyances such as the excessive projectiles, useless timer pickup, UI elements always being in the way and enemies spawning right next to you.
I'd also like to mention that at least in a Bullet Hell Shooter or SHMUP, enemies usually come at you from above or swing back around from below, that's not the case in RC, enemies spawn randomly EVERYWHERE, even right on you, there is a mechanic to STOP enemies from spawning on you but you basically have to be standing DIRECTLY on their tombstone as it pops up and it'll destroy itself. So as you're looking ahead to dodge a projectile an enemy can appear right under your feet hitting you as you're trying to dodge all the♥♥♥♥♥♥flying around the screen and that to me is probably the most ANNOYING aspect of the game because it forces you into two states, either pay attention to only your character and dodge spawning enemies or watch out for projectiles as you hear them get fired. Both of those will likely lead to your death.
Because of the random spawning this also leads to moments where it's impossible to dodge getting hit as you'll have a wave of projectiles come at you and not enough time to clear the enemies blocking your path to dodge it and using the TNT can result in two things, the explosions block your view and you'll get hit by another projectile OR they block your view of the other zombies spawning right under your feet and again, the timer is USELESS.
It's simple, it IS fun, it feels good to play, controls well, looks great, has style, etc. and the issues could EASILY be fixed by the devs though it seems there hasn't been much in the way of activity from the dev on here recently though I know they're lurking.
You could turn UI elements transparent and make them smaller or put a strip accross the bottom with all the UI elements on it and block the game from rendering behind it, as if the screen cuts off right there. Make it to where enemies can't spawn within like 10ft of you. Make the timer and TNT more useful since they're so hard to come by and expensive to purchase (Early in the game at least.), make the explosions a little less pronounced or make them transparent so we can see through them, adjust hit boxes for certain enemies. Oh, and one last annoying thing, make the collision boxes on the cars, barrels and such NOT make you get stuck when you touch them, I'd randomly get stuck by a vehicle or barrel off screen and get hit, especially in Level 1. It was highly annoying.

Stick of Truth is actually a really great RPG.  It is another title by Obsidian Entertainment (Baldur's Gate series, Pillars of Eternity, etc.).  You embark upon the most epic larping-adventure of all time with the cast of South Park, playing as the new kid in town.
I really don't want to spoil any of the humor for anyone who has never played the game before, so I won't.  What I can say is that no opportunity for satire is missed in any aspect of the game.  The battle scenarios, the overall plot, the gear, weapons, settings all feature immense content that will make you laugh intensely... all while playing what is actually a pretty challenging RPG.  Nothing else is to be expected from the creators of South Park, Trey Parker and Matt Stone, who seem to always transmute the mediums they touch into gold, whether they take the form of cartoons, musicals or now with this game.  I regard them as some of the best American satirists, even in league with Mark Twain.
If you're not from the U.S., you should definitely pick this game up.  It's a great reflection upon our contradicting, somewhat psychotic and multi-faceted culture.  Of course, it IS satire... but nonetheless enlightening on key aspects of our society and the awkward landscape of middle-class, suburban values.
The port to PC is pretty good, with some minor irritations.  Also, I am not very fond of the use of key-mashing as a mechanic in games, which Stick of Truth utilizes for a lot of the character abilities.  Still, the gameplay is really fun.  The experience makes you feel like you're a kid again, with all the fart humor, vulgarity and immaturity that made childhood great.

Visually impressive, but everything else is downgraded from previous Arkham-games.
The plot is not interresting, and it revolves mainly around the titular character Arkham Knight. Some of the old villains from previous titles are here as well, but now they are side characters whose sole purpose is to justify some repetitive minigames. Those minigames include tasks such as chasing vans, destroying enemy outposts, destroying enemy tanks, defusing random mines and solving riddler puzzles. There is not much enjoyment in doing these fillers, that serve as an excuse for gaming content.
It is a shame because the city itself is many times larger than in Arkham City. There is no enjoyment in exploring the city however, because the streets are filled with enemy soldiers and tanks. Thugs, gangs, helicopters, soldiers and tanks are present in every block, and unless you want to fight most of the gaming time, you'll end up avoinding the fights just like me to get to the next boring objective.
Avoiding is quite easy though. You are given a new model suit that has enhanced gliding properties, so now Batman can stay in the air practically as long as he wants. Faster way to travel is to use the new Batmobile though. Batmobile looks good, handles okay, and driving it through the streets is chaotic. Hold your right mouse button, and your Batmobile transforms into an agile tank that you can use to fight against those pesky tanks and soldiers. It is very clear that Rocksteady wanted the Batmobile to have a large role in the game, so you will use it (the tank mode mostly) a lot.
Of course, Batman still beats his opponents with fists and gadgets as well. Now, however, the controls are unresponsive at times and often the Batman does something that you weren't meant to do. Fighting worked so well in previous Arkham-titles, so it is amazing how it can be screwed here. While talking about the previous titles, they usually contained an area where Batman was able to look around and plan his takeouts. In Arkham Knight, there is very little of that. Either the thugs have technology to counter your gadgets or you just have no other option than to throw yourself head-on to the enemy crowds. There is just no fun in having to fight 15 thugs at a time over and over and over again.
Rocksteady has succeeded in making a Batman Arkham game that is not enjoyable. Arkham Knight is frustrating, poorly paced, boring, badly optimized and uninteresting after couple of playing hours. I found myself playing just because I hoped the game would get better.
To sum it up numerically, Arkham Asylym is 9/10, Arkham City is 10/10, Arkham Knight is 4/10.

As you kill monsters you'll receive experience which will boost your stats and mana which can be used to buy passive abilities and special moves. The game progresses quickly, you won't be spending much time on the same level so you can just drop it and pick it up anytime. With so many places I could begin this review, I might as well start with the obvious issues which is the lack content and interesting map design choices. Don't get me wrong, I like chasing shiny things in the street too, but new content updates are few and far between. One map and one or two weapons every few months just feels off especially considering the continuous updates to the "Zedconomy" (Valve tested, Ubisoft approved). Now onto the official area designs. Maps repeat the same formula of small areas with lots of narrow passages that makes me question whether the new engine can actually support large open areas. When compared to the maps from the previous game like farm or wyre it makes it seem like everything is in a clown car. As for things that this game improved upon, the new gore system is something enjoyed by most if not all.  I believe it is time for the list of a bit more subjective things I have with this game.
The first is the idea and creation of the Zedconomy. In the first game if you wanted to put pretty makeup on yourself you could look in the store and see what exactly you are going to get. Instead now you have to gamble with what is essentially keys and crates. It's not like they hold a knife out and demand your wallet because this is all purely optional but the fact that microtransactions exist with rng on a fully priced game makes me uneasy. At least there's more customization to make up for the lack of different characters.
The second is the new artistic design. The theme appears to be big and muscular equals scary and powerful but to me it just comes off as comedically oversized. Think of those before and after ads of people taking experimental performance enhancing drugs. Might as well replace the scrake's chainsaw with a giant cartoon circus mallet and use the old voice to replicate scenes from Tom&Jerry. As much as I disliked how some players would purposely block the door to the trader in the previous installment, the design of the makeshift shops were more pleasing to the eye instead of these pylons with a voice.
The third is with the perks and weapons in general. The saying of too many cooks in the kitchen almost describes the current situation with the creation of the newer perks overlapping the older ones. Berserker's reliance on parrying can become an annoyance when you have to constantly butt heads with the server everytime to see if you either blocked successfully or get reamed without lube. Commando gets to start and end airsoft rifles which are absolutely perfect if your end goal is to imitate a bee and annoy the locals. SWAT tries to copy commando's role with smgs stolen from kf1's medic but falls on its face. Field medic at least no longer has to play matrix dodge simulator so there's a plus. Support players from kf1 who loved the style of weld door from time to time and deal with a single line of enemies are in for a big surprise when muscle pounders come knocking on the door to see if they have heard about lord and savior Kevin Clamely. Sharpshooter gets less weapon variety but still can perform its job. Gunslinger is sharp's younger ADD brother that took half its weapon collection. I guess firebugs are useful as emergency flashlights when they aren't blocking your view with their particle vomit. Demolitionist gets its legs clubbed by the dev's game design with not being able to detonate explosives with other explosives, c4 being remote detonation instead of proximity, and not being able to stack enough explosions to send the boss on an improvised moon voyage. Survivalist was an interesting idea and now that I think about it, I want to know if it live up to its title by being forcefully shoved headfirst into an incinerator. For weapons, I feel as though they aren't as satisfying to fire as the ones from kf1.
I don't know, maybe I'm just remembering the first retail killing floor to be more amazing than it actually was but even so I feel as though this game at its current state is not a good successor. I've tried to like this game as much as I did the first, but every update I keep finding myself just trying the one new toy they give then burying it. If there's one thing I would like to see though, is survivalist's ashes from that incinerator.
TLDR; "There might be more microtransactions update and everything else is on hiatus but we got more gore and gunslinger finally. That's worth it, right? Right guys?" - sleep deprived simpleton

As you can imagine, bullet hells are on a whole 'nother level of hell when played with a mouse and keyboard, generally speaking.
This game, while fun, is not for those who want a story. Riddled Corpses is about gameplay, which is definitely fitting considering it is, in fact, a bullet hell. Aside from that. the pixel artwork is charming and the enemy designs are well done. They do a good job of adding to the experience.
In short, this game is about fun gameplay, and not story, If you're into bullet hell you'll probably like it.

In many ways, OOTP18 is a minor improvement on last year's version. On the other hand, last year's version was great, as was the one the year before, and so on. I'm sure the next one will be great as well, and I'm sure I'll buy it.
One feature that is a surprisingly big deal (at least to me) is the inclusion of players who never reached the majors in historical league drafts. I tend to play decades-long sims with the same team, starting from decades ago and reaching into the modern day and beyond.
This year, for example, my first game is with the 1962 New York Mets. I've reached 1966, and my Mets have become quite a respectable squad, getting good production from the likes of Bob Veale, Tony Conigliaro, Rico Petrocelli and a 17-year-old Larry Dierker. But I also have a functioning minor league system -- something that was hard to develop in historical leagues past. This adds a sense of realism to roster management, and introduces variety to replays, as some of the minor-leaguers inevitably develop into major league players. I would probably buy the game every year anyway to support the developers, but it's changes like this -- plus the ability for teams to retain partial responsibility for traded players' contracts, plus many more -- that make it easy to justify that decision and hard to imagine going back.

It follows the story of three players who participated in the tournament, and it gives some good insight into their lives, and the development of their gaming careers; not to mention how well it delves into the core aspects of competitive gaming, and how it's becoming bigger with the passing years.
For someone who isn't really into the eSports scene, like myself, it's still a great documentary. Before watching this, I knew that The International was big and all that, but more than that, I did not care. However, after watching this, my interest in Dota 2 has increased. I might not start playing it, but I'll probably follow the competitive scene. So, even if you're not interested in Dota or in competitive gaming, give this documentary a shot. At least you'll get to know why some people are so interested in these kind of games.

The gist of this feature-length documentary is not entirely original. The problems these three had growing into super stars of dota2 scene are none other than those ordinary players - i mean, fervid fans - would encounter if they would choose to pick playing a game professionally.
I consider this documentary a motivator, a promotional piece aimed to plunge more people into the world of e-sports by demonstrating to them the glories awaiting them, and or least an attempt to hold ordinary players' attention longer by fostering an elite group of esport celebrities whom, like movie stars, if you are into them, you would login onto steam to watch play.
That said, the creation of this documentary is epoche-making. It tells of the growing power dota2 and valve's steam are wielding over esport lovers. It looks back on the past few years that represented dota2's rise and replays the historic scenes deeply embedded into fans' mind in a well-crafted manner. It could very well be what fans of dota2 have always been wanting with or without them knowing. Therefore, Valve's done a great job, no doubt about that.
Content-wise, it would strike me a bit over the top, especially the very contrived bit about hyhy's former girlfriend. It's not that we don't want to gossip about that, I mean, she happened to be a looker, and know this, a dota2 player, too. It's just the genuineness of it all plants doubt in my mind. Would a game batter a person up so badly that he would put all his hopes, including regaining his ex-gf and proving to family, to a single tournament. Probably, and probably not. From an artistical point, I would say it's a beautiful bit if it's true, a cheeky insertion if not.
At the end of days, this is a good documentary chronicling the TI events Valve's given birth to and Valve had every reason to release something like this. I loved it, and the dlcs, by which, I mean Dendi's Murder of Crows in-game set (though I don't play Pudge at all), epic, isn't it?

Good Documentary!!! Even though the main game is dota, gamers that play other games can still relate to it.
Hope to see more of Valve works!!! (^_^)

A very fun and unusual game.
Saints Row IV incorporates the best features from SR3 but also enhances many of the most lacking elements of it's predecessor.  It does appear however that the game engine and graphics had changed very little or not at all, which may disappoint those wanting a significant upgrade to the visuals.  The game does look decent on the PC but does seem to be a bit behind other recent titles.
I did not think that Volition would be able to go even more "over the top" than they did with SR3, but they somehow managed to do so, and in a way that fits the game very well.  At no point did it seem that the humor in the story was forced or placed for the sake being there.
The campaign is very well scripted and dialoged.  I did particularly like the banter between the various members of the Saints.  The game has a great antagonist in the alien overload Zinyak who has a witty English accent and a very Bond-esque villain personality.  The game also finds a lot of ways to include throwbacks to the previous titles in the series, which should please those who have played those games.
The main theme behind the game borrows heavily from some favorite Sci-Fi action films like the Matrix (1999) and They Live (1988).  Most of the gameplay is in a very Matrix-like virtual city of Steelport where the player has to free other captured friends and attempt to break out of the simulation via hacking and disrupting.  Much like the Matrix, you spend a lot of time switching between a real-life ship and the virtual city of Steelport, and super powers are learned in the virtual world as the player learns more about how to master and disrupt the virtual environment.  There is a TON of missions and side activities to keep the player busy and many of the familiar side activities from SR3 make a comeback with some fun twists (though Snatch and Escort missions are omitted this time, YAY!)

Biggest complaint I would see is in the super powers that the player gets in the simulated Steelport.  While they are great fun and add a very interesting element to the gameplay, the powers will render the automobiles and many of the weapons obsolete.  The gameplay with superpowers in the open world does greatly resemble that of games like Prototype, Crackdown and inFamous, so the game does feel more like a really good super hero simulator or Matrix game rather than a GTA style crime game.  The player will also find the game not too challenging with upgrade super powers, but the great writing, over-the-top gameplay and humor makes up for the lack of challenge.
Overall the game continues to shamelessly build on the over-the-top gameplay that SR3 did and further distance itself from GTA and earlier Saints Row titles.  The result turned into something rather unique and it seems that Volition has become rather adept at creating a very fun and zany game that does not take itself too seriously.  If you liked the direction that SR3 took with the series then you will probably enjoy this game as much as I did.

Excellent game for the price. Despite the linear "plot" to the game (make your way through eight sectors of a galaxy and defeat the final boss), you are given a huge number of options in terms of HOW you tackle this task. Whether you use boarding parties, drones or just arm yourself to the teeth with powerful weapons is entirely up to you, and there is an excellent balance that makes these all viable options.
A playthrough doesn't take too long, so it's the sort of game you can play (and probably finish) in a couple of hours, or you can try out different things if you have longer. This means that it's a great game to play in either short bursts or a longer session.
The unlockable ships and hidden easter eggs are the cherry on the top that may well make you come back and play this game again and again- I know they did for me. I've now gotten 72 hours out of a game that cost barely anyting- and it's been a better experience than a few games five times the price.

This game is so beautiful. The first thing that strikes me about it is not the gameplay, characters, setting or anything like that. It is the mood it sets. From the aesthetics, the soundtrack and the pace it makes you feel great, it makes you feel like you can fly or something. You come away really feeling captivated by that spirit and wish you could emulate it.
The aesthetics need to be talked of. Bold, bright colours make the world come alive. It makes the world look surreal even though there isn't anything unreal in it. It's beautiful to look at everything in it. This is definitely one of the very high points of the game. The soundtrack is stellar. "Still Alive" is a great dream-pop sort of song with fitting lyrics that fit the basic idea of this world.
Onto more banal points. The controls are slightly tricky but you get used to it and it becomes easy. Sometimes you can get lost in the maps. The challenge is reasonable. The replay value is very high if you are into time-trials and speed runs. The story isn't so amazing, not so well fleshed out. You get the gist of what it's about, why the characters do what they do but you don't go too deep here.
All in all I say this game is pretty damn perfect. Some people have been harsher when judging it but I think this game will remain a classic for many years.

Batman: Arkham Knight picks up on Halloween night, nearly a year after the events of Arkham City, with Scarecrow as the big bad, with an army under the leadership of our mysterious titular foe. (There are comics published adding more to the lore of the Arkham universe, but they don't impact anything going forward into this game.)
Story:
This is the probably the weakest storyline of the Rocksteady Arkham games (maybe just a bit better than WB Montreal's Arkham Origins). I say it felt apart, solely because of two things; the identity of the Arkham Knight (thanks to in-game flashbacks) and the return of a familiar foe, but not in the way you think. I will however give credit where it's due, this is definitely
finest performance in the entire trilogy.
Gameplay:
Definitely the best of all the Arkham games.
Once you unlock the new Batsuit 8.01, you unlock the ability to perform Fear Takedowns (instantly takedown up to 5 enemies all at once, in lightning speed). The grapple is also improved, with now the ability to chain grapplings to navigate the vast space of Gotham City much more fluidly.
The Batmobile is a somewhat welcome addition; and I say "somewhat" because it's used far too often in the main campaign as opposed to it just being for navigation and the occasional Riddler puzzle.
Video:
Managed to get most of the game to play out at 1080p with almost every setting on Very High. There was a dip in framerate here and there. Pre-rendered cutscenes play out at 30fps which breaks the immersion (the intro and
ending cutscenes). The nVidia Gameworks settings caused Fatal Error crashes in Panessa Studios and another place (I can't remember). Better have those off just in case.
Content:
I've only done one playthrough of the game on Hard, and it's taken me approx. 80 hours (including all the Season Pass DLC at 120%). I'm yet to start any of the other character's Story Packs or New Story+, but believe me, there's lots of reasons to come back and play this.
Voice-Acting:
Everyone in the game is well-cast, although I did miss Kimberly Brooks voicing Oracle.
Overall:
Great game, but not worth full price. Definitely buy the Premium Edition on sale ($20). I did.

I don't think I've fallen in love with a game more instantaneously than I have with Antichamber. While I'm far from considering myself a "classic gamer", one thing I find a bit exasperating about almost all modern games is how they will persistently hold your hand in a manner that, even if it doesn’t remove the challenge entirely, certainly does a lot to insult your intelligence. You will not run into this problem in Antichamber, and this for me is its main charm. Much like the very first Legend of Zelda game, AC starts you out in an unknown, unexplained world and you have to learn the rules by yourself, some writing on the walls telling you how to control your newfound matter gun (which I didn't even find until maybe 2 hours in playing the game and honestly completely forgot about until I did) and upgrades the only real guides you'll be getting, aside from some delightful life lessons you only receive after completing the puzzles they refer to. The simple puzzles quickly become daunting and brain-teasing, though a small few can become a bit tedious (and one puzzle in particular, albeit optional and only leading to an extra dev room, is complete and utter BS). However, for the most part the game has an excellent track record of keeping your mind stimulated and providing many rewarding and even cathartic moments, and many puzzles are an absolute joy for me to replay over and over again.
I also love the game’s minimalist presentation. You’ll be spending a lot of your time in pure white hallways, frequently visiting rooms that sport a color scheme ripped out of an MS Paint palette, but the game finds ways to use even its graphic simplicity to its advantage (many of the game’s puzzles and tricks wouldn’t work too well, I don’t think, in a more detailed aesthetic). I’ve seen people refer to the game as “ugly”, and while it certainly isn’t too easy on the eyes, it still finds ways to look just as charming as it plays.
At a glance, the game could easily be describled as "Portal with blocks” (even though development on this game started a year before Portal was released), but what sets it apart from its mad scientist peer more than anything is while Portal follows a very linear storyline, AC is completely open, nonlinear, and ready and waiting to have every conceivable corner explored—as soon as you figure out your way around. Another important difference that makes AC stand on its own is that where Portal’s theme is based around physics, science and strict logic, AC’s theme is its complete and utter deconstruction of your preconceptions of logic and reality, and while logic isn’t necessarily completely absent from the game, it has created its own, new set of rules that, again, you have to figure out for yourself.
This game did have me stumped on more than a few occasions and I will admit have committed the sin of using a walkthrough to help me through a few of them (although all but one of them ended up being dev rooms), but after seeing the answers its clear that a player’s inability to proceed really does simply stem from their lack of ability to put pieces together rather than a negligence of giving you all the tools you need and teaching you how to use them—there are plenty of subtle, clever lessons leading up to larger problems, but it’s up to you to actually learn them and keep them in your head.
Overall, I’d say my only big complaint with Antichamber is that there isn’t more of it. There’s no real extra content aside from the hidden dev rooms, and apart from restarting your save file to finish with a faster time there isn’t exactly much in the way of replay value, and asking for a sequel to a game like this in my opinion would be outrageous. Still, if Bruce does come up with something, I’d love to see it and will be the first in line to get it. :) This game is without a doubt one of the finest I’ve played and is an absolute must-have for puzzle game enthusiasts.

I received this product from a friend, who recommended it as I played games like Dead Cell, Nuclear throne, Rogue Legacy, and Enter the Gungeon.
The game is akin to Nuclear throne and EtG, being a top-down shooter with increasing difficulty. Unlike the other two games, I have not encountered different playable characters aside from the one you start with. The customization is lacking in player choice, but is actually really strong in the equipment you pickup and the crafting menu, in comparison.
The game is very ambient, also unlike the other two games mentioned. Teleglitch is focused on ambient noises, the sound of gun fire, and all that comes with it. There is no real "Music" in the game. This I feel is a huge benefit, because it really captivates the player into focusing their attention towards the game. That said, you shouldn't play this game like you would EtG, or NT, as those games more focus on whom you are playing as, rather than what you are playing "with".
If you are looking for a rogue-like, top down shooter, similar to NT or EtG, but with nuanced differences that offer a different taste to the genre, I recommend this game. However, this game is difficult, and you may find yourself dying often. There is a tutorial, but I feel the game is better played first looking at the keybindings, and then jumping straight into level 1.
I do NOT recommend watching other videos, guides or playthroughs of this game if you can help it. What do I mean by that? The game is just better enjoyed without knowing what is where, which things do what, how the game progresses, etc. That said, I think you should watch at most, one or two short videos, especially if you are unsure if this game is for you.

In many ways, OOTP18 is a minor improvement on last year's version. On the other hand, last year's version was great, as was the one the year before, and so on. I'm sure the next one will be great as well, and I'm sure I'll buy it.
One feature that is a surprisingly big deal (at least to me) is the inclusion of players who never reached the majors in historical league drafts. I tend to play decades-long sims with the same team, starting from decades ago and reaching into the modern day and beyond.
This year, for example, my first game is with the 1962 New York Mets. I've reached 1966, and my Mets have become quite a respectable squad, getting good production from the likes of Bob Veale, Tony Conigliaro, Rico Petrocelli and a 17-year-old Larry Dierker. But I also have a functioning minor league system -- something that was hard to develop in historical leagues past. This adds a sense of realism to roster management, and introduces variety to replays, as some of the minor-leaguers inevitably develop into major league players. I would probably buy the game every year anyway to support the developers, but it's changes like this -- plus the ability for teams to retain partial responsibility for traded players' contracts, plus many more -- that make it easy to justify that decision and hard to imagine going back.

This looked like a silly time waster so I bought it on sale.  Unfortunately, its actually a rage-inducer with control issues. You will NOT be chilling out playing this!
Aside from the fact that the game is insanely hard, has no 'easy' mode, and can cause massive confusion due to constantly flashing colors and spinning shapes, there is one big issue that prevents me from recommending this to even the hardcore 'Impossible Game' fans: the controls aren't tight.
While my reflexes may not be perfect, I can tell when a game mishandles input.  With this title, there is major input response lag; it lacks precision. Push a button down and release it for the same amount of time twice and the distance the 'avatar' moves is often very different.  This feels like the little triangle is drifting on ice, which isn't ideal in the best of circumstances.  For an idea of what tight, responsive controls feels like, check out Electronic Super Joy.
Ah, and one last gripe that some people might not notice from the screenshots - that little triangle doesn't move over one 'lane' at a time (the shaded area the triangular 'avatar' is in). So pressing left and releasing it quickly may only move the triangle slightly over, but won't move to the next shaded area. This is a bit frustrating and I was misled to believe that the game functioned this way (i.e. simply tapping left + right switches between shaded areas). But apparently that wouldn't have been challenging enough!  The input response lag makes this title even more annoying.
If the controls were tight, I might give this a recommendation to people that love torture lol.  But as it is, its not polished enough.
