Simple review:
I was introduced to OOTP17 last year, and enjoyed it heartily over the past 12 months.
So if you're familiar with the best baseball sim (in manager mode or as GM) on the planet, with as many options as can be imagined...and you haven't purchased OOTP yet...what are you waiting for?
Improvements from OOTP17:
-The Negro Leagues are an incredible addition to this year's iteration of the game.
-The improvements in the 3D modeling for every current ballpark were worth the wait. Great job,dev staff! Even the crowd movements, while somewhat rudimentary, are a nice improvement over OOTP17. Additionally, in 3D mode, the player sprites are a decent improvement over the chesspiece-like sprites in OOTP17.
My only "con" would be that,after a few hundred managed games with OOTP17, and now a dozen or so in OOTP18...still NO FOUL OUTS ever! I think this is wierd and supposedly the staff is looking into this. That's IT. That's my only "con."
-The MOD folks do a great job modding the 3D stadium advertising, the player facegens and adding player photos,etc. So what the game doesn't have (and frankly the player facegens are pretty darn good), you can easily download!
-Here's THE BIGGEST "PRO" for me, a long-time baseball PC-simmer: where ELSE can you get EVERY HISTORICAL SEASON EVER PLAYED...included in the game?
Look, I LOVE APBA; I still do; along with APBA Baseball for WIndwos v 5.75, and still visit that game from time to time. I always will; it's been a part of my life for 40 years. But having to purchase each season seperately and not having a 3D option is their biggest drawback. THIS game, OOTP, has every season, current or past, all the current ballparks, and if I want past ballparks I just have to d-load them from a MOD site.
And did I mention you can manage, GM, or just watch games with current majors AND minors, with real rosters? Manage a game overseas...yours for the taking. Even weather patterns.
NOTHING is left out.
---The learning curve in OOTP admittedly is slightly steep, but not much. It's only because there are SO many options.
If you haven't purchased OOTP ever, for goodness' sake BUY THIS NOW if you're a baseball sim lover like me. And as mentioned I bought OOTP this year and the updates are worth it. Especially through Steam so the updates are automatically done.
You will NOT be sorry. And you won't be able to stop playing. I had to take time away from the game to write this review!

The shooting mechanics are great, annihilating every abomination in your way is very satisfying and while the Screen can get very worked with the amount of bullets present at times, it is exhilarating to slip around bullets like a boss, plus it manages to run silky-smooth even with a cabbage PC like mine, so I dare to say this game can be enjoyed even with 2009's Notebooks.
The Items you can use to your aid are also pretty sweet stuff, mainly the Dynamite which blows everything up and gives you cash money for every killed enemy, the Stopwatch and Turret lose a lot of effectiveness in the later Levels where mostly everything shoots at you, so they are not bad, just situational.
While the Shoot'em'up and Bullet Hell mechanics are very well implemented, the Level Up system is beyond being a tiresome chore to handle, you need to constantly rack up Gold in order to enhance your firepower and make yourself more effective, you can even purchase some other Chars that have special traits if you have enough Gold.
The Lvling starts cheap enough, but afterwards, nearing Lv20, the prices turn obnoxiously high compared to the amount of Gold you would gain from Arcade, some could call it Replayability, but considering there is only 2 Game Modes, i would rather call it padding via limitations.
.
Now if there is a slip-up, is how when using the Keyboard, the HUD remains opaque, even when there are mobs or you are nearby, so you could get pot-shotted if you don't have a sharp eye for that sort of thing, I once tried it with the X360 controller and the HUD became transparent.
There is also this bug where if you pause the game around the time a Mini-boss or Boss would spawn and the game is still paused, the game will crash, so... Patch?
Pixel Art at its finest, ladies and gents.
The level of detail in this game's art is just dumbfounding, the brilliant colors and some of the dark or bright aesthetics in the levels mix into a art direction that i love and can't get enough of, even during the most down-to-earth and dark locations, it still manages to be greatly polished, and for that, i applaud it.
In my personally opinnion, it hops up and down throughout the game, the Stage 1 theme is embedded into my head and the Stage 2 tune is pretty nice too, but afterwards, I legit am unable to hum any other theme by heart, yeah, that includes Stage 5, in which i had to replay possible more times than Stage 1, is not terrible, is just a bit roller-coaster...y.
As hinted during the
category, this game's length is entirely up to how much of a completionist you are about this, you can easily try to get better and you can Lv the base character to 20 and get through Arcade mode in like... 30 mins.
Afterwards, Survival is there to challenge you to see how much mobs can you slaughter before you rip in peace... If you are behind a Hi-score.
For so, if you are not seeking the Achievements, this game can be no longer than a pair of hours once you get some good fire and beat Arcade mode, but if you decide to go full Achievement, expect your game time to near 20 hours.
For its asking price, this game is worth checking out, specially if you are particularly interested in the cliche zombie trope and also like your Shoot'em'up to be hard as balls (Almost like a kid-friend version of Touhou at times), charming art style and very competently designed gameplay mechanics, this game is a quick but solid burst of entertainment (or sheer frustration depending on your Skeelz), perfect for a Arcade-styled game.

**QUICK THOUGHTS** Riddle Corpses is a throw back to the classic 16-bit era, but with the modern standards of grinding. Picture clicker titles like Crusaders of the Lost Idols crossed with Shmup physics and an on-rails progressing Survival Mode, and you get this very grindfest. Sadly, it lacks a good amout of definition.
The graphics are fantastic, and the score is spot on with the days of SNES and Sega Genesis. The problem is that you don't really get to choose how you progress your characters. Instead, you have the simple choice of spending money you earned in game to level up your chosen character, of which there are a number of to unlock. I'd love the option to choose strength over health or other upgrades, but that's just not the case here.
It's also a pain that uou have to exit out of Arcade Mode or Survival Mode to access the Upgrade Menu to make said purchases, making doing so more of an inconvenience. An in-game option to upgrade would also have been nice, but, alas, it is lacking. There are additional rare objects you can pick up, but aside showing up in the Upgrade Menu, I don't really see the point other than bragging rights.
This title also has local co-op, which is a nice feature. Sadly, I don't have anyone willing to join me in it, as grind-based games aren't exactly everyone's cup of tea. I'd love the option to take this title on-line, and hopefully one day the developer will put that mode in. But, until then, I'm sure a good amount of my time will be devoured by just grinding my way to level 130 on each character to unlock the game's achievements.
All that said, I do recomend this title. It's a fun little pick up and play game that grind fans will find more a casual experience to widdle the time away until your next task in reality.

Dying Light is Techlands attempt at making their own version of Dead Island after breaking off from Deep Silver.
On the surface the game is alright, the story is nothing too special though there are some moments where it might hit you in the feels if you grew attached to some of the characters, maybe not since you don't get much interaction with a lot of them throughout the game.
The gameplay is where it really shows its strengths though, whilst it has a lot of things reminiscent of Dead Island like craftable mods, leveling/ranking system and so on, one thing that is drastically different is the implementation of parkour into its gameplay ala Mirror's Edge style.
I will give that the parkour is a lot of fun to play around with especially with the Grappling hook which you unlock later in the game as you progress ranks. It lets you glide across the starting map and later on Sector 0 as you progress through the story, however that said its not always clear about exactly how extensive the range of what you can grab onto which can lead to a halt in flow or in some cases, death by gravity.
There are colletibles in this game but I didn't care much for them and challenges are also present do 'x' in 'x' time, you know the drill. Some can be hard to do though and for someone like me who can sometimes take a game too seriously it does not help when the challenge giver insults you sometimes after failing said challenge.
The crafting system is decent enough allowing you to craft things from medkits to throwing stars to elemental explosives later on when you unlock the ability to.
However that said, the last boss of the game is an absolute joke, its basically one big QTE and you'd think they would have not done this since the last boss from Dead Island was good though bs in it's own right but that's just my opinion.
In summary though I think it's a game worth playing for sure, the crafting system allows for some nice weapons, the parkour is fun and overall a good time. Though like most games it has its share of flaws.
But regardless its a must play from me, though I maybe suggest waiting for a sale either on here or other sites that might offer it for a bit cheaper.

Riddled Corpses is a twin-stick shooter set in a zombie apocalypse, with a retraux visual and audio design. Speaking of design, the game features some absolutely baffling design choices, which include:
There are a lot of things to complain about: the enemies are bullet sponges, even the random mooks. While I like fanservice as much as the next person, the female characters are all dressed like street walkers. The gameplay is slow and grindy, yet the game manages to be short as well. The biggest complaint, and the most important one, is that the game just isn't interesting or fun to play. It's dull and drudgerous right from the beginning, and it only gets worse the longer you play.

I was really hoping to like this game. Unfortunately, the shop system sucks. You and a friend will play to unlock only one character at a time, and you will share them throughout your play time. Riddled Corpses is tedious, and not in a fun way. It's a shame, because if the shop system was overhauled to give people actual options for upgrading, then this game would have been great! As it is though, you save for the next character, or pay to level the same one up some, which only gives you a shallow impression that the shop means something.

So when Killing floor 2 was released in Early access, I was severely dissapointed in the way this game was going, It felt too easy, no matter the difficulty. Back then, i didnt really have a reason to give this game a review simply because it wasnt as good as Killing floor 1. But I did give it a chance and tried it after release. This review will be a comparison between the two games.
The good!!!!
Graphics: it is beautiful. It has been a really great upgrade. from just the visual looks to the gore.
The gameplay: has been improved aswell. After the latest update introducing the newest Zeds, It has started giving a challange for solo players on Suicidal and Hell on Earth. Meaning you just cant stay in one spot. you have to move around the map conserving ammo as much as possible (Dont be afraid to spray into the harder zeds)
Weapons: Now this was the biggest concern when the game was in early access. Majority of weapons there wasnt really any point to use. the cheaper weapons were better than the more expensive. Now, the more expensive weapons are far superior in the later waves compared to the cheaper weapons.
Classes: There is plenty of classes in this game. Some people like and some dont, Demo class has got its old Risk reward style of gameplay back from Killing floor 1. Where you can badly get hurt from your own grenades just to kill the zeds. At first, it was very dissapointing, Now since the m16+203 combo came back in, its a great class. All classes are very well balanced to work with eachother in a team.
Blood: Blood, Lots of blood! xD
The bad! :(
Running: I dont know if its just me, but When you start running, it feels like the game slows your running to a walk speed. you just dont feel like you are running that fast, but the animation is too quick for the speed.
Zeds: Now I dont know if they adjust to your playstyle. They are good. But... if you try to get them lined up. The zeds respawn so they are closer to you, It creates a harder game, but it Kinda ruins the experiance by running around to get them lined up just for some to dissapear.
maps: So This game kinda lacks maps. Mostly ones with open spaces. In Killing floor one, The most iconic map was West london, Being 2 main lines where zeds can walk down, and a downstairs area aswell. This allows the sniper class more straight lines. Even Farm in Killing floor 1 was great. Big open maps, Where you can go anywhere to hold out
This game does have a little more they have to do before its fully complete, But they are heading in the right direction, You dont have to really worry about micro transactions, Due to they dont impact the game at all. Just weapons skins.
For this game i am giving it a 8/10. Some parts need to be worked on. It has really improved since it came out of early access. More content will be great, There is no DLCs yet, And at the price of $30, you cant go wrong.
I'd kill to play this game 24/7, (it was a play on words, because it's killing floor 2 and I said kill in the beginning.) English isn't my second language sorry.

Killing floor 2 is a good game.Basically it is a good successor to the original. I played the original quite a bit back in the day and I remember when the original game came out it was bare bones, meaning very little content but over time it became a legendary game because tripwire kept adding weapons and classes which made it great. Seeing as killing floor 2 has already started out as such a promising game so shortly after release brings me to the conclusion that the addons and content tripwire will put into the game will make it more than worthwhile for the purchase made now. Now with that being said it is important to note the differences in between the two. The first being that the difficulty seems rather low unless you play on hoe difficulty but at the same time the differences in tactics compared to the first game are improved. In the first game it was possible to hide in a starewell and and weld the door behind you and basically be able to hold off the hordes of the undead for a long time. In this game you can't do that because the excess fleshpounds and scrakes will cause you to retreat. So now it's actually better to defend yourself out in the open where you have plenty of escape routes in case you have to fall back. ALl the classes work really well except for commando IMO because stalkers are soo easy to kill. not only this but the variety of classes will surely satisfy anyone. Because anyone who plays this game will be able to find a class that fits their playstyle. The firebug is vastly different from the swat and the swat is vastly different from the demo man and the demon man is vastly different from the berserker. teamwork is necessary and all classes need to fill their designated position to succeed. But unfortunately that is only on harder difficulties I do hope they atlest four more difficulty options that are harder than hell on earth which is currently teh hardest difficulty in the game. with that beign said the game is absolute blast to play and I do recommend it. The last thing I will bring up is the crafting and cosmetics system they have put into the game. It's garbage in killing floor 1 you could pay five dollars and get a group of new characters or weapon skins. This is what they should do again. Five dollars for 5 new characters is a good deal so I hope they choose to do that instead.

This is a light hearted JRPG. It’s not too long nor too small. It’s perfect to spend some time.
While not particularly groundbreaking in any sense, it’s a very good game. It starts in a very comedic tone, and even when it gets into the main plot it never goes near dark.
The dungeons are somewhat repetitive, but there are no random encounters, you can see the enemies on the screen and avoid them.
The Tower is a very nifty way to take away the grind in dungeons, almost all side quest important items can be found there, and it’s a quick way to gain exp, money.
Don’t try to do everything on the first run. If you try to finish all side quests it might go for about 20h. On NG+ you’ll stomp everything that moves and are finally able to do some other side quests, recruit extra characters, get another ending (there are three different one) and focus on other stuff, like crafting.
It’s a good game. Ig you like the art style and jrpgs, this one is a good one, not the best, but good to relax form others like the Agarest series (80h a game with obligatory battles every move, it’s nuts).
About the DLCs:  the important ones are already included in the game (the tower ones). Some aren't very good (like the bath set) and other just break the game until lvl 30 zones (in first run you'll end up around lvl 40) so it's your call.

Every now and then a game comes along that sets a new bar for awesome. FTL broadcasts a new, fun and addictive experience the way games like Space Invaders, Tetris, Wolfenstien 3D, Portal and a few others have managed to do.
You and your ship and your crew of ragtag aliens are the last hope the galaxy has against the corrupt rebellion. Galaxy and zones are different every time you play. Encounters are unpredictable and combat is nuanced yet accessible whether your pounding the enemies hull or repelling boarders. Different ships offer different strategies to victory and different alien crewmen offer their own strengths and weaknesses. You'll never have the same experience twice.
The game is not easy, and you will probably leave many a wrecked hulk in the cold reaches of space before you start to win. But this really does make the experience all the more rewarding. FTL is hard, but the good kind of hard that makes you beam with pride when you see the boss finally burst into tiny ship bits.
Highly recommended! One of the best games I've ever played! You won't be disappointed!

TL;DR: It's a cutesy, singleplayer brawler that plays similarly to Super Smash Bros with RPG elements, but with out as much polish and refinment of the combat. It is very enjoyable, though is at times more fustrating that it should be. FBF is fairly short and offers replayability through NG+.
Buy? Maybe. It's an almost too cutesy, Super Smash Bros style brawler set in the Jomon forest, a place dependent on the power of a magical stone that is protected by Freesia. Combat is similar to Smash Bros where you have a simple attack/combo button, jump button, block button and special attack button based on the direction you press.
The neatest aspect of this is the ability to customize the specials from a wide variety of moves including projectiles, ground smashes, anti-air moves and more. It is presented in an RPG fashion, as more specials unlock as you level up and complete levels. This does mean that you have to figure out which moves you like or need prior to each Day (level), as some are not effective in some situations (especially moves that only work in the air or only work on ground, leaving Freesia doing nothing and wide open to attack, which isn't a problem in SSB). You can unlock all basic attacks, but you have a limit of two "passive buffs" that you can apply. This doesn't make sense to me because there are so many of these buffs and at many times, I feel like I lose so much because I can't use a couple more. Thankfully, the game will tell you if you're up against a boss or protecting a vortex in the next fight.
The combat is nowhere near as good as SSB. Combos feel good and satisfying, but often are easily interuppted by a near extreme multitude of projectiles thrown by offscreen enemies, requring you to block mid-combo to prevent damage (this may be why the combo reset timer is a bit forgiving). That same block, like SSB, can be broken if you are attacked too much, but it's shown under your HP bar in the upper left corner of the screen, instead of on Freesia, requiring you to take your eyes off the action in intense fights - VERY BAD. Offscreen enemies are a huge nuisance when they are shooting so much while you're dealing with melee enemies - you don't have the ability to deal with it, especially when your block doesn't let you evade out of the way like SSB, just hop around. Bosses never flinch like you do when you are hit mid combo (except when you beat them down to certain points of their health), so you spend most of the time in boss fights playing defensively and nicking at their HP with 2-3 hit combos, so you aren't juggled (while they can also break the block, which is your only real means of defense). I mention offscreen enemies - that means the camera is fixed on Freesia's location, which is not a problem until there enemies beyond the bounds of the screen that can ruin your day - or enemies attacking vortexes you can't see.  I got kinda irritated near the end to amost rage quitting, but thankfully, that was the last battle around 3hrs. There's replayability in NG+ and a Guardian mode that some how didn't save after I beat the game because the game crashed when I messed with resolution settings (even though I could access my 2nd save file that occured after beating the game. Oddly, it acted as if it was before the last battle.). I've seen a Dark Freesia, so there might be more bosses or levels.  This game isn't BAD, it's just isn't as polished as the early Smash Bros games. I'd love to see a really good SSB clone, that maybe has some RPG aspects like this, as well as some exploration. It's important to note that Freesias battle yaps are pretty annoying, since she screams with every attack: it may not bother you, but it will probably bother people around you if you play with speakers.

A very fun and unusual game.
Saints Row IV incorporates the best features from SR3 but also enhances many of the most lacking elements of it's predecessor.  It does appear however that the game engine and graphics had changed very little or not at all, which may disappoint those wanting a significant upgrade to the visuals.  The game does look decent on the PC but does seem to be a bit behind other recent titles.
I did not think that Volition would be able to go even more "over the top" than they did with SR3, but they somehow managed to do so, and in a way that fits the game very well.  At no point did it seem that the humor in the story was forced or placed for the sake being there.
The campaign is very well scripted and dialoged.  I did particularly like the banter between the various members of the Saints.  The game has a great antagonist in the alien overload Zinyak who has a witty English accent and a very Bond-esque villain personality.  The game also finds a lot of ways to include throwbacks to the previous titles in the series, which should please those who have played those games.
The main theme behind the game borrows heavily from some favorite Sci-Fi action films like the Matrix (1999) and They Live (1988).  Most of the gameplay is in a very Matrix-like virtual city of Steelport where the player has to free other captured friends and attempt to break out of the simulation via hacking and disrupting.  Much like the Matrix, you spend a lot of time switching between a real-life ship and the virtual city of Steelport, and super powers are learned in the virtual world as the player learns more about how to master and disrupt the virtual environment.  There is a TON of missions and side activities to keep the player busy and many of the familiar side activities from SR3 make a comeback with some fun twists (though Snatch and Escort missions are omitted this time, YAY!)

Biggest complaint I would see is in the super powers that the player gets in the simulated Steelport.  While they are great fun and add a very interesting element to the gameplay, the powers will render the automobiles and many of the weapons obsolete.  The gameplay with superpowers in the open world does greatly resemble that of games like Prototype, Crackdown and inFamous, so the game does feel more like a really good super hero simulator or Matrix game rather than a GTA style crime game.  The player will also find the game not too challenging with upgrade super powers, but the great writing, over-the-top gameplay and humor makes up for the lack of challenge.
Overall the game continues to shamelessly build on the over-the-top gameplay that SR3 did and further distance itself from GTA and earlier Saints Row titles.  The result turned into something rather unique and it seems that Volition has become rather adept at creating a very fun and zany game that does not take itself too seriously.  If you liked the direction that SR3 took with the series then you will probably enjoy this game as much as I did.

Ever feel like you have time to kill? Got something downloading in the background that's taking longer than it should and you are in need of entertainment? Watched all your favourite channels new vids on youtube? Tired of seeing bottle flip compilations and need something else in your life? Well, my friends, I think you've found a good investment right here.
Risk of Rain, a rogue like, combat based platformer which pits your character on a planet as they scrape together junk in attempts to fight for their life. Now, sounds strange from my generalisation, but theres more to it.
You don't get to determine what gear is thrown at you, the game picks for you, and you have to deal with it. (without in game modifiers, that is.) Each playthrough on vanilla settings is completely different, as the items you recieve can change how you approach the game. The items provided lean toward either offensive or defensive gameplay, by either granting you increased damage, lifesteal or gold income, or providing damage reduction, "overshield" or an aura of barbed wire, because why not. Utility items are also included, which are things like increased movement speed, auto gold generation, and increased amounts of jumps. There are plenty more different stat augments that I will let you discover for yourself.
A thing I mentioned earlier, modifiers. These can be found in each of the levels Risk of Rain provides, usually requiring a puzzle to be solved, or a jump course, or maybe even just extreme cheese strats. If vanilla is getting rough, or maybe too predictable, turn some of these on, and you can find yourself mowing down everything in your path while only being allowed to take one hit maximum, or make it so the game hates you entirely.
Another thing which I think is particularly interesting, is the difficulty mechanic. Risk of Rain has no set difficulty, but instead, a system based on how long you take in game. The difficulty increases the longer it takes you to find your way around, and the rate at which this increases can be adjusted in the form of three difficulties on the character select screen. No matter which setting you pick, the game will grow more challenging as you take longer to get through.
TL;DR A great game to kill time with, and even something to spend a decent amount of time on as you mess around with different playthroughs as you pit your luck against the random drop system. The different characters and game modifiers allow you to see what kind of crazy things you can achieve, ranging from running around at the speed of sound, jumping up to asgard itself, or decimating anything that takes a millisecond to look at you. Extremely worth the money while it's on sale, and even when it isn't, I'd say you can find enjoyment out of it. The soundtrack is also nice. Give it a go, won't you?
EDIT: forgot to add that if you want to play multiplayer, you will need LogMeIn Hamachi or a similar program. LogMeIn Hamachi is a free download, but it is true that there is better software out there, so you might want to explore a bit.

Risky Rain is a survival platformer with roguelike elements, it'd be nice if games these days were easier to explain, like what does that even mean. Well you're placed in a 2D side scrolling arena in which you have to find the teleporter to get to the next stage which has a new arena to find a teleporter in. It's a game about balance, the more time you waste finding loot and not finding the teleporter the harder the enemies get but if you rush the teleporter you'll be underequiped.
The roguelike elements come in the form of permadeath and some light random elements. The loot and its placement is random but the maps are mostly static with a few variable parts. Each stage also has a couple of maps to drop you in so each playthrough feels a little different.
Risking Rain has a steep learning curve. It took me quite a while to finish it for the first time, but as I got used to the tactics and characters I found myself consistently getting further in each playthrough. Not all of the characters are equal by the way, there are all pretty unique and valid choices for finishing the game but some are just more versatile and "easier" than others. The "better" characters tend to be more difficult to unlock though. There are also "artifacts" that can be found in the levels and activated to make the game harder or easier (mostly harder).
The game has a co-op mode but I think you've a higher chance of completing a run in single player. The enemies scale with the player count and unless your team is coordinated with loot drops so that everyone's build makes sense you'll probably underequipped and outgunned. The scaling stops at four players and you can edit the games config files to allow for more players than that, which theoretically makes things easier but lootshare will still be a problem. This would also be Risking some serious Rain too as the games net code can barely handle 4 players.
Overall I found Risk the Rain to be fun and a little addicting. The occasional bugs, gaps in the UI or crappy net code is made up for by just how fun the core of the game is.
Also this game is published by Chucklefish so they were probably watching Hopoo Games make Rain of Risk instead of working on Starbound.

Killing floor 2 is a good game.Basically it is a good successor to the original. I played the original quite a bit back in the day and I remember when the original game came out it was bare bones, meaning very little content but over time it became a legendary game because tripwire kept adding weapons and classes which made it great. Seeing as killing floor 2 has already started out as such a promising game so shortly after release brings me to the conclusion that the addons and content tripwire will put into the game will make it more than worthwhile for the purchase made now. Now with that being said it is important to note the differences in between the two. The first being that the difficulty seems rather low unless you play on hoe difficulty but at the same time the differences in tactics compared to the first game are improved. In the first game it was possible to hide in a starewell and and weld the door behind you and basically be able to hold off the hordes of the undead for a long time. In this game you can't do that because the excess fleshpounds and scrakes will cause you to retreat. So now it's actually better to defend yourself out in the open where you have plenty of escape routes in case you have to fall back. It really is too bad. Riddled Corpses looks great on the surface - good graphics, solid premise, and a decent upgrades system which incentivises continude play. Then after the first half hour you start to notice the things that aren't quite right, and they sour the whole experience.
The largest issue is visibility - large portions of the screen are obscured by the HUD, and it's just unnecessary. And it gets worse the more you play - boss bars, wave timers, and your turret (once purchased) all take up additional screen space. Environmental objects in stage 4 further hinder visibility. It's no exaggeration to say that whatever difficulty the game has, it owes to hidden enemies and blind dodges. The game makes other cheap shots with its large enemy spawns, which appear as circles but can drop enemies of any size on top of you.
Controls are another sore spot. The game was clearly designed for the X360 controller - and for the basics, this is fine; left stick moves, right stick shoots, everyone is happy. But items are assigned to the face buttons (again, no option to remap) and if you want to use them you either have to stop shooting or contort your hand into strange positions, which is ridiculous when the shoulder triggers are available. Keyboard controls are nonexistent, though there is a terrible mouse+keyboard control scheme you can use (for further irritation, the game does not even tell you which of the three item keys uses each item).
There are other smaller annoyances - the only at all effective way to grind gold is to dynamite stage 1 over and over, turning off sound effects will allow random effects to still play, pacing is quite slow (stages can be up to 9 minutes long by my timing). I'm also disappointed that Arcade Mode is not really what I expected - it's simply not possible to play like an arcade game, as it's tied in to the rest of the game's grinding system and it quickly becomes impossible without prepurchased upgrades. But Riddled Corpses would have been a fine game for what it is without its many extremely obvious (and easily addressed) flaws.
Readers might notice that I put quite a few hours into this game. It's not unplayable - as another reviewer noted, it's not a bad side activity for listening to podcasts. But it's frustrating to see a developer do so well, then start dropping the ball on things that are not small details. The strong start just intensifies how much Riddled Corpse's flaws hurt it - real fun is right in front of it, and all it delivers is mindless activity.

Teleglitch is a game that exhibits the primary negative attributes of the modern roguelike quite well. It throws one into a semi-random environment and provides little consistency in what serves to aid the fight for survival between playthroughs. The player will likely be struggling on any given run for one of two goals: to either learn the terrain, foes, and uses for scavenged materials, or to locate the necessary items to tinker, heal, and shoot to the next major waypoint. Perhaps one of the bigger disappointments is the fact that story, while quite serviceable as a roadmap and mechanism to explain to the player why one is chased by zombies or robots or weird four-armed grunty things, seems to carry less weight here than of what it is capable.
So why has the author logged over 300 hours total with this game?
Despite the game's faults, Teleglitch situates the player in a fleshy malleable shell and says "OK, run on home, and shoot the monsters before they git ya," and the player is afforded exactly that much control. It is that level of control which really embodies the experience; you are an unlikely hero who can overcome tremendous odds with skill and knowledge, and you can survive either a moderate number of heavy punches or two to three bullet wounds before you're done. You will need to put together equipment in ways unintended by its creators, get incredibly frustrated, and make every single shot count - and if you do, you will perhaps succeed in running the gamut of a labyrinthine facility and escaping alive. At certain points the game will show a kinder face and very occasionally provide checkpoints upon the completion of a level, but these are few and far between.
Two major components factor into making many roguelikes: adversarial competition, i.e. combat, and exploration/knowledge acquisition. Teleglitch is a relatively well-built animal whose focus lies entirely on those aspects from the visual aesthetic to gameplay. Combat usually exemplifies Hobbes' human nature, being difficult, quick, and painful, and yet it is often the prettiest part of the game - each bullet draws the eye as it moves through the environment, each kind of firearm looses rounds with slightly different characteristics and reports or bangs, and each impact communicates the gravitas of "a bullet just went through that thing!" (Alternatively, when one intercepts a bullet with unprotected body parts, the severity of "maaaybe one or two more of those before death comes" really sinks home.) Even in close range, trying to knife the last members of a ravening horde turns into an uncomfortable dance... each swish manages to convey a grim sense of space rapidly closing between metallic edge and target surface. And after an engagement concludes, one's reward is usually not more than a nutritious can of meat or mediocre weapon. The game's point is that fighting ought to be a means to an end - even when demolishing a troupe of robots with explosives, the enjoyment one gets from seeing the metal bits fly everywhere must be tempered with the knowledge that one no longer has those explosive materials. It is unnerving and quite involving.
On the other side of the equation, seeing the world of Teleglitch is a careful and tense experience. When one wakes up in a tiny storeroom, the limitations on the player's vision become obvious - line-of-sight is one of the most striking mechanics, and with very few exceptions danger begins as soon as a foe comes into view. Audio cues, like the hum of a door opening to admit a herd of mutants or the slamming beat of robotic legs, frequently provide the player's only warning before weapons need to be discharged. One of the author's more memorable experiences was the first time walking in front of a large pipe and discovering a dozen or so zombies swarming from its mouth, and the quick subsequent demise. At later levels, one might rush into a room to discover a shotgun-wielding foe directly inside a closed door, and then one once again realizes the benefit of detecting enemies even when unseen, and the dangers of the converse. The player equates the unseen with an unknown but qualitatively significant danger. Every step survived feels like a miniscule victory. Even if one manages to build equipment which detects enemies outside of line-of-sight, a squid lying in wait at the end of a long corridor is all it takes to reduce one to an irradiated crisp.
All in all, Teleglitch is an imperfect experience where the player embraces the frustrations of mortality and the joys of victory over great tribulation. It is certainly not for those who find difficulty in a title unappealing. But for those who are willing to give to the game, it will give an enormous amount in return.

After a few hours of playtime, I can safely say, this game is far and away the  best sports simulation game of all time. Fun, strategic, and incredibly deep, OOTP 18 is a step above all previous entries in the series.
But that doesn't mean there aren't misteps.
A major one is how there is still no major tutorial mode. While at first this game seems like a "Point and Click simulator" the reality is that this is a deep and complex series of menus, some of which are incredibly cluttered and hard to understand without expirementing or prior knowledge. If there was an optional mode or at least a "How to play" menu, I think it would reduce the pain of newer players settling in.
Challenge mode is new to OOTP 18, and it is awesome. Removing any chances of cheating, making you use all your knowledge of the game to build up a championchip contender. However, with this mode, some things are made heavily abundant. The major one being that TRADE A.I. IS HOT GARBAGE. In challenge mode, the A.I. is set to the hardest settings, which is natural, given the name. However, what results is a trade market heavily dominated by weaker players, with those players being offered for your best. (I.E. Boston Trading Babe to the Yankees for prospects) It's silly, and made worse by the fact that you can't pull that back on them. Want to run a Braves franchice? Good luck with the heavy contracts of Bartolo Colon, Nick Markaksis, R.A. Dickey, and Matt Kemp, which take up over half the total payroll, and are at maximum, 3 STARS OUT OF FIVE! That is bullcrap.
Besides those misteps though? Everything else is excellent. 3D mode is improved to feature small little animations to represent players doing things, and even minor quality of life things like celebrations of walk off hits have been added. It's nice to see the devs putting in the extra effort. Most everything else is either kept from past versions, or slightly updated, but I'm not a huge technical guy. I'll leave it at these Devs clearly love the game of baseball and the fans, so I highly reccomend OOTP Baseball 18 to any fan of the game, or even the occasional statistician.
It is a cruel, harsh, unforgiving mistress and you will it love for it.

After spending a dozen sweaty hours playing this game, I've come to several conclusions:
-- Yes, it belongs in the horror genre.  Not because the monsters are scary, but because the atmosphere makes discovery scary.  You open doors carefully; you wince at thinking about pushing a button, you make sure the coast is clear before opening a cabinet.
-- Rogue-likes are supposedly hard, but THIS is unmerciful.  It's just a hair's width from being unfair, and while I don't think it gets there, if I spend another dozen hours not being able to get past the 4th level, I'll be convinced.
-- The pixel graphics weirdly add to the scary quality of the game.  I didn't think I'd like them, and while they're not impressive, they really do ADD to the game's atmosphere in a good way
I sorta can't stop playing, and I don't know why.  The combination of anxiety and discovery and trying to balance the need to preserve my inventory against the need to say alive - it's addictive.  This might just be the most difficult game I've ever played, but it keeps bringing me back...

I really wanted to love this game. Set in a bright colorful world with just the type of characters I would expect to see.  Cute outfits and stock consumables fill the item shop in the hub city. I really liked the way you could change the story by deciding whether you wanted to release the Goddess or the Devil. The swords being able to change the dungeons was also an interesting idea. All things considered it was just what i was hoping it would be at first.  However the game became a struggle after the first 10 hours due it its restrictive combat system and sluggish leveling.
Before I get into that, there are side missions to help you get additional items, but after the first round you just pick all the ones for the area you will be visiting and you will usually complete them as you travel thru the dungeon. There were a few that had me change the monsters in the dungeon or hunt down something interesting but most were quickly forgotten as soon as I accepted them.
The combat system in this game places each of your characters facing the enemy in a small circle. For fights with 2 or less it's not a problem, but once you start going against big monsters with a full party you begin to realize just how tight the arena is. It seemed like I could make better use of the small space by increasing the character range but that leads me to my other issue. As you get more experience, each character earns points to increase various stats and buy new abilities. Some abilities are unneccessary but still i never felt i had enough to build my characters like i wanted. I had the DLC weapons on the entire time but I never felt overpowered. I pushed myself to make it about halfway through the story. (current hours 29) The battle system doesn't really get fun until you have at least a 3 move combo. While trying to balance your points between obtaining these moves, magics and other stats you realize that they don't go that far. This is when the game became too much of a grind. and when I couldn't go any further.
If a slow grind doesn't get to you in what is an alright RPG then go right ahead. But I can't reccomend it and I unfortunately will not be playing anymore of the games from Compile Heart as the battle/upgrade system is seen in all the ones I have looked into.

Obsidian Entertainment & South Park Digital Studios 2014, 'South Park: The Stick of Truth', Ubisoft Entertainment (publisher).
South Park: The Stick of Truth (SoT) is a game that was always on my 'to-do' list, however, two things ultimately detered me away from getting the game. Firstly, the price, and secondly, the censorship; the latter being the major deterent. SoT became infamous here in Australia due to censorship which entailed certain scenes being replaced by a picture of a crying koala, this being a tongue-in-cheek way of the developers/publishers poking fun at the state's strict and at times over-the-top regime regarding video game content. With the advent of the Steam Christmas sale though, I decided to bite the bullet and buy the game at a discounted price, and found a mod online that allowed me to play the game the way it was intended; uncensored. I can safely say now, on my third playthrough of the story, I have not been disappointed whatsoever. I think I should also add at this point, that I'm a big South Park fan, so my expectations were high given that Trey Parker and Matt Stone were heavily involved in game's story and development.
The premise of the game is that you're the new kid in town, promptly named ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ by the Colorado children who've become engrossed in a Dungeons and Dragons-esque game about a mystical stick that controls the universe, thus leading to some hilarious shenanighans that make the story feel like you're involved in a giant episode of South Park. Without giving too much away, you will explore the small mountain town of South Park and encounter classic and familiar characters that have made the show a classic that is still going strong. The game definitely rewards longtime or avid fans of the show as many throwbacks are made to classic moments or episodes which make the game so much more enjoyable. The game also allows control, albeit it little, over the game; most notably the ability to choose your character's style as a fighter, mage, thief, or Jew (probably closest to a Paladin in DnD law). It should be noted however that there isn't that much difference between the classes aside from unique attacks. The combat system can be a little repeative and resembles typical turn-based strategy games, however, the attacks from both your allies and yourself are pretty awesome. There's nothing quite like being able to peform a Roshambo, or a circumcision on children.
One thing that has pushed me into playing the campaign for a (now) third time is the sheer level of collectables which tie into achivement farming. If you're one of those people who love to 100% games, then this is going to provide you with some fun challenges such as collecting Chinpokomon throughout the town, some of which cannot be found outside of the story, which means you not only be able to collect them all, but also means you cannot friend the entire town on Facebook, which means you'll miss achivements...
In summary, if you're from a region where the game is censored, you can easily find a mod to play the true game in all its glory. As a fan of the show, I was not disappointed, however at the same time, I can understand how some people would be as the fights can be a bit repetative. However, the sheer amount of throwbacks and cameos from characters we've all grown to love makes this game worth it. It's like being in your own South Park movie.

Schlocky, hilarious, cleverly written and irreverent at all times, this is a game built around being as fun as possible. It manages to do so many strange and funny things in a single game while also being not only the best Enter the Matrix game but also superhero genre game made to date. Superpowers are the natural next frontier for the SR universe, and SRIV implements them admirably while refining the mission structure and types to maximize player involvement.
Listening to pulsing dubstep and bounding from rooftop to rooftop collecting things sounds pretty basic, but it's something I haven't experienced in such a open way like this game provides for you. Go buy it.

Risk of Rain is one of the most fun experiences I've had in video games. I've spent countless hours, and I'll spend many more in this game. The most important concept to learn is that you will die. Once you realize that, one can spend their time getting a little bit further and further. You can find what character suits you the most, you'll eventually figure out what each ability does, and you can learn to love the game more and more. Multiplayer/co-op is also extremely fun, though you have to port forward to play online with your friends.
tl;dr, Risk of Rain is game that is very difficult, but if you love pixel textures, rouge-like games, and light (morbid?) humor, pick this game up.
Edit: This game earns my Steam nomination for The Test of Time award. It's gameplay is honestly as mesmerizing as the day I picked it up. Definitely worth it.

(TL;DR is final paragraph)
Riddled Corpses (RC) mixes the "twinstick shooter" gameplay of Robotron 2084 with the Forward Crawl & Stage mechanic from "Beat 'Em Up" games (such as Double Dragon or Bad Street Brawler). If you're an oldschool gamer (or just old, like me) you'll recognize and appreciate the choices made here, and the respect and love that RC displays for the genre.
There's really no plot: Select a character, hold down the fire button and decimate zombies; pick up health or dynamite (what we used to call "smart bombs" back in the day); rinse and repeat. Coins dropped by zombies can be used to upgrade or unlock characters. That's it. But, really, who cares? The genre is tried and true, and still loads of fun. Better yet, Riddled Corpses features so many thoughtfully designed touches, that you don't even notice them at first.
For example, power-ups make a different noise when you collect them, so that you don't even have to see them to know that you have one (and sometimes, you
see them amidst all the on-screen chaos, so this really becomes useful). Likewise, the end of a wave also features a special sound, so that you don't have to take your eyes of the frenetic battle surrounding your character.
This type of game is, by its very nature a grind,. However, that doesn't mean it's boring. Two modes of play (Arcade and Survival), along with unlockable characters (each with their own special quality, such as a magnet that attracts money and perks) keep things interesting. Some enemies offer bullet-hell styled run-n-gunning, which also keeps the action moving. In another nice touch, each character has their own weapon and upgrades, so the graphics for each one are different. I really appreciated that; even though the level 15 weapon for one character may do the same amount of damage as another character, the fact that they look different keeps things interesting.
The music and art are well above average and, while I'm not generally into bit tunes, this is a soundtrack I'd listen to if it were available.
There are some things that could be tweaked. Boss deaths, while satisfying, create such massive and prolonged explosions that it's impossible to see what is going on in a signifcant portion of an already-cluttered and chaotic playfield. More than once, I've lost a game simply because I killed a boss and the explosion (which doesn't seem to cause any splash-back damage) allowed a baddie to slip beneath, unnoticed.
Also, the random perk drops, such as first aid kits and dynamite, seem a little
random.  I've played games (in RC) where multiples of the same perk have literally dropped too fast for me to use them before the next drop, and then I've played games where I've gone ten minutes or more without a single drop. In a game as well-structured and thought out as Riddled Corpses, this seems to be a bit of an oversight. Another curious choice is that health packs are consumed as soon as you run over them, whether or not you are at full health; it would be nice if they couldn't be picked up until after the player has taken damage, to keep from accidentally "using" them.
Finally, keys are not rebindable, which is a pretty big deal, particulary for the arcade genre. Keyboard players (such as myself) need to be able to feel comfortable with the controls, as they may be scrambling to hit the right key milliseconds before potential death. Also, menu selections (including resuming from a pause) can only be done via the keyboard, which means (if you're a keyboard and mouse player) you must either take your hand off directional keys or the mouse (firing button) in order to resume a game. If you had to pause in the middle of an intense fight, there's a possibility you'll die while trying to resume due to this (so plan accordingly). The game does offer gamepad support, although I have not tested it, so it's possible that gameplay can be resumed via a button on the pad for those gamers who use them.
(TL;DR) All that aside though, rarely have a played a game in this genre where the difficulty curve is this perfect. From the very first level, the challenge took me far enough to know that I wanted to see more, and it was an easy decision to press that replay button one more time. The developer is active on the discussion boards and seems open to improving the game. Even if he weren't, Riddled Corpses is fast, frantic, and fun, and it's one of the finest arcade games I've played in a long, long while.
Recommended.

Musics (9/10)
I found every music GREAT in this game. I mean, yeah I may have overreacting, but all of them was cool to me. There was no annoying musics and some of them was epic. Only reason I took 1 point from this one is, when you are fighting with bosses there is a music playing really cool and EVERY time you do Fairize the music of it interrupts is until you lose Fairize Mode. Yes, it is normal when you are fighting against normal mobs, but in boss fightes, a music comes that you can't listen it unless you do nothing but listen in Sound Gallery, when you do Fairize that you need it always, Fairize's music always interrupts boss fight's music and it is annoying.
DLCs (5/10)
Like in many games, you pay some cash and you are overpowered against game. They are just for boosting your power and do nothing other. One of them for costumes and it is cool I guess, but the other ones have no other meaning. Ah, there is a one for 100-750 level dungeons, but I do not need to play it to 750 level. Overall (8/10)
This game is great fun to play. It has some annoying points, but if you do not count them it is great game. Story is not boring, jokes are funny, gameplay is cool, musics are great. They all have some bad points, but they are not that big to make game bad. You should buy the game. If the game is in discount, I think you MUST buy it.

Civ is the king of all strategy games. There have been many strategy games since but Civ is the original.  Civ has been and always will be the well from which all others draw their inspiration - to some degree. Civ V specifically is one of the best in the series. It is the modernizing and refining of the Civ concept.  While I have some small misgivings with the way the Brave New World expansion added a needlessly complicated layer of sea trading. there are far more things to be happy about than sour with in this newest edition. The graphics are nicely polished, bugs mostly (if not completely) squashed, mechanics simplified and streamlined without the loss of depth. multiplayer functions well, and lastly the tutorials, learning curve, and difficulty settings have never been more accessible for new players.
If you're new to Civ, feel like trying out a new genre of game or a veteran that for some reason still hasn't picked up this latest edition there's no downside to jumping in. It is a game that easily justifies its price for the amount of content and hours you are likely to spend with it.

I've been wanting to purchase this game for awhile now, but always found an excuse not to.  Today I bit the bullet and bought it, along with some other games that were on sale for the holidays.
I jumped into the game to play, blinked and four hours had gone by.
Some of the early quests have you mining and gathering resources.  I had amassed a sizeable collection, mining deep into the planet.  Then I went to do one of the first "dungeons".  I died numerous times in the same spot because I was trying to get my stuff back.  I thought it was hopeless.  Then I remembered my character's abilities and was able to retrieve all of the backpacks.
There are many elements similar to Minecraft, but these are two different games.  Planets are small but big enough to be able to mine and explore for long hours without running out of new things to do.  Unlike Minecraft, which is one endless procedural world, you're meant to move on to other planets once you've reached a certain point.
The crafting system is much more enjoyable than Minecraft, in my opinion.  New recipes are acquired through gameplay and NPC's and you don't need to use an inventory grid to make something.  That was one thing I hated about Minecraft, the crafting system.
This is an early access game, but so far there's been enough to keep me thoroughly engaged.  I don't know how many quests there are, but it's well worth the asking price.  As it is now, it feels like I'm playing a completed game.  I can't wait to see what else they do with it.
When a game sucks you in and doesn't let go for 4 hours, I'd say that's a keeper in my opinion.  Your experience may vary, but I can't find anything to complain about.

Riddled Corpses is a pixel-graphics twin-stick shooter.  It is an overly grind-dependent repetitive experience.
As you kill enemies, they drop gold which can be spent to unlock new characters, upgrade your characters, and to buy beneficial items.  Unfortunately, this upgrade system is the root of the most critical issue with the design of the game.  Simply put, the game appears to be designed primarily to be a grind-heavy time sink rather than an entertaining experience.
Against the bullet-sponge enemies, your starting character is pitifully weak.  I'm not sure it is possible to even beat the first stage of the game with an unleveled starting character, as enemies will at times spawn faster than you can kill them.  If it is possible, it is presumably a time-consuming soul-draining process, as it takes forever to whittle down the life of even the mid-boss, much less the stage boss.
Weapon upgrading becomes increasingly expensive with each level, and the starting character can be upgraded I believe to level 20.  Alternate characters, which have beneficial special abilities that the starting character lacks, are relatively expensive.   Enemies drop gold frequently, but the individual amounts are tiny compared to shop costs.  Due to how underpowered you are, you will have to play (and die) several times just to upgrade your character enough to efficiently farm the gold to buy and upgrade (as they will also start horribly underpowered) the next character, who was apparently designed to help you farm gold a bit more easily.
Through this experience, you will either keep playing the first arcade stage repeatedly, or you will be playing the arena-based survival mode.  You should be replaying survival mode, as you can get a better gold return for time invested.
By the time you level your character enough to actually be effective in arcade mode, you should already be sick of the title.
The title does have issues beyond the grind, though.  The HUD can block the view of enemies in the upper left of the screen as well as long the bottom.  If you have to move through those areas, you will eventually take hits from unseen enemies.
Graphics-wise, the game is retro-style blocky pixels.  It isn't so bad in small screenshots, but it can be somewhat annoying at fullscreen.  There is a rather awful filter option you can use, but you might as well stick with the default look.

As the title says, you'll like the game when you're into story mode and building stuff that looks minecraftish.
The main downsides here are there's nothing much to do when you've finished the story quest. The remaining random dungeons are just more of the same and not as nice as the story boss dungeons. They will add more story and mod support but till these thing are actually here there's not much to do. The building aspect is quite nice on planets but it lacks for space and vehicle kind of structures. You even have signal logic at your disposal.
So if you're interested in dungeon/story based building, you may like the stuff here. If you're like me and you prefer aspects you know and like from Starmade, 7d2d, Empyrion... then its clearly a no go. Your stuff looks way too minecraftish and you can't build stuff like battleships etc. -  there's also no purpose for these things ingame. Its not a game centered around fps fighting or real physics. Its also not a game about building stuff that looks "real". You have more shapes than just cubes but it still has the minecraft look - a beautiful one but nontheless you have to like it the way it is.
Crafting is not super deep but easy. Just select a receipe and throw ingredients in eg the workbench and its done. Also the UI is decent and easy to grasp.
Unfortunately the enemy ai is super basic and you have just the usual few weapons at your disposal. So Don't expect a real shooter experience or a space sim. The wildlife looks super nice and i like the cute animals but once you've seen a planet you've seen (almost) all species. There's also nothing special about space - it feels just as the distance between the planets you have to cover because planets are where the real action takes place.
There is a roadmap on their homepage but its very vague concerning the future. Multiplayer also seems quite limited. Unfortunately i had no time left to test it - i'd rather went for refund.
Its a lovely game but i don't think its my cup of tea because its lacks features i like in blockbuilding and space games. I'd vote it neutral if there was such an option but since you rely heavily on storymode and hand made dungeons - it's rather a downvote since its not open ended gaming at this point. I see its future in roleplay and dungeoneering but one has to see how it turns out. Currently it looks "sweet" to me but there's nothing else i've seen not better made or more complex in other titles. Its a shame most blockbuilding titels on stem lack features or will be abandoned sooner or later. This is one of the better ones on steam but still not good enough yet.
p.s. The soundtrack is gorgeous!

One of the highlights and best parts about the game is that it throws curveballs at you. Some solutions will be obvious. Some will randomly appear without you even considering them. An hour in, and I've got to say this: The re-playability on this game is very low.
Although I got this at the low price of $3.99, I think there should be more game modes or something to earn. Like collecting badges, getting characters, upgrades, art, that type of thing. Something to work at and unlock. You also might benefit from making some type of story in the game (but don't make it the main focus) or at the very least have some type of background to characters.
The stages are long, and having to replay them again and again to get to where you were is very annoying. Try having some type of checkpoint system (They Bleed Pixels does this very well). Speaking of gameplay, there should be something on the screen indicating how close you finish the level. This is more for convience than anything else. It can be toggled in the settings if people would rather not know. The gameplay is hard, since it's a hell bullet game. Also, the spawn rate is extremely high with hordes and hordes of zombies (oh curse the boss that attacks and spawns those eyeballs) and the hitboxes are...the hitboxes. In stage one of arcade mode, there's a boss where if you try to move above it it's instant gameover. (The gameover when this happens doesn't look pretty as well---the screen shakes repeatedly and the same sound clip is spammed.) Then there's the problem of leveling. When you get to a high enough level, you're constantly bored of fighting the same weak old zombies again to get to the boss that's been giving you trouble. That's time consuming and just plain *boring*.
It's enjoyable, but I can see myself getting tired of it very quickly. What's the point of finishing all the arcade levels? To get a character to play what? The endless level for a higher score? It's not very rewarding and it also seems bland. The characters themselves are pretty pricy, and there needs to be more stats shown. If all I know is my killing stats and not how much health this character has in comparison to this character, how am I going to make the best choices in killing zombies?
All in all, it's fun to play *right now* but it probably won't be in the future. The game's hard, and some people might rage from how painstakingly hard it is to advance, but it's still kind of addicting at the same time. I recommend this game because
1. it's on sale for $3.99, so give this game a shot (if by the time you're reading this it's come back to $7.99, consider my points and see if it's worth it, because personally I'd still buy it anyways)
2. the game has nice graphics, a sweet soundtrack, and many different types of monsters
3. it's fun to play; revisiting the game will probably still be fun after a period of time not playing it
4. I like the game, honest, and I can't say I haven't been enjoying my time playing it. (it's just that the slow progression really puts me off games)

Though this is a simple game, it still has much to offer. You play as a character “Jon" and you defeat waves of enemies as you walk down the road. Every now and then you will even get waves that have small bosses and different enemies. As you defeat more and more waves you will notice an increase of difficulty that will keep you on the edge of your seat. As you achieve higher level waves, more and more zombies will come and more and more gold will drop. Though do not fret, most of the time when you die, you will have gained enough gold to purchase upgrades and do even more damage your next time around. Most of the achievements are for leveling and defeating difficult monsters.
I am definitely happy that I got this game and I will be playing this game often. The fun and chaos makes it definitely worth the price! I am also glad that its 8 and 16 bit, because sometimes its nice to fall back on easy graphics after spending hours on a high intensity graphics game. This is a nice game to sit back in your chair at night with your controller and just have a good time. Nothing to complicated, nothing too simple, just a perfect blend of enjoyment.

I was pleasantly surprised by this game. Since it's made by the same company as the Neptunia franchise, I wasn't really expecting a
story but my expectations were wrong.
Let's start off with the positives. The writing is still very anime-y but the story is told like a Visual Novel so it's able to flow nicely and coherently. The characters are pretty likeable (despite the main protagonist being unlikeable at the beginning) and there are a lot of optional skits that help develop some personality in each of them despite being a pretty short JRPG (20-30 hours for the first playthrough).
Combat is standard. If you've played a Neptunia game, it's the same thing: Turn-based in a 3D realm. A different aspect of the whole leveling process is the "Weapon Point" system where you can spend points to obtain new skills or magic in (mostly) any order you like. This lets you see noticeable differences in your strength.
Oh, and the music is pretty great. The game takes a "Tales of Symphonia: Sylvarant -> Tethealla" route with the music where the normal battle and Fairize music change after starting the 2nd half of the game. It's a nice touch that I personally love. The final boss music is fantastic as well. Without it, the final boss would not have been so great.
I noticed a lot of complaints about bland characters. The thing with that is you can easily pile any JRPG or anime character into a single archetype without regarding any of their other traits or back stories. It's just dumb to have that mindset. All of the characters, from the main cast to the villains, are very unique and memorable. One of the secret characters in particular play a great role in developing the main character's motivations which made me actually
.
Another complaint I've seen is the fact that the game re-uses assets. Without going into spoiler territory, I'll just say that the whole direction of the 2nd half of the game actually played out the way the story intended so that complaint is just moot. I definitely did
get the feeling that they were just trying to "prolong the game".
Now on to the bad. Combat. It's either way too easy or you have to suddenly start grinding. The difficulty is really...weird in this game. There are no options to select a difficulty so everything is always going to be fixed. Given that info, I'm surprised there was such a weird fluctuation in difficulty since you'd think it would be
for the devs to adjust the difficulty with only 1 setting.
Another thing that is a side-effect of the weird difficulty is how some of the fights play out. There are always cutscenes before, during, and after the boss fights which doesn't always match up to how easy/hard the boss was. For example, I completely stomped one of the bosses and right after a cutscene plays where my character is saying "I don't think we can beat him...". It's pretty awkward but it does that to fit the narrative of the story I guess. They could have fixed that by giving different dialogue options (Scene A plays if you win, Scene B plays if you lose/don't kill him in x amount of turns) but I shouldn't expect that much from a low-budget game. Thankfully the final boss' difficulty is
and that left me with a great feeling at least. There are a few other minor gripes like the moments of
random fan service but it's from the Nep-devs so what else could I expect.
Overall, Fairy Fencer F is a pretty great game with some complaints that can just be forgiven if you just focus on the drive of the story rather than the gameplay. I will give a warning for completionists though as this game is incredibly grindy if you're going after achievements.

Seriously though, I cannot recommend XCOM enough. It's hard, but with enough options to tweak the difficulty to suit your playstyle. An average mission, at least for me, takes between 45 and 90 minutes. The level design is neat, but there are only a handful of different maps. That, combined with how long it can take for your soldiers to learn how to shoot straight, makes the game extremely hard in the beginning and almost a breeze in the end - you will learn down to a square and a turn who will go where and who will shoot with what kind of success rate etc. And considering how the probabilities work out, you will need that knowledge.
If you don't want to feel like you have to sink hundreds and hundreds of hours into the same game, XCOM is the right game for you. If you're into different challenges, XCOM is the right game for you. If you like it when the mechanics tell the story, XCOM is absolutely the right game for you. XD
PS: If you're a GM and you're looking for a game that you can shamelessly copy and paste into your setting of choice for a combat-heavy adventure, XCOM is mandatory.

D-Shift utilizes the spellboost mechanic to lower the cost of their cards and to increase damage of a removal card.

Next, after spellboosting wind blast they are able to remove any of the opponent's follower. Not only that, after boosting fiery embrace multiple times for a max of 8 times, they have a 0 costs removal that they can use to remove any threats on the opponent's board.
Lastly, is D-Shift itself which can be played at a low cost due to it being spellboosted. First world:
Started digging underground after 2 hours gameplay to get resources. The gravity starts to flip out, making me stuck in an endless loop of flipping backwards and forwards and getting stuck on the walls/floor/ceiling.  Eventually, I come accross a big block of lava (I assume the core of the planet) and die, losing my inventory.
There was no way I could get my inventory back, because If I went back underground, I would just encounter the same physics problem over and over again. So I reset the game, this time making sure to disable  the default "lose inventory when you die" settings.
Get to the same point in the story again on the second world, and this time when I am mining, I encounter a similar bug. Except this time, instead of getting stuck in an endless gravity loop, I somehow manage to start to fly away in one direction. Eventually, I float above ground, and keep on going far out into space!  I quit and loaded back in hoping that I would be back on the planet, but I was still far out in space. I had to use a console command to kill myself.
If a game can't manage to get something as simple as the gravity correct, or a game like minecraft makes it so you encounter game ruining physics bugs when you start to mine, then what hope is there for the rest of the game?
Physics/cellular automata are also still unfinished, if you pick up some water for instance,instead of the hole filling up like in minecraft, it just stays a hole for ever, like if you picked up a block of stone.
When these bugs are eventually fixed, then the game will be fun to play through.

This is a fun game, actually. It's a story-mode Minecraft more than anything, but still fairly unique, and I think, better.
The mining aspect is definitely downplayed, for better or worse, with fewer instances of things to find underground, so far, and the best strategy is to build and/or mine a tunnel down an existing underground cave, since there are minerals that just appear in the cave systems themselves rather than in the ground.
The blocks are smaller than most block-mining voxel-world games and there are several shapes, and many material/color choices, so the world composed of these blocks is more detailed and beautiful, as are the creations you can make with them. The detail level is high enough that sprites are used less in favor of modeling trees and things almost entirely from the blocks alone.
It does not have a 'true' survival mode, yet, but you can start a creative game, and then switch it to 'survival' mode, which just enables some of the robot enemies pretty much. However, it does not have the same feel of even Minecraft survival in terms of enemies coming for you, or in populating the world with vilages and dungeons. The liveliness of the Story Mode vilages, rebels, and robots is gone. It's basically good for doing work in creative mode and then releasing it as a 'survival' multiplayer world. (A copy of it.)
However, a better survival mode is apparently on the list of things to do, being that it is still in Early Access and under development.
I play with Hard Enemies and Normal Death Penalty.

I recommend this game with a very large disclaimer: it's hard and you have to be willing to accept that.
Is this game perfect? No. Is it still worth playing? Yes, and here's why:
Riddled Corpses is a throw back to the arade games of the late 80's: mutants, zombies, and Engrish. It's a frenetic twin-stick shooter that demands zen-like concentration at times and a willingness to invest a few hours of grinding as well.
The grinding is what polarizes peoples opinions of this game. "Grinding? In an arcade shooter?" Yup. In order to get stronger and to get sub-weapons, you need cash. You get cash by killing enemies. Survival Mode is the best place to get cash. So you'll spend quite a bit of time there. See, at that point, RC becomes a score grind which reminds me of classic Atari-age shooters where the score was all that mattered. For that, I'm cool with it.
The graphics are bright, varied, and colorful. Enemy design is nice. The music is pretty good. It controls as well as it should. It's just the grinding. Raw skill only gets you so far with RC, and while some feel that it's a poor design choice having to grind for more firepower, it needs to be addressed that if it wasn't for the grinding and steep difficulty, this game would be over in a single sitting offering little replay value.
If you can accept nut-punchingly difficult shooting and a required sense of dedication, this game is worth the purchase.
