Riddled Corpses has decent graphics, a fine soundtrack, solid playability, BUT....
Why is it a frustratingly bland grindathon?
First off, I love the grind. Rarely do I ever need an excuse to play a game over and over just for shinier loot, some unlocks, or acquiring dollarz for the game art-galleries I'll never peruse. Arcade ports at or around full-price are a hard sell, so it never hurts to have extra modes or something to shoot for besides a hi-score. The nicest aspect of these extras is that they create another incentive for gamers to replay the game. The more they play it, the better they get. For example: By the time I filled out the art gallery in Dynamite Cop on the Dreamcast, I could beat the game without dying.
Here's the rub. When you play an arcade port, you're already given everything you need in order to complete the game. Your ability to get further is determined by practice, knowledge, and talent. Riddled Corpses gives you nothing, and expects you to work like a dog for several hours. Only by grinding enough cash can your character become strong enough to beat the game. This is a twin-stick shooter, but you start off crazily underpowered. You can be an ace in the genre, but it doesn't really matter. Without leveling up your damage-output, you will become overwhelmed and killed.
From Metroidvania to Disgaea, we are always looking for more efficient grinding methods. With Riddled Corpses, survival mode is the only way to make cash. Typically, players are given incentives to attempt the story mode. Even if they have weak characters, they should still be able to eke out some rewards to build their abilities. Not so with this game. The most baffling decision is that there are no cash rewards for completing stages. Furthermore, there is no way to increase stats in-between stages. There is a shop, but it's only for temporary items like med-kits and dynamite. So all you can really do is die, then upgrade, then give it another shot.
But why fuss around with that? Playing story mode before you've maxed out your character of choice is a waste of time. It's faster and less time-consuming to grind out Survival mode for everything you need. While this mode gets overly difficult in a short amount of time, it doesn't require any serious effort. Maybe you'll get lucky, score some dynamite, and collect an extra 700-1000 gold an attempt. This becomes a very mind-numbing experience. You may find yourself wondering why your precious hours in survival mode couldn't be spent elsewhere. Maybe you could have seen a movie? Learned a stage in a difficult 2D shooter? Trolled messageboards? Anything would be more fulfilling.
The worst part is when you're finally ready for the arcade mode.
You discover that It's too easy.
Due to the rate at which enemies/bosses appear, survival mode is eventually going to become more difficult than anything in the main mode. You've got dozens of enemies spawning from every direction and they're flooding the screen with projectiles. It's an absolutely hopeless situation. The arcade mode is breezy by comparison (provided you're sufficiently powered-up). Yes the bosses will fill the screen with projectiles but...well let me break it down.
In a 2D shooter, bosses will make use of a variety of bullet-patterns. At times they will create something mundane and easily dodgeable, but mix it up with other projectiles in an attempt to throw off your rhythm. Riddled Corpses never really moves beyond the mundane. There's a constant bullet-pattern for every boss-fight, and they do very little to deviate. You'll occasionally see one or two additional projectiles, but it's never enough to cause problems or force you to adapt. The possibility of death still exists, but it's only via running into large zombies. Also, you can always stock up on med-kits & dynamite in-between each stage.
In short: If this game didn't have the massive grind, it would be much shorter. This is a textbook example of bloat. An arcade title can be seemingly insurmountable at first, but still be well-designed. Riddled Corpses is a brick wall, and can be overcome only through nonsensical work. Beating the game didn't really feel like an accomplishment. Instead, it felt like the expected result of having too much free time.

Killing Floor 2 is a first person shooter game, where you have to survive a number of rounds against hordes of terrifying enemies called "Zeds", with a big boss fight in the last round.
You can play singleplayer, or online multiplayer co-op up to 6 players. There are competitive stats at the end of each game like: healing done, damage done, most assists etc.
There are also some pvp game modes, but I've never tried those, because KF2 has always been a stellar co-op game for me.
You are a survivor of the Zed Apocalypse. Basically, a mad scientist working in a not-so ethical Bio-Corporation, created a massive army of cloned monstrosities, which he unleashed upon the unsuspecting world. You and a few other survivors decided that the best course of action, is to grab some serious firepower and cleanse the globe from the Zeds and their insane creator.
So you get to choose one of the survivors. Each has his own unique voice acting and 3D model which comes with various cosmetic choices.
The above is what your character looks like in game. What determines your Class however, is what is called "Perk System"
There's a decent selection of classes with each focusing on different kinds of weapons and filling different roles. The classes themselves don't have active abilities but instead use a perk system that gives different kinds of passive bonuses to the character and their respective perk weapons.

Each class can gain up to 25 levels*. You get to choose between 2 perk options each 5 levels, but you can always reset those options freely.
To level up a class, you need to use a weapon from that class, that means that you can play for example as a Demolitionist and still use an SMG, (which is a SWAT's perk weapon), so each kill with the SMG will contribute to SWAT's xp bar and not the Demo's.
*All the xp you gain is permanent, not match-specific like Dota for example.
Killing Floor 2 offers a selection of classes for different tastes:
*Berserker (melee weapons, fast walking and tanking big Zeds)
*Firebug (flame damage weapons, croud control)
*Medic (healing weapons, faster and better healing)
*Demolitionist (weapons with big aoe damage, trap doors to go boom)
*Commando (assault rifles, guns with lots of bullets)
*SWAT (SMGs, also lots of bullets and some crippling effect on zeds)
*Support (shotguns, better barricades)
*Gunslinger (pistols and powerful handguns)
*Sharpshooter (very good single shot rifles)
*Survivalist (this class has some mixed perks from all other classes and can get xp points from any perk weapon)
You can change class whenever you want, even during a match if you desire, the game doesn't penalize you for it. You can even use another class' perk weapon, so for example, if you have a high level Medic, you can grab some Commando weapons to level up the latter easier.
Your objective is to survive a set number of rounds against the attacking zeds until the final boss battle. Each round becomes progressively harder, with more menacing zeds being introduced the further you survive.
Besides the obvious first-person shooting, you can also temporarily barricade doors to block some of the paths the zeds take. The enemies spawn randomly where you can't see them in set locations and rush to you directly. You can keep moving and kite them, which is usually the right play, or you can choose a location and defend, which some times can work too.
Killing zeds gives you money (DOSH!! Grab it while its hot!!), which in the end of each round you can spend in the trader to buy extra weapons, ammo, grenades, armor and bigger guns. There are also random pickups (ammo, armor, low-tier weapons) that can be found scattered across the map, these too respawn with every new round.
If you manage to survive all rounds, you get to do the final boss battle, which involves you running away from the boss, shooting everything you got at him while desperately trying to find ammo and armor pickups. Pretty intense fight everytime  although not the game's strongest part.
Besides the big bad boss, there are many different kinds of zeds to keep you occupied and each has a specific role to play. Each zed can create all different kinds of dangerous situations, that only quick thinking and experience can save you from them. Also every zed has it's own weaknesses to each weapon damage type, for example a Fleshpound is resistant to bullets but vulnerable to explosions, lots of tactical options there.
If you played Left 4 Dead, the enemies can't compare, there are no "specials" here. Kf2 is more comparable to a tower defense game when it comes to the style you face your opponents. You see them coming from afar (or you don't if you aren't paying attention, or the map is too claustrophobic) and act accordingly.
There are multiple levels of difficulty to choose from. In most FPS games when you increase the difficulty the enemies receive an arbitrary Health & Damage increase (Borderlands, PAYDAY2), which results in boring unrealistic spongy fights.
In KF2 though, enemies become faster and aquire deadlier attack moves. This results in 2 important things:
1) Your weapons always feel powerful and devastating.
2) Zeds become a real horrifying menace, instead of superficial sponges.
There is an exception of enemy health boosting and you will find it in a multiplayer game:
Three of the big zeds (Scrake, Fleshpound and the final boss) receive a health boost which goes up the more players there are. This is justified though, otherwise it would be too easy to bring down these giants by casualy shooting at their general direction.
That said, the health boost is not that excessive as in other FPS games, in fact one player can still solo-kill one of these giants if his headshots are well placed and using the proper weapon.
All other zeds maintain their original health pool though and you still get the satisfaction of purging enemy mutant hordes by the numbers.
So in the end, if you are playing solo or multiplayer, the difficulty 'feels' that is properly balanced.

-Killing Floor 2 has one of (if not), the best gunplay in a FPS game you can find. You especially notice this when Zed time (slow motion) kicks in and all the cool animations play in a super smooth framerate where you can appreciate every little detail the devs have put in.
-Very satisfying bullet (and melee) damage feedback. Limbs getting cut off, heads pop, guts spill, zeds getting knocked around, blood splatters everywhere.
You can literally paint the map red with all the zeds' blood and there's also an advanced option to enable physics rendered guts and other good gory stuff that stick to the floors and walls, (although the latter is a bit demanding on your PC).
-Beautiful graphics, HD textures, very disturbing and horrifying monster design. Fluid animations and realistic physics.
-Very good performance even on dated PCs. I used to play this on an old rig I had from 2009 and the only times the framerate dropped was when too many things exploded on screen.
-Sound assets are all top-quality, with the superb gun sounds stealing the show.
-Well made (zero lag or desync problems) Online Co-op play, up to 6 players. Dedicated servers, some official ones and the ability to "take-over" a server for the duration of your game (if you want to play with friends only).
-Easy multiplayer access for friends, both in-game and via Steam menu.
-Good server browsing with many filter options. Or a one-click matchmaking button if you prefer a fast game.
-Decent number of official maps available (very good level design on them too), but most importantly Steam Workshop integration. There are plenty of awesome custom made maps with different kinds of strategies involved in them. This makes KF2 infinitely replayable.

A fun and challenging twin-stick shooter with some flaws that sadly has "arcade mode" where you don't have checkpoints as it's main game mode. Why is this bad?
- You have to die to progress - enemies start having too much health for your firepower
- When you die, you have to start all the way from beginning.. there are LOTS of enemies to kill again.
- Upgrades are costy, characters are pretty costy and other characters have to be unlocked either at extreme cost or by repeating levels over and over again with almost the same gold gain on each level, even if they are harder.
- Slow progression
Indeed, levels take long to complete and award almost the same amount of money, with the early levels getting more and more trivial each time and only becoming a chore afterwards.
Another small problem would be the amount of things you have to look out for on your screen. Bosses themselves might be just a little challenging, but the true challenge is in the spawn system - enemies spawn anywhere on the screen and sometimes even during boss fights. Every now and then you get these extreme spawns of enemies that shoot at you right after spawning and you have to evade that while evading 10 other shots coming from all directions.
Usually you will get hit a few times from the insane spawn in such encounters unless you have money for dynamites (you most likely won't have for extra in the first few hours). In these encounters you need to:
- Run away from many shots coming from different directions
- Keep moving to avoid those shots and enemy spawns
- Avoid unkilled enemies
- Destroy high HP obstacles to have more space to move in
- Have some dynamite if your firepower isn't high enough
- Kill a miniboss while doing all this (1 hit from miniboss or boss = dead)
The game has a fitting soundtrack. Good and sort of addictive, but repetitive.
The game has some grammar errors / poor english.
Even though that's a lot of negatives, I would recommend buying or at least trying the game because of the fun factor. The idea is there, but I think it could use some polish.
Then again, I wouldn't be surprised if the "grind" is a intended feature because of recent Steam Refund update - it at least keeps people playing.

Speaking of skill, the game is VERY easy most of the way through (you can button mash through about 50% of it, and it doesn't throw much more at you until the 80% point), and even at the end it only makes it to "not very hard". Shadowverse is a solid, digital card game. It has many things to appeal to Magic and Hearthstone players alike, as well as differences that make it stand out.
1. Free to Play, not Pay to Win.
It's been awhile since my account is old, but Cygames is very generous to new/and free players. I think you get 10 packs (8 cards in a pack across 4 rarities) of each expansion right off the bat, as well as some core basic cards that everyone gets.
As of right now, there have been 5 expansions so that's an immediate 50 packs to start.
Then there are events, which have been numerous. It seems like whenever Cygames achieves a new record in downloads, translates the game to a different language, or has a tie in with another franchise (most recent was Fate/Stay), they give out free packs.
Packs cost 100 rupies, you earn rupies everyday for 4 days of logging in. Every 5th day of logging in, you get either get a free pack or a taketwo ticket (more on this later).
There are 3 dailies per day that also reward rupies or packs. If you feel hesitant about facing other players right from the getgo, you can change the dailies to "against AI bots" and still earn. Build up collection/decks and then go back to real opponents later on.
So if you're apprehensive about starting so late, don't. You won't have a perfect collection but it'll be something you can work with.
QUICKEDIT: Someone on reddit did a pretty good numbercrunch on how quick it is to build a new collection
2. The game is fast.
Even if you play "control" or "combo" decks, you will have to keep up with the fast nature of the game for your deck to function.
Shadowverse is meant to be played on phones, which means matches on the go while commuting, a break at work, etc. leads the card design to have games end around turn 7-8-9-10. Of course the game can go longer, but usually the winner is "decided" during these turns and the rest is just a formality or a play error extends the time.
This is often a criticism of the game, but just think about your time spent on other games. Magic games that go best of 3 in tournaments take 40+ minutes and have pages of rules for "extra overtime turns" if no one is dead. League of Legends matches take 30+ minutes, and you have to restart the process whenever some dodges or screws up pick/ban.
Time is important, the games are fast and you can really squeeze in alot for your hour spent. If you lose, you lose fast and move on, bringing what you learned right to the next match. If you win, you move on and refine what worked or see a clearer picture on how your deck functions. The more people you play, increases the chance that the deck they use against you might inspire you to build a similar strategy in the future.
3. FOTM or fad of the month decks, aka netdecks.
Most Shadowverse tournaments are organized play outside of the client and run by 3rd parties. These often have best of 3, players having 2-3 registered decks, and target deck bans.
In game client only has something called a Ladder system. This is best of 1, with whatever deck you choose, facing someone with their deck.
This means that the 2 environments are so different, that often the best "tournament winnning decklists" that get posted on various sites.. are actually very weak on Ladder (or they are fundamentally not optimal for Ladder).
Because on Ladder you won't be able to pick and choose based on what everyone else is bringing. You can't even "ban" a deck that you know is strong against yours.
There will always be netdeckers. But straight up copying a tourney deck for the Ladder system will make you hit a wall very quickly if you don't make adjustments.

Having grown up on MicroLeague Baseball in the mid-to-late 80's, I was always waiting for the next "pure" baseball sim to come along that would rival the managerial joy of that first classic. The 90's and 2000's were filled with some great baseball games, but they were dependent upon you being able to hit "X" at the right time.  OOTP's early offerings were the first in decades to take the MicroLeague Baseball approach, giving you full control over both existing historical teams and leagues as well as the creation of your own fantasy teams and leagues from any era.  Better yet, they're completely stat driven, with the most "in game" influence (if you want) being your job as manager.
OOTP 18 has taken the baseball sim to incredible heights.  They've built upon a core that was already strong and have refined the interface without making it unfamiliar.  Earlier versions had some quirks but they've done a great job of streamlining things in '18.  I especially love the option for animations, as this really brings back great memories of the original MicroLeague Baseball.  While I doubt we'll be able to predict an inside-the-park home run by watching how fast the batter comes out of the box, where the ball is headed, and how fast different fielders are moving to their positions (a MicroLeague classic), the animations should be a nice touch.
TL;DR ... After 30 years I am finally ready to admit that MicroLeague Baseball is the 2nd best baseball simulator ever.

Dead Rising is an open world game from 2006 created by Capcom for the Xbox 360. It's one of the earliest killer app titles for the console and was the game most people bought a 360 for prior to Halo 3. At the time it blew people away with how groundbreaking it was in terms of technology and continuously remains on top ten lists to this day.
In Dead Rising you play as Frank West. A journalist who enters the small town of Willamette Colorado by helicopter. Dropped onto the roof of the local mall, he has 3 days to figure out the origin of the zombie apocalypse that has befallen the town, and return to the roof alive in the process. Frank is the anchor the game hinges around, he's a loveable selfish scoundrel who has a ton of lines that are instantly quotable. While the rest of the characters are kind of forgettable, you want to finish the game purely because you wanna see what Frank does next.
Compared to the later games in the series and even other zombie survival games Dead Rising is very different, and infact feels foreign and hostile to the player. For starters, you have a very strict time limit. Frank has 72 hours to complete all of his objectives, and the game enforces this harshly. You can only complete your objectives within a certain time period. And this leaves very little time to explore the mall or screw around. Likewise, most of the player's weapons are household objects like baseball bats and power tools. And they break very quickly. The mall is entirely filled with zombies, and you can see up to 800 zombies on the screen at once. But the zombies aren't the player's objective, they're an obstacle. And the inherant fun of the game is finding unique ways to get around them. It is very enjoyable to carve a path through a bunch of zombies while saving all of your weapons and healing items for a tougher encounter later.
After completing the game's initial 72 hour mode, there's an additional "Overtime" mode that lasts an additional day, and a more interesting "Infinity" mode. Infinity mode spawns Frank in the mall, and you continuously lose health due to hunger. And the objective is to continuously find more food items in the mall so you can keep yourself alive. It's a really fun mode and I was slightly disappointed in later Dead Rising games they removed hunger entirely in their sandbox modes. It's one of the most immersive optional modes to a game I've ever played.
While Dead Rising was liked for it's technical innovations, it was remembered for its humor. Frank is a joy to play as but there's also this Japanese style of humor. Frank can wear silly costumes and use silly weapons like toy megabusters. This is all juxtaposed with a mostly down to Earth and relatively serious story. Compared to the later Dead Rising games, this contrast feels the most amusing and works the best.
Lastly the game was not ported to PC until 2016. I can safely say the PC port feels just right, with only a slight handful of bugs. It also allows you to play in mouse and keyboard with rebindable keys, along with gamepad support and support for higher anti aliasing, framerates and resolutions up to 4K. This really brings back the feel of mid to late 90s arcade shooters in a great way. The pixel art is nice & detailed, sound effects are sharp & crisp, and the music really gets your head bobbin'. In terms of style the game is impeccable.
The game also supports vertical monitor setups, with video options for 90-degree rotations, as well as scaling and screen positioning.
The gameplay is also really nice. There's quite a bit of enemies that show up in every stage, and also a decent amount of bullets on screen, but thankfully it never gets quite as crazy as some of the more intense bullet hell games out there, so it always feels more like you're dodging than carving a path.
There's a power-up meter at the bottom of the screen and it'll fill up with the different color power-ups you acquire. Each color will give you a different weapon, and the more you get of one color, the stronger that weapon will become, so if you're careful about which power-ups you pick up, you can customize exactly how you want your weapons to fire during the game.
The one thing I wish the game had would be a "Speed" power up. The ship feels just slightly too slow for my taste (For comparison: It's somewhere around the speed of the ship from Gradius with only one "speed up"). This makes it nearly impossible to grab all of the medals that are falling out of enemies, which don't do anything aside from give you extra points. However, high scores are a large part of my enjoyment for these games, so it seems a little disheartening to not have the extra speed.
They do have online leaderboards, which is always a nice addition. There's separate leaderboards for each difficulty as well as each stage's score attack mode once you unlock them.
Overall, aside from the ship speed, which is a relatively minor complaint in the grand scheme of things, the game is fantastic. I would definitely recommend it to anybody who is a fan of scrolling shooters, especially ones from the mid-90s, as it seems to really accurately evoke that aesthetic.

For whatever reason, DELTAZEAL is the only Triangle Service game I keep coming back to play time and time again.
It's kinda written off as just another Raiden clone by some--and it does feel a lot like any Seibu Kaihatsu or even a Psikyo game--but the weapon system, branching paths, and weapon system keep the gameplay interesting and reshreshing.
However, no game is without flaws and I have a couple complaints:
1) The enemy bullets are waaaaaay too hard to see sometimes. I'll have a near-perfect run going only to die without warning because a tiny pink bullet was hidden behind my larger pink bullets. This also applies to the powerups which are, you guessed it, the same pink color that both the player and evemy bullets are.
2) All Triangle Service games are basically straight ports of the XBox version which are simple ports of the arcade version. There are no concessions to PC gamers and how they expect a game to work these days: there's no tutorial, few instructions, no pause menu options, few graphical options to choose from, and the controls are simply maps from the keyboard to XBox controller buttons.
If you love arcade shmups and don't mind the difficulty and weird XBox-style controls and graphics, DELTAZEAL is an under-appreciated game that's a lot of fun to play. Despite my complaints, it's still by far my top pick of all of Triangle Service's games.
(Fun fact about the game: it was originally released as G-Stream G2020 by Oriental Soft for arcades, but because Oriental Soft didn't pay Triangle Service for the work, Triangle Soft now releases it under its current name)

Game wise it was an amazing experience & the variety of settings, story driven gameplay + all those little touches that Valve seem to be so good at adding, made it very worthwhile. The graphics are fantastic & the areas in the game often have a kind of gritty realism not seen before in a FPS. City 17 is an amazing backdrop for a game not to mention the surrounding areas such as highway 17, the Nova Prospekt prison complex & especially the citadel which is as alien as Xen but portrayed in a much less organic & much more mechanical Manor. On the whole the HL2 world is an amazing contrast of urban/suburban realism, a variety of outdoor locations & cold alien structures.
HL2 also attempts to build on the character interaction that was revolutionary in the first game. Later in HL2 you will be joined by resistance fighters that form into a small squad that you can control. However you have extremely limited control over this squad. You simply order them to collectively follow you or move to an area that you point out with the crosshair & that's about it.
Everything in HL2 behaves as you would expect it to in the real world & this really helps to draw you into the HL2 world. No more so then when you are first let loose with the gravity gun. This 'weapon' almost turns the game into a glorified physics engine demo but Valve have managed to implement this device in such a way that it becomes indispensable in your quest as well as an awe inspiring tool for demonstrating the physics engine.
The sound in HL2 is a very strong point. Amazing FX, background sounds & music that suits the action & seems to carve a niche of it's own. It's good to see such attention paid to an area which is sometimes overlooked in games & plays second fiddle to the graphics. In HL2 the sound is as important to the feel of the world as the graphics are. Probably some of the best sound I've ever heard in a game. I thought Doom 3's sound was amazing but HL2's is more subtle & as such often more effective.

Killing Floor 2 is a first-person shooter video game developed and published by Tripwire Interactive. It is a sequel to 2009's Killing Floor. An early access version of the game was released for Microsoft Windows in April 2015, and the game was released in November 2016 for Windows and PlayStation 4 and August 2017 for Xbox One. The game utilizes Epic Games' Unreal Engine 3. It is also planned to be released on Linux.
Killing Floor 2 is a first-person shooter video game, that can be played alone or cooperatively with up to six players. The game is based on events from Killing Floor, in which bio-tech firm Horzine's attempt to create military clones is hijacked by an insane researcher and unleashed on the UK. The clones have now rapidly spread across Europe, paralyzing the response from the European Union. Within Killing Floor 2, taking place a month after the first game, the outbreak has spread beyond Europe, causing governments to collapse and communication systems to fail.
Gameplay consists of players fighting through waves against Zeds. As waves pass, the enemy count, which scales with the number of players in the game, will increase and different enemy types are introduced with the final wave culminating in a boss fight. The boss character will be determined randomly upon the start of the last wave, with each boss having different strategies for defeating it. Players are equipped with melee weapons and firearms, a healing syringe, and a welder used to block passages. Random weapons, ammo, and armor can be found by exploring the level, though players have a limited amount of weight they can carry.
When players kill a Zed, they earn in-game money and experience points. Achieving certain types of kills, such as a head shot, will cause the game to enter "zed time", a few seconds where all game actions for all players are slowed down, which for players can be used to carefully aim their next shot or start a different course of action. The player can take damage from the various Zeds, which can be restored using their own medical syringe on themselves or having another character use theirs, among other regenerative items. Once a player's health is drained, the player-character will die and they will not respawn until the end of the current wave; the mission is failed if all players are dead simultaneously. Players gain a monetary bonus for surviving a round, which they can use to buy and sell body armor, ammo, and weapons at a store that is only open for a limited time between rounds. Game matches can be configured based on the number of rounds before the boss fight, and over four difficulty levels. A patch to be released in early 2016 will include a dynamic difficulty option, where a computer-based "Game Controller" will be able to alter the strength of subsequent waves, either making them easier or harder, based on the players' current performance.
Prior to starting a game match, the player selects one of several perks representing basic combat classes (such as "field medic", "commando", or "support") that have various skill boosts, such as better damage with specific weapon types, healing other characters, or welding doors more effectively. In the meta-game, players earn experience points for their character towards gaining experience levels any of the perks by doing actions related to those perk classes; for example, healing other players will gain "field medic" experience even if the player is not using the "field medic" perk. Most experience is earned by using weapons specific to that class, such as explosive weapons for the "demolitions" class. Each level boosts the base skill statistics of the player's character when they use that perk, while every five levels, the player is able to select one of two specific skills to enable for their character. Skills include a mix of passive and active abilities, including some that can benefit the other team members. Players also have the ability to configure their in-game character through a number of pre-made personas and options for clothing coloration and accessories, though these have no impact on gameplay.
An April 2016 patch added a player-vs-player mode, in which one or more players take on the role of a Zed to kill the mercenary players. The Zed-based players will be able to use the abilities of the Zeds as they are in game, such as a Stalker Zed remaining invisible while not charging.

I'll admit, I had my doubts coming into the game after reading many reviews for the game - although, I caught it on sale, so it wouldn't matter incredibly if it wasn't good. And yet, most of these doubts were quickly put to rest as I began to play the game.
First off, I want to say that this game is not made for everyone. If you're the kind of person to play mainstream games (specifically shooters, like CoD or Halo), I have a feeling you will fail to appreciate this game. MIrror's Edge may have some shooter elements, but its was not made to be a shooter whatsoever. That being said, let's get more detailed.
The Pros:
MIrror's Edge has a lovely full body awareness/parkour system. From start to finish I marvelled at the game's art style, and freerunning on rooftops is a very unique experience in the video game industry. Of course, it was not perfect, but I do not know of any other game that tried to pull off this concept quite like Mirror's Edge. Hopefully, the second game announced at E3 will improve on the following:
The Cons:
Cutscenes. They were sub-par, at best, in my opinion. Just look some up; it's like cheap anime, and yet not really. Second, in my playthrough I ran into a few glitches where I would leap to (for example) a pipe on the side of a wall, and I would physically touch it. I would still fall to my death because it did not register that I touched it. It can be quite annoying to be running on rooftops in the evening sunset's light, only to break the flow and die because the game didn't register something.
Debatable Concepts:
This is, in my opinion, a con; THIS Mirror's Edge was not made for combat, yet some enjoyed it. Combat was way too simple as for every fight you would do the same moves over and over again, and picking up a gun only makes it worse. I noticed myself that the combat really broke the flow of the game. From fast paced running to a sort of slow combat system. Again, some people enjoy the combat in Mirror's Edge; just not me.
The storyline is another subject that is debatable. Some enjoyed the simplicity, and others thought that DICE may have hired a 4-year old to write up a story. I do not have an opinion of it, although I do think it could have been more in-depth. I like story-driven games better than rush-shooters (*ahem* CoD). I won't speak of storyline too much so as not to spoil much of anything.
Verdict:
Mirror's Edge is unique. I highly recommend it, and if you don't want to fork up $20, wait for it to be on sale (it's on sale for $10 now at the 2014 Summer Sale).

I've meant to postpone an actual review of this game until I have finished.
Which I had done so recently at a leisurely pace with 55+ hours of gameplay and I have just barely even touched multiplayer.
The following is a review of Dying Light's single player content:
Dying Light is a highly detailed, ominous, dark and thrilling playground.  In it's zombie apocalypse setting, it has on multiple occassions, made me think twice about leaving the safety of a safehouse at night.
By day, you're this invincible, weapon weilding, parkour swashbuckler; going ninja on anything not friendly.
When night comes however, well, you're just dinner.
Think of it as a mix of Mirror's Edge and Dead Island and/or a glorious result of interbreeding of other genre - Yes, it's a good thing.
However, you may find item acquisition, items, item crafting and weaponry to be a bit lacking and repetitive. Guns are not customizable, melee weapons are almost identical to Dead Island's crafting schemes (exotics would have been nice. Like spears or whips or flails or claws similar to Riptide, etc.) Adding more to the player's arsenal would have been golden.
But still, Dying Light remains to be a game that deserves a place in your library.  The highly detailed world, the amazing voice acting and the seemless fight techs are some of the many points to why this game is quality.

In DELTAZEAL, whenever your ship is hit by a bullet, there is this perfect moment where everything stops. If only there was somebody with a camera to capture the look on my face whenever I died. I guarantee that I never made the same expression twice. A lot of 2D shooters, even brilliant ones like
, never really grasp just how horrifying and beautiful it can be. This is strange, since these deaths represent everything about the genre. When a plane or a jet or a psychic teenager is lost in a hail of neon-colored bullets, dozens of questions and emotions wash over the player. It's subtle, and if viewed from a distance, the only thought that can cross one's mind is "oh, well that stinks." But to me, every death in a shmup creates a void, and it us up to the player to reach into that void, and pull out something great. This is just one of the many reasons why I like DELTAZEAL, it values one of the most important elements of the genre.
To understand the significance of death, we must first understand life. In this game you start with three lives, and once they're gone, they're gone. The last two shooters I played were
, which handed out extra lives like candy, and
, which handed them out like oxygen. This game doesn't give you any extends, nor are there any hidden lives to discover. The impact that comes from every loss of life is soul-crushing, and it either makes you work that much harder to protect whatever remains, or you completely fall apart. The difficulty of this game is well-balanced, so the meager number of lives will last you a long time, provided you know what to do with them.
Part of what sets this game apart from similar titles in the genre, are the branching paths. There are 9 stages, but a play-through consists of 7. Stages 3 and 5 have two paths: a & b. From my experience, I tend to have more trouble with stages 3b and 5a. That's why I'm thankful for the rest of the stages remaining the same. This sense of familiarity helps in practicing sections where I'm weak at, and focusing on more efficient scoring where I'm not. If you accomplish certain tasks - such as destroying particular enemies quickly - the route within the stage will change. Stage 1 practically triples in length depending on your performance at the very beginning. More opportunities for a high-score run hand-in-hand with worse chances for survival, but that's how it goes.
Paradoxically, the better you play a shmup, the more often you're liable to die. Despite learning enemy behaviors and their bullet patterns, you'll make things harder on yourself by looking for more scoring opportunities. In DELTAZEAL, there's a medal-chaining system. While developing your route, you'll start questioning which enemies should be destroyed. In order to maintain the large medal bonuses, you might have to leave a few enemies un-touched, because they're just too far away. Keep in mind also that medals drop at a high frequency. It doesn't take very long to rebuild a good chain (IIRC they cap at 1,000 points each). The other benefit to having a high bonus is that it makes boss-fights very profitable. Your special ability is a vortex that charges over the course of the game. When used, the vortex converts bullets into medals. Of course, you still have to manage the chain, while avoiding danger, and find the right moment during boss-fights to cash in.
The weapon-system further complicates your chances at scoring and survival. Perhaps "chance" isn't the best word, since it implies RNG had a hand in your demise and/or failure to beat your hi-score. Nevertheless, the constantly revolving weapon system is another factor to account for. Three are three flavors of power-ups: red, blue, and green. Along the bottom of the screen, there are ten slots that can be filled with weapons. Basically, if you grab all reds, you'll have a very powerful spreadshot. On the other hand, the piercing ability and raw power of a laser is important, plus we need to improve our score a bit, so let's grab some blues. Unfortunately, when you grab greens (homing missiles) it's probably on accident, because they're not very good for most situations. Due to the constant rate of power-ups, you can cycle through your weapons several times over. It's something to consider, but can also be distracting in the chaos of bullets & medals. You also get bombs, but they aren't very effective as panic buttons. Enemy bullets tend to move a little too fast for that. They're best used in addition to your regular weapon, so you can obliterate bosses very quickly.
The
series readily comes to mind while playing DELTAZEAL. I've always had a fondness for those games, due to their intense pacing. The stages are a little on the shorter side, there is always huge scoring potential, and your lack of lives are balanced out by a shortage of prolonged boss-fights. All of the bosses have multiple parts and sections, all with their own weapons. There's a nice dynamic aspect to everything, so you're not just focusing a giant laser on a huge target, while threading a needle through thousands of pink death-globs. However, I will say that this game also shares
' affinity for bullets that can blend in with the background. It sounds like more of a huge deal than it actually is, and you develop a sixth sense with practice. A couple of stages in DELTAZEAL run a little long, and a roster of playable ships would have been nice, but otherwise this game is a great love-letter to a classic series.
But really I just can't get over how impressively deaths are handled in this game.  Triangle Service gives you just enough time to feel the shock, the anger, the frustration, the teetering on the precipice into confusion and failure, and it's an amazing feeling. Call me pretentious but this is part of the reason why I enjoy shmups so much. They're a great challenge in of themselves, but what really sets them apart is that they allow players to challenge their greatest rival: themselves. Although I've dabbled in competitive games (mostly FPS), I think that there are too many factors that go into winning and/or getting a high K/D ratio. When I beat a hi-score, or a final boss without continuing, or other smaller victories, I'm doing something my past-self couldn't accomplish. I'm reaching beyond my abilities to attain a new level. Alternatively, when I fail, that means I have to go back, think about what went wrong, and form new strategies. It's a constant process but the triumphs are worth more than any of my other gaming accomplishments.
So before going any further off-track, do I recommend DELTAZEAL? Yes, most definitely. It's a superb game that consistently rewards skill-ful play, and the difficulty never becomes overbearing; although the jump from the normal to the harder settings is a little surprising. It also would have been nice if the last boss didn't have seemingly a dozen forms. It's one of those final battles where it probably should have been a stage unto itself, but I guess it comes with the territory. Regardless, this game is a class-act, and deserves a place in any 2D Shooter fan's library.

FTL: Faster Than Light is a beauty. With an aura of adventure and strategy so other games cannot have, this is one of my favorite games. The game's balancing is excellent. The unlockable ships are not more powerful than the starter ship; it all depends on skill and play strategies. This game can weed out the unfit by having them rage quit because of the game's difficulty, but those who are in that crowd-myself included- can enter the Easy Mode which is less of a challenge. The permadeath experience causes you to mourn a crewmember's loss in two ways more than most games; Not only do you care about them, like in most games, but you also rebuke yourself for your foolishness if it is your fault and begin freaking out a bit when your ship starts failing. And the fealing of panic is spot-on. If there's a hull breach, then another, then six fires, you start panicking. This leads me to the excellent feature of the pause button. You can plan your attacks, repairs, and defenses. For those players who want more of a hardcore experience, you can test your skills without a pause button. The risks of death in random events are high, making you want to take part in less; this is a good feature as well. The overall experience of the game makes this incredible. The satisfaction of unlocking a new ship is incredible. The difficulty of a fire or a hull breach in your ship makes the experience even better. The difficulty and yet rewards in boarding parties is amazing as well. Everything in this game can be decided by a single variable in anything. If you have enemy boarders on your Engi ship, you're a bit screwed, but if the enemy has Human crew and you attack them with the Mantis, there is a lot less struggle. This game... Is incredible.

Half-Life 2...
Where to begin? This is quite possibly one of the most influential games of the 2000's (I mean the first decade, not the millennium). I was ten years late to the party for this game, but that didn't diminish its appeal very much for me. Sure some features seem standard issue today, like picking up random objects or using said objects in physics puzzles, but in 2004 they were revolutionary. After the people of 2004 waited through a two-hour long disc install, they were greeted with an animated title screen. Not a pre-rendered FMV title, but a full 3D title screen, rendered in real time!
...
I'm going off on a tangent, aren't I?
Anyways, enough history lessons. This game is AMAZING. After a teleportation mishap, you begin a quest to topple an extradimensional alien empire, through events I won't spoil. I
tell you about some of the methods. After a while of shooting enemies with standard firearms, you take control of an amphibious vehicle, get a tool that lets you kill enemies with extreme blunt force, command hordes of insects, and even become leader of a squad! The graphics are also absolutely amazing, even 11 years after release. The lip-sync is a marked improvement over the previous game, and sometimes even looks better than modern AAA titles. In addition, the game features a variety of mods, some of which can be found as products on Steam (Garry's mod is actually a standalone game now, but it started as a mod for this).
tl;dr : An amazing game. Even though it's ten years old, it still holds up today.  You should buy it.

Fairy Fencer F is a wonderful game. It is a charming jRPG, with a clear manga/anime flavor. Its strengths consist in the character design, rich and colorful, and an outstanding voice acting (both the Japanese and English version) combined with well-written dialogs containing the right amount of humor. You will truly enjoy each single dialog between the characters! The plot itself, while made up of interesting ideas, is maybe not developed to the highest levels, resulting quite plan and straightforward, nevertheless you will have a lot of fun through the story.
The combat system is dynamic and varied, with each character playing a distinguished role within the party and relying on spells, skills, close combat, transformations, and so on (as to be expected from a jRPG).
An intruiguing trait of the game is that you need to play at least a second run, not only to see other endings, but also to complete the most interesting side quests, and this hence improves the longevity of the game.
In summary, if you are looking for a fun and cheerful jRPG with a fantastic anime-like design, this is the right game for you!

This game is fantastic.
You'll notice that at the time of writing this review, I have 24 hours of play time. That's the amount of time it took to beat it. I haven't started another run yet, but I'm planning on it. You'll notice other reviews spouting about how hard this game is, and they're all absolutely right. This is a very difficult game, but it's difficult for all the right reasons.
Death doesn't feel cheap. At no point did I die from a "cheap death." It was my fault. It was always my fault. I could see precisely where and why I messed up, and therefore what I needed to watch out for in the future. This game will teach you. This game will break you. But when you finally conquer that level 10, this game will be one of your favourites.
Other notes:
The weapons are extremely satisfying. Nearly every gun you acquire will chew through enemies with swift ease and lethality. However, those weapons will also be in the hands of your adversaries, and they work just as well on you. This leads to a great deal of tense, slow-moving dread-filled exploration pock-marked with very short, lethal encounters. Also, enemies will actually roam, so hub-like rooms become extremely stressful as anything could emerge from any door at any time without notice.
The bosses are massive and challenging and varied and exciting and satisfying to beat. Each has their own strategies and unique features, which are very intuitively conveyed to the player directly through gameplay. Seeing the bosses (especially the final one) react to different kinds of retreat and aggression is very satisfying. Usually each boss will kill you once, and then upon reflection you can determine a more cohesive method of engagement.
The story is actually quite engrossing, I eagerly searched the terminals as I unlocked later levels, getting more and more of the story of your installation.

If you're looking for a quality game to scratch your JRPG itch, you've likely found it. In the vein of games within the "Tales Series", Fairy Fencer F is a solid (though slightly lower quality) version of those games. The story isn't incredible, but it gives you enough of an incentive to continuously engage in the entertaining combat. There is also an entertaining card collecting mechanic which assists in the modification of your characters' leveling and ability acquisition. The combat has some throwbacks to the flash the was present within some older JRPG titles and remained entertaining throughout.
+ Solid graphics
+ Flashy Combat moves
+ Comprehensive combat and controls
- Occasionally annoying characters
- Weak story
+ Great character leveling & ability system
+ Game length via plenty of content
+/- Occasionally awkward fan service
I'd recommend picking this game up if you're a JRPG vet that's played through most of your options on steam. If you can grab this game during a sale and you're really looking for some cool effects within a decent JRPG combat system, you should try this one out!

I really want to recommend this game, but its flaws are just too egregious to make the plusses worthwhile.
This leads to two major problems:
It is impossible to correctly reconfigure the controls for some generic gamepads without spending an inordinate amount of time looking up code-descriptions and reading through guides in order to figure out how to edit the .ini file and get the camera-control working.
The game uses XBox-pad icons, but these do not correspond to generic button layouts, which means you have to use an image-editing program with *.dds filetype support in order to cut-and-paste the icons around in the keyboard.dds file in order for them to be mapped properly.
This is before you even get into the game itself, and took me hours to fix.  I posted the fixes on the forums, so it's possible that people with identical setups could now have this sorted in minutes if they know what they're looking for, though.
Whether its crafting recipes that require ingriedients that do not drop in the game at all (you have to hack the code using a third-party-program like Cheat Engine to make them work), or some that require multiple copies of an ingriedient that is UNIQUE and thus you cannot get more than one of without the aforementioned hacks;
or the "Seize" (steal) skill that seems to have a misplaced decimal in its success-rate, and thus you can spend half-an-hour spamming it against enemies too weak to damage you before it actually works.
And this is before you get to the litany of frankly
.
A "magic" and "skill" system that doesn't scale properly - so instead of choosing the "right tool for the job" you always need to spam the most powerful one for it to deal any damage - even if its a screen-wide AOE and you only want to injure one enemy.
An AOE system that is worthless because each of the abilities "knocks back" the enemies - spreading them out too far for any follow-up AOEs; as well as having inappropriately scaled templates so that often a low-level AOE literally means "one or two enemies only if you're lucky."
"Magic" is largely worthless - the Mana (SP) costs are too high early on for it to be viable for builds; and late-game it's too weak to be useful as anything other than "use the most powerful spell to one-shot trash for quicker clearing".
The elemental resistance system has such a negligible effect as to be worth ignoring.
The "Skill" system is identical to magic, except it uses the same stat (Physical Attack) as your combos, and thus is simply superior - making "Magic" even more redundant.
The weapon-combo system requires an inordinate amount of "Weapon Points" (WP) to fully unlock, which forces you to sit on your hands for ages with lame-duck characters; and because you're neglecting putting WP into the "Fairy Fury" stat, the game's unique selling point (turning into a fairy-powered pseudo-robot) is generally superfluous.  Even if you do put points into it, you're just looking at a 2% buff to your stats for every unit you upgrade.
It uses a "travel back in time to the start of the game" gimmick to recycle assets and pad the length out - doubling the playtime from 5 hours to 12 hours.  This adds very little to the experience, although it does allow you to enjoy your levelled up characters a bit more and thus get juicier combat.
Unfortunately you then complete it again, and find that the "NG+" mode is essentially just another play through identical to the first; except now the enemies pose no challenge because you can one-hit them all.
Hell, if you equip the overpowered-as-hell DLC equipment the game throws at you from the start, you can have had this "I walk through the game suffering no damage and one-hitting everything" nonsense through your first play-through!
And all-the-while the side-quest system expects you to repeat zones you've already cleared using the "alternate enemies" Fury function, in order to farm those kills and their drops.
Think you've cleared all your side-quests in the Tavern?  Think you've got all the "Find a new Fairy sub-events"?  Double-checked to make sure no-one anywhere is prompting you for more?
Well, must be safe to complete the next event and move on, right?
WRONG.  Several events require you enter a dungeon - and then exit it
- in order to show up.  No indicators, no warning, no suggestion whatsoever that you should stop doing the only task you currently have issued to you and walk out of the dungeon the very second you walked into it.
The game punishes you for being efficient in how you clear the zones.  And these are MAJOR elements of content.
There's a character you can't unlock if you beat him while you're BELOW a specific level...  Whether you repeat content by grinding out the level; or by playing through the whole game in NG+ from scratch, they expect you to repeat it all again.
Whether it's a ridiculous drop-rate; or a frustrating crafting (synthesis) system; or sub-quests whose rewards are less than the value of the items they want you to turn in; or forcing you to play through AGAIN AND AGAIN AND AGAIN to maybe stumble across whatever you've missed...
Which is a shame, as the game has a lot of potential:  The characters are fun, the art-style is cool, the graphics are pretty good.
If it wasn't for the game constantly recycling its own content in order to pad out its length, it would be one I would recommend.
But ultimately there's between five and eight hours of gameplay here, but it has deliberately been padded out to about sixty hours of pointless frustrating unsatisfying and downright miserable busy-work.

- building, for nothing, no idea why someone decide to make electricity while game lack and doesn't required even concept of "base" (home), you do not need to build anything, all craft machines are there..
- balance: combat is primitive, fighting the hardest mobs (bosses) is designed for 5-years old girl, you basically CAN NOT die, and then BAM, dungeon with lazers.. and passing lazers is totally strange skill which you have to master suddenly or you just die.. overall game is too easy, AI is too stupid and such..

Game has potential no doubts, it's already polished and of very high quality overall. It's just lack enough of something to hold me any longer, more dungeons? Why? There are no even achievements.. And I hate lazers..

FTL: Faster Than Light is a beauty. With an aura of adventure and strategy so other games cannot have, this is one of my favorite games. The game's balancing is excellent. The unlockable ships are not more powerful than the starter ship; it all depends on skill and play strategies. This game can weed out the unfit by having them rage quit because of the game's difficulty, but those who are in that crowd-myself included- can enter the Easy Mode which is less of a challenge. The permadeath experience causes you to mourn a crewmember's loss in two ways more than most games; Not only do you care about them, like in most games, but you also rebuke yourself for your foolishness if it is your fault and begin freaking out a bit when your ship starts failing. And the fealing of panic is spot-on. If there's a hull breach, then another, then six fires, you start panicking. This leads me to the excellent feature of the pause button. You can plan your attacks, repairs, and defenses. For those players who want more of a hardcore experience, you can test your skills without a pause button. The risks of death in random events are high, making you want to take part in less; this is a good feature as well. The overall experience of the game makes this incredible. The satisfaction of unlocking a new ship is incredible. The difficulty of a fire or a hull breach in your ship makes the experience even better. The difficulty and yet rewards in boarding parties is amazing as well. Everything in this game can be decided by a single variable in anything. If you have enemy boarders on your Engi ship, you're a bit screwed, but if the enemy has Human crew and you attack them with the Mantis, there is a lot less struggle. This game... Is incredible.

I've played every Civ since Civ 2 and I have to say this is the best 4x game I have played to date! There are many innovations to Civ 5 that all are welcome additions and the expansions are also highly recommended. Social policy trees, city states, no more "stacks of death" from Civ 4, trade routes, ect. lots of great new features.
My only gripe is that the AI sucks at combat and that cities are too easy to defend. Games are probably too peaceful and the AI hates you too much for being warlike (even though this was normal through much of history). The AI also has unusual quirks, just like all Civ games, but with all the patches and expansions this game has gotten, they are minor (especially compared to it's competitors).
Of course games take 8-12 hours or more to finish, which is something you will learn to live with playing Civ. Of course you can stop and come back, but it's the stopping that's the hard part. I hope the implement a game mode that is designed for shorter play in the future (setting the gameplay speed to "quick" is still a very long game really).
If you like 4x games, turn based strategy games, ect. you owe it to yourself to play this game. It is the best 4x game to date now.

There isn't much to this Fairy Bloom Freesia, but since it's an indie game, I can't really hold that against it. FBF could be classified as a single-stage brawler with combat similar to Super Smash Bros, of all things! Unfortunately, it's held back by some pretty glaring issues.
The primary feature of this game is the combat, which managed to surprise me in the fact that it seems very one-dimensional on the surface, but quickly becomes frustrating if all you do is button-mash. The game is broken up into small stages, wherein you fight a great number of very squishy, very bouncy enemies. At first it's a blast to just knock them around into each other, but can become overwhelming with the amount of projectiles that can be flying around. Then come the boss fights, which require a great deal of finesse to master and can be gamepad-chuckingly difficult. I suggest 2 approaches: button mashing and flinging moves for the masses, and stamping the block button any time the bosses even twitch.
The plot is fairly typical japanese stuff filled with fairly typical japanese characters and the RPG elements are the typical japanese grind. The only substance comes from the combat, but there are simply too many things going on to really feel like you are controlling the fun. When you do finally get a good rhythm, though, it can be heaps of fun. But then it ends, cuz this is a fairly short game. At least there's "New Game +" if you're not quite ready to put it down yet.

It's been a while since I've played this game, but it is only fair to write a review by now. Let me start by saying: this game will not take you by the hand. They give you the basic controls, but nothing else, and you WILL die. You will die many, many times. You will die enough times to take a break, and then come back to die some more. Understood? It's impossible to not die the first time. Now, besides dying, the game offers a wide variety of collectibles and items you can purchase with in-game money. No, you can't buy in-game money with real money, or do you keep the money after a round of playing. These items and collectibles can help you (or sometimes hurt you) with your main goal while on this alien planet: getting off of it. You can also unlock 8 characters, besides the one you begin with, which have a variety of attacks and stats when it comes to things like damage, defensiveness, and mobility. There are also boss fights, and they are all enjoyable. You must be prepared for these fights, or they will be the finale to your short, sweet life. Perhaps the one thing I dislike about this game is that the developers no longer support it. Do not expect updates. Otherwise, to sum everything up, if the idea of dying many times while trying to escape an alien planet infested with terrifying monsters sounds appealing to you, get the game.

If you like combos and you like button mashing, then this is the perfect game for you!  Don't have Marvel in your life?  Push those buttons.  Push them.  Forever.
This is one of those fabled Japanese indie games where it's mainly a one-man show.  The total amount of people that worked on this game seemed to be around 13 people based from the credits (and that's including all of the voice actors LOL).  The stages are all mainly the same, and there's only about 5 or 6 different types of enemies throughout the entire game (not including bosses).  Some of the stages and some of the boss battles can be really challenging if you don't pick up on patterns quickly.
I didn't expect anything when I bought this game as the trailer itself looked like the same stages and the same enemies with a very basic combo system.  I'm happy with my purchase and feel like I'll be soaking in a couple of more hours into this game to unlock the harder difficulties.
The entire game is really really short, but if you like button mashing and creating combos with a wide variety of moves, then this will be a good purchase for you!  The game itself is basically like Digimon Rumble Arena for the PSX or any other 2D platform fighter.  All of the moves are things you've probably seen before from other games, but that's not a bad thing in itself.  There's skills like a teleport or a ground bouncing slash or a rising juggle uppercut and much much more.  The story is cute, and although all the voice acting is in Japanese, you can still understand what's going on from the translated dialogue.
Basically, this game brings nothing new to the table, but it's still a ton of fun.  Make sure you have a controller or stick or something to have a fluid game experience!

I picked up this game looking for a laid back, relaxing adventure/builder to play over the weekend. My husband purchased it as well and we started together in co-op mode. Within an hour we requested refunds.
The game world is cute and the starting area is very detailed. As a builder it was exciting to see all the customization. The detail only rendered up close, which was a little disappointing, but I expected as much from reading reviews. The quest line/tutorial could be more streamlined, but you find everything if you run around enough.
Where we ran into trouble was the hunger bar. One of the first things you learn is how to make berry juice, which you eat to survive. Berries are in limited supply and there's no followup about how to farm/grow berries. By the time we reached the rebel base, we had eaten all the berries inside and outside the town within visible distance and were fighting off starvation.
We could gather wheat, carrots, rabbit meat, and other things you'd expect to be able to eat, but without recipes they couldn't be processed into food. The TAB help menu says recipes are earned as you get farther, so we pushed on, but kept starving to death while digging to complete the moonstone collection quest. At that point it was no longer fun. You might get far enough to gain the other recipes if you play solo because then you're eating your food resource half as fast.
There is an option to turn off hunger when you start a game. If we did it all again, we'd select this option. The first run through was such a stressful experience, though, we weren't up for a second try. We bought it to play co-op and co-op didn't work in the environment.

Shadowverse is an attacker's choice collectible card game which draws many parallels to Hearthstone. The biggest difference with Shadowverse and its competitors is that it's extremely free to play friendly, easily the best in its genre.
An important mechanic which allows it to differentiate itself from other similar games is the evolve mechanic. This option which is primarily used as a way to swing tempo back and forth as well as balance going first vs second opens up roughly in the middle part of each match. While limited in uses, it allows followers to attack enemy followers immediately upon being played as well as activate any evolve specific effects. I find that it does its job relatively well (it could be better), although aggressive decks can easily win before such an option can turn the tides of battle.
The arena mode, which is named Take Two, brings an interesting take to drafted decks. Instead of picking one card at a time, Take Two forces you to pick a pair of cards at a time. Do you pick a game-winning card even if it's paired with a terrible one or do you go with the 2 average cards? Maybe all 4 cards are awful, which pair could be considered better? Questions like that bring an additional strategic layer to a tried-and-true drafting formula.
Something that can be considered a strength or a weakness completely dependant on each individual is the games heavy anime aesthetic. Because the art comes from many different artists (similar to Magic The Gathering), it can cause consistency issues.
Another important strength in this game compared to its competitors is from their developers. The game goes through balance patches monthly and the developers themselves are very transparent about their thoughts and future plans for the game.
Easily the weakest part of the game is the UI. While the game originated on mobile and its largest playerbase is Japan's mobile market, I do not believe that is a good enough excuse for the UI to not be improved upon for the PC version.
It's a relatively minor complaint but that's what ends up happening when the rest of the game is extremely solid.

-Exteme framerate drop even when on lowest settings for everything,
-Buggy doors,
-Buggy vehicles, (they don't despawn when you destroy them, leaving 10,000 'hoverbike' blips on your map.)
-Railmotors are extremely bugged. Expecting them to hopefully get fixed next patch (Roadmap says it's supposed to update mid-2017.)

-Losing inventory (backpack) when you die because it doesn't respawn with you.
-Having backpack blip stuck on map because you died but yet your inventory didn't go away.
and so on...
TL'DR: Overall, Stellar Overload is a great building game with interesting planets to explore and a short (for now) but interesting questline with just purely amazing dungeons, but as of right now even though it being early access as mentioned I can not recommend due to the sheer severity of the current bugs and hair-pulled frustration of trying to fly a vehicle without it glitching out leaving you either stranded on a planet or soaring above the land with 10 FPS. Give it until next update to give it a try and im sure you'll love it.
Also if you're a builder at heart and you loved being inspired and creative then this  is a game you will definitely love.

This may be first ever review of a game on Steam.
Dying Light is one of my top all-time favorite games.  I've played the game on my Xbox.  I've played and beaten it on my PC and started on the hard mode.  I'm looking forward to playing it all the way through again at my current levels while maintaining my inventory.
Something about this game hooked me quick.  I won't lie, the first few hours were a bit slow.
But believe me when I say it picks up soon after.
I'm not an excellent game reviewer, going into detail about all the aspects of the game so I'll just tell you how my daily dose of Dyling Light plays out.
When I first log in I check my inventory.  Weapon, still in good condition with plenty of repairs left.  One machine gun.  Many Molotovs.  Many Exploding Traps.
I might do a side quest or two or maybe even one of the main story line.  Or, maybe I'll wander up onto the bridge and get my thrills by farming some upgrades and killing many zombies.  Hence, Molotovs and Exploding Traps are a joy.  I sit there, up on top of a police van luring zombies my way.
Maybe they'll wander through a slick of gasoline.  Oops, there goes a molotov and there goes twenty zombies up in flames.  I'll move so that the path from me to the zombies brings them through a host of already burning zombies.
They burn too.
Once I clear a small area on the bridge I'll loot everything.  Everything helps.  I open cars, I open bags, I pick locks on police cars and vans to get the "good stuff".
I don't stop until it starts to become night.  While night time isn't near as dangrous now compared to my level, it's still fun to run back to a safe house.  Once there my abslute favorite thing to do at night is lure volatile zombies close while maintaining a close proximity to my local safe house.  From there, it's lure, burn, blow up, shoot, and chop my way to bloody satisfaction.
Oh, sure, then maybe I'll go do a quest.
Oh but wait, there's a protect side quest.  Let's do that :).
Buy the game.

Now and again you find a game which looks and sounds fantastic - on paper. This is me and Stellar Overload (which is quite a poor title to be honest). I kickstarted this game. In hope of a more advanced Minecraft (which I love in so many ways) in kind of a scifi setting.
The game runs well. It looks good (mostly) and there seem to be plenty of blocks, materials and such to do stuff with. You have quite advanced building and crafting tools. Even machines to ride and explore the world with.
Despite all this, which sure looks and sounds good, I can not recommend it. Everey time I try it I get my hopes up. Everything looks so good. It clearly are in flux and development. Things are happening. BUT then comes the BIG hurdle (in my view at least): how the player interacts with the world. The general user interface.
Before actually doing anything in the world it all looks so full of promise. But then you start doing things and it is like bashing your head at a brick wall. The Ui feels downright un-natural. It is clumsy and (I feel) gets in the way. Nearly nothing works the way you think. It is not intuitive at all. There are WAY to many key combos and they are strangly mapped. You can can change them, which is good. But they are still to many.
I know the intentions and ideas are good. I'm the first to applaud the initiative. After all I did kickstart the thing. But everytime I try to get into the game I get turned off in a major way. It happens fast too. That is why I have so little in game time. I find it offputing in a serious way.
Until this, what ever it is, changes I simply can not recommend the game at all.
The user interface is in dire need of a total conversion - and soon at that. Sorry but I call it as I see it. No hiding it. The game is FAR, FAR from ready.

This is a classic game, it's the first Dead Rising and one of the first games i got to play for a very long time, a very long time ago.
It's the weirdest and most bizarre game of the three, which in my opinion makes it more honest, as well as more unique, there are the classic psychopaths roaming around the Pasadises Mall that you Frank West a photojournalist are trying to explore, uncovering what exactly it's going on in the small town of Willamette, based on your actions, how many cases you explore, how many people do you help, how many things do you uncover, the game will always have a different outcome, as well as different rewards depending on what you actually end up doing, some of the endings are devastating while some of the other ones are fullfilling and amazing, it all depends on your actions, you of course can now find a lot of guides on the internet to get the "best" ending, even then i would recommend you for the first time going in to go alone and blind, discover what the game has to offer, welcome the mistakes that you surely will make considering how difficult the game is in some cases, and pretty much just enjoy yourself.
In terms of the port, it seems very basic, frankly the options menu only withholds an entire screen and that's pretty much it, you don't have two pages of options it's what i'm getting at, that being said, it runs, and looks, pretty darn great for a ten year old game, but really if you're gonna play this game it's not going to be for the graphics, it will be for the narrative, and it's gameplay, the game it's different than all the other Dead Rising games focusing a lot more in delivering a more "authentic" experience while at the same time keeping the "fun aspect" of the game intact. This is done by making the silliness and humor feel incidental, by letting YOU be the one that ends up causing the things that are fun and enjoyable to happen, in this game everything it's a weapon, from pretty standar stuff like chainsaws, axes, and baseball bats, to more rare stuff, like frying pans that you can put on top of stoves to then melt zombies faces with it, or maybe even throwing at them some oil so you can see how they fall down and take pictures of them.
Dead Rising is in my opinion one of the few games that while not being "genre defining" it's certainly a game that holds a place in a lot of people's hearts, if you're getting this game it's probably going to be because of the nostalgia that brings to you, or simply because you wanted it to play it again, in my opinion the asking price it's excellent and in that sense capcom has really outdone themselves, remember what happened with something like the ol dlc on disc, and all the other controversies.
I like the fact that i can actually finally feel like i own this game, even if i still have my old copy from way back in the day.
P.s. The font seems to have been fixed as well, it took ten years, but it's finally here.

This movie projects a full-scale visual picture of what Dota 2 really has become and explains its humongous popularity, once you begin giving sight to the movie everything will slowly fill your mind and make you completely open up to its depth.
To write it nice and shortly, this movie follows three of Dota 2s most proffesional players in a life-documentary on how they slowly become induced and self-convinced to strive for higher achievments in gaming. Following the hardships and sacrifices they made to the decision of skiping school, be separated from their families and dive into the Realm of Dota, they became the most proish individuals of the game and begin aiming for the top spot in the Dota 2 Internationals in their respective teams.
The Movie starts of with an animated intro sequence which shines beautifully in your eyes as heroes of Dota 2 appears in full 3D-animated scenes, at first i imagined a full 3D-movie coming to life giving the potential of Valve creating such fine visuals, afterwards the real point begins where we follow the players in their stories about the players. One very important note i must give is how fine these animated sequences blended in during their moments of competitive match moments. This movie is a feature-lenght documentary, but at the same time it gave me a glimpse of how nice and fitting it would be for Valve to crate a full-lenght movie featuring the heroes of Dota 2 considering their personalities, lores and the feel of epicness thoose animated moments gave me. I hope we will see a movie like that surface in the near future.
Recommended for both beginners and veterans of Dota respectively for a "true sight" of what Dota is.
I hope you find my review useful and that it motivates you to inspect its finesse.
