This is a good game, it can get annoying at times because there's a simple formula that the game doesn't change through its entirety, after a while of just playing it feels as if the game is somewhat trying to "artificially" extend its duration by just having you go to, admittedly, different locations, or levels, that sadly just look different, but have the exact same objectives, and challenges than all of the others.
The enemies do get tougher as you progress, usually they require you to crush them by jumping over them, but eventually they'll require you to do the same while being of an specific color.
The idea of the game is that you get this massive areas that are both black and white, the objective is to color them by touching them, or alternatively, interacting with them, in certain cases, under specific circumstances.
As you move through this massive levels, that probably will take you more than 20 minutes or so to complete each of them, you'll find certain challenges that follow the same structure and are given by different characters.
One gives you objectives that are specifically related to painting massive "tactical" buildings, you do this by interacting with some form of station that makes you sacrifice a particular number of your life.
Your life is measured by how much paint you consume, you consume paint by crushing, similarlly to other enemies, units of specific colors.
The colors you can get are always primary colors, that then you can combine to create more elaborate color combinations, but combinations that are still limited.
They are diversive enough however, to give you an actual feeling of change, and energy after every "consumption".
Then you have other activities, ones that are races in which you need to follow "flares", others in which you need to beat a series of enemies that spawn when triggering the specific challenge, and finally, and probably my least favorite of them all, some that require you to paint certain structures with an specific color.
Given that you need to change colors sometimes between each set of structures, and the only way you can paint said structures is by touching them, this resulted in a lot of different accidents that would make me have to repeat certain challenges.
The game never got frustrating because I was loosing or anything like that, the game frankly for the most part is fairly easy, but the frustration comes from the way its difficulty is implemented, not so much because it relates to the same difficulty you've encountered in other games.
One of the most enfuriating things I found about this game, ended up being the sense of direction, what I mean by that, is that in plenty of different cases, I just didn't know where to go, and I would just remain during the same area, painting stuff, and messing around with respawing colored sentries until I would get bored, desperate, or both, and simply started wandering through the map, avoiding obstacles, and enemies, as well as even the act of painting certain buildings, just to try and find the exit.
The other issue I have with it is that the game just keeps going on, and on, and on.
Had the game skipped the last couple of... Say... 4 levels, it would have been fine, its not that I hated those last 4 levels, is that they felt unnecessary, because the formula of the game is the same, the objectives are the same, and so it starts fun, but frankly, the execution of this very simple concept can, and will, at times get redundant and tedious to partake into.
Even then, however, the game has such a fantastic charm to it, I mean just the simple idea that the whole game is about coloring the world, quite literally, I just think that's a very creative way of handling a very beautiful, and relatively "basic" thought.
The characters are fun, and even if they don't talk that much besides in cutscenes, they managed to actually be quite distinctive from one an another, whilst also oozing charm, I didn't want anything to happen to this characters while I was playing it.
And even if the game at times, can surprisingly, be incredibly dark, for the most part it always had a positive, and genuinely "fun" result.
I really liked the game, but it isn't exempt of issues, and repetition, induced by its poor sense of direction, and its "artificial" lenght.
For the most part tho, I really enjoyed the game, it is a very beautiful, and charming experience, it's fun, and it's pure, it's innocent, but it respects my intelligence as a human being, it isn't a "dumb" game by any sense of the word.
I recommend it, just, developers, if for one reason or another you're reading this, just make sure that you "promote" this game a bit more, I don't even know if that's possible up to this point, but I heard of this release because I frequent websites like reddit, and other similar ones, users, and fans, let me, as well as others, know about the existence of this version, then, an upcoming one at that.
I believe the low player count has to do with that, and it can't be only attributed to the fact this is in a way a "cult classic" that at one point an time, was only available for a now, "defunct" platform.
I guess I can only thank for the preservation of this game, the fact that this is an actual good version to play, run, looked, and played with a regular 360 controller perfectly fine.
So I recommend it, just get it on a sale if you can, and come open minded to it, you won't regret it.

is a pretty simple and straightforward game. Now admittedly, when I first saw screenshots for the game, and even the first time I watched a video on it, I really had no idea what the hell was going on. This was a combination of the trippy visuals, and just how simplistic it is graphically.
You play as a triangle, which circles around a hexagon at the center of the screen. You simply use the arrow keys to move clockwise and counter-clockwise. As you circle around the center, lines will move from the outside of the screen towards the center hexagon. If the lines hit you, you “die.”
The game has 6 levels, 3 you begin with, and 3 that are hard modes of the levels that you unlock for completing the corresponding basic level. To “complete” a level you must survive for 60 seconds. I put complete in quotes in that last sentence, because levels last until you die, there’s no set end point. However, the game rewards you with an achievement for lasting 60 seconds and considers it as beating the level.
Levels are comprised of different patterns of lines that you must dodge, for each 10 seconds that you survive, you unlock an additional set of patterns (up to the first 60 seconds). On some levels the center hexagon even morphs into a pentagon or a square to shake things up a bit. Other than that, there’s not a whole lot else to the gameplay.
The music in the game consists of 3 different electronic songs, and they fit the game pretty well, correctly matching the trippy visuals, with rapidly changing colours. I just wish there were than only 3 tracks in the game, as while the tracks are good, it’d be nice to have a few more.
The gameplay itself is pretty damn difficult, much more than one would likely expect from such a simple game. As such, I’ve not been able to beat the game, and I’ve so far only managed to last the full minute on only the first two levels. I’m not sure that I’ll be able to complete any other levels, though I’ll likely play it a bit more here and there. Chances are though, that even if you can’t beat the game (quite likely), you’ll probably be able to get at least 3 hours of entertainment out of it before you move on to another game. Given that the game is only $3 normally, and sometimes goes on sale for $1, I think that’s a reasonable price to pay for what you get.
isn’t a must have game, but it’s still a fun little time killer now and then. Chances are you won’t beat it, but it’s more of an arcade game where you see how long you can last anyway. Give it a chance if that’s your sort of thing.

When this game first came out, it was very glitchy and had lots of issues, and usually couldn't even start for a lot of people. A ton of people got this when it first came out and they made a ton of money from this game. The developers could have easilly walked away from the project, but even though they knew the cost benefit would most likely not be worth it they worked constantly on fixing all the issues this game had, and probably spent a lot of money doing that, so I really want to thank the developers for not making the same mistake Ubisoft did with Assassins Creed Unity. That being said, now onto the game. There are a lot of new things in this game that made it so much better than the previous ones. This includes getting the freaking batmobile and being able to just tank people to death which can be so fun you can completely forget about the story for a few hours. Another thing is the new combat system. It has very usefull combinations to help you in almost any situation and is also easy to use, improved 3rd person to easilly see your surroundings, and more weapons. The world is also very nice. I have played over 50 hours as of now, and have not noticed any copy pasted buildings. There is lots of detail in everything, and the map size is huge. I know graphics is not everything to people but just flying over the city is so fun and it's really beautiful. For the story, there could not be a better ending to the Batman series. A lot of other games have long stories that can just become boring to people and they don't even like it at all, but this game is not that. The story is long, and very fun and engaging, so you will never get bored with this game. Optimisation is also very good for this game, so you don't need to have such an expensive GPU as other games. I have a $130 1050ti and I can run this game at the max settings at an average of 80 fps on 1080p, and 24 fps on 4K. I Really love this game because they blended in a large and fun open world map, an amazing combat system, and a long rich story all into one game, so I 100% reccomend this game.

Since this game came out in 2009, this review will mainly focus on the port quality.
Despite originally being a 2009 Wii game, De Blob's port runs at an unlocked resolution and framerate. The game takes full advantage of my 1440p 144Hz monitor, which I legitimately wasn't expecting due to the game's origins. Sure, it's completely barebones otherwise and the keyboard+mouse controls make unmodded Dark Souls 1 feel like Quake, but it's a pretty good experience with a gamepad, especially since the original was full of Wiimote waggle which is replaced with the A button.
Things to note:
The level of detail was made for the Wii's 480p resolution. The level of detail was not modified in the PC version, so pop-in is extremely noticeable at high resolutions.
Once again, a gamepad is absolutely recommended for this game. Although there are keyboard button prompts, the game is close to unplayable using a keyboard.
This is a straight port, so there are no quality of life improvements whatsoever apart from the gamepad controls. Issues in the first game (such as only saving at the start of its fairly lengthy levels) have not been improved upon.
Menu assets and FMV cutscenes are still in SD resolution.
So it's a completely barebones port, but the unlocked framerate, good performance, and gamepad button prompts make it preferable to emulating it in Dolphin.
Now a short few words about the game itself.
I really liked this game as a kid. The graphics were almost on par with Mario Galaxy, and the gameplay (though it had problems that annoyed me even in my young age) was fairly enjoyable. Playing it now, it's still quite a good game, with an aesthetic reminiscent of Jet Set Radio and gameplay similar to the painting part of Splatoon. I wouldn't say it aged perfectly, but I'd still recommend it.

FTL man... Let me tell you about FTL.  FTL is one of those games where you just look at it, and you know the game is good.  The interface idle, by itself, is entertaining.  It's cool looking.  FTL is one of those games where you're hooked after the first time you try it.  You spend the next week telling everyone you know about it.
In FTL, you are the captain of a spaceship.  This spaceship is holding vital information, and is on the run from the evil space empire.  You must succesfully navigate from sector to sector while keeping your ship intact, your resources managed and your crew alive.  You will encounter other ships on your journey.  Some of these will be space♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥that will try to ♥♥♥♥ your♥♥♥♥♥♥up.  Others will be space angels who just want to give you stuff.  Going from point to point, just to see what kind of encounter or random event each has to offer, is addicting.  That word gets thrown around a lot these days, but it is truly addicting.  Your first few runs will be some of the most fun you've had with a game in a long time for this reason.
Battles are frantic and difficult, but rarely cheesy.  You may be frustrated after a wipe, but when you calm down and think about it, there is almost always something you could have done to save your ship.  Conversely, the feeling you get after barely winning a battle, jumping into the next sector with half of your ship still on fire and your oxygen low, is pure elation.  This feeling intesifies as you upgrade your ship.  You start with space trash, but soon, you will know what it is like to wield a space laser like a samurai sword.
As with most games in the (I'm starting to hate this word) "Rogue-like" genre, unlocks are a big part of the game experience and replay value.  There are several new ships to unlock, and there are two versions of each ship.  Each ship/version comes with a different starting crew and loadout.  As you would imagine, every one of these variations changes the game flow drastically.  You have a lot of room to experiment and find out both what works best for you, and what you most enjoy.  There are many, many different ways to play and enjoy the game.  Also, it will take you a while to unlock all the goods.
Overall, it's hard to point to one thing that FTL does particularly well because nearly every part of the game is fluidly executed.  Most of the games systems feed into one another, creating what I like to think of as "fun synergy".  I would tentatively call this one of the most robust indie games I have ever played.  A lot of indie games are fun, clever, and truly excellent.  Very few feel as complete as FTL.  One of my favorite gaming experiences in recent years.

is a pretty simple and straightforward game. Now admittedly, when I first saw screenshots for the game, and even the first time I watched a video on it, I really had no idea what the hell was going on. This was a combination of the trippy visuals, and just how simplistic it is graphically.
You play as a triangle, which circles around a hexagon at the center of the screen. You simply use the arrow keys to move clockwise and counter-clockwise. As you circle around the center, lines will move from the outside of the screen towards the center hexagon. If the lines hit you, you “die.”
The game has 6 levels, 3 you begin with, and 3 that are hard modes of the levels that you unlock for completing the corresponding basic level. To “complete” a level you must survive for 60 seconds. I put complete in quotes in that last sentence, because levels last until you die, there’s no set end point. However, the game rewards you with an achievement for lasting 60 seconds and considers it as beating the level.
Levels are comprised of different patterns of lines that you must dodge, for each 10 seconds that you survive, you unlock an additional set of patterns (up to the first 60 seconds). On some levels the center hexagon even morphs into a pentagon or a square to shake things up a bit. Other than that, there’s not a whole lot else to the gameplay.
The music in the game consists of 3 different electronic songs, and they fit the game pretty well, correctly matching the trippy visuals, with rapidly changing colours. I just wish there were than only 3 tracks in the game, as while the tracks are good, it’d be nice to have a few more.
The gameplay itself is pretty damn difficult, much more than one would likely expect from such a simple game. As such, I’ve not been able to beat the game, and I’ve so far only managed to last the full minute on only the first two levels. I’m not sure that I’ll be able to complete any other levels, though I’ll likely play it a bit more here and there. Chances are though, that even if you can’t beat the game (quite likely), you’ll probably be able to get at least 3 hours of entertainment out of it before you move on to another game. Given that the game is only $3 normally, and sometimes goes on sale for $1, I think that’s a reasonable price to pay for what you get.
isn’t a must have game, but it’s still a fun little time killer now and then. Chances are you won’t beat it, but it’s more of an arcade game where you see how long you can last anyway. Give it a chance if that’s your sort of thing.

Batman Arkham Knight is a 2015 Action-Adventure, Open-world, Superhero game that is developed by Rocksteady. It is the fourth and last installment in the Arkhamverse officially. The game is based on the characters on DC Comics.
Batman Arkham Knight, I had high hopes for back when it released but unfortuantly for the PC version, it came off a very very rocky journey, the game was delayed constantly and the game was very broken on PC. If I am correct, only 20% of Steam could run the game. I was one of thoses 20%. The rest had to wait for patches but even I felt sorry for them as they tried patch after patch and they just couldn't get the game running how they wanted too. Till today, a few players can't get the game running still.
To talk about the gameplay, it's more or less the same for previous installment, just added abilities that Batman can do. It also introduces new features like Driving the Batmobile and teaming up with sidekicks such as Robin and Nightwing.
Batgirl is a sidekick but I will come back to that shortly.
The game focuses on Batman's final adventure where he goes to war against Scarecrow, only to find that he has made a new ally called "The Arkham Knight", the identity of the Knight was revealed as Jason Todd or The Red Hood. In order to defeat scarecrow and save Gotham, Batman had to reveal his identity to the public of Gotham.
The Good:-
- Big world to explore, Gotham is yours to explore
- No loading screens
- Great action in combat
- Great graphics  and visuals
- Batman, Robin, Nightwing, Oracle, Gorden, Scarecrow and a few other villians were the best parts
- The batmobiles and costume DLC are fantasticly made.
Bad:
- Story was mediocre
- Arkham Knight was too obvious to identity
- Joker shouldn't of been in the game, I don't really care if it's just in Batman's head.
- Too much batmobile
- Not many boss fights like previous games
- the DLC stories are quite♥♥♥♥♥♥except the Matter of family with Batgirl and Red Hood's story.
- Rocksteady lied on a few things such as timed exculsive content, A lot of hours put into the DLC story.
- Rocksteady hired a company that made disgusting port for PC.
Final result:-
If am honest, I don't really know weather to recommand this game or not. I am in the middle. Arkham Knight was enjoyable at first but it just got mediocre. I did feel it was the weakest Arkhamverse game to date which is a shame because normal the final game is normally the best at times. If you want a Batman open-world adventure-action with a lot of Batmobile and no boss fights. Do you want a mediocre story? then this game is for you.

For those that, for some reason, don't know about this game: This game is a turn-based strategy game based on starting from scratch as post-cavemen and working your way up to a large empire. There are many ways to beat the  others. Some examples are Diplomatic, Scientific, and Domination. Diplomatic is being voted the "World Leader" by the other Civilizations. Good luck with that. Scientific is being the first to win the space race. Sounds easy, right? Build a rocket? It would be, if it wasn't so time consuming and every civilization wasn't trying to stop you. Finally, my personal favorite, domination. You basically go to war with every last Civilization in the game. If you emerge victorious in every battle, you win. This is especially fun when working together in a team with a friend. And now that I brought up the topic of friends, you have the option of being in the same team as a friend. You share almost everything, except for your army and resources. However, any way you play, either you being alone or with a friend, you will still have a blast.
Just a P.S: If you ever meet Gandhi in this game, try to stay on his good side. At least, before he gets nuclear weaponry. You'll thank me later.

If you’d have to choose just one thing to admire about de Blob, that would have to be its refreshing looks, despite the fact this game made its debut on the iOS and Wii platforms in 2008. That’s a nine-year gap between the original version and its solid PC port. You got that right since de Blob is a great remake, if you will. It runs and looks best on its PC version, but that’s hardly news for Steam gamers. I never played the console or mobile counterparts, so I really didn’t know what to expect and I was still pleasantly surprised. The concept and characters are the initial project of several students from the Utrecht University. THQ were impressed by what they saw and bought the rights to de Blob franchise.
The Wii version was apparently very popular and the sales figures alone, prompted developer Blue Tongue Entertainment and publisher THQ, to begin work on a sequel, which launched in 2011. If we ever wish to see de Blob 2 on the Steam Store, then we should hope that the current title fares as well with the buyers and players as it does with the critics. And in case you were wondering (since Blue Tongue closed its doors in 2011), this PC port has be skillfully adapted by Blitworks, industry veterans which have ported to PCs, countless quality games in the last decade. History lesson’s over.
Players assume control of “de Blob”, a cute little abstract creature formed from certain liquids such as water or paint. We’ll just call him Blob from now on and refer to him as male, despite no clearly defined gender. Our hero is part of the revolutionary Color Underground. A guerrilla on a mission to free their homeworld and its capital, Chroma City, from the evil clutches of the INKT Corporation. The antagonists are more likely resembling  an oppressive regime and an occupying army, than a firm. Comrade Black is their supreme leader and his goals seem simplistic and confusing at the same time. INKT wishes to rid the world of color and impose a literal black & white vision in regards to all aspects of life.
I am fully aware that de Blob is geared towards a younger audience, but that’s no reason for adults not to enjoy it and look for a deeper meaning than “those are the bad guys and you fight for the good ones”. Some mature themes do surface, such as intolerance and how to perceive or deal with it, along with tyranny and complicity to it. The silent majority and the need for a providential savior. Do not get me wrong, the game is light-hearted in nature and that is perfectly fine. Yet it is far from superficial since it contains sufficient metaphors for most gamers to enjoy discovering them.
The graphics engine in de Blob is custom made in-house while getting some assistance from the Havok physics engine. This practice of using middleware is quite common for the video games that can afford it and Havok  physics are among the best in their branch. It would have been easy to just say that the game has aged well, but de Blob has been adapted to PC. I hope you realize that console or mobile games have to sacrifice “minor details” such as antialiasing or shadow and lighting effects in order to ensure at least 30fps. The PC port I’m reviewing today? Runs buttery smooth on 4K@60fps. No crashes, no glitches or bugs. The camera controls are a bit finicky, but that’s not something practice won’t correct, by the time you spent an hour in-game. Soon enough you’ll be doing all sorts of stunts while wondering how you became so skilled at it, in such a short time span.
If you think de Blob is just another 3D platformer on Steam, well the soundtrack insists on proving you wrong. Most platformers I played so far on Steam, had a handful of annoying or repetitive sounds which couldn’t even qualify as a worthy OST. Blob gets to bring Chroma City back to life (and color) while being constantly accompanied by a selection of jazz and disco songs. These instrumentals playing in the background offer players the chance to choose between them, at the start of each new area. They are designated as “moods” and they really offer a replayability factor of their own. As a self-declared fan of instrumental music (from epic to jazz), I couldn’t be more happy with what I heard while playing de Blob!
Watching the game’s hero paint the city, one building at a time, you begin to understand why the gameplay is so captivating and even inspired the Splatoon series. Chroma City under INKT is a literal blank canvas just waiting for the skilled hands of a determined painter. Blob takes his freedom figher role very seriously and he’ll get plenty of help in his crusade to bring color back to every corner of the city. Speaking of which, Chroma is divided into separate areas which you may revisit anytime after you brought them back to their former glory. Based on how many challenges you completed already, new sections and unlockables become available.
It may seem like grinding but it pays off in the end, to paint a large percentage of each distinct area of the city. In a way, de Blob also reminded me of Lantern, an indie game which featured a similar mechanic of bringing color back to an otherwise black & white environment. For something as simple as this, it’s satisfying to see it in action but Blob ups the ante by performing all sorts of stunts which really portray him as Chroma City’s very own superhero.
As you can imagine, Comrade Black and his henchmen will put up an increasingly more concentrated fight against your efforts to restore peace. INKT shall not only summon tough foot soldiers carrying their titular ink guns, but also throw all kinds of mechanized units, which require both patience and dexterity from Blob, if players wish to succeed in defeating them. Ink will quickly deplete your hitpoints (more precisely, paint points) so you must find a water source as soon as you get hit by “inkies”. You can discover most of the painting mechanics by yourselves and the game features some very thorough tutorials along with low-difficulty initial challenges which manage to accommodate even genre beginners.
De Blob’s hands down one of the best 3D platformers I ever played and since I no longer own a console nor do I intend to own one in the foreseeable future, I’ll have to contend with the genre representatives on PC. Most console ports to PC are abysmal from a technical perspective but luckly, de Blob is a noteworthy exception. For the sheer amount of activities and replay value, I’m more than willing to agree that its current Steam price tag is justified, even without those extras which Steam collectors covet. Perhaps Trading Cards may be added within a future update? I’m hoping more for a de Blob 2 Steam edition, to be honest. It has to happen sooner rather than later.

Please note - I've not played many JRPGs since I was a child, so this review is heavily based on the core game itself, and contains no comparisons to other games. Thus, avid JRPG fans may have a much different view from mine.
As many other reviews state, the game takes about 20-30 hours to complete your first runthrough of it, and boy is it worth it. The gameplay itself is good enough for what it is, and although the combat isn't anything revolutionary, the strategy in it is solid enough to make it very enjoyable. And as far as the story and characters... that's where the game comes into its own. There are three main characters, and a decently sized supporting cast that the game does a great job of fleshing out, which is surprising for side characters. Be prepared to laugh as well, as the main character's personality is hilarious at times, and the other characters all have their quircks that come out and incite laughter. Another amazing thing that I love about the game is the varied endings. There are three main endings, as well as multiple "secret" characters that you do things to obtain, all of whom affect the dialogue.
~~~
Pros
+ The cutscenes are quite nice, with high quality texture models and animations
+ Fairly in-depth combat, which is easy to grasp but also satisfying later in the game once you learn the ins and outs
+ AMAZING story, which will likely draw some tears at some points, and of course a plethora of laughs
+ The characters are all amazing in their own way, there will be some you despise, some you love, and some you just accept. There also is much development in the characters relationships to one another, and yes - there are love routes you can attain (which are done very tastefully, and this comes from a person who typically despises romance novels, animes, and games)
+ GREAT attack animations, which can actually keep you entertained at times, and I found myself sometimes just letting the animations play out rather than skipping them
+ Well done soundtrack, with over 50 songs that play at various times, and although some of them begin to get old (ESPECIALLY if you choose to grind), it's undeniable that a majority are actually very enjoyable to listen to. If you enjoy them enough, you can also use a converter to extract the soundtrack from the game files (.ogg to .mp3), and listen to them outside of the game.
Good/Bad
~ The main story requires little to no grinding, which I personally am fond of. I normally prefer to not need to bore myself of a game because I'm forced to grind in order to have a chance. If you play through the game with minimal grinding, you'll have some trouble at parts, but IMO that's the fun of it when you have your back to the wall, fighting with all you've got. Some grinding will be fine, especially in the second arc of the game, but DO NOT OVERGRIND! The main story will become very boring to play when you become OP.
~ Some purposely cringeworthy dialogue from the main protagonist, which will make you cringe but also laugh, and the side characters call him out on it.
~ Personally, I'm not a fan of the hilariously oversized weapons, but they do look awesome, and they're a standard characteristic of games of this type.
Bad
- Aside from a few dungeons, most of them are fairly bland, and the textures are often muddled. Of course, it's not the main purpose of the game to look beautiful, but I'd much rather the dungeons be more interesting
- Keyboard is fully playable, but if you have access to a controller I'd recommend you play it with that. However, I did make it through the game on nothing but M&K without changing controls, so it's not the worst I've seen
- Fps drops even on a good rig at times (GTX 970, i7 4790k, 16gb RAM), usually when loading the world map or a new dungeon where enemies are spawning, but it's brief and still only drops to about 30.
Good GAme

It's hard to recommend this, even on sale. The gameplay is okay but can rapidly become repetitive. The power curve is so fragile that if you grind even a bit, you readily break it, and it turns into fractured splinters by the end anyway as the game hands you tools to trivialize every combat - yes, even the final boss.
Speaking of bosses, the game has a really bad habit of letting you spank them hard and then halting the fight to declare they're so unstoppably powerful that now you need to run the exact same fight again only with this specific plot contrivance that makes them beatable. Usually because the writers had no other idea how to introduce a new character except to say you need their help, when they have all-around far worse stats and will struggle to catch up because they weren't there for all those Weapon Points you already earned and spent to increase your characters' skills.
Also: skills. And spells. They're useful for the first couple hours and then rapidly outpaced by basic combat once you put any points into combos. It's a whole side of character advancement you can safely ignore, which is honestly just bad game design. Every enemy is weak to some kind of weapon, usually at least one that each character has, so there's really no tactical choice. Combined with new characters coming in way behind on the WP, it makes everyone but your preferred three party members feel completely superfluous.
Unfortunately the writing doesn't really carry it. It's a serviceable plot with some good ideas that could stand to be fleshed out more, but genuine humor feels more accidental than intentional, and your actions never quite feel like they have a notable impact on the world. Which is unfortunate given the mid-game "twist" that seems to exist mostly to let them to shamelessly re-use the game's assets all over again. If you can't use a twist like that to meaningfully change the setting, then why are you even writing it?
In the end I mostly finished it out of spite, and to make certain I didn't feel tempted to come back later to something I left hanging. At least I'm not going to be tempted if we ever get the remake.

I have owned this game for a while and I very highly recommend it. If you like platforming, brawling, beat-'em-up games, cute fairies, lolicon knights, talking trees... or cute fairies that jump on platforms, brawling and beating up all enemies, including a lolicon knight, to protect a forest and a talking tree... then this game's for you!
*Ahem* In all seriousness though, the game is very fun with a lot of replay value. The game consists of many good qualities.
Story Mode - It's fairly short (a few hours), but it consists of a good storyline. It's not too deep, but it's a fighting game and not a Visual Novel. There are multiple difficulties unlocked as you beat the Story Mode, and it includes a New Game+ feature where you can start over from the beginning with the skills you had unlocked on previous playthroughs.
Guardian Mode is especially fun - you can unlock it after finishing the story mode and it consists of fighting through 99 days of increasingly difficult battles (some of which include fighting bosses...or multiple bosses) and ends with you fighting a special boss, who I won't spoil. Your save data from Story Mode does not transfer over to Guardian Mode.
It's definitely fun and definitely worth the money in my opinion. You can find out yourself if you like the combat style by playing through the demo. I never played the demo so I don't know how long it is, but I've heard it's just the tutorial.

XCOM:UFo Defence.Now that name should strike fear into even veteran RTS gamers,if you are as old as me.This franchise was the staple of horror and fear and nightmarish scenarios for many people when it first came out in 1994.It was a brutally hard game,really unforgiving,and extremely likely to absolutely murder you the moment you made a small mistake.You felt like you were always behind in that game,until you finally got the technology from your hardworking scientists and engineers to stand toe-to-toe with the alien invaders.Horror and tension ran the game and you always were afraid of what would happen afterwards.
And now.We have this.XCOM:Enemy Unknown. This game often seems to be overlooked for some reason,and i am unable to decipher why.But to the point.
Enemy Unknown is a turn-based RTS game,You are tasked with the role of Commander for humanity's first and last defence against the alien invaders,the XCOM project. Your  job is to defeat your otherwordly invaders at any cost.
Now,for the game itself.This game feaures 2 kinds of modes.Geoscape mode,which allows you to customize soldiers at the barracks, research alien technologies in the Labratories, and then build these items in the ENgineering Bay.This is also from where you will monitor the situation of the world and take mission requests from a group of united nations known as The Council.
The other mode is the Battlefield.When an UFO lands,ALien Abductions are spotted,or aliens terrorize cities,your soldier are fielded onto whereveer the current situation demands.You will then control them with a Turn-based system to find aliens,neutralize them(be it lethally or non-lethally(Lethally,i prefer,curse those damn Berserkers)),rescuse civillians,,escort VIP's,disarm Bombs,or sequre important cargo.
The game offers a good amount of different types of weapons,amrour and items to equip your soldiers with.Equip your squads with the best that humanity has to offer in conventional weapons,from shotguns,rifles,LMG's,SNiper rifles,and rocket launchers,add grenade sinto thee mix and with a pistol for a sidearm,and you are good to go..right?
Not really.You will not last llong in the world if you rely on human weaponry.WHich also makes it important to capture or build alien weapons of your own.through the research systems,you will be able to research new technology for the engineers to later build in the form of  amrour that turns your soldier invisible, laser rifles,or the almighty Fusion Launcher,an auto-targeting(Presumably) plasma-fuelded warhead which will destroy everything within many blocks,be it cover,enemies,or your own damn team!But weaponry alone is not going to cut it for humanity's finest.You will have to rely on the world to aid you in keeping your soldiers alive.Aka you must find suitable cover for your soldiers to hide behind.Everything form boulders,trees,cars,walls, PLANT POTS!Pillars,and even UFO flight computers can provide you with cover which willl be your squad's main survival tactic. Aliens will utilize the same amount of cover as you do,with the exepction of more..feral aliens like the Muton Berserker and the infamous Chryssalid.
However,all those things will have no say in the matter if you are not allowed to go a bit off the rails in terms of'realism'. Enhance your soldiers with 'Psionic Power'if they,in the game's terms'Gifted'.These powers will allow soldiers to damage,defend,de-rail enemy fire(Like Fortune's *Luck* in metal GEar Solid 2:SOns of Liberty)induce panic and disorder,or take contorl of an enemy's mind and use him against his fellow aliens-in-arms.
As the game progresses,you will want to prioritize squad survival with better armour and weapons.Armours come in many forms,form what i said before,turning you inviisble,hhave grappeling hooks for height scaling,a jetpack,Psi-armour,which enhances Psychic soldier's already face-melting powers,or the almighty Titan amrour,which provides the best amount of health,and also Immunity to fire and poisons(Noteably from Thin Men)
However,once you have reached the staple of technology in the game,you should never construct things like Carapace armour or Laser weaponry,as it becomes obselete in the long run.
But the war cannot be won solely on our own soil. The sky is filled with bogeys,and it is X-Com's job to shoot these UFO's down with their Interceptors.Initially equipped with the traditional missiles at first,you must shoot these things down before they can reach their objectives.Then you get on the ground and assault them.
But the enemy has no shortage of tech of their own. Creatures like the Psionic Sectoid Commander,Notiroius Cryssalid,or the devestating Sectopod tell you that the alien invaders mean buisness on a worldwide scale.Aliens are very likely to always outman and outgun you at every turn,yurning a potential mission sucess into a desperate scramble to get the hell back to your Skyranger,X-Coms aerial transport craft in order to save your soldiers(Or soldier,depending on how badly the escape goes).The enemies show absolutely no mercy on normal mode,and classic mode induces the same level of terror as the Original game from 1994 did.
The game is more action-packed and cinematic then its predeseccor,allowing for immersion and the joy of being in a firefight(Although you only select what abilities a soldier can do).
The Expansion pack,called Enemy Within,improves on a lot of these features.it also adds new feaures to the game.genetically modify soldiers to jump 2 stories,regenerate wounds,or allow electric detection through the skin,letting you find aliens without looking directly at them,or enhance the eyes to allow for etter shots after each miss.You also have the option of making a new soldier class,of which i will explain in a moment.You cna augument soldiers with the'Squaddie'rank by amputating their arms and legs to allow them to be fit into cybernetic suits known as MEC's.
The MEC is a new soldier type in the game who is what it sounds like,its a mech,but with a living perosn insade.The operator has acess to a lot of abilities which cna be built upon with a new resource known as Meld(WHich is also used for genetic modification)to mount a flamethrower on the arm,allow for a high-powered Falcoon punch,prximity mines,grenedad elaunchers,and electromagnetic shockfields to shut down robotics or fry organics alive.
Now,for the classic soldiers.Assault,which can be equipped with a normal rifle or a shotgun for CQC,and with traits to evade enemy fire or allow for an automatic'Reaction shot'when an enemy comes close.They are your team's main frontline comba tunit,alongside the mEC trooper.SNipers are your long-range attackers,able to fire from exxtreme range,and can often be the doom of even the toughest alien if left alone.Support does what supports do.they should carry medpacks with them to heal your squad,or provide smoke-grenades or combat drugs to enhance defence and attack.The heavy class carries the LMG and a rocket launcher to devestate enemy installations and ruin cover,exposing them to more accurate shots.They can also be outfitted with traits that can turn them into'tankbusters'or lock-down enemy personel with supressing fire,and are the general demoilition's expert of the team.
The game has Multiplayer,as well.Jump into the role of humans or aliens,or just mix them togheter.But the Multiplayer has a lot of issues.Bugs,lag,and glitches seem to be offputting for several people,me included.
As for how the general game feels,is it good?Without question!This is a must.buy for everyone who loves RTS games.I still enjoy it to this day!

This review will change if my experience changes after the first two hours.
Stellar Overdrive has a ton of competition. Empyrion, Space Engineers, Starbound, Star Citizen, Elite Dangerous, Rodina, even No Man's Sky- Each of them accomplishes its own goals in its own way. Empyrion has survival and crafting, with plenty of aliens. Space Engineers is all about physics and ship building, putting things together in space. Starbound and NMS have their infinite lineup of procedurally generated world's. Star Citizen and Elite Dangerous focus on the realism of quotidien life as a spacefarer. Rodina is a lonely experience, exploring four unique but barren planets, learning about a story
But not one of these has yet given me the range of emotions an hour's play of this game has. The basic gist: Minecraft on cube-shaped planets, with more to craft, people to talk to, storylines, real vehicles, and the voxel variability that Minecraft is missing. But more than that, this game explores something Minecraft never did but the games in my aforementioned list do: Gravity. Each side of the cubic planets has a different time of day. And gravity reorients as you move. Want to dig to China? Go for it. See how the game handles it when you get closer to the core, and then when you go beyond. Want to fly through space to a forest planet, a desert planet with deep canyons, an ocean planet with little islands and trenches that go almost to the core? How about a moon? How about a lava planet? Build a ship...and go there. Each planet has a different ecosystem with different dangers, monsters, fauna, and enemies. It's a closed system, not open or infinite. But the groundwork is there for the story to expand, the variety to multiply, and the game to evolve.
I know this review isn't very detailed. I'll be updating it after the game leaves Early Access. For now, let me close with this:
If you are a fan of Minecraft but wish the world were a bit more sci-fi; if you're a fan of Elite: Dangerous but wish it were more colorful; if you're a fan of No Man's Sky but were turned off by the lackluster release; if you're a fan of Starbound but want a similar experience in 3D; if you're a fan of Space Engineers but want more survival; a fan of Empyrion but want a more thoughtful art design; or a fan of Rodina but want a game that's more polished with more variety...
...you know what to do. ;)

I've played every Civ since Civ 2 and I have to say this is the best 4x game I have played to date! There are many innovations to Civ 5 that all are welcome additions and the expansions are also highly recommended. Social policy trees, city states, no more "stacks of death" from Civ 4, trade routes, ect. lots of great new features.
My only gripe is that the AI sucks at combat and that cities are too easy to defend. Games are probably too peaceful and the AI hates you too much for being warlike (even though this was normal through much of history). The AI also has unusual quirks, just like all Civ games, but with all the patches and expansions this game has gotten, they are minor (especially compared to it's competitors).
Of course games take 8-12 hours or more to finish, which is something you will learn to live with playing Civ. Of course you can stop and come back, but it's the stopping that's the hard part. I hope the implement a game mode that is designed for shorter play in the future (setting the gameplay speed to "quick" is still a very long game really).
If you like 4x games, turn based strategy games, ect. you owe it to yourself to play this game. It is the best 4x game to date now.

Played it on the XBOX 360 when it came out. Big hype around it. And well worth the wait.
It's a whole lot of fun pulling off those parkour moves that this game bases on. The story wasn't that interesting or original but the main character is likeable and fun to control. Oh, the controls. They take some getting used to but man oh man are they great when you finally start landing a bunch of cool tricks/moves.
It's short, lacks a bit of content but for what it has to offer I definitely recommend picking this up but at a discount price.

+ Gameplay/Controls
The Gameplay of dying light is very good. You have various ways to distract zombies and kill them. The World is also filled with traps which can be used given the player unlocks skills to use them. After unlocking the third and last tier of abilities the game really is fun to play. With help of the grappling hook your way of traveling through the world and avoid obstacles completely changes. While climbing up something can be fun getting down is a complete different story. I died many deaths just to get down a tower. At times this can be even a frustrating experience. Thats why I am thankful for the existence of objects like  zip lines and trash heaps which can be found at most places.
~ Inventory, Items, Crafting and Upgrading
At the beginning the player can only carry four weapons.  Of course it is possible to increase the amount of items the character can carry with the skill system. Weapons can be repaired 3-5 time depending on their rarity until they are completely useless. While limiting the amount of possible repairs is realistic it defeats the purpose of an upgrading and crafting system. Why create new items when they degrade that fast by using them? The only weapons which don’t degrade are guns.  I personally did not upgrade or create many items as the degradation through use takes all the fun out of the upgrading and crafting system.
- Main Campaign
The main campaign is probably the worst campaign I ever played in my life. Many missions just allow for certain ways to play it. While the game is open world the story missions don’t allow for different approaches. Items like the grappling hook are essentially useless for most missions. There even is a mission where you are forced to use quicktime events although no other mission before even indicated that quicktime events were even part of the game. During the campaign some important character die. However the game utterly fails to create an emotional bond so you would care for the characters. All in all the story combined with the level design of the missions is a complete disaster.
~ Skill system
The skill system has three main trees: survival, combat and agility/acrobatics. The agility tree improves by climbing obstacles. The better you are the easier and faster you can jump and climb obstacles. The combat tree improves by fighting and killing enemies. The combat tree mainly focuses on melee combat and improves strength and attacks on enemies. Lastly there is the survival tree. It improves by doing quests and reacting to random events which occur in the world. Improving these abilities increases their levels which in turn gives points with which it is possible to unlock improvements for the character. Some Unlocks allow for increased inventory space other unlock a grappling hook or even a shield. Unfortunately the system is misused as an “unlock” system rather than being skilltree which reflects the growth of the character. Best example would be the inventory system. So what do I mean by that? There is an unlock for the ability to carry more weapons. However combat unlocks which improve strength of attacks which logically could increase carry weight don’t affect the number of carryable weapons. Unfortunately this is a problem with most games which try to combine Action with RPG mechanics.
+ Enemies
The enemies are diverse enough for a zombie game. Many enemies have their weak spots. While most of the time you will encounter the “walker” zombie which is slow there are areas where you can encounter stronger zombies, venom spitting zombies or “runners”. Also fighting humans forces you to a different strategy. As every human is a master of self defense in melee combat you are bound to use guns. That way you are forced to decide whether you use guns and attract zombies with the gun fire or just avoid them.
- Dying light vs. Dead Island
The game was developed by the studio which created Dead Island so is it better? Dying light is in terms of gameplay is a step forward as opposed to Dead Island. In Dead Island I had many encounters which to me were just unfair. The problem was it’s combat system. In comparison to that I never had that feeling in Dying light. If I died in the open world (not the story missions) I died because I made a mistake which I easily could avoid. In dying light it is also more important to be aware of the surroundings. Your approach is much more tactical. After all you can lure your enemies in deadly traps, use firecrackers to distract them or kick them of roofs. Unfortunately this is the only instance where Dying light shines. I rather prefer the tropical atmosphere of Dead Island. Although Dead Island has not the best story - it is a zombie game for crying out loud - I felt more connected to the characters in Dead Island than in Dying Light.
Dying Light strifes to be more realistic in its approach. It does not have levelling enemies and hitting enemies where it hurts is more rewarding. The Skill system has no super powers and you have access to all the abilities with your character, there are no more classes. Still as the story missions are extremely lacking. You end up with a game where just the controls and non levelling enemies are better than Dead Island.
- Conclusion
Dying light has really good controls running and jumping from roof to roof can be fun. Unfortunately this is the only good part of the game. Story, characters, item system and many more just aren’t good enough at all. Back when Dead Island first came out it got a very harsh critique. However at least that game allowed me to keep my weapons and had characters I felt some emotional connection. Not to mention of the campaign. It seems as if the developer behind dying light were only interested in creating an open world and good controls to move around in it.

XCOM:UFo Defence.Now that name should strike fear into even veteran RTS gamers,if you are as old as me.This franchise was the staple of horror and fear and nightmarish scenarios for many people when it first came out in 1994.It was a brutally hard game,really unforgiving,and extremely likely to absolutely murder you the moment you made a small mistake.You felt like you were always behind in that game,until you finally got the technology from your hardworking scientists and engineers to stand toe-to-toe with the alien invaders.Horror and tension ran the game and you always were afraid of what would happen afterwards.
And now.We have this.XCOM:Enemy Unknown. This game often seems to be overlooked for some reason,and i am unable to decipher why.But to the point.
Enemy Unknown is a turn-based RTS game,You are tasked with the role of Commander for humanity's first and last defence against the alien invaders,the XCOM project. Your  job is to defeat your otherwordly invaders at any cost.
Now,for the game itself.This game feaures 2 kinds of modes.Geoscape mode,which allows you to customize soldiers at the barracks, research alien technologies in the Labratories, and then build these items in the ENgineering Bay.This is also from where you will monitor the situation of the world and take mission requests from a group of united nations known as The Council.
The other mode is the Battlefield.When an UFO lands,ALien Abductions are spotted,or aliens terrorize cities,your soldier are fielded onto whereveer the current situation demands.You will then control them with a Turn-based system to find aliens,neutralize them(be it lethally or non-lethally(Lethally,i prefer,curse those damn Berserkers)),rescuse civillians,,escort VIP's,disarm Bombs,or sequre important cargo.
The game offers a good amount of different types of weapons,amrour and items to equip your soldiers with.Equip your squads with the best that humanity has to offer in conventional weapons,from shotguns,rifles,LMG's,SNiper rifles,and rocket launchers,add grenade sinto thee mix and with a pistol for a sidearm,and you are good to go..right?
Not really.You will not last llong in the world if you rely on human weaponry.WHich also makes it important to capture or build alien weapons of your own.through the research systems,you will be able to research new technology for the engineers to later build in the form of  amrour that turns your soldier invisible, laser rifles,or the almighty Fusion Launcher,an auto-targeting(Presumably) plasma-fuelded warhead which will destroy everything within many blocks,be it cover,enemies,or your own damn team!But weaponry alone is not going to cut it for humanity's finest.You will have to rely on the world to aid you in keeping your soldiers alive.Aka you must find suitable cover for your soldiers to hide behind.Everything form boulders,trees,cars,walls, PLANT POTS!Pillars,and even UFO flight computers can provide you with cover which willl be your squad's main survival tactic. Aliens will utilize the same amount of cover as you do,with the exepction of more..feral aliens like the Muton Berserker and the infamous Chryssalid.
However,all those things will have no say in the matter if you are not allowed to go a bit off the rails in terms of'realism'. Enhance your soldiers with 'Psionic Power'if they,in the game's terms'Gifted'.These powers will allow soldiers to damage,defend,de-rail enemy fire(Like Fortune's *Luck* in metal GEar Solid 2:SOns of Liberty)induce panic and disorder,or take contorl of an enemy's mind and use him against his fellow aliens-in-arms.
As the game progresses,you will want to prioritize squad survival with better armour and weapons.Armours come in many forms,form what i said before,turning you inviisble,hhave grappeling hooks for height scaling,a jetpack,Psi-armour,which enhances Psychic soldier's already face-melting powers,or the almighty Titan amrour,which provides the best amount of health,and also Immunity to fire and poisons(Noteably from Thin Men)
However,once you have reached the staple of technology in the game,you should never construct things like Carapace armour or Laser weaponry,as it becomes obselete in the long run.
But the war cannot be won solely on our own soil. The sky is filled with bogeys,and it is X-Com's job to shoot these UFO's down with their Interceptors.Initially equipped with the traditional missiles at first,you must shoot these things down before they can reach their objectives.Then you get on the ground and assault them.
But the enemy has no shortage of tech of their own. Creatures like the Psionic Sectoid Commander,Notiroius Cryssalid,or the devestating Sectopod tell you that the alien invaders mean buisness on a worldwide scale.Aliens are very likely to always outman and outgun you at every turn,yurning a potential mission sucess into a desperate scramble to get the hell back to your Skyranger,X-Coms aerial transport craft in order to save your soldiers(Or soldier,depending on how badly the escape goes).The enemies show absolutely no mercy on normal mode,and classic mode induces the same level of terror as the Original game from 1994 did.
The game is more action-packed and cinematic then its predeseccor,allowing for immersion and the joy of being in a firefight(Although you only select what abilities a soldier can do).
The Expansion pack,called Enemy Within,improves on a lot of these features.it also adds new feaures to the game.genetically modify soldiers to jump 2 stories,regenerate wounds,or allow electric detection through the skin,letting you find aliens without looking directly at them,or enhance the eyes to allow for etter shots after each miss.You also have the option of making a new soldier class,of which i will explain in a moment.You cna augument soldiers with the'Squaddie'rank by amputating their arms and legs to allow them to be fit into cybernetic suits known as MEC's.
The MEC is a new soldier type in the game who is what it sounds like,its a mech,but with a living perosn insade.The operator has acess to a lot of abilities which cna be built upon with a new resource known as Meld(WHich is also used for genetic modification)to mount a flamethrower on the arm,allow for a high-powered Falcoon punch,prximity mines,grenedad elaunchers,and electromagnetic shockfields to shut down robotics or fry organics alive.
Now,for the classic soldiers.Assault,which can be equipped with a normal rifle or a shotgun for CQC,and with traits to evade enemy fire or allow for an automatic'Reaction shot'when an enemy comes close.They are your team's main frontline comba tunit,alongside the mEC trooper.SNipers are your long-range attackers,able to fire from exxtreme range,and can often be the doom of even the toughest alien if left alone.Support does what supports do.they should carry medpacks with them to heal your squad,or provide smoke-grenades or combat drugs to enhance defence and attack.The heavy class carries the LMG and a rocket launcher to devestate enemy installations and ruin cover,exposing them to more accurate shots.They can also be outfitted with traits that can turn them into'tankbusters'or lock-down enemy personel with supressing fire,and are the general demoilition's expert of the team.
The game has Multiplayer,as well.Jump into the role of humans or aliens,or just mix them togheter.But the Multiplayer has a lot of issues.Bugs,lag,and glitches seem to be offputting for several people,me included.
As for how the general game feels,is it good?Without question!This is a must.buy for everyone who loves RTS games.I still enjoy it to this day!

Okay, here's my thoughts on this game.  Value them as you may.
Graphics: 3/5.  Heavy on the polygon side, some of the characters seem to have some hit boxes still rather than a more smooth circle or sphere.  The dungeons look nice, but there aren't that many of them.  I would say that some of the dungeons probably were underdeveloped or potentially rushed.  To be sure, they could have put a tad more thought to it.
Audio: 3/5 The voice acting is solid enough in both English and Japanese.  There are some minor problems with the English characters (a couple of them sound whiny even when they're talking normally, which tended to grate on me).  The music is a little generic, but the songs used for the "speical power" mode do fit nicely.
Battles: 1/5 There's not a lot here.  It's a button smash, where you don't need to use the special abilities.  Almost EVERY fight, including the final boss, can be beatdown with a faceroll.  This detracts heavily from the overall "fun" factor.
Gameplay: 2/5 There isn't a lot of gamplay per se.  You go to a dungeon, of which there are 8 or so, kill the stuff that needs killing and go back to town.  Given all the dungeons are just a matter of moving the cursor and hitting "enter", it's not that hard to find.  There's no real "overworld" like you expect in a RPG, or even some adventure games.  Town options are limited.
Story: 2/5.  It's pretty standard fare: gather X and save the freaking world.  How it goes about it is somewhat different though.
Fun factor: 3/5.  The characters have some great lines between them.  Some of them are unlikable and the ones that ARE likable are ones you can get behind.
DLC: 3/5.  The good news here is that it's CHEAP (I think it's $5 or less for all of it).  The bad news is that the DLC adds in some extra dungeons (mainly rehashes or established ones at higher difficulty levels), and practically unbalances the game.  I mean, you don't need to buy ANYTHING in-game with the weapons the DLC offers.
Overall: It's not a great game by any criteria you can apply to it.  It is an easy enough romp, and stuff you can go through without a guide or instructions.  I'd probably call this a "weekender".  If it's on sale, it'd be worth it.

Killing Floor 2 : A short review that became a bit long.
First off, if anyone is wondering the game totally lives up to it's predecessor the one and only original Killing Floor we all know and love. The major change is the amazing gun play, the weapons feel realistic and do the ammount damage you'd expect from a certain caliber and they handle like how you'd think. From the peashooter AR-15 to the AA-12 that'll kick 'em in the head all guns still feel useful and semi-powerful. The visible change that is very noticeable is of course the graphics, Killing Floor 2 look beautiful and you don't need a NASA supercomputer to run the game either! A decent graphics card and a 2nd gen I-7 still does it at 60 fps on high settings, of course if you want the best graphics and you want to spoil yourself like the PC master race 2nd coming of Jesus you are I'd suggest getting a NVIDIA graphics card (Or if you already have one, good job you.) Personally I have a GTX 980 (MSI) you can enable special physics for blood. Now this might seem as something silly "Oh physics for blood? In other games blood dissapears after like 4 seconds. Why would I want extra physics for something stupid like blood for 4 seconds?" But no, in Killing Floor 2 you're like a professional painter, a Picasso.. With Zed blood instead of paint, the blood of deceased Zeds stay on the map, you start off with a clean(ish) map and the further you get into the match, the more rounds you survive you'll see that the map is turned into modern art. The walls, the floors, the f*cking ceiling... Blood is everywhere. If you play the game on high(er) settings Zeds will also explode into magnificent gibs; a bit of brain, the intestines and so on.
There is also Zed time, you remember the amazing slowmo's in the first Killing Floor where you felt like you were Neo from the Matrix? Well that has returned but 83% more epic (percentages may vary). Everything that is red, mainly the artwork you created with the blood of Zeds but also red camouflage on your weapons or the red jacket your character is wearing or Mr. Fosters patriotic Union Jack GP-5 gasmask lights up, while all the other colors fade to grey.
Furthermore the perk system feels balanced yet really good. It's worth the grinding, being rewarded by getting getting XP and rewarding you more by giving you special abilities per 5 levels of your perk such as ; 50 extra HP or just simply more damage for perk weapons and faster reload times and many more! And for the love of god use the weapons for your perk! Don't go running around with beserker weapons as a commando or field medic.
That's about the end for my short review turned long. If I haven't convinced you to treat yourself on a fun game or to give tripwire a pat on the shoulder for yet again making a wonderful game then I don't know what will.

Review in French and English :P  French is further below, english just down here.
--- English
For having tried it in Beta really extensively and now rediscovering its current form, the game has made giant leaps and you can really say that Stellar Overload has what it takes.
Three main branches in the game: building, creating and adventure/missions.  You can do it all: lose yourself for hours in building houses, fortresses, vehicles (mobile ones that you can take for a spin!) ; go out building new tools and equipment with the extensive crafting mechanisms, head out and discover the huge planets (yes…more than one), use your jet pack (just great to go visiting canyons) or just follow the missions… you’ve definitely got the bucket load with this one.
And you don’t just have to follow the story and go in the dungeons: you can make your own! If you weren’t crazed enough with the possibilities, you can now try and trap your future visitors for good.  Just need to share your dungeon on the community via the workshop and see lost souls try and have fun in your tortured structures.
On the Stellar web site, you can also see that it’s not a dead fish… they are still working on the game and they are going to build an automation system (via cabling) and it will soon come out.  Seems quite promising.
If you like adventure, tinkering and building, Stellar is the deal.
It is still in "early access" now, so some things are still buggy (the vehicles get lost sometimes and so on), but for an early access game, it is definitly worth the spin.
--- French
Pour l’avoir beaucoup essayé en beta de manière étendue puis maintenant en redécouvrant les sauts de géants depuis, on peut quand même dire que Stellar Overload en a dans le ventre.
Trois grands axes : bac à sable/construction, fabrication et aventure/missions.  On peut tout faire : se perdre pendant des heures à construire des forteresses et des véhicules (mobiles !), fabriquer de l’équipement (crafting) vraiment expansif, partir à la découverte de ses immenses planètes, faire du jet pack (si si !) ou juste carrément suivre les missions qui sont proposées, on a de quoi faire.
Sans compter qu’il n’y a pas qu’une histoire à dérouler et des donjons à explorer et vaincre : on peut créer les siens ! Histoire de laisser libre cours à sa fantaisie pour de bon.  Ensuite, reste plus qu’à offrir son donjon à la communauté (via le Workshop) pour voir d’autres âmes perdues se faire plaisir dans les constructions tortueuses face à nos horreurs.
Et les gars de Stellar ne s’arrêtent pas là.  La bête n’a pas fini de préparer son coup.  Sur leur site, ils parlent qu’un système d’automatisation (via câblages à installer) va bientôt voir le jour sur le jeu ! Que du bonheur.
Si vous aimez l’aventure, le bricolage et la construction, feu vert pour Stellar.
Le jeu est encore en "early access" alors il y a encore quelques petits bugs (vehicules qui se perdent, etc), mais pour un early access, ça vaut vraiment le coup.

An OK movie.
First off, what is up with the title? Very misleading. This game is not about the state of free to play games, but about DOTA, some of its top teams players, and the International tournament.
I watched this after "Indie game the movie" and I felt that free to play was a more mechanical, by the book (production wise) movie. It tries to come up with personal stories and even if they are not fabricated, they come up a bit off... Fear posing with his desk, dendi fishing at the end, all the attempts at building story arcs and preaching at the end that the tournament kind of solved the player's issue? or delivered a kind of happy ending... it felt a bit too forced and preachy to me, especially the little rant at the end about how pro gamers will make 250k a year and travel the world in 10-15 years, WTF? It's like they went off track for the whole movie since the start with personal stories, then at the very end they wake up and remember they did this movie to promote the competitive scene so they drop that random propaganda without any support, proof, logic, or even a transition leading to that statement.
Indie game did a better job at being genuine and simply showing passionate people doing what they love to do. For instance, indie game shows game developers and the challenges they face while making their games, which is spot on what you want from it, there just enough personal stuff to make it right but it never became the main focus of it. Free to play feels like it goes off track getting into the personal history and intimate details of player's life, again and again, and for what? It has nothing to do with the competitive scene, the free to play model, Dota, or anything really significant, even if I didn't mind learning some details about the people we have been watching in tournaments I was expecting more.
That being said Free to play is not bad, it just end up being OK-ish, and seeing as it is free there is no reason to not give it a watch.

I purchased this game on a whim.. I wasnt expecting it to be anything good.
Ohh how wrong I was.
Short version : If you like JRPGs in general this is a good one. PC port is good, has keyboard cues & mouse support.Has English voice overs
Long Version :
But first I should mention that Im already a fan of Animes & JRPGs & other popular Japanese stuff in general even tho im not one. So I dont really find fantasy stories & themes like this awkward as some others do.
I dont usually play games for long stretches unless its a competitive multiplayer game or a really hard game which im tryin to beat but cant(example:dark souls). But occasionally there will be compelling games which you just cant put down because they give u just the right amount of depth & enjoyment.I guess thats what the RPG genre is known for but many RPGs fail in some way & end up being a boring chore. It can be uinteresting characters to unresponsive world.
Fairy Fencer F is not even an open world RPG. Its a typical JRPG,safe city zone where u manage ur party & dungeons for questing & grinding. But even then It kept me going... I just didn't get bored at all, the grind did not feel like boring grind. I cared for the characters & enjoyed the music & combat animations. Its not one thing which makes it good. Its all the little bits that combine & polish this to near perfection. Add to that english voice overs & a PC port which does not disappoint. It even shows keyboard button cues on screen, yes you can play with keyboard & mouse just fine. And just like most JRPGs it has very in-depth(sometimes confusing)Player development(I mean stats.. like buffing up your character in different ways).Although all confusion can be cleared by reading through the mini-teaching sections which pop up everytime you open a new menu or encounter something new.Im not even mentioning the absoulutely hilarious conversations the lazy protagonist has with his companions, which are a treat to listen to everytime.
At last.. this game is a typical JRPG & a good one at that & the fact that its a JRPG so it may not be for everyone, as the title mentions that its a turned based combat game. But if you're into that sort of thing like me, then look no further.
If you're still in doubt I suggest you buy the game & play it for 1 or 2 hours & then decide whether its your taste or not, you can refund it if you did not spend more than 2 hours  & 15 days on it. The first 2 hours of the game will stand a good judge of the game trust me.. unlike some other games which start off good & fade into boredom.
Now if you'll excuse me.. I'll go back to gathering more Furies or food
PS: I've never played Hyperdimension Neptunia so I cannot compare, but others say its similar so if you like that... you may like this.

I had high, high hopes for this game and not once did it or has it disappointed. With the more than epic storyline, game-play mechanics, graphics, more in-depth character stories being revealed and filling in gaps between killing aliens in the simulation, it is a game you will never tire of. However, that aside, there is also a lot of community made mods and what not ranging from more clothes to extra missions or activities. Quite similar to Steam workshop, with the only difference being that this game can pretty much be converted into your own personal sandbox.
Literally the only thing Saints Row IV has against it is, when coop'ing, it will have a few kink's and silly glitches, but so does any game once multiplayer comes into the picture.
I commend Deep Silver for bringing out yet another epic game in this installation, yet again not disappointing fans and I hope for more.

Unfortunately, especially for me, the sequel to Syberia really isn't as good as the original.
The big thing is that it lacks the atmosphere of the original, which is probably the biggest factor in the original being so good. Why did it lack it? There's a bunch of reasons. The soundtrack isn't as catching, imagery isn't as distinctive (due to all the snow), seemingly more stilted dialogue/VA, and etc. The game also includes a subplot which, frankly, is more distracting than complimenting.
Another big reason is that there aren't as many locations. The original Syberia has four distinct locations -- Syberia 2 has two. Both games have areas 'in-between', but, even then, the 'in-between' areas of the original carried a far stronger impression because there is more unique imagery. The 'in-between' areas of Syberia 2 is mostly bland snow.
So all of the above combined to dramatically decreased the atmosphere of Syberia 2 to its detriment. However, I still recommend it for fans of the original because the game is a major plot continuation of the story from the first game. I suppose if you don't care for the original's story, that won't matter, but I grew to love Kate/Oscar/Hans so I really wanted to know what happens next.
On its own, I honestly wouldn't recommend it, but if you love the original and/or, like me, preparing for the upcoming release of Syberia 3, this game would be a worthy purchase.

Creative Mode:
So this part is more on just the game mechanics than really the mode itself, I just put it here since in Creative mode you get to TRY OUT EVERYTHING the game has to offer without any restrictions, so I honestly should have started with Creative mode first. I usually refrain from it though since it ruined my Fallout 4 experience when I activated God Mode half way through the game lol.
The electrical system is pretty dang genious, it's like redstone from Minecraft but with a bit more polish. Theres this one item that just lets you displace a HUGE amount of blocks which reminded me of all the mods in Minecraft, but it's actually a feature, not a mod, which is nice.
Overall:
So for an Early Access Game, and the trend I've been seeing with the amount of updates it gets, I really feel like I can trust the developers to keep working on the product with the same amount of care as the previous update. They aren't going to pull a "Stomping Lands" or any of those other god aweful early access scams.
For a Final Release Game, I'd say i'm still a bit shakey, due to the lack of a finished story. But even then, the Creative mode is a blast, along with the community, and the Steam Workshop integrated system that allows you to share creations EXTREMELY EASILY with others. Haven't played any other "Minecraft"-esque game that executes this so well.
Assuming the end product is to be as promised, the $20 price tag is worth it, but if you don't want an unfinished game, then you can wait. If you do want to be part of the community while it grows and give your feedback (they do listen on their forums) I'd say it's worth 4 Starbucks coffees.

You wake up in a peaceful village greeted by fitness nerd joe your neighbour, and as you try to find your brother to speak to him he’s missing! I first heard about this game during it’s early years on Kickstarter going by name Planet³. The premise of a voxel-based world that promised interactive NPCs, beautifully cubed worlds, fully customizable space vehicles and more. Years later the game changed names to Stellar Overload, and many of these promises during the campaign were fully realized with more updates to come before Christmas.
The music is the first “stellar” characteristic that either creates a comfy atmosphere or a feeling of urgency. The colours and views are a sight to behold upon my hoverbike showing vast voxel imagery and worlds across the distance. The mechanics largely differ from similar games like Minecraft, allowing huge placement customizability rather than the standard one block. Many of the in-game mechanics like fighting are solid and well thought out, providing a great tutorial system that allowed my story to begin. Multiplayer also came very naturally, as a friend popped out of nowhere while I was adventuring and we teamed up together.
Voxel-based games that weren’t Minecraft have always felt like copycats, but I feel that Stellar Overload is a completely separate entity. It's well thought out story, visuals and mechanics have created an addicting experience that pushes me to explore the cubed worlds that are nearby.
