Never before has an indie game make me sweat bullets as much as this one. Super Hexagon is the most intense game I think I've ever played. From the first stage to the last, I am kept tensing up and jumping around in my chair while listening to the excellent music.
From a regular standpoint, this game may not look like much. You play as a triangle that must avoid hexagons (and sometimes other shapes) that try to close in on you. A very good idea, I'd say. The gameplay was executed perfectly. You can either use a controller, your mouse, or your keyboard to navigate the triangle. Movement is fluent and not sticky. Each stage has a different movement speed of the actual triangle that you must get used to as well. There are 6 stages, which, naturally, increase in speed and difficulty. You start the game with three of the stages, and every time you beat a stage you will unlock a "Hyper" mode, which is a faster, much more difficult version of the same stage. These features make gameplay exciting and not repetitive in the slightest. You can try to complete the stages to make it to the final stage, or you can also select an "Arcade mode" in which the object of the game is to simply beat your high score. This mode is fun to play with friends.
The soundtrack is perhaps where this game shines the most. The 8-bit drum and bass music style gets you so pumped up upon entering a stage, or when you're close to beating your high score and the music is almost cheering you on. No complaints about the music, I couldn't have asked for a better soundtrack in this game; it fits perfectly.
Now let's talk about the difficulty. It goes without saying that this will be the most difficult game in your Steam library, hands down. More than often, this game will cause you to shout, slam your fist into your keyboard, and rage quit. Beating a stage, however, is so satisfying, it makes you want to keep on playing. The addictiveness overshadows the difficulty. The game can be annoying, and you will rage quit more than once, but you will keep on coming back to it.
In conclusion, Super Hexagon is an amazingly addicting game that will keep you busy for a while. Excellent music and a great art style, paired with insane difficulty, will earn Super Hexagon a final verdict of:
9.2/10.

[DISCLAIMER: This was the first Civ I got to play for more than a few hours. So I'll review the game as it is per se, and not as the fifth installment of the series, since I don't have enough knowledge to compare it to previous iterations.]
Short version: Cool game to chill and relax with friends, unstable online and a few bugs might make it a bit frustrating. DLCs are mandatory to have the best experience though.
Long version: As I said, this is the first Civ I played. And I must admit I got into it pretty fast. It's not that hard to learn, even though the UI might not be that clear. You get to play your favourite historical leader, and see your civilization rise and fall. Simple to learn, with many civilizations each having special abilities/troops to increase the depth and variety, the game is really newbs-friendly and easy to get into. The combat is simple, it's easy to have an estimation of wether you're going to win a fight or not, the informations you get allow you to pick the fights you want to take. The visual style is pretty generic, but it's not bad either, and for each civilization you get a different song playing as background theme. So there go the good points.
Now the cons. The tech tree doesn't always seem to make sense, not all Civs are balanced, there are still gamebreaking bugs ("PICK A CONSTRUCTION" button not going away, which makes it impossible to skip turn, visual tearing that makes it either very ugly or impossible to play...), the loading screens take forever to actually load, and the online is very, VERY unstable. I didn't actually finish a multiplayer game without a problem at some moment. Plus, even though there are a few different victories, the most rewarding one always seem to be the way of the warrior. Science victory is possible though, as well as the diplomatic one, but as soon as one player decides to go on his destruction spree, you just can't get any of these. Not even mentionning the cultural victory since it is basically impossible as long as there's at least one civ that doesn't want you close. It feels quite unbalanced, and only the science and war endings are reached most of the time.
So yeah. Easy to pick up, enough depth to stick around, definitely funnier with friends (Go play Venice and become the richest motherf*cker around, then pay the leaders to fight each other, that's guaranteed entertainment), but beware, it is STILL filled with bugs that might get you to grind your teeth and mechanics that might not always make sense. Hopefully the next game will fix these issues as well as the civs balance.

My RCF Review overall
Alright, Elite Rift here, and some of you may know me from older times, like RC2 where I was named Elite Hunter 39, and RC1 where I was named Excalibur 38.
Now I have been playing Red Crucible for 5 years now.
As a long-time player, I would like to say that Red Crucible has gone from a simple multiplayer tank-fighting game, to an all-out infantry and tank hybrid war in RC2.
Now I understand RC2 had lesser graphics.
I understand how RC2 allowed you to carry multiple weapons AND switch the weapons in the battlefield, but those weapon-switching days are gone.
Seriously, I found it fun too, but look at other games like COD or Battlefield. They don't allow loadout changing in the battlefield. And thus it was removed.
The RGS has gone for a more realistic development to the game, and are currently working on releasing a new map called "The Favela".
RGS has improved the graphics from RC1, and quite frankly, they're still starting out, atleast two months fresh from the update, optimization can still be possible.
As for the cons in the game, there are some, and I will list down four of them.
1. Improve the sounds for almost all the weapons. Sure the new sounds compared to RC1 show a vast improvement, but if you're going for realism, you have to be able to FEEL the power of a 7.62 mm caliber-rifle firing out.
2. Some rifles in RCF are designed in such a way that the IRL stats compared to the RCF design doesn't fit. The SCAR for example. Designed as a SCAR-L ( 5.56mm ), however it's stats indicate that it's a 7.62mm gun. It also carries the normal 30 round 5.56mm magazine, and it's easily OP.
3. Optimization. I understand you guys are working hard to release Favela and other gun updates, but I would like to suggest that you work on Optimization for even a bit more before moving on.
4. OP weapons. I'd like to give an example but I think you know what I'm talking about.
5. Katana length makes it looks like a Fang already.
RCF is a major improvement to the game.
The graphics, how the guns have been "balanced".
They have come a long way from RC1, and I'd like to say that they've certainly improved.
I would like to say however, those cons above are suggestions for improvement.
RCF has great gameplay indeed. But it certainly holds room for improvement. A lot more, in fact.

Killing Floor 2 : A short review that became a bit long.
First off, if anyone is wondering the game totally lives up to it's predecessor the one and only original Killing Floor we all know and love. The major change is the amazing gun play, the weapons feel realistic and do the ammount damage you'd expect from a certain caliber and they handle like how you'd think. From the peashooter AR-15 to the AA-12 that'll kick 'em in the head all guns still feel useful and semi-powerful. The visible change that is very noticeable is of course the graphics, Killing Floor 2 look beautiful and you don't need a NASA supercomputer to run the game either! A decent graphics card and a 2nd gen I-7 still does it at 60 fps on high settings, of course if you want the best graphics and you want to spoil yourself like the PC master race 2nd coming of Jesus you are I'd suggest getting a NVIDIA graphics card (Or if you already have one, good job you.) Personally I have a GTX 980 (MSI) you can enable special physics for blood. Now this might seem as something silly "Oh physics for blood? In other games blood dissapears after like 4 seconds. Why would I want extra physics for something stupid like blood for 4 seconds?" But no, in Killing Floor 2 you're like a professional painter, a Picasso.. With Zed blood instead of paint, the blood of deceased Zeds stay on the map, you start off with a clean(ish) map and the further you get into the match, the more rounds you survive you'll see that the map is turned into modern art. The walls, the floors, the f*cking ceiling... Blood is everywhere. If you play the game on high(er) settings Zeds will also explode into magnificent gibs; a bit of brain, the intestines and so on.
There is also Zed time, you remember the amazing slowmo's in the first Killing Floor where you felt like you were Neo from the Matrix? Well that has returned but 83% more epic (percentages may vary). Everything that is red, mainly the artwork you created with the blood of Zeds but also red camouflage on your weapons or the red jacket your character is wearing or Mr. Fosters patriotic Union Jack GP-5 gasmask lights up, while all the other colors fade to grey.
Furthermore the perk system feels balanced yet really good. It's worth the grinding, being rewarded by getting getting XP and rewarding you more by giving you special abilities per 5 levels of your perk such as ; 50 extra HP or just simply more damage for perk weapons and faster reload times and many more! And for the love of god use the weapons for your perk! Don't go running around with beserker weapons as a commando or field medic.
That's about the end for my short review turned long. If I haven't convinced you to treat yourself on a fun game or to give tripwire a pat on the shoulder for yet again making a wonderful game then I don't know what will.

Overall, this is the most impressive strategy/turn-based, board-game-esque programs I have ever experienced. The level of immersion is wonderful; you can set about to win via military, scientific, cultural, and diplomatic means, or by having the highest score in a time-based playthrough. One of the greatest accolades I can attribute to this program is the degree of learning, historical or otherwise, which playing as the various civilizations and through the included scenarios bestows. As Kamehamaha, you can build moai and field maori warriors. As William of Orange, you can build polders and control the seas with sea beggars. You can ally with city-states, build infrastructure, and wage war on all terrain types. Although there are a few historically inaccurate aspects and scenarios like Wonders of the Ancient World are not well-made, much of the experience is about making your own story and challenging yourself to prevail in situations with the limitations you are dealt. And best of all, there is a grandiose amount of high quality modding available for this program. In the 5 or so years I've had it, I am yet to utilize the multiplayer aspect, but I have heard that it needs significant improvement. Also, this program is processor-intensive and is a good gauge of your computer's max capabilities. In any case, the developers of Civilization 5 have created an enduring and artful product for the ages. I consider Civ 5 to be one of the best video-games, up there with Sim City 4 Deluxe. Some changes/additions I would like to see with respect to content woud be a more realistic set of ramifications resulting from ideology choice, exemption from the world congress if desired (maybe isolationism as a social policy?), as well as the option to privatize various aspects of the player's civilization to the point of market anarchism. There is a great deal of potential for future installments when you consider the prospects of sport, seasteading, banking, subterranean & undersea exploration and even natural disasters. It's the good old formula that got this series of games popular in the first place, nothing wrong with that, but I feel that their attempts to shake up the means of experiencing this formula fall slightly flat.

The humor is standard kid's game affair, with a bit more of a self referential edge, because Deadpool; otherwise the writing is the usual flanderisation of every character in a franchise, with some bits of genuinely funny dialogue and scenario writing.
All in all, despite it's numerous niggles present here and there, it's pulls through remarkably well with solid gameplay, fun puzzles and jokes that are sure to entertain any kid in the audience, and even some adults. Just don't expect a masterpiece.

While it may not have been a worthy successor to KF1 back when it was in early access, it definitely is a great sequel to Killing Floor in its current state. It's still not entirely complete, with new features, fixes, balances, etc. being added in the future. But what content it has now, & the quality of that content, is very much worth the fair price tag in my opinion.
I haven't played the original Killing Floor in a long time, so I may be sort of biased towards liking KF2 too much. But either way, I think Killing Floor 2 is great. It gives Killing Floor a great new coat of paint & polish, setting the old clunky-chunky graphics of KF1 far back. Each character is uniquely voiced, while not needed, does give a nice new level of polish. The game is optimized pretty well too, as my older PC can run this at a good framerate with good graphical settings as well. The maps, enemies, characters, and especially weapons are all pleasantly polished to look & feel satisfying.
The combat, teamwork, & classes all work very well. KF2 adds multiple new classes to play as, each suiting different & fun types of play-styles. While I think that there is still room for some balancing (Some classes are still just better than others, at least until they are majorly leveled up) they are still fun & worth playing as if anything just to try something new. Playing single-player solo matches works pretty well too, as the game is balanced not only by difficulty but by how many players are in the game. Beating an entire match on hard by yourself is entirely possible provided you're good enough, and you choose a decent map to play on. (Some maps are much harder when playing alone as you can't properly watch your back)
It might be a little disheartening to some players when you see that Killing Floor 2 has a CS:GO/TF2-esque item & economy system. But as I kept playing on I was more & more open to it, as the item economy in this game is less offensive than it is in games like CS:GO & TF2. Maybe it's just because KF2 is primarily a Co-op game & not a competetive game. But either way I found the cosmetic item system in this game to be fairly balanced & un-offensive. It's absolutely completely optional, you get pretty much a guarantee of 1 random item a day, and the quality of the items is decent. Even if you don't want to buy or spend any money on cosmetics, you will most likely get decent items daily to customize with, and you'll be able to sell anything you don't want for Steam money on the marketplace. So that's a plus.
Overall Killing Floor 2 is a great, skillful, challenging & fun game that has a good price. It looks good, it's well optimized, you can make some of your money back on the Steam market if you don't care about cosmetics, and overall I feel that it's a good improvement to Killing Floor 1. It's had a lot of updates to get it to where it is now & if it keeps getting even more great updates, then the game will continue to be worth playing (In my opinion). I recommend this game whether you're new to Killing Floor, or if you're a Killing Floor 1 player.

Now that KF2 is out of beta/EA with all 10 classes released, I can review this game after 450+ hours.
Long story short, KF2 is like KF1 but better in every way, from graphics, gameplay, and perk-system. For those who are new, KF2 is a FPS, wave-based survival co-op game that pits you against bioweapons called "zeds". You start out with the basic weaponry, you kill things, earn dosh (money), buy stuff at a trader pod at the end of each wave, and repeat. Highly repetitive, but the gunplay is top-notch along with the enemy types/behavior that you will find yourself going back to. With 10 classes and 25 levels per class (aka perks), you can spend a lot of time grinding for that max level for maximum perk power. A bit grindy in that regard... but I feel you'll get your leverage by playing classes you truly want to play as so you're not forced to grind everything to max.
Obviously KF2 is not perfect, and further balancing and content is required for sure. After a rocky early access, and the zed-economy (think CS:GO mtx system, which I don't care for), the game has come far though with the help of it's playerbase and a dedicated dev team. Any fan of FPS that likes co-op, zombies, PvE, easy entry but high skill ceiling, this is the game for you. Decent vidcard required though.
Final Score: 5/5

Pros:
Cons:
For an early access game that was released less than 3 months ago, it's got a lot going for it.
But of course due to it being Early access, it isn't feature complete. Meaning that once you complete the first main questline on your starting planet, you are left with only a side mission taking you to the newest planet added (which is gorgeous and massive) Aside from that, there really isn't much wrong with this game.
I went into this expecting nothing special, but I was left pretty surprised.
The Story aspect kept me very interested, to the point that I'm excited for more Story centered updates in the future.
The world design is beautiful, which is shown the second you start your game,the starting town is really reflects how pretty this game gets. And with the tools given to you for building, you can creation some pretty amazing stuff yourself.
You're able to build your own Hovercylces and Space Ships by hand, using the blocks you've gathered to make it really special. You're also able to scan, and save your builds to either spawn (given you have the materials required) or share with other people Via the Workshop.
One of the best things about this game is how the planets are layed out. They're cube shaped, so when walking to the edge of a planet, you're able to go over the edge and land on the other sides. And while this can be extremely jarring at first, it's a really cool mechanic and makes the planets pop.
The combat isn't too much to sneeze at, Typical FPS stuff, but if you're not careful you're going to find yourself stuck in a loop of getting your butt handed to you. The dungeons are the best example of this, especially at the end of the main quest. That dungeon alone took me about 2 hours to get through.
Speaking of which, the Dungeons are pretty tricky at times. Laser grids, Parkour challenges, Mazes, Enemies around every corner, Platforming and Minor Puzzle Solving, They have pretty much everything you could ask for in a challenge.
This is a really solid game, even if it is in Early Access right now, it has enough to satisfy 10 hours or so with it's story content, and if you're a builder you'll find yourself spending even more time playing.
If you're not a fan of Early Access, you should definitely buy this when it comes on sale, or wait until future updates before buying. However if you're willing to trust the developers, which is a good idea in this case, then I would definitely recommend buying this full price and enjoy watching it grow.

I think this game is worth picking up solely on it's merits as a game in the South Park Universe. The games does an amazing job of looking and feeling like you're actually in the world of South Park. Additionally, the amount of references they managed to pack into this tiny game is amazing. Even more amazing is the fact that it somehow feels like a natural progression of things instead of them just trying to pack in as much stuff as possible. The humor is spot on; I chuckled, chortled, and cackled throughout the game. It felt like I was playing something Matt and Trey had written, not some intellectual descendent or knockoff.
Surprisingly, I would also recommend this game based solely on its gameplay; it is a surprisingly good RPG. It's standard turn-based RPG but with a bit of agility-based flair that I found fun throughout the entire game. It becomes clear after a bit that the system itself is often pretty simple; however, the designers intentionally include lots of opportunities throughout the game to use your brain to avoid fights. There's also at least one achievement related to doing so.
Despite my overwhelming positive review, the game does have some flaws that become readily apparent after a bit of time spent with the game. Some might take issue with how short the game is. I only spent 20 hours on the game, yet I still managed to beat it on the hardest difficulty and get 100% of the achievements. This time also includes a reasonable amount AFK time while the game was running. I got the game on sale for 7 or 8 USD so I was pretty okay with this; however, I would not have been happy had I spent the full price of 50 or 60 dollars.
To make matters worse, I have trouble seeing how you could really reply this game. There are no real storyline choices in the game; the only variability is in what class/build you choose. Even then, there are only 4 total classes and each class only has 4 total moves. After my playthrough I went back and played around with another class for a few minutes and it didn’t feel new or interesting enough to merit another playthrough. Based on other comments on the interwebs, this feels like I may be in the minority.
Probably the biggest issue is just how simple the combat system is. You don’t have that many options in combat. I found that picking my favorite two skills and just spamming those skills was super effective. Variation wasn’t rewarded since the upgrade system encourages you to go all in on one or two skills. Those skills then become significantly better to the point where it’s not worth really using the other skills. Like I said earlier, this fault is somewhat masked by the fact that the game itself is short, and you’re encouraged to use your brain to avoid an awful lot of the fights.
Overall, I still recommend this game if you're a fan of South Park or you love RPGs. Just make sure you get it for a reasonable price (probably less than 10 USD).

Cute, little rogue-like spaceship sim game.
The role is simple, fly on the other side of galaxy map to warn your fleet about upcoming rebel invasion and it's weaknesses.
Flying through 8 sectors, each containing many systems you have to hold on and maintain many encounters of enemies, random events and threats by space phenomena.
Given yourself the ship of your choice, you can upgrade and set pretty much anything giving you so large options of Micromanagement. From manning the ship systems with your crew to weapons, shields, drones and ship's energy power distribution. During combats you can also pause the game any moment, thinking and planning your moves ahead which comes handy in most of the chaotic situations.
Destroying enemy ships provides you with gear and scrap for which you can buy better stuff in Stores scattered over the space. Not only by simply destroying enemy ships you get victorious, you can also either disable their life support systems or send in the Assault team both resulting in killing the enemy crew, giving you much more rewards.
Getting through the game makes you unlock more new ships or their new weapon/system/crew layouts after successfully completing achievements with each of them. Can you save yourself while getting through the space with Rebel fleet chasing your tail making you not to stop for long in each sector?
Personally I am not much of a fan of Rogue like games but this one can be hard, fun and still mannageable at once.

I was really looking forward to this game and... oh my god I was not disappointed!
I'll begin with a short prologue. Many game developers nowadays don't make good quality games anymore, instead they regurgitate some sort of a dodgy half-baked product to try and get as much money from the public as possible. Rarely, however, we get a chance to play a quality game truly worth of our attention and this one fits perfectly into this recently impoverished category.
And now about the game. To start off this is a good quality polished product with only some very minor issues/bugs. The game performs well in terms of stability and only has several minor bugs, however I tend to think that it could have been optimised slightly better. Don't get me wrong, it's a beatiful game but you need quite a powerful machine to be able to enjoy it on full graphics. The gameplay is fun and highly immersive but can seem a bit dull at first. Although once you level up your character and get new abilities the game becomes extremely fun! There are so many ways you can kill zombies. To name a few: you can smash them, burn them, slice them up, impale them, blow them to pieces and much more. I won't say much about the graphics except that he game looks great and visually appealing. The storyline is not that great and is not original at all. From what I heard it's a bit similar to far cry series. You can pass the main story fairly quickly but I would strongly reccomend that you explore the city and do side quests because that is where the game shines. Side quests are quite fun and introduce to many interesting/weird characters that got trapped with you inside the city. Some of the quests are quite touching and let you feel the full scale of madness that is consuming the city. The multiplayer experience is what makes this game truely special. You can grab your friends and do quests, go to parts of the city that you don't dare exploring alone or to try and survive the night without being eaten by the hunters (other players). You will be terrified and feel like a prey when facing those nasty creatures, especially in early stages of the game.
Overall this is a fun game which will probably keep you hooked for quite some time. I would definitely recommend it to anyone who likes killing zombies and having fun in multiplayer.

The show that takes it's shot at absolutely anything takes a shot at a video game. ( A decent one this time around.) Any south park fan will love this game. Runs like a breeze on a TABLET (although you might need to mess with the resolution occasionally in the options, as the cutscenes would displace the main character or background a bit.) , and has picturesque open world, even though you can't cross the street.
They really do touch on so much of the lore in the show, from Tom Cruise still in the closet, to the subtle references to items in the background in closets, garages, and homes. As for the map of south park, the game holds true to the layout in the show. While not spatially expansive, like one would find in a game akin to the Elder Scrolls  or Fallout franchises, what it lacks in space, it makes up for in progressively unlockable, and carefully hidden nooks and crannies. This made the gameplay not as daunting in unlocking achievements and completely exploring, as the aforementioned counterparts, but also retained the games intended challenge.
Now on to it's age rating. It's South Park. Gotta use common sense here. If you don't have it, you should probably not be on steam. At all. All I can say in describing the content without spoiling it, is what they can't show on the air,  they hang out to dry here.
The combat doesn't need too much praise. Or rather I could praise it, but then make a wall of text to add to what I have already. To keep it short, the combat is simple and easy to get the hang of, in any turn based rpg, but still keeps the player engaged with quick time events built into the combat. Weapons, equipment and modifications that only a kid in south park would use, (and probably RandY Marsh,) along with a myriad of snacks. The classes speak for themselves in the game. Fighthers use brute force, with high armor, mages use high damage out put attacks, with potions, and so on. ( To unlock everything, You'll probably need to play them all. and a couple times.)
All in all, this game is the perfect satirical take on an rpg, It delivers to major fans of the show, and of the genre. Absolutely recommend. gr8 r8 m8 I r8 8/8

While this is not the best game In the series, it is still a fun and approachable first step into the shadows. I recommend it, but it isn't the best in the series.  It's biggest flaw lies in the writing of the campaign.  Feeling more like a fanfiction, with cheesy, almost comical treatment of several shadowrun setting tropes and characters.  Jake armitage is a potent ally, but his character treatment is silly.  The main hub feels extremely forced and clichéd, and while there are interesting NPCs to talk to, it just feels hollow.
Don't get me wrong, there is a reasonable plot arc and mystery here, you will feel good when you reach several plot points.  But some of the linear mission structure's will Rob you of a strong feeling of accomplishment.  With only one real open path mission with multiple solutions.   It ends up feeling a but like an old school libear adventure game with better combat.
The game also doesn't treat every etiquette (a special dialogue trait you select at character creation and again if you level up charisma) dialogue equally, with some etiquettes popping up almost every few scenes, and others appearing once if at all.
What irks me, is This isn't quite the gritty, dark, and deadly shadowrun I grew up with, it's a pg rated tech demo with a few great parts (by the end I was eager to play more)
What you need to know is that this setting deserves an open world treatment, with a Skyrim style radient mission system to give the player a real sense of being a runner.  Obviously that's not what this engine is remotely capable of, but some sense of open world transit would have been great.
Looking at the creation tools they could have done this, but I'm sure most of the Kickstart money went into the engine, not the campaign. The creation tools are are easy to learn if you have any modding experience, especially if you ever used the original nwn module toolset.
I didn't make any myself but, messing around in it was pretty intuitive.
Overall if you plan on playing only one of the shadowrun games in this series, you should skip this one and do dragonfall or Hong Kong.  But if you got the nuyen to buy all three, at least try this campaign, even if only to see how much they improve on the next ones.

Being that this film was from valve, where their top 3 games are free to play or monetized through virtual transactions, I expected something about the business of f2p and how that has changed the landscape of gaming.
But what we get instead of a bog standard "guys getting ready for a video game tournament film", with short interviews with their mothers and all that "e sports" coverage fluff, it was substance free. I don't know why this film with such a name decided to just cover one game, Dota2 exclusively. But for the sake of argument even if that were fine, it fails miserably in showing how any of this matters. There is already another video game movie which did all this correctly, it was called "King of Kong", and that film explained why things mattered, how the game worked,  and what the players had to over come to reach their elite status.  Even people who have never played donkey kong come away with an understanding of the game, its challenges and the strategies used by elite players after watching that film. This free to play film however shows you nothing but some random characters bashing each other on screen, and to make it worse they then zoom in close with what I'm guessing are post rendered depictions of whats happening, just to show off action scenes without context that tell you nothing about the game. Unless you play Dota2 already you have no idea whats going on, what strategies are in play, why it matters at all, why should I care.... instead you just see the shots of the players making faces, shouting, hammering away, and senseless action. The only suspense is who wins the million dollar prize, but how they do it, and why should I care is never covered in an effective way.
This really was a wasted opportunity. It really should have been titled Dota2, the quest to win a million dollars or something like that, because other than being a marketing video for tournaments and Dota 2, its not really much of a documentary.  Its really not much more than the same type of puff piece athlete bio's NBC likes to use as filler during the olympics.
For people who don't care about video games, this won't enlighten you. It shows Dota2 in a way that is indistinguishable from mindless button mashing. For people who care about video games, the film provides zero insight.
The only thing this film has going for it is that its free.
Do yourself a favor if you haven't watched king of kong already, rent that instead and see how things can be done, the special features alone on the dvd are better than this film.

I'm cautiously recommending this game, as while it can be fun, it has some issues that I can't overlook.
This game seems like it really wants to be skill based, but it sadly ends up relying much more on luck than anything else. If you don't get the items that your chosen character REALLY wants, you'll end up falling behind the difficulty rating. It's very easy for a minor setback in this game to rapidly snowball into an uncontrollable situation where very little can be done. The enemies become bullet sponges, and unless you have damage items, there's very little you can do. During a teleporter event, you're forced to deal with whatever amount of enemies the game decided to throw at you, and you'll have to slowly chip away at their absurd HP pools from afar. By the time you're done with them and can move on to the next level, you've already lost too much time. You're done for. Add this to the fact that the game can spawn green enemies that can heal those around them, and it just leads to a tedious and un-fun scenario, and you're forced to start over again...
Luckily, the game has an unlockable that allows you to somewhat alleviate item randomness, and lets you select what item you want depending on rarity. But even with this, the game can still bombard you with things you don't need. For some reason, I'm constantly stuck with green and orange item boxes, when I just want some basic attack speed, crit, or speed items.
That said, the game IS very fun once you get a good run-through going, but the situations where you slowly realize that there's nothing you can do are incredibly tedious and unfun. I'm going to recommend this game to people that can look past a couple of bad runs, and have fun being an unstoppable monstrosity. I doubt that this game will ever be updated again, even less that these issues will be fixed, but here's hoping for a sequel?

I am a total sucker for adventure games. My love affair with them started way back with Colassal cave, Scott Adams Adventures, and the famous Infocom games. Back then things were text based. Wishbringer, Hitchhiker's Guide to the galaxy, Enchanter, Suspended, Planetfall, Bureaucracy, The Lurking HOrror, and the everpopular ZORK were among my favorites. Adventure games have one game play premise. The Barter System (and right now the This for That Schoolhouse Rock song is playing in my head).  But that is the essence of the system. I have this, I give this person THAT and get another thing in return or they do something for me. Thus I progress in the story.
Now the purpose really is to tell a fun and interesting story while loading up with these puzzle exchanges. Graphics adventures of the sort were inevitable. THe best known were the Sierra company's titles like the King's QUest series, thus the POINT AND CLICK adventure was born. Thus a problem. Instead of getting a description of a room and things you can pick up, you are given a picture and have to see that these blocky pictures are actually objects as well as that there are exits...and sometimes not. Sure you can hover over an area to see if you can interact, but therein lies the problem. You HAVE to make things logical enough so that people will not only be able to tell where to go and that there might be something you can pick up.
Syberia 2 suffers bigtime from both obstacles. It is a sequel to a previous Syberia game, but that doesn't really matter. YOu can pick up easily that the lead character Kate has been away from work for awhile...and never wants to return. She instead sets off on another journey with an elderly friend to find Syberia, a place of myth and legend. It's an intriguing beginning that basically leads nowhere fast. Like King's Quest V, it suffers from lots of illogic in tasks you must do. Give a alligator to this character to get a key? No that's an exaggeration but there are some of the puzzles like that. THere is a lot of bait and switch in it. Oh I need a small key to get through this door. Rats. It doesn't work I think. Am I doing this right? I need a coin for this contraption. I have many coins. They don't seem to work. I have no idea what to do now.
This uncertainty is there because of the gameplay engine. When you hover it is a bit ambivvalent in what's happening. It uses a weird symbol to indicate that you CAN'T do something that is small and unclear and most importantly unlabeled and uninstructed. There is NO instruction whatsoever in fact. So you will waste a lot of time, say....trying a key in a door and wondering what you are doing wrong, not totally realizing that....it's just the wrong key....go find another one. It doesn't tell you it is wrong in ways that are obvious. Other games have big eyeball icons for looking, speech ballon for talking, hand for grabbing. Can't really say I can identify what the cursor is doing at any particular time except that it changes. Another gameplay issue is objects. You can use objects in your inventory to interact with objects in a given location. That isn't really obvious either. Mixed with the obtuse icons and cursors it takes a bit to figure it out when a simple 1 minute training area would have taken care of this.
It also definitely lacks logic in that it won't let you say and do things that seem obvious. Example. You talk to someone. They have a broken thing. You have a long conversation about your goal, your traveling companion, his ability to invent and fix things and that the two character even KNOW each other. THen in the end nothing becomes of it. It is obvious that you should go back to your friend and talk to him to tell him to go fix the thing right? But when you do it doesn't give you that option. Why not? I think the characters stand around asking themselves that.
The characters are indeed very good characters, some a bit natural, some cartoony. The lead character especially is appealing. However most of the characters don't want to help you with anything. Then out of nowhere they do. Then instead of actually saying logical things that flow, they clam up simply waiting around...bored in their existance. They almost look like they are frustrated about having nothing interesting to say. Talking with someone is easy. Just click on them and it gives you a series of topics to discuss. But that soon becomes a complete grind. They recycle information SO MUCH within each topic. Nothing goes in sequential order. You can get 5 layers deep in ONE topic conversation only to be told the exact same thing 2 layers down in another. And those conversations seem to go on forever without really getting to the point.
I do like the characters in general. The stories of each person are fine and make you want to know them more. The lead character is appealing enough to easily get most people on her side. But....this game and story is a bit of a depressing downer right from the getgo. I love the beginning of how her bosses are worried about her and that she hasn't come back to the office. "She's gone." says one. Meaning...wanderlust has totally consumed her. She's a different person now and will never return. Kate does indeed to be fulfilling that role...trying to help her dying old inventor friend find the mythical Syberia. So good strong beginning instantly sent on a downward depressing spiral dealing with an elderly friend whose mind is not all there and whose health slowly declines...in fact there are a series of interactions and puzzles dealing specifically with that. I don't want to watch a man dying and have to go through a lot of things just to get him treated just to be told he's going to die. On the upside this is a world like MYST, like Likehouse. Full of robots and contrption. Granted it has this supercharged locatamotive run by a robot and still has to use coal. What's with that? It then goes through a town whose economy is nonexistent because it has no travelers or money coming in on the last stop to nowhere. No wonder all the characters just stand around fidgety waiting for something to happen (which never does)
Overall there is no brightness at all to this game. Not in puzzles, not in interaction, not in story, not in logic. THere are some things that you just happen upon and they work. THere are others you didn't even realize and never would have guessed. THen there is the problem of having to constantly go from one of a towen to the other to your train back again, etc. It's a grind. Not fun at all. Especially when location logic too seems to suffer. LEt's see if I go under the train track I should be here then back this way I'm at the stairs. No wait I'm now at an engine. BUt that should be over by the house. Location placement is a bit off and not logical either making that running grind worse. Putting things as far apart as possible just to lengthen gameplay and then confuse you in how to get there....is a very very bad idea.
At end, the only great thing to say about this is that the characters are well formed, the scenerey gorgeous, the voice acting is great, especially Kate and the pearshaped Russian guy that sounds like Boris Badenov from Bullwinkle.
The singleplayer experience in this game is amazing. If you are getting this with only multiplayer in mind then just so you know, its extremely difficult to set up.

Antichamber is a sometimes difficult, sometimes simple, puzzle game that can be frustrating and satisfying. You don't really know what the aim of the game is; you just try to solve whatever you feel might be a puzzle.
The game offers little sayings before and/or after challenges but there is little guidance or direction, although that's not necessarily a bad thing. Sometimes the aim of the puzzle is clear (eg. get to the other side of the cliff) and sometimes you have no idea until you complete it (eg. run into a wall by accident and go through it). There are also lots of things that happen or things you can do that don't make sense in the real world. The game has witty comments such as "Things are not always as they first appear" but it sometimes felt like a bit of a cheat to me and not a proper puzzle.
That said, I would definitely recommend this game to anyone. Antichamber is pretty unique. Basic graphics, simple gameplay, but still a challenge!

A great follow up to Cyberia. The exciting feel of something fresh and new that I felt with Cyberia is somewhat diminished during playing the second part, but the world is so immersive that I was happy as hell playing this. The game is also somewhat shorter than the first one, if you have good problem solving skills you should be able to do this in one day.
Animations are quicker so you don't loose time watching Kate going up&down the stairs like an old lady like in the first game. Some minor improvements have been also made, like the conversation list updating and hiding topics that can't be discussed further at that point, and so on.
Puzzles are still fairly clear and manageable by yourself. Sadly there are also puzzles that the game does not give you any hints on how to do, and important objects are still not lit or highlighted in any way. You can end up searching little pieces for hours because of this, and can't progress until you find them. I also noticed one "bug" that can ruin the game, so saving the game is very advisable, at least in the beginning of levels.
So while I gave Cyberia something like 4.5/5, I give this 4/5.

I started playing this game whit not many expectations but it is the best game I got for free by far. It creates a tense atmosphere throughout the entire game  by having a great sound design,minimal graphics and by forcing the player to always think before shooting because the ammo is scarce and there are no continues.

Unfortunately, the devs took the worst aspect of Syberia and *emphasized* it in Syberia 2: the entire game is designed around assuming that the only "right" way to approach solving a problem is by thinking the same way the devs do, so all you get is mounting frustration as Kate refuses to do what seems "obvious" to you, particularly in the form of dialog choices.  Also bad: the game keeps violating Chekhov's Gun, where game elements are not present until you need them, so you will vet an area as empty, then solve a puzzle, and have no reason to realize that the heretofore empty area now has the next element you need to pick up.
Stay away, and play a GOOD point and click, like Dreamfall.

As a roguelike, FTL manages to meet all my requirements for a worthwhile play: it's got better than average visual and musical presentation, gameplay that demands your attention, a gruesome difficulty curve (that you can tone down as needed), a wide selection of extremely varied starting ships, plenty of unlockables and optional challenges, and more than enough story and scripting to keep it from becoming a straight numbers game. On top of that, the real-time, action-heavy combat hides many of the more onerous aspects of roguelikes really well, making FTL an excellent choice if you're looking for a way to introduce friends to the genre without boring them silly. An excellent game overall, even if it is extremely painful at times.

The show that takes it's shot at absolutely anything takes a shot at a video game. ( A decent one this time around.) Any south park fan will love this game. Runs like a breeze on a TABLET (although you might need to mess with the resolution occasionally in the options, as the cutscenes would displace the main character or background a bit.) , and has picturesque open world, even though you can't cross the street.
They really do touch on so much of the lore in the show, from Tom Cruise still in the closet, to the subtle references to items in the background in closets, garages, and homes. As for the map of south park, the game holds true to the layout in the show. While not spatially expansive, like one would find in a game akin to the Elder Scrolls  or Fallout franchises, what it lacks in space, it makes up for in progressively unlockable, and carefully hidden nooks and crannies. This made the gameplay not as daunting in unlocking achievements and completely exploring, as the aforementioned counterparts, but also retained the games intended challenge.
Now on to it's age rating. It's South Park. Gotta use common sense here. If you don't have it, you should probably not be on steam. At all. All I can say in describing the content without spoiling it, is what they can't show on the air,  they hang out to dry here.
The combat doesn't need too much praise. Or rather I could praise it, but then make a wall of text to add to what I have already. To keep it short, the combat is simple and easy to get the hang of, in any turn based rpg, but still keeps the player engaged with quick time events built into the combat. Weapons, equipment and modifications that only a kid in south park would use, (and probably RandY Marsh,) along with a myriad of snacks. The classes speak for themselves in the game. Fighthers use brute force, with high armor, mages use high damage out put attacks, with potions, and so on. ( To unlock everything, You'll probably need to play them all. and a couple times.)
All in all, this game is the perfect satirical take on an rpg, It delivers to major fans of the show, and of the genre. Absolutely recommend. gr8 r8 m8 I r8 8/8

I was really looking forward to this game and... oh my god I was not disappointed!
I'll begin with a short prologue. Many game developers nowadays don't make good quality games anymore, instead they regurgitate some sort of a dodgy half-baked product to try and get as much money from the public as possible. Rarely, however, we get a chance to play a quality game truly worth of our attention and this one fits perfectly into this recently impoverished category.
And now about the game. To start off this is a good quality polished product with only some very minor issues/bugs. The game performs well in terms of stability and only has several minor bugs, however I tend to think that it could have been optimised slightly better. Don't get me wrong, it's a beatiful game but you need quite a powerful machine to be able to enjoy it on full graphics. The gameplay is fun and highly immersive but can seem a bit dull at first. Although once you level up your character and get new abilities the game becomes extremely fun! There are so many ways you can kill zombies. To name a few: you can smash them, burn them, slice them up, impale them, blow them to pieces and much more. I won't say much about the graphics except that he game looks great and visually appealing. The storyline is not that great and is not original at all. From what I heard it's a bit similar to far cry series. You can pass the main story fairly quickly but I would strongly reccomend that you explore the city and do side quests because that is where the game shines. Side quests are quite fun and introduce to many interesting/weird characters that got trapped with you inside the city. Some of the quests are quite touching and let you feel the full scale of madness that is consuming the city. The multiplayer experience is what makes this game truely special. You can grab your friends and do quests, go to parts of the city that you don't dare exploring alone or to try and survive the night without being eaten by the hunters (other players). You will be terrified and feel like a prey when facing those nasty creatures, especially in early stages of the game.
Overall this is a fun game which will probably keep you hooked for quite some time. I would definitely recommend it to anyone who likes killing zombies and having fun in multiplayer.

Another day, another asset flip. That seems to be my life lately. Today's installment is another Tonguc Bodur gem, Nephise Begins. This prequel to the complete non-entity that is Nephise is basically the same game with a few slight improvements.
You play as a young but fragile girl named Nephise who can jump off of sheer cliffs stories high and needs exactly ten mushrooms. While mushroom hunting, she finds some skulls and uses them to persuade a fox to let her enter a cave, where she learns that she'd rather be an orb collector.
Things you do in this game include: walking into a house, pick up mushrooms, pick up animal skulls for no stated reason, turn vases around, kill a harpy through your leprous touch, walk through a cave, wake up a fox, and collect one orb. That's it. So that's not much to do in a game.
The pros of this game are that you move at a relatively normal speed (which you don't in the first game), you don't have to do any puzzles that lie to you (which, again, the dev had trouble with last time), there are a couple of fun-ish missable achievements, and the stock music was better this time.
The cons are that everything in this game is stock except the narration, which merely leaves no impression at all on you. I was meditating on these games a bit, and it occurred to me that one of my main complaints with the series is that the storytelling (and "progression") is all delivered via narration. A piece of advice for Mr. Bodur: show, don't tell. Particularly in video games, one of the most interesting ways to deliver information is organically, through in-game experiences. On the other hand, these games suck all the fun out of the point of being a game by telling you exactly what to do in words and not giving you really any information that YOU can glean from the audio and visuals.
One of the reasons this sucks so much is that this tell-don't-show method ruins even the slightest amount of immersion you might otherwise have had, since Nephise the character, dwelling in a world with no narrator, would have no reason to solve the game's two puzzles or do anything besides collect mushrooms and go home.
A side note: despite what the Store page says, there's no fog in this game. It doesn't really matter, but it is a lie.
One of the most damning criticisms a game can get is the ratio of playtime to achievements unlocked. Take me, for instance. I have no need to play this game ever again, and I got 100% of the achievements in about 40 minutes. And that was with a lot of dicking around, like futilely trying to find a lose state or climb the ladder in the game. If that doesn't tell you that this game isn't worth your money, I don't know what will. Yes, the Unreal engine is pretty. The stock assets used here are pretty. The lighting effects are pretty. The stock music is soothing. But there's nothing of value here. Play a game where someone made original textures or music in the Unreal engine. Play a game where someone implemented controls outside of the most basic FPE settings. Play a game where something happens, or you do something that sounds like it might matter. Do people even make games like that anymore?
What have we done?

I'll tell you a story.
Once, I went to my grandma's house in March- the THIRD month of the year. It was also the THIRD. I arrived at my grandma's house at 3:33. She has THREE houses on her block. I went up to the door, which had THREE chips on it, and knocked THREE times. After THREE seconds, she said: "Be right there!"- it had THREE words in it. She came up to the door and took off THREE locks on her door. She invited me into the kitchen for cookies, while all of her THREE cats ran past me, one of which had THREE spots on him. She told me to sit down next to the table, which had THREE chairs. She handed me the platter with THREE cookies on it, and said that her THREE cats took THREE of the cookies THREE times. So we sat down for THREE minutes, and talked about THREE subjects: Major companies, Games, and Numbers. After that, we sat in my grandma's living room, and watched THREE different channels. After a while, she started to get thirsty, so I generously got up from one of the THREE sofas, went into the kitchen, and opened the fridge. I spilled THREE drinks, but I got more for my grandma. When I came back into the room, she was watching a commercial for a product that said: "If you don't get it in THREE days, it's free! Only $33.33!" I sat down and started reading a magazine for children- the THIRD issue. It was on how to add. 1+1-1+1+1=3. That didn't seem appropriate for a children's book, so I went on the computer in my grandma's bedroom, and found out the company had been in buisiness for only THREE years. Now it made sense. It was time for me to leave because I was going to a party with THREE of my friends. My grandma gave me THREE seashells as a present, which I thanked her THREE times for. So then I left out the door, walked to my car, and drove away.
So, what I'm trying to say is that I had a great time at my grandma's house.

Saints Row IV feels like some sort of Matrix mod for Saints Row The Third. It's graphically the same. Even the characters are exactly the same. The last part is a bit obvious of course, since it's a sequel, but still, it would've been nice if they mixed things up. You know, different city, different characters, things like that.
Instead Volition took the easy way out. That doesn't mean Saints Row IV can't be fun, because it can be but I'm sure it will give you that 'been there, done that' feeling, too.
There are plenty of side activities to be done though. It's in no way a small game. It's big, You could play for 25 hours and you still wouldn't have finished it 100%. No, content wise this game is amazing.
It's just that the city isn't worth exploring anymore, especially since you've seen it all in the third game. But it wasn't worth exploring in the first place. There are (almost) no awesome landmarks or anything. It feels like a city but... a regular, simple one. Nothing like the cities of the Grand Theft Auto games, which are epic in scale.
Saints Row IV, for me, is enjoyable and disappointing at the same time.
However, if I had to choose one of those two terms 'disappointing' would be my first choice. Let's hope a possible sequel will give us a better, newer and more fun experience.

Pretty fun, unique, interesting, that sort of thing. The whole first-person view thing can go both ways though. It's a good thing in that it makes the game interesting, but it's terrible in the sense that it can make it difficult to judge your jumps. The game sometimes has clear indications of where to go, but other times it leaves you hanging out to dry. Since the game has such an emphasis on speed, and often times that's the difference between dying or getting to the next area, it can be frustrating if you can't think on your feet and find the correct pathways without any sort of indication. Often times you're doing so while being sprayed with gunfire, which just makes it even more difficult. Combat feels a bit sticky and frustrating, but it's achievable. The parts where combat is required are rare and most times you just focus on running away, so not a big deal. Overall, I'd say it's a good game, but it can be difficult in a number of ways. Or maybe I'm just terrible at it, who knows? Also mine was screwing up due to "physX" being turned on in the settings menu. If you have a simular issue with tons of lag, try shutting that off. It was smooth sailing after that.

Couple Warnings:
1) This review covers both Syberia games.
2) While I'm saying I don't recommend it, I'm not saying it's a bad game. Hear me out, here.
Not too long ago they had the "Syberia Bundle" on sale, so I thought I'd buy it with nothing to lose. It couldn't be that bad, if there's another sequel on the way, right?
Again, as an adventure game, it's not bad. In fact, I think it did pretty good at setting up some challenging puzzles. But it's also nothing special. In a game like this, solving a puzzle is supposed to mean advancing the plot, but this game has barely enough plot to write a single novella, even if you use 100% of content from both Syberia games.
Here's a quick TL;DR:
1) The plot is weak and nonsensical.
2) World building and character development were thrown out the window altogether. You just have to take everyone's word for it that "Kate's Changed," because I can't tell a difference.
3) The game features some glaring samples of bad level design, forcing the player to deal with issues that game devs had known were bad ideas for at least a decade before.
((((SPOILER))))
Plot of the first game can be summed up as "Young Lawyer Kate Walker goes to France to finalize paperwork on an automaton factory's takeover after the owner dies. However, the owner reveals in her will that her brother was still alive, and therefore she wants all her assets sent to him. All things considered, this should have still been the end of Kate's job, but her boss tells her not to come home until she gets that paperwork signed, so she travels to Russia hoping that just sort of maybe this brother will be there. On her way, we learn that her boss is an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and that her boyfriend is cheating on her with her best friend. All things considered, it's somewhat understandable that she chooses to run away with this brother, Hans, once she finally meets him." Sure, there's a train whose engineer is a robot who is your companion, but he refuses to lift a finger to assist in any way beyond "drive the train."
Second game, Kate's traveling with Oscar the robot train driver and Hans the mammoth-obsessed idiot whose only redeeming feature is his ability to make Automatons. Hans gets sick and nearly dies, but he gets better after killing Oscar and turning his body into a brace. In the end, you make it to the magical island of Syberia, where wooly mammoths are still alive. ((((END SPOILER))))
Considering what I know about the story so far, Syberia III is most likely going to just be "Kate goes back to civilization after completing her journey" and that's all we're going to get. And the worst part is, Kate's motivation is never clear. If these games made anything clear about her, it's that she isn't an idiot by any stretch of the imagination. Plus she was a lawyer. She knew her rights. She knew that her boss couldn't exactly fire her just because he didn't know all the facts before sending her into the field and it turns out the situation was more complicated than they expected. If she loved her job so much that she was willing to travel from France to Russia just to get one document signed, she would have known that travelling from France to Russia alone with no help was beyond her job description. Why the hell did she decide to throw away her relationships just to make her ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ boss happy?
My other major complaint about the game is that there is next to no world building or character development, although I guess I already talked about poor character development. One of the main staples of point and click adventure games is that you can click on things to learn about them, or at least what the character knows about it. This helps you understand your environment and your character, but it's something that was sorely lacking from this game. Even some of those stupid Putt Putt and Freddie Fish games from the late 90's/early 2000's for kids 6 and under (which I played when I was 6 and under) did a better job of this, and they did it for an audience with a much shorter attention span. This game was for the 16-20 audience, and failed to deliver on one of the simplest questions anyone could ask of a story: "Why should I care?" Due to the fact you're surrounded by  strange devices, the sci-fi loving part of me cared from the first cutscene, but I could never rationalize caring beyond that.
Lastly, although I've said many times that the game aspect was good, this game is the poster child for bad level design. In Syberia I, you are forced to run from one area to another multiple times, and half the areas in between bear no relevance to solving any puzzles or continuing the story. In Syberia II, they don't fix it. In fact, the only thing that got an update as far as I could tell was the layout of the train interior. That made no sense to update, though, since there would have been no time or reason for our characters to renovate it. I mean, Syberia II picks up one stop after Syberia I as far as I can tell. But that's the biggest gripe I think you can throw at any game series: This was a problem in the first game. You didn't fix it.
Last thing. You know how the bullet points here on Steam say that the game has "Rich and intriguing new characters with new, realistically detailed 3D environments?" ignoring the game's age, I can't tell a difference between the graphics from the first game and the  second game. Also, the new characters? One's a dog, the other's a thief who follows you. I will say, though, that the dog is a good boy.
I regret to say that once Syberia III costs 12.99 or less, I'll probably cave and buy it as well, but I can't see it being anything other than a quick cash grab.

Syberia II picks up where the last game left off, taking place one week after the finale of the last one. Kate Walker has abandoned her life in New York, and instead continued her journey with Hans Voralberg on the special clockwork train that is on the rails that leads to the departing location to the ever mysterious island of Syberia. An island that is said to inhabit the last surviving mammoths on Earth. Despite the fact that the island may be a myth and that no human being has seen a living mammoth for the past 10,000 years. Hans is determined to go to the island and witness the site of the mammoths that he'd dreamed of since childhood. Kate, who previously spent a lot of time hunting down and learning more about Hans, is also determined to help the kind elderly automaton builder fullfill his dream. During their travels, they encounter both kind folk and intimedating foes, as well as dangers of the wilderness that effects the journey in some ways. Meanwhile Kate's law firm had previously sent out a private eye to hunt her down because of A. She has the paper work for the merger of the automaton factory and toy company and B. Kate's family is worried sick and are demanding for her safe return. Despite all of the odds, Kate will go out and beyond to help Hans get to Syberia at all costs. This sequel is just as great as the first game, while the majority of the game is set in the wilderness, you do get to see a good number of automaton technology like in the first game. The graphics are slightly improved and the locations are just as beautiful as the first game. Originally this plot was going to be part of the first game, but it was decided that it should split into two games instead. Which was a wise choice as it would of been a really long game if it did. Anyone who played the first game must play this one as the story that was left open is wrapped up very nicely for this sequel. A strongly recommended game by Benoit Sokal.

Risk of Rain is a wonderful roguelike platformer with so very much to offer. When it was released in 2013 I had no idea how many hours I'd eventually sink into this little gem with my friends, as well as on my own. My friends and I would get together every weekend and attempt to take on the challenge of "Monsoon" difficulty. We'd get further and further into each randomly selected level each time and fail. We'd all beaten Rainstorm together and individually, and Monsoon gave us a challenge we all found to be a driving force. We'd all regroup weekend after next talking about the characters we'd unlocked and how we got them, what achievements and items we'd unlocked, and our plans for our next Monsoon run. We'd share the loot from each level, sometimes we'd call every item first come first serve, but no matter how we played we always had a good time. We'd play late into the evenings, run to the nearest 24/7 grocery store for snacks in the middle of the night, and return to do it all over again until the sun rose. This game is among many other fond memories I have of gaming growing up. At this point, it may only be three years since we started playing, but so much can happen in three years time and it has felt like Risk of Rain has always been a game I could return to with or without friends. Singleplayer is even more of a challenge and I for one am always itching to see how far I can get through Monsoon on my own. I highly recommend this game to others who are in search of a game that's challenging, quirky, unforgiving, and extremely rewarding. Going through the bestiary entries and item descriptions in the menu reminds me of how much I've put into the game and how many memories it gave me in return (not to mention the super rad item drops that come with unlocking new items and use-items). The lore is absolutely enticing and the longer you play the more you're immersed in the world, as well as with your character. Good luck, bring an umbrella.

FTL is a strategy game set in space, and what a game it is. Before you begin, you get to choose either Easy or Normal difficulty. While these don't sound relatively menacing, in a regular game these equate to Extremely Hard and Impossible difficulties. During the game, you take on the role of a captain of a spaceship and will usually fail horribly at it. But sometimes you won't. Sometimes you will get to the Last Stand (with a great deal of hope and lots of preparation), telling yourself that you will win and everything will turn out fantastically. 2 minutes later, you will admit a soul-crushing defeat and begin crying on your bed. When you stop crying, you will play this game over and over again and you will love every minute of it, because this game is absolutely brilliant. So if you have a soul, and it is due for a bit of crushing, buy this game. If you don't have a soul, buy this game anyway. You will not regret it.

Oh Shadowverse. Where do I even start on this one.
Never have I played a game that I both loved and loathed at the same exact time. I am fast approaching 900 hours on this computer, and that doesnt include phone or tablet hours. Overall I would imagine I'm close to 1000 hours of play.
Let's begin!
The Good:
-The game itself is absolutely brilliant. It combines the ease of Hearthstone with a mechanic that drastically changes the games around from moment to moment in the form of the Evolve system.
-It has the worlds easiest to use interface in this history of all games. Nothing is confusing, you can click on anything at any point to find out what it is or means, and you almost never have to wonder "how does this even work?"
-Each class is very much their own class. It's not a game of "pick a couple class staples and fill in the rest with neutrals" (though you can do that) but rather it has a lot of synergies and ways to play almost every class.
-Unbelievably generous reward system. They practically throw packs at you on a daily basis, on top of regular events and such and ANYONE can make a top tier deck probably from the very start of the game.
The Bad:
-Each new expansion release comes with one or more ridiculously broken meta-warping cards. It usually get's fixed EVENTUALLY, but it can make entire chunks of the games life miserable to play.
-Some decks are incredibly unfun to play against. I skip playing against the Rune class entirely.
-Most decks get "solved" in a day or two. In other words, experimenting and messing around with cards is usually pointless, as a highly optimized perfect-in-slot deck will exist before some people have even gotten a chance to try the new cards out.
-Aggro is king. This is a personal bias, but I strongly dislike losing a game by turn 3 or 4 if you go second versus a aggro deck. It makes most decks just feel like they can't exist.
Overall:
It's just the best card game out there, and its not even close. It's a shame it has no twitch userbase going. I didn't play for close to 1k hours because of obligation, I played because I wanted to.

After playing this game, I honestly feel the story could have easily, and maybe should have stopped with the end of Syberia 1. I'm not saying this game wasn't good, but I feel Kate's arc really developed and ultimately crescendos in the final scene of the first game and maybe that storyline was more important than the journey. She doesn't really need this game because her story was, in essence, over. The story felt less important to me because instead of acting on your main character's motivations you are doing this for Hans, who is a one dimensional character, thus making the games progression very predictable and it doesn't feel as much like an adventure as just wrapping up the subplot in the first game.
But this game was made and of course I played it, needing to know what happened next. I recommend it to fans of the first game because it adds a satisfying closure to the tales of Hans, Oscar, and the Youkol people. The cast of new character introduced in this game were not as memorable as the first, except for Youki. The 'bad guys' seemed to be shoehorned in just to get the train to stop at a couple extra location and I felt they ultimately detract from the story.
The game continues directly after the first, also featuring identical gameplay. You will read journals that outline the history of locations and using these to clue into the answer to the puzzles and slowly jog between screen after screen just to find out you need to backtrack. The backdrops were not quite as good but there are still some interesting areas.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a must for anyone. It's is both difficult, fun, and easy to get sucked in. I'd say the best reason why I like it is the fact that it's not a FPS (2011 and 2012 was nothing but shooters) and it was keeping me glued to my chair.
The good is that it's easy to understand how to play, no 2 games play the same (so it's got high replay value), and it's challenging. The ailens will use the same stradegy as you. Use cover, flank you, and take you out as quick as possible. But with every play comes interesting results. You can fight to gather resources for weapons and armor for your troops along with building your base and Earth's defences.
The cons are that at times it can be glitchy on occasions. I've seen a few that were odd but nothing bad. But while XCOM is challenging it's also unforgiving. One screw up on a battle will basically force you to restart your game. I've had to restart 6 times so far but I personally can deal with that.
If you are a XCOM fan or a tactical game fan I highly recommend XCOM: Enemy Unknown. It gets a 4.5/5 in my book. And with that, good luck Commander!

I initially backed this game on Kickstarter a few years ago after being thoroughly impressed by the proof of concept. I pretty much forgot about it until I got the email that it was on Steam, so I gave it a try and well, I'm blown away with how far it's come. It's not perfect, but it's by far the one of the most complete Kickstarter games I've seen, and out of all of the unfinished ones, it's certainly the one with the most promise.
Pros: The gameplay is very nice. It's smooth, sensible, and while the learning curve is pretty steep initially, once you come to grips with it, it makes sense. I'm a big fan of the huge inventory. Creative mode is a lot of fun, and I've barely scratched the surface. The campaign seems fun, but I'll get into that in the next section.
Cons: The campaign runs completely terribly on my machine and I have no idea why. In Creative Mode, I can crank the settings up to max with no issue and get a steady 60fps (albeit while making my GPU cry), but in the campaign, I can't get a stable framerate even with the graphics set to their lowest and the game itself in a tiny window. It just doesn't work right now.
Overall, for an Early Access title, it's in really good shape, and they're updating it frequently. I'm excited to see where things go from here.
Also, if you use the command "/exec fov <x>", you can enhance the default terrible FOV, a very handy feature.

Nephise Begins is the prequel to Nephise, and a small, encapsulated vision of Nephise's journey to become an Orb Hunter. As far as Tonguc Bodur's catalog goes, this one was probably my least favorite, and yet it still carries a lot of appeal as its own entity.
As mentioned above, this is the prequel to the game Nephise, and in Nephise Begins, we get to see how she becomes an Orb Hunter. While the significance of such is still left a mystery, it is a satisfying explanation as to how she found her way to the events of Nephise and why she has issues with excess (or addiction, if you will).
She starts out as a mushroom hunter, but as she starts to find the skulls of the dead, she is drawn into an adventure to find the origins of said doom.
7 out of 10
As with Nephise, Nephise Begins is set in a small and encapsulated, circular area that she will explore to find mushrooms and animal skulls, which are also the impetus for her finding the path to becoming an Orb Hunter.
This is exactly the same style of gameplay as Nephise and similar to other of Tonguc's entries. As such, you can expect a seamless experience with no bugs or glitching.
There is one primary puzzle much as with its predecessor, and this is easily solved, yet clever in its design and application.
All in all, solid effort here. 9.5 out of 10
The graphics in Nephise Begins is where I really see an actual decline from previous entries. Running with the same specs on each game, Nephise Begins was far less distinct and crisp as previous entries. The colors were a bit more blurred, and everything had a less vibrant feel about them (outside of the skulls and mushrooms which really popped in contrast to everything else). I don't know if this was a conscious decision so as to emphasize the mushrooms and skulls, but it just wasn't as effective in my estimation as it could have been. Some of the other stuff, like the guardian fox and the harpy were quite nice looking, and the temple was really cool. So, it is still a visually pleasing game. Just not at the level I expected it to be.
8 out of 10
The audio tracks in Nephise Begins aren't too different than in Nephise itself. The old lady narrator was the same and the orchestration was at least similar. Everything was as such both effective and pleasing.
9 out of 10
It might seem I'm a bit down on Nephise Begins but I'm really not. It's still a definite cool experience. I just wasn't AS pleased with it as with past efforts by Tonguc. This game still rates highly though.

Fairy Fencer F is a light hearted and funny "budget" JRPG with lots of charm.  You play as a reluctant hero trying to unite the powers of ancient fairy fueled weapons to save the world or at least score some free food along the way.  The combat is an absolute blast with lots of characters to build, weapons to customize and power ups to manage.  The action is fast paced and satisfying, although a bit easy at times and gets repetitive.  The presentation is the "budget" part unfortunately.  The story is told with 2D cartoony cut scenes, with fantastic voice work and some genuinely funny dialog.  However you never really get to explore the towns, country side or world you are trying to save, just the dungeons.  This lack of interaction results in a fantasy world that lacks any weight to it.  I lost interest about half way thru the experience once I grew tired of the combat and party management strong suites of the game.
If you love JRPG's, especially the combat and character development, then you will enjoy Fairy Fencer.  However the lack of interaction with the story and the out of dungeon world will be a turn off to those looking for a more polished and complete RPG experience.
