Fairy Fencer F is a turn-based, action, role-playing game loaded with charming characters. The action takes place in a world where a God and Goddess were in a fight to the death. Their terrible struggle left a fantastic assortment of powerful weapons littering the landscape. You will find not everyone who tries has the ability to wield these relics. It is only those who are worthy of them that can pull them free. Fencers wield these weapons with the assistance of the fairy that resides within the weapon. For once, you are not really saving the world. At the beginning, there really is no peril that a hero/heroine must raise to defeat. In fact, the protagonist of this game isn’t even really a hero at all.
The game is a mixture of a visual novel and an action role-playing game. The story is driven by discussions the playable characters hold as well as their interactions with the NPCs. During the discussions, a static image of the characters is on screen. To emphasize which character is doing the talking, that particular character will have an animated mouth. Emotions are conveyed through a mixture of symbols and facial expressions. If the characters are having a story based discussion, it will be fully voice acted. If it is a random conversation, it will generally be just text on the screen. This works quite well although I do prefer the voiced sections over the just text sections.
When in town you simply select between the various options and you enter into the related screen. You do not need to walk to the item shop or inn when you arrive at the town. This is handy because it saves you from having to remember where each place is and having to run back and forth between them constantly, but I still prefer to have explore-able towns. Dungeons are thankfully free to explore when you get to them. The world map is simple to navigate, it shows places you have already opened and explored. It also conveniently has your next destination(s) flagged on the map as well as where any events or sub-events may be taking place.
Dungeons are where you are going to spend most of your time (outside of dialogues between characters). You are free to roam around as you please. Monsters can be seen wandering around and you have the option to fight them or attempt to avoid them. If you choose to fight them, you can attempt to get a preemptive strike by swinging your weapon right before the battle screen is triggered. If successful, all your characters will get a chance to strike the enemy first. If you fail or if the enemy sneaks up on you, you will be the one ambushed giving the enemies the chance to strike first. Just walking into an enemy will put your characters and enemies in that standard cue to fight. The fight cue is always displayed and lets you know who will get their turn next. When you are controlling a character in combat, you have a movement circle. You can move anywhere in that circle before you take your action. Once you take your action, your turn ends and the next in cue gets to take theirs. Since each weapon type and ability has its own range and effective arcs, it makes for a nice variety when playing.
The game has a lot of customization options available to you. While you can’t change your weapon, you can reconfigure it so it changes into a different type of weapon during combat. You are given free choice of what armor and accessories you want to wear as well as your secondary fairy. To make up for the fact you can’t change your weapon, you are given weapon points after battles. These can be spent on how you want to customize the weapon and your related weapon abilities. If you prefer to do a lot of simple physical attacks, that is great. You can set yourself up that way. Do you prefer getting really high combo scores? Well you can buy new combos too. There are a ton of customizations options and luckily you are not locked into your decisions as taking one of the ability does not preclude you from taking a different one later. With enough grinding, you can max out everything for every character.
Fairies make this game more interesting. They do that in three ways.  The first is the fact that when your Tension gauge fills (fills when you do damage or takes damage, but reduces when you miss or heal yourself), you gain the ability to merge with your weapon’s fairy and become much more powerful. Another way the fairies are interesting is that you can acquire new ones as you play. While you can never swap out your main fairy (fused to your weapon) you can swap out your secondary fairy. You can customize the abilities of the secondary fairy to some degree as well. When you acquire a new one, if you equip it, it will level up and gain new abilities. You can also merge it with one of the sealed weapons found impaling the fallen God and Goddess that I mentioned earlier. By merging it, you gain new abilities for the secondary fairy. The third way they are interesting is the fact that you can stick a fairy imbued weapon into the ground to “shape the world” using the shaping abilities of the fairy. This changes up how dungeons work as well as adds extra levels to a tower in the game. By sticking the shaping weapon into the ground, you will get positive and negative effects that will change how the dungeon will play out. You may get extra experience while doing the dungeon, but you will take more damage from magical attacks. It might even change the enemies in the dungeon making it feel a little different when you go through it.
The story and characters in this game diverge a little from the standard clichés for this type of game as well. Instead of being a band of heroic figures rallying to save the world, you have a band of misfits each doing it for their own personal and selfish reasons. The protagonist of the game doesn’t even want to do it. He just pulled a sword out of the ground because someone told him it would grant him any wish he could think of. All he wanted to wish for was a nice meal. He accidentally became linked to the fairy in the sword who then forced him to go on the quest because she has amnesia and wants the other fairies to help her remember her past. Another Fencer is out for her own personal gains and is really full of herself. Another is just studying fairies… you get the idea. None of them are actually real heroes! That makes this game much more fun than the cliché, “let’s save the world from evil” shticks of other RPG games.
Overall, it’s another enjoyable Idea Factory game. If you like the story telling, humour and fan service found in their other games, such as the Hyperdimention Neptunia series, you will likely enjoy Fairy Fencer F as well. If you are looking for a fun dungeon crawler style RPG that has zany characters, by all means give Fairy Fencer F a go.

is a nice little mixture of visual novel and RPG style game mechanics and combat. You play as Fang, a guy who ends up acquiring a Fury without realising the responsabilities that come with it. Furies are swords left on the planet long ago after a battle between the Vile God and the Goddess, and each of them has a fairy inside. The fairy inside your Fury, Eryn, explains to you that the Fury is only able to use to those who are destined to fulfill the wish of its fairy. She then explains to you that she wishes you find 100 Furies in order to awake the Goddess. This is where your journey begins.
We could say that the gameplay of this game is divided into two very different genres. For me, the real meat of the game is the combat, which despite being somewhat repetitive, allows for a lot of different approaches due to the variety of abilities that you can use. Combat is turn based, and in each turn you move your character freely inside a circle and must get within range of the enemy in order to attack. If you get close to this outer circle you can attempt to escape the battle. You’ll be able to to switch between Fencers on the fly, once you have more on your party, but doing so while in combat will end your turn. As you acquire more Furies, you’ll also gain access to more fairies which you can use to increase your stats and get hold of more abilities. Not only that, but acquiring more Furies allow you to start working your way to free the Goddess, or the Vile God if you prefer, and will also enhance your fairy abilities.
The other part of the game plays pretty much like a kinetic visual novel, in which the player has no actual impact on the conversations and outcomes. That said, I find the dialogue to be rather amusing, if somewhat uninspired. If you’re looking for a deep story, great plot and memorable characters you probably won’t find that here. Still, I find the dialogue rather funny with the ocasional joke here and there, and most of the characters behave like teenagers which gives the game a less serious tone. Also, most of the main story dialogue is fully voice acted, while optional conversations are not.
You’ll be spending a lot of your time revisiting
the main city in the game. Here you can go to different places and talk with random people. You’re also able to buy and sell items, get side missions (kill & fetch quests) and acquire information about the whereabouts of the next Fury. Still, the city feels somewhat lifeless since everything happens through a menu screen. There is no depth to the places and to the different people you find there, they are pretty much there just for the sake of being there, and this made me care less about the actual game world.
There is also a world map where you can go to various different locations, such as dungeons. There you’ll battle enemies and find varied items. Inside dungeons you can move freely and see enemies wandering, and if you manage to get in close and attack them you’ll trigger an ambush and the battle will start, thus allowing to attack first. Of course, if the enemy gets the drop on you, you’ll be the one getting ambushed. This is probably where I spent most of my time, grinding in dungeons to level up my characters and fairies, doing side quests, collecting items and selling them so that I could afford potions, etc. If you’re not too fond of grinding, you might have a hard time later on with some enemies.
If you’re looking for a memorable story and unique characters you might want to steer away from this, unless you’re a hardcore fan of the Neptunia games and the likes of Idea Factory. The story might be interesting for some people until a certain point, and most of the character reactions are rather predictable. Still, if you’re looking for a solid RPG experience with a very robust turn-based combat system this might be something right up your alley. There are tons of unlockables for you to track down, and if you’re into completing side quests there are always some for you to do. Thus, revisiting old dungeons will always yield some kind of reward.

The Lego games are probably the best couch co-op games there are, and this is probably the best Lego game, so this is definitely recommended.
Lego Marvel Super Heroes is appropriate and playable for all ages and skill levels.  This is even a game that an older gamer could play co-op with a very young and inexperienced player, since the better player can kinda "carry" the weaker one by doing the tricky stuff. The bonus Deadpool levels are also a lot of fun!  Just walking through New York with different characters has a lot of charm as well.  The public walking around will crack jokes and make references to your characters with a very New York style.
There are a couple of bugs, like you can get stuck in an infinite loop or fall through the earth, requiring restarting that section, but its uncommon and not too bothersome.  The only serious bug I found was in playing with a laptop and exporting to HDMI, the game absolutely insisted to send the sound to the laptop speakers instead of through the HDMI, whatever setting I used either in game or in Windows.  I don't know if anyone else had this bug.
Anyway, I highly recommend you play this, especially if you want a fun and relaxing local co-op game!

Risk of Rain is a wonderful roguelike platformer with so very much to offer. When it was released in 2013 I had no idea how many hours I'd eventually sink into this little gem with my friends, as well as on my own. My friends and I would get together every weekend and attempt to take on the challenge of "Monsoon" difficulty. We'd get further and further into each randomly selected level each time and fail. We'd all beaten Rainstorm together and individually, and Monsoon gave us a challenge we all found to be a driving force. We'd all regroup weekend after next talking about the characters we'd unlocked and how we got them, what achievements and items we'd unlocked, and our plans for our next Monsoon run. We'd share the loot from each level, sometimes we'd call every item first come first serve, but no matter how we played we always had a good time. We'd play late into the evenings, run to the nearest 24/7 grocery store for snacks in the middle of the night, and return to do it all over again until the sun rose. This game is among many other fond memories I have of gaming growing up. At this point, it may only be three years since we started playing, but so much can happen in three years time and it has felt like Risk of Rain has always been a game I could return to with or without friends. Singleplayer is even more of a challenge and I for one am always itching to see how far I can get through Monsoon on my own. I highly recommend this game to others who are in search of a game that's challenging, quirky, unforgiving, and extremely rewarding. Going through the bestiary entries and item descriptions in the menu reminds me of how much I've put into the game and how many memories it gave me in return (not to mention the super rad item drops that come with unlocking new items and use-items). The lore is absolutely enticing and the longer you play the more you're immersed in the world, as well as with your character. Good luck, bring an umbrella.

FTL is a strategy game set in space, and what a game it is. Before you begin, you get to choose either Easy or Normal difficulty. While these don't sound relatively menacing, in a regular game these equate to Extremely Hard and Impossible difficulties. During the game, you take on the role of a captain of a spaceship and will usually fail horribly at it. But sometimes you won't. Sometimes you will get to the Last Stand (with a great deal of hope and lots of preparation), telling yourself that you will win and everything will turn out fantastically. 2 minutes later, you will admit a soul-crushing defeat and begin crying on your bed. When you stop crying, you will play this game over and over again and you will love every minute of it, because this game is absolutely brilliant. So if you have a soul, and it is due for a bit of crushing, buy this game. If you don't have a soul, buy this game anyway. You will not regret it.

Some game developers can go for years without coming up with a game design half as good as Planetoid. This game is a wonderful example of a great idea, implimented horribly. It will probably always just be that interesting game that you can play for an hour maybe, then forget about for months on end. If it was priced at $10 or $15, and the developer actually knew what he was doing, or had some help, this could be a really fun space tower defense game.
Right now, all I can say is if you enjoy tower defense games, and this looks like it could be up your alley, don't waste you money right now, but keep an eye on it. I will definitely check it out again and hopefully it will have gotten better with some updates.

Teleglitch (DMe) has been growing on me slow but strong. I wasn't entirely sold after first few hours of play. The graphics work well in the context, leaving just enough for the imagination to immerse you into the world of forsaken horrors of the bases your roam. The sound is equally top-notch. The first hoop I had to jump to properly appreciate the game was the controls. I started off on my Xbox One controller and that was a terrible mistake. In my humble opinion, Teleglitch was made for good old mouse and keys. After ditching the gamepad, immersion is the world became instantly more intuitive. The second hoop was accepting the fact of dying while pushing through the first few levels. It is only after three or four hard won teleports that the adrenaline really kicks in since there is no way to save and hence protect your investment in time. Most of the time, the game keeps your supplies to the bare minimum. Facing a swarming horde of monsters with your final clip and a pack of explosives really makes every shot count. Nor does being armed to the teeth - as rare as that is - make you invincible. There have been plenty of times when I thought I had the upper hand with a bunch of medkits, several weapons and a sackful of ammo just to be ambushed by a throng of zombies and killed in a heartbeat. As frustrating as this sounds, it is memories like this that really drive your heart rate as you progress further and further towards that elusive save point beyond the first five teleports. Whoever played the original Doom on hardest difficulty knows that bloodrush well. I therefore find the criticism of random deaths misplaced. As frustrating as it may be, it is an absolutely fundamental element in immersing one into the gameworld and pumping that adrenaline. An experience very different from - and ultimately more rewarding - than hitting F5 to quicksave around every corner. Progressively generated levels ensure that the experience never gets monotonous. I recently realized with some amazement that two of the most-played titles in my library - Europa Universalis IV and Teleglitch - were both fathered by Paradox Interactive. Given how different these two games are, I can only conclude that these guys know their gaming inside and out! My highest recommendation to anyone looking for a heart pounding claustrophobic challenge!
TIP: Remember to combine the items in your stock to make new stuff! Took me a while to figure this out... Also, shotguns can finish a secret wall if you're out of explosives or simply get stuck!

I was really looking forward to this game and... oh my god I was not disappointed!
I'll begin with a short prologue. Many game developers nowadays don't make good quality games anymore, instead they regurgitate some sort of a dodgy half-baked product to try and get as much money from the public as possible. Rarely, however, we get a chance to play a quality game truly worth of our attention and this one fits perfectly into this recently impoverished category.
And now about the game. To start off this is a good quality polished product with only some very minor issues/bugs. The game performs well in terms of stability and only has several minor bugs, however I tend to think that it could have been optimised slightly better. Don't get me wrong, it's a beatiful game but you need quite a powerful machine to be able to enjoy it on full graphics. The gameplay is fun and highly immersive but can seem a bit dull at first. Although once you level up your character and get new abilities the game becomes extremely fun! There are so many ways you can kill zombies. To name a few: you can smash them, burn them, slice them up, impale them, blow them to pieces and much more. I won't say much about the graphics except that he game looks great and visually appealing. The storyline is not that great and is not original at all. From what I heard it's a bit similar to far cry series. You can pass the main story fairly quickly but I would strongly reccomend that you explore the city and do side quests because that is where the game shines. Side quests are quite fun and introduce to many interesting/weird characters that got trapped with you inside the city. Some of the quests are quite touching and let you feel the full scale of madness that is consuming the city. The multiplayer experience is what makes this game truely special. You can grab your friends and do quests, go to parts of the city that you don't dare exploring alone or to try and survive the night without being eaten by the hunters (other players). You will be terrified and feel like a prey when facing those nasty creatures, especially in early stages of the game.
Overall this is a fun game which will probably keep you hooked for quite some time. I would definitely recommend it to anyone who likes killing zombies and having fun in multiplayer.

Overall, I loved the game, from its soundtrack, to the turnbased combat, to the competent writing.  The controls were fluid and intuitive. Improving your character on the fly was great, too.
Now for the negatives:
1) Way too short.  I clocked it 25 hours playing it, but that's a misnomer, as I had the game running for several hours while I was away a few times.  If someone sits down and plays it seriously, they can blow through it in day or two.
2) Certain classes are useless.   I played the game as a Decker, and I thought I would be able to go into the Matrix and score some creds on the side. NOPE.  I expected an open world, what I got was an encapsulated snow globe.  Seriously, don't bother playing as a Decker, as there will be characters way more competent than you, and you will only use decking a handful of times.  Also, don't be an Adept, as you will be literally be bringing swords to a gunfight, which there are many.
3) Linear.  The game is far from open world.  It's "Go to Point A.  Talk to/Perform Action B.  Leave Board to go to next area."  I think the lack of control as to where to go and the dearth of side quests soured me a bit on this game.
In closing, it's fun but incredibly short.

Nephise Begins is the prequel to a game called, oddly enough, Nephise (that's pronounced "Neh-fee-see", by the way, and is the name of the young female protagonist in both games). For those who haven't yet played the original, I wouldn't worry: they're very similar and there's little to no plot or character to speak of, so it's much of a muchness which order you play them in.
That said, I must confess to having enjoyed this one slightly more, perhaps because the first one felt a bit circular in its mapping - you basically just walk around a circular path, as well as exploring a small area in the middle - while the mapping in this one is a bit more expansive and requires a mite more exploration to find all its nooks and crannies. Sure, the puzzles are slightly fewer and even easier than those in the first installment, but if you're buying games like this for the puzzles, you really do need to reassess your purchasing habits.
It's short (under an hour, with all Achievements), beautiful to look at, has lovely music, and is genuinely relaxing provided you're in the right mindset. And, well, whad'ya know...it's also cheap as chips. Oh, and in spite of not being a "horror" game per se, it does have a very creepy bit right at the end (which I won't spoil with further details)!
When all is said and done, it's little more than a brief indulgence for your sense of wonder, but isn't that something worth indulging from time to time? Not every game needs to be as long as Skyrim, as hard as Dark Souls, or as "deep" as Dear Esther. If you're the kind of person who, like myself, desires something short and soothing upon occasion, you won't find much to complain about here. And if you're still set on being stingy about the price, i'm sure you'll find it on sale often enough. Done deal.
Verdict: 7/10.

Just as its name suggests, Nephise Begins is a prequel to Nephise. As of this writing, both are Tonguç Bodur latest creations and they are the developer’s attempt towards a new direction. Obviously, this separates the Nephise series from the Drizzleplath one, yet even if I didn’t know who developed these last few titles, just by looking at them for a few minutes, I would have pointed out towards Tonguç. He really knows how to pick these abstract ideas and turn them into something beautiful. Still, dreams can quickly turn to nightmares and the abstract subgenre in the case of walking simulators, always features a double-sided coin.
The titular character is a young female which doesn’t share any of her thoughts or give voice to her concerns. Players shall have to find details from her life, through the help of a female narrator which speaks on Nephise’s behalf. The journey begins in the middle of a relatively vast forest and the main objective is to get past the Forest Guardian. A giant fox, because we needed to be reminded of the abstract nature of this title. Nephise shall have to find the four animal skulls scattered across the woodland and also pick up ten red mushrooms, as a secondary objective which doesn’t alter the storyline in any manner at all. Pretty straightforward and there aren’t many hidden meanings or symbols behind this quest and journey.
Powered by Unreal Engine 4, Nephise Begins forced me run it in 2K, since stability at 4K resolution would result in less than 30 frames per second. Screenshots look great, regardless. It may be a brief forest exploration, yet I still found enough screenshot opportunities and I’m certain that part of this game’s charm comes from relaxing and taking in the sights. There are no situations which might endanger you, so why hurry? It goes without saying, that you’ll be able to accomplish your objectives if you are patient enough and keep your eyes peeled.

Repetitve tune or not, I enjoyed the soundtrack and the narrator was a pleasant touch as well, even if I would have preferred to hear the heroine herself and her own perspective into the trip and mysterious encounters. No reason to complain, though. It’s a walking simulator, not an audiobook.
I think I already cleared the key aspects of the gameplay in the Story section above. Don’t expect me to spoil even the few elements of the game I haven’t discussed yet. It is indeed rather short, you should be able to see it though in less than two hours, perhaps just one if you don’t care about the Achievements for finding the mushrooms and hidden N symbol. But if you really lack the patience for peaceful exploration, than I really don’t think that this might be the genre you’d enjoy playing anyways.
There’s no action, you don’t fight anything, not even for your survival. Had my fair share of “survival in the woods” indie games and I’m glad Nephise Begins isn’t instructing me to collect twigs for a campfire, only to get mauled to death by a wolf pack. You just explore the surroundings, at your own pace and on a fairly large map. Visual cues in the form of small floating orbs, shall make the discovery of the mushrooms or skulls, much easier than it might seem at first glance. There are some structures to visit as well, but for the majority of the gameplay, you’ll be heading outdoors.
The shortest of the Bondur creations to date, Nephise Begins still packs the beauty and symbolism worthy for any self-respecting walking simulator. It certainly won’t bother fans of the genre and perhaps even new players might find the brief gameplay, to be an excellent introduction to more complex, future forays into this particular type of video games which have no expectations from their playerbase other than to relax while taking a hike across a peaceful environment. Rest assured, you get your money’s worth from this title.

She told me to sit down next to the table, which had THREE chairs. She handed me the platter with THREE cookies on it, and said that her THREE cats took THREE of the cookies THREE times. So we sat down for THREE minutes, and talked about THREE subjects: Major companies, Games, and Numbers. After that, we sat in my grandma's living room, and watched THREE different channels. After a while, she started to get thirsty, so I generously got up from one of the THREE sofas, went into the kitchen, and opened the fridge. I spilled THREE drinks, but I got more for my grandma. Overall, this is the most impressive strategy/turn-based, board-game-esque programs I have ever experienced. The level of immersion is wonderful; you can set about to win via military, scientific, cultural, and diplomatic means, or by having the highest score in a time-based playthrough. One of the greatest accolades I can attribute to this program is the degree of learning, historical or otherwise, which playing as the various civilizations and through the included scenarios bestows. As Kamehamaha, you can build moai and field maori warriors. As William of Orange, you can build polders and control the seas with sea beggars. You can ally with city-states, build infrastructure, and wage war on all terrain types. Although there are a few historically inaccurate aspects and scenarios like Wonders of the Ancient World are not well-made, much of the experience is about making your own story and challenging yourself to prevail in situations with the limitations you are dealt. And best of all, there is a grandiose amount of high quality modding available for this program. In the 5 or so years I've had it, I am yet to utilize the multiplayer aspect, but I have heard that it needs significant improvement. Also, this program is processor-intensive and is a good gauge of your computer's max capabilities. In any case, the developers of Civilization 5 have created an enduring and artful product for the ages. I consider Civ 5 to be one of the best video-games, up there with Sim City 4 Deluxe. Some changes/additions I would like to see with respect to content woud be a more realistic set of ramifications resulting from ideology choice, exemption from the world congress if desired (maybe isolationism as a social policy?), as well as the option to privatize various aspects of the player's civilization to the point of market anarchism. There is a great deal of potential for future installments when you consider the prospects of sport, seasteading, banking, subterranean & undersea exploration and even natural disasters. Thanks and goodnight!

I never played the old XCOM games; but I've spend many hours on various types of strategy games (RTS, TBS, 4X), and this is one of the better ones that I've played.
Pros: Good, solid story, logical progression, and decent side missions available as DLC.  Resource management is minimal, but that is not a drawback in this type of game; and it works well with the theme.  Enemies scale well, and have an interesting range of abilities that keep you on your toes.  Combat is intuitive and highly tactical, and requires a wide range of weapons and tactics to suvive; and there is often more than one way to beat a mission.  Advancement and tech trees are pretty standard, but well implemented; and there are few useless items/paths in the game.  Plays well on multiple playthroughs as well, thanks to a good range of optional challenges.  The visuals are excellent for a strategy game; and one of its strongest points.  The mission maps in particular are excellently designed; much better than is usual for this type of game.  Voice acting is good, and not too monotonous.
Cons: The maps again.  While the art is excellent, the number of maps is very limited, and you'll wind up playing the same ones over and over a lot.  The game would have benefitted greatly from procedurally-generated maps.  Mission types are also very limited -- elimination, find and deactivate, rescue, and escort.  And the playstyle for all mission types is nearly identical.  A greater variation in mission type would have also been an improvement.  The controls are also sub-optimal.  This is a port of a console game, and it shows.  Most of the time the controls are easy enough to use; but are overly simplified and lack the sort of power and flexibility standard for PC games.  When it comes to free-aiming grenades and missiles, however, the controls become clumsy and difficult; and can make those weapon types unreasonably difficult to use.
Overall, a solid but not earth-shattering example of the genre.  Additionally, there are some references, overt and subtle, to the original XCOM games that fans of the original should appreciate.

Crimson Room: Decade is a 3d first-person take on the popular flash game series that served as the inspiration for very many “escape the room” themed games. Locked in a red room, you must search every nook and cranny for items or interactive elements to aid in solving puzzles and eventually find your way out of the room. This particular installment takes place almost entirely in one location but manages to stay interesting due to a few perspective-based mechanics and an underlying plot delivered to the player via written messages scattered around the room.
Having a bit of a background in room-escape games, I managed to solve this game in around 2 hours only stumbling on a bit of a pixel-hunt (or 3d equivalent) in the very beginning as the points of interest don’t always seem to “snap” the cursor over them. Given the overall shortness of the game, I would recommend waiting for it to go on sale for 50% off or less (I got it for $4) so you don’t end up feeling cheated if you happen to blow through it. Other than the short length though, it’s faithful to the series and has a decent production value.

Saints Row IV is a great game in it's own right. A game that I am grateful to see having not fallen out due to THQ's closure.  While the game does ramp up the silly and grant a massive amount of freedom that it's predecessors did, it all comes at a cost.
Overall the main arc of this story is about revenge, much like Saints Row: The Third, and while I myself am a fan of alien invasions, the aliens took a very familiar, very cliche (to the point of the game itself pointing it out and having a laugh) evil alien overlord trying to do... something to Earth that just doesn't make sense in the long run.
Visually the game is almost indistinguishable from Saints Row: The Third, with only an aesthetic change to help push the game towards a more vibrant arena, which can cause a bit of an eyesore at times. The field of view and camera angles are still a bit problematic with a right-only over-the-sholder view and an obscenely tight angle in certain portions of the game that make it hard to be able to enjoy. Motion sickness is a distinct possibility here, even for those who didn't have issues in Saints Row: The Third.
With having to manage specal abilities on top of weapon changes, controls seem to falter some on the PC. Weapons being selected via mousewheel or the number keys are a given, but special abilities were chosen primarily with the F1 through F4 keys with subsets of those special abilities activated by double-tapping them. This was extremely finicky to deal with and the UI didn't lend itself well to PC play, meaning it was too easy to forget which ability you had active at any given time.  There are still issues with previous PC-Port like issues such as aim assist always being on and no option to truly disable the HUD.
With everything said and done, the game itself is pretty easy to beat even on it's Hardcore difficulty, and doesn't exactly add much to replay value. Since the side missions are essentially just minigames in themselves with no major story impact, I found myself getting quite tired of them about a third of the way through the game, feeling like it was nothing but a chore to get what I wanted.
That said, there are some truly impressive "wow" moments that really give you the feeling that you are playing as a badass and there's not a damn thing anyone can do about it. The game is pretty good, fun with a friend, just like the previous Saint's Row.

I bet that when the Disney executives were playing Lego Batman 2 they got cold feet and immediately rang up Travellers Tales to have them make something just like that, but with Marvel characters. Turned out pretty good.
Lego Marvel Superheroes is exactly like Lego Batman 2 except that it uses the Marvel Universe instead of DC. Controls are the same, gameplay is identical and everything revolves around golden bricks and character coins. New in the game is the Megafigure, a considerably larger minifigure that gives shape to characters like Hulk and The Thing.
Like Lego Batman 2 (you’re going to hear this a lot) the story stays true to the comics and puts a set of heroes into a unique adventure. Loki is up to no good and has recruited a number of villains to his cause. You controls a host of iconic heroes who need to stop his dastardly plans, whatever they may be.
Being a newly written story it combines certain heroes in ways you don’t often see them ; mostly due to licensing issues. The detachement from the current marvel cinematic universe allows the combination of Xmen, Fantastic Four, Spiderman and Avengers with no problem at all. The character pool is massive as usual with many characters becoming much sought after very fast to help clear content effectively.
The voicework is delivered by the current cartoon casts and overtime by Steve Blum and Nolan North. In fact, the latter is so omnipresent that he is more of a bother than an actual improvement. While it all fleshes out into a cohesive package that will keep you busy for hours on end, it’s not all perfect. Technically, this game is one of the least refined Lego games yet, with shoddy controls, badly executed character missions and a crash here and there.
When all is said and done, this is still the best Marvel Game you can get on Steam right now, especially for younger players. Fans however will also find lots to do and enjoy the many references and Easter eggs.

This game is not terrible -- but it has enough flaws that unfortunately do not allow me to recommend it in good conscience.
is an escape the room puzzle game with an unsettling mood. The puzzles themselves are the primary source of trouble. There are two primary ways to approach puzzle design in video games. You either create puzzles that organically come to from the games story and purpose, or, you create puzzles that might not be directly related to the game's thematic but serve as a level obstacle that rewards the player in some way, adds an element of analytical thiking to the level or extends the overall runtime of your game. Moreover, a key factor in puzzle design is the delicate balance between difficulty and purpose. You might design a unique puzzle that beautifully relates to the story
serves to progress it forward, but, for instance, if the solution is not intuitive (or deductive) enough, or the gamplay is repetitive and boring, or the intended time spent on it is too long, then you might take the player out of the game and ruin the overall feel of your level.
, unfortunately, does exactly that. The puzzles are challenging, sure, but not only do they feel that they were simply implanted in the game with no clear context, or purpose, but the solutions sometimes do not seem logical and the time spent on each one does not seem satisfying relative to the price of the game and the ending. This brings me to my other two supplemental criticism for this game: price and writing. For the frist, it's quite simple. I believe this game is too expensive for both the content it provides and the time spent playing it. For the latter comment, it is a bit more complicated.
The writing, in of itself, is not terrible -- but the manner by which its presented is not effective. The story is inherently convoluted, and the method by which the player figures it out does not help. You learn about your situation and why you're stuck in crimson red room by finding anachronistic pages of a journal someone else wrote. Moreover, the text is small, filled with out-of-context quotes and motif and devoid of fleshed out characters. All of this makes it hard for the player to care, particularly after solving seemingly random challenging puzzles, about the story or the characters. The ending, for example, is incredibly surrealistic, and instead of reading as a thematic twist, it just seems unnecesary and ineffective.

With games like these, sometimes I wish there was a "Mid-way" other than "Recommended" and "Not Recommended".
Let me tell you why.
Personally, I think that this game is gonna be mostly enjoyed by old-time fans of the original series (like me).
The game is the Escape from the Room type, but this time with a first-person perspective instead of simple point and click.
The idea works rather well and the creepy atmosphere without cheap jumpscares really makes it worth. The puzzles can be quite challenging but some of these might need to think REALLY outside the box, for example it's just by accident that I discovered that
.
However, the new mechanics really made the experience refreshing for me and made me really like the few hours I had with it. The ending is... err... no, not gonna say that. But I'm pretty sure you're gonna exclaim at least a "... WHAT?!".
But now... it's time for the cons.
The game is REALLY short. In two or three hours you'll probably finish it (even less if you played the demo first) and the only thing that MIGHT make you continue are the achievements... but most of them are extremely simple to get, except one, maybe. Once you get everything and finish the game once... well, you won't be able to play the game anymore because by now you'll know the solution and everything will become extremely easy. You'll probably play it again only if you want to live again the experience (that's why I finished Entwined Story Mode on PS3 multiple times, for example).
OR... you can call a friend at home, make them play and watch them struggling trying to find the solution while you look at them smiling evily because you know.
I kinda wished for more content, like Crimson Room Reverse on PSP, but... eh, it's still pretty nice. I'm hoping for the realease of "Viridian Room Decade", "Blue Chamber Decade" and "White Chamber Decade".
Can I recommend this to everyone, however? Nnnnnot really, not full price at least. Maybe wait for a price drop and remember that it's gonna be a short but tense experience.
Oh a final note, which I think is mostly subjective: you may get motion sickness after a while, probably due to how the area is small.

This game is good, hard and fun. The gunplay is very good, the graphics are strong and create an eerie feeling (be warned, big chunky squares, but expressive none the less) . The story is a little like Doom, you are a scientist in a research lab overrun by mutants and killer robots, and have to fight your way out.
The levels are procedual, so even if some rooms are always the same, you have a different level to explore in every run.
Ammo and items are scarce, so scavenging and resource management are key factors.
The DLC adds some nice starting weapons, but you can enjoy the game with out it.
Now that it isn't a buggy mess, I really enjoyed this game.  I got it on sale, and i recommend it.

Note: I never played the original. I rate this one as a lean to the recommend side. More so if your the type that is a big fan of "Escape from the Room " games. If so , then this is for you.  There are only a couple of points of more than mild frustration where you may want to leave for an hour or a day and then return with a fresh look on things.
Solving the puzzles is mildly rewarding. They are on the clever side but not analytical like chess games or solving a code. My biggest complaint is that on some puzzles, once solved, the resultant activity that automatically occurs has no logical bearing to the solution. For example, why would playing a record on a record player cause the door to the room to explode open? Why would smacking a light bulb cause it to thunder and lightning outside?  Why would anyone want to put a postcard in a microwave oven and then why would putting a post card in a microwave oven cause the postcard to turn into a toy boat? Minor things like that. It's a world where logic, even the shaky logic of the gaming world, does not apply.
Note: You can reach the end of the game without reading all the hidden letters.
The hardest puzzle is the safe combination lock. Finding the combination is not intuitive and I believe that each player of this game will have a different combination. I'm not 100% sure on this , so anyone chime in if you know.

Shadowrun Returns is Harebrained Schemes first Shadowrun game, while it misses the mark for what it was trying to do in a few places, it is still a very good game and I recommend it to anyone who likes to play tactical turn based games or likes the Shadowrun world.
Set in the future where magic has returned, along with the rise of metahumans (humans changed by magic into sub races) governments have fallen and now the world is ruled by mega corps, corporations who own everything (including their workers) and constantly vie for more power. You play a shadow runner, someone who is a disposable asset to the mega corps, but who is willing to run in the shadows against other corps for prestige and money.
It has some great extras from the original Super Nintendo and Sega versions, with old characters joining your crew as you try and avenge a friend’s death (and I don’t know why how Jake survived in the Super Nintendo game when he is so crap in this one, though I think they nailed his personality). Jake is an example of how to not build a character with options that oppose each other. The plot contains enough twists and turns to keep you involved, but there aren’t many options to sway the outcome. You get a few more choices for your companions, but again it’s limited.
The game is pretty straight forward with doing a mission, filling in back story for your companions, upgrading your equipment and then back into the fray again. Customising your character is easy and straight forward, with missions allowing you to pick who you want (there are a few instances of forced companions).  The missions themselves give you enough room to mess around in (hack your way in, talk your way past a guard with the right etiquette, or go in guns blazing (which is always a good option).
The biggest gripes I have are with some of the upgrades, most of the Etiquettes options aren’t really needed (they expand back story) in most places. I thought it was a missed opportunity, something they have fixed in the subsequent sequels. There aren’t many other checks in the game as well (pass tests based on character stats), again this is something that is fixed in the sequels. Your companions fulfil their roles nicely, however by the end of the game I couldn’t say I was invested in them like I was with Dragonfall and Hong Kong.
Once you have finished Dead Man’s Switch (the main scenario available) you can download others that the community have created.

I didn't know crap about the setting before playing this, so at least I got some level of enjoynment from being introduced to it. The premise of the story is neat as well, seemingly framing it as a contained and slow-paced murder mystery.
That is not the case, of course, and the game has the audacity to be cheeky about it. The plot is completely unremarkable, the narrative feels borderline impersonal and the flavor text is
dully presented.
Best stuff writing-wise was happening at the Seamstress Union and the last section of the game. The player desperatedly needed at least one more visit to the hub and the place itself some more eventful, varied things happening inside. By "last section" I really just mean the introduction of potentially interesting and messy (at least one of 'em not original) characters + a fine ending. At these sections it seemed like the writers suddenly woke up and started caring about their work. Mind this is still run-of-the-mill writing I'm talking about.
The bad stuff was happening during the runs. It's concerning how basically the biggest part of the game felt like filler (even the plot-moving parts!) for the majority of the time. The linearity didn't help of course. Your runner is basically incapable of expressing any views or emotions besides the absolute minimum and their actions have no impact on the story. So nothing of
personal significance can really happen. Actually, the protag's barebones characterization reminds me of Neverwinter Nights.
Characters were just bundles of traits vaguely connected together. Drama felt inorganic because of that (especially the central family conflict). The only permanent party member had their arc finished the moment you were able to hire them for missions. At least they spoke a couple of lines from time to time.

When I played HL2 for the first time, I wasn't sure how I felt about it. I wanted to love it, praise it, say that it is exactly as good if not better than the first Half-Life. But, HL2 just didn't have the same effect on me like Half-Life. I was almost disappointed, but HL2 was still a very playable, enjoyable, solid FPS, that my teen self forgave it for not being like it's predecessor.
However, I've found myself to appreciate Half-Life 2 more and more after each year. It simply doesn't get dull, boring, or bad. You can spend hours and hours playing it, always finding new details and nuances. It's all in the design. I could write for hours why is it possible that thousands of players are still playing the same maps in Counter-Strike or Left 4 Dead 2 after years of their release. Half-Life 2 is the same breed: perfectly balanced and paced FPS game that offers entertainment for countless of hours. You just need more than one playthrough to reveal all of HL2's details and nuances. HL2 has a high replay value, which might manifest itself as you wanting to experience all of it's goodness after a year or two since the previous playthrough.
What also makes me appreciate HL2 more after each year, is the simple fact that all of the FPS games released after HL2, frankly, are not that good. Sure I have enjoyed a lot of FPS games after HL2, but none of them can rise to the level of HL2. I am still dumbfounded how immersive HL2 is compared to any other FPS game in the market. For example, the characters in HL2 feel alive, their facial animations and lip sync are yet to be beaten. You can compare this to any other FPS game in the market and try to challenge my opinion. Half-Life 2 was ahead of it's time, and after each passing year that fails to represent a better game just underlines it more.
This is simply unmissable game for the fans of FPS genre. But because it's such a good game, it can and it should be recommended to anyone who likes to play games. Imagine it to be like the Godfather; no matter what's your taste in movies, you should see it.

[DISCLAIMER: This was the first Civ I got to play for more than a few hours. So I'll review the game as it is per se, and not as the fifth installment of the series, since I don't have enough knowledge to compare it to previous iterations.]
Short version: Cool game to chill and relax with friends, unstable online and a few bugs might make it a bit frustrating. DLCs are mandatory to have the best experience though.
Long version: As I said, this is the first Civ I played. And I must admit I got into it pretty fast. It's not that hard to learn, even though the UI might not be that clear. You get to play your favourite historical leader, and see your civilization rise and fall. Simple to learn, with many civilizations each having special abilities/troops to increase the depth and variety, the game is really newbs-friendly and easy to get into. The combat is simple, it's easy to have an estimation of wether you're going to win a fight or not, the informations you get allow you to pick the fights you want to take. The visual style is pretty generic, but it's not bad either, and for each civilization you get a different song playing as background theme. So there go the good points.
Now the cons. The tech tree doesn't always seem to make sense, not all Civs are balanced, there are still gamebreaking bugs ("PICK A CONSTRUCTION" button not going away, which makes it impossible to skip turn, visual tearing that makes it either very ugly or impossible to play...), the loading screens take forever to actually load, and the online is very, VERY unstable. I didn't actually finish a multiplayer game without a problem at some moment. Plus, even though there are a few different victories, the most rewarding one always seem to be the way of the warrior. Science victory is possible though, as well as the diplomatic one, but as soon as one player decides to go on his destruction spree, you just can't get any of these. Not even mentionning the cultural victory since it is basically impossible as long as there's at least one civ that doesn't want you close. It feels quite unbalanced, and only the science and war endings are reached most of the time.
So yeah. Easy to pick up, enough depth to stick around, definitely funnier with friends (Go play Venice and become the richest motherf*cker around, then pay the leaders to fight each other, that's guaranteed entertainment), but beware, it is STILL filled with bugs that might get you to grind your teeth and mechanics that might not always make sense. Hopefully the next game will fix these issues as well as the civs balance.

Saints Row IV is a great game in it's own right. A game that I am grateful to see having not fallen out due to THQ's closure.  While the game does ramp up the silly and grant a massive amount of freedom that it's predecessors did, it all comes at a cost.
Overall the main arc of this story is about revenge, much like Saints Row: The Third, and while I myself am a fan of alien invasions, the aliens took a very familiar, very cliche (to the point of the game itself pointing it out and having a laugh) evil alien overlord trying to do... something to Earth that just doesn't make sense in the long run.
Visually the game is almost indistinguishable from Saints Row: The Third, with only an aesthetic change to help push the game towards a more vibrant arena, which can cause a bit of an eyesore at times. The field of view and camera angles are still a bit problematic with a right-only over-the-sholder view and an obscenely tight angle in certain portions of the game that make it hard to be able to enjoy. Motion sickness is a distinct possibility here, even for those who didn't have issues in Saints Row: The Third.
With having to manage specal abilities on top of weapon changes, controls seem to falter some on the PC. Weapons being selected via mousewheel or the number keys are a given, but special abilities were chosen primarily with the F1 through F4 keys with subsets of those special abilities activated by double-tapping them. This was extremely finicky to deal with and the UI didn't lend itself well to PC play, meaning it was too easy to forget which ability you had active at any given time.  There are still issues with previous PC-Port like issues such as aim assist always being on and no option to truly disable the HUD.
With everything said and done, the game itself is pretty easy to beat even on it's Hardcore difficulty, and doesn't exactly add much to replay value. Since the side missions are essentially just minigames in themselves with no major story impact, I found myself getting quite tired of them about a third of the way through the game, feeling like it was nothing but a chore to get what I wanted.
That said, there are some truly impressive "wow" moments that really give you the feeling that you are playing as a badass and there's not a damn thing anyone can do about it. The game is pretty good, fun with a friend, just like the previous Saint's Row.

I love escape games (I work at a live escape room venue) and I loved the Crimson Room original, so when I saw they had made a new, beefed up adaptation I had to have it. The nostalgia factor is high, and they play that card in the best possible way--rewarding you for remembering certain item locations and holding on to just enough of the original images to validate the returning player, while still adding new mechanics, perspectives, and atmosphere to make a completely new game.
The puzzles were medium to dificult. Some of them seemed a bit arbitrary, but par for the genre. A few times I consulted the guide to find that I had been using the right item(s) but hadn't clicked in *exactly* the right spot to activate the next step, which was annoying. Despite having multiple 'levels' (or phases) the game didn't seem to increase in difficulty or change dynamically as it progressed, which is my major complaint against it. The narrative 'plot' was a little stupid to me ('OH NOES COMMUNISM' is overdone and dated, imo) and felt tacked on. It would have been exactly the same game without the documents/letters that dictate a plot to the player.
Overall: a fun, short game that will please returning fans. Probably doesn't hold up as well if you don't have nostalgia for the old game.

So, first of all, what kind of game is Teleglitch? It is a [relatively] random generated ,,dungeon"-crawler Topdown-shooter with a perma-death mechanic, great crafting, micromanagement, many enemies and a striking [horror-kind of] atmosphere, made by some cool sounds and your limited vision set in an abandoned sience-fiction apocalyptic scenario.
The story/setting: Something went wrong in a research station on a planet in outer space. They wont respond, so you and your team were sent to find out what is going on. Turns out, everyone turned into mutants and all the androids and robots are infected with some kind of virus. You managed to lock yourself into a room, but your supplies are limited and you can´t contact anyone from your current location. So, the only way to get out of this hellhole, obviously, is to search the whole station for a way to communicate with someone to get you out of there.
The gameplay: You basically try to gather supplies, craft new useful stuff and shoot everything in your way. You have a variety of cool weapons and ineresting tools. Micromanagment is also a big deal in this game, as you can´t drag everything you have into the next level and have to decide if you will leave weapons, health-kits, tools or stuff to craft witch maybe be important later on. But *What I like most about the game* is the sense of progression! After every level I finished I thought that, no matter how hard I would try, I wouldn´t be able to make it to the next level because I used all I had and only just made it to where I was. But then I would try it again and get much further. Also, getting to the new location, getting/craftin the new weapons and tools and seeing and defeating the new enemies adds much more to that sense of prgression.
One last thing: Look at one of the screenshots, just to be sure you can handle the graphics ;] I find them pretty cool.
Also, your skill in gaming should be atleast average, maybe better as this game isn´t easy. I would also recommend to bring some patience/ passion. Also, don´t use the music.

As with the original Crimson Room from 12 years ago, this one kept me stumped for a little too long.
Crimson Room: Decade is a remake of the original Crimson Room game by TAKAGISM. Other than the name, the room and a couple of items and references, everything else is new. Instead of point'n'click, now you actually walk around the tiny room and look for clues and items to help you escape and uncover the secrets of La Crimson, the ship that the main character's grandfather spent his last days in.
Unlike the original, where sometimes you had to click on random places to get what you needed (I'm looking at you, you
battery), most of CR: D is logical (except for some bits after a
twist).
Throughout the game, you can find diary papers that show pieces of the history of the protagonist's grandfather that you can put together to have an insight of the true purpose of the room. And if you played the original back in 2004, it'll also take you on a trip down memory lane. In my case, it took me back to my childhood, when I was a 9 years-old boy learning how to use the internet.
The game is great, it's not so hard, and if you can't logically do something, you can always click on everything like in other point'n'click games. Or, like on the good old times,
to solve the mystery.
There's a bit of nonsense to it, specially at the end, and some of the puzzles rely on it as well. But hey, the original one had a movie of a man dancing pointing you to a safe hidden behind a fake panel on a wall, so...
Other than that, the game is very good. If you're already acquainted to Crimson Room or other Escape the Room games, give this one a try, you won't regret it. And if you've never played, then this is a good one to start with.

A real gem of a game. Feels like a mix of Dead Space, Loaded from ps1, Aliens, crossed with the Item collection of Symphony of the night; tons of item play. The game lacks music, but it's fixed easy by playing StarCraft 1 music on your own.
The game throws curve balls at you, and also lets you choose which path you take when going in teleporters, so if you've never played before, it gives you a feeling of choice, and facing the unknown.
You never know what you'll face so it requires thinking, and good choice making.
You can craft things like experemental drugs that make you faster, altar guns into things like full atuo pistols, and also craft things like enemey detectors.
But you always need to question... which choice is right for now, and what happens if I'm mobbed.
The game starts you out sort of slow, and if you don't watch it, you could get a false sense of security, enter a room, and get mobbed so bad you'll be in a corner dead in seconds.
You'll think you're rolling like an ace, then BAM!! wrong place wrong time.
There's also a story element that's text based, it's really well done, and mixes modern symbolism; like mentions of people arguing over the best robot types for days on online fourms x,D.
And there's the desire to know what the items do; the more you discover the more is added to the data base in menu, and the world at large in game can be uuncovered slowly by using computer terminals in game; stuffs really interesting if you're a reader.
There's allot of info in game you can discover that paints a picture of the world and story, and it really does a good job of it; it's never drawn out too much.
If you dig mystery, survival, light crafting, and you have stones of brass, get this game.
It really is fun, but it pulls no punches, it's a thinking man's game.
Craft nail bombs, make stims, or use the explosive to try and get into a secret area? The game will make you question each move you make.
Don't give it your all, or don't think hard, and you'll end up dead.
Really well done top down survival shooter with a realisitc pace; slow to frantic getting jumpped situations, for those with the stones and mind to brave it.

Very short, (I beat the storyline in 5 hours) but very fun.  Picked it up for $5 on sale and it was absolutely worth it.
The movement is amazing.  With about half a dozen techniques to use, you can approach most of the game from a variety of (literal) angles.  There's also a time trial mode to really test yourself.
What little combat there is is intentionally clunky as you're a "runner" not a "fighter."  But if you master the movement, you can do some amazing combat techniques too.  I, however, settled on repeatedly doing a running slide and kicking every single opponent in the junk over and over.  Crude, yet effective.
The platforming never felt "cheap" like in a lot of platformers, where you need nearly pixel-perfect precision.  In this game, if you're having trouble with a jump it's more than likely you're using the wrong techniques.
There's not much to the story, so don't expect anything wonderful there.  Someone wronged you, you're trying to figure out who they are and why they did it.  Nothing epic or grandiose like saving the world, it's pretty much just personal revenge with a bit of a political background.
I had a few minor issues, including one slowdown/crash that was remedied by simply turning off PhysX in the options.  Other issues were my character not grabbing ledges that I clearly thought she should, or at one point I must have "stubbed my toe" mid wall-run because I just stopped and fell off the wall.
Due to the extremely short length of the game, I can only recommend picking it up on sale.  It has difficulty settings, time trials, and some collectible items, so there's a small bit of replay value to it.

I have played 10hrs or so, exhausted the main story and mucked about in the sandbox mode for quite some time since the main story only lasted about three hours.  However, I could only play for 40/50min stretches before requiring a break since I get mild motion sickness from the severly restricted field of view.
Conceptually this game is fantastic.  The physics of the cuboidal worlds is genious. The environment is great to look at, the caves are fun (but too dark on my system), and the character models match well with the overall voxel scheme.
So far 5/5 for just about everything, though I will eventually take a star off if the devs fail to add FOV and GAMMA sliders to the gfx settings.  Frankly, given the amount of time this game has been in development I am surprised these two extremely basic settings are missing.
A little worrying that there seems to have been some stagnation over the past year - hopefully this isn't vaporware/conware like Cubeworld.  I found a let's play series on the yubtubs from around a year ago and the guy seems to be having so much more fun in his survival sandbox world than what I had in the current release.  Why did the devs fail to release the Steam version with a 'survival single player' mode?  It seems like it's been a possibility for a long time!
Here's hoping the devs pick up the pace now that they've got the Steam release done. Hopefully there will be an open sandbox mode whereby you can fly off to other planets with friends to see interesting terrain, structures, settlements, allies and enemies.  Hope, hope, hope.  Assuming all that I just barely recommend this game, but only to the hard core and patient,  And only for the purposes of encouraging these guys to keep going strong with a game that has the potential to be absolutely massive.

This game is, to best describe it, a first person puzzle adventure game, teaching morals in the most minimalistic ways possible. I can't stress how much this game can teach you, and you can look back on each and every lesson in the central area if you wish to return there.
I loved this game. While I'm one to get frustrated at games when I can't get past a certain point, this game's puzzles were so calming and relaxing that I couldn't get upset. (Except for that one puzzle towards the end of the game, f*** that puzzle).
Again, I loved this game. I recommend it to anyone who wants their mind to be constantly blown, to anyone who wants to think and expand their mind, to learn lessons of actual value, and to anyone who doesn't mind throwing up rainbows at least 6 times during a playthrough. Of course if any of these are a detriment to your gaming experience, this game might not be the best for you.

Stellar Overload: AKA Gravity is Trying to Murder My Brain.
My first impression of Stellar Overload was that it looked very good, had a great take on the block-based style and would surely be a lot of fun. After more than half an hour of talking and fetch quests though I was beginning to tire and really wanted to just dive into survival a la Minecraft. So far in my misguided quest to save the village I had managed to fill in large amounts of the well with dirt when I got frustrated trying to climb out of it, destroyed all the farms (and much of the surrounding area) whilst trying to harvest carrots and finally ripped down half the wall of a quest giver’s house by tunnelling straight through the berry bush I was harvesting and into their front porch. Compare this mass destruction to the tree punching start I was expecting and it was quite a culture shock.
I don’t know if the grabber has the ability to specify the type of block you are trying to break rather than it’s default WMD setting... but if it does I haven’t found it.
So for the sake of my sanity (and for the good of the villagers) I quit out to look for a survival mode without a story but only found Creative, where I was immediately overwhelmed by the sheer number of block types and items in my inventory and realised I’d likely have to play through the story to understand half of them. At the moment it appears there is no Survival mode and this is sorely lacking since repeating the story over and over is unlikely to be all that enjoyable.
I jumped back into the story and was almost immediately given a jet pack after one quick chat and then I found a hover bike cunningly concealed behind a semi-transparent bush. So much for the usual grinding and saving of resources to build something cool. Apparently I would ‘require’ the jetpack for cave exploration which as explanations go is kind of on a par with ‘I require this armour-piercing-high-explosive ammunition for pest control’.
Texas state law aside, it sounded like after completing the quest to find 20 Moonstone I’d probably get a rifle and armour too. Apparently I needed an upgrade... despite so far having only used my 200 rounds of pistol ammunition pot-shotting peacoc ks for their (assumedly) delicious meat that I have no way of cooking. In fact I had yet to encounter anything more scary than a squirrel who jumped out of a bush and startled me.
It is quite a long way from those early Minecraft days of rationing your torches and being terrified to go outside in the dark because you have no health or food but need three bones from a skeleton in order to make fertilizer... in order not to starve... in order to continue on to actually make a sword rather than trying to fight with a spade.
Needless to say I just wasn’t exactly feeling the sense of survival and achievement that similar games have offered...
Nonetheless I persevered and after crashing the hover bike into one too many squirrels I found a nice big hole in the ground to jump into. Almost instantly I was overwhelmed by dozens of glowing crystals in various colours, none of which were the illusive Moonstone and still I found none by the time I’d reached the bottom of the cave.
So out of frustration I decided to see what would happen if I attempted to tunnel directly through the centre of the Earth.
For the first minute or so I wasn’t really aware that I was actually making any progress on my journey down as my screen was basically solely occupied by a single block which had constant particles coming out of it and then occasionally changed colour. Much like mining obsidian I thought it was simply taking ages to break the blocks. After all there was no way it could be so easy to go so deep, so fast at the start of the game right?
It was only when I looked up into the black abyss that I had apparently created above me that it dawned on me that even blocks way down deep in the planet break instantly and how deep down I could go was basically just equal to how long I held the mouse button down for. It seemed that my suspicion was correct and that like some other games mining was just going to be unchallenging, boring and somewhat of an obligatory requirement tacked on to every block-based resource gathering game.
Then I reached the middle of the planet and proceeded to spend the next half hour in a battle against the laws of physics.
I assumed one of three things would happen when I dug straight down: A. I would die in lava, void, a rock monsters gastrointestinal tract etc. B. I’d hit bedrock and it wouldn’t let me reach the core. Or C. Gravity would get all screwy, it is after all a cubic planet.
C is in fact correct however it is C to the power of ‘Ow my brain hurts’ screwy. I assumed (if I survived) then gravity would simply flip but I had failed to factor in the fact that I was not drilling through the centre of the quadrilateral planet and merely skirting through a layer of the cubic crust, nowhere near the magma and iron cube core.
If there was an audio transcript of my experience it would be something like this:
“Dig, dig, dig, down I go... what the... *incomprehensible screams*... WHERE IS GRAVITY? ...ok I’ll go this way then... *muffled*...what is happening? ...I’m scared. Help me.”
Etc.
I won’t spoil the fun of saying precisely what happened or how I got out of the middle of the planet as the first time you try it it’s like an escape the room puzzle... only where Newton’s first law of motion is plotting to murder you.
However I will dictate the things that went through my head at the time:
“I understand why they gave me a jetpack now.”
“HOW? How do I have thirty seven thousand limestone blocks in my inventory.”
“I hear birdsong. The surface! At last. I wonder what side of the planet I am on? Wait is that my hover bike?”
...
“I still have no Moonstone.”
----------
To give some slightly more helpful feedback and information however...
Currently there isn’t a huge amount of content in the game past the first part of the story. Hence I spent a large amount of time finding ridiculous things to do in creative mode instead...
Resources are so easy to find in huge quantities that there is scarcely a need to bother mining, farming or anything else. Most containers dotted around in the little hamlets, crashed ships, observation posts and the robot fortress contain stacks of hundreds of all the common elements and more medicine, food and ammo than you would need to survive against an entire armada of angry machines. Not that it matters because even if you die you don’t lose anything in your inventory and the only penalty is returning to your clone machine.
If you do decide to mine then you can rack up thousands of coal and ore by just digging straight down for five minutes and jetpacking back out of the hole so you quickly end up with dozens of storage containers filled with stuff you have no use for other than building ten foot high carbon steel statues of yourself everywhere...
I flew to most of the planets in creative mode and was impressed to find they actually exist even if at the moment they are basically just different biome templates with nothing much to do there. It would be great in the future if you could play on large multiplayer servers with people flying back and forth between planets in cobbled together spaceships. At the moment though the only way of getting a craft into space it seems is to build an extremely high pole that reaches space and launch the ship from the top since it wants to just hover ten foot off the ground otherwise. This works but the ship remains fixed to the gravity of the face of the planet you launched from so you are limited to two dimensional movement and can basically only reach planets in line with you.
When the game is more complete and these issues are addressed I can see it being very addictive.

Shadowrun Returns couldn't hold my attention. At first the game invites you into a fascinating cyberpunk world but then proceeds to quickly enclose you in a very linear storyline without any depth to the tactical side.
You can, for example, hire runners but you can't use them to hack. Why not? Because your main character is not a hacker.
Buying upgrades for any of the other classes other than the one you are playing has no effect. You can not equip your temporary runners, only yourself. And with the limited equipment available, you quickly find yourself doing the same thing over and over.
The RPG side to the game is minimal. Sometimes the game offers you different routes through a map but the further in you get, the fewer the possibilities and you'll just find yourself running down corridors clicking on the text that has no real consequence on the game world.
There is very little interaction with NPCs as well. See all those buildings in the screenshots? You're not going to be allowed to enter any of them. There are no vehicles and you will continuously be brought back to the same place (namely the bar you see) from where you 'coordinate' your attacks. I say coordinate loosely because you're basically taken on a roller-coaster ride. The storyline is rather silly but acceptable..
At some point you also run into invincible enemies which, if you ask me, is just a lame excuse to make up for poor AI and lack of proper map design. I got through that fight and got bored with the game.
Too much on-rails, too little NPC-interaction, too little exploration and too little character customization make this a very mediocre RPG with a kick♥♥♥♥♥theme.

Dying Light is the best zombie-game up to this date. Atmosphere filled post-apocalypse with strong emphasis on survival. Fighting and movement/parkour feels fantastic and quick. The world is huge and very detailed, and hence very satisfying to explore. The world is very immersive with some varying weather and day-night cycles, where it gets much more dangerous during the dark. The story is interesting enough: epic at times, but overall standard and sometimes cheesy. The character you control is fun and sarcastic, overall adding to the shifting sense between dramatic and humoristic world. Overall this game excels as a an action game with a rich world to explore.
The game reminded me of Stalker some times, where you can never be too sure how an encounter or a situation will end. Other times it reminded me of Fallout, where if you pay attention to details when exploring, you can find small clues telling a short story of i.e. what happened to that corpse in the bed. The game's graphics are fantastic (but I am aware that some people have experienced technical problems), especially the lighting is very immersive and atmospheric.
Dying Light lets you play the way you prefer. You can be quick and fast, practicly flying and sliding through the city. Or you can be slow and explore your surroundings. The best part is that both approaches are rewarding in their own way, but I would suggest the slower exploring style, due to all the fantastic detail that can be observed.
The zombies are traditional, in that sense that they are almost no match for you when you single one out. But once you are surrounded by a group, everything changes. And as is standard in many classic zombie stories, man can often turn out to be your worst enemy.
Dying Light also offers many side quests, some of which are really epic, both in terms of action and humor. Some other quests are simple fetch-tasks, but are complimented by the main characters reactions: such as tossing the fetched package at the quest-giver angrily and insulting him/her. It' satisfying that way.
The game offers lots of variety in terms of surroundings, enemies, side quests, items, and locations. An approximate estimation is that it will keep you entertained and engaged for 40-50 hours. If the modding tools deliver in the future, this game could have so much more.
I played mostly single player and found it superior to coop. Coop was too simple, where the otherwise threatening world turned into a easy playground. I hope this gets adressed in the coming hard mode.
The infamous night mode is a very strong aspect of why the game feels so fresh, but here I also found a loophole. It is very easy to avoid the dangerous zombies through the mini-map, which literalily makes the night time a breeze. I found it much more engaging when trying my best to ignore the game's clues, and relying on hearing only (since it is otherwise dark..). This hopefuly will be attended to in the hard-mode which is coming from the developers.
