I beat Syberia a year or two ago and while I really enjoyed it and knew that the journey continued in Syberia II, other games and life called me away. When I learned that Syberia 3 was in the works, a fire got lit underneath me and I finally played and finished Syberia 2 in preparation. I am so glad that I didn't play Syberia 2 until 3 was announced because I think I would have some seriously unanswered questions, but lets start from the beginning.
Syberia II starts immediately after Syberia ends, so it is not so much a sequel as it is a continuation of the story. Now if you think that a game that has the story of a New York lawyer named Kate Walker going to Eastern Europe to wrap up a business deal and ends up instead helping an old man who is a genius with building automatons (NOT robots) go to the supposedly fictional island of Syberia where mammoths still live is boring, then move along. If however you think that that plot has possiblities you have to play it. I dare say it will be unlike any game you play. I know it stands out for me.
Where to even begin? I love the world that Benoit Sokal has created. Even though it is mostly snow, and blizzards and vey remote locations on the fringe of civilization, it is gorgeous. The cut scenes are exciting, beautiful, and add to the overall mystic feel of the game. The soundtrack is a wonderful blend of regular orchestral music or a tribal feel, depending on where you are in the game.
I love the characters. Seriously, if I were to pick a favorite heroine, it would be a tie between Commander Shephard and Kate Walker. I think Kate is that amazing. She doesn't save the world, but she questions the importance of having the ideal job in an ideal place. In her case it's a promising career in New York City. She learns how important it is to follow your dreams, and help others realize theirs, despite how crazy or off the beaten path they are. It's a real life lesson, and I think that is what makes her so special. The cast of characters that surround her are also memorable. I love Oscar. He may come off as annoying to some but personally I would love to go on a train adventure with him. The story really focuses on Hans, whom Kate is helping reach Syberia. It is his dream that is the focus and what drives Kate. The dynamic between these three makes this game special, and at times heartbreaking.
Of course, you can't have an adventure game without the puzzles. The key is to talk to everyone about everything you can. This will give you clues about where to go. Each area feels like a kind of level, so there are only so much backtracking. The puzzles are everywhere from pretty easy, to definitely having to think. It will just depend of your experience with adventure games.
Now I must address one thing - the ending. They got it right, mostly. Once the journey is over, there is definitely a loose string - Well, what now Kate Walker? Luckily, we will be getting the answer in Syberia 3, and I can't wait to see what new adventure she finds herself in.

Some multiplayer free-to-play games, players who are willing to pay for special items or downloadable content may be able to gain a significant advantage over those playing for free. Critics of such games call them "pay-to-win" games. A common suggestion for avoiding pay-to-win is that payments should only be used to broaden the experience without affecting gameplay.[25] Some suggest finding a balance between a game that encourages players to pay for extra content that enhances the game without making the free version feel limited by comparison.[26] This theory is that players who do not pay for items would still increase awareness of it through word of mouth marketing, which ultimately benefits the game indirectly. In response to concerns about players using payments to gain an advantage in game, titles such as World of Tanks have explicitly committed to not giving paying players any advantages over their non-paying peers

Fairy Fencer F is a JRPG that ticks most of the right boxes, and carries a certain amount of charm with it. However, it has a lot of untapped potential that bears mentioning-- potential that other games made by the same company might fulfill better.
The premise of the game is somewhat bland-- there's a good deity and an evil deity, they hate each other, and mortals want them revived. They can do this by collecting Furies, which are magic weapons scattered around the world. Mostly by accident, the main character Fang gets wrapped up in the plot because he unseals a Fury by accident.
The story is lighthearted for the most part, barely dipping into troubled territory later on. Expect a lot of self-referential humor and Anime Silliness sprinkled throughout, and enough fanservice to bear mentioning, but not enough to feel egregious. I got the feeling that the story was played very safely, barely deviating from several common anime tropes. While it was certainly done well enough, it wasn't really the strongest part of the game overall, especially later on when you must repeat several areas of the game.
Locations are greatly varied, but none of them really stuck out to me, and the enemy design and overall art direction was also pretty standard anime fare. Expect a lot of reskinned enemies and common thematic areas-- the fire zone, ice zone, desert zone, windy zone, etc.. Overall, the setting works for the game, but like the plot it feels like it was just playing it safe. The best part of the locales is the World Shaping ability, which allows players to give unique effects to areas like increasing EXP gains and drop rates in return for losing HP gain or silencing spells.
The combat is the standout part of the game. You command a group of three Fury-wielding fighters, and take turns against your enemies on a 3D map. Characters can move within a circle around them and attack within a smaller range around them. If you've upgraded a Fury to do so, basic attacks can combo together for more damage overall, and since Furies are magical, they can shift their form to several different weapons. Most monsters have specific weaknesses to certain weapon types, and attacking these can chain together even more attacks from allies nearby. Attack animations are quick and flashy, with big effects and pronounced swings. Skills and Magic are also available, and are even flashier, with full-screen animations. However, while each character's skills and attack spells are unique, characters have at most 9 different skills and attack spells. Since some spells and skills are stronger than others, I found myself seeing the animations for the stronger skills (like Fang's Eruption Edge) over and over again later on, which made a flashy, cool animation somewhat mundane.
Characters can also Fairize, a transformation power that combines them and their weapon for more power. It's very flashy and changes the music, as well as making almost every encounter laughably easy. It also unlocks the use of an HP draining ultimate ability, but I rarely used these. Strangely, the devs decided to give every character a skill that they can use while not transformed that's more powerful and cheaper than the ultimate skill. This added up to more viewings of Eruption Edge, and more frustration. Characters also have a special ability, but to be honest, I never used these. They take a turn to toggle or use, and I usually felt that it was better to just deal damage.
However, the combat is marred by its sheer volume. While it's easy to get from story point to story point, since characters join the party with effectively no training, if you get a new character you like, you have to stop and grind. Even with World Shaping to take the edge off, the grind will take up many hours of a standard playtime.
At a discount, Fairy Fencer F is a good purchase for JRPG fans. There's even DLC to raise the level cap by 900 levels for some reason (???).

A classic Point and Click slow-pace puzzle game set in a beautiful surrealist world. I have to admit that the art is what first draw me to this game.
The game consists of seven acts (“dreams”) where you play as a ghost named “reader” aiming to go to “the other side”. Helped by your sidekick “writer”, you advance in the game by solving puzzles.
Some puzzles are kind of hard to figure out. You will need perseverance, good observation skills and to pay careful attention to the dialogues with your different encounters in order to not miss any clues. You will also have to take notes, and for some puzzles you need to brainstorm on paper and do some trials and errors to figure them out. There is just one pixel hunting puzzle that required me a solution map to be solved (in fact, even with the map showing me where to click, I still had a hard time doing it right… even with a ruler… ).
Dialogues and monologues are a big part of the game. Voices were purposedly muffled to give them a more ghostly effect. Filled with humor or bad jokes, the dialogues make us discover some interesting imaginary ghost world.
The interface is simple (there is no inventory and you can “go to”, “look at”, “interact with” or “talk to” an object by switching the cursor of your mouse) and the menu is very basic (you can only save, load and exit the game). There are some instructions in the art book about how to adjust your display settings to see the game art just right. F12 is not enabled, so you will have to use the print screen key to save any clues you find. You can use some screen capture freeware like Snapper to easily save screenshots while in-game.
The art book (or “commentary book”) was an interesting read (it can be downloaded from the “manual” link located on the right side of the game library page). I did not know much about a developer’s work, so it gave me some insight about how the thinking and making process during game development works, but it could be a boring read for some. It also gave me some understandings about some aspects of the dream world in the game, and it contains some hints and solutions of the puzzles if you are stuck (but the pixel hunting puzzle solution map can be found on the forum).
If you forget the awful pixel hunting puzzle, it was an interesting game to play. If you enjoy puzzles games and reading while exploring some imaginary surreal world, I would definitely recommend this game to you.

This game was never on my radar due to the early access model it took, I never played KF1.  I don't early access, I filter em out , won't get into that.  I am playing the finished game ...it's an amazingly fun co op fps zombie slayer.  I got this game on sale with a RL friend, we have been playing it daily since.
I'll get into what I like and leave out my opinions on what I don't.  My negatives don't relate to current build but rather what I would like to see in the future ... I.E , More boss variety/modes/etc.
My Reasons why you should play it:
1.) Co-op game-play is intense and team-play is a must on later difficulties.  If you don't work together, game over ... that simple.  It feels like the left for Dead series to the 100th power.  Bigger teams, more weapons, and tons of customization items for the little snowflakes.  Now even has a pvp mode if that's your thing, I just love hunting the AI with pals.
2.) Time Vampire.  There are different match length's available based on how much time you have, but can easily meet a nice group and kill hours without noticing.
3.) The weapons.  Each feels different and have there own roles to play, huge replayability factor.  The sub machine guns shoot different than assault rifles, all with unique recoil , feel, and game-play.  Something for everyone.
4.) Perk leveling system - Each perk (or class) has their own unique passives that gain points per level.  Every 5 levels you have access to a deeper build system, being able to select one active for every 5 levels.  This makes two people playing the same perk, be able to play the same class uniquely.  Example, two berserkers.  One might select passives as a tank, the other dps big mob hunter.  Together , a bloody well paired almost unstoppable duo that complement each other.
5.) Blood and gore, slaughter for hours.  The game looks and plays great, play on ultra with all the carnage options on.  Can't have slaughter without the laughter, and I love Gore in all forms.  Always ear to ear smiles when time slows down and you paint the walls with your closest zed.  At the end of the round you look like you left a Gallagher show and forgot the tarp ... or just left a Gwar or Cannibal Corpse show.
6.)  The soundtrack.  Is great and fits well with the game and encounters.  Even if metal aint your thing, it is an enhancement to the experience.
7.)  There is a server/client MP infrastructure so you join hosted servers.  No local nonsense.  Games are not hosted off their local machines , but dedicated hosted servers in which you connect to as a client.
8.) It is difficult, you will die and loose but I like harder games.  You will die or your team will get wiped out, could happen for many reason from team comp to perk level ... or people not sticking together late game.  I suggest this as a guide for difficulty based on perk level, this keeps it feeling challenging.  Normal (0-5) , Hard (6-12), Suicidal (13-25) , and Hell on earth (25+ only).
Looking for a game that you can play all day or just pick up when bored...this might be a fit for you.  Play with friends if you have them and if not join a random server and make some.

Note: The Art Book is not missing- you grab it from the Store Page using the link to the "manual" on the right. Yes, it helps a LOT to have this, but the puzzles aren't impossible without it. Just old-school hard.
This is a game to buy if you have very particular tastes. It is a game to avoid if you won't find its weird logic compelling, as without that, its flaws would make it more annoying than charming.
Things some will like:
Surreal Art Style
Unusual Story
Old-school Adventure Game Puzzles
Things some will dislike:
Wordy, reverb-heavy dialogue
Old-school Adventure Game Puzzles (yes, this is a plus or a minus, depending on your taste)
Rather abrupt ending
The art style is an obvious one, either you like it or you don't. The Art book is available on this page as the "manual" in the links to the right, but I recommend care if you decide to check it out- it includes many spoilers, including a section that gives the answers or very strong hints to all of the puzzles.
The story is the part that hooked me, despite being initially drawn in by the art. While, structurally, this could be considered similar to many other adventure games, the details and world were very different than the usual fare. For this reason, I was willing to forgive a great deal.
The puzzles are a mixed bag for someone who doesn't really remember pixel hunting with any fondness. There are two pixel-hunt puzzles, and I would have been much happier with something else, but they serve their purpose well. Most of the others are more about brain power and less about stubbornly looking for a hotspot. I was mildly annoyed that the characters implied I couldn't have known the answer to one (very simple) puzzle without the walkthrough, but that could be considered a nod to the fact that in their world, ours is basically a myth, and thus what is common or easily acquired knowledge here could be esoteric there.
The dialogue... left me in a weird place. I found some of Reader's lines of conversation annoying, but at the same time, they drew me further into the world, in some cases even as I speed-clicked through topics I had seen before. The reverb didn't really bother me, but I know some people find it very annoying. Definitely find a Let's Play video or something and watch a tiny bit of the game to see which camp you fall into. For me, it just corresponded to the pulsing of the scenery- of course the sound is going to be odd.
The ending... everything important gets dealt with, it's just that there's no epic ending cutscene to help you feel accomplished. There is a mildly entertaining non-epilogue, which served just fine for me, but this is the money brick wall many indie games run into, so I am a bit used to it, I suppose.
All in all, I am pleased that I played it, and pleased to own it, but I definitely do think this is a niche piece, for those of us who like their surreality without a strong horror overlay. YMMV.

I got this game as a gift, not from the devs or anything. TLDR: it's cool but broken/unplayable.
I was really excited, because it's a really neat looking game, but also the kind of thing I probably wouldn't buy for myself. The fact that it was a gift gave me extra incentive to actually play it, rather than let it linger in my library.
It's a really cool game.
The production value is good. The sound is really nicely done. The visual effects work really well, so well that I was mad that I couldn't use the Steam screenshot function. The narrative is engaging, the writing is not boring or bad or anything. I enjoyed playing the game and would like to play it more.
So why the negative review?
The game is unplayable.
You start in a room with a guy. You can talk to him. You can go through two empty rooms. You can talk to a second guy in a fourth room. That's it.
After talking to both guys, you have to options: either 1- follow a walk through, step by step, for the rest of the game, or 2- download a random compressed file from some sketchy hosting site.
The "60 page art book (with puzzle guide)" promised on the store page is not included anywhere in the downloaded files, and it is the key to solving every single puzzle in the game. If you check the community forums, someone has posted a link to a random file hosting site, claiming it's the art book, but it's not hosted by the devs on their own site nor has it been uploaded to Valve's servers and updated to the downloadable files.
Figuring out the obscure puzzles is 2/3s of the game's content. Following a walk through on your first play through, you might as well just watch a Youtube play through, then. Downloading who knows what from some sketch site, honestly not a great idea.
Hopefully the devs will add the artbook and fix this problem, and I will be able to turn this into a positive review, but until that happens you should NOT BUY this game, even though it has lots of cool things about it.

One of the few games that gave me motion sickness, so personally I cannot recommend Antichamber in that sense. On the technical side, it was probably a mixture of weird FoV and the mouse movements, which seemed to have a mind of their own. The visual style is quite striking, I must admit.
As a puzzle game, I did not enjoy the style where there is seemingly no coherent set of rules. Yes, that's part of the design and charm of the game, but nevertheless it made solving the puzzles frustrating instead of stimulating. It's probably unfair to compare this to an AAA game like Portal, but Portal, with all of the surreal stuff you could do, had a very intuitive set of rules about what and when you could pull off. Here, instead of trying to fit these pieces into the puzzle, I was instead resorting to running around the rooms trying to find elements to interact with, or trying to figure out when I could place a block from my gun or not. Combined with the non-linear (okay, this is usually a good thing) progression I found myself often tracking back and redoing some parts. These are elements I do not particularly enjoy in any game.

I have to say that I'm intrigued by this little game. I've always been a fan of the space frontier/freelancer sort of genre, and this reminds me a lot of Escape Velocity: Nova in terms of theme, but in terms of actual gameplay it's a completely different beast. In many ways, it's sort of like Theme Hospital or Dungeon Keeper, albeit set in space. You don't actually ever see your ship or the enemy ship moving, but you can control various rooms and doors, keeping systems online as you order your crew (read: imps) around to keep things working.
For what it is, the graphics are very nice; I wish there were a little more of a visual elements to the interesting text scenarios, and after 10 hours it's gotten a little repetitive, but I'm still having fun trying different ship layouts. The one thing about this game that keeps it replayable after you've hit every encounter is the difficulty level; even on "easy," this thing tends to kick your butt. The final boss is an order of magnitude harder than the rest of the game, and it's always fun to try different strategies with it.
I look forward to seeing more from this developer, and more games like this in general! It doesn't have to be flashy to be incredibly entertaining, and FTL pulls that off without looking tacky or feeling like a waste of money.

Dying Light isn't a long game, and it doesn't have a unique story, but its the dead island we wanted and more. I couldn't enjoy kicking zombies as much as I can in this game, with the amount of variety available to me in combat, the possibilities were endless. The attention to detail in this game is superb, not to the tiniest detail like GTA V, but to the point where you can find supreme beauty in the environment, despite the crisis. The story itself is not original, but it is delivered fairly strong, with some missions with such impact on the player by playing with their emotions, and linking you to some of the characters. The serious tone however, is lost in co-op mode, which I find as a good thing, as dead island had co-op that made the game seem like party fun with your friends, this same theme is matched in Dying Light, but to a more enjoyable extent, thanks to the freedom the group has in the world, and the hilarious antics that will most definitely ensue. Multiplayer however, completely changes the game for most, since you never expect to survive a prolonged encounter at night, this can be worsened by the fact that there is now a player-controlled super-zombie running around eating you and your friends. In my personal opinion, dying light lives fully and beyond expectation, and can proved a good 20-50 hours of entertainment depending on how you bide your time, this game is definitely worth full price, but if you feel like waiting for a better price, don't feel bad, a good game is awaiting you anyways.
Side note: physics is good but still has flaws, hilarious flaws. I swear to god Techland if you fix the funny physics I will flip a concrete/gold table forty feet off of the peak of mount everest into space and destroy the sun.

It's XCOM.
What else do you really need to know?
Look, a lot of people don't like the game. Their reasons are FAIR. Mainly, they play fantasy games to get away from real life, and the very concept of their major characters dying violently with random elements playing a role is something many players are not willing to put up with.
It's trying to simulate military seriousness. In real life, it's hard to fight a war without casualties. It forces the character to really consider their moves and recognize that everything is at stake based on you and what they are about to do. You don't think the police feels outgunned sometimes? There really are situations where the enemy just doesn't give a ****. Everyone is expendable for the cause. The game is sending you against a superior enemy, up the hill, with the sun in your eyes.
Front Mission and Final Fantasy tactics are great games, but they are created to be of a more forgiving style. You might be surprised to know that you still lose characters in those games too, but that's because the story forces on you. Alma didn't have to die at the end of chapter one. She should have thrown herself out of the way of the crossbow bolt; or maybe if it hadn't been scripted, then the enemy could have had a chance to miss - but the game didn't even give you the chance. It just took her from you. Most of Delita's character design and choices are based on losing his sister. Besides the trailer section, Xcom instead puts the tools in your hands. It's up to you to sharpen the sword, or die.
That's the way it works, and that's why Xcom is so beautiful, because of it.

After playing the criminally underrated base game, I couldn't wait for more content to be added - paid or otherwise - and imagined what could be added. I didn't imagine the frustration and cruelty the Tropical Ice pack would cause me to endure. This pack offers 3 new Championships, one for each of the car classes, featuring two new seasonal maps and two new game modes. The maps are the real show-stealer, or at least they attempt to be. One takes place inside a beach bar, the other on a wintry holiday resort. There's surprisingly little re-use of assets, and most of the maps' setpieces seem completely original. Even reskinned items are done cleverly and don't detract at all from the map. The actual tracks themselves need a lot more work done to them. The amount of times one gets hung on corners, or misjudges what should be a fairly easy slide are innumerable, leading to crashes and falling off the tracks many a time. Mercifully the game's unfairness is really just kept to its tracks - the difficulty in the modes seems genuine.... for the most part.
I don't remember the controls pre-Tropical Ice Pack being as grindingly wound up as they are here, with even the Supercars failing to make sharp turns and recover from the speed drop quickly enough. Considering how fast you have to be in the highly demanding time trials and against the speedy AI, this makes the game feel meanspirited. I don't mind the rival racers being faster than me, especially when there's powerups galore, but when the cars don't feel as responsive as they should (especially now the other cars' collisions are a lot harder on you), it's like Playrise Digital are spiteful of you beating the game and paying for the priviledge of paying for new stuff out of enthusiasm.
The modes are the only good thing about this pack, and if they were incorporated into the original cups I'd gladly redo them all just to experience them. Checkpoint and Overtake are self-explanatory; the former requires you to go through a slalem of checkpoints, awarding time for each one you go through successfully and deducting time for when you miss them. Overtake mode requires you to overtake as many vehicles as possible before time runs out. With these game modes I felt like I was constantly making progress with each checkpoint and car overtaken, whereas the constant fear of wasting 3 minutes in the hope of getting just one measly star so I can progress in the Championship made me miserable. There's new special events too, so if you want to replay these specific modes and maps you'll get bonus coins and XP for trying the individual maps and modes.
But what is there left to spend gold on? There's no new skins or cars, so unless you own the other DLC there's virtually no point in playing this unless you fancy getting riled up about poor controls and frustrating time requirements. It's a shame given how I love both the Hawaiian and icy setting (two of my favourite kinds of place), but it's marred by its wonky design and unrealistic requirements to progress.
Given how I'd waited months for the controller support issue to be fixed so I could play this, you can't say I went in expecting to hate it (especially if you see how much time I've put into the game). It gives a horrific first impression, and only continues to be a slog that reminds you there's another cheaper DLC you could've bought. If you're desperate for this, wait for a sale. It's not even worth its low price of £3.99.

Yeah, there's a reason why the Tropical Ice DLC for Table Top Racing: World Tour has mixed reviews as of me writing this: It's kinda frustrating.
For comparison's sake, the base game was a competent kart racer that didn't have a strong sense of identity. The Supercharger DLC gives you free cars that make the game too easy. This DLC adds two new locations, NO CARS, that are more frustrating than fun thanks to physics glitches. "Life's a Beach" is the nicer looking of the two IMO, but the scenery is ruined by some really annoying bug where your car will get bumped off track because you went down an incline too quickly. "Yellowsnow Piste" adds an arctic locale to the game's location list, which sounds cool on paper, but sadly gets tedious thanks to rogue snowballs that will nearly knock you off course with no warning. With time, you'll BARELY see them coming, but that's it and they can slow you down a lot if you're not using a bigger vehicle. (And that's without mentioning the bumpy snow section of the course.)
What a shame, too, that the two DLC's to this game have only made it worse. One makes the whole game too easy, and the other adds new events that can drive you insane if you're not careful, and if being careful doesn't sound fun in a kart racer, then yeah, trust me when I say that it's not.

Risk of Rain is a new indie release on Steam where you play as a stranded survivor on an alien planet with only your guns, your reflexes, and your wits keeping you alive against the numerous hordes of enemies that populate the planets you travel to.
I honestly enjoyed Risk of Rain's gameplay... to a certain extent. It's smooth and effective and shooting enemies is satisfying. But while I enjoyed the different upgrades, I'm not a big fan of the randomness of their appearance. I get that it adds a level of tension to the game and adds to the arcade feel of it, but I'd rather upgrade because I've been doing good at the game, not cross my fingers and hope that the next item in the chest is a Warbanner.
Along with that, the game can get a little ridiculous with the monster spawning. I was on one ledge and nearly 7 monsters with insanely large health bars appeared leaving me almost defenseless against their attacks. I'd try to run away, but even more monsters would spawn and the whole thing would just turn into a sh**-show.
The music is good, for however many times you like to hear the same loop over and over again. And the graphics are very retro, but at the same time very appealing to look at.
I feel like after 4 hours, I got my satsifaction from Risk of Rain. I killed the three main bosses, and that was good enough for me. I know some people are willing to take the challenge, and go the extra mile, so if this looks like that kind of game then don't let me stop you from playing it. But I'm giving it a 6/10.

Okay, so I bought this game for my brother and I. $18 each or whatever, no big deal. Played solo co-op. We couldn't put it down until we reached the end of the alpha content (and even then, we went on to monkey around in Creative mode).
Even if those 10 hours are all I ever get for my $18 (x2), they were WELL WORTH IT. This game is incredible. The graphics are very charming and pretty. I was correct in my impression that this is not really a mining/crafting game... that's all very much secondary.
The game surprised me time and time again. Luscious graphics, wonderful shaders, well written story, amazing hand-crafted feeling to the building designs populated on your planets, and the sheer fun factor of cube-shaped worlds. Once we got the jetpack, my brother and I started playing around on the edge of the planet where the faces converge, and we ended up just having a blast with that for an hour or so (you haven't lived until you've base-jumped from one face of the planet to the other).
We got kind of confused on only one mission where you have to find 20 moonstone. Those can be found 150 blocks DEEP, you don't need to actually mine to the center of the planet (although this is a recommendable experience in creative mode).
I think if they keep pushing out story-mode content every few months and wrap up this game in a year and a half, I could be okay with that. It's not hard to see beyond the fun if you're paying attention and there's a lot of missing content here. Most importantly, they need to get planetary-travel space-ship building in the game. You can build hoverbikes, but that's about it for now. The game needs a lot of graphics settings options to be configurable that aren't currently, namely vsync checkbox, AA tweaking, FOV slider.
This game makes you constantly want to test the sandbox universe with "can I do that?". Part of the fun for me was having the ultimate questions answered in Creative mode, so do play around with that!

I would recommend Killing Floor 2 if you’re into zombie killing. In this game, you kill zeds, experimental zombies that escaped from a lab called Horzine. You will face zeds like a crazy man wielding a chainsaw (scrake), a female creature that turns invisible (stalker), a human spider (crawler) and more. You can have varieties of zed killing weapons. From a weapon that is a combination of a chainsaw, crossbow and a saw blade to a gun that freezes the balls of zeds. There is a quite a few exotic weapons you can find in the game. Also, there are perks or classes. You can play as a berserker, who focuses on using melee weapons like a katana, a gunslinger, who focuses on shooting guns like revolvers and aiming for the head, medic, who focuses on healing other players, and more. They also have multiplayer. You could play with over players on PvE (Player Vs Enemies) or PvP (Player Vs Player). Killing Floor 2 can use the Steam Workshop, which means you can subscribe and play on other maps or just vote for skins to be part of the game. Speaking of skins, yes, just like CS:GO, they have skins for their weapons. Micro-transactions... yeah... Skins outta the way, Killing Floor 2 has difficulties. It has Normal (zeds have low health, walk slow, and less of them), Hard (zeds have a little higher health, sometimes can run and a little more quantity of them), Suicidal (zeds have more health, most of them run, and there is a larger amount of them), and Hell on Earth (zeds have got more health, run faster, and has a large♥♥♥♥♥amount of zeds). A last thing to mention is the bosses. There are so far 4 bosses. Hans Volter, a german scientist (i think) that has an exo skeleton from COD: AW who throws grenades and gas grenades like ♥♥♥♥. Patriarch, the head of the company Horzine who transformed himself to one ugly♥♥♥♥♥who has a minigun, rockets, invisibility system, and syringes he uses to heal himself with. King Fleshpound, a buff zed that has a giant rolling pin for arms to smash people with, summon quarter pounds (little minions), and uses a huge ♥♥♥♥ing laser on his chest like iron man. The last one is Krampus, a monster that has armor on it’s head, body and his backpack or something. Krampus also has the ability of Kirby, which is sucking people in and killing them.
In conclusion, this game includes lots of zombie killing, kinda fun bosses, skins for weapons (don’t try to get em), an extremely hard difficulty, cool weapons, classes, and a use of the steam workshop. Again, it is recommended in my opinion for people who are into zombie games like L4D2 or 1 and No More Room In Hell.

This game was never on my radar due to the early access model it took, I never played KF1.  I don't early access, I filter em out , won't get into that.  I am playing the finished game ...it's an amazingly fun co op fps zombie slayer.  I got this game on sale with a RL friend, we have been playing it daily since.
I'll get into what I like and leave out my opinions on what I don't.  My negatives don't relate to current build but rather what I would like to see in the future ... I.E , More boss variety/modes/etc.
My Reasons why you should play it:
1.) Co-op game-play is intense and team-play is a must on later difficulties.  If you don't work together, game over ... that simple.  It feels like the left for Dead series to the 100th power.  Bigger teams, more weapons, and tons of customization items for the little snowflakes.  Now even has a pvp mode if that's your thing, I just love hunting the AI with pals.
2.) Time Vampire.  There are different match length's available based on how much time you have, but can easily meet a nice group and kill hours without noticing.
3.) The weapons.  Each feels different and have there own roles to play, huge replayability factor.  The sub machine guns shoot different than assault rifles, all with unique recoil , feel, and game-play.  Something for everyone.
4.) Perk leveling system - Each perk (or class) has their own unique passives that gain points per level.  Every 5 levels you have access to a deeper build system, being able to select one active for every 5 levels.  This makes two people playing the same perk, be able to play the same class uniquely.  Example, two berserkers.  One might select passives as a tank, the other dps big mob hunter.  Together , a bloody well paired almost unstoppable duo that complement each other.
5.) Blood and gore, slaughter for hours.  The game looks and plays great, play on ultra with all the carnage options on.  Can't have slaughter without the laughter, and I love Gore in all forms.  Always ear to ear smiles when time slows down and you paint the walls with your closest zed.  At the end of the round you look like you left a Gallagher show and forgot the tarp ... or just left a Gwar or Cannibal Corpse show.
6.)  The soundtrack.  Is great and fits well with the game and encounters.  Even if metal aint your thing, it is an enhancement to the experience.
7.)  There is a server/client MP infrastructure so you join hosted servers.  No local nonsense.  Games are not hosted off their local machines , but dedicated hosted servers in which you connect to as a client.
8.) It is difficult, you will die and loose but I like harder games.  You will die or your team will get wiped out, could happen for many reason from team comp to perk level ... or people not sticking together late game.  I suggest this as a guide for difficulty based on perk level, this keeps it feeling challenging.  Normal (0-5) , Hard (6-12), Suicidal (13-25) , and Hell on earth (25+ only).
Looking for a game that you can play all day or just pick up when bored...this might be a fit for you.  Play with friends if you have them and if not join a random server and make some.

I dont know what to put here so, here is waffles receipe:
Ingredients
1 3/4 cups all-purpose flour
2 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1 3/4 cups milk
1/2 cup cooking oil or butter, melted
1 teaspoon vanilla
Directions
In a medium bowl stir together flour, sugar, baking powder, and salt. Make a well in center of flour mixture; set aside.
In another medium bowl beat eggs slightly; stir in milk, oil, and vanilla. Add egg mixture all at once to flour mixture. Stir just until moistened (batter should be slightly lumpy).
Pour 1 to 1 1/4 cups batter onto grids of a preheated, lightly greased waffle baker (use a regular or Belgian waffle baker). Close lid quickly; do not open until done. Bake according to manufacturers directions. When done, use a fork to lift waffle off grid. Repeat with remaining batter. Serve warm.
Makes 12 to 16 (4-inch) waffles

One of the few games that gave me motion sickness, so personally I cannot recommend Antichamber in that sense. On the technical side, it was probably a mixture of weird FoV and the mouse movements, which seemed to have a mind of their own. The visual style is quite striking, I must admit.

It's probably unfair to compare this to an AAA game like Portal, but Portal, with all of the surreal stuff you could do, had a very intuitive set of rules about what and when you could pull off. Here, instead of trying to fit these pieces into the puzzle, I was instead resorting to running around the rooms trying to find elements to interact with, or trying to figure out when I could place a block from my gun or not. Combined with the non-linear (okay, this is usually a good thing) progression I found myself often tracking back and redoing some parts. These are elements I do not particularly enjoy in any game.

Very addictive "roguelike" game, best played in bursts. You have to play with the hand you're dealt, whether it's for better or worse, and that's where a lot of the fun comes from. You get to choose the order in which you upgrade the different systems on your ship, and it can make a big difference on how you succeed in your current sector, the next, and the final sector. There is much strategy involved.
For instance, say you have an intruder on your ship. If you bought yourself some door control upgrades, your doors take some time to break through, and if the intruder is near an airlock, you can just vent the air from the room and the rooms adjacent to it. Shut off your life support while you're at it to make this go faster. Or if you have a crew that can handle hand-to-hand combat (i.e. not Engi), then send them to the same room as the intruders to take care of them. A combined strategy is to put your crewmen in your medbay with it powered and vent all the spaces leading to the medbay, forcing the intruder into it to deal with your crew, whom are regenerating health as they fight. Or if you're feeling particularly dangerous and you have a rockman crew, set fire to the rooms the intruders are in (ideally non-system rooms) then send your rockmen in to fight them off. In addition to the damage your crew deal, the fire will burn the intruders, dealing extra damage.
That's just one instance of something that may happen while you're on your merry scrap-collecting journey. You can save and quit if you want to take a break, but death is death, and you can't go back without starting a new game. This game can be rather unforgiving at times, but also very rewarding. Definitely a game worth playing if you're into this kind of game.

Given this is an early access, I imagine the first thing people want to know is if Cubical Drift has been reliable and trustworthy with Stellar Overload. I have been following the game since it first came out on Kickstarter as Planets³, and I believe I bought it sometime after their second alpha release once I had confidence in backing. Thus far, no regrets.
The game has certainly been making fantastic progress from each and every alpha release, and the Steam release is no exception. Like a true early access, there have been performance issues, stability issues, and bugs. This release is so far the most stable from what I have experienced. The devs, with the current scale of the community, are listening and responding really well and always seeking player feedback on the gameplay and technical issues, with surveys, constant forum threads, responding to the comments in their blog posts, and so forth.
As for the actual game, it promises to be an open world, or open space, block based, RPG FPS adventure game. A polygonal voxel system is used, with infinite view distance, encouraging destruction and building. The story mode shall go across 10 planets, with multiplayer optionally available for players to use. A creative mode is also available, in the same way Minecraft has one essentially.
With the latest release, as they add more content to utilize the technological foundation they have spent so much time making, has progressively gotten more fun. Navigating bumpy terrain on foot can and probably always will be jarring at first, as your camera constantly bounces up and down, though you do get used to it... somewhat. The gunplay is a bit basic, allowing you to switch between currently two different types of ammunition, but it has been opening itself up, with more gun variety,  block throwing weaponry, a sonic blaster, grenades, and a basic armour system allowing you to handle more shots. Enemies also have a wide variety of weaponry, from deadly close range tasers, lasers, to short range utility teleportation.
Performance and examining the required specs for the game is something you will need to check before purchasing, as it is currently fairly demanding. The devs are considering increasing the price as they approach release, so keep that in mind.
TLDR; I like it and trust it with my backing, devs are active with the community, make sure you can run it, and price will probably increase towards release.

I don't know what to say, honestly.
The game is fun, I've spent 43 hours as of this review and I've done nothing more than play around, and I am yet to find things. The game is big, and made for people who like to explore. But if you like to kill, then this is also your game.
I'll explain myself here. Dying light can be seen and loved by many points of view. There's a leveling system that will level according to what you do most. There is Agility that specializes on escaping Zombies and climbing, Parkour. Then there's Power, which is the one that specializes in killing zombies and giving you fun and diverse ways to kill them.
Storyline:
Although I am not yet done with the Dying Light storyline, I'll tell you one thing: If you go straight trying to speedrun through the storyline, you'll end the game quickly, perhaps too quickly too. The game is aimed for you to explore, and enjoy, so if you are not the type to enjoy exploring and looking around looking for the highest place you can climb or how much you can find, how rich you can become, this is not your game. But I will give it to the storyline, I've found myself ignoring countless sidequests and opportunities to explore because I wanted to see what would happen next. Overall, I'd say the Storyline is fun, can hook you on but not something to speedrun through.
Exploring:
Like I said, this game has an AMAZING exploring system. If you go around and explore you'll find that there are collectibles for you to find, and chances are on first look you're not gonna find them all. There are three sorts of things you can find around the world. Zombie Statues, Flags and Notes. That is all I am gonna say. There are 30 Flags, like 100 Zombie statues and 67 notes. If you are the type to play this game and find everything and enjoy everything. You will find yourself enjoying this game to the maximum. Because there is a lot to explore and exploring is rewarded. Easter eggs can be found and the game will last a lot longer.
Fighting:
Although I will say, I died a LOT on this game, most of it was not because the Zombies took the upper hand and killed me. Zombies will seem threatening and even a bit scary at the early stages of the game. Where it takes you 5 hits to kill them and it is really satisfying to kill your first Zombie, your first 10, and soon your first 100. Zombies are fun to kill, even a bit relaxing after a while and if you get overwhelmed, even a bit hard to beat. There are many types of Zombies, I will not get into detail with them because that is for you to find out, but personally, I am satisfied with the fighting on this game. The Zombies don't follow Ragdoll physics, so if you kill one by kicking them off a cliff, they will look almost human falling off a cliff.
Parkour:
The Parkour in this game is very fun, at first a bit confusing but really fun in general. You will be able to find the highest place you can climb to and even find yourself just parkouring out of the actual questline or sidequest you were doing. Some fun things about Parkour is that there are some things you can find in some houses that you would not have found had you not gone ontop of a house or even a building. Overall, there is not much to say about parkour more than it's fast, exciting, and I would definitely say it is fun, although I found myself raging because I would die from fall distance, and whatnot but that's because I'm stubborn.
Co-op:
Co-op adds a LOT to this game. I found myself constantly running off from my partner just to see what I could find, and eventually both of us meeting somewhere and exchanging what it is that we found. Ranging from Weapons that perhaps he liked the bat and I liked the Cleaver, or anything, really. Co-op adds a different element to this game, that allows you to survive a Zombie Apocalypse with a friend, not alone. I would definitely reccomend it.
Customization:
Although this game is lacking whether I can be a female Runner or not, I would say it was quite disapointing. My Co-op friend also being Kyle Crane kind of killed the entire fun of two survivors and it made it seem more like that was just my twin running around. Outfits are pretty, I will admit that but they are not the maximum customization I would have wanted from this game. Overall, a bit disappointed.
Overall:
Dying Light is a game that can reach out to a lot of people. I, for one adore every aspect of the game whether it is getting Airdrops to rank up on Survival. Parkouring and jumping over Zombies to see if maybe I can find another note, another flag or another Zombie Statue or to see just what else I can discover. And also the fighting on the game that can be extremely satisfying with the slow motion, succeeding on the game making me feel indeed as a Hunter at Day and Prey at Night. I'll reccomend this game to any person. Even if it's just to do the storyline, it is a lot of fun. My rating for this game would be 9/10.

This is a strangely addictive game which has found a difficult to obtain balance between battles and base management, done well enough so that each element could have carried the game on its own. The battles themselves are well designed and organic and feel well linked into the base management aspect e.g. researching weapons and armour that benefit your troops in the battle. The base management is very fun and well designed, with new aspects being unlocked at a good pace as the game progresses. The aliens are an entertaining enemy to combat with you them being mysterious enough so that each new revelation about them and their plans being eagerly awaited!
It’s one of the few games I’ve played where I’ve actually felt like I’m fully in charge, not just told I'm in command of this base and then led through the game in actuality. If you neglect your troops, base or preparations before the battles, you will fail and then still be expected to continue fighting the ever increasingly difficult invasion. Overall I’d highly recommend this game; it’s immersive, addictive and just simply fun!

Generally I'd say it's an alright RPG but emphasis on the "alright". It's nothing phenomenal, sublime or even unique. Only difference I've seen compared to other RPGs is the decking sub-game, where you traverse the matrix but it's just a version of the normal game.
Atmosphere is really fleshed out, both in writing and graphically, and the style is quite pleasing and aesthetic, conveying the gritty dystopian cyberpunk that Shadowrun represents.
Combat is similar if not identical to XCOM 2 as in you can shoot first and follow up by moving. Movement is based on action points, each point allowing an action such as move a distance, shoot or use item.
Leveling system is like Mass Effect. You have a succession of unlockable skills in a pillar that are accessed by leveling character stats.
One MAJOR pitfall as an RPG especially one with such potential in assets is the lack of character stories. I meet a character called Armitage in a morgue and was interested in him and his backstory. Then after a single mission I learn nothing more of him.
There are puzzles in this game, but I never encountered a situation, where I could just click something and have it solved instantly. Same goes for the "skill checks". I can count all the skill checks I used in this game not counting combat with the fingers of one hand.
I suppose it's a modern RPG, considering how most of the missions are in very linear dungeons and more emphasis is based on the combat. Modern also on how short it is: As I write this review I completed the game on normal exploring all the side quests I could find as well as talking to everything. That took only 9 hours, which is unacceptable for an RPG in my opinion. Had I ignored everything apart from the main quest, it would've been 1-2 hours.
It's saving grace might be the editor, but honestly I don't know.
The score I would give it: 6-7/10 as in OK but not good. It was fun in the short time it lasted but turned out to be a disappointing experience. Like I said, get it in a bundle with the other games and DLCs.

I spent 800 hours and about 50 bucks on Shadowverse. At first I geniunely enjoyed the gameplay. Later I mostly played for the gorgeous art and the thrill of opening card packs. I uninstalled the game recently.
The developer's aim is to create a game where every single meta deck has a winrate of 50%, give or take 2%. This doesn't translate to a balanced game environment but a game where every single match in the "competitive" ranks boils down to luck. The play point system severely limits your options in the early game to the point where there are very few meaningful choices you can make. And by the mid-game, most matches are already decided. Honestly, it's mind-numbingly dull.
In addition, experimental, or "fun" decks are virtually useless for laddering, and even doing the daily missions can be a chore with subpar builds in the higher ranks, as they fall prey to the 2-4 meta decks that are out there in any given season.
This means that there's nearly zero skill involved in both deckbuilding and actually playing the game. If you're a sucker for cute anime girls, love gambling on card packs and don't mind losing for reasons that are completely beyond your control, you can give this game a try. For everyone else, Shadowverse offers nothing.

Few games give people a lot of freedom of movement or the feeling of fluidity as they transition from one area to the next. Mirror's Edge, on the other hand, makes it all effortless and smooth. No other game has made me feel quite as mobile and agile as controlling Faith as she moves across the rooftops.
Faith can stop and fight if she really wants to, and she'll do alright at it. However, the game gives us a second and often wiser choice: run away. Faith moves faster and better than any other enemy in the game, so the cops can't catch her once she's past. As in Thief and Dishonoured, it's possible to play through with minimal combat, though it's arguably a lot easier to do in Mirror's Edge. This isn't a combat game at heart.
I like games that try to do something different, and I especially like games that succeed. Mirror's Edge shows that a game can be all about movement, to the point that combat, though present, is largely unnecessary.

I don't know what to say, honestly.
The game is fun, I've spent 43 hours as of this review and I've done nothing more than play around, and I am yet to find things. The game is big, and made for people who like to explore. But if you like to kill, then this is also your game.
I'll explain myself here. Dying light can be seen and loved by many points of view. There's a leveling system that will level according to what you do most. There is Agility that specializes on escaping Zombies and climbing, Parkour. Then there's Power, which is the one that specializes in killing zombies and giving you fun and diverse ways to kill them.
Storyline:
Although I am not yet done with the Dying Light storyline, I'll tell you one thing: If you go straight trying to speedrun through the storyline, you'll end the game quickly, perhaps too quickly too. The game is aimed for you to explore, and enjoy, so if you are not the type to enjoy exploring and looking around looking for the highest place you can climb or how much you can find, how rich you can become, this is not your game. But I will give it to the storyline, I've found myself ignoring countless sidequests and opportunities to explore because I wanted to see what would happen next. Overall, I'd say the Storyline is fun, can hook you on but not something to speedrun through.
Exploring:
Like I said, this game has an AMAZING exploring system. If you go around and explore you'll find that there are collectibles for you to find, and chances are on first look you're not gonna find them all. There are three sorts of things you can find around the world. Zombie Statues, Flags and Notes. That is all I am gonna say. There are 30 Flags, like 100 Zombie statues and 67 notes. If you are the type to play this game and find everything and enjoy everything. You will find yourself enjoying this game to the maximum. Because there is a lot to explore and exploring is rewarded. Easter eggs can be found and the game will last a lot longer.
Fighting:
Although I will say, I died a LOT on this game, most of it was not because the Zombies took the upper hand and killed me. Zombies will seem threatening and even a bit scary at the early stages of the game. Where it takes you 5 hits to kill them and it is really satisfying to kill your first Zombie, your first 10, and soon your first 100. Zombies are fun to kill, even a bit relaxing after a while and if you get overwhelmed, even a bit hard to beat. There are many types of Zombies, I will not get into detail with them because that is for you to find out, but personally, I am satisfied with the fighting on this game. The Zombies don't follow Ragdoll physics, so if you kill one by kicking them off a cliff, they will look almost human falling off a cliff.
Parkour:
The Parkour in this game is very fun, at first a bit confusing but really fun in general. You will be able to find the highest place you can climb to and even find yourself just parkouring out of the actual questline or sidequest you were doing. Some fun things about Parkour is that there are some things you can find in some houses that you would not have found had you not gone ontop of a house or even a building. Overall, there is not much to say about parkour more than it's fast, exciting, and I would definitely say it is fun, although I found myself raging because I would die from fall distance, and whatnot but that's because I'm stubborn.
Co-op:
Co-op adds a LOT to this game. I found myself constantly running off from my partner just to see what I could find, and eventually both of us meeting somewhere and exchanging what it is that we found. Ranging from Weapons that perhaps he liked the bat and I liked the Cleaver, or anything, really. Co-op adds a different element to this game, that allows you to survive a Zombie Apocalypse with a friend, not alone. I would definitely reccomend it.
Customization:
Although this game is lacking whether I can be a female Runner or not, I would say it was quite disapointing. My Co-op friend also being Kyle Crane kind of killed the entire fun of two survivors and it made it seem more like that was just my twin running around. Outfits are pretty, I will admit that but they are not the maximum customization I would have wanted from this game. Overall, a bit disappointed.
Overall:
Dying Light is a game that can reach out to a lot of people. I, for one adore every aspect of the game whether it is getting Airdrops to rank up on Survival. Parkouring and jumping over Zombies to see if maybe I can find another note, another flag or another Zombie Statue or to see just what else I can discover. And also the fighting on the game that can be extremely satisfying with the slow motion, succeeding on the game making me feel indeed as a Hunter at Day and Prey at Night. I'll reccomend this game to any person. Even if it's just to do the storyline, it is a lot of fun. My rating for this game would be 9/10.

Syberia II is a disappointing sequel to me, since the first one started strong and introduced an amazing cast, as well as some of the best character development in a video game. This sequel undermines everything that made Syberia great, and to top it all off, the whole plot is boring and you can see everything happening a mile away. The content is comparable to modern story DLCs where the final chapter of a game is seperated from the main storyline and is sold seperately. Syberia II doesn't work well as a standalone, and it isn't accomodating to new players who didn't play the first game; the story is a hodgepodge without proper context from Syberia. There's no character development and not much has been changed on the gameplay side of things - it's like the studio were assuming that only players of the first title would be interested this sequel. Overall, it's not a bad game, but don't get your expectations too high or you'll just be disappointed at the end.
:
*For fans of Syberia, the game ends in a very satisfying manner and Kate's wanderlust has proven to be worth it
the journey towards their goal is so drab and boring. Side characters have no lasting impact on both Kate and Hans, the antagonists are comical, and key plot points reveal in an unsatisfying manner. Syberia II just didn't work for me since this game is all about fulfilling an agenda, rather than satiating Kate's desires of discovering herself, and expanding the mythos surrounding Hans Voralberg.
*The backtracking had been minimized considerably

puzzles are so obscure and complex, you have to scour every inch of the levels and read every note to find the solution, making the player backtrack a lot, regardless of the improvements made to counter that. True story: I never consulted guides during my playthrough of Syberia, but Syberia II prompted me to do otherwise.
And there you have it.

Where do I even start to tell you how magnificent, how awesome, how utterly mind-blowing this documentary film resonates with every gamer. It's not just a movie that only details the struggles of three individuals in the first ever International for Dota 2. It's not just a movie that can sympathize with every other person who struggles to compete on a higher professional level. It's not just a film where E-Sports marked a great change. No, its something bigger, something awe-inspiring to see.
After watching it 3 times, One for the whole movie, then again with "Fear' commentating and again with "Dendi," I can say you don't have to know about Dota 2 to understand what's going on in the film. It's easier to know beforehand to grasp what they're trying to say.
'Breaking Boundaries'
To give a bit of background of the E-sports tournament/championship/etc. Gaming, decades back was never hugely popular like popular general big sports around the world. Soccer, Football, Olympics, Baseball, you name it. It was slowly increasing. Because of the natural fact that games were not seen as hugely competitive or spread something as noteworthy.
The most you would ever see back then, would be LAN tournaments or places to go through with friends and hook-up your computers right next to each other then play against them. I can't even remember one advertisement commercial, Bill-board, or anything that comes to mind in spreading news about a competitive tournament featuring video-games. However, momentum still rose, small but slowly increasing. Games we often know of today that contribute to the rise of E-Sports in gaming would be Starcraft and expanding internationally with South Korea. Perhaps Halo:combat evolved on the P.C. Or even the infamous Counter Strike. Slowly but, surely some games pushed gamers and audiences to become ultimately a truly competitive area to go against one another. As more and more people become interested the falling of dominoes fall into place and now we see a huge surge into commercialized gaming around the world.
"Turning the Abnormal to Normal"
Gamers back then were common. You, Your friend, Hell even an employee or family of yours probably played a game in the arcade. Playing Pac-man, or Dance-Dance-Revolution and more! We were seen as people who just want to have some fun. Then it expanded, hand-held consoles and consoles erupted onto the market and with it the rise of gamers around the world. Sitting on the sofa, on the chair, or exercising on the Wii or Kinect. The term 'Gamer' had become a social term, created by people who enjoyed enthusiasticlly to play other games more often than not. But, with this change comes a stereotype of not amounting to reality.
The reality of which: Can you make a living off of gaming? The question if asked many decades ago when the internet was still brand-spanking brand new would probably be "No, Preposterous, Are you crazy?" It's fair to say most of the general population would answer with that answer long ago. But, times are changing and with the out of place gamers being picked on we see a new day come forth. A new age. The Professional Gamer.
Where once Gamers were ridiculed, frowned upon, looked un-note-worthy to praise for has slowly begun to change the trend that has been stereotypically associated with Gamers. Now. Tournaments in S. Korea for Starcraft 2, League of Legends in North America and Europe. Counter Strike amongst nearly every part of the world. And more and more!
Are now looked up! As role-models, celebrities, hell even professionals now! They have re-shaped the landscape and structure of Gaming around the world. And thus have brought a new age of Gaming everywhere...
"The New Player"

It's difficult to describe. The feeling that emerges when you try out something new, and eventually seek to take it to the next level. 'Free To Play' The movie is without spoiling much a film where it displays not just the a new emerging E-Sports. But, as something that gives hope. Silly, I know but every gamer out there is probably pressured already about their life and are at a crossroads to see where they end up. Is Gaming right for me? Can I make a living playing Videogames.? The movie doesn't go all philosophical on you, to give you the right answers. It can only show you something and leave it in your hands with what to do with it.
'Free To Play' May seem like a film to advertise that gaming is growing massively with prizes becoming larger and larger. But it's not only that. The film dives into the heart and struggles of reaching the top. Perhaps not all the way. But close enough to feel it.
The New Player, is someone who tries something new in gaming, perhaps playing for the 1st time on Dota 2 and sucking so bad probably dampen your feelings and self-esteem and then uninstall the game entirely before finding some other enjoyable game. The New Player might in some cases quit to seek a living wage in the world, never able to accomplish the one wish to become the very best. Then there's The New Player with the drive, the motivation, and ambitition to get atop the pedalstal and become a professional gamer like Dendi, Hyhy, Fear.
It's an incredible historical movie. One every gamer should see.

Notes for this review: I am a third of the way through the story mode at this point. The original LEGO Star Wars was one of the first video games I ever played. I have played through all of the original LEGO Star Wars story mode, a good chunk of the LEGO Star Wars II story mode, and 100% of LEGO Indiana Jones.
PROS:
- Wide variety of characters with unique abilities
- The usual LEGO gameplay that is just challenging enough
- It's not based directly on any movies, so the plot is new
CONS:
- "Open world" setting -  I don't think it really works for LEGO games
- At one point during a level, both characters needed to do something at the same time, but the other character wasn't doing it, so I had to go into 2-player mode and control both characters at once. From there I couldn't figure out how to get out of 2-player mode so I was stuck in splitscreen until the end of the level.
- I've only had two sessions so far, but both times when I tried to exit the game it froze the game and my laptop. The only way to get out, since I couldn't open Task Manager, was to completely shut down my computer by holding down the power button.
EDIT: For the second con, it turns out you actually have to switch to the other character if you need two characters to do something at the same time - I was used to the character doing it automatically in the Star Wars games. The point about not being able to get out of 2-player mode still stands, though.
Rules, Plotlines, Creative Writing, there is none of that.  An unpolished carbon copy DLC of Saints Row the Third, and much worse off.

So, here we are again, another jrpg game...
Now before I go into detail about certain game elements, I want to tell you that the recommandation is completely biased and you should try to decide for yourself if the game is worth the money or not. Also, you might've noticed I played this game for over 40 hours but I'm not reccomending it, and well, the reasons for that are explained below, if you want to read them.
First of all let's start with the gameplay, it's the usual IF dungeon turn-based combat in which you have certain characters to select from and you make a party of maxium 3 and go beating up monsters and leveling, and all those other elements you'd expect to usually find in a rpg. The combat is alright, and the controls aren't that bad either, considering the guys that made neptunia made this it's bound to be good right...
Next let's talk a little about the story and characters. The story is so blend it makes me puke, it's the usual ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t there's an evil God and a good Goddess and you must revive the goddess and stop the guys who want to ressurect the God, and all that nonsense, seriously, the plot is also a mess, and they try to squeeze in all these elements inside just to cover up for certain plot holes. The easiest element that can do this for you: time travel... And the ending is exactly what you'd expect it to be if you have this kind of stories.
Well, you might be thinking, okay, if the story is bad, maybe the characters might help. Well, the characters are so typical, and tehy're the sterotypes of anime, which is what I hate the most about games such as this, unoriginal character concept is seriously a turnaway. You've got a typical lazy mc who wants to do nothing, two main love interests a tsundere and a yandere, the usual loli, the big boobed chick that's there for fanservice and don't get me started on the fact that there's a cat that talks or whatever that thing is. Now, don't get me wrong, the characters are what they are but there is certain plot development.
Next, let's go in detail about the music and voice acting. The voice acting is decent, I would say good, but that's still not enough to sell this game for what it is, considering the music feels repetitive and every song feels like the other, seriously I'd rather listen to my own songs than to the ingame music at some points.
The final element I'd like to talk about are the achievements, and how insensitive some of them are. Now don't get me wrong, getting the achievements is not a matter of skill but rather a matter of time in this game, with that being said there are a couple of achievements which are if not impossible, then they would take about a couple hundreds of grinding without using any dlc. All in all Fairy Fencer F is not a bad game, neither a good one, it's in the middle and everyone can have an opinion about it. I'm a little biased, since I wrote a very large mod for this title, but... well, I ~cared~ enough to write a very large mod for this title, which should tell you something.
I think Teleglitch is a game which needs a sequel that's much more polished.  It has a brilliance that shines through much of its crudity and balance problems.
It is, frankly, one of the few procedural-dungeon twin-stick shooters I'd honestly recommend to anybody to give it a go, because it gets a lot of things right, even if it doesn't get everything right.
Teleglitch, vanilla, is a Nintendo-hard twin-stick shooter that is basically about stabbing zombies with a knife over and over and over whilst not getting hit.  It also has guns and a crafting system and bombs and a bunch of other things, but most of them don't matter, because there is so little ammo available that it's basically a game where ammo-hoarding to deal with certain enemies is the only way to survive the entire game.
I don't think all of that was well-done; I made a mod that basically re-configures the experience into something I personally found more fun.  You can find it by reading through the comment threads here.
But the core idea- that you're alone in the dark, you cannot see everywhere, you're going to be constantly worrying about the next critter around the corner- these things are brilliantly realized.  Few games, let alone games so simple, have been able to so convincingly create a real sense of worry and dread in Yours Truly; I don't think I've been so jump-scared since I played the original Resident Evil and the dogs crashed through that window (a reference most of you won't get, but trust me, it's one of the first truly Scary Things in video-game history).
I'd really like to see a better Teleglitch engine, with higher-resolution graphics, tighter gameplay and multiple difficulty settings so that it isn't so forbiddingly hard for newbies to the genre.  Sadly, I doubt if we ever will see a sequel unless somebody else writes one, but it's a game where I think that the central feel and core will stick with me always.
None of what Teleglitch did was really "new", but it was all brought together pretty well, and even though there are rough edges and areas that I felt could have been better, it is far more fun than the many, many, many boring "roguelight" games that are essentially just variations on Smash TV, with their boring, square arenas and no sense of place and poorly-designed RNG systems under the hood taking skill out of the equation.
Teleglitch, by comparision, is almost entirely a game where a player's death is almost always the player's fault, not the fault of some developer's poor understanding of statistics; it's a game where exploration is risky but properly rewarded, and if the knife just worked a bit better and it had difficulty settings, it probably would have sold a lot more copies.

A revival of one of the first great entries of Cyberpunk video games, Shadowrun Returns offers tactical combat and a full spread of character customization options. The inclusion of a magic system prevents the game from defaulting to a guns only affair while cybernetic enhancements allow for a more traditional sci-fi experience.
There are five races to choose from pulling from the traditional fantasy settings (Human, Elf, Dwarf, Orc, Troll) and six pregenerated classes (Street Samurai, Mage, Decker, Shaman, Rigger, or Physical Adept) along with a custom build option.
The combat is team turn based allowing you to position and act with all your party members before moving over to the enemy team. Action Points dictate many times you can move or act with the amount increasing over time. The story revolves around solving the mystery of a friend's murder.
All in all it's an excellent game and worth the time and money. It also tends to be extremely affordable when put on sale just because of how long it's been out. This is the first part of three entries, the other two being Shadowrun: Dragonfall and Shadowrun: Hong Kong. Both of which are excellent games as well.

Okay, let's be real honest for a moment. South Park is arguably one of the most offensive shows on TV. It's also arguably one of the funniest. So, I expect that people are going to be pretty polarized about a game featuring the same humor as the show. For that reason, I'll seperate this review into two parts, first covering the game mechanics, sound, etc., and then covering the content.
Mechanics: 4/5
The mechanics of the game, i.e. input notification and intuity, are actually very good. Combat is turn-based and thus is not hard to learn. Some bosses seem to be fairly hard to beat, but that's not necessarily a bad thing. Attacking and defending is based on a "Quick Time" prompt where you press a button when you see a flash of some kind. Not hard to learn, but some people may have problems with poor quality controllers.
It should be obvious to most that a Port-to-PC is going to work better with a controller, but it was still very easy to play with M-n-K.
Controls: 5/5
The game has some pretty snappy, dead on target controls as long as you are using a controller like the Logitech F510 or the Microsoft controller. Sometimes when using the M-n-K there was a missed response or a failed timing, and a few embarassing wrong key presses, but overall it was still quite playable without a controller.
To be honest, the game played much better than I had expected and very similar to any top dollar game. As I said, I had a few issues with using computer keyboard and mouse, but when I switched to using my Logitech F510 controller, they all went away. If you're using the Microsft console controller you shouldn't have any problems, as I tested that as well. No gaurantees on how other controllers will perform.
The only issue I had, was with learning some of the "dragon shouts" as they didn't seem to convey the steps input moment needed quite accurately.
Sound: 5/5
The sound is actually very impressive, filling my headphones perfectly with directional audio. Given that the game primarily focuses on 1 axis of movement, I would have been very disappointed if the developers couldn't get left and right audio cues correct.
Music: 5/5
The music is really good, parodying "recent" RPGs like Skyrim with the main BGM and portraying a good feeling of immersion overall in the various locations. In addition, many places had radios that would play the various songs from the show, which was funny as heck.
Graphics: 5/5
Uh... It's a South Park game so, the characters look like paper-cutouts filmed with some sort of stop motion to show speech, motion, and facial changes. It looks very much like the show, so if that doesn't bother you the game won't either. I never bothered to check FPS or anything like that since the system requirements are so low, but there's been no lag whatsoever on my rig, even while it's not running to spec due to ram speed issues.
If you've got a "modern" PC with a dual-core running @2GHz, a video card that's come out in the last 5 years  and 4 GB of ram then you should have no problems.
Now I'll cover the content of the game. These won't be rated as it's entirely subjective to the individual.
Humor:
South Park's humor tends to be crass, disgusting and politically incorrect, not unlike a number of other popular TV shows like The Simpsons, Scrubs, Just Shoot Me, or Married With Children, and this game follows that theme reliably. From the Unplanned Parenthood Clinic, to Chef singing on the radio, to Aliens probing you rectally the humor is in your face and unapologetic. Parents, this is not a game I would let young children play, just as I wouldn't let them watch the show, but teens would probably be fine.
Characters:
You have all the usual South Park charactors, from Cartman to Kenny, Token to Tweek. In addition, you have many "Guest" characters as well, such as Mr. Hanky and Al Gore. If you're familiar with the show, you'll be happy.
Overall, I'd recommend this game if you like the show and like RPGs.
